14721-speeches-letters-of-abraham-lincol:
Edited by Merwin Roe, this volume gathers Abraham Lincoln's speeches and letters from 1832 to 1865, with an introduction by James Bryce. Early letters on national policy sit beside later state papers, and the arc runs from a young Illinois politician to a wartime president.

Readers meet the Gettysburg dedication of November 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation, the second inaugural address and the last address to the American people, among other pieces. Bryce's introduction frames Lincoln as a voice that fell like winter snow, impossible to answer. The collection suits readers who want Lincoln in his own words, plain, legal and moral at once.
20587-integration-of-the-armed-forces-19:
Integration of the Armed Forces, 1940-1965 is an official United States Army history of how the services ended racial segregation. It covers the years from the first wartime pressure for change to the civil rights era. Orders, boards, and battles over policy fill its chapters.

Its author, Morris J. MacGregor, Jr., took his degree in history at the Catholic University of America. He continued graduate study at Johns Hopkins and at the University of Paris on a Fulbright grant. Before joining the Army's history staff, he had trained for years in archives. His book remains the standard account of the policy fight.
21566-the-good-old-songs-we-used-to-sing:
O. H. Oldroyd gathered Union veterans' songs in The Good Old Songs We Used to Sing, '61 to '65. First published in 1882 and reissued in 1902 at ten cents, the book is dedicated to veterans of the war. A photo of General Grant from life, dated 1864, fronts it.

Sherman's March to the Sea leads the set, with tunes drawn from sheet music at the Library of Congress. Other songs recall Resaca, Kennesaw, and the long march down to the sea. Linda Cantoni transcribed the music from the Civil War Songbook and old prints. Old soldiers could sing their war again from these cheap, plain pages.
26958-captain-richard-ingle-the-maryland:
Edward Ingle's paper, read before the Maryland Historical Society on May 12, 1884, retells the career of Captain Richard Ingle, the Maryland pirate and rebel of 1642 to 1653. Ingle raided the colony, sided with Parliament against the Catholic proprietors, and destroyed records, leaving his episode wrapped in obscurity.

Ingle works from the scraps that survive: assembly acts, pardons that name Ingle alone as excepted, and the conflicting verdicts of later historians. The paper weighs whether Ingle was pirate, rebel, or both, and shows how one man's raids helped shape Maryland's early struggle over who would rule it.
33708-the-irish-ecclesiastical-record-vo:
The Irish Ecclesiastical Record for August 1865 opens with a history of the see of Dromore, founded by St. Colman. For several centuries the see comprised little more than Colman's abbey and its immediate territory. The synod of Rathbreasil in 1118, defining diocesan boundaries, makes no mention of Dromore. The acts of Kells some fifty years later are likewise silent, as is Cencius Camerarius compiling his list of sees in 1192.

Still, the abbot of the monastery called de viridi ligno, which gave Newry its name, governed this diocese with a bishop's authority in the second half of the twelfth century. The last episcopal abbot, Gerard, a Cistercian of Mellifont, was chosen bishop in 1227 and died in 1243, after which chapter and monastery disputed his successor.
4154-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-33-jan:
January 1664 to 1665, a Lord's day, finds Pepys long in bed after a busy late night, then up to his office to order accounts and papers. He reviews last year's gains and expense, which he finds very great, and sets about dividing the new year's business.

The volume opens the year before plague with a clerk counting his fortune and planning its growth. Accounts, not adventure, drive these winter entries, and that is their charm. Readers who like Pepys the bookkeeper will find a satisfying start to 1665. Gains counted in January cast a long shadow over the plague year ahead.
4155-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-34-mar:
March 1664 to 1665 opens on a promise long made to his wife: twenty pounds to lay out in clothes against Easter. Despite last night's falling out, wife and husband come to peace, though Pepys boggles mightily at parting with his money.

The volume follows a marriage through shopping, quarrels, and reconciliations, beside office work and the coming war. Pepys's money worries and his wife's Easter clothes share equal weight on the page. Readers get a tender, funny portrait of a household where love and accounts are never far apart. Easter clothes and office papers share the same anxious attention.
4156-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-35-may:
May 1665 sends Pepys to Mr. Povy's bedside for a good while of talk. Povy insists on the difficulty of getting money, and would have Pepys join in thinking of another way to dispose of the Treasurer's place to one Mr. Bell.

Pepys seems to agree while holding his own counsel, in the diary's familiar dance of office politics. Plague gathers at the edge of these entries, but money talk comes first. Readers see the Navy's purse strings pulled tight in the spring before the sickness peaked. Money talk at a sickbed shows how office worries outranked even plague news.
4157-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-36-jul:
July 1665 calls Pepys up betimes, weary and sleepy, by appointment with Mr. Povy and Colonel Norwood to talk Tangier payments. They gone, he sits among Navy papers all morning, then dines at home and goes to the Duke of Albemarle's by appointment.

Plague summer presses on every entry, yet the Navy Office grinds on, paying, ordering, and answering. Pepys records the strain without flinching, from Tangier accounts to ducal audiences. Readers meet the diary at its most serious, when duty continued while London sickened around it. Tangier money and ducal orders keep the office turning through the sickness.
4158-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-37-aug:
August 1665 finds Pepys sleeping long, then visiting a bridegroom and bride, both up and red in the face, well pleased with their night's lodging. The groom has gone to dress himself, and the household bustles around the new couple.

Plague year weddings went on even as death lists grew, and Pepys notes the contrast without comment. The volume mixes weddings, offices, and river journeys through a sick summer. Readers get August 1665 as life stubbornly continuing, with joy beside fear. A wedding in plague time reminds readers that life refused to stop.
4159-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-38-sep:
September 1665 finds Pepys visiting Lady Pen and her daughter at the Ropeyard, breakfasting and chatting a good while. Then to his lodging at Mr. Shelden's, where Captain Cocke joins him for a bit of dinner, and the two go to Greenwich by water.

Good discourse fills the boat ride, even as plague empties the city they leave behind. The volume follows Pepys between lodgings, yards, and river trips, keeping office life alive in a scattered London. Readers see how friendship and work persisted when the town itself seemed to pause.
4160-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-39-oct:
October 1665, a Lord's day, calls Pepys up about four in the morning to dress and board the Bezan. Finding all his company asleep, he will not wake them, but walks the deck till break of day, then sleeps in the master's cabin.

The volume follows Pepys afloat in plague autumn, between ships, lodgings, and offices scattered by sickness. His quiet deck walk opens a month of movement and waiting. Readers get the diary at sea and ashore, with dawn light over a city in trouble. Dawn on deck opens a month spent between ships and scattered lodgings.
4161-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-40-nov:
November 1665 keeps Pepys long in bed, discoursing with Mr. Hill on the things of a man's life. Little merit prevails in the world, they agree, but only favor, and Pepys owns that chance without merit brought him in, while diligence alone keeps him there.

Living among so many lazy people, as he puts it, Pepys resolves to work harder still. The volume closes plague year with reflection rather than triumph, a clerk weighing luck, merit, and effort. Readers will find these entries among the diary's most thoughtful, plain about how careers are really made.
4809-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
The ninth volume of Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic, dated 1855, covers 1564 to 1565. Chapter five opens with return of the three seigniors to the state council, the policy of Orange, and corrupt character of government. Efforts of the Prince in favour of reform, influence of Armenteros, and painful situation of Viglius follow, with his anxiety to retire.

Secret charges against Viglius, transmitted by the Duchess to Philip, join ominous signs of the times and Philip's attention to details of persecution. Execution of Fabricius and tumult at Antwerp close the sampled scope, as reform efforts meet a king who watches persecution's details himself. Orange presses for change inside the council, while Viglius, caught between prince and king, longs to retire. Readers get Motley's account of a council divided, and a persecution gathering force.
4971-the-great-intendant-a-chronicle-of-:
Thomas Chapais's Great Intendant chronicles Jean Talon in Canada from 1665, when New France stood weak and destitute after more than half a century. Champlain's colony, founded on valour and devotion, had been stifled by trading companies whose narrow mercantile selfishness blocked its growth, and by neglect from home.

Talon arrives to rescue the colony, organizing settlement, trade, and defense along the St. Lawrence. Chapais follows the intendant's reforms and their limits. Readers get a clear short history of French Canada's turning point, when a colony run for profit began, at last, to be governed as a country.
8918-life-of-johnson-volume-1-1709-1765:
James Boswell, a young Scots lawyer, set out to record the life of Samuel Johnson, the great English writer and maker of the Dictionary. This first volume of the Hill edition covers Johnson's life from his birth in 1709 to 1765, with letters, talks, and early works set in time order. Boswell knew Johnson well and wrote down his speech with rare care.

Johnson's school days, his hard youth, his Grub Street grind, and his rise to fame all unfold here, in his own words as much as Boswell's. The book is prized as the finest life story in English, a close portrait of a brilliant, flawed, and deeply human man.
arnold-essays-criticism-1865:
Matthew Arnold published Essays in Criticism, First Series, in 1865, a landmark in literary study. The opening essay, The Function of Criticism at the Present Time, argues for disinterested inquiry. Criticism, Arnold says, must see the object as it really is and spread the best ideas. Other essays treat poets and prose writers of Europe.

He writes on Homer, Heine, and the Celtic element in literature, among other topics. His touchstone idea judges verse by great lines held in mind. The book in effect invented modern literary criticism as a public task in English. Arnold's calm, lucid style set its tone. Scholars still teach these essays.
arxiv-2509-00165:
Türkü Özlüm Çelik, Pierre A. Haas, Georgy Scholten, Kexin Wang, and Giulio Zucal study ecological coexistence in 2025 through algebraic geometry. The Lotka-Volterra system models how species grow, compete, and prey in a shared habitat. Equilibria, the steady states of the system, matter most when they are both feasible, meaning all counts stay positive, and stable.

Those two conditions split the parameter space into strata, or layers, of semialgebraic sets. The team encodes the layers on a real Grassmannian, a space of planes, through a parameter matrix form. Oriented matroid theory and Plücker relations then drive a symbolic algorithm that tests sign patterns. Some interaction networks are proven impossible, since no pattern extension can meet both conditions at once.
arxiv-2509-00365:
Zhenxin Li, Shuibing He, Jiahao Guo, Xuechen Zhang, Xian-He Sun, and Gang Chen present CRouting in 2025, a routing strategy that cuts distance calls in graph-based nearest neighbor search. Approximate search finds near neighbors fast in high-dimensional data, a core step in retrieval and AI. Graph methods lead on speed and accuracy, but repeated distance computations in high dimensions dominate their cost.

CRouting skips needless distance computations by exploiting angle distributions among vectors. It plugs into existing graph search with minimal code change. On two leading graph indexes, HNSW and NSG, distance calls fall by up to forty-one and a half percent. Query throughput rises by up to one point four eight times in the tests.
arxiv-2509-00465:
Jiading Fang's doctoral thesis sets out embodied spatial intelligence, the aim of giving robots a grasp of space so they can act on spoken instructions in the real world. Large language models handle words well but lack a direct tie to physical places.

Fang works on two fronts. For perception, he builds scene models with implicit neural methods, including self-taught camera calibration, detailed depth fields, and large-scale rebuilding of scenes. For reasoning, he adds a navigation test set, a way to ground language, meaning link words to places, in three dimensions, and a feedback method for long tasks. The thesis lays groundwork for robots that see their surroundings and follow complex commands.
arxiv-2509-00565:
Athulya P and one co-author, Sandeep Kumar Verma, introduce an A-Laplacian in the Dunkl framework, a version of calculus shaped by a root system and a multiplicity function that weights directions. The A-Laplacian generalizes the usual Laplacian, an operator that measures how a function spreads, by first applying a given map A to the Dunkl gradient.

Athulya and Verma derive local and global Caccioppoli-type inequalities, bounds that control a function's gradient by the function itself, for functions in a Dunkl-Orlicz-Sobolev space that satisfy a stated differential inequality. Using that bound, they give a sufficient condition, a test that guarantees the result, under which no nonzero solution can exist. The work extends classical energy methods to this weighted setting.
arxiv-2509-00665:
Weilong Yan, with two co-authors, Xin Zhang and Robby T Tan, tackles monocular depth estimation, judging distance from a single image, in bad weather such as rain, fog, snow, and night. Ground truth is scarce in such scenes, synthetic data brings domain gaps, and self-supervised methods break when light patterns change.

Yan and his co-authors fine-tune vision foundation models efficiently using only a small amount of clear-weather data. Their Selecting-Tuning-Maintaining strategy splits pre-trained weights by effective rank measures, chooses ranks and directions to tune, then regularizes key directions to preserve prior knowledge. Across four real benchmarks, the method beats other efficient tuning methods, full fine-tuning, and even models trained on synthetic bad-weather data.
arxiv-2509-00965:
Amin Jafarimoghaddam and Manuel Soler propose a new framework for long-term contrail evolution. Contrails are trails of condensed vapor left by aircraft. They are now seen as a major driver of aviation warming. Their impact can rival that of carbon dioxide. Mitigation needs accurate, efficient models to guide avoidance.

Contrails evolve from formation and rapid growth to dissipation. They may also turn into cirrus clouds over time. That late phase critically sets their climate effect. The framework includes wind changes across space and time. It adds nonlinear diffusion that can model blocking effects. A multiphase model gives the settling speed of ice particles. Ice-crystal habit dynamics are included as well. Adjustable factors can be tuned with ground-truth data.
arxiv-2509-01065:
Soft robots bend and stretch, which makes them safe and able to adapt, but also hard to steer with care. Sumitaka Honji and Takahiro Wada tackle control of a soft robotic finger whose motion is random and hard to predict. Fixed models tend to fail because they ignore that spread of possible motion.

Honji and Wada instead control the spread itself, using the Fokker-Planck equation, a rule that tracks how a cloud of likely states moves over time. Their method looks ahead and picks actions that shape that cloud toward a goal. Two test cases in simulation show the approach handles the finger's uncertain motion well. The work points toward safer control of flexible machines.
arxiv-2509-01265:
Choosing self-employment can say something about a worker's talent, because the results become public, while firm jobs hide individual performance. Georgy Lukyanov, Konstantin Popov, and Shubh Lashkery study that signaling role in a steady labor market. Risk-averse workers know their own lasting talent and choose each period which path to take.

Because workers decide whether to add another public result or apply to a firm, both the record holders and the applicant pool are shaped by those choices. The authors build market beliefs in two stages, from the flow of types through each history, then from the current choice. They show an equilibrium exists under a stated condition, with talent cutoffs guiding choice at each record. That equilibrium need not be unique, and firm work persists under stated conditions.
arxiv-2509-01365:
Bacteria move, and some species can speed up or slow down their neighbors after recognizing who they are. Mattia Mattei, David Soriano Panos, Mahantesh Halappanavar, and Alex Arenas model that recognition-driven control of motility, movement, in microbial communities. Cells respond to local signals from other species that either boost or suppress their motion.

Large simulations and a simplified stochastic model show a sharp transition driven by nucleation, the seeding of clusters. As motility-suppressing links grow denser, the system flips from a fully mixed, moving phase to one of large, still bacterial clusters. With many species, the flip can be triggered by reshaping the interaction pattern alone, holding species and link counts fixed. The work shows how structured interactions, not just their amount, organize microbial space.
arxiv-2509-01765:
Skand Peri, Akhil Perincherry, Bikram Pandit, and Stefan Lee save robot energy without hurting task success. Common training adds an energy penalty to the reward, but the weight needs careful tuning. Too much weight makes the robot fail its task to save power. Their method instead projects learning updates so energy and task goals do not clash. The idea borrows from work on learning many tasks at once.

Tests on standard motion benches cut energy use by about two thirds while task scores held steady. A four legged robot also ran the learned policy in the real world. The method needs only small code changes in standard training setups. It offers a clean swap for hand tuned reward shaping.
arxiv-2509-01965:
Wei Chen leads five co-authors in predicting masses of pentaquarks that hold two charm quarks. Pentaquarks are exotic particles built from five quarks, beyond the usual two and three quark states. The team covers cases with no strangeness and with one strange unit. Their tool is the QCD sum rule method, which links quark level theory to particle masses through correlation functions.

Parity projection splits the signals of opposite parity states, which otherwise mix in the counts. Interpolating currents stand in for each pentaquark candidate in the formulas. Results predict several possible bound states in this doubly charmed family. Such forecasts guide collider searches that hunt for these rare states. The method keeps both parity channels cleanly separated throughout.
arxiv-2509-02065:
Matthew Burfitt, Jie Wu, Stephen S-T Yau, and Shing-Tung Yau compute singular simplicial homology for directed graphs and quivers. Large systems are often modeled as networks of pairwise links with direction. Homology of the directed flag complex is popular but not the only option. New singular theories for quivers across morphism types have recently appeared, with little computational work behind them.

The team builds homotopy theory that turns those homologies into homologies of ordinary spaces. Chain groups for those spaces come in compact form at least as handy as the flag complex. Naturality under the isomorphisms suits persistent homology, which tracks features across scales. Efficient algorithms for persistent homology are given for each theory covered. The work brings abstract quiver homology within practical reach.
arxiv-2509-02165:
Jeremy Mould and Jarrod Hurley propose that primordial black holes seeded globular cluster formation before galaxies assembled. Globular clusters are dense ancient star balls among the oldest structures known. The quantum chromodynamics phase transition in the early universe may have created black hole nuclei. Once thousand solar mass nuclei formed, they would persist and gather matter.

Accretion and star formation following that seeding are the focus of the model. Whether such nuclei are common in the oldest clusters remains an open, hard question. A possible contribution to the cosmic gravitational wave background is another open thread. The proposal reframes cluster origins around early universe physics. Tests will need careful comparison with cluster age and mass data.
arxiv-2509-02465:
Ruben Aylwin, Göksu Oruc, and Karsten Urban wrote a 2025 numerical analysis paper on fractional differential equations, where derivatives have non-integer order and remember past states. Their equations use Riemann-Liouville derivatives with diffusion and reaction coefficients that vary in space.

The authors derive a variational form, meaning a weak equation tested against trial functions, and prove the continuous problem is well-posed, and its finite element version too. They then apply the reduced basis method, which builds a small surrogate model through a greedy search over parameter values. Convergence behaviour, including decay of the Kolmogorov width, depends on the fractional order. Numerical tests confirm the theory. The work supports fast simulation of fractional models with changing coefficients.
arxiv-2509-02565:
Eric J. Michaud, Liv Gorton, and Tom McGrath wrote a 2025 paper on sparse autoencoders. These tools rewrite a network's inner activity as a sparse mix of feature directions. How well they rebuild activity, as features grow, follows scaling laws. Those laws need an account.

The authors adapt a capacity model from scaling research. Some features form multi-dimensional manifolds. A manifold is a surface, not a single direction. Such features change the picture. Distinct scaling regimes seen in practice reappear in the model. In one regime, manifolds cause a pathology. The autoencoder learns far fewer real features than it has slots for. The authors ask if practical autoencoders sit in that bad regime. The answer bears on trust in interpretability claims.
arxiv-2509-02965:
Alexis F. Vasseur, Yi Wang, and Jian Zhang proved a 2025 result about shock waves in a scalar conservation law with viscosity. A conservation law tracks a quantity that moves and spreads without being created or lost. Viscosity adds a smoothing effect, turning a sharp shock into a steep but smooth profile.

The authors study polynomial flux, where the flow speed follows a power of the quantity itself, for powers from two to four. They prove that large shock profiles pull nearby solutions toward them in a strong average sense over time. Their method uses a weighted contraction idea with a shift that moves as time passes. When the starting disturbance is also small in a total sense, they derive an explicit decay rate.
arxiv-2509-03065:
Charles-Philippe Diez, Luis da Maia, and Ivan Nourdin documented a 2025 experiment in which a large language model tried research-level mathematics. A report that GPT-5 had solved an open convex optimization problem in August 2025 prompted their test. They chose the Malliavin-Stein framework, a tool for proving that random quantities behave nearly like bell curves.

Their challenge asked the model to strengthen a known fourth-moment theorem. The original result says closeness holds, but gives no speed; the task was to add explicit convergence rates. They posed it in both Gaussian and Poisson settings, where such rates had not been published. The paper records what the model produced and discusses what the attempt means for machine help in mathematics. Claims here are the authors' report of their experiment.
arxiv-2509-03165:
Anirban Bairagi and Benjamin Wandelt introduced PatchNet in 2025, a method for squeezing cosmological information out of dark matter maps. Modern galaxy surveys will map matter in fine detail, but standard summaries like the power spectrum waste much of the pattern in clumpy, nonlinear regions. Simulation-based inference learns the link between settings and simulated universes directly.

PatchNet cuts a simulated cube of dark matter into smaller patches and reads each patch with a neural network. It then combines those local readings with classic large-scale statistics. That hybrid design cuts memory needs and training data demands compared with reading the whole field at once. On the Quijote simulation suite it captured more information than analytic summaries. Its yield matched a very different wavelet-based approach.
arxiv-2509-03365:
Paul-Gauthier Noé and 4 co-authors studied how calibrated likelihood functions are spread in 2025, extending a two-class theory to many classes. Calibration asks whether stated likelihoods match reality. Evidence claimed as strongly supportive should be right at the matching rate. For two hypotheses, such functions compress into log-likelihood ratios, a well-studied case.

With more than two hypotheses, ratios no longer suffice. The authors use the Aitchison geometry of the simplex. That framework treats probability lists as points with their own arithmetic, and it restores Bayes' rule in an additive vector form. They extend the meaning of calibration, and the idempotence property, a self-consistency demand, to a transformed version for many classes. An application to discriminant analysis yields parts that form a calibrated likelihood over the classes. That improves how well the method can be read and trusted.
arxiv-2509-03765:
Ilya Nemenman and one co-author review a 2025 modelling strategy for high-dimensional biology: build random systems, but only ones respecting biological constraints. Traditional models of living systems use a few finely tuned interacting parts and work beautifully for simple cases. Modern data instead describe thousands of heterogeneous components interacting at once, where fine tuning becomes hopeless.

The reviewed works argue that many observed biological behaviours are typical, meaning most random systems with the right constraints show them too. Case studies span neuroscience, ecology, and evolution, each tying the random-with-constraints approach to real experiments. Random matrix style models can then predict dynamical and statistical features of high-dimensional data without fitting every detail. The authors present this stance as a minimal modelling philosophy for biology. It trades exact mechanism for robust, testable patterns that survive across particular systems.
arxiv-2509-03965:
A mid-infrared ring laser integrating optical fibre and chip waveguides is what Tinghui An and nine co-authors examine in a 2025 research paper. Mid-infrared light serves sensing and spectroscopy, but compact sources in that band remain difficult. Their design inscribes directional couplers, which split light between two paths in controlled ratios, into fluoride glass.

Femtosecond laser writing carves the couplers, forming low-loss waveguides whose refractive index rises, tuned for light near 2.7 micrometres. Varying the coupling gap and interaction length sweeps splitting ratios from full transmission to a balanced split. One coupler, with a seven-micrometre gap and an eighty-twenty split, joins a pumped erbium-doped ZBLAN fibre to close the ring cavity. The device lases stably near 2717 nanometres with milliwatt output. The authors call it the first mid-infrared laser fully integrated across fibre and chip, opening three-dimensional integration in fluoride glasses.
arxiv-2509-04065:
A Tobar and five co-authors offer a new way to split national figures into regional ones in a 2025 economics paper. Countries often know total output for long spans but lack matching yearly data for each region. Standard splitting methods work over time yet ignore links between neighbors. Trade and commuting mean one region's economy affects nearby ones, so that gap can distort the estimates.

Their method joins time splitting with a spatial model and guide data from related indicators. Tests with simulated data held up across many settings. Applied to Spain, it produced yearly output estimates for all seventeen autonomous communities covering 2002 through 2023. Known national totals stayed respected throughout.
arxiv-2509-04265:
Yuanchao Xu and four co-authors let a learning agent choose where to collect data for analyzing complex systems in a 2025 research paper. Koopman analysis rewrites nonlinear motion as linear change in measured quantities, exposing decay rates and repeating modes. Standard estimators falter when most recorded paths start in dull regions carrying little spectral information. Their method, Reinforced SDMD, pairs an estimator called SDMD with reinforcement learning, where an agent earns rewards for good choices.

The agent picks starting regions, the estimator updates, and a consistency reward grades the fresh estimates. A bonus keeps exploration broad. Tests on three classic wobbly systems, including the Duffing oscillator, showed sampling shifted toward informative regions. Error analysis traces how estimator mistakes flow into the learning bounds.
arxiv-2509-04365:
Anaclara Alvez and three co-authors compute heavy meson masses inside the Curci-Ferrari model in a 2025 physics paper. Mesons are particles built from a quark and an antiquark, and the nonrelativistic ones here pair charm and bottom quarks, the heavy flavors. The model gives gluons, the strong-force carriers, a mass. Starting from a single gluon exchange, the authors build an energy Hamiltonian and add a Cornell potential, a standard confining term that keeps quarks bound.

Solving the Schrödinger equation gives the main energy levels, and small corrections follow perturbatively, as refined approximations. Five model settings, with two allowed to drift with energy scale, are fitted to measured spectra of charmonium, bottomonium, and mixed mesons. Agreement is very good, favoring a nonzero gluon mass.
arxiv-2509-04465:
Sushrita Rakshit and four co-authors study how emotional expressions steer buyer-seller disputes in a 2025 research paper. In conflict, displays of anger or warmth shape what the other side thinks and does. Automatic emotion reading from text might reveal that influence at scale. The team mined a large corpus of dispute dialogues, asking how emotional expression connects with subjective feelings and objective outcomes like settlement.

Large language models annotated emotion intensity far better than older methods, closely matching human judges. Patterns fit existing theories of how emotions escalate or defuse conflict. Agent-based systems that recognize rising emotion could help manage disputes, the authors suggest, perhaps by cooling exchanges before they harden.
arxiv-2509-04565:
Ofer Aharony and two co-authors analyze conformal fixed points of Chern-Simons-matter theories with several flavors in a 2025 physics paper. These three-dimensional theories couple matter to a special gauge field and settle at scale-invariant fixed points. The multi-flavor quasi-bosonic case resists easy generalization because three relevant and three marginal couplings interact, with the marginal ones drifting slowly at large particle number. The authors compute the drift functions, called beta functions, in several weak-coupling limits and map their general shape.

Stable infrared fixed points exist for some flavor counts and coupling values but not others. In one case, fixed points merge and vanish in pairs as coupling grows. Semi-critical theories, tuned on fewer knobs, receive the same treatment.
arxiv-2509-04665:
Scattering calculations for atomic nuclei rely on optical potentials that can depend on position in a nonlocal way. Laina M. Stahulak and one co-author examine that nonlocality in a 2025 nuclear theory paper. Their potentials come from chiral effective field theory, a systematic low-energy theory of nuclear forces.

Using the Perey-Buck ansatz, they link energy dependence in local potentials to spatial nonlocality of Gaussian form. They find spatial nonlocality explains most energy dependence in the real part, while the imaginary part mainly reflects genuine time nonlocality. Results cover the calcium isotope chain and how shape parameters change with isotope number.
arxiv-2509-05165:
Long conversations with a language model fill its key-value cache until memory becomes the bottleneck. Dmitry Akulov, lead author with five co-authors, propose KVCompose, a structured cache compression framework, in a 2025 paper. Earlier methods use rigid rules, break tensor layouts, or need special kernels.

Their method first pools attention scores to judge which tokens matter. It then picks tokens per attention head and aligns the picks into composite tokens that keep the uniform cache structure. A global mechanism shifts retention budgets toward layers with more informative tokens. The approach cuts memory while preserving accuracy better than prior methods in their tests, and it stays compatible with standard inference engines.
arxiv-2509-05565:
Walls that reflect radio waves in a timed pattern can protect wireless links while sensing their surroundings, Zhihao Tao, Athina Petropulu, and H. Vincent Poor propose in a 2025 wireless engineering paper. Their targets may themselves be eavesdroppers, so sensing and secrecy must be designed together.

The time-modulated reflecting surface is tuned so legitimate users receive clean data while signals in every other direction appear scrambled. A generative flow network learns a sampling strategy over the huge space of surface settings, guided by rewards mixing data rate and sensing beam strength. Against exhaustive search and earlier security methods, their design sampled far more efficiently and held up more robustly in tests.
arxiv-2509-05765:
A faster way to solve a stubborn class of optimization problems is proposed in a 2025 paper by Yuqia Wu and four co-authors. The problems mix a smooth twice-differentiable part with a prox-regular part, a function that is rough yet well behaved near a point. Such problems are both nonconvex and nonsmooth, so standard solvers can stall.

The team first shows when the proximal mapping, a key building block, stays single-valued and steady under small changes. They then blend proximal gradient steps with semismooth Newton steps into one globalized method. The full sequence settles at a stationary point, and under extra conditions it speeds up to a superlinear rate near the end. Tests on sparse-norm problems show it matching strong second-order rivals.
arxiv-2509-06065:
Do language models stay truthful in Filipino? Lorenzo Alfred Nery and two co-authors build the test in a 2025 paper introducing KatotohananQA, a Filipino translation of the TruthfulQA benchmark. Truthfulness benchmarks exist mainly in English, leaving low-resource languages unmeasured while models happily answer in them. The team assessed seven free-tier proprietary models in a binary-choice format.

A clear gap appeared: truthfulness in Filipino lagged English, though the newest OpenAI models showed strong multilingual robustness. Performance also varied by question type, category, and topic, so some content transfers across languages worse than others. The authors argue that fair, reliable deployment needs routine evaluation in the languages people actually use, not just in English.
arxiv-2509-06265:
Composite fermion theory is generalized to fractional Chern insulators in a 2025 paper by Hao Jin and Junren Shi. Composite fermions, electrons bound to flux, explain the fractional quantum Hall effect; Chern insulators offer a lattice cousin without a magnetic field. Adapting the quantum mechanics approach to composite fermions, the authors obtain an effective Hamiltonian and a recipe for the waves in one stroke.

Band geometry supplies the scalar and vector potentials the composite fermions feel, and state counting in their phase space needs a small fix away from half filling. Applied to the twisted bilayer MoTe2 insulator at a chosen filling, both electron-based and hole-based models track exact solutions for small systems, the electron version closer. The insulator's transition coincides with a topological transition in empty composite-fermion bands.
arxiv-2509-06465:
Predicting where an antibody will grip its target is the goal of a 2025 computational biology paper led by Hongzong Li, with seven co-authors. Such binding sites matter for designing antibody medicines. Older methods used only a protein's letter sequence or only its shape, and often missed sites that are specific to one antibody.

Their system, CAME-AB, merges five kinds of evidence, from raw amino acid codes and substitution tables to language-model features, shape data, and biochemical graphs refined by a graph network. A fusion module learns how much weight each kind deserves for each input. A transformer with a mixture-of-experts design, plus contrastive training that pulls similar cases together, completes the model. On standard test sets it beats strong rivals across several accuracy measures.
arxiv-2509-06765:
Flocking models with noise settle into aligned motion at rates Alexandre Surin pins down in a solo 2025 analysis paper. The model is a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation derived from the Cucker-Smale flocking system with noise added. Noise strength decides a phase transition: strong noise leaves one symmetric, unpolarized steady state, while weaker noise allows a whole continuum of polarized steady states.

Above the threshold, solutions converge to the unique radial steady state, even though that state is unstable in the symmetry-breaking range. There, polarized states attract all solutions whose entropy starts low enough. Surin proves convergence in a weighted norm happens at an exponential rate, and the average speed also converges exponentially to a unique limit. That limit selects a single polarized steady state, resolving which of the many possible aligned outcomes a given flock reaches.
arxiv-2509-06865:
Quantum error-correcting codes built around easy state preparation are introduced by Matthew B. Hastings in a solo 2025 quantum information paper. Most code families are designed for simple stabilizers, the checks that detect errors. Hastings takes the opposite organizing principle: simplicity of preparing a code state, at least when no noise is present.

Certain known codes turn out to belong to this cyclic class, including a family of rotated two-dimensional toric codes. Other small examples were found by computer search, showing the class is not just a redescription of one known family. The paper closes by discussing how to prepare these codes fault-tolerantly, so that the preparation process itself does not introduce errors faster than the code can handle. Preparation-first design could matter for near-term devices, where state preparation is a practical bottleneck.
arxiv-2509-07065:
Black hole images computed with gradients, so fitting models to telescope data becomes far cheaper, are presented by Pedro Naethe Motta and two co-authors in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Event Horizon Telescope imaging has relied on searching huge precomputed libraries of models, an approach whose cost grows as data sharpen. Their code, Jipole, makes a standard radiative transfer code automatically differentiable.

Gradients show how each model parameter, such as the black hole's spin or the viewing angle, changes the image pixel by pixel. The code was validated against the original in analytical tests, and its derivatives matched finite-difference estimates. Parameter recovery on an analytical model then succeeded in a few optimization steps for ideal, blurred, and noisy test images, failing only at extremely low signal quality with heavy blurring. Gradient-based fitting could speed future black hole imaging substantially.
arxiv-2509-07265:
Erin Barillier's 2025 paper, with 7 co-authors, sets limits on dark matter boosted by blazar jets using xenon detectors. Blazars are galaxies whose relativistic jets, streams of matter moving near light speed, point toward Earth. Those jets can strike light dark matter in the host galaxy and fling it toward us at high energy, where giant xenon tanks can catch its recoil.

The search models the full chain, from jet acceleration to the detector response, using public data from XENON1T and LZ aimed at the blazar TXS 0506+056. No signal is claimed; instead, the team draws exclusion regions for dark matter near one MeV in mass. The limits shift with how dark matter is spread near the central black hole, which the authors flag as the main uncertainty. Light dark matter below detector thresholds gets a new, if model-dependent, test.
arxiv-2509-07665:
Adem Kikaj and 4 co-authors present DeepGraphLog in 2025, a neurosymbolic framework that lets neural and symbolic layers alternate freely. Neurosymbolic AI joins neural learning with symbolic reasoning. It aims for both structure and interpretability. Systems such as DeepProbLog fix the flow, though. Neural processing always comes first, and symbolic reasoning second. That fixed order restricts complex dependencies, above all on graph-shaped data.

DeepGraphLog extends ProbLog with Graph Neural Predicates. Symbolic representations are treated as graphs, so graph neural networks can process them. Components can then stack in any order, across many layers. The team shows the framework on planning tasks. They also test it on knowledge graph completion with distant supervision, and on graph neural network expressivity. The authors report that the framework captures complex relational dependencies that fixed-flow systems miss.
arxiv-2509-07965:
Fabio Apruzzi and 4 co-authors build a field theory for spacetime symmetries in a 2025 physics paper. Most symmetry theories deal with internal traits, like charge. This one deals with the symmetries of space and time themselves. Those include shifts, turns, and changes of scale. The trick is to add one extra dimension.

In that added dimension, the theory takes a simple BF form for the whole symmetry group. When the base dimension is even, extra terms can encode known anomalies, the small ways quantum effects break classical rules. The team works out the edge conditions and how such symmetries break. For scale symmetry, they recover the action of the dilaton field. One frame now covers many cases.
arxiv-2509-08265:
Tracking an object in hyperspectral images, which record many narrow color bands, promises robustness when ordinary cameras fail. Long Gao and 4 co-authors propose HyMamba in a 2025 research paper. Earlier trackers converted the data to false-color images or fused modes in ways that lost spectral detail. Temporal links and interactions across network depth were also underused.

HyMamba unifies spectral, cross-depth, and temporal modeling with state space modules, an efficient sequence modeling family. A spectral integration module refines features progressively across depth and time. Inside it, a dedicated module scans in three directions to learn space and spectrum together. Tests on seven benchmark datasets put HyMamba at state-of-the-art level. Rich material signatures, it turns out, help most when the tracker actually keeps them intact.
arxiv-2509-08665:
Marcello Porta and 2 co-authors study the large scale response of interacting one-dimensional Fermi systems in a 2025 paper. Weakly interacting, gapless fermions are disturbed by a small force that varies slowly in space and time. The authors track charge and current density in a large system limit.

Linear response, where output grows in proportion to input, is proved valid and asymptotically exact as variation vanishes. An explicit formula for the response is given. The proof uses Euclidean correlation functions with sharp bounds from renormalization group methods. A cancellation linked to bosonization and chiral Ward identities makes the result exact.
arxiv-2509-09065:
Projective representations of almost unimodular groups are studied by Aldo Garcia Guinto in a 2025 paper. Almost unimodular groups are groups whose Plancherel weight, a key measure in harmonic analysis, is almost periodic. Projective representations allow a phase twist in how group elements combine.

The basic construction for a natural inclusion is shown to be a twisted group algebra of a larger group. A group is almost unimodular exactly when a related central extension is, under stated conditions. Formal degrees of square integrable projective representations then behave like ordinary ones. An Atiyah-Schmid formula is obtained for groups with a finite covolume subgroup.
arxiv-2509-09165:
Naritaka Oshita and 3 co-authors probe direct waves in black hole ringdowns in a 2025 paper. After two black holes merge, gravitational waves ring down as the remnant settles. That signal carries rich information about spacetime dynamics.

Waves from comparable mass and extreme mass ratio binaries are analyzed from simulations and perturbation theory. The authors argue prompt direct waves, emitted as the holes collide, dominate the signal. The remnant's potential screens them selectively, and spin can make them mode-like with stable frequency. For a GW150914-like system, detectability with current detectors looks strong. Direct waves may become a robust observable for ringdown studies.
arxiv-2509-09365:
Xiaodong Wang and 3 co-authors mix plug-and-play methods with diffusion models for image sensing in a 2025 paper. Single pixel imaging must rebuild a full image from very few measures, an ill posed task. Plug-and-play and diffusion tools solve such tasks in distinct ways.

The pair first map how the two families differ in denoising and sampling. Diffusion is then split into three stages: denoise, enforce data fit, and sample. A hybrid fit module blends several fidelity terms and fixes the denoised image in place. Image fit improves with no break to the sampling path. Tests on single pixel tasks show better rebuild quality than rival methods.
arxiv-2509-09465:
Weak light carries hard limits for ordinary cameras, and Aleksandr Mokeev and 3 co-authors show in 2025 how quantum processing might loosen them. Standard imaging adds up detected signals and cleans the result afterwards, so shot noise piles up and caps clarity. Their alternative stores light amplitude coherently inside qubit registers as signals arrive, out of step with one another.

Quantum algorithms then work on that stored information directly. For imaging point sources too close together to separate, the authors build a concrete method and apply it to finding exoplanets. Under realistic conditions they report gains of orders of magnitude. Notably, the processors needed are described as relatively small in scale.
arxiv-2509-09665:
Richard Stiskalek and 6 co-authors measure the present expansion rate of the universe in 2025 using Cepheid stars alone. The Hubble tension, a stubborn mismatch between expansion rates found by different routes, motivates a leaner check. Their ladder has just two rungs: Cepheid periods and brightnesses in anchor galaxies with known distances, plus redshifts of the host galaxies, all drawn from carefully vetted SH0ES data.

Fresh rigour in modelling how hosts were selected, plus a detailed local density and velocity map, tightens the result considerably. Their value lands lower than the supernova-based SH0ES figure, within a modest statistical distance of it. The authors warn the answer still leans on how the host sample was chosen, which remains unclear.
arxiv-2509-09865:
Kristian Behrens and 1 co-author pin down a family of utility functions in a 2025 economics paper where people's caution toward risk follows a linear fractional rule. The family is wide enough to contain several utility forms that separate literatures had used in isolation, and the authors express it neatly through Gauss hypergeometric functions. That unity lets one analysis speak to many older models at once.

Carried into monopolistic competition, the family yields the profit-maximising price through a generalised Lambert W function. Firm data then get the final say sector by sector: whether relative risk aversion rises, falls, or stays flat decides whether markups shrink, grow, or hold steady as marginal costs change. Theory hands over a dial, and the data turn it.
arxiv-2509-09965:
Hiroshi Hakoyama's 2025 paper builds confidence intervals for extinction risk that stay honest when wildlife records are short. Population viability analysis is often dismissed as useless with little data, because the uncertainty looks overwhelming. Working with a classic drift model of population change, Hakoyama reparameterises the problem so the key estimates follow a known statistical distribution, giving intervals whose coverage matches their promised level.

Precision turns out to depend on the risk level itself, not just on record length: very low or very high extinction chances can be pinned down even from brief series. A second estimator handles observation error and short-term correlation. Applied to sixty-four years of Japanese eel harvest records, the method returns extinction chances far under the thresholds that mark threatened status.
arxiv-2509-10165:
Matthew J. Schneider and 2 co-authors explain, in a 2025 paper, why data anonymization has not spread through business practice. Companies hoped methods like differential privacy and synthetic data would give simple compliance answers. In practice, each use demands hard choices: what data range to cover, which units to protect, where protection must hold, and what counts as protected.

Each choice changes what the privacy promise actually means, yet the same label gets used for all of them. The authors argue that anonymization works mainly when the patterns a firm needs are much larger than the unit being protected. Because firms must keep the patterns that drive profit, solutions end up custom-built and hard to scale.
arxiv-2509-10765:
Owen Mayer and 3 co-authors tune camera color processing with words instead of sliders in this 2025 paper. Every digital photo passes through an image signal processor, and its color block sets the look of the final image. Tuning that block by hand takes expert trial and error. Their method lets a user simply describe the wanted style in a text prompt.

The team rebuilt the color block so its settings can be adjusted by gradient descent. A pre-trained vision-language model scores how well the processed image matches the prompt, and that score drives the tuning. Tests show different prompts producing different looks, and the paper compares which vision-language models and optimization choices work best.
arxiv-2509-11165:
Waikit Xiu and four co-authors present Traffic-MLLM in this 2025 paper on self-driving cars. Safe driving depends on lessons from rare, awkward traffic situations, and the authors want a system that reasons from past cases without looking them up one by one at driving time.

Their model builds case knowledge directly into training, learning from a mix of traffic videos and large sets of visual questions and answers. A curiosity-driven step, based on random network distillation, pushes the model to learn deep patterns near the edge of what it knows rather than surface resemblances. On two driving benchmarks the system improved at dynamic reasoning, rule understanding, and transfer to new domains, reaching its best scores on real-world street imagery.
arxiv-2509-11365:
Mohamed Tarek and 2 co-authors report their system for an Arabic health question answering contest in this 2025 paper. The AraHealthQA 2025 shared task asked systems to answer clinical questions in Arabic, both multiple-choice and open-ended. Their entry took second place in both sub-tasks of the general health track.

For multiple choice they used a large commercial model with few-shot prompting, cleaned inputs, and an ensemble of three prompt variants voting together. For open answers, one unified prompt cast the model as an Arabic medical expert, again with worked examples, plus post-processing to keep replies concise. The paper documents a prompt-centered recipe that needs no model training at all.
arxiv-2509-11465:
Amirhossein Abaskohi and four co-authors present CEMTM in this 2025 paper. It is a topic model for documents that mix text with images. Topic models sort documents into themes a reader can grasp. This one aims at coherent themes for short and long documents alike.

CEMTM draws embeddings from a fine-tuned large vision-language model. The embeddings carry context. A distributional attention step weighs each token's share in theme inference. A reconstruction aim keeps theme-based forms close to the document embedding. Several images per document are handled with no repeat encoding. On six benchmarks, the model beat text-only and multimodal rivals. Extra tests show help for few-shot retrieval. Visually grounded meaning in scientific articles was captured too.
arxiv-2509-11565:
Samuel W. Yee and thirteen co-authors measured the tilt of a Neptune-sized planet's orbit. This 2025 astronomy paper studies TOI-2374 b. The planet sits in the Neptunian ridge. That is a crowd of planets between Neptune and Saturn in size. Their orbits run three to six days. They may have arrived like hot Jupiters did, by a violent path.

The team watched the planet cross its star with the Keck Planet Finder. They caught the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect. That is the wobble a transit stamps on starlight. The orbit came out strongly tilted, near polar. Star rotation timing gave the true three-dimensional tilt. It too was near polar. Ridge planets on polar paths are piling up.
arxiv-2509-11765:
Kai Chen and Jie Zhu connect quantum state geometry to electrical response in leaky systems. This 2025 condensed matter theory paper treats non-Hermitian systems. Their energies and responses can be complex. The object of study is the quantum geometric tensor, for a system with a spectral line gap.

The tensor's symmetric part is the quantum metric. Here it takes complex values. It generates an intrinsic nonlinear conductivity. That conductivity ignores scattering time. The full tensor drives a second, distinct conductivity. It depends on the width of the wavepacket carrying the current. No counterpart exists in ordinary Hermitian matter. One- and two-dimensional models confirm the links. State geometry and wavepacket size jointly encode transport in open quantum matter.
arxiv-2509-11965:
Kidney exchange programs match donors to patients in cycles, but what if one participant group can veto a matching that shortchanges them? Bart M. P. Jansen, with two co-authors, studies that rejection-proof variant in 2025 as a problem in parameterized complexity.

Several agents own the graph's vertices, and an agent rejects a packing of disjoint swap cycles when a different packing would cover more of its own patients. The authors use the sunflower lemma on a set-packing formulation to build a kernel whose size is polynomial in the target for fixed cycle length. From it they get an algorithm whose running time they prove essentially best possible under a standard complexity assumption. A generalized version, where a parameter bounds how far agents may rewrite a packing, drops in difficulty yet resists single-exponential algorithms.
arxiv-2509-12465:
Training a quantum neural network on pooled medical data promises stronger pattern finding, but pooling genomes is a privacy hazard. Gaoyuan Wang and two co-authors propose in 2025 to encode each group's data ensemble as a single mixed quantum state, so training runs on the mixture and never touches a raw record.

The scheme needs just one round of communication per participant, trains fast, and lets new analyses reuse the shared states without asking participants again. Theory backs the privacy claims against attempts to recover individual points or test membership. Tests on three datasets, centered on genomics, show the approach works in practice.
arxiv-2509-12665:
Bond-orientational measures tell crystal growers how ordered a particle soup is, yet they never directly measure symmetry itself. Domagoj Fijan and three co-authors introduce Point Group Order Parameters in 2025, a family of scores that continuously quantify how strongly a particle's neighborhood obeys a chosen point group symmetry.

The new measures are tested across several crystalline systems and compared head-to-head with the standard bond-orientational metrics. Computations for every non-infinite point group ship inside SPATULA, an open-source toolkit written in fast parallel code with a Python front end. The authors argue symmetry-first scores sharpen the study of how crystals nucleate and grow.
arxiv-2509-12765:
Zihan Wang leads nine co-authors in 2025 on InfoGain-RAG, a better way to pick source texts for chat models that search before they answer. Search can help models avoid made-up facts, but it also pulls in weak or false pages that hurt the final answer.

The team scores each page by how much it lifts the model trust in the right answer when the page is added. Those scores train a ranker that keeps the most useful pages and drops the rest. Across many tests the method beat older search setups by clear gaps, with gains also seen on a top paid model.
arxiv-2509-12965:
Silvia Zottin and 4 co-authors report a competition on segmenting text lines in ancient handwritten documents in a 2025 paper. Text line segmentation is a critical step in analyzing handwritten document images. Historical documents add irregular handwriting, faded ink, and complex layouts with overlapping, non-linear lines, and large annotated data sets are scarce.

The FEST competition, held at ICDAR 2025, tasks members with segmenting text lines using only three annotated images per manuscript for training, a few-shot setting. Its data set collects diverse ancient manuscripts with wide-ranging layouts, degradation levels, and non-standard formatting that reflect real-world settings. By emphasizing few-shot learning, the competition aims to promote robust, adaptable methods for historical document study.
arxiv-2509-13165:
Alessandro Antonucci, Eric Rossetto and Ivan Duvnjak test in 2025 whether fairer calls in chance models also tend to be more accurate. Fairness here means stable calls when private traits are nudged. Robust calls may track truth more closely.

Fourteen sets with fairness stakes are tested with Bayes nets as the base models. Hard robustness checks are recast as best-explain tasks in a side field model. That recast makes multi-trait checks tractable. Results back the link: robust cases are more often right. The link hints at ways to ease the classic fairness versus accuracy trade.
arxiv-2509-14165:
Michal Szczepanski, Martyna Poreba, and Karim Haroun ask where tokens go in a vision transformer in a 2025 paper. Transformers for image segmentation are powerful but expensive at high resolution, because every image patch becomes a token carried through every layer. Their framework, STEP, cuts that cost by merging patches into superpatches and pruning tokens the model already predicts confidently.

A light convolutional policy network decides the merging, and early exits inside the encoder retire high-confidence supertokens before the final layers. Applied alone, the merging cut token counts by a factor of about two and a half against standard patching, more than doubling throughput. The full framework reached up to fourfold lower computational complexity with an accuracy drop of at most about two points.
arxiv-2509-14265:
Siyuan Chen, Zhichao Lu and Qingfu Zhang present Evolution of Kernels in 2025, a system that uses large language models to write fast low level code for RISC-V chips. RISC-V is a newer chip design with a thin software base, so good kernels, the core routines programs call often, are scarce.

Their system mines old kernel libraries for reusable design ideas, stated as plain principles and concrete tips. It then guides many language model attempts in parallel, adding RISC-V facts through retrieval and favouring ideas that worked before. Tests reported in the study suggest the search can find strong kernels even where handbooks and sample code are thin. That matters because weak basic software can hold back a whole new hardware platform.
arxiv-2509-14465:
Shifra Mandel and thirty-nine co-authors present a multiwavelength study in 2025 of MAXI J1744-294, a black hole candidate near the Galactic centre in outburst. It is the first bright transient in the central parsec in nearly a decade. The source matches a previously known Swift transient.

Data span five X-ray telescopes plus radio and near infrared observations. The team tracks the outburst as it moves from a high soft state to a low hard state. Relativistic reflection features in the X-ray spectrum give a high spin estimate and a modest viewing tilt. Those values agree with measures for the earlier Swift source, supporting a single identity. A well watched Galactic centre outburst is a rare laboratory for accretion physics.
arxiv-2509-15265:
R. Maria del Rio-Chanona and four co-authors review what is actually known about AI and jobs in a 2025 economics paper. Generative AI is changing work processes and organizational design, yet headline claims about employment run far ahead of settled evidence. The review organizes theory and measurement at three levels.

First comes the evolution of economic models, from aggregate production frameworks to task- and expertise-based accounts of automation. Second, the authors quantitatively compare occupation exposure measures across studies and find them converging on high-wage jobs as the most exposed. Third, they assemble after-the-fact evidence from randomized trials, field experiments, and digital trace data such as platform and code repository records. Productivity gains look sizable but context-dependent, and the employment picture stays genuinely unresolved.
arxiv-2509-15365:
Błażej Żmija, a lone author, works on a pure math problem about number patterns. Some whole numbers can be written with set forms called binary quadratic forms. He asks how long the gaps can grow between one such number and the next, when several forms are used at once. Long gaps mean wide stretches where no form reaches.

Żmija proves a lower bound on how large these gaps must get as the numbers grow. His result sharpens and widens an earlier one by five other mathematicians. Along the way, he also improves a known bound on character sums, a tool used across number theory. The paper is short, dense, and aimed at specialists.
arxiv-2509-15465:
Eric Bittner and Andrei Piryatinski study how light trapped in a cavity makes photons act on each other. Their setting is a topological insulator, a material with special edge states. They use a chain model, called SSH, to keep the math clear. The link between two photons runs through the material's bands.

The pair build a diagram based theory for these links. A key term in their math steers how photon colors tangle and how a strong beam can shift light's speed in the material. They map a phase chart for this effect. They also find how empty cavity light shifts the bands, and which shifts symmetry forbids. The work ties band shape to light and matter links.
arxiv-2509-15565:
Yixuan Jia leads a team that matches data seen by robots at different times or places. Matching, called data association, is a base step for robot work. Repeated or symmetric scenes make it hard. Most tools return one best match set, yet hard cases often have many near equal answers. Committing to one too soon can fail.

Their frame keeps many candidate answers alive as particles. Each particle moves by a set rule to cover the peaks of the answer spread. The method takes in limits from the matching problem itself. It also gains speed from graphics chip parallel work. Tests on mock and real data with much ambiguity show it finds the true spread.
arxiv-2509-15765:
Xiao-Huang Hu leads a team that sorts a family of exotic baryons. Baryons are particles made of three quarks. The family here holds a strange and a charm quark, and a recent collider find anchors the study. That state, seen at the LHCb detector, is read as a spinning excited state of a set type.

The team use a chiral quark model plus a decay rule to place the other states. Two known states form a close pair of one excitation type. States near a higher mass mix two excitation modes. Another fits a radial excitation. A further pair forms a second doublet, and one more state takes the same class. The scheme calls for more lab tests.
arxiv-2509-15965:
Chao Yu leads a very large team that builds a faster system for reinforcement learning at scale. Such training mixes many unlike steps, so hardware often idles and runs crawl. Their system, RLinf, starts from one observation: flexibility is the main bottleneck. A new design pattern breaks big workflows down and rebuilds them as tuned flows.

The pattern, called macro to micro flow transformation, splits workflows in time and space. Worker tricks like context switching and elastic pipelining carry it out. A profiling guided scheduler picks the best plan. On reasoning and embodied tasks, the system beats top rivals. Speedups range from slight to well over double the throughput.
arxiv-2509-16065:
Grid worlds where cells flip to one fixed state and never flip back pose a sharp question: how hard is it to predict a cell's future state? Pablo Concha-Vega and three co-authors study this freezing majority rule, where a cell adopts the most common state among its north and east neighbors in an L shape.

For the smallest L shapes, they prove the task can be solved fast in parallel. For larger L shapes, they prove the task is complete for a class tied to step-by-step work. So a small change in the shape of the neighborhood flips the problem from easy to hard.
arxiv-2509-16265:
Quantum annealing can stall when two low-energy states nearly cross, forcing the system to tunnel through a tiny gap. Vicky Choi studies this stall for a class of set-packing problems with many tied local best states. The analysis shrinks the system to a core model built from the local and global best parts, then solves it in a tilted basis.

That route yields the tiny gap in closed form, with no need to treat the drive field as small. The stall comes from rivalry between the tied states and the true best state. A companion work uses this picture to design drives that bypass the stall.
arxiv-2509-16465:
Health risks shown as bar charts versus rows of little person icons can steer choices in different ways, even at equal numbers. Jade Kandel and four co-authors run a series of studies on how chart type and layout shape value comparison and later decisions. Layouts placed charts side by side, labeled values plainly, or did both.

Icon arrays with plain labels plus side-by-side layout gave the best mix of accurate gap reading and low bias. Accuracy and good decisions did not always move together, and reading skill split the results. Design advice should fit the audience, not just the chart.
arxiv-2509-16865:
Xia Jiang and co-authors use language models as direct solvers for hard planning puzzles in a 2025 paper. Such puzzles, in logistics and factories, once needed bespoke algorithms and deep expertise. Past language approaches detoured through code or called an outside solver. That limited their reach. This team tune a modest model to solve the puzzles end to end.

Tests span seven classic hard problems. The tuned model produced valid plans at a high rate. Its gap to the best known answers stayed small. It beat large general models, reasoning models, and hand-built heuristics. A single language pipeline could widen access to optimization for smaller firms.
arxiv-2509-16965:
Minchan Kwon, Junwon Ko, Kangil Kim, and Junmo Kim improve preference training for small language models in a 2025 paper. A popular method teaches from pairwise wins and losses. That binary signal is thin for small models with limited capacity. The team distill richer value-based signals from reinforcement learning into the preference step.

Their method fits into the standard training frame with no extra rollouts. Tests show steady gains across benchmarks and model sizes. Richer feedback could let small models align with human tastes without huge training runs. That matters for teams that deploy compact models on phones and local servers.
arxiv-2509-17265:
David Liu, Erik Weis, Moritz Laber, Tina Eliassi-Rad, and Brennan Klein study a skew in recommendation systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. These systems push popular items too hard and starve niche items that many users would love. The authors look closely at the users who favor niche goods, as a step toward fixing that skew.

Across three benchmark data sets, users split by activity and by taste. One group stands out: power-niche users, who are both very active and fond of niche items. There are more of them than chance would predict. Their records turn out to be gold for training, lifting suggestions for niche and mainstream users alike. Past fixes boost all niche users, active or not. The team's PAIR method instead weighs training by both activity and item popularity at once.
arxiv-2509-17465:
Nina Smirnova, Muhammad Ahsan Shahid, and Philipp Mayr built a web portal for political text research. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents PoliCorp, a platform for structuring, searching, and analyzing large political collections. The launch collection holds transcripts of German parliament debates that span more than seven decades of proceedings.

Researchers can search with logical operations that combine or exclude criteria across many fields. That power makes it easy to carve out custom subcollections tuned to one question, then download them in JSON form for deeper study. Extra processing steps prepare the texts for web search and add features. A key draw is that the interface needs no programming skill, so historians and social scientists can query processed texts directly. The authors frame the portal as shared infrastructure for discourse research over long spans of time.
arxiv-2509-17565:
Zhi Gao, writing alone, reports on searches for new physics at the BESIII experiment in a 2025 arXiv conference paper. BESIII is a symmetric electron-positron collider that runs at modest energies and has gathered the world's largest threshold data set. Its samples hold billions of J/psi and related particles, plus rich sets of charm meson pairs.

That wealth lets the collaboration test the Standard Model with care, hunt exotic low-mass particles, and probe forbidden or rare decays. Gao surveys recent hunts for axion-like particles, dark photons, and QCD axions, plus invisible decays of the neutral kaon. A second thread covers rare charm decays: lepton and baryon number violations, flavor-changing neutral currents, and weak decays of charmonium. Each null or hit result trims the space where physics beyond the Standard Model can hide. The paper reads as a status report from the collaboration's front line.
arxiv-2509-17665:
Katharina Simbeck and Mariam Mahran look inside language models for traces of religion, violence, and place. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that bias research has dwelt on gender and race, while religious identity gets little attention. The pair ask how models represent five religions internally, and how those pictures tangle with violence and geography.

Their method is mechanistic: sparse autoencoders pull apart the model's inner features, read through the Neuronpedia interface across five models. They measure how far religion prompts and violence prompts light up the same features. All five religions show similar internal cohesion. Islam, though, links more often to features tied to violent language. Geographic links mostly mirror real-world religious demographics. The authors argue that auditing inner structure catches stereotypes that output checks alone can miss.
arxiv-2509-17765:
Jin Xu leads a large Qwen team that built one model for text, image, sound, and video. Their 2025 technical report calls the model Qwen3-Omni. It aims to match models that handle just one kind of input. Sound tasks are a clear strength.

Across many sound and sound-plus-video tests, the model ranks at or near the top. It can chat in text in many tongues, hear speech, and speak back in real time. A split design pairs a part that thinks with a part that talks. The first sound comes back fast, in well under a second.
arxiv-2509-17865:
Paul Bannmuller and 3 co-authors help grid staff find more than one good way to rewire a power grid. Their 2025 paper deals with grid strain from more solar, wind, and electric use. Tools that suggest fixes can miss real limits or staff tastes, since their models are not exact.

Their loop asks a human expert to react, then makes fresh, varied switch plans. Tests on two standard grid cases show the loop can use that feedback well. The result is a set of strong, distinct plans, not one brittle pick. Staff keep the final say on which plan to run.
arxiv-2509-17965:
Sai Samrat Kankanala, Ram Chandra, and Sriram Ganapathy compare humans and machines at picking speech out of a mix. Their 2025 study deals with the cocktail party task, in more than one tongue. A listener must lock onto one voice while others talk over it.

Human listeners did far better in their home tongue than in a second one. Speech language models matched or beat humans when one clean voice spoke. With two voices at once, the models often failed to focus on the target. Folk lean on focus cues tuned to their home tongue, while models tend to pull all speech at once.
arxiv-2509-18065:
Parna Mandal, Nigel J Mottram, and Sean McGinty model how food supply shapes slime growth on medical implants. Their 2025 paper deals with biofilms, layers of bacteria that cling to a surface and resist drugs. When food runs low, some cells turn dormant and can survive a drug course, then regrow.

Their model links food flow to live cells, dormant cells, dead cells, and the slime they shed. Switch rates between live and dormant states rest on two food thresholds. Sims show low food keeps the dormant share high, while rich food brings growth back. Dormant peaks mark key times to strike the film.
arxiv-2509-18265:
Saranyo Moitra and Inti Sodemann Villadiego prove that a famed quantum liquid can melt into a gapless state as a field turns patchy. Their 2025 paper deals with the Laughlin state, a gapped, top-ordered phase that lives in flat Chern bands. Those bands act like Landau levels in a field that varies in space.

A neat map turns the wave state into a classic Coulomb gas. Known plasma results then show a phase shift at the set third filling. The new state has power-law links and no gap, yet no broken symmetry. Its link power slides in a smooth way with field patchiness.
arxiv-2509-18365:
Plasma physics has a classic result from 1973 on how waves and particles trade energy over time. Alain J. Brizard revisits that result in this short 2025 paper. The topic is oscillation-center quasilinear theory, which tracks the slow drift of particle motion under fast waves. The setting is a plasma with no magnetic field.

Brizard re-derives the theory of Dewar using a Lie-transform method, a step-by-step way of reshaping the equations of motion. The note is brief and technical, aimed at plasma theorists. It offers a cleaner path to a known result rather than a new claim.
arxiv-2509-18565:
Word problems trip up language models because they mix reading, reasoning, and arithmetic. Mitchell Piehl, Dillon Wilson, Ananya Kalita, and Jugal Kalita present a checking method that lifts model scores in this 2025 paper. Their approach first splits the problem into parts. The model then writes equations from those parts, and a symbolic solver computes the answer.

A second pass asks the model to estimate the answer, the way teachers urge students to sanity-check. If the estimate and the computed answer clash, a repair loop runs until they agree. The method set new best scores on standard numeric and algebraic word problem sets, gaining about two points on average. It also handled trigonometry problems, a type not tried before in this line of work. The team releases two new test sets to push the area further.
arxiv-2509-18665:
When two neutron stars merge, the wreck keeps ringing with gravitational waves. Christian Ecker, Tyler Gorda, Aleksi Kurkela, and Luciano Rezzolla show that long ringdown carries clues about matter at extreme density. Their 2025 paper runs full relativity simulations of mergers. The inner recipe of neutron star matter, its equation of state, is unknown at the highest densities.

The team varied that recipe across the plausible high-density range. They found a robust link between the late signal's lost energy and angular momentum and the core recipe. Applying that link to a real post-merger signal would shrink uncertainty where no direct limits exist. That zone sits at several times the density of atomic nuclei. Inspiral waves, size measures, and theory each cover other zones. The ringdown thus adds a fresh probe of the densest matter known.
arxiv-2509-19165:
Matching the two views of a stereo camera to judge depth works well in clear weather and badly in rain, fog, or darkness. Yun Wang and five co-authors make self-supervised stereo matching robust to such conditions. Rain and glare corrupt the image features their networks rely on, especially on shiny or textureless surfaces. The usual training signal, which assumes matching pixels share brightness, also breaks down in degraded regions.

Their system, RoSe, borrows strong visual priors from a large foundation model to steady the feature extractor. It also builds training pairs with realistic weather damage that keep the same scene layout and depth, so supervision rests on scene correspondence rather than brightness alone. Training then aligns results between clean and damaged views in two steps. Across experiments, RoSe beat existing self-supervised methods under adverse weather.
arxiv-2509-19265:
Do commonsense skills learned in one culture carry to another? Saeed Almheiri and six co-authors test that transfer across the Arab world, where countries share language and history yet differ locally. They use a commonsense reasoning dataset grounded in thirteen Arab countries. Lightweight alignment methods, from in-context examples to a demonstration-based reinforcement technique, are compared with heavier fine-tuning and preference optimization baselines.

Just twelve culture-specific examples from one country improved performance in others by about ten percent on average, inside multilingual models.
