Surprisingly, examples from Indonesia and the United States sometimes matched or beat in-culture examples for multiple-choice reasoning. Commonsense, it seems, transfers across cultures more than expected. The findings suggest a cheap path to adapting language models for low-resource cultural settings: borrow alignment from richer ones.
arxiv-2509-19365:
Topic models sort piles of posts into themes, but social media text is noisy and sparse, so the themes multiply and overlap. Wannes Janssens and two co-authors pair the BERTopic framework with large language models to tame that sprawl. BERTopic first builds topics from transformer embeddings and clustering. The language model then reads a representation of each topic and merges the ones that mean nearly the same thing, round after round.

The team tested the pipeline on three Twitter/X datasets with four different language models. Merging raised topic diversity and often coherence too, compared with BERTopic alone. Results did wobble with the dataset and with starting settings, which the authors note honestly. Unlike full language-model topic modeling, the hybrid keeps computing costs modest. It offers a practical route to cleaner topic maps of social media at scale.
arxiv-2509-19665:
Clouds hide the ground from methane-hunting satellites, and their shadows darken it further. Manuel Perez-Carrasco and fourteen co-authors train deep learning models to mark clouds and shadows in data from MethaneSAT and its airborne partner MethaneAIR. Both craft read the spectrum of light at fine detail, far sharper than global survey satellites. Clean cloud masks must come first, or methane readings will be skewed.

The satellite fills a middle niche: wider views than point-source imagers, finer detail than coarse global mappers. Its airborne twin flies at even finer resolution, which helps build and check the models. The team applies modern learning methods to the marking task. Reliable masks let the missions turn raw spectra into emission maps and rates. Those maps are the point of the missions: finding who emits methane, and how much.
arxiv-2509-19765:
Water stores more heat per degree than almost any common liquid, a fact that steadies both bodies and climate. Motoyuki Shiga and three co-authors compute that heat capacity from first principles. Their simulations track atomic interactions with high fidelity. Light hydrogen atoms force them to include nuclear quantum effects through path integral dynamics.

Such runs are costly, and heat capacity needs wide sampling of energy fluctuations. Machine-learned potentials stand in for the expensive force calculations, cutting the cost sharply. The goal is a microscopic account of why water holds heat so well. Hydrogen bonding networks are the usual suspect, but proof needs numbers that match experiment. First-principles values also test the learned potentials themselves. The study bridges quantum simulation and a property known since school physics.
arxiv-2509-20065:
Language models often fail on tricky inputs because they misread them at the start. Maggie Mi, Aline Villavicencio, and Nafise Sadat Moosavi study this failure mode in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their goal is to predict errors before the model writes any answer. They look at idioms, figurative phrases, and other context-sensitive text.

Their method uses only the input text itself. It builds features from how likely each token seems, guided by ideas about surprise and even information flow. These features flag local uncertainty in how the input is understood. Tests on five hard language datasets beat standard baselines. Span-level features help larger models most, while smaller models gain more from global patterns. The method needs no outputs or hidden states, so it stays light and general.
arxiv-2509-20365:
Turbulence simulations must guess what happens below their grid, and Karan Jakhar, Yifei Guan, and Pedram Hassanzadeh report a better guess in a 2025 arXiv paper. That guess, called a subgrid closure, strongly affects accuracy and stability. Earlier analytical and machine-learned closures for two-dimensional turbulence proved unstable in large-eddy simulations. The team combined physics reasoning with an AI search over equations.

Their search, guided by how energy moves between scales, found a closed-form closure from modest simulation data. Simulations using it stayed stable and matched direct simulation statistics, including extremes. The team then showed the formula follows from a fourth-order Taylor expansion. Earlier work had stopped at second order, which explains the instability. The result joins data-driven discovery with a classical derivation that others can inspect.
arxiv-2509-20465:
Three famous claims in labor economics are larger in print than in life, argues Ricardo Alonzo Fernandez Salguero in a 2025 arXiv synthesis. The work merges reviews of reviews on three linked themes: informal work, minimum wages, and the market power of employers. It asks what drives each theme, what follows from it, and which policies help. One shared model is built to hold all three themes at once.

The advice is to doubt big numbers. Cutting the cost of going formal barely cuts informal work on its own, while enforcement at the edge works better. Job losses from minimum wages stay modest next to the pay gains. Bias in what gets published inflates effects in all three fields, and fixed estimates often sit near zero. The shared model, with mixed firms, employer power, and a free choice of formal status, matches the real patterns well.
arxiv-2509-20865:
Majority voting can cycle in circles unless voters' rankings come from a well-behaved set. Bei Zhou and Klas Markstrom present an algorithm for listing all such sets in a 2025 paper on Condorcet domains. A Condorcet domain guarantees that pairwise majority voting yields a consistent ranking.

Their orderly algorithm generates every non-isomorphic maximal Condorcet domain for a given number of alternatives. Orderly generation avoids producing the same domain twice under renamed options. The method adapts to important subclasses of domains as well. Using their implementation, the authors extend existing enumerations for several subclasses. They release both the data and the code publicly, giving social choice researchers a larger catalog of voting domains to study.
arxiv-2509-20965:
Carbon capture pipelines carry dense carbon dioxide blends that can split into liquid and gas when pressure drops. Pardeep Kumar and Patricio Rosen Esquivel rework the phase math for such flows in a 2025 engineering paper. Safe pipeline design rests on modeling those sudden events well.

Their framework joins a homogeneous equilibrium flow model with an equation of state built on Helmholtz energy. Phase states come from a UVN-flash computation, recast here for two-phase blends with many components. A stability check spots when a blend will split and seeds the flash with good first guesses. The target use is moving carbon dioxide-rich blends, a core part of carbon capture and storage. Getting depressurization right guards pipelines against fast-running cracks and other failures.
arxiv-2509-21065:
A CubeSat mission needs a laser tuned to excite fluorescent quantum light sources, and space is an unforgiving place for optics. Sven Schwertfeger and eight co-authors report building and qualifying such a laser in a 2025 paper. The system emits at a wavelength of six hundred ninety-eight nanometers.

The design uses an external-cavity diode laser, fiber-coupled, with custom driving and thermal management electronics. The team chose the optical and mechanical layout for space compatibility from the start. Off-the-shelf components were put through validation tests for satellite deployment. Everything is integrated into a compact package sized for CubeSat platforms. The manuscript documents a step toward orbiting quantum light experiments, where sources and their excitation lasers must survive launch and vacuum.
arxiv-2509-21865:
Feeding a whole document to a language model is now possible, but it wastes tokens and buries key facts in the middle. Seongwoong Shim, Myunsoo Kim, Jae Hyeon Cho, and Byung-Jun Lee propose a middle path in this 2025 paper, accepted at ICLR 2026. Fetching only some passages, the older approach, risks grabbing text that distracts the model. Their retriever learns to avoid exactly that.

The method, called LDAR, learns to fetch passages in a way that cuts interference from distracting text. It aims for the balance between covering the needed facts and keeping noise out. Across several model designs and six knowledge-heavy benchmarks, LDAR gave higher performance while using fewer tokens than long-context approaches. The results held up across the tests. The authors argue that how a retriever handles distraction matters as much as how much it retrieves.
arxiv-2509-22165:
Eunhee Ko and five co-authors forecast how well a coming sky survey will estimate galaxy distances from colors alone. The 7-Dimensional Sky Survey will image the sky through forty narrow filters, giving rough spectra for huge numbers of objects. From such photometric data, astronomers compute photometric redshifts, which stand in for true distances. Their 2025 paper, accepted by The Astrophysical Journal, builds mock catalogs for the survey's three main programs and tests the estimates with standard software.

The five-year wide survey should give reliable redshifts for bright to moderately faint galaxies, with few catastrophic failures. The medium-band data capture a key spectral break and emission lines well. Adding data from other surveys helps further: near-infrared coverage breaks the confusion between near and far solutions. Combining an all-sky infrared survey with the wide program cut the failure share sharply for faint, distant sources.
arxiv-2509-22265:
Hao Wu and six co-authors simulate how electrons gain energy during a solar eruption, in work accepted by The Astrophysical Journal. When a magnetic flux rope erupts from the Sun, a vast current sheet forms beneath it. Inside that sheet, tearing instabilities spawn many small flux ropes. The team combined high-resolution three-dimensional magnetic simulations with test-particle tracking that follows electrons through the evolving fields.

Electrons get temporarily trapped inside the small ropes, where they accelerate and travel in ways that differ sharply from simpler models. These fine structures proved to be efficient accelerators, beating single reconnection sites and pushing electrons to high energies. Electrons from different ropes follow distinct paths and land on opposite sides of the flare ribbons. The paired bright sources at the ribbons thus come from separate acceleration regions, not one shared field line as previously thought.
arxiv-2509-22465:
Dylan Elliott and 3 co-authors blend a physics weather model with a learned part and test the mix in forecasts. The base model, SPEEDY, solves the core equations of the atmosphere. Reanalysis data stands in for the true sky. The team made fake noisy observations over thirty years for training and one year for testing, then blended them into analyses with an ensemble filter.

In one run the physics model alone made the background forecasts. In three others a hybrid model did, each trained on a different data set. Hybrids improved both analyses and ten-day forecasts. Training on reanalysis gave the cleanest analyses, while other training sets gave larger forecast gains after a few days.
arxiv-2509-22865:
Seda Aslan and 10 co-authors simulate catheter-based repairs of leaking heart valves in an open-source framework. Edge-to-edge repair clips and annuloplasty devices treat mitral regurgitation, but their mechanical interplay is poorly understood. The team modeled four MitraClip geometries in the FEBio finite element solver, with leaflet grasp and clip motion under realistic pressure. Band annuloplasty shrank the ring by boundary displacement; suture annuloplasty used discrete nodal constraints.

Cases covered prolapse and a dilated ring. Clips restored closure in prolapse but raised leaflet stress. In dilation, clips alone left residual leakage, while annuloplasty improved closure. Combined clip and band repair minimized leakage and contact loss, with stress between the single-strategy levels.
arxiv-2509-23165:
Surgeons who thread catheters through vessel trees need maps that keep the traits that matter. Guillaume Houry and 3 co-authors flatten 3D vessel scans into faithful 2D maps. Their maps preserve topology, length, and curvature, the traits navigation depends on. A recursive embedding algorithm keeps the global orientation of the network. Optimized filters prepare the scan in seconds.

Demos cover brain, pelvic, and knee artery networks from real procedures. Clinicians could pick devices with more confidence before and during work. That may cut failure risk and narrow the expert gap between centers. The maps also mimic dissection displays for anatomy study. Code ships in an open Python library.
arxiv-2509-23465:
Finding the shortest tour through many stops is easy to state and hard to solve at scale. Zhuoli Yin and 3 co-authors use vision language models to guide the search in their framework, ViTSP. The model looks at a picture of the tour problem and picks small patches that look promising. A standard solver then polishes those patches, which lifts the whole tour.

No training is needed at the user's end, since the vision model comes pre-trained. On real tours with one thousand to eighty-eight thousand stops, ViTSP left gaps near zero in most cases and beat other learning-based methods. Given equal time, it also beat the strong LKH-3 solver, most clearly on the largest tours.
arxiv-2509-23665:
A model can be accurate yet badly calibrated, stating ninety percent confidence while being right half the time. Kristina P. Sinaga and Arjun S. Nair study post-hoc calibration, the fixes applied after training to align confidence with reality. They analyze two standard fixes, Platt scaling and isotonic regression, with convergence guarantees, cost bounds, and finite-sample measures.

Controlled experiments vary how informative the input features are, from clean signals to spaces padded with noise. Real data sets and several model designs show steady gains in calibration metrics. The authors turn the results into practical guidance for picking a calibration method under given data and compute limits.
arxiv-2509-24365:
One model that both understands and generates images and text is elegant, but the two modes can fight during training. Jitai Hao and 4 co-authors pinpoint gradient conflicts between vision and text in shared transformers, worst in the shallow and deep layers. The clash traces to the different low-level statistics of images and text, while middle layers, where features turn abstract, stay calmer.

Their design, Uni-X, separates the two ends and shares the middle. That X shape removes conflicts at the ends and eases what remains in the shared layers. Scaled up, Uni-X matched or beat larger unified models while scoring strongly on generation and understanding alike.
arxiv-2509-24465:
One-dimensional quantum systems are a bedrock of many-body physics, but carving them from solids leaves disorder and crude confinement. Elie Vandoolaeghe and 8 co-authors report a bottom-up route: such matter emerges at the atomically sharp seam between two monolayer semiconductors. Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, sit pinned to that junction.

Light measurements resolve the excitons into a ladder of discrete states, proof of nanoscale confinement. They carry huge permanent electric dipoles and drift for microns along the seam only. Adding charge collapses the dipole and cuts the light-emission lifetime twentyfold. That live tunability makes lateral seams a platform for one-dimensional excitonic circuits.
arxiv-2510-00665:
Galati, Falcetta, and four co-authors present a multi-domain brain vessel segmentation framework in this paper, published in the journal MELBA in 2025. Tracing the brain's arteries and veins guides treatment of vascular disease, but segmentation models usually work for one scanner type or one vessel kind only. Hospitals differ in machines and protocols, so models often fail when moved. The authors avoid harmonizing the data and instead adapt the model itself.

Their framework disentangles image properties in a latent space, so vessel appearance can be translated between domains while shape and location stay fixed. That label-preserving translation lets one model segment across medical centres, imaging modalities, and vessel types. A semi-supervised design keeps the annotation burden low, and ablation studies probe how few labels suffice. The authors report strong robustness across the varied domain gaps they tested.
arxiv-2510-00765:
Wilson and Jiang report fast, sensitive readout of a semiconductor quantum dot in this 2025 arXiv preprint on quantum devices. Quantum computers based on silicon quantum dots must measure electron charge states quickly and accurately to correct errors in time. Older charge sensors sit beside the dot and can be slow or hard to scale. The authors instead couple a silicon-germanium double quantum dot directly to a niobium microwave resonator built on the same chip.

Their key trick is enlarging the gate lever arm, guided by quantum dot simulations, which strengthens the dispersive signal without exotic high-impedance resonators. The device reached a signal-to-noise ratio of one with an integration time of about thirty-five nanoseconds. Its charge sensitivity ranks among the best reported for such sensors. The same setup also performed noise spectroscopy, exposing low-frequency charge noise in the device.
arxiv-2510-01265:
Hatamizadeh and co-authors at NVIDIA move reinforcement learning from the end of model training into pretraining itself. Today's reasoning models learn by predicting text first and only practice thinking during final polishing. Their objective, RLP, instead rewards a reasoning passage by how much it helps predict what comes next.

Thinking becomes an exploratory action scored by information gain. Models learn to reason for themselves far earlier, as a habit rather than a finish. Gains persisted and compounded after later alignment stages. Compute-matched comparisons across datasets and architectures favored the reinforcement-pretrained models consistently. Chain-of-thought becomes the action, and likelihood gain becomes the reward. Hybrid large models scaled the objective without collapse. Independent thinking is the behavioral target named by the authors. Exploration, long postponed, moves into the foundation phase. Pretraining objectives quietly shape everything downstream of training.
arxiv-2510-01365:
Saberi, Barati Farimani, and Jamali simulate complex fluids with a transformer that learns flow physics instead of solving equations each time. Non-Newtonian fluids remember their history, which makes their mathematics slow and fragile. Retraining for every new condition compounds the cost.

Their model, RheOFormer, uses attention to capture spatial interactions inside viscoelastic and plastic-like flows. Benchmarks against ground-truth solvers covered several named fluid families and tricky geometries. Accuracy held even when training data stayed limited. One trained operator generalizes across conditions that defeat narrower data-driven methods. Scalar and tensor quantities both fall within the model's remit. Giesekus and Oldroyd-B fluids are among the named benchmarks. History dependence is the trait that defeats simple solvers. Neural operators supply the function-space viewpoint behind the design. Thixotropic fluids, which thin under stress, complete the test set. Simulation becomes a query, not a campaign.
arxiv-2510-01465:
D'Alessio, Varsano, Molinari, and Rontani show that exciton condensation helps hold sliding ferroelectricity in place in a two-layer material. Sliding one atomic layer over another flips an electric polarization at tiny energy cost, a trick first seen in tungsten ditelluride bilayers. Standard density-functional calculations understate how stable the polarized state is.

Bound electron-hole pairs renormalize the energy bands substantially in the ground state. Their condensation adds real stabilization energy when the layers slide. The effect should generalize across two-dimensional materials, where screening is weak. Ferroelectric control of quantum phases becomes a richer design space. Van der Waals bonding between layers is what makes sliding cheap. Reduced screening in flat materials strengthens electron-hole attraction. Band renormalization moves the energetics beyond textbook calculations. External fields could switch quantum phases through the dipole. A prototype material carries the general argument.
arxiv-2510-01965:
Yuan and Lu prove how one-way resonances persist as structures change in this 2025 photonics paper. These special modes radiate light to only one side of a periodic structure, even though both sides are open. Any small fabrication error usually breaks that one-way behavior. Finding such modes seemed to demand delicate tuning.

The authors build a strict theory for how these modes depend on parameters. With a single radiation channel, a resonance can persist continuously as one structural parameter varies. The trick is to tune a second parameter that compensates for a generic perturbation. Starting from a bound state in the continuum, one can always generate a whole family of one-way modes this way. That route yields modes with very large quality factors. The proof writes the shifted mode as a power series in the shift size.
arxiv-2510-02165:
Wauyo and four co-authors build a real-time fraud detector for public transit in this 2025 paper. Fare evasion drains transit systems, and manual inspection cannot watch every gate. Their system fuses closed-circuit video with audio from the station environment. A video transformer extracts features from the footage, while an audio spectrogram transformer analyzes sound.

A tensor fusion network combines the two streams, explicitly modeling single-mode and cross-mode interactions. That fusion targets the subtle cues that separate evasion from ordinary crowding. The work comes from a Rwandan deployment context, with the national utilities regulator among the partners. Real-time operation is a design requirement, not an afterthought. Multimodal evidence should cut both missed violations and false accusations against honest riders. The authors frame fairer enforcement as the goal: catch evasion without harassing the compliant. Tensor fusion, proven in sentiment analysis, migrates here to civic infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-02765:
Ninou, Kadmon, and Cayco-Gajic show that learning rules with curl can still optimize, until they cannot. Their 2025 theoretical neuroscience paper questions gradient descent in brains. Artificial networks train by following loss gradients. Real synapses follow many varied plasticity rules. Some mixed rules add a rotational, non-gradient component. Such dynamics optimize no single objective exactly. The authors study feedforward student-teacher networks analytically. Flipping the sign of plasticity in some neurons injects curl. Small curl leaves the solution manifold stable. Learning then looks much like gradient descent.

Past a critical curl strength, behavior changes sharply. Rotational flow starts to dominate the dynamics. The paper maps where that threshold lies. Excitatory and inhibitory wiring naturally breeds such terms. Brains may exploit curl rather than avoid it. The result reframes what counts as learning machinery. Non-gradient paths deserve study as features, not noise.
arxiv-2510-02965:
Dosti, Vorobyov, and Charalambous speed up a core task in optimization. Many data jobs minimize a cost built from two parts. One part is smooth, and one part is rough or kinked. Such composite costs are convex, like a bowl with a crease. First-order methods use gradient steps to descend the bowl. Their design tool is the estimating sequence, a chain of bounds. The team widens that tool with memory of past steps.

The new sequences reuse facts stored in earlier iterates. A fresh accelerated method grows out of them. It finds its own step size through backtracking search. No exact knowledge of the cost's smoothness is required. The method also shrugs off a wrong guess of strong convexity. Tests on fake and real data sets followed. The method beat standard rivals in speed and reliability.
arxiv-2510-03165:
Tenison, Murphy, Beauville, and Kagal bring federated learning to tiny edge devices. Federated learning trains one model across many devices in place. Raw data never leaves the device that holds it. Small gadgets, though, lack memory, power, and bandwidth to spare. Slow stragglers also drag down classic training rounds. Their engine, FTTE, answers with a semi-asynchronous design. Only sparse slices of the model cross the wire.

Server aggregation weighs each update by age and variance. Stale or wild updates thus count for less. Tests spanned many models and skewed data splits. Networks reached five hundred clients in the trials. Nine in ten clients could lag without breaking training. Convergence ran far faster than the synchronous baseline. On-device memory fell by about four fifths. Message sizes shrank by roughly two thirds. Accuracy matched or beat a leading semi-asynchronous rival.
arxiv-2510-03865:
Deng and colleagues at Westlake University wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on why reinforcement learning can cap a language model's reasoning. Training with checkable rewards improves math problem solving at first. Yet with many attempts allowed, trained models often lose their edge over their base model. The authors blame the usual penalty term, which keeps the model in familiar territory and blocks exploration.

Their algorithm, RAPO, swaps that penalty for one that rewards stepping outside the base model's comfort zone. It also reweights the reference model to encourage smart exploration within familiar ground. They trained two sizes of the Qwen2.5 model on a small math dataset with no supervised fine-tuning. RAPO improved scores on two AIME competition benchmarks at every sampling budget. Trained models even solved problems that the base model never could. The results suggest exploration, not just reward, drives reasoning gains.
arxiv-2510-03965:
Shu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper with a new public dataset for predicting corporate earnings surprises. An earnings surprise, when reported profit beats or misses market expectations, often moves a company's stock price. Research on predicting surprises has relied on costly, private, text-only data. The authors release a large open alternative built from real earnings calls.

Their dataset, FinCall-Surprise, covers more than twenty-six hundred calls from 2019 to 2021. Each call includes a word-level transcript, the full audio recording, and the presentation slides. The team benchmarked twenty-six leading language models, both text-only and multimodal, on the data. Many models looked accurate only because positive surprises dominate the real data, a class imbalance trap. Adding audio and slides helped only modestly, since models still fuse the signals poorly. The dataset sets a harder, fairer test for financial prediction research.
arxiv-2510-04265:
Hariri and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper arguing that the popular Pass-at-k metric for grading language models should be retired. Pass-at-k reports whether any of k samples solves a problem, but with few trials it produces unstable, misleading rankings. The authors replace it with a Bayesian framework estimating each model's underlying success probability. Evaluation outcomes are modeled as categorical with a Dirichlet prior, yielding closed-form posterior means and credible intervals.

Under a uniform prior, the posterior mean turns out order-equivalent to average accuracy, explaining that metric's robustness while adding honest uncertainty. Simulations with known ground truth and real results from AIME, HMMT, and BrUMO competitions showed faster convergence and stabler rankings than Pass-at-k variants. Non-overlapping credible intervals supply a transparent rule for when a gap is real. Reliable rankings at small sample counts save the community substantial evaluation compute.
arxiv-2510-04465:
Zhiping Zhang and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a tension inside AI agents that act for users. An agent needs personal data to tailor its work, yet using that data can feel invasive. How much freedom the agent has may change that balance. The team ran a controlled experiment with 450 participants. Each person used an agent set to one level of personalization and one level of autonomy.

Personalization that ignored privacy wishes raised concern and lowered trust in the agent. It also lowered the wish to keep using the agent. Autonomy changed the strength of those effects in a surprising way. A middle level of autonomy, where the agent checks before sending sensitive content, flattened the harm. Full autonomy and no autonomy both let the harm grow larger. Giving users the right amount of control may matter as much.
arxiv-2510-04565:
Borkovits and a large team of coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on ten studied triple star systems. Each system holds a close pair of stars orbited by a third star, and all three eclipse in turn. Data from the TESS space telescope revealed more than a hundred such systems. The tightest of them complete an outer orbit in under about one hundred days. Those ultracompact triples let astronomers pin down masses and orbits with rare precision.

The team combined eclipse timing curves, light curves, and energy distributions in one photodynamical study. Ground telescopes added data for two of the systems. Outer periods ran from about 47 to about 101 days across the ten. Four systems showed fast apsidal motion forced by the third star. One system was a double twin, with both inner and outer mass ratios near one. All ten systems were nearly flat, with orbit planes tilted by under five degrees.
arxiv-2510-04665:
Eva Sciacca and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on interactive visualization for astronomy data. Telescopes and simulations now produce petabytes of data, far beyond what a laptop can explore. The team wired the VisIVO visualization framework into a supercomputing service at Cineca in Italy. Astronomers reach graphics enabled compute nodes through browser based notebooks. Custom Python wrappers and notebooks hide the machinery of the cluster.

The setup lets a user load a simulation and shape three dimensional views on the fly. Test cases used galaxy formation runs from the GADGET code to show the workflow. Views of the large scale structure of the universe rendered inside the same gateway where analysis runs. That closeness cuts the loop of downloading data, rendering offline, and uploading results. Reproducibility improves because the notebooks record each step of the session. Science gateways of this kind aim to give domain tools the power of infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-05065:
Kumar Abhinav, Partha Guha, and Indranil Mukherjee explain a curious near-conservation law in this 2025 arXiv paper. Some wave equations are integrable, meaning they conserve infinitely many charges exactly. Slightly deforming such an equation usually breaks that magic. Yet in these deformed models, many charges still come back to conservation over long times.

The authors trace that behavior to PT symmetry, the combined flip of space and time. In the PT-symmetric phase, the deformed system's Lax pair has definite symmetry properties. Those properties force the anomalous parts of the charges to cancel asymptotically. The construction covers deformed KdV, nonlinear Schrödinger, and nonlocal Schrödinger systems. It turns an observed pattern into a general mechanism.
arxiv-2510-05365:
Irtaza Sajid Qureshi and Zhen Ming Jiang grade how language models turn bug reports into tests in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generating a reproducing test from a prose bug report is a key software task. The authors organize the evaluation around Bloom's taxonomy of cognitive skills. Its layers run from Remember up through Create, probing ever deeper reasoning.

They tested StarCoder and GPT-4o on Defects4J and GHRB benchmarks, plus mutated variants. Both models mostly reproduced prior results with minor deviations. Rephrasings and translations were handled with partial robustness, sometimes surfacing new reproducible bugs. Identifier mutations, though, cut success by more than 60 percent. Near-identical worked examples in an open-book setting tripled success rates, exposing reliance on surface cues.
arxiv-2510-05465:
Gupta and colleagues built a benchmark that asks a deeper question about language models. Safety tests usually check whether a model refuses banned requests or avoids toxic text. Those tests say little about whether a model holds steady values on public debates. Their 2025 benchmark, VAL-Bench, measures that steadiness directly.

The set holds 115,000 prompt pairs drawn from contested sections of Wikipedia. Each pair frames the same issue from opposing sides. A judge model then scores how much the two answers agree in stance. A steady model keeps one view, while a shaky model flips with the framing. Claude models scored nearly three times higher than GPT models on this measure. Across leading models, scores varied widely, and refusal-heavy models often dodged value questions entirely. The authors offer the benchmark as a shared tool for tracking value consistency over time.
arxiv-2510-05865:
Baraldi and colleagues review the safety of world models for embodied agents. World models let robots and self-driving cars predict future environmental states. Those predictions guide planning, so unsafe predictions become unsafe actions. Their 2025 review covers autonomous driving and robotics with safety center stage.

The authors collect predictions from state-of-the-art models and inspect them empirically. Common failure modes are identified and categorized as pathologies. Quantitative evaluation then measures how often each pathology occurs. Scene generation and control generation each get dedicated safety criteria. The taxonomy gives evaluators a shared vocabulary for unsafe generations. Physical conformity and traffic adherence remain weakly measured so far. Generated futures must respect physics intrinsically, not by prompting tricks. Self-improving methods are flagged as a promising repair direction. Safety certification for deployed agents is the end goal.
arxiv-2510-06165:
Butler, Feng, and Djuric build a theory of higher-order feature attribution in a 2025 machine learning paper. Attribution methods estimate how each input feature pushes a model's prediction. That reading is clear when features act independently, but it blurs when features interact.

They develop the theory on Integrated Gradients, a widely used attribution method. Extending it to higher orders credits combinations of features, not just single inputs. They uncover natural connections to statistics and to topological signal processing. Several theoretical results establish the framework, validated on a few examples. The payoff is a principled way to explain models driven by feature interactions. Interactions are common in real data, so single-feature explanations often mislead. A shared theory lets explainable AI, statistics, and signal processing borrow each other's tools.
arxiv-2510-06365:
Kettinger classifies quasi-elliptic surfaces in characteristics two and three, settling questions about unexpected plane cubics in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. Quasi-elliptic fibrations exist only in these small characteristics, where elliptic geometry behaves exceptionally. A complete inventory of such surfaces had been missing.

Kettinger categorizes every isomorphism class of quasi-elliptic surfaces in characteristic two or three. For each surface, all blow-down sequences to the projective plane are classified. Those categorizations drive the second result. Every unexpected plane cubic in characteristic two is identified explicitly. In characteristic three, he proves no unexpected cubics exist. The blow-down census is the engine that makes the cubic classification possible. Both questions were open before this work, based partly on his thesis. Unexpected curves violate naive dimension counts in interpolation problems. Closing the classification removes a stubborn gap in the theory.
arxiv-2510-06465:
Sterzinger, Kosmids, and Moustaki build a softly penalised likelihood method curing Heywood cases in factor analysis in a 2025 statistics paper. Exploratory factor analysis often returns boundary estimates. These Heywood cases show non-positive variances and break the fitting search. They mislead judgments about factor scores and model choice.

The authors derive the needed conditions on model and penalty. Under them, penalised estimates exist inside the allowed range. The results keep consistency and asymptotic normality. The key point is softness: the penalty adapts as information builds up. The paper first proves that two classical penalties meet the needed conditions. They come from Akaike and from Hirose and co-authors. Their vanilla versions can go wrong in finite samples, so the method adjusts them with care. Proper scaling keeps penalties strong enough to repel boundary estimates yet tiny in the large-sample limit. Tests and real datasets confirm good finite-sample results.
arxiv-2510-06665:
Michael Wurm and colleagues test a recipe for loading a neutrino detector liquid with tellurium. Their 2025 paper supports the hunt for neutrinoless double beta decay, a rare nuclear event. Seeing it would reshape our picture of neutrinos. One promising route is to dissolve a candidate isotope into a detector's liquid scintillator.

The team used the high-grade scintillator liquid from the Borexino detector as their base. They loaded it with tellurium compounds called Te-diols at several concentrations. A new water-free synthesis, done at room temperature in a non-acidic setting, made the loading possible. The loaded liquid kept nearly the same glow spectrum and transparency as the pure liquid. Light output dropped only moderately, reaching about 8,400 photons per unit of deposited energy at one percent loading. Light pulses from alpha particles also became faster as tellurium rose. Those traits matter for spotting the rare decay signal.
arxiv-2510-06965:
Bryan Christ, Penelope Molitz, Jonathan Kropko, and Thomas Hartvigsen enlist language models to write math word problems for classrooms. Their 2025 paper presents EDUMATH, a system for generating problems aligned with education standards. Word problems work better when tuned to a student's interests and level. Teachers rarely have time to customize them for every child.

The team evaluated over eleven thousand generated problems with a human and model judging process. That produced the first teacher-annotated dataset for this task. A compact twelve-billion-parameter model trained on it matched larger open models. A classifier trained on the same data let a thirty-billion model beat closed commercial baselines. Its problems read more like human-written ones. The researchers then ran the first classroom study of customized generated problems. Students performed about as well with them as with standard materials. Released annotations should help others build classroom-ready generators.
arxiv-2510-07065:
Ajinkya Gaikwad, a single author, maps the difficulty of pruning a network into tight clusters. The 2025 paper studies s-Club Cluster Edge Deletion in computer science. The task is deleting few edges so every remaining cluster has small diameter. The diameter cap, called s, controls how spread out each cluster may be.

For s equal to one, the problem is easy, and for three it is trivial. Gaikwad proves the in-between case, s equal to two, is NP-hard even on split graphs. That closes the complexity gap for the problem. He designs a kernel for that hard case, the first known. An open question from 2023 falls as a side result. The problem is hard when measured by pathwidth, so the diameter bound looks essential there. Under other measures, like neighbourhood diversity, the problem becomes tractable again. The paper draws a map of where the boundary lies.
arxiv-2510-07165:
Santos and Boschi-Filho build a model of a superconducting junction using gravity theory. Their 2025 paper works inside Horndeski gravity, an extended theory with an extra scalar field. A Josephson junction links two superconductors through a weak bridge. Current flows across it without voltage, guided by a phase gap. The authors describe such junctions through a hologram-like match between a gravity world and a material system.

Two junction types are studied: a pinched constriction and a normal-metal bridge. Below a critical temperature, a charged condensate forms in a smooth phase shift. The condensate turns out to consist of pairs of quasiparticles. The gravity theory's settings tune how much supercurrent the junction carries. The current follows the classic Josephson relation between current and phase. The work shows how gravity tools can mirror quantum material behavior. That mirror may guide later work on exotic superconductors.
arxiv-2510-07465:
Wang and co-authors grow ultrathin films of a magnetic garnet whose internal compass can be tuned to order. Their 2025 paper concerns bismuth-substituted yttrium iron garnet, a material prized for spin-wave devices. The team deposited nanometer-thick films by high-temperature sputtering onto garnet substrates of several kinds. Strain from the substrate, stretching or squeezing the film, proved a precise control knob. Films stayed fully strained and defect-free up to sixty nanometers thick despite lattice mismatches near one percent. Microscopy and chemical mapping confirmed clean, coherent growth with little mixing at the interface.

By choosing strain between compression and tension, the team exactly canceled the film's total magnetic anisotropy. Deposition angle and oxygen flow offered further tuning through the film's chemistry. Optimized films showed a resonance linewidth of one millitesla at ten gigahertz even at ten nanometers thick.
arxiv-2510-08165:
Tambovtsev, Kristinsson, and Jónsson wrote this 2025 computational chemistry paper on how chlorine substitutions change light-driven molecular motors. These second-generation motors rotate in steps powered by light and heat. Chemists tune them by swapping atoms at the stereogenic center. Fluorine substitutions had been studied, but chlorine never had. The authors computed effects for five well-characterized base molecules, comparing two chlorine swaps at the center.

The trichloromethyl swap sped rotation up, more than the fluorine equivalent did. Extra bulk destabilizes the metastable state, shortening its lifetime before the thermal inversion step. It also widened the separation between the isomers' absorption peaks, easing selective activation. The single chlorine swap backfired. It flipped which isomer is more stable and raised the barrier above the backward one, quenching rotation. The same element, placed differently, either upgrades the motor or stops it.
arxiv-2510-08265:
Rafael Costa and co-authors work out how to define work for quantum fields in curved space in a 2025 arXiv paper. Work distributions track the spread of energy changes in small systems. In relativity, the usual two-measurement scheme for work breaks down for quantum fields. The team instead uses Unruh-DeWitt detectors, small devices that click when they absorb field energy.

They extend a Ramsey-style protocol, first built for flat space, to static curved spacetimes. From it they derive an exact formula for the field's characteristic function, which encodes the work spread. For heat-bath states, the resulting distributions obey the Crooks theorem and the Jarzynski equality. These are two core laws linking work, heat, and free energy. For a pointlike detector, they get compact formulas for the first two moments. At high heat, the classic fluctuation-dissipation relation comes back as expected.
arxiv-2510-08365:
Yukai Song and co-authors design a two-stage system to detect suicide risk in social media posts, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many at-risk people avoid formal help yet share distress online, often in indirect ways. Metaphor, sarcasm, and subtle cues hide much suicidal ideation from simple tools. Light models catch blunt signals cheaply, while large models read nuance at high cost.

Stage one uses a lightweight BERT classifier to settle clear, high-confidence cases fast. Stage two sends ambiguous posts to one of two paths. One path runs a multi-perspective large-model vote to maximize recall on hidden ideation. The other uses an ensemble fed with psychological indicators that large models extract as structured features. On explicit-heavy Reddit data the system reached an F1 score of 98.0 percent, and it hit 99.7 percent on an implicit-only data set.
arxiv-2510-08565:
Changyao Tian and a large team rethink how multimodal language models should be trained from scratch in a 2025 arXiv paper. Standard models bolt a pretrained vision encoder onto a pretrained language model, then train the seam between them. This compositional habit makes scaling behavior hard to study, since parts train separately. The team instead explores native end-to-end training under realistic data constraints.

Through careful study of design choices, they identify a meta-architecture balancing performance and training cost. They then map how native models scale, finding visual encoder and language model sizes should grow together in positive correlation. Their model, NaViL, pairs this architecture with a simple, cost-effective training recipe. On fourteen multimodal benchmarks, NaViL performed competitively against existing models. The authors offer their findings as guidance for future native multimodal model design.
arxiv-2510-08765:
Amiri and Amiri propose a lean way to locate a signal source in three dimensions, in this 2025 arXiv letter on wireless networks. Their setting is the Internet of Things, where many small devices need to know where a signal comes from and towers may be scarce. The method needs only two measurements. One is the gap in arrival times at two receivers, and the other is the direction the signal arrives from.

A single ground station plus a drone that relays the signal supply both measurements. The authors turn the geometry into a closed-form weighted least squares estimate, which is a formula that balances the errors in each measurement. Tests and analysis show the estimate nearly reaches the best accuracy that theory allows when noise is moderate. The small measurement count makes the scheme cheap to run on limited hardware.
arxiv-2510-08965:
Xuan, Chen, and Li improve the search for the best design in problems with very many knobs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Bayesian optimization guides such searches by learning a stand-in model of the costly true objective. In high dimensions the stand-in starves for data. A popular remedy compresses designs into a small latent space with an autoencoder, but rebuilding designs faithfully does not guarantee the objective behaves the same in latent space.

The authors first pin down why reconstruction-only training causes that mismatch between the two spaces. Their framework, HiBBO, then builds consistency between the spaces into the compression itself. It borrows HiPPO, a method designed to remember long sequences, to shape a latent space whose geometry respects the original. On high-dimensional benchmarks, it converged faster and landed better solutions than rival autoencoder approaches. The authors point to uses in architecture search and materials design.
arxiv-2510-09065:
Takahashi and co-authors teach a video-to-audio generator a second career as a sound separator, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Given a video or text query, the model pulls out just the sound the query names. Dedicated separators usually train from scratch, discarding the rich knowledge inside large pretrained audio generators. This team instead fine-tunes such a generator, trusting what it already learned about how sights and words map to sounds.

Their model, MMAudioSep, was compared against existing separators of both classic signal-processing style and generative style. It beat the baselines on separation quality. Notably, the fine-tuning did not overwrite the original talent: the model could still generate audio for a video from scratch. They present this as evidence that foundation sound models can be retreaded for downstream listening tasks. The work comes from Sony research groups.
arxiv-2510-09165:
Hernández-Díaz and colleagues mine the TESS planet-hunting telescope's sky survey for the orbital periods of magnetic vampire stars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A polar is a binary where a white dwarf's strong magnetism funnels gas from a companion star. Knowing each pair's orbital period confirms candidates and reveals their evolutionary state. The team searched TESS light curves, month-long brightness records, for ninety-five polars with four period-hunting methods.

Eighty-five systems gave periods matching published values, confirming the approach. Four asynchronous polars, whose white dwarfs spin out of step with the orbit, showed the orbital period, the spin period, and their beat frequencies separately resolved. Four systems disagreed with earlier claims and two were too noisy to measure. The team also mapped how noise grows with faintness and built a reliability framework. Their warning: beyond roughly magnitude seventeen, TESS period detections grow unreliable.
arxiv-2510-09365:
Valentin Biller and six co-authors present a generative model for brain tumour images in a 2025 arXiv paper. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scans are central to brain care, and filling in missing or damaged regions is called inpainting. The team's model is guided by voxel-level tumour concentrations, meaning a number for each tiny cube of the scan that says how much tumour it holds.

Their latent diffusion model also reads tissue maps, and it produces three-dimensional scans that stay coherent and anatomically plausible. Setting the tumour values to zero turns the same model toward restoring healthy tissue, the task set by the BraTS 2025 inpainting challenge. The authors report quality scores of eighteen point five for healthy tissue restoration and seventeen point four for tumour inpainting. They release their code so other groups can build on the approach.
arxiv-2510-09565:
Rajath Radhakrishnan, Adar Sharon, and Nathanan Tantivasadakarn recast a new kind of quantum error correction in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dynamical stabilizer codes replace the fixed check group of a static code with a sequence of measurements that do not commute. The moving structure opens new routes to fault tolerance, but errors must now be tracked across space and time together.

The authors map the measurement sequences of these codes onto non-invertible symmetries in a gauge theory with four space axes plus time. The sequences become fusions of the symmetry operators. Error detectors correspond to surface operators that can end, and their endpoints define line operators. Detectable errors are exactly the surfaces that braid in a linked way with those lines. The framework also recovers, in a natural way, the spacetime stabilizer code linked to each dynamical code, giving the area firm physical footing.
arxiv-2510-09665:
Yuhan Liu and ten co-authors present LMCache in a 2025 arXiv paper, a system for storing the memory of large language models outside the graphics processor. During generation, models keep a key-value cache that speeds decoding, traditionally held in scarce GPU memory. Reusing that cache across queries and engines requires moving it off the device, and the team's usage statistics show stored cache volumes growing far beyond GPU capacity.

LMCache extracts caches from modern engines such as vLLM and SGLang, stores them across processor, storage, and network layers, and shares them between engines and queries. Its speed comes from batched, pipelined data movement, a modular connector decoupling it from fast-changing engines, and a flexible control interface. Combined with vLLM, it improved throughput up to fifteenfold on workloads like multi-round question answering and document tasks. The system is open source and already widely adopted.
arxiv-2510-09865:
Fredy Maglorio Sobrado Suárez and co-authors analyze a model of double-walled carbon nanotubes in this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics. A double-walled nanotube has one tube nested inside another. The authors model the pair as two Timoshenko beams, a beam theory that counts both bending and shear, coupled by the van der Waals force between the walls.

Their study concerns analyticity, a strong smoothness property of the solutions over time that also implies the system settles in a well-behaved way. The model adds Kelvin-Voigt damping, friction tied to the rate of strain, plus an intermediate damping term. The authors examine under what conditions the coupled beam system keeps this analyticity. The question matters because damping choices decide whether vibration energy fades smoothly.
arxiv-2510-09965:
Zhao and co-authors study state aggregation in Markov decision processes in this 2025 arXiv paper on reinforcement learning theory. Aggregation groups similar states together to shrink a decision problem. The catch is that a policy tuned on the grouped problem must still perform best on the original one, a property called optimal policy equivalence.

The authors use homomorphic mappings, maps between decision processes that preserve their reward and transition structure. Such maps give a principled way to merge states without losing value. Their work ties the mapping view to the equivalence property, showing when solving the smaller problem is guaranteed to solve the real one. That guarantee is what makes aggregation safe to use in large problems.
arxiv-2510-10065:
Higgins, James Liley, and Eilidh Cowan calibrate answer probabilities in verbal autopsies in this 2025 arXiv working paper in global health statistics. Across most of the world, causes of death go unrecorded. Verbal autopsies interview people close to the deceased and estimate the likelihood of each cause.

Those estimates rest on a probbase, a table giving how often each interview answer occurs for each cause of death. If the table's probabilities are miscalibrated, the cause estimates inherit the error. The authors study how to calibrate the answer probabilities so the final likelihoods can be trusted. Better calibration improves the cause-of-death statistics that health policy in low-resource settings depends on.
arxiv-2510-10265:
Lin and co-authors defend language models against backdoor attacks in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI security. Backdoors are hidden triggers planted in a model, often through public checkpoints, that make it misbehave on cue. Existing defenses assume things about the trigger that real attackers need not respect.

The authors propose Locphylax, a defense that needs no prior knowledge of the trigger. It works by aggregating known backdoors, using studied attacks to expose and remove unknown ones, an approach they call backdoor collapse. Removing the need for trigger assumptions makes the defense usable on models pulled from public hubs. The work targets the supply chain risk of shared model checkpoints.
arxiv-2510-10365:
Jiang and co-authors present PointMAC in this 2025 arXiv paper on 3D perception. Point cloud completion fills in missing parts of a scanned object, a core skill for robotics and augmented reality. Existing models infer once, statically, and lean on biases learned in training, so novel shapes and sensor distortions at test time trip them up.

PointMAC adapts at test time through meta-learning, training that prepares a model to adjust quickly. The method updates itself on each new input to stay robust against unfamiliar structures and noise. Safety-critical uses cannot retrain in the field, so a model that safely self-adjusts is valuable. The authors aim for completion that degrades gracefully outside its training distribution.
arxiv-2510-10565:
Pankaj K Jha and four co-authors report beating a classic precision limit of light based measurement, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The standard quantum limit, also called the shot noise limit, says how much the quantum flicker of light blurs a phase measurement. In a Mach-Zehnder interferometer fed with ordinary laser light, that limit ties the phase uncertainty to the average photon count. The team changes the inputs to do better.

They feed the interferometer a single photon added coherent state together with a weak coherent state. Working in the low photon regime, with fewer than ten photons on average, they demonstrate phase sensitivity beyond the standard limit. Many rival schemes need large photon numbers, so succeeding in this faint light regime is the point. The authors argue this opens a path to sensitive devices for quantum sensing and spectroscopy where light must stay faint.
arxiv-2510-10865:
Ahmed Alanazi, Duy Ho, and Yugyung Lee present a unified framework for robots navigating cluttered, changing spaces, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such robots must combine perception, symbolic reasoning, and spatial planning, and generalize across layouts and object types. Existing methods lean on static priors or thin memory, which limits adaptation when views are partial and meanings ambiguous. Their framework, GRIP, builds dynamic 2D grids and plans symbolically over them.

GRIP comes in three variants. The lightweight version optimizes symbolic navigation on semantic occupancy grids. The full version adds multi hop anchor chaining and language model introspection. A real world version targets physical deployment under perceptual uncertainty. The system grounds open vocabulary objects and plans with object co-occurrence in mind. On AI2-THOR and RoboTHOR benchmarks, GRIP gained up to 9.6 percent in success rate and more than doubled path efficiency on long horizon tasks.
arxiv-2510-11165:
The ALICE experiment at CERN controls its detectors through a framework called ALFRED, but its new Fast Interaction Trigger detector speaks a different protocol. Franciszek Urbanski describes the fix in this 2025 arXiv instrumentation paper. The trigger electronics use the IPbus protocol, which clashes with the GBT-based slow-control protocols that ALFRED currently supports, and the detector must run without firmware changes.

Urbanski built a bridge layer named ALF IPbus, written in C++ and linked with DIM services, that converts SWT frames into IPbus transactions. Benchmark tests showed median execution times below 4.2 microseconds per frame for sequences above 512 words, comfortably meeting the control system requirements of the experiment. Long-term stability tests in the FV0 detector reached uptime close to 100 percent from implementation onward. The same bridging approach can serve other ALICE subdetectors and similar experiments.
arxiv-2510-11565:
Labeling a 3D point cloud by hand is slow, so interactive tools let an annotator click a few points, or type a phrase, and receive a segment. Aniket Gupta and co-authors unify those interactions in one model, SNAP, in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Earlier tools were confined to a single domain, indoor or outdoor, and a single prompt type, and training one model on many datasets hurt through negative transfer between domains.

SNAP trains on seven datasets spanning indoor, outdoor, and aerial environments, using domain-adaptive normalization to prevent that negative transfer. For text prompts it automatically generates mask proposals with no human help and matches them against CLIP embeddings, covering both panoptic and open-vocabulary segmentation. In experiments the model reached state-of-the-art results on eight of nine zero-shot benchmarks for click-based segmentation and stayed competitive on all five text-prompted benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-11865:
Nathan Chen and David Yang study what small shapes can live inside a curved surface. In algebraic geometry, a hypersurface is a shape cut out by one equation in projective space. Take a general such surface of high degree, meaning a generic, twisty one. Which subvarieties, smaller shapes sitting inside it, can have small degree? Their 2025 arXiv note shows the answer is: only the obvious ones.

The first theorem handles subvarieties of degree up to the surface's degree plus two. Any such shape must have exactly the surface's degree. Moreover, it must arise by slicing the surface with a flat linear space. A second theorem loosens the bound to a fixed multiple of the degree. Then every small subvariety still comes from intersecting the surface with another variety, and its degree must be a whole multiple of the surface's degree. The results answer an earlier question for hypersurfaces.
arxiv-2510-11965:
Ouri Karni, Chirag Vaswani, and Thibault Chervy solve the problem of peeking inside an optical cavity without slowing it down. High-finesse cavities trap light for a long time, which strengthens light-matter interaction but makes the stored light hard to read quickly. Their 2025 arXiv paper demonstrates an ultrafast gating scheme inside a microcavity built with a thin film of lithium niobate, a nonlinear crystal.

A femtosecond gate pulse slips through the cavity mirrors, which are transparent at its color. Inside, it up-converts the stored field by sum-frequency generation, and the converted light exits as one short snapshot pulse. The team tracked several resonant modes ringing inside a plano-concave mirror cavity, and the snapshots matched analytical models closely. Running the process backward by difference-frequency generation also loaded cavity modes within femtoseconds. The scheme works at low temperatures, opening real-time control for quantum light storage experiments.
arxiv-2510-12165:
Butkovsky presents lecture notes from a mini course on stochastic sewing, given at Edinburgh and Beijing in 2025 and posted on arXiv. Stochastic sewing is a technique for building solutions to equations driven by noise by stitching together many small local approximations. The notes aim to introduce the method to researchers in stochastic analysis, the branch of mathematics that studies random processes.

The lectures show how sewing handles several hard problems in the field. These include regularization by noise, where added randomness makes an equation with bad coefficients solvable after all. They also cover well posedness for stochastic partial differential equations with irregular drift, a study of averaging operators and local time, and the analysis of numeric algorithms. Worked applications run through the notes so readers can see the technique in action rather than only its abstract form.
arxiv-2510-12365:
Avrachenkov and Bobu study how to find a hidden clique, a fully connected group, planted inside a random geometric graph, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. In geometric graphs, vertices are points in space and edges link near neighbors. A planted clique is an anomaly hidden in that random structure, and finding it matters for anomaly detection.

The authors compare two algorithms. One uses vertex degrees, counting each vertex's neighbors, and the other uses common neighbors shared by pairs. They analyze both across regimes set by average degree and clique size. Exact recovery holds with high probability as the graph grows, in a specific parameter range. The common neighbor method greatly outperformed the degree method. In the connectivity regime it could identify even tiny planted cliques, down to a single edge. Simulations confirmed both algorithms work in practice, with the common neighbor approach clearly stronger.
arxiv-2510-12665:
Rivasseau argues that the way Facebook upgrades its password hashing quietly weakens the security of stored passwords, and shows an exploit, in a 2025 arXiv computer security paper. Password hashing protects stored credentials so a database leak does not directly reveal passwords. Platforms periodically upgrade hash algorithms to keep up with norms, sometimes chaining hashes together to save cost rather than rehashing from scratch.

Meta's scheme for its services, used by several billion monthly users, is presented as a case where such an ad hoc upgrade introduced unforeseen vulnerabilities. Rivasseau presents what he describes as the first concrete exploit demonstrating the weakness of Facebook's password storage scheme and discusses its implications for large scale credential storage. The paper states that proper ethical disclosure guidelines plus vendor notification were followed before publication. The work is a warning that composing standard components can degrade security even when each component is sound.
arxiv-2510-12865:
Jin and Rhee test which neural network designs best infer cosmological density parameters in this 2025 arXiv paper. The targets are today's matter and dark energy densities, normally estimated from the universe's expansion history with slow statistical sampling methods. Building on an earlier approach called ParamANN, the authors ask whether the best architecture depends on how noisy the expansion data are.

They generated synthetic expansion curves from the first Friedmann equation, then added realistic noise at high, normal, and low signal levels modeled on forty-seven real observations. A bidirectional recurrent network performed best on cleaner data across four metrics, while a convolution-recurrent hybrid using gated units won on the noisiest data. All their networks agreed with the earlier approach, though most differed significantly from the Planck satellite's traditional results.
arxiv-2510-13065:
Bagirov and co-authors introduce absolute indices for judging clusters in this 2025 arXiv paper. Clustering algorithms group data points, but different methods disagree, and the usual validity indices are only relative: they compare one clustering against another rather than certifying quality outright. Their success also depends heavily on the data's structure, which makes choosing the true number of clusters unreliable.

The new indices measure compactness and separability on an absolute scale. A compactness function scores each cluster and the whole distribution, while sets of neighboring points between cluster pairs define margins that quantify separation. Combining both sides lets the method identify the true number of clusters directly. The authors tested the indices on synthetic and real-world datasets and compared them against widely used validity indices, reporting stronger performance at recovering the intended cluster counts.
arxiv-2510-13165:
Chen and Yin complete the basic theory of the fifth-order Camassa-Holm model in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The model generalizes the famous shallow water wave equation with two length parameters, and earlier papers had established only partial results on when its solutions exist and behave well. The authors treat the initial value problem in function spaces built from frequency decompositions.

First they improve the known local well-posedness results, tightening the conditions under which solutions exist, are unique, and depend continuously on their starting profiles. Next they give blow-up criteria and, complementing them, conditions guaranteeing solutions exist for all time. Finally, at a special parameter value, they prove ill-posedness in two Besov spaces through norm inflation, where arbitrarily small starting data can produce disproportionately large responses. The three parts together delimit the model's good and bad regimes.
arxiv-2510-13765:
Garg classifies type Ia supernovae from light curves with an interpretable gradient-boosting model tuned by Bayesian search. This 2025 arXiv paper serves cosmology, where type Ia explosions act as standard candles for measuring the universe. Telling them apart from other supernovae using brightness alone is hard. Classes are lopsided and deep learning rivals are heavy and opaque.

The model trains on the Supernova Photometric Classification Challenge set of over twenty-one thousand events. Non-Ia events outnumber Ia ones by more than three to one there. Garg stresses precision-recall area and F1 scores over plain accuracy for such skewed data. The tuned XGBoost ensemble scored 0.993 in precision-recall area and 0.923 in F1 score on the challenge data, rivalling deep networks while using far fewer resources. Balanced errors mean spectroscopic follow-up time gets spent more wisely. The approach suits the coming LSST survey's flood of events.
arxiv-2510-13865:
Lee, Lee, and Kwak revive the classical edge filter inside deep networks, high-pass filtering the features rather than the inputs. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests a hypothesis about where networks store what they learn. Task-relevant meaning, they propose, rides in high-frequency parts of deep features. Domain-specific bias accumulates in the low-frequency parts instead.

The Deep Edge Filter subtracts a low-pass filtered copy from each feature map. What remains is the high-frequency, supposedly generalizable component of the representation. The host architecture stays untouched, keeping the method easy to bolt on. Experiments span vision, text, three-dimensional data, and audio tasks. Performance improved consistently across all those domains and model types. Analysis shows the filtering sparsifies features as predicted by the hypothesis. The authors frame handcrafted signal processing as a complement, not a relic, in deep learning.
arxiv-2510-14065:
Gaoyuan Liu and co-authors merge reinforcement learning skills into task and motion planning, the robotics method that sequences symbolic actions and computes the motions to execute them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Planners handle deterministic actions well, but actions with uncertain outcomes remain a challenge, while reinforcement learning produces versatile short-horizon manipulation skills that cope with uncertainty yet lack long-horizon reasoning.

Their method defines each learned skill not only by its policy but also by data-driven logical components, so a symbolic planner can deploy it like any other action. A plan refinement subroutine then handles the inevitable effects of uncertainty during execution. In experiments, they compare against baselines from both the planning and reinforcement learning fields. Embedding learned skills extended the planner's reach to domains with probabilistic skills and improved planning efficiency over previous methods. The hybrid inherits the strengths of both traditions.
arxiv-2510-14265:
Xukai Wang and co-authors propose MorphoBench, a reasoning benchmark whose difficulty adapts to the models being tested, in this 2025 arXiv paper. As reasoning models grow stronger, static benchmarks saturate and lose scope, so evaluators cannot tell genuine progress from memorized ceilings.

The team curated over thirteen hundred complex questions from existing benchmarks and Olympiad-level competitions across many disciplines. MorphoBench then adjusts difficulty in two ways. It rewrites questions using key statements harvested from a model's own reasoning process, making analytical challenges that target current abilities. It also generates questions with simulation software, allowing dynamic adjustment at minimal cost. The authors iteratively recalibrated the benchmark against the reasoning of frontier systems such as o3 and GPT-5. By letting the test evolve with the test-takers, MorphoBench aims to keep reasoning evaluation comprehensive and valid rather than letting it expire as models improve.
arxiv-2510-14465:
Adem Ait and co-authors sketch a vision for governing software projects where humans and AI agents contribute side by side, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Open-source projects struggle with governance: policies about who may review, merge, or release are often implicit or unclear, and adding autonomous agents with different capabilities and failure modes makes explicit rules urgent.

The authors present the foundational concepts of a domain-specific language for defining and enforcing rich governance policies in such mixed teams. The language is meant to express rules about stakeholders, human contributors of varied backgrounds as well as software agents, in a form machines can check and enforce automatically. They frame the design as a pathway toward more robust, adaptable, and ultimately automated governance. It aims to make collaboration in software projects, especially open-source ones, more effective. It should also make projects less dependent on unwritten conventions and maintainer vigilance.
arxiv-2510-14765:
Catalano and Soccini tackle, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the holes in maps of Mars. Virtual reality systems for mission planning and astronaut training need accurate three-dimensional terrain. Satellite heightmaps of Mars contain missing patches, lost in acquisition or transmission. On Earth, rich datasets let conditional learning fill such gaps. Mars data are too sparse for that, and simple interpolation often breaks the terrain's coherence.

Their method trains an unconditional diffusion model, which learns the texture of Martian terrain itself, on an augmented set of twelve thousand heightmaps from NASA's HiRISE survey. A rescaling step preserves features across scales before images are shrunk to the model's fixed size. On a thousand-sample evaluation set, the method beat inverse distance weighting, kriging, and a Navier-Stokes inpainting algorithm. It improved reconstruction accuracy by four to fifteen percent and perceptual similarity by twenty-nine to eighty-one percent in the reported metrics.
arxiv-2510-14865:
Liu, Neubig, and Xiong investigate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a training phase that many language model builders use but few understand: midtraining. After ordinary pretraining on raw text, builders often mix in higher-quality, instruction-formatted data near the end, before fine-tuning. The practice is popular, yet why it helps had not been studied systematically.

The authors ran controlled experiments, pretraining models from scratch and fine-tuning them in several domains. Midtraining helped most in mathematics and code, exactly where it can shrink the syntactic gap between pretraining text and posttraining data. There it beat continued pretraining on in-domain loss and on how much pretraining knowledge survived fine-tuning. Ablations on code showed timing matters more than mixture proportions: earlier specialized data gave larger gains and preserved general language ability better. The authors frame midtraining as a domain adaptation tool in its own right.
arxiv-2510-15365:
Maonan Wang and fourteen colleagues release a shared virtual testbed where drones and ground vehicles learn to work as one traffic team. Their 2025 arXiv paper, presenting TranSimHub, notes that air and ground systems increasingly share city streets and skies. Progress has been slowed by the lack of one simulation environment that covers both sides at once.

TranSimHub renders synchronized views for air and ground agents in color, depth, and semantic labels, so both domains perceive the same scene consistently. It lets the two sides exchange information during a run. A causal scene editor builds controlled scenarios, letting researchers insert accidents, change weather, or add obstacles and then rerun counterfactual versions. The platform is open source and supports end-to-end research on perception, sensor fusion, and joint control. The authors aim it at next-generation city traffic management that blends aerial and street-level intelligence.
arxiv-2510-15465:
Alicja Wierzcholska and Hubert Siejkowski pull apart two overlapping components in the x-ray glow of a distant blazar. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies 1ES 0229+200, a galaxy whose jet points near Earth and whose gamma-ray spectrum is exceptionally hard. They combine sixteen years of Swift observatory data with hard x-ray observations from NuSTAR.

Most past snapshots showed a smooth x-ray spectrum with no cutoff past a hundred kiloelectron volts. One NuSTAR look in August 2021, catching the source in a low state, showed something new. The spectrum bent into a concave shape with an upturn near twenty-five kiloelectron volts. That kink may mark the handover between synchrotron emission and inverse Compton emission. It could also signal photohadronic processes, which would make the blazar a source of high-energy neutrinos. The authors discuss a possible third bump in the spectrum as a testable consequence.
arxiv-2510-15565:
Vinicius Moraes de Jesus and Andre Georghton Cardoso Pacheco present Colepp, a free tool for gathering clean data from wearable devices, in this 2025 paper written in Portuguese. Smartwatches and fitness trackers produce heart rate and motion data that researchers need for new algorithms. Public datasets are small and collection conditions are hard to control, which slows that work.

Colepp uses a smartphone as a hub that collects from a Polar H10 chest strap and a Wear OS smartwatch at once. It records heart rate from ECG and optical sensors plus motion from accelerometers and gyroscopes. A custom protocol keeps the streams synchronized, and results export as tidy CSV files. A friendly interface lets researchers design their own collection sessions. A use case in the paper shows the tool producing consistent, well-aligned signals, aimed at activity recognition and heart rate estimation studies.
arxiv-2510-15965:
Mohan Zhang leads five co-authors in an attack that traps large reasoning models in endless thought. Reasoning models solve hard problems by writing long chains of thought, yet that loop is also a new surface for abuse. Their Deadlock Attack trains a malicious embedding that pushes the model to keep inserting transition words after each step, so it never lands on a final answer.

Turning a continuous embedding into real trigger tokens tends to kill the effect, a gap the team closes with a backdoor implantation strategy. Across four advanced reasoning models and three maths benchmarks, the attack succeeds every time in their tests, driving output to the token limit. Benign inputs lose almost no utility, and existing overthinking fixes do not stop it. The findings expose reasoning inefficiency itself as a security risk.
arxiv-2510-16065:
Lunchen Xie, Zehua He, and Qingjiang Shi cut the communication bill of personalised federated learning by sending only the parameters that matter. Federated learning trains across scattered clients whose data differ, and personalised variants give each client its own model. Parameter decoupling helps quality, yet many methods still ship so much data per round that deployment stalls.

Their framework, FedPURIN, chooses critical parameters for transmission through an integer programming formulation, a mathematically grounded selection rather than a heuristic trim. That selection feeds a sparse aggregation scheme, so rounds carry far less traffic. On standard image classification benchmarks under varied non-identical data splits, performance stays competitive with leading methods while communication falls by a measurable amount. Edge intelligence systems with mixed data sources stand to gain most, the three authors argue.
arxiv-2510-16165:
