Across six actinide nuclei, the calculations show a low-energy enhancement, an unexpected rise in strength at low gamma energies, marking the first evidence that the effect survives in these heavy nuclei. A scissors mode resonance also appears in all six, matching recent Oslo-method measurements. The results matter for nuclear reaction modeling used in astrophysics and reactor studies.
arxiv-2511-11665:
Sameeksha Sriram and three co-authors revisit rotary positional embeddings. This widely used method tells transformer models where each token sits. It works by rotating embedding vectors. Extensions to higher dimensions rotate vectors on spheres instead of circles. But sphere rotations do not commute, so rotation order becomes unclear.

Their method, QuatRo, uses quaternions to set the rotation axes. Quaternions are the classic algebra for three-dimensional rotation. The goal is to keep the shift property that makes rotary embeddings work. At the same time, richer spatial inputs should be handled well. For models that reason about three-dimensional scenes, a cleaner rotary code could improve how position is represented.
arxiv-2511-11965:
Howard Hao-Tse Huang and Wenbin Lu model how massive black holes can make close binary stars. A black hole can tear a binary apart, the Hills mechanism. That usually makes one hypervelocity star and one captive star. But breakup takes a long time. Tides have time to work on the binary itself.

Over many pericenter passages, the black hole pumps the inner orbit to extreme eccentricity. The stars then pass within a few stellar radii of each other. Dynamical tides between them take over at that point. Outer orbital relaxation, black hole perturbations, and inter-star tides are combined in one model. Chaotic tides offer a route to tight binaries near galactic centers.
arxiv-2511-12265:
Rui Wang, Zeming Wei, Xiyue Zhang and Meng Sun stabilize adversarial training against many kinds of attack at once. Neural networks can be fooled by small crafted changes, and training against several attacks is a natural defense. Computing every attack at each step is costly, while random sampling can push the parameters too far in conflicting directions.

Their method, Calibrated Adversarial Sampling, recasts the choice as a multi-armed bandit problem. At each step it samples just one attack, balancing exploration of new attacks with use of known hard ones. Experiments show stronger overall robustness at low computing cost, with less conflict between attack types during training.
arxiv-2511-12365:
Yiqing Shen and Mathias Unberath propose DT-R1, a learning framework that lets a language model reason about images and video by first building a digital twin of the scene. Visual reasoning tasks range from drawing masks to answering questions, and each has usually needed its own model design and training data. That blocks shared solutions.

DT-R1 trains the model with reinforcement learning to construct a structured, high-level representation of multimodal input, then reason over that representation for any task. A new reward checks both the structure of the twin and the accuracy of the final answer. Across six benchmarks, two modalities and four task types, the method beats task-specific state-of-the-art models, in their report.
arxiv-2511-12665:
Saverio Salzo extends a recent breakthrough in optimization theory. Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, in its composite form called FISTA, is a workhorse for minimizing functions that mix a smooth part with a simpler structured part. For years it was an open problem whether the method's iterates themselves converge to an optimal point, and two recent papers settled that question. Salzo asks whether the answer survives the messiness of real computation.

He proves that it does. In infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the iterates still converge, in the weak sense, even when the gradient is computed with errors or is random, and when the proximity operator is also inexact. That matters because large problems rarely allow exact steps. The result tells practitioners that the method's good behavior is not a fragile artifact of perfect arithmetic, but a property that tolerates noise and approximation.
arxiv-2511-13065:
Reeshoon Sayera and four co-authors present RobustGait, a benchmark for testing whether gait matching survives the real world. Systems that identify people by how they walk perform well in controlled datasets, but nobody had systematically measured their robustness to corruption and to errors in extracting body silhouettes. RobustGait varies four things at once: perturbation type, silhouette extraction method, model architecture, and deployment scenario, across three established data sets plus wild footage.

Fifteen corruption types at five severity levels expose how damage propagates. Noise applied to the raw image reflects real degradation better than noise applied later. Scores proved highly sensitive to which silhouette extractor was used, an overlooked source of bias in earlier benchmarks. Robustness also depended jointly on the corruption and the design. Noise-aware training and knowledge distillation helped. The authors aim the benchmark at builders of surveillance and identification systems that must work outside the lab.
arxiv-2511-13165:
Pieter Braam and five co-authors compute freeform optical surfaces that serve two targets at once. Inverse design in optics starts from the light pattern you want and works backward to the lens or reflector shape that produces it. Most methods handle one source and one target. This one takes a source distribution described by two planes and delivers two separate target distributions. The surfaces control where rays start and end and their directions at both ends.

Energy conservation yields Jacobian equations for the optical mapping, and the optical path length supplies generating functions for the surfaces themselves. A three-stage least-squares algorithm solves the resulting equations numerically. The authors demonstrate the method on examples with complex source and target distributions. Two-target designs matter for lighting systems that split one source into two beams.
arxiv-2511-13265:
Yu-Hao Zhang and 5 co-authors present TransFit-CSM, a fast model for bright transients powered by a blast wave hitting gas around a dying star. The tool couples shock motion to the spread of light from a moving heated edge. Both the escape path for light and the diffusion time shift as the shocks expand.

TransFit-CSM reproduces the known sequence of a dark start, a slow rise and peak, and a cooling tail. Fits to two famous supernovae gave accurate curves and clear physical readings of the star and its lost gas. The speed suits large surveys and careful fitting of many events at once.
arxiv-2511-13365:
Ruijun Deng, Zhihui Lu, and Qiang Duan propose InfoDecom, a defense against privacy leaks in split inference. Split inference lets a user run part of a model locally and send only middle data to a server. Attackers can rebuild the raw input from that middle data, which breaks the promised privacy.

The authors trace the weak trade-off in older defenses to noise dumped on redundant parts of the data. InfoDecom first splits and removes redundant information, then adds noise tuned to give a proven privacy guarantee. Tests in vision tasks showed a better balance of usefulness and privacy than leading baselines, even when the local model is shallow.
arxiv-2511-13565:
Jingyi Zhao and 4 co-authors propose Human-Symbiotic Health Intelligence, a full-stack framework for AI-driven wearable health systems. Older wearables lean on trial-and-error material design and basic signal handling, which limits personal fit. The new concept joins sensor networks with edge-cloud computing and a hybrid of data-driven and knowledge-based modeling.

The system adapts to differences both between people and within one person over time, shifting care from passive tracking to active partnership. AI tunes materials and micro-structures, multi-modal signals are read jointly, and population insight merges with personal adaptation. Reinforcement learning and digital twins close the loop with tailored interventions and feedback for prevention-focused care.
arxiv-2511-13865:
James Bono, Beibei Cheng, and Joaquin Lozano ran a controlled trial of an AI agent that helps manage access rules in Microsoft Entra. The agent supports four tasks: merging policies, finding gaps against a zero-trust baseline, planning staged rollouts, and matching users to policies. In the trial, 162 identity administrators worked with or without the agent.

Those with agent access were much more accurate overall, and they finished tasks faster at the same accuracy level. The biggest gains came on the hardest thinking tasks, such as spotting baseline gaps. The authors present the trial as early hard evidence that purpose-built agents can raise both speed and quality in identity administration.
arxiv-2511-14065:
Felipe A. Torres, Alejandro Weinstein, Jesus M. Cortes, and one co-author explain why bigger brain networks hum more slowly. When neuron populations synchronize, a collective rhythm emerges, and imaging shows large networks oscillate slower than fine parcellations of the same volume. The mechanism behind that size law was unresolved.

The authors start from a Kuramoto model whose couplings carry delays, like signals traveling along fibers. Linearizing near synchrony gives a closed formula: the resonance frequency is set by the inverse of total delay-weighted coupling. Only growth scenarios that respect real geometry follow the law. Simulations with varied delays confirm the prediction and measure how delay spread degrades it.
arxiv-2511-14365:
Prathamesh Kalamkar, Ned Letcher, Meissane Chami, and three co-authors fix a mismatch between how language models read chemistry and how chemistry is written. General-purpose tokenizers chop molecular strings such as SMILES into fragments that carry no chemical meaning, a tokenization bottleneck that blurs what the model can learn. Their remedy extends the model's vocabulary with chemically salient tokens.

After the vocabulary surgery they continue pretraining on chemistry-domain text so the new tokens settle into the model's knowledge alongside natural language. The empirical demonstration shows stronger performance across a range of downstream chemical tasks. The authors present the recipe as a principled way to unify text and molecular structure in one pretrained model.
arxiv-2511-14465:
Clément Dumas built nnterp, a software tool for studying how transformer models work inside. Such models power most modern language systems. Researchers need to probe their inner steps, yet each model design often needs its own custom code. That custom work can also change the numbers the model would normally give.

nnterp wraps a known library so the same probe code runs across many model types. It works with more than fifty model variants from sixteen design families. It includes common probes and checks that users can run on their own models. The tool aims to keep results exact while making tests far easier to share.
arxiv-2511-14565:
Minyoung Hwang and three co-authors propose Masked IRL, a method for teaching robots user preferences from demos plus language. Demos alone show how to act, but not what matters, so reward models can latch onto spurious details. Language can state what matters, yet instructions are often vague on their own. The key idea is that the two signals complement each other.

Large language models help combine demos and language to resolve reward ambiguity. The framework masks state details that language marks as irrelevant. That focus should improve generalization from limited data. The method targets household and assistive settings where preferences differ per user. Better reward learning means robots adapt without extensive new demos.
arxiv-2511-14665:
Milan Rosko argues that some famous hard problems are hard for a logical reason, not for lack of clever methods. When global decision problems are written in arithmetic form, they gain a self-referential structure. Checking the fixed points that arise seems to need reflection steps beyond finite means, in the style of Feferman.

Rosko applies this lens to uniform complexity claims, including the P versus NP question. The claim is that their difficulty comes from this built-in self-reference, not from weak tools. The paper does not claim to separate the classes. Instead it clarifies what kind of statement such claims are, and why standard techniques may keep falling short.
arxiv-2511-14865:
Dwipam Katariya, Snehita Varma, and four co-authors build FinTRec, a transformer system for ad targeting and personal feeds in financial services. Banks face long user histories that mix online and branch activity, plus many linked products that must be promoted together. Goals for different products can also pull in opposite directions.

Tree-based models have long been the default in finance because they are easy to explain and satisfy regulators. The authors argue FinTRec can handle the mixed timing and linked products while staying practical for real-time use. Their study presents the transformer route as a workable shift for a field that has been slow to adopt it.
arxiv-2511-15265:
Hengyuan Zhang, Jielong Zhang, and seven co-authors settle a heated dispute over the crystal structure of a nickel oxide superconductor under pressure. The compound La3Ni2O7 superconducts only when squeezed, and rival groups had claimed three different symmetries for that squeezed state. Using high-pressure Raman spectroscopy down to near absolute zero, the team tracks the structure as pressure climbs.

A single transition appears, from one orthorhombic form to another, right where bulk superconductivity switches on. Careful symmetry rules for the Raman signals show the persisting symmetry rules out the claimed tetragonal form in these samples. Pinning the true structure is a prerequisite for any theory of how this material superconducts.
arxiv-2511-15565:
Daniel Bermuth, Alexander Poeppel, and Wolfgang Reif re-examine human pose forecasting, the task of predicting future body poses from past motion. Such forecasts support action recognition, sports analysis, and human-robot interaction. The authors argue progress is hard to judge because studies use varied preprocessing, mismatched scoring code, and only partly shared artifacts.

They audit many recent methods, find several reproducibility problems, and build one shared training and scoring pipeline for absolute pose forecasting. Under that fair protocol, mature sequence models borrowed from speech recognition gave the lowest errors. A paired noisy data set, built from a pose estimator rather than clean motion capture, showed detector noise hurts results badly, though retraining on noisy poses recovers part of the loss.
arxiv-2511-15765:
Harun Basmaci and Hasan Ozgur Cildiroglu show that a parity anomaly appears naturally in two-dimensional Dirac fermion systems threaded by gauge fields. Dirac fermions are fast, light-like particles described by a first-order equation, and a parity anomaly is a quantum breaking of mirror symmetry. The setting uses regions with holes, where an Aharonov-Bohm phase arises as a charged particle loops a magnetic flux it never touches.

Using the Fujikawa method, which tracks how the quantum measure changes, they show the anomaly reproduces both that phase and its spin-based cousin, the Aharonov-Casher phase. They compute the induced topological currents explicitly. Their divergence-free form provides a direct signature of this parity-anomalous topological phase.
arxiv-2511-15865:
Thomas Donlon, Lawrence M. Widrow, and Sukanya Chakrabarti introduce a new way to estimate how much mass sits within a sphere centered on the Sun. Their data are the line-of-sight accelerations of millisecond pulsars, spinning neutron stars whose signals reveal tiny changes in their motion. Applying the divergence theorem, a calculus identity linking a volume total to surface flow, turns those accelerations into a mean mass density without assuming a model shape.

Results agree with earlier analyses, and paired with a baryon model they give dark matter density as a function of distance rather than one number. Current data cannot yet isolate the local dark matter signal cleanly, but growing pulsar data should soon allow it. Density asymmetries across the galactic midplane are also estimated.
arxiv-2511-15965:
Luning Sun, José L. Safanelli, and seven co-authors build a self-supervised framework to forecast soil traits from spectra. Soil spectroscopy reads how soil reflects light in mid- and near-infrared ranges to infer traits cheaply. But labeled samples are scarce, and the richer mid-infrared libraries are costly to use in the field. Their method first learns from unlabeled spectra alone.

A variational autoencoder compresses the large mid-infrared library into embeddings, compact learned summaries. Scan repeats augment training. A frozen decoder then turns cheap portable near-infrared scans into forecast mid-infrared spectra. Downstream models use raw spectra, forecast spectra, and embeddings to predict nine soil traits, matching or beating baselines on a gold-standard test set.
arxiv-2511-16565:
Tianjun Li, Qi Sun, Rui Sun, and Lina Wu widen the landscape of three-family supersymmetric Pati-Salam models built from intersecting D6-branes in type IIA string theory. Earlier constructions forced one stack of branes to sit parallel to another's orientifold image; this work drops that restriction by generalizing the three-family conditions.

With the relaxed conditions, four new classes of models appear, with intersection numbers that the parallel construction could not reach. The authors also use a modified renormalization group evolution for a left-handed gauge coupling. That coupling is obtained by breaking a product of two SU(2) groups, with canonical normalization imposed before running. That mechanism strongly suppresses a problematic coupling ratio and restores the string-scale gauge coupling relation for the new models as well.
arxiv-2511-16865:
Tai Hyun Yoon designs a tabletop quantum optical simulator for the Unruh-DeWitt detector model, the standard model of a detector interacting with a quantum field along a spacetime path. Effects such as the Unruh effect are far too weak to see directly, so an analog platform that mimics the mathematics is valuable.

Entangled nonlinear biphoton sources, built from phase-controlled single-photon frequency combs, supply the hardware. Signal-mode excitations play the detector, and coherently seeded idler modes play the field. The author derives the effective Hamiltonian and master equation for two seeded units and solves for the photon number and correlation dynamics in closed form. Simulations confirm phase-dependent behavior of the Unruh-DeWitt type. They show controllable fidelity, interference visibility, and entanglement entropy, putting analog tests of vacuum fluctuation physics within reach of current optics.
arxiv-2511-16965:
Jigyasa Gupta, Soumya Goyal, Anil Kumar, and Ishan Jindal build a system that imagines how food will look as it cooks, and watches cooking progress, on edge devices inside smart ovens. Rendering browning, texture, and structural change convincingly is hard for image generators, and the heavy ones cannot run on appliance hardware.

The team contributes the first oven-based cooking progression dataset with chef-annotated doneness levels. Their generator takes a raw food image plus recipe and target state guidance, so users aim at their preferred result rather than a preset. A culinary image similarity metric, designed for this domain, doubles as training loss and progress monitor, enforcing temporal consistency and plausibility. The model beat baselines on realism scores by wide margins on both the new and public datasets while staying edge efficient.
arxiv-2511-17365:
Evangelia Gazaki studies zero-cycles, formal combinations of points, on bielliptic surfaces, a class of surfaces built as quotients of a product of two elliptic curves by a finite group. The algebraic object in question, the Chow group of zero-cycles, measures when configurations of points are equivalent under a geometric relation. Gazaki focuses on the kernel of the Albanese map, which sends degree-zero cycles to points of an associated abelian variety.

She proves that, over any field whose characteristic is not two or three, this kernel is a torsion group. Its exponent is a small power of two or three times the order of the group, depending on the surface's type. Explicit examples over p-adic fields show the kernel can contain genuinely nontrivial elements, built by pushing forward cycles from the covering abelian surface. The note sharpens the arithmetic picture of these surfaces.
arxiv-2511-17565:
Sarthak Chakraborty and four co-authors cache language model responses more cleverly for repetitive work. In agentic and workflow settings, prompts recur with small variations on a shared structure. Exact-match caching misses those near-hits, while semantic caching can return a response that ignores a critical difference. Their generative cache instead learns the reusable response patterns across similar prompt structures and synthesizes a customized answer for each new request, aware of what changed.

The system reached an 83 percent cache hit rate while keeping incorrect hits minimal on datasets without repetition. In agentic workflows it raised the hit rate by about twenty percent over standard prompt matching and cut end-to-end execution latency by about a third. The work targets a real cost center: organizations rerunning near-identical model calls thousands of times, where a smarter cache pays for itself quickly.
arxiv-2511-17665:
Hadi Khodaei Jooshin and Inna Partin-Vaisband speed up a bottleneck step in chip design: batching nets for global routing. Global routing gives early estimates of a circuit's routability, and top routers process nets in batches to parallelize the work and control congestion. Conventional batching heuristics are expensive and flawed, producing oversized batches of conflicting nets or so many batches that parallelization suffers. The authors enhance batching with a Wasserstein generative adversarial network, which learns to propose fewer, higher-quality batches in less time.

Tested on the latest ISPD 2024 contest benchmarks, the GAN-assisted algorithm cut runtime by up to forty percent and degraded routing quality by only a tiny fraction of a percent. The result targets a practical pressure point: as circuits grow, routing preparation must scale with modern parallel hardware instead of against it.
arxiv-2511-17765:
Darren Chiu, Zhehui Huang, Ruohai Ge, and Gaurav Sukhatme present LEARN, a navigation system for teams of tiny flying robots. Such nano drones have very limited sensing, communication, and computing, so methods that need sharp cameras or heavy planners cannot run on board.

LEARN pairs low resolution distance sensors and a simple planner with a compact learning policy that pays attention to key inputs. In simulation it beats leading planners while using far fewer resources. Flights with six small quadrotors indoors and outdoors, through narrow gaps, show the system works fully on board in cluttered spaces.
arxiv-2511-18365:
Dangyang He studies a key transform on a cone shaped space with a Schrödinger operator that holds a potential. The space spreads like a cone over a closed curved base. The Riesz transform, which trades a function's size for its slope size, is a core tool in this analysis.

He first adds endpoint bounds of Lorentz type at both ends of the range where the transform stays bounded. He then proves a sharp reverse bound: the half power of the operator is capped by the slope plus a term scaled by radius. The bound holds just for a set range of exponents tied to the base spectrum. Such sharp two way bounds pin down how heat and waves act on cone spaces.
arxiv-2511-18565:
The KM3NeT Collaboration tunes its deep sea neutrino telescope to catch a Galactic supernova. When a massive star's core collapses, a burst of neutrinos escapes the dense core and can reveal the hidden dynamics. KM3NeT's glass modules, each with many light sensors, watch for a sudden rise in hit rate that marks such a burst.

New per module measures exploit the shape in space and time of the hits, which sharpens the split between a true burst and background noise. The team also probe the systematic doubts that cloud the signal. A better burst watch turns the telescope into an early alarm for a rare event in our Galaxy or the Large Magellanic Cloud. Partner observatories can then point in time.
arxiv-2511-18965:
Susanne Hindennach, Mayar Elfares, Céline Gressel, and Andreas Bulling measure how eye tracking researchers reflect on ethics and privacy in their own work. Eye tracking now serves health care, marketing, and surveillance, all high stakes uses. Guides exist, yet how scholars weigh these issues in practice was scarcely studied.

Two tools, built with input from over seventy researchers, frame the study. REFLECT is a qualitative questionnaire; SPERET is a quantitative scale for ethics and privacy reflexivity. Findings show a field that cares about user privacy, knows its method limits like sample bias, and holds a nuanced sense of duty that grows as a project matures. The tools let the field grade its own conscience.
arxiv-2511-19065:
Jin-Young Kim and seven co-authors dissect and then speed the training of MeanFlow, a generative model that promises fine samples in few steps. MeanFlow learns two velocity fields at once: the instant field and the average field over a time span. How the two interact in training was unclear, which left schedules to guesswork.

Three findings guide their fix. A sound instant field must form before the average field can be learned. The instant field gains from the average field at small time gaps and loses at large ones. Smooth learning of large gap averages, the key to one step generation, rests on prior sound instant and small gap fields. Their scheme builds the instant field fast, then shifts weight from short to long spans.
arxiv-2511-19265:
Bianka Kowalska and Halina Kwaśnicka survey mechanistic interpretability, a research program that tries to read the actual algorithms inside neural networks. Deep networks work well but hide their reasoning, which blocks trust in sensitive uses. Mechanistic work reverse engineers inner computations and restates them in human terms.

The article offers a unified taxonomy of approaches and walks through key techniques with concrete examples and pseudo-code. It places the field within the wider explainability landscape, comparing goals and methods with other strands. A history traces its roots and recent rapid growth. The authors argue this line of work is central to building AI systems people can understand and trust.
arxiv-2511-19465:
Theo Demessance, Chongke Bi, Sonia Djebali, and Guillaume Guerard predict where tourists will go next, using the traces they leave on social networks. Travelers post comments and photos during trips, and those posts reveal their paths through a city. Knowing likely next moves helps tourism marketing and planning.

The method learns tourist movements with a grammatical inference algorithm adapted for very large data, and packs the result into a hidden Markov model for a group of tourists. That model stays flexible and can be updated with fresh data. Paris serves as the test case, where the approach models visitor flows through the French capital.
arxiv-2511-19865:
Mingkai Chen, Zijie Feng, Lei Wang, and Yaser Khamayseh propose a network for teams of smart embodied devices in future 6G systems. In tasks like disaster rescue, many devices must fuse images and radar, share meaning, and coordinate work. Older systems struggle with this fusion, with adaptive communication, and with explaining their choices.

Their network, CC-EIN, joins several modules: PerceptiNet fuses image and radar data into shared semantic features, while coding and power adapt to task urgency and channel quality. A semantic mechanism splits tasks and coordinates devices without conflict, and a separate module visualizes decisions for transparency. Rescue simulations after an earthquake show high task completion and efficient transmission.
arxiv-2511-19965:
Hongji Yang and six co-authors present HiCoGen, a system for images that must match complex, layered prompts. Diffusion models handle simple prompts well but often drop objects, mix up parts, or compose scenes poorly when prompts have many objects and nested structure. The authors replace one-shot generation with a step-by-step build.

A language model first splits a complex prompt into minimal semantic units. HiCoGen then synthesizes the units one by one, each new image giving visual context for the next step. Reinforcement learning tunes the process with rewards judged at global, subject, and relationship levels, and a decaying randomness schedule widens exploration early on. A new benchmark, HiCoPrompt, tests the method on layered prompts.
arxiv-2511-20065:
Xiaoge Zhang and six co-authors present FLaTEC, a method for compressing LiDAR point clouds. Compressors must trade file size against reconstruction quality, and the trade is awkward because low-frequency structure and high-frequency texture behave differently at the same resolution. A full scan needs a high ratio without losing either kind of content.

FLaTEC converts voxel embeddings into triplanes, a compact stand-in that cuts sparsity, cost, and storage. A frequency-disentangling step stores compact low-frequency content and gathers high-frequency detail across scales, both in binary form. During decoding, a modulation block restores the full spectrum step by step, while a frequency-based attention step rebuilds local links and can output points at any resolution. The method beats standard codecs clearly on two driving datasets.
arxiv-2511-20265:
Zheng, He, Kang, Cai, Huang, and Wymeersch predict car-to-roadside radio beams with flowing math. Their 2025 paper uses rectified flow for millimeter-wave links. Vehicle-to-infrastructure beams misalign constantly in moving traffic. Repeated beam sweeping wastes time and spectrum. Roadside cameras can anticipate the best beam instead.

Discrete sequence predictors accumulate errors over long horizons. Recurrent networks and LSTMs wobble as predictions stretch out. The new method treats beam motion as continuous flow. An ODE-driven vector field carries the latent beam state. A terminal constraint keeps long predictions globally consistent. Top-K accuracy beat the recurrent baselines clearly. Performance approached large language model approaches. Inference ran about ten times faster on GPUs. On CPUs the speedup reached ten-thousand-fold. Edge units at roadside stations can host it. Smooth trajectories replace jumpy index guesses.
arxiv-2511-20365:
Armadillo, Devoto, Dradi, and Vicini grind through second-order corrections for lepton pair production. Their 2025 paper tackles the infrared structure of the Drell-Yan process. Colliders make lepton pairs from quark-antiquark collisions constantly. Those events pin down the W and Z boson masses. Precision targets now demand two-loop electroweak accuracy.

The team computed the QED subset exactly. Their OCEANN framework keeps exact numbers at every stage. Amplitudes stay exact all the way through. High-energy excess terms were cleaned away step by step. Low-energy pieces were taken out to leave finite results. The inclusive cross section emerges fully corrected. Agreement with published work validates the machinery. Cancelling terms could easily have destroyed precision. Boson masses are known to a hundredth of a percent. Bright future running will push errors below one percent. The full electroweak case is the next target. LHC measurement work gains a verified engine.
arxiv-2511-20465:
Shao and colleagues review how well science can predict solar flares. Their 2025 survey covers data-driven forecasting for space weather. Flares blast radiation and particles toward Earth without much warning. Satellites, communications, and astronaut safety all face risks. A major flare releases around ten to the thirty-two ergs of energy. Forecasting within a day is the operational target.

The review traces methods from physics models to deep learning. Early statistics gave way to machine learning. Convolutional networks read spatial patterns in magnetograms. Recurrent networks track how active regions evolve over time. Transformers capture long-range links through self-attention. Multimodal large models are the newest entrants. Real forecasting platforms are assessed for daily performance. Datasets often span less than one full solar cycle. Severe class imbalance plagues the training data. Physics models explain mechanisms but miss accuracy deadlines.
arxiv-2511-20665:
Tcharlies Schmitz proposes in 2025 a way to turn text into numbers for computer comparison without any training at all. Standard embeddings, the lists of numbers that capture a word's meaning, are learned from huge text collections and cannot be run backwards. Schmitz's method, Harmonic Token Projection, converts each word's Unicode values, the standard codes for characters, into waves on a circle using fixed maths, so the original text can always be recovered exactly.

Because similar words end up with similar wave patterns, the method can judge how alike two sentences are in meaning, the task set by the Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark. On that benchmark it reached a Spearman correlation of 0.68 in English, a score where higher means closer agreement with human judges, and it held steady across ten languages. Each sentence pair took under a millisecond to score, with no training data, no stored vocabulary, and no random steps.
arxiv-2511-21765:
Hariprasad M, of IISc Bengaluru, proves a convex bound in the Hölder inequality family and puts it to work across analysis and number theory, in 2025. Hölder's inequality, a workhorse for bounding integrals and sums, relates norms of different orders. The paper asks what can be said about a middle norm knowing only a smaller and a larger one.

Given three exponents in increasing order, the result bounds the middle s-norm from above using the l-norm and the m-norm on either side. The bound is then applied several ways. It estimates odd zeta values, controls binomial sums, and bounds gamma and beta functions. Along the way it settles a concrete inequality posed by Dinu Teodorescu, about three positive numbers summing to one, by applying Hölder's inequality repeatedly. One interpolation estimate thus unifies scattered bounding problems.
arxiv-2511-21865:
Vallarino argues long-term development depends heavily on which institutional club a country belongs to, not just its own policies. He compares Spain, which joined dense European institutions, with Uruguay, which stayed inside the weaker-coordinated Latin American regime, despite similar starting human capital and democratic traditions. Their paths diverged sharply.

To test what belonging is worth, Vallarino trains a generative AI model, a Wasserstein GAN, on data for 80 countries from 1960 to 2020, covering institutions, economic complexity, and human development. The model then simulates counterfactual histories, scored by a new measure called Expected Developmental Shift. Spain transplanted into a Latin American institutional setting suffered significant developmental decline in the simulations, while Uruguay placed inside a European regime gained complexity and resilience in the model's output. Development thus emerges from network position, making institutional access itself a policy lever.
arxiv-2511-21965:
Benedek and colleagues examine a promising quantum bit in silicon carbide, a mature semiconductor. The ClV centre, a chlorine atom beside a missing silicon atom, was flagged by screening as a high-spin defect emitting at telecom wavelengths. Experiments have since seen its infrared photoluminescence lines after chlorine implantation, but a working qubit also needs ODMR, optically detected magnetic resonance, to initialize and read out its spin state optically.

Using wavefunction theory, CASSCF with NEVPT2 corrections, they computed the centre's states and the rates connecting them, including intersystem crossing, which makes ODMR possible. Their calculations strongly suggest the centre is ODMR active, with a predicted zero-field splitting of 1.0 to 1.3 gigahertz and emission around 0.8 to 0.9 electronvolts in their results. That combination would make ClV an optically addressable spin qubit that plugs naturally into fibre networks.
arxiv-2511-22565:
Brunink and colleagues stress-test a fashionable claim about neural question answering over knowledge graphs. Complex query answering systems learn embeddings and neural operators, and are widely believed to infer answers that plain graph traversal cannot reach. The authors compare state-of-the-art neural systems against a simple rival: query relaxation, a training-free strategy that loosens a query's constraints and counts resulting paths, ranking candidates by simple statistics.

Across multiple datasets and query structures, no neural model consistently beat the relaxation baseline; in several cases they performed about the same despite the baseline involving no learning at all. The two approaches also return largely different answers, with little overlap, and combining their outputs improved performance consistently. Neural and symbolic methods thus capture complementary reasoning patterns, progress claims need stronger non-neural baselines. Future neural systems should borrow relaxation's principles.
arxiv-2511-22765:
Li and colleagues report first bench tests of a second generation of ultrafast light sensors for future neutrino detectors. Large-Area Picosecond Photodetectors are flat panels timing photons to tens of picoseconds. They are precise enough to separate instantly emitted Cherenkov light from slower scintillation light in novel water-based scintillators, sharpening reconstruction in proposed detectors such as Theia. Pairing them with fast readout electronics is the untested link checked here.

The team coupled them to two commercial systems-on-a-chip from Nalu Scientific, the HDSoC and the AARDVARC, full-waveform digitizers sampling at roughly one and ten samples per nanosecond. Firing a picosecond laser, they measured timing jitter between a pair of channels, the spread limiting how precisely arrival times can be compared. With intrinsic jitter of 5 to 10 picoseconds, the setup demonstrated the timing performance precise applications need, validating the sensor-plus-chip architecture.
arxiv-2511-22865:
Ryu and colleagues teach self-driving systems to know when it cannot see well. End-to-end planners learn directly from camera input to trajectory, but treat perception as perfectly reliable, so in ambiguous scenes the planner charges ahead with unjustified confidence, sometimes steering into non-drivable areas. SUPER-AD is camera-only and estimates aleatoric uncertainty, the data's irreducible noise, directly in bird's-eye-view space.

The uncertainty feeds a dense drivability map carrying semantic structure and geometric layout at pixel resolution, so the planner can discount regions perception itself flags as doubtful. A lane-following regularisation adds what data alone teaches poorly: traffic norms. It stabilises trajectories and supports rule compliance while preserving flexibility for overtaking. On the NAVSIM benchmark it reached state-of-the-art performance overall, with substantial gains on the challenging NAVHARD and safety-critical NAVSAFE subsets, evidence that explicit uncertainty measurably improves safety.
arxiv-2511-23065:
Thornley and colleagues look inside porous gallium nitride mirrors, called distributed Bragg reflectors, that are made by electrochemically etching a layered crystal so some layers become spongy and reflect light strongly. The etching is defect-driven: it travels along threading dislocations, natural line defects in the crystal, but how the pores connect in three dimensions was not known.

Using focused ion beam tomography, slicing the material and imaging each slice, they produced the first three-dimensional reconstructions of such mirrors, comparing five-pair stacks etched at 5 and 8 volts. The images support a new cascade model, in which etchant runs down vertical nanopipes and then spreads sideways through the doped layers. And they show individual dislocations switching on and off, which explains broken pipes. Higher voltage made etching follow the older, simpler kebab pattern more often, giving makers a knob for tuning pore structure.
arxiv-2511-23365:
Kipp and colleagues study on-chip terahertz spectroscopy, which measures how two-dimensional materials respond electrically at terahertz frequencies. The samples are far smaller than the wavelength of the light, so the team traps the waves in metal transmission lines on a chip. What the measurements mean is not always clear, because a metal sample can answer in more than one way.

A true Drude response reflects charge flow limited by scattering. Another answer is plasmonic resonances, standing waves of charge bouncing inside the sample. The team identifies a third regime, called Phantom-Drude. It mimics a Drude response, but is really several resonances piled on top of each other. It appears depending on sample size and shape, line geometry, and gate material. Direct sample-to-line contact gives the most reliable Drude signal, and the authors' guidelines, favoring standard graphite gates, help future studies avoid the trap.
arxiv-2512-00265:
Estimating cause and effect with instrumental variables gets hard when there are more parameters than observations. Eleftheria Kelekidou writes an exposition in 2025 on high-dimensional penalized linear instrumental variable estimation. The methods covered are BRIDGE and adaptive LASSO, used inside two-stage least squares.

Both stages of the procedure can have parameter counts that grow with the sample size. Penalization keeps such problems solvable by shrinking weak coefficients toward zero. The exposition helps applied researchers in economics and health choose and understand tools for settings where traditional instrumental variable methods break down. Two-stage least squares is the classic estimator the penalized methods extend. Growing parameter counts are now routine in genetic and economic instruments. For folks who work with scant data and many loose ends, the gain is a set of tools that stay put. They hold up when the old rules break down at scale.
arxiv-2512-00365:
People reason about physical objects through rough internal body representations, coarse shapes that capture an object's extent. Andrey Gizdov and co-authors test whether vision models develop comparable representations in 2025. Human psychophysics suggests we use such approximations for intuitive predictions about motion and physics.

The team probes models trained for segmentation, asking whether their internal structure contains body-like representations. The internal structure of human representations remains largely unknown, so models offer a testable comparison. Findings could connect machine perception to cognitive science and improve models that must predict how objects will move and collide. Segmentation models are a good probe because they must carve the world into objects.
arxiv-2512-01065:
Carlos Martínez-Ranero and Lucas Polymeris construct a set-theoretic model with a rare combination in a 2025 paper. Suslin lines are dense linear orders with special countability properties, long studied in set theory. The Open Graph Axiom is a statement about coloring edges of large graphs, with strong consequences for such orders.

The authors build a model where the Open Graph Axiom holds, yet a 2-entangled Suslin line exists. As a consequence, that model has a 2-entangled uncountable linear order, but no such order that is separable. Careful models like this show which combinations of axioms can coexist.
arxiv-2512-01365:
Swati Kumari and co-authors build a guard for networks in smart devices. Homes and plants now link many small devices to the web. Odd traffic on those links can signal an attack. Spotting that traffic fast is a key safety task.

Their method mixes quantum and classic computing. A quantum support vector tool sorts traffic as normal or odd. A quantum wavelet step cleans the signal first. The mix is tested under the noise of today's small quantum machines. Strong scores would hint that quantum aids can help guard real device networks.
arxiv-2512-01465:
Hongnan Si and co-authors fill gaps in water quality data. Sensors that track river and lake health can fail. Long records then hold holes where data is lost. Holes make trend checks and alerts hard to trust.

Their network blends convolution with a Tucker form. That form squeezes the data while keeping its main traits. The net learns from the sound parts to rebuild the lost parts. Full records help staff spot pollution early. They also give a truer view of how water health shifts over months and years. The squeeze form also keeps time order intact, so seasonal swings and slow drifts in water health stay visible after gaps are filled.
arxiv-2512-01565:
Alex Oshin and co-authors speed up nonlinear programming with deep unfolding. Quadratic programs sit inside many control and planning tasks. Solvers must stay feasible at each step, which can be slow. Their solver, FlexQP, is built to stay feasible by design.

Deep unfolding turns solver steps into a learnable network. Training tunes those steps for speed on real task families. An always-feasible solver can run in tight loops, like robot control. Learned speed with firm feasibility could cut compute in autonomous systems. Unfolded steps keep solver structure, so the learned solver stays readable to control engineers who must certify it before real use.
arxiv-2512-01865:
Adel Moumen, Guangzhi Sun, and Philip Woodland interleave languages to lift speech language models. Speech models learn language straight from audio units. That widens access for tongues with little written text. Progress has stayed English-centric due to scarce data and tests elsewhere.

Cross-lingual interleaving mixes speech units across languages in training. Shared structure can then transfer to low-resource tongues. The team tests whether that transfer holds in practice. Gains would bring voice tools to many communities now left out of language technology. Interleaving needs no parallel corpora, a key gain for tongues where aligned speech pairs across languages simply do not exist yet.
arxiv-2512-02165:
The Higgs boson occasionally decays into pairs of photons, or a photon and a Z boson, and these rare decays are precision tests of particle physics. Alexander Khodjamirian, Kirill Melnikov, and Arkady Vainshtein estimate in 2025 the leading corrections to those decays that come from non-perturbative effects in the strong force.

The corrections originate in how light quarks contribute to the decay, a corner where perturbative calculation, the usual step-by-step method, runs out. Sizing them up tells experimenters how much of any future mismatch with theory could be mundane strong-force physics. Rare Higgs decays are prized because new particles could shift them, so every known contribution must be accounted for first.
arxiv-2512-02265:
Clinical machine learning must be accurate, fair across patient groups, and explainable enough for doctors to trust, and improving one can disturb the others. Joshua Anderson and Shyam Visweswaran examine in 2025 a neglected link in that triangle: how enforcing fairness changes a model's explanations.

It was already known that fairness work can move predictive performance, but its effect on explainability was little studied. If explanations shift when fairness is enforced, clinicians may see different reasons for the same prediction, which affects trust. The study maps that interaction for healthcare models, where explanations are an essential ingredient of safe use.
arxiv-2512-02465:
Xingwang Li and nine co-authors tackle a practical gap in city weather data: rain gauges are sparse. Fast city growth and more extreme storms make fine grained rain maps vital for safer, smarter cities. Their 2025 study uses signals from commercial microwave links, the radio links that carry phone traffic.

Those links weaken when rain crosses them, so they can act as rough rain sensors. The team presents TabGRU, a design that reads link data to estimate how hard rain falls across a city. Such low cost sensing could help cities track storms street by street. City crews could use such maps to warn streets that face fast floods.
arxiv-2512-02665:
Jing Ma tests whether the order of documents changes what a language model concludes from them. Models now summarize several long documents at once, as in AI search overviews. Whether they weigh every source equally has been unclear.

Ma built forty triplets of news articles on abortion, mixing pro, neutral, and opposing views. Each triplet was fed in all six possible orders to Gemini 2.5 Flash, which wrote a neutral overview. Comparing outputs across orders shows if early or late placement tilts the summary, a fairness concern for news synthesis. That tilt, if real, means the same facts can read as slanted or fair based on list order alone.
arxiv-2512-03265:
Heat that spreads and fades follows patterns over long times. Carmen Cortázar, Fernando Quirós, and Noemí Wolanski study a nonlocal heat equation in this 2025 work. Nonlocal means heat jumps across distance, not just to nearby points, and an absorption term removes heat.

The authors focus on the case where absorption dominates and the starting heat decays fast. They describe how solutions behave after long times. Such results help model spread in biology and materials where long jumps occur. They also test the limits of classic diffusion theory. Long-time limits reveal the final shape of a solution, long after early details fade.
arxiv-2512-03565:
Luis Gall and colleagues squeeze more speed from molecular dynamics by reordering how atoms are loaded into processor registers. The AutoPas simulation library already tunes its algorithms while running. Their 2025 paper asks whether the vectorization order itself should join the runtime tuning menu.

Pairwise force calculation dominates these simulations, and the best loading order shifts with particle density and neighbor-finding strategy. Benchmarks confirmed that matching order to conditions considerably speeds the force step over the library's previous fixed approach. The team extended AutoPas so it chooses the winning order on the fly. Energy consumption, not just time, entered their comparisons.
arxiv-2512-03665:
Steffen Gommel and co-authors propose catching light's electric field in a single shot at near-petahertz bandwidth. Fieldoscopy reads ultrafast light-matter events without labels, but current setups scan and average many pulses, blurring one-off events. Their 2025 design stretches time itself to freeze the waveform.

A nonlinear time lens zooms in on the fleeting optical signal so electronics can record it in real time. Their math shows bandwidth near a petahertz with attosecond resolution. The wide time window suits transient fields thrown off by solids and liquids when excited. Uses stretch from electronics at that scale to watching ultrafast events that happen just once.
arxiv-2512-03765:
Companies holding large amounts of Bitcoin face a pointed question: prove the funds are sound without revealing wallet layouts or trading plans. Jose E. Puente and Carlos Puente answer with the Treasury Proof Ledger in a 2025 security preprint. Their system logs treasury activity on Bitcoin itself, treating exposures across domains as a conserved state machine.

A ledger instance records snapshots proving reserves, receipts for cross-domain movements, and policy metadata. Each stakeholder sees only a permitted view. The authors define an idealised model and name the guarantees a deployment should aim for, covering soundness of holdings, completeness of policy, and freedom from conflicting histories. They show practical versions are achievable by combining known reserve proofs with hash-based commitments anchored on the blockchain. A stylised corporate example shows how such a system could support responsible transparency.
arxiv-2512-03865:
The standard map is a toy model of Hamiltonian chaos, a kicked rotor whose orbits mix order and randomness. Yunzhe Li asks an inverse question about it in a 2025 preprint. Can the map be deformed while keeping features of infinitely many periodic orbits exactly fixed? The features are the symplectic actions and the Lyapunov exponents, which measure orbit stability.

Li constructs deformations preserving the actions, or separately the exponents, of infinitely many periodic orbits piling up on an invariant curve. The proof works through resonant normal forms, tracking how those orbits depend on Fourier coefficients of the dynamics, then applies a contraction argument to find the right deformation. The result mirrors a nonrigidity phenomenon known for lengths of closed geodesics on surfaces. It raises the same question for convex billiard tables, where such rigidity may also fail.
arxiv-2512-04165:
Deep learning theory keeps drowning in detail: exact accounts of feature learning produce high-dimensional nonlinear equations that only heavy numerics can solve. Noa Rubin, Orit Davidovich, and Zohar Ringel propose a shortcut in a 2025 machine learning preprint. Borrowing the spirit of scaling arguments from physics, they ask at which data and width scales each pattern of feature learning switches on.

Their heuristic analysis is far simpler than the exact theories it imitates. It reproduces the scaling exponents of several known results, the first test any shortcut must pass. It then goes further, predicting behaviour for more complex toy architectures: three-layer nonlinear networks and attention heads. The authors argue that such scale analysis extends first-principles theorising to problems where the full equations are impractical. It gives researchers a cheap way to anticipate which learning regime a network will occupy.
arxiv-2512-04265:
The TRAPPIST-1 system offers the strongest atmospheric transmission signals of any planetary system. But the star keeps shouting over them. Its flares contaminate half or more of transits, far above the level of an atmosphere. Ward S. Howard and a team attack that contamination in a 2025 exoplanet preprint.

They analyse five and a half hours of Webb near-infrared observations covering six flares, fitting them with RADYN radiative-hydrodynamic models across a grid of electron beam parameters. Moderate-intensity beams fit best, though every model over-predicts the Paschen jump. The team builds two mitigation pipelines, one empirical and one model-based, by binning spectra at similar flare temperatures. They clean the data down to residuals near fifty to sixty-five parts per million. Injection tests suggest carbon dioxide atmospheres with features above one hundred fifty parts per million could be detected at three sigma.
arxiv-2512-04565:
Peter Fisher and Anuradha Annaswamy propose a new route to adaptive control for the linear quadratic regulator, a benchmark problem in control theory. The regulator steers a system at least cost, but the system's traits are often unknown at the start. Existing adaptive methods carry practical baggage: some need a working stabilizing controller up front, some keep stability only by constant probing, and some are heavy to compute. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets one class of discrete-time systems free of those burdens.

The algorithm blends direct model-reference adaptive control with an epoch-based schedule. Early epochs adapt and stabilize; later ones learn and optimize. The authors prove a high-probability regret bound that rivals the best known rates. Simulations show the method settles quickly without risky probing. Such designs matter wherever a controller must learn on the job, from drones to power converters, without a safe starting policy.
arxiv-2512-04765:
Pooja Singh, Sandeep Kumar, and co-authors present AdiBhashaa, a community-built benchmark for translating into four Indian tribal languages: Bhili, Mundari, Gondi, and Santali. Mainstream language technology barely sees these tongues. That invisibility deepens gaps in schooling, public services, and digital life for tribal communities. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the first open parallel corpora and baseline translation systems for the four languages.

Native speakers helped create the data, and human checks kept it sound. The team tested both classic encoder-decoder translators and large language models on the new sets. Results show how far current systems fall short and where they already help. Beyond scores, the project models a fairer way to do language research: local experts lead, and the community owns the resource. Such corpora are a first step toward digital access in one's own language.
arxiv-2512-05065:
James Flemings and five co-authors tackle a privacy problem created by personal language-model agents. Programs that act for a user often must decide whether sharing a piece of the user's data is acceptable. Letting the model decide alone works poorly — general privacy norms miss what a particular person wants, while feeding the model past decisions as examples yields shaky, hard-to-explain reasoning. The team proposes a hybrid that pairs the model with explicit logic.

Their framework, ARIEL, checks whether a user's earlier decision on a similar request logically implies the same answer for the new one, and only then applies it. Tested with advanced models on datasets, ARIEL cut the error rate for sharing judgments by a large margin compared with example-based reasoning, especially on requests the user would approve. The approach gives automated privacy decisions that are both more accurate and open to inspection.
arxiv-2512-05165:
Vincent Laude and David Röhlig offer a shortcut for spotting bound states in the continuum — waves trapped in a structure that, unusually, never leak energy away. Such states are normally hunted through quasi-normal modes, the structure's decaying resonances, which means computing complex eigenvalues. The authors note that a truly bound state should not care about the world outside the structure at all, and they turn that indifference into a test.

They vary the artificial boundary that closes the simulation domain and watch the spectrum respond: leaky modes shift, bound states stand still, and the contrast shows up cleanly in spectral histograms. The method matches the standard matched-layer analysis on two examples — a periodic array guiding surface waves, and a whispering-gallery resonator built from it — while skipping the imaginary parts entirely. Integral reciprocity results then explain why the trick works, grounding a practical time-saver in mathematics.
arxiv-2512-05565:
Jie Liu, Renhui Qin, and Ligong Bian take on a stubborn flaw in studies of how the early universe changed as it cooled. Their 2025 paper looks at the electroweak phase transition. At that moment, bubbles of a new state of matter formed and grew. Work on how fast these bubbles appear has long given answers that shift with choices made in the math. That flaw is known as gauge dependence.

The team works within a three dimensional thermal field theory. They prove the true rate at which bubbles form does not depend on those choices. The proof holds up to a demanding level of detail in the sums. It removes a large source of error from later work. That firmer ground sharpens forecasts of gravitational waves sent out by the young cosmos. It also helps tests of how matter gained its slight edge over antimatter soon after the Big Bang.
arxiv-2512-05865:
Florent Draye, Anson Lei, Hsiao-Ru Pan, Ingmar Posner, and Bernhard Schölkopf show that a transformer's attention web can be thinned almost to nothing, and the model still thinks as well. Normally that web is dense. Their post-training method adds a flexible sparsity pressure under a firm constraint: the original training loss may not rise. On models up to seven billion parameters, the loss held while attention kept well under one percent of its edges.

Sparsity acts as a structural prior, forcing the model into a tidier organization that humans can inspect. Local sparsity cascaded upward: the circuits that solve particular tasks shrank dramatically, with up to a hundredfold fewer edges linking their parts. Attention maps that were once hairballs become legible diagrams. Much of what dense attention computes is redundant. What remains is closer to the model's real algorithm.
arxiv-2512-06265:
Yinjie Guo and a large team map how superconductivity shifts as they twist two thin sheets of a tungsten selenium crystal by small angles. Twisting stacked sheets makes moire patterns that can turn plain materials into superconductors. Two past studies, at two twist angles, seemed to show two quite distinct maps of where the state appears, which raised doubts about whether the states share one cause.

The team made devices across the full span between those angles and charted each one. The superconducting state shifts smoothly as the angle changes, with no break between the two old maps. At every angle it sits near a reshaping of the electron surface, likely tied to opposed magnetic order, but not locked to two other features once blamed. The smooth trend gives fresh clues to the state's origin, and shows these twisted crystals make a clean lab for such states.
arxiv-2512-06365:
Xiang Guo, Zhihai Wang, and their co authors study a special quantum state that can hide inside a channel for light and stay put. These bound states in the continuum sit within a sea of passing waves yet do not leak away, which makes them prized for boosting the interplay of light and matter. The team places two rows of atoms along a chain of linked resonators, a setup from waveguide quantum optics, and varies how strongly each row couples over time.

They show a standing wave of light forms as one of these bound states. That mode can carry an unknown quantum state from one row of atoms to the other with very high fidelity. The transfer holds up even when the setup has flaws or loses energy along the way. The result marks bound states as durable tools for moving quantum information inside future devices.
arxiv-2512-06465:
Haijun Zhao and three co authors study spiral magnetic patterns that form at the surface of chiral magnets, where the magnetism twists by nature. Inside such a magnet, cone shaped spirals carry a hidden in plane direction set by a phase factor. In long spirals that direction averages away, but in short spirals and thin films it steps forward and shapes what forms at the borders between regions.

Simulations of the magnetic texture at borders between a plain aligned region and a conical one show surface spirals hugging those borders. Their shape and swirl charge are steered by how the cone's in plane direction resets at the border. In flat borders the spirals look like eyebrows, and film thickness sets the angle between top and bottom sets. The team also found them on skyrmion cluster faces, and confirmed them under a microscope in a cobalt zinc manganese film.
arxiv-2512-06765:
Vincent de Heij and three co authors estimate traffic across a road network using the road users themselves as sensors. In their framework, roadside sensors and connected vehicles act as cooperative sensing nodes. Each forms a local picture of density and flow. Each then shares it with nearby nodes over vehicle to everything links. No central brain gathers everything; the picture is built by agreement among neighbors.

Their estimator is a distributed Kalman filter tuned to a second order model of traffic flow, with a consensus step that fuses the differing local estimates. Projection steps keep the fused numbers physically sane. In microscopic simulations of a highway hit by passing congestion, the estimator rebuilt the nonlinear shockwave pattern faithfully, even with sparse fixed sensors and patchy vehicle links. The study also maps how the share of connected vehicles changes what the network can see, with sharp thresholds in observability.
arxiv-2512-06965:
Manfried Faber argues against a textbook claim: that the electron is a point with no size at all. Quantum field theory usually gives that answer, he notes, yet the same theory dresses each electron in a cloud of virtual particles that spreads its charge. Scattering experiments, where electrons are fired at targets at high energy, should be able to settle which picture the data favor.

Faber works through the theory's own formulas and the measured cross sections. Both, he argues, fit an electron whose extent matches the classical electron radius, a small but nonzero length from older physics. He offers a simple reading: at high energy, the electron's energy can be viewed as the cost of deforming its spread-out charge. The article also separates nearby terms, point-like, structureless, and substructureless, and answers the usual objections to a measured size.
arxiv-2512-07165:
Muyu Xu and co-authors make three-dimensional scene reconstruction from just a few photos far cheaper to train. The modern approach scatters a scene into millions of soft blobs and renders new views from them. Pose-free feed-forward versions lean on big pre-trained vision transformers, but adapting those backbones fully eats graphics memory and time. MuSASplat instead tunes the backbone lightly, through a small multi-scale adapter that touches only a fraction of the parameters.

A second piece, a feature fusion aggregator, merges information across the input views directly, replacing the memory banks earlier systems used. That swap keeps the geometry consistent between views while cutting memory, complexity, and cost. Across diverse data sets, the framework reached state-of-the-art rendering quality from sparse views while demanding far fewer trainable parameters and training resources than its rivals.
arxiv-2512-07265:
Bhavana Akkiraju and co-authors build the first careful benchmark for translating spoken Telugu into English text. Telugu is spoken by tens of millions, yet its rich word-building makes speech translation research thin on the ground. Their corpus draws on forty-six hours of manually verified recordings, split into training, development, and test portions. With it they stage a fair contest between the two standard architectures: a cascade that first transcribes, then translates, and end-to-end systems that go straight from sound to English.

A cascade pairing a Telugu-tuned recognizer with a dedicated translation model still scores highest, thanks to its heavy diet of language-specific data. But a fine-tuned all-in-one model came remarkably close while using far less Telugu material, suggesting end-to-end systems can compete in low-resource settings with careful tuning and modest parallel data.
arxiv-2512-07365:
Arieh Iserles studies the matrices that represent differentiation itself in spectral methods, the numerical schemes that expand a function's solution in a basis of special polynomials. When the basis is chosen well, the differentiation matrix acquires a semi-separable structure, a kind of low-complexity skeleton that fast algorithms can exploit. Laguerre and ultraspherical bases were known to give such matrices of the lowest rank, one.

Iserles extends the census to bases built from Jacobi polynomials, the broad family that contains many classical choices. Their differentiation matrices prove to be semi-separable of rank two, still strikingly lean. Getting there requires new results about semi-separable matrices in general, which the author notes may interest readers well beyond spectral methods. The practical stakes are design guidance: a basis whose derivative operator has a known.
arxiv-2512-07665:
R. Patrick Xian, Garry Gabison, Ahmed Alaa, Christoph Riedl, and Grigorios Chrysos wrote this 2025 paper on building reliable AI agents. Agents based on large language models are spreading through society. With that spread come hard questions of coordination, control, delegation, and accountability.

The authors look for answers in an older field: organization science. Human organizations have long balanced the same tensions between freedom and reliability. Evidence-based theories describe how they design roles, scale up, and manage members. The paper maps those frameworks onto the world of language-model agents. Three preliminary accounts carry the argument. Agent design must balance agency against capability in each role. Agent scaling must weigh resource limits against performance gains. Agent management needs both internal and external checks to stay reliable. The bridge between fields, they argue, should run in both directions. Social systems and AI systems can teach each other how to integrate well.
arxiv-2512-08365:
Yi Pan, Wenbo Qian, Dedong Xie, and colleagues, computer systems researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their tool, Magneton, hunts wasted energy in machine learning software. Training and running models burns enormous power, and while hardware keeps getting more efficient, sloppy software design quietly wastes energy through redundant or poorly chosen operations that developers cannot easily see.

Their idea, differential energy debugging, exploits a simple observation: rival systems doing the same job often use wildly different amounts of energy. Magneton profiles energy at the operator level and compares similar systems, pinpointing the code regions and settings behind excess use. Applied to nine popular systems, from language model inference to image generation, it found every known inefficiency case put before it. It also uncovered eight unknown cases, most later confirmed by developers, giving teams a practical way to cut power bills without new hardware.
arxiv-2512-08465:
Alexandre Gracia Calvo, Francesca Rossi, Eduardo Iraola, and colleagues, power systems engineers in Spain, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Modern grids face growing risk of cascading failures as they grow more complex and absorb more wind and solar power. The standard safety check asks whether the grid survives losing any one component, but operators increasingly need the far heavier check of losing any two.

Their framework runs that double contingency analysis with small signal stability checks, using high performance computing to make it tractable. A probabilistic risk index ranks components by combining how severe a failure would be with how often the parts involved actually fail. On a standard test grid, the system processed tens of thousands of scenarios and isolated assets prone to trigger cascades, catching critical components the single failure criterion overlooks. The workflow is offered as replicable, near real time support for operator decisions.
arxiv-2512-08665:
Sreelakshmi Nair, Aabhaas Vineet Mallik, and R S Patel study a layered magnetic material made of iron, germanium, and tellurium. The material draws interest because it stays magnetic at fairly high temperature and has strong magnetization, yet its behavior is complex. Part of that complexity comes from several distinct iron sites and from missing atoms in the lattice.

The team presents detailed temperature dependent Raman spectra for the bulk material, among the first full studies of that kind. They find an odd peak shift near a set low temperature, and discuss its link to a known odd lattice expansion at a nearby temperature. Magnetization tests also show how that expansion affects magnetic direction. The findings matter for future spintronic devices that might use this material.
arxiv-2512-09265:
Wei Teng, Sheng-Nan Wang, and Yu Zhang study the shapes of xenon atomic nuclei with mass near one hundred thirty. Such nuclei sit near a shape phase transition, a switch between prolate shapes, stretched like a rugby ball, and oblate shapes, flattened like a lens. The authors use the interacting boson model, an algebraic way to describe collective nuclear motion.

Their scheme adds the shape transition into the model in a simple form. It predicts unusual soft vibrational modes near the transition point, marked by quadrupole moments with a distinctive sign pattern. Those predictions help explain measurements in the xenon isotopes, especially a nearly vanishing quadrupole moment that experiments had found puzzling. The authors present the result as fresh insight into how gamma-soft deformed nuclei, which wobble rather than hold one shape, are put together.
arxiv-2512-09565:
Faraz Ali and colleagues present DNS-HyXNet, a model for spotting DNS tunneling in real time. Tunneling abuses the domain name system, the internet's address book, to smuggle data out of a network or control malware, hiding traffic inside name queries. Graph-based detectors are accurate but slow, because they parse and rebuild graphs for each sequence.

Their model instead reads packet sequences directly. It combines tokenized domain name embeddings with normalized DNS features and feeds them through a two-layer long short-term memory network, which learns the time patterns. That removes graph reconstruction and allows single-stage multi-class classification. Trained and tested on two datasets with tuned settings for low memory and fast inference, the model reached accuracy above ninety-nine percent with near-perfect averaged precision, recall, and F1 scores. Detection times ran at millisecond scale per sample, below a millisecond, suitable for commodity hardware.
arxiv-2512-09765:
Shraosi Dawn, Subrata Ghosh, Chandrakala Meena, Tim Rogers, and Chittaranjan Hens ask where instability begins in dynamical systems spread over undirected networks. Such systems appear in fields from disease spread to biochemistry. The authors study the spectrum of the Jacobian matrices tied to a broad class of networked systems. That spectrum shows how a small disturbance at a steady state grows or fades over time. They find that stability is always set by one outlying value in the spectrum.

Where trouble starts, though, depends on the details of the model. Instability may begin at nodes with unusually few connections, at nodes with unusually many, or everywhere in the network at once. Finite network size matters a great deal as well. The authors check their theory on epidemic dynamics and on gene regulatory systems, and they suggest the results could help monitor networks to predict or prevent sudden failures.
arxiv-2512-09965:
Tamiaki Yoneya builds a statistical field theory for Nambu dynamics, an old broadening of classic mechanics. Standard dynamics runs on one Hamiltonian function. Nambu dynamics uses several Hamiltonians on an equal footing, tied by a wider canonical structure. Extending the theory to interacting systems without breaking that structure has been an open problem. Yoneya borrows tools from quantum field theory and classical statistical dynamics, casting the system as a field theory on Nambu's generalized phase space, in operator form with a probabilistic reading.

Within it, he gives a simple model of self interaction in a many body Nambu system. The closed system obeys an H-theorem, the drive toward equilibrium. Starting from certain non equilibrium states, continuous random processes carry it toward generalized microcanonical and canonical ensembles, the latter marked by many temperatures rather than one.
arxiv-2512-10165:
Matt Miller, Dan Sinykin, and Melanie Walsh present BookReconciler, an open source tool that cleans up messy book metadata. Library staff and scholars often hold spreadsheets with little more than titles and authors. The tool enriches such rows with trusted identifiers like ISBNs, and clusters records that represent the same underlying work: editions, translations, and formats grouped as expressions and manifestations of one work. It plugs into OpenRefine, a popular data cleaning application, and queries major bibliographic services, from the Library of Congress and WorldCat to HathiTrust, Google Books, and Wikidata.

A hands-on interface lets users judge matches and decide what counts as the same work. Tested on prize winning American books and contemporary world fiction, the tool reconciled American works almost perfectly. Scores dropped for global texts, exposing structural weaknesses in bibliographic infrastructure for non English literature.
arxiv-2512-11165:
Lucas Domingos and colleagues clean up sound recordings of moving targets whose echoes blur the original signal. Passive listening is a cheap way to monitor ships and aircraft, but reflections arriving by several paths, plus motion effects, tangle source and echo together. Existing filters ignore how the local environment shapes those reflections.

Their method filters the spectrum's cepstral form, which separates source structure from echo structure, using an adaptive band stop filter. The filter widens or narrows itself according to the strength of echo related components. On simulated aircraft noise across a wide speed range, the method improved signal quality and distance measures. It also raised ship type classification accuracy on two underwater datasets. The authors aim next at preserving signal strength and handling several sensors at once.
arxiv-2512-11365:
Ilja Honkonen, Riku Jarvinen, and David Phillips present a new method for simulating magnetised fluids on grids that refine themselves where detail is needed. Magnetohydrodynamics models plasmas from solar wind to fusion devices, and physical consistency demands the magnetic field keep zero divergence everywhere, a condition sloppy numerics easily break. Their scheme builds on the constrained transport method, which preserves that condition by building.

The method works on staggered meshes, where magnetic quantities live on cell faces, and supports cell based adaptive refinement, so resolution follows the action. A temporal substepping feature lets fine regions advance in smaller time steps than coarse ones. Resolution changes are handled directly on the logical grid, with no interpolation or projection between levels and no coupling machinery between them. That simplicity makes high resolution plasma model run cheaper to run and easier to maintain.
arxiv-2512-11665:
Atte Keitaanranta and co-authors simulate how giant black holes pair up and merge in young, compact galaxies. Their zoom in simulation follows a galaxy that reaches 8.5 times ten to the tenth solar masses by redshift 5. A new code, KETJU, tracks black holes from seeding down to their final merge.

All nine big galaxies in the run pass through a tight, gas rich phase between redshifts 7 and 9. They look much like the Little Red Dots seen by the Webb telescope. Dense star packed cores then drag paired black holes together fast, in just 4 to 35 million years once bound. The team also tracks the full gravity wave signal, from slow pulses to the final chirp.
arxiv-2512-11865:
