Smart farming robots that see with RGB cameras and act with arms face a weak spot: light based attacks. Shifts in hue, brightness, or noise can fool their perception and cause wrong moves. The authors counter with an explainable, attack resistant Vision-Language-Action model built on OpenVLA-OFT.

An added Evidence-3 module spots photometric tampering, meaning light based fakes, and explains the cause and effect in plain words. In tests the model cut current action error by 21.7 percent and next action error by 18.4 percent versus the base model. Accuracy and clear explanations rose together under attack. Such pairing matters for field robots that must be both tough and auditable.
arxiv-2512-11965:
Pradip Kattel, Abay Zhakenov, and Natan Andrei show the multichannel Kondo effect can live inside superconducting leads. The classic effect needs several metal channels screening one magnetic impurity, more channels than the spin can absorb, yielding strange non Fermi liquid behavior. Metals were thought essential, since superconductors are gapped.

Their system couples one spin half impurity to several one dimensional superconducting channels with quasi long range order. Using the Bethe Ansatz, they find four phases: an overscreened Kondo phase, a zero mode phase, a Yu-Shiba-Rusinov phase, and a free local moment phase. In the Kondo phase the boundary behavior matches the gapless theory exactly, gap or no gap. Entropy formulas are given for each phase.
arxiv-2512-12465:
Uriel Singer and Yaron Lipman explore the design space of Transition Matching in a 2025 paper. Transition Matching is a new generative modeling approach that generalizes diffusion and flow matching. Like them, it turns noise into data step by step, but an inner generative model performs each transition, making steps more expressive. A big backbone plus a smaller head module keep it tractable.

The team trained 56 text to image models of 1.7 billion parameters, giving 549 evaluations, to test head design, training, and sampling. An MLP head with a specific time weighting and a high frequency sampler ranked best overall. A transformer head with sequence scaling and low frequency sampling came second, excelling at image aesthetics.
arxiv-2512-12765:
V Prayag and many co-authors report twelve new radio pulsars in the Large Magellanic Cloud in a 2025 paper. The finds come from the TRAPUM survey with the MeerKAT telescope, using L-band receivers and eighteen new pointings with two hour integrations. The survey total rises to 19 pulsars, and the known LMC radio pulsar count to 44, an 80 percent increase.

The new set includes PSR J0454-6927, the slowest extragalactic radio pulsar known, with a spin period of 2238 ms. Another, PSR J0452-6921, shows the highest dispersion measure among extragalactic radio pulsars, at 326 pc per cubic cm. The fastest new spin is 245 ms. Timing solutions for seven earlier pulsars show isolated, canonical pulsars with ages up to 8.8 million years.
arxiv-2512-12865:
Jean Goubault-Larrecq studies barycentric algebras, abstract structures that capture the idea of weighted averages, much as convex sets do. His paper, at 98 pages, looks at versions of these algebras that also carry a sense of closeness, called topology. A 2008 study of cones by Klaus Keimel is his model.

He proves results on free structures, on when one kind of algebra can sit inside another, and on forms of local convexity. A running theme is the barycenter, or average point, of a measure-like object. The paper ends with a broad theorem that such barycenters exist. Valuations, close cousins of measures, are a key example throughout.
arxiv-2512-12965:
Thayssa Rocha and co-authors study remote and hybrid work for people with disabilities on software development teams. Working from home has grown fast in tech. It brings fresh chances for inclusion, and fresh barriers as well.

The study asks how remote work shapes the daily experience of disabled developers on mixed teams. It focuses on the problems that arise at a distance and on the tactics people use to handle them. The aim is practical: to name both the challenges and the enablers clearly. That naming can guide teams that want remote work to include disabled colleagues fully, not just in name.
arxiv-2512-13165:
Jakub Lyskawa, Jakub Lewandowski, and Pawel Wawrzynski present SACn, a version of the Soft Actor-Critic algorithm that learns from multi-step returns. Soft Actor-Critic is a leading method for online reinforcement learning without a model. Multi-step returns speed learning, but combining them with this algorithm has been tricky.

The usual fix, importance sampling, corrects for changed action probabilities yet can turn numerically unstable. Their approach applies that correction in a stable way with simpler tuning of its settings. They also rework entropy estimation to cut variance in the learning target. The final algorithm was tested on MuJoCo simulated control tasks, a standard check suite for such methods.
arxiv-2512-13365:
A. I. Perminov presents a parallel random search method for cutting the added cost of fast matrix multiplication schemes. Fast schemes trade multiplications for additions, so trimming additions via common subexpression removal matters. Exact scoring of candidate rewrites is expensive, which slows the search.

His method scores candidates with fast heuristics instead, including a new greedy intersections strategy. Many separate removal runs proceed in parallel, swapping random pairs and sharing promising partial solutions. Over 149 ternary schemes, it beat the prior best method on 102, matched it on 45, and lost on only 2. It also ran much faster, with all software open source.
arxiv-2512-13665:
Wenhan Chen, Sezer Karaoglu, and Theo Gevers build Grab-3D, a detector for AI-generated videos based on 3D geometry. Diffusion models now make highly realistic videos, so reliable detection matters. Past detectors barely used the 3D patterns hidden in video frames.

The authors use vanishing points as an explicit sign of 3D geometry and find clear gaps in geometric consistency between real and fake videos. Grab-3D is a transformer with geometric positional encoding, temporal-geometric attention, and a smoothed classifier head. They built a data set of static scenes for stable geometry checks. In tests, Grab-3D beat top detectors by a clear margin and held up on unseen generators.
arxiv-2512-13865: Simion Filip surveys recent work on measure rigidity beyond homogeneous dynamics. Rigidity results show that invariant measures in a dynamical system are often far more constrained than they first appear. Classic results rely on a Lie group acting homogeneously, which limits their reach. Filip shows how some measure and topological rigidity results now extend to quite general manifolds. The article, written for the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians proceedings, gives a guided account of that extension in 20 pages.
arxiv-2512-14065:
Y. S. Liu and X. Z. Zhang study how a tunable long-range hopping term breaks integrability in spin chains, in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian versions. Ergodicity breaking in complex quantum systems is a central question in nonequilibrium physics. Their one-dimensional model uses the hopping term as a bridge between the two regimes.

Using level-spacing statistics, Krylov complexity, and entanglement entropy, they show the term acts as a universal control driving the move from integrability to quantum chaos. Statistics cross from Poissonian to Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble form as its strength grows, in both regimes. Despite global chaos, a tower of exact nonthermal eigenstates survives as quantum many-body scars. Those states keep low entanglement and coherent dynamics even under strong non-Hermitian perturbations, a route to preserving coherence.
arxiv-2512-14365:
Filip Klimovic, Jens Paaske, and Tomas Ostatnicky analyze the terahertz response of a confined electron hole pair in a 2025 paper. The pair sits inside a semiconductor nanoparticle, and the question is how confinement and their Coulomb attraction jointly shape the response.

The interplay causes large renormalizations and energy shifts in the terahertz linear conductivity of the nanocrystal. The authors build models for the strong and weak confinement regimes to treat the Coulomb effect correctly. In the weak regime, solutions look like a Wannier wavefunction whose size shrinks under confinement. Those states scale down to the strong regime, so one theory can describe exciton response for nanoparticles of any size.
arxiv-2512-14465:
Siyuan Zhu and three co-authors tackle context choice for question answering over long documents. Giving a model too little text risks missing the answer, while too much buries it in noise. Fixed-size retrieval cannot adapt, especially for simple factual questions that need only a few lines of evidence.

Context-Picker learns to find the smallest set of passages that still suffices. Training runs in two stages, first rewarding wide recall, then rewarding trimming. Because good example sets are scarce, the team mined them offline by removing passages one at a time. On five long-context and multi-hop benchmarks, answers beat strong retrieval baselines.
arxiv-2512-14565:
Fabian Haak and Philipp Schaer work on measuring linguistic bias in news and social media, a judgment call that is subjective and short on trusted labeled data. Instead of scoring texts one by one, annotators can compare pairs and say which is more biased. Pairwise judging is easier per item but explodes in cost, so the authors hunt for cheaper designs.

Simulations with built-in noise and biased fake annotators tested three cost-aware variants and their settings. The best setups then faced real human-labeled benchmarks, against direct scoring by large language models and plain pairwise labels. The results support pairwise comparison as a workable base for quantifying subjective language traits.
arxiv-2512-14765: Justin Jung proposes a way to guide discrete diffusion models so they can solve constraint satisfaction problems. Such problems ask for an answer that obeys strict rules all at once. He tests the method on Sudoku, the number puzzle where each row, column, and block must hold each digit exactly once. The guided model solves the puzzles without supervision, meaning it is never shown worked answers. The result points to a new use for diffusion methods, better known for making images, in tasks that call for step by step reasoning.
arxiv-2512-14865:
Advait Gosai leads a team of eleven authors who built a tougher test for voice based AI assistants. New spoken dialogue systems take in raw audio and reply in speech, skipping text entirely. Older tests used fake speech and single exchanges, so they missed how well systems handle real, messy conversation over many turns.

Their open benchmark, Audio MultiChallenge, holds 452 conversations from 47 speakers, scored with 1712 tailored rubrics. It tests memory for past details, holding onto instructions, staying coherent, and a new skill: coping when speakers fix their own words mid sentence. Ambient sounds and tone of voice also count as clues. Even the best model tested, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, passed only 54.65 percent of cases. Coherence faded as talks grew longer, showing where voice AI still falls short.
arxiv-2512-15165:
Giacomo Albi and two coauthors model how opinions spread in social networks where popularity feeds on itself. In their kinetic model, both the flow of opinions and the making of contacts depend on how popular agents are and how prominent their views seem. A new feedback loop runs the other way too: opinions shape which contacts form.

On top of this coupled system they add control laws, stand ins for awareness campaigns or moderation policies. The controls promote contact with popular individuals and amplify dominant opinions, acting on both opinion formation and connectivity at once. Simulations show the controls can blunt polarization, foster consensus, or steer the whole opinion distribution in a network that keeps rewiring itself. The work gives policy minded readers a math test bed for interventions in online social life.
arxiv-2512-15365:
Gajendra Doniparthi and three coauthors build ArcBERT, a search engine that lets researchers explore biological metadata in plain language. Research data management systems hold structured metadata for huge collections of multi omics datasets. Classic search tools demand keyword queries, which forces users to guess the exact terms in the records.

ArcBERT uses a large language model trained for the domain, so it matches meaning rather than keywords. It also understands the structure and hierarchies inside the metadata, not just the text. That lets it handle many styles of user questions about integrated datasets. The system points to a shift in how scientists find data: ask naturally, and let semantic matching do the digging. For data stewards, it offers a template for smarter discovery across research repositories.
arxiv-2512-15765:
Melissa Tamine and co authors make Shapley based data valuation practical for language model alignment in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. When a model is aligned on several data sources, Shapley values can score each source's contribution. The standard method needs a separate alignment for every coalition of sources, an exponential cost.

For direct alignment algorithms, the authors show that sequential training, source by source, makes each stage add a known amount to response log probabilities. Any coalition's score can then be rebuilt from the base model and one model per source, cutting cost from exponential to linear. Experiments across base models and reward models show how source contributions vary by evaluation criteria.
arxiv-2512-15965:
Annalivia Polselli presents xtdml, an R package for double machine learning in panel data models, in a 2025 paper. Double machine learning pairs machine learning prediction with statistics to infer a target parameter while controlling for many confounders. Panel data add fixed effects for each unit, which the original methods did not handle.

The package carries out methods for partly linear panel models with low dimensional fixed effects and many controls, following Clarke and Polselli. Users can learn nuisance functions with learners from the mlr3 ecosystem. Unseen unit gaps are handled by first differences, within group changes, or correlated random effects, and controls can be rescaled or expanded. Simulated and real panel data show the package in use.
arxiv-2512-16065:
Sean Breckling and eight co-authors test an extreme imaging task in a 2025 paper on arXiv. Tomography rebuilds a 3D picture of an object from X-ray views, usually from many angles. The team asks how well a learned method can do with just one view, when the target is symmetric around its axis.

They use Learned Primal Dual, a neural method that has done well with few or limited views. Training data came from exact math formulas for parallel X-rays and from physics-based ray tracing for a cone-beam test setup, with blur and noise added. The paper compares the learned reconstructions against standard numerical inversion methods. The results probe how far data-driven imaging can go when measurements are scarce, a question that matters for inspection and security scanning.
arxiv-2512-16465:
Jinwu Chen and seven co-authors automate GPU programming in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. CUDA kernels, the small programs that run on graphics cards, decide the speed of AI workloads, but tuning them demands rare hardware expertise. Language models paired with evolutionary search can write kernels, yet weak agent designs hold them back.

Their framework, cuPilot, coordinates several agents around an intermediate representation called strategy, a semantic sketch of how a kernel should be optimized. A strategy-coordinated evolution algorithm, roofline-guided prompts that reason about hardware limits, and strategy-level seeding of the population are its main parts. On a benchmark of 100 kernels, cuPilot's output ran on average 3.09 times faster than PyTorch. On matrix multiplication tasks it found sophisticated optimizations with high hardware utilization. The kernels are open-sourced.
arxiv-2512-16965:
Akila Wickramasekara and coauthors introduce AutoDFBench 1.0, a framework that automates testing of digital forensic tools under the NIST Computer Forensic Tool Testing programme, the de facto standard for validating such tools. No shared automated bench covered its diverse tasks before.

The bench spans five task areas: string search, deleted file recovery, file carving, Windows registry recovery, and SQLite recovery. Ground truth holds 63 test cases and 10,968 scenarios, scored through a REST API with precision, recall, and F1 outputs whose average forms the AutoDFBench Score. The design lets vendors, researchers, and standards bodies compare tools and AI-written code fairly and repeatably.
arxiv-2512-17065:
Dhruvesh Patel and coauthors release XLM, a Python package for non-autoregressive language models, which write text in parallel rather than word by word. Interest in such models has revived, but code was scattered and bespoke, blocking fair comparisons.

Each model family used to need its own data collation, loss, and prediction logic. XLM shares those parts so new methods can be built fast and tested alike. A companion package, xlm-models, ships small pre-trained models for the community to use at once. The authors aim to give non-autoregressive research the standard tooling that autoregressive work has long enjoyed.
arxiv-2512-17365:
Fryderyk Falniowski and Elżbieta Pliś model what a brand-new product does to a whole market. Their frame follows Joseph Schumpeter, who saw economies churn as fresh goods destroy old ones. In their population game, two kinds of firms share the market: innovators who launch new products and imitators who copy them, settled in one stable balance.

A new product shifts the mix of goods on offer, and the team tracks how that shift in diversity moves the stable balance. The effect depends on the traits of the new product itself. Their result casts diversity change as a driving force of innovation, a hidden engine behind creative destruction. For policy and strategy, the mix of products matters as much as their number.
arxiv-2512-17565:
J. Jarecki and coauthors track how energy races through nanoscale copper layers in a stack of platinum, copper, and nickel. They fire ultrafast x ray pulses at the stack and read the motion from how the nickel layer expands, which reports how fast heat and hot electrons arrive.

As the laser fluence changes, the nickel response follows a diffusive transport model and not the ballistic one. The team concludes that diffusion rules once the copper is thicker than twice the electronic inelastic mean free path, a length of about 25 nanometers, so the crossover sits near 50 nanometers. The result guides how thin metal films in fast electronics move energy on the shortest time scales.
arxiv-2512-17665:
Zhouhang Mao works in p-adic geometry, a branch of algebra that studies numbers and shapes through p-adic completions. His long paper links three topics: de-completed topological periodic cyclic homology, the Segal conjecture, and a smoothness condition called F-smoothness. The results connect homology theories used to probe rings and their geometry.

Mao proves that a motivic filtration on the de-completed homology is complete for rings with a weakly finitely generated cotangent complex. For F-smooth rings, he shows the Segal conjecture holds for their topological Hochschild homology. He also builds filtrations on Hodge-Tate cohomology and deduces that weak and strong F-smoothness pass along in a transitive way.
arxiv-2512-17865:
Sofia Chiarenza leads a large team measuring a faint clue about the infant universe, called primordial non-Gaussianity. The clue would show whether the first seeds of galaxies grew in the simplest way or a richer one. They cross match 1.2 million quasars from the DESI survey with a lensing map from the Planck satellite.

The quasars fall into three distance bands, letting the team track the signal across cosmic time. Their best fits sit close to zero, with values of 2 and 6 under two assumptions about how quasars respond. The limits are about 35 percent tighter than the best earlier quasar study, which sharpens tests of how the universe began.
arxiv-2512-17965:
Zachary J. Wegert leads a six author team studying plates that turn ocean waves into electric power. Each plate pairs two layers that make voltage when bent, split by an elastic core. The team asks whether such a plate gathers more energy floating on the surface or sunk below it.

They derive the plate's motion from the full laws for such materials and solve it with a panel method. Across many settings, sunk plates beat floating ones at soaking up wave energy. Edges held firm also beat edges left loose, by a small margin. Two materials were compared, and the team's code is shared in the open for others to test.
arxiv-2512-18065:
G. Tiago and four coauthors build a tabletop way to fake a key kind of quantum noise. The depolarizing channel scrambles a quantum state in every direction at once, and engineers use it as a standard test of quantum gear. Their setup uses light whose spin and path are locked together in a compact circuit of lenses and mirrors.

Several test states passed through the circuit and came out matching the ideal scrambled forms. The match also held against a second method, a Solovay-Kitaev breakdown of the same channel, shown here for the first time. A cheap, honest noise faker helps labs check error handling before they scale up.
arxiv-2512-18165:
Hamza Abdelhedi and coauthors present Coord2Region, an open source Python package for brain imaging research. Feed it a 3D brain coordinate, in MNI or Talairach space, and it returns the anatomical region that the point falls in, across several atlases at once.

The package then links each region to the published literature through NiMARE, with direct ties to Neurosynth and NeuroQuery. An optional language model feature writes short summaries of the linked studies and draws pictures of the regions. That aid sits next to the peer reviewed sources, not in place of them. Coord2Region runs single points or large batches, works from the command line or a web page hosted on Hugging Face, and aims to cut manual errors in coordinate based workflows.
arxiv-2512-18365:
Badr Moufad leads a seven author team making image inpainting cheaper to run. Inpainting fills a missing or marked patch of a photo with plausible new content. Ready trained diffusion models can do it with no extra training, but the best zero shot methods pay for each step with costly passes back through the denoising network.

Their new stand in score gives plain bell shaped update steps that skip those backward passes entirely. In tests the fills stayed true to the kept parts of each photo and looked clean and whole, rivaling versions that were fine tuned for the task. The savings in memory and time were large, which brings high grade editing closer to everyday hardware.
arxiv-2512-18765:
Andrea B. Rava and three co-authors separate real physics from hardware flaws in a Rydberg atom quantum simulator. Their chain of atoms realizes an Ising model with both transverse and longitudinal fields. Experiments ran on QuEra's Aquila processor, with large-scale emulations from the JUQAS simulator for comparison. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, tracks how correlations spread through the chain.

In the ideal case, the longitudinal field confines domain walls into meson-like bound states, shrinking the correlation light cone step by step. With realistic imperfections added, correlations instead stop at a finite distance even where theory expects freedom, a localization caused by emergent disorder. The close match between noisy emulation and experiment lets the team name the dominant error channels. Confinement survives as a robust, programmable tool for building non-ergodic dynamics.
arxiv-2512-19265:
Zun-Xian Zhang, Mengchu Cai, Bolun Hu, and Xiangyu Jiang measure a key constant of mixed-action lattice QCD, where the quarks used to generate gauge fields differ from those used to measure. The constant, Delta mix, captures the leading mismatch effect in the low-energy theory. Knowing its size helps correct mixed-action results.

The team computed it on ensembles with up, down, strange, and charm quarks, using HISQ fermions and an improved gauge action at four lattice spacings. Comparing with other actions and a three-flavor case, they find the fermion action matters most. The gauge action has a smaller, real effect, and charm loops are negligible for now.
arxiv-2512-20165:
Aviad Eisenberg, Sharon Gannot, and Shlomo Chazan build a speaker extraction system that does not fully trust its own clues. Pulling one voice from a noisy multi-channel mixture usually leans on spatial cues, where the speaker is, or spectral cues, what the voice sounds like, and each can be wrong in practice. Their algorithm feeds both cue types into a dedicated network trained to balance them dynamically.

When one cue degrades or misleads, the network learns to down-weight or disregard it in favor of the other, keeping extraction stable. Evaluation simulates the sloppy conditions of real deployments, using a simple direction-of-arrival estimator and a noisy enrollment process to generate flawed references at test time. The system still extracted the target speaker under substantial reference inaccuracies.
arxiv-2512-20665:
Nicolas Bueno, Luis F Ayala, and Yashar Mehmani write the first kinetic theory of bubbles trading mass underground. In porous rock, trapped gas bubbles differ in size and composition; through Ostwald ripening, big bubbles grow at the expense of small ones. Underground hydrogen storage, with its cycles of fragmented gas, is the motivating application.

Single-component theories existed for porous media, but mixtures had none. The new formulation tracks a number-density function over a three-dimensional state space of pore size, bubble saturation, and composition. A population balance equation, closed by mean-field approximations respecting pore-size correlations and mass conservation, governs the evolution. Validation against pore-network simulations across four network types agrees well with no adjustable parameters. Predictions can now exceed the pore scale.
arxiv-2512-21265:
Matteo Vezzelli, Carsten Gachot, and Maria Clelia Righi compute why a lubricant performs unevenly from floor to floor. Black phosphorus and its layer phosphorene slide well, but experiments show the lubricity depends on the substrate underneath. Using density functional theory, the authors measure adhesion energies for pristine and oxidized phosphorene resting on aluminum, copper, iron, and chromium, and on each metal's oxide. They match the numbers against measured friction.

Oxidized phosphorene sticks harder to all of them, thanks to oxygen's non-bonding states reaching for empty substrate states. Bare metals grip more strongly than their oxides, with iron and chromium strongest because of their partly filled 3d orbitals. That matches the drop in friction seen once scratching strips iron's oxide skin away. Some interfaces even turn the phosphorene metallic. Tribology engineers gain a design rule: a solid lubricant is only half the system, and the interface's chemistry decides the rest.
arxiv-2512-21465:
Kenzo Imamura, Suguru Otani, Tohya Sugano, and Koji Yokote examine how economists measure assortativeness in matching markets. Assortativeness describes whether similar types tend to pair with each other, as in marriage or hiring markets. A 2025 study by Chiappori and co-authors proposed indices such as the aggregate likelihood ratio and the odds ratio, with axioms claimed to single out each one.

The authors give a counterexample showing the characterization of the aggregate likelihood ratio fails as stated. They identify exactly which class of indices the original axioms do characterize. Adding new axioms, which they supply, recovers the intended characterization. They also flag errors in the axiomatizations of other measures from the same study. Finally, they generalize the odds ratio from two-type markets to multi-type markets. The note audits the foundations behind widely used matching statistics.
arxiv-2512-21665:
C. L. Liu, Baoqing Sun, and D. L. Zhou answer a question about entanglement transformations. Two parties holding an entangled quantum state can manipulate it using local operations and classical communication, called LOCC. For pure states, the rules for which transformations are possible are well understood. Mixed states, though, can be prepared as many different ensembles of pure states.

The natural hope was that transformation rules for mixed states could be read off from their pure-state ensembles. Liu and his co-authors rule this out. They show that satisfying the inequalities for every convex-roof entanglement measure is not enough to guarantee an LOCC transformation between two mixed states. Likewise, comparing average entanglement across ensembles, for all entanglement monotones, does not ensure an ensemble-to-ensemble transformation exists. The result closes off a tempting shortcut and settles open questions. Mixed-state entanglement must be treated on its terms.
arxiv-2512-21765:
Samir Bhatt, Ruriko Yoshida, and their co-authors review the tropical Grassmannian as a tool for phylogenetics, the reconstruction of trees. The number of possible tree shapes explodes with the number of species, making tree space hard to search and summarize. The classical Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann space gives tree space a nice geometry but brings computational difficulties.

Tropical geometry, a piecewise-linear shadow of algebra, offers an alternative. Speyer and Sturmfels showed that the tropical Grassmannian for two-planes coincides with the space of trees. The paper explains that structure and presents algorithms for working with it, including procedures for sampling trees from the tropical Grassmannian. Sampling matters because biologists need to explore the distribution of plausible trees, not just find one best guess. The authors aim to make the machinery accessible to biologists and seed new work where algebraic geometry meets phylogenetic inference.
arxiv-2512-21865:
Yihan Hu, Xuelin Chen, and Xiaodong Cun decompose a video into layers: foreground, clean background, and cast effects such as shadows and reflections. This task, video omnimatte, usually relies on slow multi-stage pipelines that waste generative models' power.

Their insight is that an inpainting model fine-tuned to remove a foreground and its effects must already perceive those effects, so it can be fine-tuned again to extract them. A naive fine-tune gives good alpha mattes but misses the effects. The authors trace this to specific transformer blocks where effect cues live, suppressed when adapters are applied everywhere. EasyOmnimatte trains two experts: an effect expert adapted only on the sensitive blocks, and a fully adapted quality expert for matte refinement. Sampling uses the effect expert at noisy early steps, the quality expert later, in one pass. The method sets a new state of the art.
arxiv-2512-22265:
Bachir Bekka and Christian Brouder examine symmetry in infinite crystals. In that setting the usual finite-crystal shortcuts break down. Textbook treatments use a finite crystal with periodic boundary conditions, making the Brillouin zone a finite point set. Covering continuous crystal momentum, and whether band energy levels vary smoothly, requires truly infinite crystals whose symmetry groups are infinite and non-compact.

For such groups, character theory cannot be used. The authors instead build the tools from harmonic analysis. It includes the group algebra, the regular representation, and induction of irreducible forms from projective forms of point groups. They cover magnetic and non-magnetic groups in any dimension. Later sections treat restriction to subgroups and tensor products of induced forms.
arxiv-2512-22465:
R. J. Fries and seven co-authors work out the quantum mechanics of quark coalescence, the moment a quark and antiquark bind into a meson inside high-energy collisions. Their non-relativistic quark model assumes a harmonic oscillator potential and Gaussian wave packets for the incoming quarks. The special emphasis is excited meson states, which simpler treatments often leave out or handle inconsistently.

The formalism systematically includes excited states listed by the Particle Data Group. It adds further states the quark model predicts, up to high orbital angular momentum and masses near 2.2 giga-electronvolts for light flavors. Mass and decay estimates are provided for unconfirmed states. A phase-space picture matches the quasi-classic information Monte Carlo simulations supply, and the authors show excited mesons are populated abundantly in typical jet configurations.
arxiv-2512-23065:
Melikşah Türker and co-authors introduce TabiBERT, a language model built for Turkish. Encoder models like BERT remain the workhorses for classification, tagging, and retrieval. Yet Turkish had no monolingual encoder trained from scratch with the modern improvements of the ModernBERT design, such as rotary embeddings and long context. TabiBERT fills that gap, pretrained on one trillion tokens drawn from a multi-domain corpus of web text, scientific writing, code, and mathematics.

The model handles contexts of more than eight thousand tokens, sixteen times longer than earlier Turkish BERT models. For fair measurement the team built TabiBench, a benchmark of twenty-seven datasets across eight task categories with standardized splits. TabiBERT led Turkish models in five categories and beat the previous best, BERTurk, in six, with the biggest gains in question answering and code retrieval. Weights, configurations, and evaluation code are released for reproducible Turkish research.
arxiv-2512-23665:
Tim Vieira, Ryan Cotterell, and Jason Eisner build tooling that analyzes algorithms the way compilers analyze code. Researchers in natural language processing routinely design dynamic programming algorithms over rich formal structures. They then prove by hand that the running time is bounded, that derived quantities have the right types, and that no part of the computation is dead or redundant. Those proofs are tedious and error-prone.

Their system automates much of that analysis, inferring types, flagging dead and redundant code, and deriving parametric runtime and space bounds for the algorithm as written. Applied to a range of NLP algorithms, it reproduced the analyses their designers had done by hand, sparing each new tool's author weeks of checked proofs. The manuscript dates from 2021 and was accepted by the Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, though it was not revised for publication.
arxiv-2512-23765:
Tiancheng Su, Meicong Zhang, and Guoxiu He tweak speculative decoding, the trick that lets a small draft model propose tokens for a large model to verify, speeding up text generation. Normally the technique is used purely for acceleration, and output quality stays capped by the large target model. Their variant, Entropy-Aware Speculative Decoding, needs no training and aims at quality as well.

The method watches for a suspicious pattern: both models are highly uncertain, yet their top predictions overlap strongly. In those uncertain-agreement cases it rejects the agreed token and resamples from the target model's distribution, stopping a shaky guess from steering everything after it. On hard reasoning benchmarks the approach consistently beat standard speculative decoding and reward-guided variants at comparable speed, and it sometimes outperformed the target model running alone.
arxiv-2512-24065:
Nicolas Fournier and Stéphane Mischler prove a basic result for the Boltzmann equation. That equation governs how gas particles collide and spread. The claim is called propagation of chaos. It says a large system of colliding particles matches the equation's smooth solution. In the limit, the particles act as if independent.

The pair prove this for moderately soft potentials. In that regime, slow particles collide very often. The math becomes singular and delicate. They adapt recent work by Imbert, Silvestre, and Villani. One estimate does the key work. Fisher information never grows along solutions of the particle system's master equation. That bound tames the singular interaction. The result closes a gap between particle-level randomness and the continuum picture of gases.
arxiv-2512-24165:
Zefeng He and five colleagues challenge how AI models that handle images and text do their reasoning. Most such models think in words alone. That serves them poorly on long tasks built around pictures. Fine spatial detail suffers as well. The team proposes reasoning in images instead. Their framework is called DiffThinker. It turns the reasoning task into an image-to-image one. Diffusion models do the work.

A head-to-head comparison brings out four traits of the new approach. It is leaner, easier to steer, able to work in parallel, and able to team up with other tools. Tests span four domains. They cover step-by-step planning and hard search problems. Rule-based puzzles and spatial layouts complete the set. DiffThinker beat top closed models by wide margins. It also beat a fine-tuned large open model.
arxiv-2512-24365:
Krishna Kumar benchmarks scientific machine learning for geotechnical engineering. Neural methods promise alternatives to standard numerical workflows. Four families face finite-difference and particle-based references. They are plain perceptrons, physics-informed networks, operator networks, and graph network simulators. Extrapolation, cost, transfer, and physics accuracy are the yardsticks.

The results counsel caution. A perceptron fit two years of consolidation data well. At year ten its predictions scattered wildly by activation choice. A physics-informed network matched a damped oscillator inside its training window. Outside that window it failed, since its residual constrains nothing there. For a wave problem, its training ran tens of thousands of times slower than finite differences. Operator networks avoided retraining but cost millions of solver runs to train. Differentiable physics solvers won the inverse test outright. Kumar assigns neural methods a careful role: interpolation inside validated domains.
arxiv-2512-24465:
Ava Polzin and a long list of co-authors write a white paper on keeping women in astrophysics. Women are underrepresented in the field. They also leave at higher rates at every career stage. Performance on the job does not explain the gap in outcomes. The Picture an Astronomer project formed in response. It pairs public outreach with professional discussion.

In March 2025, over two hundred astronomers met in hybrid form. The symposium examined the field's state for female scientists. Scientific exchange mixed with policy discussion. This paper records the resulting recommendations. The practices target gendered attrition specifically. The authors argue they would improve the climate for all scientists. Retention of talent is the stated goal. The paper is a community document, built from a field talking to itself about who it loses.
arxiv-2512-24565:
Zixiang Liu and five colleagues benchmark AI agents that use tools through the Model Context Protocol. Agents increasingly call external tools this way. Existing evaluation sets lean on live external services. They also ignore task difficulty. The new benchmark, MCPAgentBench, is built from real-world tool definitions instead.

Authentic tasks pair with simulated tools in a dynamic sandbox. Candidate tool lists include distractors on purpose. Agents must select and discriminate, not just call. Metrics cover task completion and execution efficiency together. Leading language models were tested on the suite. Performance differed sharply on complex, multi-step tool use. Some models handled the chains well; others stumbled. All code is open source. The benchmark aims to make agent tool use measurable without fragile live dependencies.
arxiv-2512-24965:
Siyuan Hu, Kevin Qinghong Lin, and Mike Zheng Shou build ShowUI-pi, a flow-based generative model that acts as a dexterous hand inside graphical user interfaces. Existing interface agents predict discrete click points, which blocks free-form closed-loop actions like dragging a slider that need continuous perception and adjustment. Their design unifies discrete clicks and continuous drags in one shared model.

Flow-based generation produces smooth trajectories rather than single points, enabling on-the-fly correction during a drag. AI agent readers get a step toward human-like digital manipulation. Many real tasks, from drawing to data entry with sliders, require exactly that continuous control rather than isolated clicks.
arxiv-2512-25065:
Rohit Dwivedula, Divyanshu Saxena, Sujay Yadalam, and others present Vulcan, a framework that uses language models to synthesize systems heuristics focused to each deployment copy. Resource management in operating systems and networks relies on hand-designed heuristics, but varied hardware and workloads make manual focus costly. Generated heuristics must run safely, integrate correctly, and still perform well.

Vulcan defines language-model-friendly surfaces that isolate core choice logic from surrounding system code, then searches for verifiable heuristics through that surface. Systems readers get automated heuristic design with safety checks. Instance focus could replace one-size-fits-all tuning across varied fleets.
arxiv-2601-00065:
Xiaoze Liu, Weichen Yu, Matt Fredrikson, Xiaoqian Wang, and Jing Gao expose a weakness in a method for moving tokenizers between large language models. The method rebuilds word-piece rows for a donor model's extra vocabulary as mixes of shared anchor rows, then reuses those mixes on a base model. Their 2026 paper shows the same mix can reach different sets of points in the two models.

Using that gap, the team builds breaker tokens: mixes that look inert in the donor yet create a strong signal in the base. One donor checkpoint allowed this against thirteen different bases from five model families. Common filters missed the flaw, and a standard fine-tuning fix only partly helped. The authors discuss misuse risks in the open-weight supply chain.
arxiv-2601-00165:
Alon Danai works with Joshua Kou, Andy Latto, Haran Mouli, and James Propp on a tiling style puzzle in graph theory. Take a grid graph built from paths or cycles. Can the edges of a complete graph split into exact copies of that grid? Each copy must be disjoint from the others. When the answer is yes, a grid design exists.

For a torus grid with prime or prime squared size, the answer is yes. The path grid case is less even. The three by three path grid admits no design. The four by four path grid does admit one. That last case links to the Connections word game. It scrambles the puzzle so each word pair sits adjacent exactly once. The constructions use arithmetic in finite fields. A party puzzle and pure design theory turn out to meet.
arxiv-2601-00265:
Prem Talwai leads five coauthors in hiding demand news inside the shape of a retailer order stream. Their supply chain has two tiers and no direct sharing channel. A downstream retailer orders from an upstream supplier. The supplier must forecast from those orders alone. Order timing can carry signal if shaped well. The authors name that shaping information delay.

Pure delay turns out to be strictly wasteful. Fractional delay tools reshape order correlation instead. Forecast skill rises and system inventory costs fall. A Hardy space method builds a workable policy family. The family stays close to a known ideal filter. Its information delay traits survive the approximation. Policy complexity gets sharp cost guidance. Memory limits on the supplier change the right answer. Sometimes a fancier policy backfires badly. Simple can beat complex when memory is short.
arxiv-2601-00465:
Dennis Christmann and colleagues propose cleaning up orbit with swarms of tiny satellites run by low-power autonomous agents. Old spacecraft and debris already crowd Earth's orbit and threaten working satellites. Small nano-satellites could approach debris pieces and push them down to burn up in the atmosphere, but they must act on their own with very little energy.

The team builds on recent work on autonomous agents for resource-limited devices. They implemented their agent software on wireless microcontrollers and ran experiments on a specialized test bed. Their simplified approach proved feasible and energy efficient in those tests. The work is an early step toward practical, self-directing debris removal swarms rather than a finished orbital system.
arxiv-2601-00565:
Marek Rogatko proves a uniqueness result for charged black hole spacetimes that also contain a massive particle sphere, a region where heavy particles can orbit. The setting is a four-dimensional, static spacetime governed by Einstein-Maxwell theory, carrying both electric and magnetic charge and flat at infinity. Earlier classification work dealt mainly with photon spheres, where light itself orbits.

Rogatko shows any such spacetime with a non-extremal massive particle sphere as an inner boundary must be exactly the Reissner-Nordström solution. His version covers whole families of particle spheres at different energies, not just one. The proof leans on conformal positive energy and positive mass theorems together with carefully chosen conformal transformations, extending black hole uniqueness to this richer boundary case.
arxiv-2601-00965:
Tianshuo Yang, Ryan Rabinowitz, Terrance Boult, and Jugal Kalita ask whether text classifiers can admit they have never seen a category before. Transformer classifiers score superbly on known classes but behave brittly on inputs from unseen ones, a routine situation for deployed language systems. The authors port an idea from computer vision, the feature attenuation hypothesis behind the COSTARR framework, to language.

They test it on two modest models trained to sort papers into one hundred seventy-six arXiv subject areas, against simpler confidence scores such as maximum softmax probability and maximum logit. COSTARR transferred to text without retraining, but it gave no statistically significant gain over the simple baselines, and a free-energy score lagged behind. The negative result is itself useful guidance.
arxiv-2601-01265:
Nick Lindsay, Caroline Trippel, Anurag Khandelwal, and Abhishek Bhattacharjee build CounterPoint, a framework for checking what a computer chip really does inside. Chips expose hardware counters that count events like cache misses, but the counters are vaguely documented, noisy, and hard to read. Mental models of the hardware often go untested against them.

CounterPoint lets experts state a model of a chip part as a decision diagram, then tests it against counter data. When the data disagree, it points to hidden features that could explain the gap, using confidence regions to tame the noise. Applied to Intel's Haswell memory unit, it uncovered several undocumented behaviors, including a queue-side prefetch helper and page-table walkers that merge or abort. The framework gives hardware experts a disciplined way to reconcile guesswork with measurement and to surface secrets that manuals omit.
arxiv-2601-01465:
Six authors led by Ze Peng tighten the theory of why stochastic gradient descent generalizes, why models trained by it work on data they never saw. Information-theoretic bounds explain this by tying the model to the training data, but the older bounds ignore a known clue: descent favors flat minima, and flat minima generalize better. They also tend to be numerically loose.

The new bound builds flatness in. It says models generalize better when the directions where the final weights vary most are directions where the loss surface curves gently. The authors verify on deep networks that the bound tracks flatness correctly and is far tighter than its predecessors. A flexible proof technique behind it also improves worst-case risk bounds for plain gradient descent on a standard problem class. Sharper bounds matter because they turn folk wisdom about flatness into a measurable, testable claim.
arxiv-2601-01665:
Neural solvers trained with deep reinforcement learning can plan routes and pack loads while balancing several goals at once, but their weakness on hard or unusual cases is poorly understood. Wei Liu, Yaoxin Wu, Yingqian Zhang, Thomas Bäck, and Yingjie Fan build a unified framework for testing and strengthening these preference-guided solvers.

Their attack method learns to generate problem instances that expose a solver's weak spots, measured by how much solution quality drops. A matching defense then trains solvers on those hard cases while varying the balance among goals, reducing overfitting. Experiments on routing and knapsack problems with multiple objectives show the defense clearly improves performance on difficult and unfamiliar instances.
arxiv-2601-02065:
Farmers who speak Bengali need agricultural advice locked inside English manuals, and cloud language models are too costly and unreliable in low-resource languages. Md. Asif Hossain, Nabil Subhan, Mantasha Rahman Mahi, and Jannatul Ferdous Nabila build a cross-lingual retrieval system that answers Bengali questions from curated English sources such as FAO and IRRI manuals.

A question is translated into English, enriched with domain keywords that map farmers' everyday words to scientific terms, answered by dense retrieval over the manuals, and translated back to Bengali. Running entirely on open-source models and consumer hardware, the system gave source-grounded answers, firmly refused off-topic questions, and responded in under twenty seconds on average, a deployable pattern for low-resource advisory services.
arxiv-2601-02265:
Long acting injectable drugs release medicine slowly after one shot, so patients with chronic illness need fewer doses. Karla N. Robles and Manar D. Samad ask whether machine learning can predict that release from the recipe of the injection. Getting the release right normally takes long trial and error work on the chemistry of the mix.

Working with data from 321 formulations, they predict release after one, two, and three days, sort release curves into types, and predict the full release curve over time. Early release predictions track the true values well, and the type sorting scores strongly. A method that explains model choices points to which material traits push release faster or slower, giving makers clear levers to adjust.
arxiv-2601-02365:
Tushar Vatsa and four co authors at Adobe improve how a multimodal creative assistant searches for and recommends content. The assistant splits a user goal among subagents for layout, style, retrieval, and generation, and retrieval can fail at several points, from misreading intent to poor ranking. Sending raw images through every step is also expensive.

Their system, FUSE, replaces most raw image prompting with a compact grounded design representation, a structured JSON record of canvas elements, layout, styles, colors, and the user's selection. Seven strategies for budgeting context are compared, from full prompting to minimal zero shot use. A pipeline attribution layer turns subagent signals into a diagnosis of where a failure began, so weak stages can be fixed directly.
arxiv-2601-02465:
Hitoshi Murayama explores whether the QCD axion, a particle proposed to solve the strong CP problem. Could be far heavier than usually assumed, in the GeV range, if the Peccei Quinn symmetry breaks below the QCD scale. In that case the axion may hide among the already observed eta resonances and would be immune to quantum gravity corrections.

Only the right handed up quark carries the new charge, and flavor changing effects stay surprisingly small. The author argues that all accelerator and astrophysical limits can be evaded. With the sharpest constraint coming from the mass split between charged and neutral pions, and sketches collider signatures for a completed model.
arxiv-2601-02665:
Mu-Tian Wang and a team of co authors report two planets around the F type star TOI-4495, a smaller sub Neptune and a larger Neptune like world. The orbits last about two and a half and five days. That spacing sits close to a two to one mean motion resonance, where one planet circles twice for each circle of the other. Transit timing analysis of TESS light curves, using a photodynamical model, pins down both masses from how the planets tug each other.

Both planets carry volatile rich gas envelopes. A Rossiter McLaughlin measurement and the Doppler shadow of the outer planet show its orbit is well aligned with the star's spin, and the two orbits are nearly coplanar. The pair sits near, but not in, the resonance, and the authors argue the planets likely arrived there through overstable migration, a drift in which a resonant lock overshoots.
arxiv-2601-02865:
Houda Haidar and forty co-authors use the James Webb Space Telescope to study dust near the bright centers of eight nearby galaxies with active black holes. In four of them, they resolve dust structures stretching one to two hundred parsecs along the narrow line region, the zone lit up by the central engine. The dust shapes closely track both the radio jets and glowing silicon gas in these galaxies.

Measuring the dust's heat glow across wavelengths, the team finds it warmer and steeper in spectrum than dust in star-forming clumps, reaching roughly 150 to 220 kelvin. Light from the black hole alone cannot explain that extra heat, even under generous assumptions. Shock waves moving a few hundred kilometers per second through dense gas can, which suggests shocks help heat the dust.
arxiv-2601-02965:
Phat Tran and three co-authors work on reading Bahnar, a minority language of Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, from scanned paper documents. Bahnar faces preservation risks because research and digital data for it are scarce. Scans are often degraded, with broken or blurred areas that cause many optical character recognition errors and hurt later information retrieval.

Their approach first detects tables and non-table regions to clean up the input, then applies probability-based heuristics that correct likely recognition mistakes after the scan is read. In experiments, recognition accuracy rose from about seventy-three percent to about seventy-nine percent. Beyond Bahnar itself, the study offers a framework that other minority language digitization projects can adapt to their own low-resource settings.
arxiv-2601-03065:
Yifan Yang and ten co-authors present FCaps, a large dataset for teaching machines the fine details of speaking style. Existing speech-text models learn from coarse captions or narrow task labels, and detailed style annotations are hard to scale. FCaps holds about forty-seven thousand hours of speech with nineteen million fine-grained free-text captions, produced by a pipeline that grounds captions directly in the audio.

Because the captions are not rewritten by a language model after the fact, the pipeline avoids the error build-up of cascaded methods, and judge-based evaluations rate its captions above cascaded ones. On top of FCaps, the authors train CLSP, a contrastive model that mixes global and fine-grained supervision. It performs reliably across retrieval, zero-shot classification of speech traits, and style similarity scoring.
arxiv-2601-03265:
Kai Hu and eight co-authors introduce Jailbreak-Zero, a red teaming method that probes language models for safety weaknesses using policies rather than fixed example lists. Example-based testing covers only the attacks someone already thought of. Jailbreak-Zero instead uses an attack model to generate a large, diverse volume of adversarial prompts, then fine-tunes that attacker on a preference dataset.

The authors report that the method reaches Pareto optimality across policy coverage, attack strategy diversity, and how closely prompts resemble real user inputs. It achieved significantly higher attack success rates than leading techniques against both open-source and proprietary models, including GPT-4o and Claude 3.5. The prompts remain human-readable, and the pipeline needs minimal human intervention, making the approach scalable for ongoing safety evaluation.
arxiv-2601-03365:
Boubakeur Khantoul and Ahmed Tedjani solve exactly a quantum oscillator problem that mixes several twists at once. Their system is a two-dimensional Pauli oscillator: an electron-like particle with spin in a magnetic field. It is rewritten with Dunkl operators, which bake reflection symmetry into the momentum. An Aharonov-Bohm flux threads the system, adding a topological phase. Both the mass and the frequency are allowed to change with time.

Using the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method, they obtain exact energy levels and spinor wavefunctions. The flux turns out to constrain the Dunkl parameters. It ties the reflection symmetry to how angular momentum is quantized, which reshapes the energy spectrum. The authors suggest the interplay of topology and symmetry could matter for quantum simulation work, such as cold atoms and quantum dots.
arxiv-2601-03865:
Rakesh Arora and Tuhina Mukherjee study the Fučík spectrum of the logarithmic Laplacian, a set of parameter pairs for which a certain nonlinear equation has a nontrivial solution. The Fučík spectrum extends plain eigenvalues by letting the equation's response differ for positive and negative parts of the solution. The domain is a bounded region with a smooth boundary, and solutions must vanish outside it.

The authors show that two lines through the first eigenvalue lie in the spectrum and are isolated within it. They establish the first nontrivial curve in the spectrum and study its shape, proving it is Lipschitz continuous, strictly monotone, and describing its asymptotic behavior. They also give a variational portrait of the second eigenvalue. Such spectra govern resonance and jumping nonlinear terms in partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-04165:
Samuel T. Badman leads twenty-six co-authors in a review of magnetic switchbacks in the solar wind near the Sun. A switchback is a sharp fold in the magnetic field: the field swings away from its background direction while keeping about the same strength. Field and flow swings track each other as outward Alfvénic waves, forming a jet.

Parker Solar Probe finds switchbacks almost everywhere within a fraction of Earth's orbital distance from the Sun. The review covers how they are spotted and measured, the traits of single switchbacks, and how they gather into patches. Badman and his twenty-six co-authors sort which traits enjoy strong agreement and which rest on thin support. They close with open questions and advice for future studies of these energetic structures.
arxiv-2601-04265:
Weihao Shen and six co-authors anonymise user text by protecting only the private details that the writer's intent does not need. Blanket anonymisation can hide facts that are central to what a text is trying to say. The challenge is to choose which attributes to shield, and how far, while keeping meaning, tone, and function intact.

Their method, IntentAnony, models the writer's pragmatic intent and traces chains of clues that could reveal each attribute. Given the intent, each attribute receives an exposure budget, and only clue paths outside the intent are suppressed. Tests use privacy inference success, text utility scores, and human judgement. The team reports a gain of about thirty percent in the overall privacy and utility trade-off over prior leading methods, with anonymised text staying notably more usable.
arxiv-2601-04465:
Ignacio Sastre and Aiala Rosá teach a language model a new word for an idea, and nothing else, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their Concept Tokens method adds one special token to a pretrained model's vocabulary and learns only that token's embedding. From natural-language definitions of a target concept in which the concept's name is replaced by the token. The model itself stays frozen throughout.

Two testbeds show the token genuinely steers behaviour. A token trained on hallucination can be asserted to increase invented answers in closed-book questions, or negated to suppress them, mostly by making the model abstain. A token for recasting, a language teacher's correction technique, shows the same directional control and follows other instructions better than stuffing the definitions into the prompt. A qualitative study with the Eiffel Tower and an invented Austral Tower probes what the embedding has and has not captured.
arxiv-2601-04765:
Santiago Acevedo, Alessandro Laio, and Marco Baroni ask whether a giant language model keeps grammar and meaning in separate drawers, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Working inside DeepSeek-V3, they average the hidden-layer vectors of sentences that share syntactic structure, and separately of sentences that share meaning, producing syntax and semantics centroids for each.

Subtracting the syntax centroid from a sentence's vector wrecks its similarity to syntactically matched sentences while sparing semantic matches. vice versa — showing both kinds of information are encoded at least partly linearly, as directions that can be added and removed. The two signals also peak in different layers and can be partly decoupled from each other. The result gives interpretability research a concrete handle: inside the largest open models, form and content are not hopelessly entangled.
arxiv-2601-04865:
Konstantin A. Rybakov's 2026 paper gives a way to build random systems that stay on a set surface. Such systems use rules with a noise term, so their paths shake as they move. Staying on the surface means each path, noise and all, must keep to a smooth curved surface in the space of states. The surface here is set in a round-about way, as the set where a smooth function is flat.

His method is made to run well in software that works with math symbols, not just numbers. It rests on a basis, a small set of arrows that span the flat sheet that just grazes the surface at each point. The work serves folks who need random models that obey hard shape rules, such as motion held to a sphere.
arxiv-2601-05265:
Mile Stankovic's 2026 paper changes how documents are chopped up for retrieval-augmented generation. Chunking quality largely determines how well a RAG system answers, yet current methods partition each document alone. Complex questions, though, need information scattered across several sources, a knowledge fragmentation problem that single-document chunking cannot fix because related facts land in separate, unconnected chunks.

Stankovic's cross-document topic-aligned chunking rebuilds knowledge at corpus level: it finds topics that span the whole corpus, assigns each segment to a topic, and synthesizes unified chunks. On a multi-hop reasoning benchmark he reports faithfulness clearly above contextual retrieval and semantic chunking baselines. Better chunking is unglamorous but decisive, since a retriever can only return what the chunker chose to keep together.
arxiv-2601-05565:
Pengyu Sun and 2 co-authors extend, in a 2026 paper, a consistency property of the lattice Boussinesq equations to a larger cube. Lattice equations assign values to grid points, and consistency around a cube is a strong sign of integrability, meaning the system has deep exact structure. The standard notion uses the eight corners of a small cube.

The authors show the nine-point lattice potential Boussinesq equation stays consistent on a twenty-seven-point cubic sublattice. They also construct a new three-component system, the lattice BSQ-Q3 system, as the analogue of a known classified equation. A gauge transformation between Lax pairs produces the new system, and a limiting form yields an invariant equation generalizing an earlier Schwarzian version.
arxiv-2601-05865:
Federico Mazzone and 2 co-authors present in 2026 the first method for detecting change points in time series that stay encrypted throughout the analysis. A change point is a moment when a series' statistical behavior shifts, such as its mean, variance, or frequency content. Detecting those shifts normally requires seeing the raw data.

Their approach uses the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, which allows computation on encrypted values. Unlike differential privacy methods, no noise is injected, so accuracy stays comparable to plaintext baselines. Tests on synthetic data and real healthcare and network-monitoring series support that claim. The authors report processing a million points within three minutes, suggesting encrypted monitoring could be real-world at scale.
arxiv-2601-06065:
Long convolutions let some neural networks handle very long inputs, but the memory they need exceeds what small chips hold. Peter Wang and 2 co-authors present a fix in a 2026 paper on field-programmable gate arrays, chips whose circuits can be reconfigured. Their setting is the Hyena architecture, which uses fast Fourier transform convolutions.

Their method splits the work into chunks and rebuilds the result with an overlap-add step. On an Alveo U200 chip with very limited block memory, they ran convolutions where both sequence and filter reached about 450,000 in length. Throughput grew with chunk size, and the longest runs lost only a small share of speed. Careful memory management made long-context work fit on edge hardware.
arxiv-2601-06165:
Real users ask vague questions and let the picture fill the gaps. Dasol Choi and 9 co-authors show how much that hurts vision-language models in a 2026 benchmark paper. Standard benchmarks use clear, explicit prompts, which flatter the models. Everyday queries from Korean online communities look nothing like that.

Their HAERAE-Vision benchmark holds 653 real visual questions, filtered from about 86,000 candidates, each paired with an explicit rewrite. Among 39 models tested, even the strongest scored under half on the original wording. Rewriting the query clearly added large gains, especially for smaller models. Web search did not close the gap. Much apparent model weakness, the authors conclude, is really query underspecification.
arxiv-2601-06265:
Tests for odd quantum links often rest on a push: change one part, watch the rest. Santiago Zamora and 4 co-authors find a new kind of push in a 2026 paper. When all seen parts sit too far apart in space, a push on them tells us too little. Their fix works on the parts we can not see.

The new step, called latent splitting, acts on hidden quantum states in the net. It joins plain watch data with push data in one test. On a three-node net, the team built fresh tests that prove the odd link with room to spare. The tests cover the small case of two-state parts. They also stretch the zone where past tests could show the effect. The work gives labs a way to prove nonclassical links when old pushes fail.
arxiv-2601-06565:
Code that moves money on a blockchain cannot afford small mistakes. Pei Yang and 5 co-authors introduce EVM-QuestBench in a 2026 paper, a benchmark for generating transaction scripts from natural language on Ethereum-compatible chains, where errors can cause irreversible user losses.

Evaluation is execution-grounded and dynamic: instructions are sampled from template pools, numeric parameters drawn from set intervals, and validators check outcomes against those exact values. The 107 tasks split into atomic single actions and composite multi-step workflows. Scripts run on a forked chain with snapshot isolation. Twenty models were tested, revealing large performance gaps. Split scores exposed a persistent asymmetry: models handle single actions far better than multi-step workflows, whose completion decays with each added step.
arxiv-2601-06665:
Sinchan Rej, Snigdhadev Ray, and Bimalendu Deb propose a Rydberg atom parity gate in 2026. Quantum computation requires two- or multi-qubit controlled gates, they note. Controlled-NOT and controlled-phase gates are the usual building blocks used.

They propose an alternative pathway using a three-qubit parity gate. The gate lives in a Rydberg atom array, they describe. Its basic principle is control by the parity of control qubits. The target qubit's operation depends on that combined parity value. They discuss constructing the gate based on dark state resonances. Parity gates could simplify some simulation and computation circuits considerably. Quantum hardware readers get a design grounded in Rydberg physics. Dark states protect the gate from some common disturbances there.
arxiv-2601-06865: A 2026 arXiv preprint by HALIMA GIOVANNA AHMAD and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers quantum Circuit-Based adaptation for credit risk analysis. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Noisy and Intermediate-Scale Quantum, or NISQ, processors are sensitive to noise, prone to quantum decoherence. And are not yet capable of continuous quantum error correction for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07065:
Eric Feltham wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on two tools for the Julia language. One tool is called FormulaCompiler.jl, and the other is called Margins.jl, and both run in Julia. They deal with marginal effects, which show how a result shifts when one input shifts a bit. Such effects help readers make sense of a fitted model.

Tools in use now can be slow when the data set is large. That slowness caps the size of work a team can do. The new tools aim to lift that cap. Margins.jl gives a clean two-function API. Its plan is a grid with two rows and two cols. One axis picks the base for the test: the whole group or a single profile. The other axis picks the target: effects or forecasts. The paper shows how the grid keeps each task clear and fast.
arxiv-2601-07465:
Jakob Robnik, Uroš Seljak, and colleagues revisit the hardest planet searches from the Kepler space telescope. Kepler's main goal was finding Earth-like planets in the habitable zone around Sun-like stars. Those planets produce tiny, rare dips in starlight when they cross their stars. At that detection limit, Kepler's own pipeline produced unreliable candidates.

False alarms are the central problem: noise and instrument effects can mimic a planet transit. The authors build a pipeline for detection plus false alarm vetting at this limit. Careful vetting decides which faint signals deserve trust and follow-up. The work matters for squeezing real planets out of archival data and for designing searches with future telescopes.
arxiv-2601-07565:
Jiaqi Qiao and colleagues present EGMF, a framework that reads emotion from several signals at once. Emotion recognition names discrete feelings, while sentiment analysis scores overall positive or negative tone. Both tasks benefit from combining text, audio, and visual cues. A face, a voice, and words together say more than any one alone. Their 2026 preprint unifies the two tasks.

EGMF uses expert-guided multimodal fusion together with large language models. Expert guidance shapes how the different signals are merged. The framework handles both discrete emotion labels and continuous sentiment values in one system. That unity simplifies building tools for customer feedback, media analysis, and human-computer interaction. The paper targets scholars in affective computing.
arxiv-2601-07665:
Andrea Martin and Giuseppe Belgioioso teach an algorithm to solve fixed-point problems faster, without losing its safety net. Fixed-point iterations underlie optimization, control, and machine learning. The Krasnosel'skii-Mann iteration is a standard method for nonexpansive mappings. The authors build a learning to optimize framework around it. Their 2026 preprint deliberately adds small perturbations to the standard steps.

The perturbations are summable, meaning their total size stays bounded. That choice improves average performance on a chosen family of problems while keeping convergence guarantees. Speed without guarantees is risky in control and safety settings. Keeping the proof while gaining speed is the paper's selling point. Optimization scholars who distrust black-box learned solvers should find the approach appealing.
arxiv-2601-07765:
Igor Sterner, Alex Lascarides, and Frank Keller teach a model to spot the events that matter most in a story. Narrative salience marks which events drive a story's progression. Their 2026 preprint presents a contrastive learning framework for modeling it. The key device is narrative twins: stories that share the same plot but differ in surface form. Twins let the model separate plot importance from wording.

Contrastive learning pulls matching stories together and pushes others apart in representation space. With twins, the shared signal is the plot itself. A model that learns salience could summarize stories better and track long narratives. It could also help writers see which scenes carry the story. The paper speaks to scholars in computational narrative and natural language processing. It offers data design as the main innovation.
arxiv-2601-08065:
Samuel I. Akinwande and colleagues verify neural controlled systems by working backward from the goal. Reach-avoid specifications demand that a system reach a target while avoiding danger. Forward reachability analysis dominates verification of neural feedback systems. Backward methods have lagged because they scale poorly. Their 2026 preprint introduces algorithms computing both over- and under-approximations of backward reachable sets. Those sets collect states that can reach the goal safely.

Two-sided approximations bracket the true set from outside and inside. That bracket tells engineers how much trust a verdict deserves. Neural controllers in robots and vehicles need such checks before deployment. Backward reasoning starts from the goal, often a smaller set than the start region. The paper serves formal methods and control scholars. It strengthens a weaker side of the verification toolbox.
arxiv-2601-08265: Sebastian Cocks, Salvador Dreo, and Feras Dayoub wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sets out AIMC-Spec, a test set for a radar task. The task is automatic intrapulse modulation classification, or AIMC, used in electronic support systems. It names the kind of modulation built into a single radar pulse, read from its in-phase and quadrature parts. A lack of shared test sets has held back work, above all for weak signals. AIMC-Spec shifts the noise level to test how tools hold up.
arxiv-2601-08365: Malors Espinosa and Zander Karaganis define a generating function for a class of buildings in group theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with buildings of affine type A1, which are trees. The buildings carry an added filtration structure that enriches the count. The authors prove the generating function recovers the zeta function of certain quadratic orders. That bridge links combinatorics of trees to number theory objects. It may give new ways to compute or interpret zeta values through building counts.
arxiv-2601-08465: V. Gorbounov and A. Kazakov wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on round networks of wires and what their edge reads can tell us. The authors use a broad form of the Temperley trick. That trick maps each round network into a totally non-negative Grassmannian. From that map, they show that the true resistance between edge nodes has the Kalmanson property. They then give a full account of which flat networks meet that trait. Such results can help rebuild a hid network from reads at its edge.
arxiv-2601-08765:
Hoang Ly, Emina Soljanin, and Philip Whiting study codes that let a lost part of data be fixed from a few near parts. Such codes guard files spread over many drives. If one drive fails, staff can fix its part with low cost. Most past work set bounds and built codes, but did not test them under real flaws.

The team tests a simple fix rule based on the most common value near the loss. They study its work under both lost parts and wrong parts. Chance math lets them track how often the rule heals the file and how often it fails. A reader who stores large data sets gets a plain rule with clear odds. It may suit fast, cheap fix jobs.
arxiv-2601-08865:
Christopher Lowrance and John Rogers test a class task to lift deep thought in control work. Their class is in mechatronics, the mix of machines, circuits, and code. Two ways to guide a machine are set side by side. One is the classic PID rule. The next is fuzzy logic, which uses soft rules such as a bit too hot.

Pupils work with both rules on like tasks. The pair then check if the side by side work lifts high thought skills. Those skills are to break a task down, to build a fix, and to judge if it works. A reader who teaches such classes gets a task plan with a clear aim. It uses a real clash of methods to push thought past rote steps.
arxiv-2601-08965:
Luisiana Cundin gives a more plain proof for a known wave rule in math physics. The rule is the Newell-Whitehead-Segel equation. It sets how a wave like pattern grows and spreads in space and time. Past work proved the best fit for it is the null, or zero, form. But the path there used deep nests of sums that are hard to read.

New facts on how a mix sum acts let her cut that path short. The new proof gives forms that are far more plain to check. A reader in wave work gets the same end point with less fog. Plain proofs help peers trust a result and teach it with ease.
arxiv-2601-09065:
Yinuo Xu and David Jurgens survey how to treat split calls by human marks in text work. Marks split oft on soft tasks, such as if a text is rude or which side it backs. Old work treats split as noise and takes the most common call. New work says split is a sign. It can show that a text reads in more than one fair way.

The survey gives one view of split aware methods. It spans how to keep split in train data, and how to model each mark hand. It also covers how to grade a tool that may give more than one call. A reader who marks text gets a map of a shift in the field. The crowd may be right in more than one way.
arxiv-2601-09265:
Bei Huang and six co-authors join physics sims to a fast 3D form that can show crisp breaks. The form is built from Gaussian blobs, soft dots that can paint a scene in real time. Past joins of sims to blobs dealt with soft stuff, such as cloth or gel. Hard stuff that cracks was left out. Blobs have no firm in side, so a crack has no place to start.

Their tool is called GaussianFluent. It gives blobs a sound in side with true shade, and a crack aware sim to split them. A reader in film and sim work gets breaks that look true and run fast, a pair that past tools could not hold.
arxiv-2601-09365:
Biswesh Mohapatra and five co-authors study a basic problem in spoken dialog: how people build shared understanding as they talk. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at common ground, the set of things, events, and links that speakers treat as mutually known. The setting is situated dialog, where talk happens in a shared space and stretches over time.

Keeping that shared record straight is hard for machines. The authors argue that dialog systems must store references in a form they can call back later in a chat.
