The need grows as embodied agents and social robots join human talk. A clear account of common ground would help such systems stay coherent and avoid losing track of what was already settled.
arxiv-2601-09865:
Jacob Sander, Brian Jalaian, and Venkat R. Dasari squeeze large language models for edge deployment. Their 2026 arXiv paper combines Muon-optimized distillation with quantization. Big models strain the compute, memory, and energy budgets of small devices.

Three problems must be solved together: getting task-specific data, fine-tuning for performance, and compressing the model. Distillation trains a small model to mimic a large one; quantization stores weights in fewer bits. The authors optimize the distillation step with the Muon optimizer. A tighter pipeline brings capable language models to phones, drones, and field gear.
arxiv-2601-09965:
Atharva Dange, Ramon Lopez, Nimish Shah, and Louis Deslauriers test an AI tutor for physics work at home. The tool is named aiPlato. It was used in a large first year physics class. The class was at the University of Texas at Arlington.

aiPlato gives step by step hints as pupils work. Two tools sit at its core. One checks a pupil's work on the spot. One is a chat tutor that guides with prompts. The aim is to help while the hard parts stay with the pupil. The paper is a first look at how the class used it.
arxiv-2601-10065:
Vincent Chen, Berndt Müller, and Xiaojun Yao run a gauge theory on a small grid. Gauge rules rule the strong force. The full math is vast. The team cuts each link down to three states. Those states are the null state and two charge states.

With that cut, the model is as lean as it can be. It is named a qutrit cut. The team writes out the full energy rule for two grid shapes. One is a chain of square cells. One is a honeycomb grid in two dims. They then track the pull of a string in the model, a key sign of force bind.
arxiv-2601-10365:
Yan Liu and co authors teach a humanoid robot to run up stairs. For a human, stairs are a small task. For a biped robot, they ask for speed and balance at once. A slip can mean a fall. Most past work walks the robot up at a slow pace.

The team aim for a run, not a walk. Their robot is named FastStair in the work. It learns a gait that is both fast and firm. Steps must land clean at speed. The work tests the gait on real stairs. A fast stair gait would widen where such robots can work.
arxiv-2601-10565:
Dávid Ferenczi, Jean-Gabriel Young, and Leto Peel infer signed ties in social nets from how oft people meet. A signed tie can be warm, cold, or not there at all. Meet data shows who was near whom. But a cold tie and no tie can both yield few meets. Past tools can not split those two.

The team built a tool that can. It asks if a lack of meets came from no chance to meet, or from a wish to avoid. Work and home facts can bound chance. With those in the math, cold ties can be told from null ties. The work sharpens maps of real social nets.
arxiv-2601-10765:
Zubair Shah and Noaman Khan frame neural network pruning as an evolutionary process. Networks are often trained with far more parameters than they need. Many weights turn redundant as learning proceeds. Most pruning methods cut by decree, using importance scores or penalty terms set from above.

That view treats pruning as a central decision imposed on a trained model. Shah and Khan instead stress selection dynamics inside training itself. Sparsity can emerge as some connections win and others fade. The frame borrows the logic of natural selection for model design. It may lead to leaner networks that grow sparse on their own, without a separate cutting stage.
arxiv-2601-11865:
Truong Nguyen, Phi Van Dat, Ngan Nguyen, and their co-authors move preference lessons between models that split text in unlike ways. Distillation lets a small student learn from a big teacher. It is much used in training, but less for aligning models with human taste.

The cross-tokenizer case is the real world case, since models rarely share a text split. That split clash has blocked fine, direct transfer of taste data. Their method, named CTPD in the work, works past that clash. It could let small models gain taste lessons from any strong teacher.
arxiv-2601-11965:
Wanli Wang, Kaixin Zhang, and Yuda Cheng study the far tails of a biased random walk model. The model is the continuous-time random walk, used for how grains spread. Many tests and sims show it fits such spread well.

They treat two cases: Gaussian jumps and discrete jumps. For each, they compute the place spread at short times. They show that a bias brings out exponential decay in the far tails. Tail forms matter, since rare long moves can rule risk and dose.  Short time tails are the core case in their proofs.
arxiv-2601-12165:
Severin Schraven and Simone Warzel give a new matrix product form for fractional quantum Hall wavefunctions. The set spans the Laughlin state and its kin. Their form rests on a strict version of correlators from a chiral quantum field theory.

The form lets them control the coefficients of the Laughlin function times any monomial symmetric polynomial. The expansion uses a Slater determinant or permanent basis. Firm control aids proofs on these topologic states. It also links Hall physics to field theory in a strict way.  The basis is built for states with any particle count.
arxiv-2601-12465:
Miao Peng and five co authors work on teaching language models to reason over long texts. A method called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has boosted short context reasoning. Its gains fade when the context grows long, though. Long tasks need both exact grounding in the text and strong reasoning across far apart parts.

The team propose a fix they call process advantage shaping. The name points to shaping the rewards given to steps of the reasoning process. Better step level signals may push a model to reason in depth, not just skim. The work targets a clear gap: models that ace short problems but falter on long ones. Closing that gap matters for real tasks like long document review.
arxiv-2601-12765:
Zhi Cai and four co authors tackle object detection across domains without source data. Source free object detection adapts a model to a new domain without revisiting source images. That setting fits privacy and storage limits in real deployments. Existing methods suffer from source bias, though: the adapted model stays skewed toward the source domain.

That skew leads to poor generalization on the target domain. It also causes error accumulation during self training, as bad labels reinforce themselves. The team use vision foundation models toward unbiased adaptation. Their work was prepared for a pattern recognition journal. Reliable source free detection would ease deployment of vision systems in new places.
arxiv-2601-12965:
Doheon Kim studies the sampling dynamics of score based diffusion models under a special conditioning trick. Diffusion models generate samples by learning the score function of a diffusion process. Theory explains their success through differential equations tied to sampling. Earlier work by Song and Ermon showed a puzzle in this story.

Neural networks using multiplicative noise conditioning still generated satisfactory samples. That fact sits oddly with the standard theoretical picture. Kim examines the deterministic dynamics of sampling in that setting. Clarifying why the trick works could improve sampler design. The work serves the theory of generative modeling, a fast moving field.
arxiv-2601-13165:
Bradley McCoy and Binhai Zhu study a watch tower task on rough ground where heights are not exact. In one form the ground is a bent line that moves in one plane, with set cross spots but loose heights. Each height must lie in a given span. In the next form the ground is a mesh of triangles in space, with set flat spots but loose heights.

The team takes the bright side view. They ask for the best tower spot when the true heights turn out as kind as they can. A watch tower must see all of the ground. Their work fits guard and sensor place tasks where ground data is coarse. It shows how to plan well when some facts are spans, not points.
arxiv-2601-13265:
Pedro H. Pereira and co-authors give a micro level theory of quantum friction. Friction at the quantum scale is the drag that two neutral objects feel as they slide past each other. Their route looks at two atoms, both in their low state, in shared motion.

The drag springs from how the atoms' spread out charge clouds reply to the slide. The team states the force as a sum in powers of the slide speed. That form shows which terms lead and which fade. A micro theory of this drag helps staff who build tiny machines and cold atom rigs. At that scale such faint drag can no longer be brushed aside.
arxiv-2601-13365:
Kevin Slote, Jeremie Fish, and Erik Bollt ship a Python pack for causal net finds by an entropy rule. The rule is called optimal causation entropy. It can pull a true causal web from time data of a live system. It can tell a straight link from a path that runs through a mid node.

Their pack is named CausationEntropy. It runs that rule plus key speed ups and growths of the method. The paper marks the pack at its version one state. For teams who study linked oscillators or other live webs, a sound open pack cuts time. It speeds the path from data to a causal map they can test.
arxiv-2601-13465:
Yimeng Min and Carla P. Gomes show that a graph neural net can turn into a heuristic for hard route tasks just by one train run. A heuristic is a fast rule that gives good, not sworn best, answers. Their test task is the travelling salesman task, to find the short tour of a set of towns.

Their net bakes global form binds in as a built in bias. It then gives a tour in one forward pass. No search, no teach marks, and no step by step picks are used. That a plain train path yields a sound tour tool is a surprise. For opt teams, it hints that form bias may swap for search in more tasks.
arxiv-2601-14365:
Tianhong Lu and Luiz H. Santos study paired quantum particles in this 2026 paper. Their materials are transition-metal dichalcogenides, thin crystals known as TMDs. These crystals host topological electronic states with no external magnetic field. They also show a strong optical response from long-lived excitons, bound pairs of an electron and a hole.

The team joins those two traits. They study an interacting fermion-boson system made by coupling an exciton to a quasihole. The quasihole sits in a fractional Chern insulator at filling fraction one third. Their title points to spectral fingerprints, marks in the spectrum that would show the exciton-anyon binding they study.
arxiv-2601-14465:
Máté Jánosik, Artúr Nádor, Nagy Zoltán Lóránt, and László Bence Simon study grid patterns in this 2026 math paper. They ask for the maximum size of a subset of the n by n integer grid that avoids specific geometric configurations. The problem is a variation on classical work begun by Erdős and Purdy. Extremal problems ask how large a set can be before a pattern must appear.

Three-point patterns, such as collinear triples and right triangles, are well studied. Four-point configurations in the grid are much less explored. The team works on avoiding configurations of small size. Readers get new bounds and constructions in a corner of discrete geometry with many open cases.
arxiv-2601-14565:
Dylan Danese and four co-authors work on quantum measurements of time in this 2026 paper. The temporal degree of freedom of light is powerful for modern quantum technologies. It enables large-scale quantum computing architectures and record key-rates in quantum key distribution. Yet one task stays a unique experimental challenge.

That task is the generalized measurement of large, complex quantum superpositions of a photon's time of arrival. The team works on programming such measurements inside a complex medium. A complex medium scrambles light in rich ways, which can be turned into a tool. Readers get methods for measuring when a photon arrives, even when its time state is a broad superposition.
arxiv-2601-15265:
Wiesław Płaczek, Maciej Skrzypek, Bennie F. L. Ward, and Scott A. Yost review two workhorse simulation tools for electron-positron colliders. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Bhabha scattering, the collision of an electron with a positron. Two Monte Carlo generators cover the process.

BHLUMI handles small-angle scattering, and BHWIDE handles large angles. Both must be extremely precise, since Bhabha events calibrate a collider's luminosity. The authors present the tools in brief and discuss how to improve them. The planned future electron-positron colliders set the high precision bar they must meet in practice.
arxiv-2601-15465:
Mehrnoosh Sadat Shirvani and eight co-authors look at chatbots that copy the user in a 2026 arXiv paper. As digital tools take a larger role in mental health care, these self-clone bots offer a new kind of support. A self-clone is trained on a person's own chat patterns. Users can then talk with a digital copy of themselves. The authors frame this as a path to self-exploration and self-derived support.

The promise comes with clear risks, and the paper takes them head-on. A clone may blur a user's sense of identity. It may reinforce harmful thoughts rather than ease them. It may also blur who is in control of the exchange. The authors build a framework for design that keeps such bots safe and therapeutic.
arxiv-2601-15565:
Alex Terrasson and three co-authors build a bright source of squeezed light in a 2026 arXiv paper. Squeezed states of light cut noise below the standard quantum limit. That allows more precise measurement than classical light permits. One target use is nonlinear microscopy. There, performance is limited by two things: photodamage to the sample and quantum-limited noise. Brighter squeezed light could ease both limits.

The title calls the source pulsed and bright. Pulses suit microscopy, where samples can only take so much light. Quantum-enhanced precision is the goal named in the title. If the source works as hoped, microscopes could image delicate samples more gently. They could also pick out finer detail at the same light dose. The work sits where quantum optics meets practical imaging.
arxiv-2601-15665:
Kwang-il Seon and a large team set out a science theme for the K-DRIFT project in a 2026 arXiv paper. The theme joins two faint targets in the sky. One is galactic cirrus: wispy dust clouds in our own galaxy. The other is the circumgalactic medium, the gas halo around galaxies. The record's abstract opens with the note that galaxies are surrounded by such material, then turns to author and institute lines. Korean astronomy institutes lead the author list.

Faint, diffuse light is hard to image, yet it traces how galaxies gain and lose gas. A survey theme paper like this tells the community what the project will chase and why it matters.
arxiv-2601-15965:
Yongda Zhu and a large team study clumps inside young galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. Massive star-forming clumps are a prominent feature of high-redshift galaxies. They may trace gravitational fragmentation in gas-rich disks. They may also trace feedback and the growth of galactic bulges. The team analyzes clump-like structures statistically. Their sample holds about 3,600 galaxies. Redshifts run from about two to eight, deep in cosmic time.

The images come from deep JWST NIRCam data in the JADES GOODS-South field. Mass scaling and radial trends are the paper's focus, per the title. How clump mass varies, and where clumps sit in their galaxies, test formation theories. Big samples turn anecdotes about clumps into population facts that models must match.
arxiv-2601-16065:
Chenyang Li and a large team trim waste tokens in robot vision and action models. Their 2026 preprint notes a flaw in such models. By default, the models may gaze too much at parts of the view that do not serve the task. The team calls those parts stray tokens. Stray gaze can hurt the acts the robot picks.

Their fix, named DTP, cuts stray tokens from the chain. The cut keeps gaze on the parts that guide the act. A lean chain should run fast and act with more care. The method is framed as plain yet strong. It targets models that join sight, words and acts for robot tasks in real rooms.
arxiv-2601-16165:
Mikhail Ivanov and coauthors rerun the first DESI data set for tight cosmos values. Their 2026 preprint joins many DESI probes in one fit. DESI maps star systems to trace how space grows. The fit uses the field theory of large scale form. It adds photo based star sets and lens cross links as well.

The team also pushes the three point fit to smaller scales. All parts use one firm frame for the fit. Tight joint fits test if the cosmos frame holds as one. They also weigh the case for the plain mass rank of neutrinos. The work gives per cent grade bounds from the joint data.
arxiv-2601-16365:
Yu Wei Soh and co-authors map the magnetic structure of a thin film of the compound EuZn2Sb2. The film is grown as a single crystal. It belongs to a class of materials where magnetism and charge transport are tightly linked. In such materials, the europium spins and the charge carriers sway each other in strong ways. That link is what the team sets out to map.

The 2026 preprint studies how the spins order inside the film. Work of this kind matters because the magnetic order steers the electrical behavior. A clear map of the structure gives later work a firm base. It shows where the spins point and how they line up across the film.
arxiv-2601-16665:
J. Seo writes on quantum machine learning, where computers use quantum states to learn from data. Quantum neural nets can hold rich patterns with ease. Yet training them on near-term machines is hard. Their error curves swing up and down a lot. Noise in the hardware adds to the strain. Seo's 2026 paper seeks a steadier way to train.

Most training now tweaks weights by small steps down a slope. That path can be slow and jumpy. It can also stick at sharp, poor spots. Seo puts forth a fix based on algebra. The fix uses weights tied to chance, to smooth the search. The goal is faster, calmer learning on real quantum gear.
arxiv-2601-16865:
Rowan Cherodian and Guy Tchuente build a new tool for cause work with weak mean shifts. Some policy shifts move a trait's whole spread, not its mean. A shift may lift the low tail while the mean stays put. Old cause tools key on mean moves and miss this case. Their 2026 preprint names this trait distributional relevance.

Their tool reads cause from the full spread shift. A quantile least squares fit does the gauge work. Such shifts show up in wage, school, and health plans. A tool that sees them can judge plans more fair. It keeps real gains from view loss by blunt means.
arxiv-2601-17465:
Akram Youssry and five co-authors boost quantum sensors with graybox machine learning. Quantum sensors beat classical ones in sharpness and sensitivity. In practice, noise and flawed control drag them down. State preparation is never perfect either. A graybox model mixes known physics with learned parts. It can absorb those unmodelled effects.

That mix aims to keep quantum gains in real labs. Uses span materials science and healthcare. Sensors that hold up outside ideal tests widen that reach. The work gives sensor teams a way to learn the flaws they cannot write down. It treats the device as it is, not as theory wishes it were.
arxiv-2601-17665:
Shan Gao comments on a claim about the Aharonov-Bohm phase. That phase shifts a charged particle even in field-free zones. Marletto and Vedral argued it is locally mediated. Their model uses entanglement between the particle and the quantized field. They claimed gauge independence for non-closed paths. Gao critically analyzes that model.

He argues the phase arises from interaction in a way their account misses. The debate is about what counts as local in quantum physics. Locality claims shape how field theory is taught and used. A sharp comment keeps a bold claim honest. Gao's record includes two papers on this effect in this set. The comment serves readers who track the locality debate.
arxiv-2601-17765:
Julius Giesler writes on a deep topic in algebraic geometry called Jacobian rings. His 2026 preprint links those rings to a part of Hodge theory for a smooth surface inside a torus. The link runs through a quotient space built from a lattice. The paper sets up a period map, which tracks how the shape of a variety shifts as its terms change.

Giesler then studies the slope of that map and works out its kernel in clear terms. The kernel is pinned down with the help of Laurent polynomials. As a payoff, the work bears on the infinitesimal Torelli theorem. That theorem asks when the period data is rich enough to fix the variety itself. Precise results here serve pure geometry.
arxiv-2601-17865:
Jia Gu, Liang Pang, Huawei Shen, and Xueqi Cheng study a trade-off at the heart of language models. Their 2026 preprint names two model types, D-models and E-models. The same next-token scores that drive a model also guide search, buying choices, and agent actions. So how a model samples its next step has effects far past the chat window. Spread and steadiness pull against each other.

A model that samples widely gives varied outputs but can drift off track. A model that plays safe can turn dull or stuck. The paper frames this as a diversity-stability trade-off. It studies how sampling choices shape that balance. The stakes grow as models take on more tasks where each next step is a real choice with real costs.
arxiv-2601-18065:
Aryan Roy, Zekun Wang, and Christopher J. MacLellan ask whether seeing makes a model more human in how it feels word concreteness. Their 2026 preprint compares vision-language models with text-only ones. People sense that some words name things you can touch, while others name abstract ideas. The team tests whether models share that sensitivity. They run a controlled comparison between matched Llama text backbones and their vision counterparts, using text-only prompts for both.

Keeping the prompts text-only makes the test fair. Any edge for the vision models must come from what image training taught them. The result bears on how grounding shapes language skill. It also informs debates about whether text alone can teach human-like word sense.
arxiv-2601-18365:
Giovanni Barbarino writes a short note on a topic in graph theory, the study of networks made of points and links. For a plain graph, one can build a blended table that mixes two simpler tables. One table shows which points are linked. The other lists how many links each point has. A single dial sets how much of each table goes into the blend.

Barbarino looks at the largest value that comes out of that blended table. Two past claims gave floors for that value, and it was not clear which floor was higher. He shows that one floor beats the other, as long as no point in the graph sits alone with no links at all. Notes like this keep the tools of the field sharp for later work on networks.
arxiv-2601-18465:
Mihir Durve and five colleagues study how drops of water move on live leaves, and they find that the leaf charges it-self as drops slide. How a drop runs, sticks, or slips on a leaf shapes how the plant deals with rain and dew. Those same moves guide the design of new stuff that sheds or holds water by plan.

The team show that a charge builds on the leaf skin as drops pass. That charge then pulls back on the next drops and shifts how they run. A force that teams had not weighed thus turns out to shape the whole dance. The find could change how plant staff read leaf wetness. It could also spark new films and coats that use charge to steer drops.
arxiv-2601-18865:
Rei Nishiura, Shoma Kamijima, and Kunihito Ioka study how a fierce radio burst can be bent by the cloud it is born in. The bursts are brief, bright flashes from far space. Some come from stars with huge fields, called magnetars. In-side that field sits a thin soup of bits and their anti-twins. A burst that climbs out must pass that soup, and the soup can scatter it.

The team check old maths of that scatter with a sim that tracks each bit. They find the scatter, though curbed by the field, still grows step by step till it must shape the burst. That growth could dim some bursts or stretch them in time. It sets a trait that burst tools should look for. A match in real bursts would back the maths and map the soup at the burst's birth.
arxiv-2601-18965:
Sabrina Poulsen and a large team hunt for planets around dead stars with the James Webb telescope. Their survey, called MEAD, images nearby white dwarfs, the dense cores left when stars like the Sun die. It points Webb's mid-infrared camera at dozens of these stars, all close to Earth.

The team looks for extra infrared glow, dips from gas effects, and faint companions near each dwarf. Around one star, WD 0644+025, the excess glow points to a probable planet. A planet that outlives its star's death would tell us how planetary systems end and what can survive.
arxiv-2601-19165:
Yi Lyu, Yiyin Shen, and Takashi Matsuzawa build the simplest database system that can still teach the craft. A database management system stores and processes large data sets and can optimize freely, as long as results stay correct and ordered. The authors draw on a known undergraduate course at UW-Madison.

Their prototype strips the system to its bare teaching core. Students can read the whole thing and see how storage, queries, and correctness fit together. A small, clear system serves learning better than a vast pro tool whose internals no beginner can hold in mind at once.
arxiv-2601-19665:
Yan Jiang and six colleagues work on keeping power grids stable after a disturbance. When a fault hits, the grid's frequency swings and must be brought back. Modern inverter-based devices can shape the average frequency of the whole system nicely. In weakly connected grids, though, that average hides swings between areas.

Those inter-area oscillations can damage equipment or trigger wider failures. The authors develop a frequency shaping control aimed at damping them. Their design uses a root locus method, a classic tool for tuning feedback systems. The control is meant for grids where regions are tied by weak lines. As renewable inverters replace spinning machines, such controls become central to grid safety.
arxiv-2601-19865:
C. Munting and five colleagues report lab tests of using lasers to control electron beams. Future colliders like the FCC-ee need bunches of matched intensity. An instability called flip-flop can grow when colliding bunches differ in strength. Laser-driven Compton backscattering has been proposed to trim bunch intensity.

Lasers have also been proposed as indestructible collimators, scraping off stray beam particles without material jaws. The team tests these laser control ideas in the laboratory. Proof at small scale comes before any collider adopts the schemes. Beam control is a quiet bottleneck in collider design. The results inform whether light can do a job now done by matter.
arxiv-2601-19965:
Mingxuan Luo and colleagues tackle a misleading metric in online recommendation. Conversion rate counts clicks that end in purchase. It ignores refunds, so it overstates how happy users really are. Net conversion rate instead counts purchases that are kept, better reflecting true satisfaction and business value.

Predicting it is hard because of cascaded delay feedback: refunds arrive long after clicks and purchases. The authors present a benchmark, insights, and solutions for this prediction problem. Industrial recommender systems allocate traffic by such predictions, so errors waste money and annoy users. A metric that counts kept purchases aligns ranking with real outcomes. The work brings the delay structure of refunds into the model design.
arxiv-2601-20065:
Rishabh Sharma, Chitrasen Jena, and Volodymyr Vovchenko study the cooling phase of heavy-ion collisions. After quarks and gluons recombine, the system lives briefly as a gas of hadrons. That hadronic phase shapes the final abundances of particles detectors count. The authors model gold-gold collisions at RHIC across a wide energy range.

Their model is a hadron resonance gas in partial chemical equilibrium. It tracks how abundances freeze as the system cools and expands. Matching the model to data across energies tests our picture of the collision's late stage. The hadronic phase is easy to overlook next to the quark-gluon plasma. Yet it edits the very yields used to claim plasma properties. Careful modelling keeps those claims honest.
arxiv-2601-20265:
Yuenong Ling and Adrian Lozano-Duran build a subgrid-scale stress model for large-eddy simulation of turbulent flows. Such simulations resolve big eddies and model the small ones. Their model extends a data-assimilation approach so that the learned stress agrees with the numerical scheme of the flow solver itself.

The method handles flows with two directions of variation and is applied to turbulent boundary layers under adverse pressure gradients. Those are the flows along wings and blades where prediction is hardest. A model that matches the solver's own math could give steadier, more accurate results for engineering design.
arxiv-2601-20465:
Yang Li and four colleagues present BMAM, a brain-inspired memory framework for language model agents. Agents that act over long horizons struggle to keep time-grounded information and stay consistent across sessions. The authors name this failure soul erosion. BMAM models memory as a set of specialized subsystems rather than one unstructured store.

Each subsystem plays a distinct role, echoing how brains divide memory work. The architecture is meant to be general-purpose, serving agents of many kinds. Agents that remember who said what, and when, could serve users over months without slowly drifting away from their instructions and facts.
arxiv-2601-20865:
Emmanuel Pio Pastore and Francesco De Rango argue that some immune complexity cannot be computed at all. Their 2026 paper gives a certificate-based view of immune reactions. The frame rests on algorithmic information theory. A fixed executor maps a short advice string to a candidate response. A response counts only if a validity check accepts it. That check may be decidable or only semi-decidable.

Gaps then appear between what can be certified and what can be computed. The authors call these information gaps under effective constraints. The immune system is their test case for deep limits on prediction. If this complexity is noncomputable, no algorithm can shortcut the biology. The paper joins immunology with the math of what can be known.
arxiv-2601-20965:
Drake Deming and eight co-authors propose a third way to probe the air of rocky planets. Their 2026 paper concerns temperate exoplanets, worlds that could hold liquid water. Detecting their atmospheres has proven hard for JWST. Transit spectroscopy of the TRAPPIST-1 planets suffers from spots and faculae on the host star. Secondary eclipses have found hot rocks, but evidence for atmospheres stays elusive. A new observable is needed.

The authors champion color phase curves. A phase curve tracks a planet's light as it orbits. Color adds which wavelengths rise and fall. Together they can betray an atmosphere without a transit. The paper lays out this option for temperate rocky worlds. It offers observers a path around stellar contamination. The idea could guide future telescope time toward clearer answers.
arxiv-2601-21165:
Miles Wang and a large team of co-authors, including OpenAI staff, build a test of expert-level science skill for AI. Their 2026 paper introduces FrontierScience. The benchmark evaluates AI capabilities for expert-level scientific reasoning. It consists of two tracks. The Olympiad track holds international olympiad problems at the level of the physics, chemistry, and biology olympiads. The Research track holds PhD-level, open-ended problems. Those mirror sub-problems in real scientific research.

Most benchmarks top out at undergraduate knowledge. FrontierScience aims at the frontier its name claims. Open-ended research problems resist simple grading, so the design matters. The benchmark can track whether AI systems approach working-scientist ability. It also exposes where they still fail like students. Labs and funders get a sterner yardstick for scientific AI.
arxiv-2601-21365:
Prateek Puri warns that small AI models pose safety risks that current policy largely ignores. AI brings clear gains to fields like medicine and materials work. Most governance so far, though, judges risk by the computing power behind a model.

Small models need little compute, so they slip under those thresholds. Yet they can still be capable, cheap to copy, and easy to misuse. The paper maps the challenges these models create for oversight. It argues that rules based on size alone will miss a growing class of threats. Policy, the author urges, should track what models can do, not just their cost.
arxiv-2601-21665:
Vijini Liyanage and François Yvon adapt word-piece tokenizers to special domains. Tokenization chops text into pieces that a language model reads. Standard practice trains one general tokenizer for everything, then uses it for training and serving alike.

A generic piece set wastes effort on text from narrow fields or specific languages. Rare terms get shredded into many tiny pieces, which costs speed and accuracy. The authors adapt the popular BPE method to build specialized tokenizers. A fitted tokenizer could make domain models, from law to medicine, cheaper to run and sharper on their own vocabulary.
arxiv-2601-21765:
Augusto Fasano and Giovanni Rebaudo, based in Torino, work on a common statistical problem. Picking which variables matter when the outcome is simply yes or no. Their approach is Bayesian. It uses a probit link for the binary outcome. Its prior lets most coefficients sit at zero while a few stand out.

The standard tool for such models, Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, gets painfully slow when the data have many dimensions. The 2026 preprint instead develops a mean-field variational Bayes method, which replaces slow sampling with a faster approximation. Fast, reliable variable selection matters wherever binary outcomes are predicted from many possible factors, from medicine to economics and social science.
arxiv-2601-21965:
Deeksha Shama, Dimitra Emmanouilidou, and Ivan Tashev work on measuring mental effort from brain signals in real time. Brain-computer interfaces that adapt to how engaged a user is need a reliable read on cognitive load. Brain waves recorded by EEG offer a cheap, non-invasive way to get that signal.

Older methods, though, struggle when a new person wears the headset, and they often need training for one specific task. The team's 2026 preprint uses brain foundation models, large models pretrained on neural data, together with interpretability tools. Their aim is load estimation that transfers across people and tasks, which would make adaptive learning systems and assistive interfaces far more practical.
arxiv-2601-22065:
Ksenija Kovalenka and co-authors show that mess can create a phase of matter, not just kill one. In clean solids, some phases guard the flow of charge in odd ways. Dirt and flaws tend to blur those phases. The team uses a toy model of such a phase, the Haldane model, to ask what dirt does in truth.

They find that dirt does more than shift the edge of a phase. It can hold open a new phase that clean solids do not show. In that phase, the guard on charge flow exists thanks to the dirt itself. Their work is a hint to labs: a bit of mess, placed with care, may give solids traits that pure ones lack.
arxiv-2601-22365:
Yisi Ke and five co-authors use large language models to attack a famed open guess about tree lengths. The Gilbert-Pollak guess says a Steiner tree, which may add new points, can beat a plain spanning tree by only a set margin. Their 2026 preprint takes the plane case, open since 1968.

The team set models to hunt for proofs, counter-cases, or new bounds. A machine-led search can scan far more shapes than a human team. Win or lose, the hunt shows what models can do in hard math. It may also crack a guess that has stood for decades.
arxiv-2601-22665:
Mayukh Mukherjee and Utsab Sarkar study sharp thresholds in boundary problems on curved spaces. The problems involve the Escobar quotient and a family of Gagliardo–Nirenberg functionals, both tied to how shapes bend and stretch. On compact manifolds with boundary, solutions can either settle or blow up in bubbles.

Their unified framework sorts when each outcome happens, using chart-scale maps and stability checks. They also reduce hard cases to finite-dimensional ones under set conditions. Such results guide the study of optimal shapes and inequalities in geometry. The framework covers both attainment and bubbling cases, the two fates that compete in these boundary-critical variational problems.
arxiv-2601-22765:
Rohit Varma and Santosh Nannuru complete distance matrices the Bayesian way, under geometric rules. A Euclidean distance matrix holds all pair gaps between points; often only a few, noisy gaps are known. Their 2026 preprint notes that the task feeds sensor location, room acoustics, and molecule shape work.

Older tools use rank tricks or semidefinite programs to enforce the geometry. A Bayesian route adds honest doubt ranges to each filled gap. That doubt matters when the map guides real choices. The work blends geometry with sound inference. It aims for maps that know their limits.
arxiv-2601-23065:
Xijie Yang and six co-authors rebuild indoor scenes so they can be edited with correct lighting. Radiance-field methods like NeRF copy rooms with high visual fidelity, but edits fail because lighting is baked in. Physically based rendering handles light properly, yet needs exact geometry that real rooms rarely provide.

Their EAG-PT joins emission-aware Gaussians with path tracing to get both fidelity and editability. Rooms that relight correctly can be restyled for design, film, and virtual tours. The blend aims to end the choice between pretty and editable.
arxiv-2601-23265:
Dawei Zhu and five co-authors present PaperBanana, an agent framework that draws academic illustrations automatically. AI scientists powered by language models now run much of the research workflow. Producing publication-ready figures, though, remains a labor-intensive bottleneck done by hand.

PaperBanana aims to lift that burden with an agentic pipeline for diagrams and illustrations. Automatic figures matched to a paper's content could speed every stage of writing and review. The work targets the unglamorous steps that quietly consume researcher time. Publication-ready output is the bar, not rough sketches, because journals demand figures that survive print production.
arxiv-2602-00065: Hiba Arnaout and colleagues argue that tests for AI mental health tools are fragmented and poorly tied to clinic work, social setting, and lived user experience. They review 135 recent publications and find heavy use of generic scores that miss clinical validity, therapeutic fit, and user experience. Input from clinicians is thin, and care for safety and equity is weak. Their answer joins clinical soundness, social context, and equity, with a taxonomy of assessment, intervention, and information synthesis tools.
arxiv-2602-00165: Arthur Negrão and colleagues use Benford leading digit patterns as a prior for post training quantization of large language models. Low bit quantization suffers when the codebook mismatches the true weight and activation distributions. Across model families, they find a split: transformational linear weights tend to follow Benford patterns, while LayerNorm parameters deviate in a systematic way. Their method, BenQ, uses a simple log spaced grid for scale broad layers. It keeps stability critical parameters at higher precision, beating uniform rounding in 4 bit tests.
arxiv-2602-00265: Dong Liang and colleagues present World-Shaper, a single frame for 360 degree wide editing. Perspective based editing methods fail to model panorama spatial structure, and cube map splits break the whole picture. World-Shaper reformulates editing directly in the equirectangular projection domain, joining making and editing in one design. To fix the shortage of paired data, controlled making makes diverse paired examples for guided learning. A geometry aware learning step then keeps the whole picture intact against round image distortion.
arxiv-2602-00365: Ashkan Alibabaei and team develop fundamental limits of large momentum transfer in optical lattices. Such transfer improves atom device sensitivity. Current tools using Bloch oscillations or Bragg diffraction suffer imperfect pulse success. The authors build a Floquet framework giving a unified account of elastic light atom scattering across regimes. Within that frame, they find regimes with far lower losses and better phase accuracy than previous tools. The paper is aimed at readers who work with atom optics and want a clear map of where losses fall and why.
arxiv-2602-00465: Jiaqi Yin and team formalize Budgeted Relational Multi-Instance Learning, a new framing of miRNA-mRNA targeting as bag prediction. Each transcript yields candidate sites, yet only pair labels are observed. Prior methods max pool site scores, ignoring relational patterns, but using them matters. Naive relational aggregation costs quadratically, yet cheap scans discard driving interactions. Here, the compute budget is key, so at most K instances per bag receive costly encoding. Approximation quality and generalization are governed by the budget rather than the raw bag size.
arxiv-2602-00665: Lakshan Cooray and colleagues ask whether small language models can handle multi-turn customer-service question answering. Here history is carried forward as a summary. Large models perform well but cost too much to deploy in constrained settings. Small models remain little tested on dialogue continuity. The study evaluates nine instruction-tuned small models against three commercial large models. It uses lexical and semantic scores plus human and model-based judgement. Results vary widely. Some small models approach large-model quality. Others lose track of context.
arxiv-2602-00865: Brandon Leblanc and colleagues offer a 72M student cutting size 9x, speeding answers 5x, and keeping structural consistency versus a 650M teacher. They distill 3D foundation models into compact students taught on a single PC. Their Distill3R method uses offline caching to split heavy teacher work from training through compressed supervision. A confidence-aware distillation loss uses teacher uncertainty to enable commodity-hardware training. The student trains in under 3 days on one PC, where the teacher needs GPU clusters for up to a week.
arxiv-2602-01065: Qianwan Yang and co-authors fix patchy blur in wide-field glow microscopes that use small optics. Field-linked flaws, dim edges, and cut sensors blur views by place, while past learning plans grow too big as pictures grow. Their SV-CoDe plan tunes its fix kernels by place with coordinate-tuned filters, so patch-wise training stays free of field size. Trained only on physics-made fakes, it read bead tests, thin brain slices, and free-moving worms well, beating past plans on fake and real views.
arxiv-2602-01265: Jiangnan Zhu and co-authors build BicKD, a two-sided contrast teach plan for model distillation. Plain distillation lines up teacher and student odds case by case but skips class-wise contrasts and sets no shape rule on the odds space. BicKD adds a two-sided contrast loss that pushes unlike class zones apart while holding like-class zones tight. That twin form lets teacher and student compare both case-wise and class-wise odds at once. Tests show BicKD beating top distillation plans across net forms and test sets.
arxiv-2602-01365: Wang Yang and co-authors map how domain order shapes GRPO thought tuning across math, science, logic, and puzzles. GRPO now rules thought tuning, yet sequential versus mixed domain training stayed little probed. Single-domain transfer proves lopsided: other-domain training lifts math scores sharply while barely moving logic and puzzles. Order also bites hard: math-then-science training beats science-then-math training by a wide margin on science scores. No single plan rules all domains, with sequential plans favoring math and mixed plans favoring science and logic.
arxiv-2602-01665: Hayeong Lee and colleagues build TABX, the Totally Accelerated Battle Simulator in JAX, a high throughput sandbox for multi agent reinforcement learning tasks. Existing benchmarks highlight key challenges but cannot support custom evaluation scenarios. TABX gives fine control over environment settings, letting researchers probe new behaviors and trade offs across a range of task levels. Running on graphics processors through JAX, it runs in parallel and cuts overhead, offering a fast, open base for future multi agent research.
arxiv-2602-01765: Bingzheng Wang and colleagues hunt diffusion backdoors without weight access. Detoxification trades success against quality, while white box or query heavy detection fails. They reveal Temporal Noise Consistency: backdoors disrupt noise consistency between adjacent timesteps, while clean inputs stay stable. Their TNC-Defense offers TNC-Detect for auditors, using noise data to detect backdoors and find timesteps. TNC-Detox serves providers, correcting the path in a timestep aware way. Across five attacks it lifts detection by eleven percent, and blocks nearly all triggered samples with mild quality loss.
arxiv-2602-01865: Shaopeng Chen and colleagues build GRAB, a generative ad ranking system that predicts click through rates, fixing deep recommendation models' generalization and long sequence limits. Its Causal Action-aware Multi-channel Attention mechanism reads time patterns and action cues in user behavior. Full scale online deployment beats established deep recommendation models, with revenue up over three percent and click through rate up over three percent. Expressive power also grows monotonically and approximately linearly as longer interaction sequences are used.
arxiv-2602-02165: Kaining Zhang and colleagues develop AQER, a loader moving classical and quantum data into quantum circuits with less overhead. Approximate loaders balance fidelity against circuit complexity. Most existing methods are heuristic or guaranteed only for narrow inputs, and no general theory tied them. The team unifies prior loaders in one framework and derives information-theoretic error bounds linking infidelity to entanglement entropy across subsystems. AQER then builds circuits by systematically reducing entanglement in the target state, with tests up to fifty qubits showing gains in accuracy and gate efficiency.
arxiv-2602-02465:
Jana Zeller and 8 co-authors test whether AI models reason better when they think in pictures, in a 2026 arXiv paper. New unified multimodal models can generate images mid-reasoning, much like human mental imagery. The hope is that sketching intermediate steps helps solve multi-step problems.

Their benchmark, MentisOculi, is a procedural suite of stratified reasoning problems designed to suit visual solutions. Strategies from latent visual tokens to fully generated imagery were evaluated. Visual strategies generally failed to improve performance. Unified models could often reason correctly in text and sometimes draw correct visuals, yet generation errors compounded, and even ground-truth pictures went unused. The authors conclude that visual thoughts do not yet benefit model reasoning. The benchmark now exists to measure progress on closing that gap.
arxiv-2602-02565:
Huanran Li and 2 co-authors fill in missing entries of data matrices whose columns gather near a handful of subspaces, in a 2026 arXiv paper. This high-rank completion problem shows up wherever readings are partial and structured. Prior solvers often came without guarantees, were hard to interpret, or needed more observed entries than information theory requires.

The new solver groups partial columns by assigning each a stand-in subspace. It then tunes two geometric costs on the Grassmannian, the manifold of subspaces. One cost is how far each column sits from its assigned subspace, measured chordally. The other is how the chosen subspaces relate to one another along geodesics. On synthetic and real data the method ties the best rivals when observations are plentiful. When observations grow scarce it pulls clearly ahead, closing much of the distance to the floor set by theory.
arxiv-2602-02765:
Haruhiko Murata and 1 co-author modify vision transformers so they attend to the object instead of the scenery, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. Self-attention operates globally, with no built-in way to tell foreground from background. Transformers can therefore waste capacity on background clutter and lose classification accuracy.

Their model, SVD-ViT, uses singular value decomposition to put foreground features first. Three components extract and combine the singular vectors that carry object information, damping task-irrelevant factors such as background noise. Tests show improved classification accuracy over standard vision transformers. The learned representations say more about the foreground and less contaminated by background. The approach treats a classical linear algebra tool as an attention guide, steering a foundation-scale model toward what human viewers would call the subject of the image.
arxiv-2602-02965:
Tests written to reproduce a specific bug are characterized by Andre Hora and 1 co-author in a 2026 paper. Such tests fail while the bug lives and pass once it is fixed. They then stay in the suite to catch regressions. Whether they differ from ordinary tests was largely unstudied before this work.

The authors analyzed hundreds of bug-reproducing tests across fifteen real Python systems. On size, assertion counts, and complexity, these tests looked much like other tests. Two small differences stood out. Bug-reproducing tests used slightly more exception-handling blocks and more weak assertions, such as checking that values are merely unequal. Most reproduced a single bug. A small share reproduced several bugs at once.
arxiv-2602-03365:
Higher-spin particles extend the holographic symmetry algebra in work by Shamik Banerjee, with 3 co-authors. Holography relates gravity in a volume to a theory on its boundary, with soft particles, those carrying very low energy, making symmetry algebras. The authors discuss what changes when higher-spin particles join the gravitons and gluons usually considered in that soft symmetry form at the boundary of spacetime.

In the presence of higher-spin particles, the soft algebra gains a subalgebra made by conformally soft higher-spin particles. That subalgebra does not commute with the one made by soft gravitons. Colored higher-spin particles similarly make their own subalgebra. The authors verify the colored soft algebra using a four-point amplitude from higher-spin Yang-Mills theory. Extensions to a deformed algebra with nonzero cosmological constant are also discussed.
arxiv-2602-03565:
Model checking verifies software by exploring its states, but the state space explodes faster than memory allows. Damien Morard and Didier Buchs propose a symbolic encoding for Petri net markings in a 2026 paper. Instead of vectors of intervals, as in interval decision diagrams, they use generalized intervals over whole vectors.

The authors give these intervals a formal footing and show they support homomorphic operations for checking CTL formulas, the standard temporal logic of branching behavior. A standard form gives the structure good performance traits. The method targets global model checking, which finds every state satisfying a formula at once. Tests on model checking contest examples, using saturation and clustering methods, look promising.
arxiv-2602-03665:
Moral judgment rarely comes in yes-or-no form, yet vision-language models are usually trained on binary labels. Eunkyu Park and 10 co-authors build MM-SCALE in a 2026 paper, a dataset for multimodal moral reasoning with graded supervision. Human annotators rate image-scenario pairs on a five-point acceptability scale and mark which modality grounds each judgment.

The scalar ratings feed listwise preference optimization over ranked sets of scenarios, giving finer calibration than pairwise signals. Models fine-tuned on the data reach higher ranking fidelity and steadier safety calibration than models trained with binary supervision. The authors argue that capturing the continuous, pluralistic character of human moral reasoning is what makes the alignment signal useful.
arxiv-2602-03965:
Neighbors often suffer the same internet slowdowns at the same time. Taveesh Sharma and 5 co-authors study shared latency anomalies in home broadband using four months of measurements from ninety-nine Chicago probes. Their 2026 paper asks whether affected devices see similar jumps in round-trip time.

Many shared anomalies did show consistent size across users, especially within one provider. Building on that, the team designed a sampling method that keeps representative probes and drops redundant ones. It captured nearly all anomaly impact with under half the probes. Cheaper measurement networks mean studies can cover more neighborhoods for the same money.
arxiv-2602-04065:
Ryan T. Low and 1 co-author chart how waves travel through plasma hotter and more magnetic than almost anywhere on Earth. Their 2026 paper studies electron-positron plasmas near magnetars, where fields approach the Schwinger limit at which quantum effects turn strong. Both charge-neutral and non-neutral plasmas are analyzed.

The strongest field and temperature effects cut the plasma frequency cutoff, making the plasma transparent where it should be opaque. The refractive index also shifts in a temperature-independent way matching cold quantum plasma behavior. Such eigenmode maps guide interpretation of magnetar signals and design of extreme laser-plasma experiments.
arxiv-2602-04165:
An exploit that prints a success marker may never trigger the bug. Derin Gezgin and 5 co-authors tackle unreliable proof-of-concept generation by language models in a 2026 paper. Their PoC-Gym pipeline targets Java vulnerabilities from the CVE catalog.

Static traces, tailored prompts, and coverage feedback guide iterative candidate generation. Each candidate must pass three validations: complete execution, a genuine success signal, and reaching the target sink in the trace. Across twenty vulnerabilities and hundreds of runs, many candidates failed these stricter tests. The work gives security researchers a generation loop whose successes mean something.
arxiv-2602-04465:
Radar images of cities can mix signals from objects at different heights into a single pixel, an effect called layover. Pia Addabbo and 4 co-authors address that detection problem in a 2026 paper on SAR tomography, a radar method that builds three-dimensional views.

Their detector uses ideas from information theory to test several hypotheses at once, meaning it checks competing explanations for a signal together. It works in one stage and adapts to the data. A compressive sensing method, which recovers signals from few measurements, estimates the unknown values. Tests on simulated and real radar data compared the design with rival methods. The approach aims at better building and infrastructure monitoring.
arxiv-2602-04565:
Blur, noise, and low light each damage images in measurable physical ways. Guanzhou Lan and 7 co-authors argue in a 2026 paper that vision-language models describe such damage well in words but poorly in numbers.

The team reframes degradation understanding as predicting the damage type, its parameter names, and their continuous values together. They prove these parts fit one prediction scheme. Their model, DU-VLM, trains with fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on structured rewards. A new dataset pairs clean and degraded images with physical annotations. The model beat general baselines and could also steer an image generator to restore pictures without retraining it.
arxiv-2602-04765:
J. V. Wijesekera and 7 co-authors trace how dust dims star-forming galaxies across cosmic time in a 2026 paper. Dust absorbs ultraviolet light and re-emits it in the infrared, so the balance between the two reveals how much starlight was hidden.

The study uses a large sample of galaxies in two well-studied sky fields, with quiescent and starburst systems removed. Infrared luminosities came from stacking images from space and ground telescopes. The team related the infrared excess to ultraviolet slope, stellar mass, and redshift out to high values. At fixed slope, the relation changed systematically with mass, so they built mass into the formula. Their relations can correct galaxy samples for dust absorption consistently across surveys.
arxiv-2602-04865:
Juliana Coelho and Renata Costa characterize a special family of algebraic curves in a 2026 paper.

The curves are stable and irreducible. Those are technical conditions from the theory of curve moduli. The curves are called (d,h)-elliptic when they arise as limits of smooth curves. Those smooth curves admit finite maps of a given degree. The maps land on smooth curves of a given genus, with genus at least one. The authors use admissible covers to give the characterization. Admissible covers are a tool for describing such maps in the limit. That tool lets them pin down exactly which stable curves have the stated property.
arxiv-2602-05065:
Does stochastic gradient descent prefer flat valleys or sharp pits in the loss landscape? Yizhou Xu and 3 co-authors settle part of that debate in this 2026 machine learning paper with a model simple enough to solve exactly. Folklore links flat minima to good generalization, yet evidence has pointed both ways, and this work looks for a causal answer.

In their solvable model, the training rule itself has no flatness preference at all. What it prefers is small gradient fluctuations. The data then decides the ending sharpness: flat minima win only when label noise is spread evenly across output dimensions, and with lopsided noise the model can settle into arbitrarily sharp solutions. The team reproduced the effect in controlled tests on multilayer perceptrons, recurrent networks, and transformers, suggesting the lesson reaches beyond the toy model.
arxiv-2602-05165:
Group-relative policy optimization trains reasoning models by comparing answers within a small group, but small groups make for noisy lessons. Kevin Han and 8 co-authors propose a stabilized version in this 2026 machine learning paper. Two failure modes drive the work: high variance when few responses are sampled, and vanishing gradients when every response in a group fails and earns the same zero reward.

Their method, EBPO, borrows strength from the model's own history. An empirical Bayes shrinkage estimator blends each group's local baseline with a global prior that accumulates over training, updated online. Theory promises strictly lower estimation error, bounded entropy decay, and penalty signals that survive total failure. Experiments on benchmarks including AIME and OlympiadBench beat the original method and other baselines, with the largest stability gains at small group sizes, plus extra benefit from ordering training by difficulty.
arxiv-2602-05265:
Underwater robots inspecting flooded pipelines cannot rely on cameras in murky water or on GPS at all. Kalvik Jakkala and Jason O'Kane give such a robot a minimal kit in this 2026 robotics paper. The kit is an inertial unit, a pressure sensor, and two sonars, one pointing down and one sweeping full circle. The pipe's radius is known, and the robot must center itself and swim the pipe's length.

A fast method extracts range estimates from single-beam sonar intensity, which stays reliable amid noise and echoes. A closed-form geometric model turns the two sonar ranges into an estimate of the pipe center, and an adaptive proportional-derivative controller, weighted by confidence, holds the alignment. Trials in a submerged 46-centimeter pipe with a commercial remotely operated vehicle achieved stable centering and a full traversal. They succeeded despite currents and pipe deformations, with no Doppler log or external tracking.
arxiv-2602-05765:
Robot policies that learn from fake worlds suffer when training waits on slow, uneven physics engines. Haoran Sun and 15 co-authors build an out-of-step reward learning frame for vision language action models, the policies that drive embodied agents. Standard frames switch strictly between runs and tuning, treating each run as one whole unit, a design taken from language model training.

Their system lets fake-world runs, guessing, and training run at once, with smart batch planners and flexible world splitting. Tests span several fake-world backends, model shapes, and learning rules. Throughput rose up to eighty five percent over lockstep rivals while sample use stayed the same. Scaling held from a handful of graphics chips to hundreds. The authors describe the system as the first fully out-of-step frame built for vision language action training. It targets robot teams whose choke point is setup, not rules.
arxiv-2602-06665:
Bowen Zhang, Meiyi Wang, and Harold Soh study a side effect of the extra training that makes language models helpful. Their answers become less varied and start to repeat themselves. Drawing on evidence that different layers of a model do different jobs, they test whether the sameness can be traced to specific layers that changed during that training.

Using a designed practice task with a clear set of valid answers, they found a trade-off between variety and quality. This showed up as different layer ranges were restored to their pre-trained state. Their method, selective layer restoration, builds a hybrid model by rolling back only the chosen layers, at no extra running cost. Across writing, question answering, and reasoning tasks and three model families, it recovered much of the lost variety while keeping quality high.
arxiv-2602-06865:
Amir Mostaed draws a hard line in arithmetic geometry between two kinds of objects. One side holds classes that come from automorphic forms; the other holds cycles built by geometry. The Hodge conjecture asks if certain classes come from cycles, and this paper shows that even an automorphic class may be out of reach for every known geometric build.

The block is one concrete class on a Shimura variety tied to the group SO(2,26), built by lifting a weight-two form of conductor 11. Mostaed proves the class sits outside the interior part, while special cycles, lifts, transfers, and boundary pushes all land inside. The proof leans only on settled tools, and it turns the conjecture from a yes-or-no question into one about what can actually be built.
arxiv-2602-06965:
Ankan Deria and five co-authors present MedMO, a medical model that reads images and text together. Such models have been held back in medicine by narrow domain coverage, shaky links between images and words, and weak grounded reasoning. MedMO trains only on large-scale medical data, with a multi-stage recipe built for the domain.

Early stages line up visual encoders with a medical language backbone, and instruction tuning spans captioning, visual question answering, report writing, retrieval, and disease pinpointing. A final reward stage checks facts and spatial accuracy to sharpen grounding and step-by-step reasoning. The larger model beat strong open medical rivals across radiology, eye, and pathology tasks, with big gains on expert question answering, while the smaller model stayed competitive.
arxiv-2602-07065:
A. N. Maria Antony and two co-authors estimate material traits from image series alone, with no touch on the sample. Contactless measurement matters in engineering and medicine where direct probing is impossible. Old approaches rely on slow iterative alignment algorithms and numerical solvers, such as finite element methods. Those do not suit high-throughput data.

Their deep learning framework uses two nets. One handles image alignment. One estimates how much a sample can be squeezed. Together they yield shifts of the continuum and squeeze traits end to end from the image series. The framework beat old approaches on both speed and score. Notably, it gauged squeeze traits well even when the alignment map strayed far from the reference shift field. The authors credit higher-order traits, such as swirl in the vector field, rather than plain local traits of shift.
arxiv-2602-07165:
Many scientific problems come down to a ratio of two counts, and treating that ratio naively understates the uncertainty.  Matthew LeDuc and one co-author present PoissonRatioUQ, an R package for Bayesian modeling of count ratios, built on the ratio of Poisson means rather than the ratio of observed counts.

The package offers several ways to recover the quantity of interest, with or without spatial information, plus added tools for intensity-ratio problems of a common power-law form.  Users who analyze count data get a ready-made, principled way to report uncertainty instead of a single shaky number.
arxiv-2602-07265:
Mixture-of-experts models save compute by activating only some experts per token, but batching and speculative decoding activate far more experts than expected, eroding the savings.  Daniil Vankov and five co-authors present XShare, a method that treats batch-aware expert choice as an tuning problem.

Greedy methods pick experts to maximize total gating score for each batch, with no retraining and adaptation to every batch, including mixed data sets.  Reported gains include up to 30 percent fewer expert activations under standard batching and up to three times lower peak GPU load in expert-parallel setups.  Inference builders get a drop-in efficiency win for production MoE serving.
arxiv-2602-07565:
Identifying people at a distance is hard when faces and fingerprints cannot be captured, so gait recognition offers a useful option.  A large team led by Jingzhe Ma reports on the Human Identification at a Distance competition, HID 2025, which has run annually since 2020.

Since 2023 the competition uses the SUSTech dataset with wide variation in clothing, carried objects. Viewing angles, supplies no dedicated training data, and regenerates testing splits with a fresh random seed each year to limit overfitting.  The paper surveys challenges, methods, and results.  Biometrics teams get a fair, cross-domain benchmark record for gait identification in real settings.
arxiv-2602-07865:
Tuned learning software usually tunes content by test scores, missing how focus rises and falls, especially for neurodivergent learners. Satyam Kumar Navneet and two co-authors present AttentionGuard, a method that infers focus states from privacy-keeping action signals and tunes the screen in response.

The system models four focus states drawn from ADHD research and offers five tuning patterns, including support that answers both low input and high input. Its finder reaches 87.3 percent closeness on a large open learning dataset and aligns with clinical ADHD profiles. A small study with eleven adults with ADHD traits found lower cognitive load and better comprehension in the tuned condition, suggesting focus-aware design is worth pursuing.
arxiv-2602-08165:
Industrial control systems mix Linux, proprietary real-time systems, and Windows, and translating the IEC 62443-3-3 security standard into concrete Windows checks is painstaking. Miguel Bicudo and six co-authors propose a transfer-learning method that maps Windows Common Configuration Enumerations to the standard's system security requirements using labeled Linux data.

That labeled dataset makes automated compliance checks possible, along with analysis of which requirements appear most, and comparison of cross-platform similarities and differences. Configuration enumerations thus bridge abstract standards and concrete settings. Security engineers for industrial systems gain automation, traceability, and clarity for Windows compliance work that previously relied on manual mapping.
arxiv-2602-08265:
High-order perturbation theory for many-body systems drowns in a rapidly growing configuration space, and judging convergence is itself hard. Xin Zhen and three co-authors offer perturbation theory quantum Monte Carlo, a stochastic method that pictures the perturbative wave function as random walkers moving through configuration space.

The walker picture avoids the exponential scaling of conventional high-rank excitation operators. Benchmarks on the Richardson pairing model reproduce exact perturbation coefficients up to sixteenth order, even where series diverge strongly. Combining the method with resummation yields stable, precise energies where naive series fail. The authors also propose an real configuration count as a global complexity measure. Nuclear and condensed-matter theorists gain a usable route to high-order math.
arxiv-2602-08365:
Making jet fuel from captured carbon dioxide and green hydrogen could cut aviation emissions without new planes or engines. Nils Erland L. Haugen and seven co-authors simulate a key step: the catalyst-free reverse water-gas-shift reactor that turns carbon dioxide into syngas. Their arXiv paper asks how turbulence and chemistry interact in that reactor.

Catalysts degrade, clog, and crack, so a catalyst-free design is attractive if its chemistry is understood. The simulations find that even small oxygen traces in the carbon dioxide stream boost carbon monoxide output markedly, through a larger hydroxyl pool. The effect is strongest at atmospheric pressure. A standard combustion turbulence model also proves to work well for this endothermic reaction. Readers get design clues for cleaner fuel plants.
arxiv-2602-08465:
Phones in public invite shoulder surfing and accidental camera exposure, yet few studies test privacy tools in real life. Andreas Tjeldflaat and four co-authors run a two-week field study with twenty-two participants using a screen filter and a camera slider. Their arXiv paper mixes questionnaires with interviews to track attitudes, habits, and social dynamics.

Screen-filter users report changes in visibility comfort and stop actively covering their screens as often, suggesting their sense of risk shifted. The camera slider surfaces subtler themes around awareness and how others might judge them. Readers get grounded evidence about tools people actually carry, plus a reminder that feeling private and being private are different things.
arxiv-2602-08765:
Coding agents are proliferating, but there is no rigorous way to compare how prompts, skills, tools, and multi-agent setups affect capability and cost. Micah Villmow introduces Scylla, an evaluation framework based on structured ablation studies across seven testing tiers of rising complexity. His arXiv paper centers on Cost-of-Pass: the expected dollar cost to obtain one correct solution.

The framework is model-agnostic and works with any command-line tool, demonstrated with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and judged by multiple models from the same vendor using direct tests, rubrics, and qualitative assessment. Results suggest architectural complexity does not always improve quality. Readers get a reproducible way to price agent designs against their actual outcomes.
arxiv-2602-08865:
Heavy rain at its rarest is hard to predict, and Rishikesh Yadav and one co-author offer a lean method for it. Their entry in the EVA2025 data challenge models extreme rainfall from many runs of the CESM2 climate model. First, target levels are estimated at lower thresholds, then a simple regression grounded in regular-variation theory stretches them to very high quantiles.

Seasonal swings show up clearly, but no strong long-term trend appears across years, and runs can be treated as independent. Confidence bands come from a block bootstrap. The straightforward two-stage approach earned a joint second place in the challenge, trading some accuracy for far less computing than full likelihood methods.
arxiv-2602-08965:
Teams of AI agents that cannot talk to each other struggle to coordinate, and shared random numbers help only so far. John Gardiner and four co-authors propose letting agents share quantum entanglement instead, a resource that enables a wider class of coordination without communication. Their framework trains agents through a differentiable policy design that optimizes over quantum measurements, splitting joint policies into a quantum coordinator plus local actors.

Learned purely from experience, the agents reach quantum advantage in single-round cooperative games treated as black boxes, beating every shared-randomness strategy. The machinery also learns advantageous policies in a sequential multi-agent problem. It is the first training framework of its kind for entanglement-assisted coordination.
arxiv-2602-09165:
Text-to-image models often garble scenes with several objects, traits, and spatial links. Hirunima Jayasekara and four co-authors ground making in scene-graph structure, swapping rigid pre-set layout maps with a zero-shot guiding setup that creates soft visual guidance during use. At its core sits the ASQL Conditioner, which encodes trait, size, count, and spot through a light language model.

That guidance steers spread making via use-time tuning, keeping text-image match while keeping outputs linked and varied. Unlike fixed layouts, soft guidance bends without breaking the whole. The approach aims to make complex prompts render true, a lasting weakness of photorealistic makers.
arxiv-2602-09365:
Rosa Paten and Dora Woodruff extend three Schur positivity results to the world of key polynomials, replacing Schur polynomials with flagged Schur polynomials throughout. Their 2026 paper first shows that Temperley-Lieb immanants of many flagged Jacobi-Trudi matrices are key positive. From that base, it derives a combinatorial rule for expanding most products of flagged skew Schur polynomials in the key basis, plus a log concavity result inspired by Lam, Postnikov, and Pylyavskyy.

The proofs run through Demazure crystals and the recently defined shuffle tableaux of Nguyen and Pylyavskyy. To make the argument work, the authors develop a new characterization of Demazure crystals building on Assaf and Gonzalez, a tool they expect to prove useful elsewhere. The paper is thus both a positivity result and a piece of crystal combinatorics with wider potential.
arxiv-2602-09965:
Graphs built from permuting multiset strings offer a test bed for coloring questions. A 2026 paper by Italo J. Dejter studies the multiset star transposition graph, whose vertices are strings with each symbol repeated a fixed number of times, joined by swaps with the first position. The question is when such graphs admit list and total colorings.

Dejter shows the graphs are choosable under stated conditions and therefore admit total colorings. The proof generalizes efficient dominating sets to a multiset version and builds vertex partitions extending earlier work. For a special case, the graphs admit total colorings with a matching count of colors, each color class an efficient dominating set at distance three.
arxiv-2602-10165:
Artificial intelligence promises much for science, but its spread through research deserves restraint, not celebration alone. A 2026 essay by Roberto Trotta argues that academia's primary aim must be guarded: advancing knowledge for humans. The piece warns against indiscriminate adoption, meaning uptake without discrimination about where AI helps the aim and where it undermines it.

The essay's case runs as follows. Promise alone does not justify adoption without discrimination, because the stakes are academia's defining purpose itself. If adoption proceeds indiscriminately, that purpose risks erosion. Restraint, on this view, is the safeguard: a deliberate choice to let human knowledge-advance set the terms on which AI enters research.
arxiv-2602-10465:
Mohan Rajagopalan and Vinay Rao propose a trust layer for enterprise AI agents in a 2026 paper. Agentic systems automate workflows, but current defenses like guardrails and meaning filters are chance and routinely bypassed. The paper argues security must instead rest on four edges: prompts, tools, data, and context.

Their authenticated workflows enforce intent and integrity at every crossing, combining cryptographic proof with runtime policy checks. Work either carry valid proof or are rejected, which the authors call deterministic security. A new policy language, MAPL, expresses constraints that evolve as agents and contexts change, scaling far better than flat rule lists. The design aims to make agent security provable rather than hopeful.
arxiv-2602-11165:
Language models now answer fresh questions, but do they match what people actually say? Pushwitha Krishnappa and four co-authors offer RECOM, a benchmark of fifteen thousand recent Reddit questions from September 2025 with community-derived reference answers. Four open models are tested against those answers.

A striking gap appears: models score near-perfect semantic similarity yet tiny lexical overlap, meaning they preserve sense through heavy paraphrase. Larger size does not predict better scores, and direct contradictions stay rare. The authors argue that lexical metrics misjudge abstractive answers, and that tests must weigh meaning across several aspects, not surface word match alone.
arxiv-2602-11265:
Condensates that exist only over a finite range of scales are a peculiar phase-transition effect. Álvaro Pastor-Gutiérrez and two co-authors show that thermal precondensation occurs in gauge-fermion theories in the chiral limit, near the thermal chiral transition. The precondensation regime grows more pronounced and wider in heat as fermion flavour count rises.

The underlying motion are shared across fermionic systems, from condensed matter to high-energy physics. Domains, pseudo-gapped phases, and spatial inhomogeneities all connect to this effect. The authors discuss relevance for physics beyond the Standard Model, where precondensation may shape phase structure in ways balance models alone miss.
arxiv-2602-11365:
Clique complexes record which vertex sets form cliques, but toughness asks for more. Marek Filakovský, writing alone, studies k-robust clique complexes, where a set forms a simplex unless it contains an independent set of size k. The setting is square sequence graphs, built by attaching four-cycles iteratively, including rectangular grids.

For k equal to two and three, the homotopy type is a wedge of spheres in a dimension set by k, extended to general k under structural constraints on attachments. König's theorem decomposes the complex into tractable pieces, enabling an inductive proof with standard topology tools. Alexander duality then links the results to total-k-cut complexes, generalizing recent grid-graph findings.
arxiv-2602-11465:
Back pain assessment needs movement data outside the clinic, but motion capture is costly and impractical at home. Jared Levy and six co-authors propose MT-AIM, a deep learning pipeline for Motion Tape, a low-cost fabric wearable sensor. Small, noisy data sets are the central obstacle for this new sensor.
