MT-AIM meets that obstacle with conditional generative models that synthesize Motion Tape data for desired movements, plus predicted joint kinematics as extra traits. Built data and trait augmentation jointly yield leading scores in classifying lower back movements. The work bridges physiological sensing and movement analysis, aiming to help clinicians prescribe physical therapy from remote, everyday movement data.
arxiv-2602-11665:
Online bilevel optimization usually depends on hypergradient descent, which needs costly Hessian-vector products that can dominate computation. Tingkai Jia and one co-author remove that requirement entirely, reformulating the problem as a single-level online problem with inequality constraints and building a sequence of Lagrangian functions. The resulting algorithm uses only first-order information, yet still achieves regret bounds that grow slowly with time and with changes in the problem.

An improved variant with an adaptive inner-iteration scheme drops one dependence in the bound and reaches a cleaner logarithmic-plus-variation rate. The same first-order approach extends to the stochastic setting with a sublinear regret guarantee. Numerical experiments confirm the method works in practice and support the theory, offering a cheaper route to bilevel problems that arrive as a stream rather than a fixed batch.
arxiv-2602-11865:
AI agents now tackle complex tasks, and ambitious goals demand splitting problems into manageable parts and handing those parts safely to other agents or humans. Existing splitting and handoff methods lean on simple rules, failing to adapt as conditions change or to handle unexpected failures robustly. Nenad Tomašev and two co-authors propose an adaptive framework for intelligent AI delegation, treating delegation as a sequence of decisions about task allocation.

The framework also covers transfer of authority, responsibility, and accountability, plus clear specs for roles and boundaries, clarity of intent, and mechanisms for building trust between parties. It applies to human and AI delegators and delegatees alike in complex delegation networks. The authors aim to inform protocols for the emerging agentic web, where delegation chains will be routine rather than exceptional.
arxiv-2602-11965:
Learning from past domains to predict future ones grows costly as backbones scale, since dynamics models must encode every adapted parameter. Zekun Cai and five co-authors propose LoTiC, a method that splits temporal updates into shared low-rank bases and a compact core. The bases define a stable update subspace while only the core changes over time, so change is learned in a small core space, not the full adapter.

The split is justified through the geometry of weight increments and supports continuous, recurrent, and time-conditioned core models. Across six controlled and real-world benchmarks, three data types, and both classification and generation, LoTiC ranks first in 14 of 15 settings. That includes near-perfect future-domain accuracy with an 8-billion-weight backbone. It adds only a tiny fraction of trainable parameters beyond LoRA and trains about two to seven times faster than dynamics baselines.
arxiv-2602-12065:
Training robots needs data, and hand-building simulated tasks is slow. Xiang Liu and six co-authors present Scene2Demo, an automated framework for offline embodied data generation from a single scene image and a user query. Five role-focused modules handle task understanding, symbolic breakdown, configuration building, object-size adjustment, and action-flow planning, sorting task specs and action transitions as path search over a scene-linked object-action graph.

Failed or incomplete executions are refined by two feedback agents: a safety checker giving step-wise visual critiques and a task lead fixing action sequences from rollouts and evolution history. Across 102 automatically generated scene-task pairs, execution succeeds about 72 percent of the time, and feedback refinement improves long-horizon task success over primitive-only execution. Cloning policies reach 96 percent and 92 percent success on two representative tasks, showing the produced data supports downstream learning.
arxiv-2602-12265:
Hecke operators turn up in many corners of two-dimensional conformal field theory, from permutation orbifolds to code ensembles and the AdS3/RMT2 program. Nico Cooper works alone here, using an equidistribution theorem for Hecke operators to show a shared pattern across large-N limits. In each case, a whole heavy sector of the partition function is averaged away.

What survives comes only from Poincaré series of light states, giving a direct holographic reading as a sum over semiclassical handlebody geometries. The paper then speculates on wider meanings for equidistribution, including a possible ergodicity claim. Readers get a single averaging principle that ties disparate conformal theories to the same geometric picture.
arxiv-2602-12365:
Energy-based finite-element methods describe complex mechanics from one global energy functional, whose derivatives give the governing equations. Mohit Pundir led this work with two co-authors, tackling a trade-off in automatic differentiation. Global differentiation is expressive but hard to scale, while local differentiation scales well but limits the physics and couplings a frame can express easily.

Their framework, tatva, defines physics as a single global functional and differentiates it globally to yield residual and tangent operators. Jacobian-vector products power matrix-free solvers, and colouring-based sparse differentiation builds sparse tangent stiffness matrices when needed. The design scales linearly on GPUs, handles millions of degrees of freedom without running out of memory, and covers constraints, mixed-dimensional coupling, and neural networks.
arxiv-2602-12665:
Logic gives a controlled testbed for scoring LLM-based reasoners, yet standard SAT-style tests often mix surface hardness, such as length, wording, and clause order, with structural factors that decide satisfiability. Naïm Es-sebbani led this work with three co-authors, giving a diagnostic test set for 2-SAT built from tuned families of structured 2-CNF formulas. There satisfiability is read from the implication graph and can be tuned along clear axes.

Generators isolate distinct skills and failure modes. They include contradiction-cycle UNSAT cores with tunable size and imbalance, SAT cases with a set share of free variables, and cases probing unit propagation and pure literal elimination. Tests of reasoning models reveal steady weaknesses, including sensitivity to surface features and failure on structured UNSAT cores, even when surface hardness is held fixed.
arxiv-2602-12965:
BMS balances describe how space-time looks from far away, but their usual presentation leans on bulk space-time ideas. Xavier Bekaert and three co-authors offer lecture notes that build the theory purely from shape at null infinity, valid in any dimension, sidestepping the traditional bulk realisation as long-run balances. The notes are self-contained and group-theory throughout.

Topics include the semidirect structure of the BMS group, BMS transformations as conformal Carrollian balances at null infinity, and holographic reconstruction of Minkowski space-time from good cuts. A one-to-one link between good-cut subspaces and Poincaré subgroups, or vacua, is covered, alongside a basic introduction to unitary representations. For readers entering the field, the notes provide a clean shape doorway into BMS theory.
arxiv-2602-13065:
Manganese telluride has drawn intense attention as an established altermagnet, prompting fresh looks at its properties. One puzzle is a Raman-active feature near 175 inverse centimetres, long assigned to an E2g phonon, that does not fit that assignment. A popular hypothesis blamed leakage of a forbidden phonon through symmetry lowering. Bishal Thapa and two co-authors check that idea with first-principles calculations.

They decisively rule out the leakage hypothesis and propose instead that the mystery mode is electronic in nature, a plasmon made possible by hole self-doping. The distinction matters for understanding electronic transport in MnTe: a plasmon points to charge dynamics, not lattice vibrations. Further experiments will be needed to confirm the picture, but the calculations redirect the search for the mode's origin.
arxiv-2602-13665:
Agentic AI turns user intent into structured function calls, but three redundancies inflate latency. They are reprocessing a large function library per request, using a large slow model for whole predictable token sequences, and regenerating fixed boilerplate parameter syntax. HyFunc eliminates all three with a hybrid-model cascade. A large model distills intent into a single soft token, which guides a lightweight retriever to pick relevant functions and steers a smaller prefix-tuned model to generate the final call.

Dynamic templating injects boilerplate syntax on the fly inside an extended vLLM engine, removing syntactic redundancy. On the unseen BFCL benchmark, HyFunc reached 0.828 seconds latency, beating all baselines, with 80.1 percent performance, surpassing models of comparable scale. Weibin Liao leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14165:
Deepak R and three co-authors design a 2026 arXiv signal chain for quantum processors at 4 Kelvin. Superconducting qubits need precise control signals and faithful readout, but room-temperature controllers sit far from millikelvin chips. The paper bridges that gap with a full bidirectional cryogenic analog path.

The control path uses a phase-locked loop for a stable local oscillator, I/Q modulation for gate operations, and a cryogenic power amplifier. The readout path pairs a low-noise amplifier with 14 dB gain and 8-PSK demodulation to tell quantum states apart. SPICE simulations with cryogenic MOSFET models at 180 nm report I/Q phase error under 2 degrees, image rejection above 35 dB, and symbol error below one in a million.
arxiv-2602-14265:
Zachary Bamberger and five co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv method for inference-time compute. Methods such as Best-of-n and Tree-of-Thoughts aim for high-quality, diverse outputs, but high-temperature sampling often fails to deliver real diversity. They also give users little control over how reasoning proceeds, limiting interpretability.

STATe-of-Thoughts instead searches over high-level reasoning patterns. A controller picks actions that encode reasoning choices, a generator writes steps conditioned on those choices, and an evaluator scores candidates to guide search. Because branches are discrete, interpretable textual interventions rather than token samples, action-guided steps reliably steer generations and yield greater diversity than temperature sampling, as shown in an argument-generation case study.
arxiv-2602-14365:
Shun Kato and four co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv medical imaging problem: spotting joint inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis from home photos. Early diagnosis and tight follow-up matter, since ongoing inflammation can permanently damage joints, yet specialist care often takes a long time to reach. RGB hand images captured at home could speed detection.

The task is hard: positive samples are scarce, data are imbalanced, and inflammation is visually subtle. The paper quantifies that difficulty by building a dedicated dataset, and proposes a detection method designed for small, imbalanced RGB data. The goal is a tool that flags joint inflammation early, helping patients reach care before damage becomes irreversible.
arxiv-2602-14865:
Chenyang Ma and colleagues present EmbeWebAgent, a framework for embedding web agents directly into customised user interfaces, rather than driving them through screenshots or raw document trees. Enterprise settings allow control of frontend and backend alike, and EmbeWebAgent exploits it with lightweight frontend hooks, curated ARIA and URL observations, and a per-page function registry reached by WebSocket.

A reusable backend workflow reasons and acts, supporting mixed-granularity actions from GUI primitives to higher-level composites, across React, Angular, and other stacks. Agents stop guessing at pixels and start using the application's own functions. Enterprise web automation gains an insider's route.
arxiv-2602-15165:
Plunkett and colleagues map the three-dimensional kinematics of the oxygen-rich supernova remnant G292. Young core-collapse remnants reveal the chemical makeup of progenitors and the geometry of explosions. G292 is one of only three known oxygen-rich remnants in the galaxy where relatively pure ejecta fragments can be seen. Earlier proper motion work on several dozen ejecta knots used images spanning 22 years. It found transverse velocities proportional to distance from a common expansion center, implying little deceleration since the blast about 3000 years ago.

The team now adds optical spectra from Cerro Tololo, measuring radial velocities for 93 knots. Assuming un-decelerated expansion, radial velocity should scale with line-of-sight distance from the center, just as proper motions scale with transverse distance. The knots generally follow a broad bi-conical distribution, suggesting the explosion drove broad jets of ejecta, a structure seen in some other young core-collapse remnants.
arxiv-2602-15665:
Kovarik and Rossaro present Hardy-type inequalities for magnetic Dirichlet forms with singular integral weights. Hardy inequalities bound a function energy from below by a weighted integral, and the magnetic setting adds the twist of a magnetic field shaping the underlying form. The authors examine when their integral weight is optimal, treating local and global optimality in turn. Several examples worked in detail show how the weight behaves in concrete cases.

The paper also carries the results into spectral theory, giving estimates for magnetic Schrödinger operators as an application. Readers of analysis and mathematical physics will find a careful treatment of a singular weight class, with optimality questions answered and examples that make the abstract machinery tangible. The spectral application shows the inequalities doing work beyond their own statement.
arxiv-2602-15765:
McGlynn and Hebborn develop an accurate formalism for two-neutron halo nuclei, using carbon-22 as a case study. Away from stability, loosely bound systems form few-body cluster structures such as two-neutron halos, born from interplay between many-body and few-body degrees of freedom and strong coupling between bound and continuum states. Models must therefore capture few-body dynamics while enforcing shell effects.

The work has two goals: enforcing the Pauli principle correctly in few-body models, and enabling more robust, cheaper three-body calculations. A three-body hyperspherical harmonics formalism combined with the R-matrix method is used, comparing phenomenological interactions with two methods for removing Pauli-forbidden states, projection and supersymmetric. The projection method proves more accurate, convergence holds for bound and scattering states near K-max of 40, and one efficient channel truncation cuts compute cost by 20 percent.
arxiv-2602-15965:
Chang and colleagues give the coming low precision floating point standard a machine checked foundation. The P3109 standard breaks from fixed formats by letting bit width, precision, signedness, and domain vary, reaching down to a single bit of precision. It also adds stochastic rounding and saturation arithmetic, features that leave a verification gap for future hardware and software.

Their Lean formalization, called FLoPS, models the standard in full and proves basic properties within it. Working through the model turns up surprises: one classic summation routine gains an exact overflow error property under saturation, while a known extraction routine fails at one bit of precision. The result is a verified base on which numerical tools for P3109 can be checked rather than trusted.
arxiv-2602-16065:
Kevin Wang leads a team of three researchers asking whether generative AI can survive training on its own outputs without degrading. As AI-made content spreads, models increasingly learn from what earlier models produced. That raises the risk of progressive collapse. The authors give rigorous theory results showing that, under mild conditions that do not depend on the model type, the model converges to the true data source distribution.

The speed of convergence is set by the slower of two limits. One is the model own intrinsic rate. The other is the share of real data at each training step. That split marks a phase shift between data-limited and model-limited regimes. For biased real data, correcting the bias stops early bias from persisting and growing over iterations. Simulations and tests on real images and texts back the theory, giving conditions for long-term stability in contaminated training.
arxiv-2602-16765:
Ira Wolfson proposes the first hands-on plan to rebuild the inverse-temperature four-vector of a relativistic medium from stochastic fields alone. Since van Kampen and Israel, that four-vector has been the accepted account of relativistic equilibrium. Yet no test has ever recovered it as one observable. Old routes infer rest-frame heat and flow speed from separate measures.

The new plan draws both parts from one passive source: field fluctuation links from a drifting medium. A plain electric-magnetic cross-spectral ratio yields drift speed from Lorentz mixing. Angle-resolved noise power yields rest-frame heat by a ratio trick that cancels absolute size. Monte Carlo runs tuned to a dual high-power laser-plasma site show sub-percent heat precision. That enables a first direct test of how thermal states transform.
arxiv-2602-17165:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports the first evidence for a rare triple-boson event: two Z bosons plus one photon produced together and caught by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The measurement uses the full Run-2 dataset of proton-proton collisions. It focuses on the fully leptonic final state of four leptons and one photon, chosen in a region where photon radiation effects are minimized.

Only a handful of events passed selection against a small expected background, yielding evidence-level significance for the ZZ-gamma final state. The measured cross-section in the fiducial region agrees with the Standard Model prediction. The result confirms a rare electroweak process at the LHC and sharpens the toolkit for probing triple-boson production.
arxiv-2602-17265:
Jonathan Stéphano led a five-author team building a multi-scale model of airflow in a personalized human lung. The lung envelope and large airway shapes come from CT scans, while smaller airways are grown by a physiologically consistent algorithm. Tissue mechanics use nonlinear elasticity under small deformations, coupled with local air pressure from fluid dynamics in the bronchial tree, with airflow accounting for inertia and static airway compliance.

Simulations run on finite elements. With this model, the team explores how ventilation variables, airflows, and shear stresses distribute across space and time in the lung. The work gives researchers a personalized, physics-grounded window onto breathing mechanics, from whole-organ shape down to small-airway flow patterns.
arxiv-2602-17565:
Hien Dang led a three-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on self-distillation in ridge regression. Self-distillation retrains a student on true labels mixed with the teacher's predictions, using the same architecture and data. It often improves generalization, but formal guarantees have stayed limited. The paper studies the unconstrained setting, where the mixing weight may fall outside the unit interval.

Conditioning only on the training data, and assuming nothing about distributions, the authors prove the optimally mixed student strictly improves on the ridge teacher wherever teacher risk is nonstationary. They give a closed-form optimal weight and a sign rule tied to the slope of teacher risk. Exact deterministic equivalents quantify the gain as sample and feature sizes grow proportionally. A consistent one-shot tuning method estimates the optimum without grid search, sample splitting, or refitting. Tests on real data and pretrained features support the theory.
arxiv-2602-17765:
Dominik Nemeth and team show that collective spin boundary time crystals, or BTCs, can carry new topological winding numbers in operator space. BTCs break time-translation symmetry. They show long-lived, tough swings that ignore starting points. The paper explains that toughness as topology, not accident.

Expanding the density operator in a spherical tensor basis maps Lindblad motion onto a local hopping problem. Spin traits label sites of a new 2D operator lattice, where topological blocks force spread of operator modes. That spectral spread explains the tough swings. With one-way transport of operator weight, the route also yields shared long-time motion across many starts, linking BTCs to non-Hermitian skin effects.
arxiv-2602-17865:
Andrzej Podobiński and Jarosław Chudziak show how generative rival networks can boost scarce financial time series data for forecasting. Forecasting matters across fields from engineering to economics, yet jumpy finance data shortage yields suboptimal training and poor carry-over. The core challenge is reliably boosting scarce financial time series to lift deep learning forecast accuracy.

The authors train a long short-term memory forecast model on data boosted with fake data from a transformer-based GAN, TTS-GAN, and find clearly improved forecast accuracy against real data alone. Results hold across Bitcoin and S&P500 price data and varied forecast spans. A novel, time series targeted quality metric combining dynamic time warping with a tweaked deep dataset gap measure reliably monitors training progress and judges generated data quality. The findings support GAN-based boosting as a practical tool for financial prediction.
arxiv-2602-17965:
Trent Ralph and team show real-time monitoring of paramagnetic chemical reactions with spin relaxometry using fluorescent nanodiamonds. Spin readings with nanodiamonds already sense many targets such as free radicals and metalloproteins with high sensing power, yet T1 spin relaxation readings are often slowed by slow capture speed.

The team shows T1 spin relaxometry from thousands of gems using a tuned cuvette-based system with an avalanche photodiode in linear mode and a fast field-programmable gate array for data handling. They show chemical tracking of copper reduction from Cu(II) to Cu(I) in-solution with a fifteen-second window using a tuned T1 sensing protocol. The method runs more than two orders of magnitude faster with an order of magnitude lower cost than older techniques. With further technical gains, the in-solution method could extend to sub-second chemical kinetics of molecules in solution.
arxiv-2602-18065:
Eduard Moos and team use femtosecond time- and angle-based photoemission spectroscopy on Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene with a single atomic layer of silver. They find that photoinduced interlayer charge transfer briefly shifts the energy landscape across the silver-graphene edge. The transfer acts as an ultrafast light gate, driving momentum-linked band renormalizations and opening a transient band gap on femtosecond timescales.

At the same time, the light-made hot-carrier numbers boost electronic screening, later closing the band gap beyond its thermal equilibrium value. The findings reveal two routes for light-driven control of the band structure in bilayer graphene that can reverse: charge transfer between layers and hot-carrier screening. They offer a general path for fast control in graphene-based stacks, opening pathways toward fast devices and the study of linked quantum phases off balance.
arxiv-2602-18565:
Pouyan Navabi and one co-author tune atomic layer deposition faster. Their 2026 paper notes ALD development is hindered by slow, precursor-heavy tuning cycles to find saturation points. The team introduces a physics-informed Bayesian framework that autonomously sets pulse times by integrating a Langmuir model into the Gaussian Process kernel.

A two-stage strategy splits noise filtering from physical fitting: the Gaussian Process first smooths noisy data, then Langmuir parameters fit smoothed values, separating signal from noise. Against a standard Gaussian Process across four simulated cases, the framework converges in five rounds, improves accuracy fourfold, and cuts precursor usage two to fourfold. Lab tests with titanium dioxide coating confirms saturation times for high targets, with deviations at lower saturation showing desorption.
arxiv-2602-18965:
Facial authentication must resist print, replay, and mask attacks, ideally on a phone alone. Shujaat Khan, writing alone in 2026, proposes CASO-PAD. It takes one RGB frame and adds content-adaptive spatial operators, known as involution, to MobileNetV3, to capture localised spoof cues.

Unlike shared convolution kernels, the operator makes kernels that vary by location, share across channels, and depend on the input. That improves spatial selectivity with minimal overhead. The model stays lightweight, with a few million parameters and low compute, trained end-to-end with a standard binary cross-entropy objective. Tests on four benchmarks show near-perfect accuracy and area under the curve, with very low error rates. On a large-scale benchmark, it also performs strongly. Ablations show that putting the adaptive operator close to the network head, with moderate group sharing, gives the best accuracy-efficiency balance.
arxiv-2602-19865:
Sweeping a system through a quantum critical point should, by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, leave a universal power-law density of defects set by equilibrium critical exponents. A 2026 arXiv paper by R. Jafari and Alireza Akbari shows that correspondence does not hold in general.

In models drawn from a wide class of quasi-one-dimensional Fermi systems, defect density can fall faster than Kibble-Zurek predicts, even for quenches that cross a critical point. Conversely, standard Kibble-Zurek scaling can hold for quenches that miss a critical point. The paper pinpoints when universal defect scaling does emerge, clarifying how defect generation relates to equilibrium criticality. Readers gain a sharper test for when Kibble-Zurek reasoning applies.
arxiv-2602-19965:
Magneto-mechanical resonators are a new kind of passive sensor: oscillating magnetic fields excite them, and inductive coils read their response, revealing pose and environmental parameters. A 2026 arXiv paper by Sarah Reiss and seven co-authors develops the estimation methods such sensing needs.

Sensing with these devices means solving a nonlinear inverse problem in real time, from induced signals plus a forward model. The paper has two aims. It introduces a reference model and simpler models for resonator dynamics and inductive readout. It also supplies robust methods that estimate model parameters fast enough for real-time use. All methods recover the measured signal, and the simplified ones cut estimation time dramatically, at the cost of only a small deviation even at large deflection angles.
arxiv-2602-20265:
Jiajie Cheng and four co-authors use a single spin qubit placed near a superconductor to listen for magnetic noise. Their 2026 study asks how an applied magnetic field changes that noise in thin, two-dimensional materials. A field disturbs a superconductor in two ways. It stirs up pairing fluctuations, and it creates vortices, tiny whirlpools that each carry a fixed amount of magnetic flux.

The authors read the noise from how fast the qubit loses its spin alignment. Near the superconducting transition, the noise departs from what quasiparticle excitations alone would predict. That departure points to critical fluctuations strengthened by a weak field. Vortex noise also separates one vortex phase from another. It yields pinned-vortex oscillation rates, vortex-lattice wave patterns, and vortex spreading rates in a liquid-like state. Noise measurement thus offers a non-invasive way to map superconducting motion in a field.
arxiv-2602-20365:
Moein Khalighi and four co-authors show how memory reshapes stability landscapes and regime shifts in living and ecological systems. Standard landscape readings assume memory-free dynamics, yet in many real systems the present depends on past states and forcing. Using a minimal bistable model with a fractional-derivative memory term, the authors link landscape shape to resilience and resistance via basin curvature and threshold-crossing push.

Memory flattens basin floors, slowing recovery, while raising the push needed for a transition. That trade-off pits resilience against resistance. Because the landscape depends on history and changes over time, memory creates behaviors absent from memory-free models. They include delayed collapse or recovery after stress ends, rebound after an apparent transition, and widened hysteresis under slow change. Fitting a memory-free model to memory-driven data can match trajectories while shifting equilibria and tipping points, risking wrong diagnoses and management.
arxiv-2602-20765:
Vadym Kurylenko and one co-author study lattice polytopes, shapes whose corners sit on a grid, and a number that sums up their fine structure, the Hodge vector. They compute this vector for a joined shape called a Cayley polytope and link it to a volume-like measure of its parts.

The formula yields endless high-dimensional shapes that share one Hodge vector yet are not simple joins. A special case, named Lawrence twists, extends a classic transform with symmetric pairs of vectors. The work also builds many new thin polytopes, answering questions posed by Borger, Kretschmer, and Nill, and gives a fresh account of why B_k polytopes are thin.
arxiv-2602-21165:
Patient messages, surveys, and interviews carry the patient voice, including social determinants of health, but manual coding cannot scale across health systems. Samah Fodeh and eight co-authors introduce PVminer in this 2026 arXiv paper, a domain-adapted framework for structuring patient voice in secure patient-provider communication. Detection is framed as multi-label, multi-class prediction.

Patient-specific BERT encoders combine with topic modeling for thematic augmentation and fine-tuned classifiers for code, subcode, and combined labels. Topic representations enrich inputs during fine-tuning and inference. Scores reach about eighty-two percent at code level, about eighty percent at subcode level, and up to about seventy-eight percent combined, beating biomedical and clinical baselines. Models, code, and documentation will be released publicly.
arxiv-2602-21265:
Language models more and more use tools over long spans, but yardsticks rarely control tool access. Hyeonje Choi, Jeongsoo Lee, Hyojun Lee, and Jay-Yoon Lee present such a yardstick in this 2026 arXiv paper. ToolMATH turns step-by-step math answers into reusable Python tools with accounts and typed schemas. Each problem pairs with a setting needing step-by-step tool use, middle-output reuse, and linked tool-call chains.

Gold tools and graded decoys control catalog hardness, while conduct-tuned measures go beyond final hit rate. Three axes sort trials: adjusting when gold tools vanish, toughness under decoy noise, and linkage across long tool chains. Trace-level failure study reveals distinct model patterns, from steady tool use to dodging and tunable swap.
arxiv-2602-21465:
Nahom Seyoum alone authors a paper extending concentration inequalities for independent random vectors under sublinear expectations. Li and Hu had recently proved variance-type bounds decaying like one over n for the sample mean in that setting. This work pushes those results into the exponential concentration regime.

For bounded, independent vectors under a regular sublinear expectation, the author proves five results. A general principle reduces vector tail bounds to scalar martingale inequalities via a three-layer architecture. An Azuma-Hoeffding inequality gives sub-Gaussian tails for distance to the Minkowski average of expectation sets. A Bernstein inequality interpolates between sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential regimes. A dimension-free bound swaps an exponential covering factor for a polynomial one. An explicit construction shows the sub-Gaussian rate is optimal.
arxiv-2602-21565:
Seokwon Yoon and five co-authors offer a way to mix pre-trained GFlowNets at run time for multi-objective tasks. GFlowNets sample varied options in line with reward, suiting science search where many good options matter. Multi-objective settings draw growing interest, since real tasks involve many clashing goals.

Older methods need joint training for each goal mix, so any change in goals forces a fresh train from scratch. The new design mixes pre-trained GFlowNets with no fine-tuning or retrain, handling reward mixes from weighted sums to curved rules, often handled apart in older work. The authors prove exact recovery of the target mix for weighted sums and gauge closeness for curved rules with a warp factor. Tests on a synthetic 2D grid and real molecule tasks match baseline scores.
arxiv-2602-21765:
Alignment and adaptation in language models lean on reinforcement learning from human feedback. Theory for its generalization remains premature, especially when the reward can shift and the KL control is estimated and clipped. Kenton Tang and two co-authors build generalization theory for RLHF covering two issues. Reward shift means reward models train on preference data from earlier or mixed policies while RLHF optimizes the policy on its rollouts. Clipped KL regularization means the KL term is estimated from sampled log-probability ratios, clipped for stability.

Their generalization bounds trace error to sampling error from prompts and rollouts, reward shift error, and KL clipping error. Special cases cover initializing with a uniform prior over a finite space and training by stochastic gradient descent as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. The theory yields guidance on the optimal KL clipping threshold and on budget allocation across prompts, rollouts, and preference data.
arxiv-2602-21865:
Luis Villarin and one co-author give a new analytic model for a force-free jet of electromagnetism shot out from a disk-fed spinning black hole. The jet is force-free to first order in spin. It comes from a step-by-step build based on older analytic tools. The jet shape tends to a parabola far out. It is set by where current piles up and flips sign on the thin disk, magnetized and lying in the equatorial plane.

Jet traits barely change with the disk trait. That hints at a shared pattern for slow-spinning black hole jets, no matter the disk build. The model matches key traits hoped for from the Blandford-Znajek process. The authors stress this near-independence as a sign of a broad rule, not a quirk of one disk.
arxiv-2602-21965:
Joseph Margaryan and Thomas Hamelryck design compact neural network layers for settings where memory and uncertainty both matter, such as medicine, robotics, and self-driving systems. Their layers are circular convolutions with weights that live in the frequency domain. That choice makes it easy to impose spectral structure, run structured Bayesian inference, and compute exact spectral norms for robustness checks.

Placing a Gaussian prior on the frequency support yields an exact stationary Gaussian-process prior over the filters. The authors pair it with a practical variational posterior. In tests spanning Bayesian image classifiers, classification heads on frozen features, and vision transformer projections, the compact layers match strong baselines with far fewer parameters and tighter robustness certificates.
arxiv-2602-22165:
Most space plasmas are ruled at large scales by Alfvén waves, slow magnetic ripples in magnetized gas. Stanislav Boldyrev and Mikhail Medvedev study the opposite regime: non-neutral pair plasmas, like those around pulsars, magnetars, and rotating black holes. At large scales there, hybrid whistler-Alfvén modes rule, turning into pure Alfvén modes at small scales. The reversal reshapes how turbulence works there.

The authors derive the nonlinear equations for whistler-Alfvén modes in ultrarelativistic, magnetically dominated pair plasma, and discuss the turbulence spectrum they govern. Their analysis covers pulsar and magnetar magnetospheres, black-hole jets, and some lab plasmas. Astrophysicists gain the governing equations for a plasma regime where the usual large-scale picture runs backward.
arxiv-2602-22265:
Modern image makers move a simple starting spread into data along timed paths, but standard flow-matching goals do not police the shape of the journey. Chika Maduabuchi proposes Entropy-Controlled Flow Matching, a rule that enforces a global entropy-rate budget along the paths. Low-entropy choke points that can starve meaning modes are thus ruled out by design.

The math behind it is a convex optimization with a full set of optimality rules, matching a Schrödinger bridge with an explicit entropy term. In pure transport it recovers entropic transport geodesics, and it proves mode coverage and density floors with stable behavior. Image makers gain flows whose mode coverage is enforced, not hoped for.
arxiv-2602-22365:
Crowdsourcing platforms juggle four tensions at once: allocation quality, workforce sustainability, operational feasibility, and strategic contractor behavior. Chayan Banerjee formalizes the quartet as a dilemma. Existing methods resolve at most two tensions together: greedy methods buy day-one quality at the cost of burnout, while bandit methods kill burnout only through infeasible full workforce utilization.

The author introduces FORGE, a physics-grounded multi-agent simulator where each contractor declares its own load-acceptance threshold from its fatigue state, turning a passive bandit problem into a genuine Stackelberg game. Inside FORGE, a neural-linear allocator fuses embedding nets with physics-informed models. Platforms gain a testbed for splitting tasks that respects both quality and worker stamina.
arxiv-2602-22465:
Language models more and more face real-world choices framed as constrained optimization, but current benchmarks test whether models can write solver code, not whether they can solve on their own. Joseph Tso and three co-authors offer ConstraintBench, a benchmark for direct constrained optimization across ten planning domains, with ground truths checked by a top solver. Each task gives a setup with items, constraints, and a goal.

Models must return a set-format answer that a fixed-rule checker tests against every constraint and the solver-proven optimum. Across two hundred tasks and six frontier models, meeting the rules, not best score, proves the main hurdle: the best model meets constraints only about two-thirds of the time. The benchmark thus tests a distinct skill: giving answers that are truly allowed, not just nearly optimal.
arxiv-2602-23165:
Yichen Peng and nine co-authors tackle gesture generation for digital humans in two-person conversation. Existing tools map one audio stream to one speaker's motion. They ignore social context and the back-and-forth between partners. DyaDiT, a multi-modal diffusion transformer, instead reads audio from both speakers, with optional social-context tokens, and produces motion that fits the exchange.

The system fuses both speakers' signals to capture interaction dynamics. It draws on a motion dictionary for motion priors and can use the partner's gestures to respond more naturally. Trained on the Seamless Interaction data set and tested on standard motion scores plus user studies, it beats prior methods on the objective measures. Human viewers also strongly prefer its motion, pointing to more socially convincing virtual conversation partners.
arxiv-2602-23265:
Gauri Umesh Rajmane and three co-authors test whether sign language can work in virtual reality through body-mounted 360-degree cameras. The study, called VRSL, asks ten participants to identify American Sign Language signs from videos recorded at three mounting positions: head, shoulder, and chest. Making VR signing legible matters for accessibility and collaboration for Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, who often face text-only options in virtual spaces.

The shoulder-mounted camera scored highest at 85 percent accuracy, though gaps between positions were not statistically significant. Peripheral distortion in 360-degree video hurt clarity, and participants flagged camera angles and distortion as areas to improve. Overall comprehension reached 83.3 percent, and participants preferred signing over text-based communication in VR, suggesting video-based signing is a viable path if mounting and optics improve.
arxiv-2602-23465:
Abdul Wadood Asim and two co-authors examine how digital money adoption affects women's financial inclusion in Pakistan. Financial inclusion remains a longstanding concern in underdeveloped communities, especially for women, yet data-driven measures for guiding policy have been scarce.

Using nationally representative Global Findex data from the World Bank, they study how mobile money use, moderated by phone ownership, internet access, and education, shapes women's access to formal financial services. Women who adopt mobile money show markedly higher odds of formal access. Internet access alone, however, shows no significant effect, pointing to socio-cultural constraints. The findings support women-centric fintech design and digital literacy reforms to narrow the gender gap.
arxiv-2602-23565:
Adhyyan Narang and three co-authors study learning when users choose among competing platforms. Platforms draw data from the same user pool, and each user picks the platform serving them best. Prior work focuses only on learners' local losses on observed data.

The authors find cases where existing algorithms almost surely converge to models with very poor global performance, even when models with low full-population loss exist. The mechanism is an overspecialization trap: learners optimizing for current fans grow less attractive to outsiders, narrowing observed data further. Inspired by knowledge distillation, they propose letting learners probe peer models' predictions to learn about users who do not select them. Probing converges almost surely to a stationary point with bounded full-population risk when probing sources are informative enough, such as a known market leader. Semi-synthetic tests on MovieLens, Census, and Amazon Sentiment data verify the findings.
arxiv-2602-23665:
Brandon Yee and two co-authors present Geodesic Semantic Search, a search system learning node-specific curved-space metrics on paper-link graphs for shape-aware meaning search. Standard vector search relies on fixed flat gaps, but GSS learns a low-rank metric tensor at each node, giving a local valid metric.

That setup ensures valid metrics while keeping the model tractable. Search runs via multi-source Dijkstra on learned shortest-path gaps, then maximal marginal relevance re-ranking and flow sifting. On paper-link forecast tests with 169,000 arXiv papers, GSS achieves twenty-three percent gain in Recall at 20 over SPECTER plus FAISS rivals. A Bridge Regain Guarantee states when shortest-path search beats direct likeness in kind, with a margin gap result linking training loss to search quality. Layered coarse-to-fine search with k-means pooling cuts compute cost four times while keeping ninety-seven percent search quality.
arxiv-2602-23765:
Heinrich Dinkel and ten co-authors present DashengTokenizer, a single-layer tool that turns sound into a compact form for both understanding and creating audio. The 2026 paper reverses the usual design: it starts from frozen meaning features and adds sound detail, rather than training a sound codec first.

In tests across many tasks, the method beats earlier audio codecs and encoders by a clear margin, while keeping sound rebuild quality competitive. Gains show up in speech emotion, music understanding, and scene sorting. For creation, it beats standard variational autoencoder methods on text-to-audio and text-to-music, and it works well for speech cleanup too. The authors argue that such autoencoder designs are not required for audio synthesis.
arxiv-2602-23865:
Matt Wilson and two co-authors develop the theory of supermaps, higher-order operations that transform quantum channels themselves, for general circuit theories. The 2026 paper proves a Yoneda lemma for categorical supermaps, a result that ties abstract supermaps to a concrete representation.

The lemma says that when a theory has a suitable channel-state duality, its supermaps can be represented through that duality, removing guesswork in defining them. As an application, the authors characterize supermaps on Boxworld, a theory of non-quantum correlations, through a weakened version of a recently proposed principle for higher-order processes there. The same lemma also yields a stable definition of supermaps in real quantum theory, widening the frame beyond standard complex quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2602-24065:
Zaiyan Yang and seven co-authors introduce EvalMVX, a unified benchmark for neural three-dimensional reconstruction under diverse multiview setups. The 2026 paper notes that current real-world datasets mainly benchmark multiview stereo from color images. Multiview photometric stereo and multiview shape from polarization, both vital for high-fidelity surfaces and sparse inputs, have never been assessed together with it.

EvalMVX contains many objects, each photographed with a polarized camera under many views and lighting conditions, including one-light-at-a-time and natural illumination, yielding thousands of images. Each object carries an aligned ground-truth mesh for quantitative benchmarking across all three techniques at once. The authors evaluate many recent methods, record the best performers, and identify open problems across varied geometry and reflectance. The benchmark aims to guide research toward reconstruction methods that work across capture setups, not just one.
arxiv-2602-24265:
Saber Zerhoudi and Michael Granitzer present a framework for inferring cognitive traces in search, moving user simulation beyond reproducing actions to modeling thought. The 2026 paper notes that user simulators are essential for evaluating search systems. They copy what users do without modeling what users think or feel, such as confusion or satisfaction.

The method uses a multi-agent language-model system. It annotates three public datasets with hundreds of thousands of cognitive labels across tens of thousands of sessions. Cross-dataset evaluation with a shuffled-label control shows cognitive labels help most where behavioral features are weakest. On a movie dataset the cognitive model improves over the behavioral baseline and above the shuffled control. The annotation collection, tool, and code are released to support cognitively aware user simulation. In short, thoughts beat clicks. Clicks miss the mind. Human minds guide the work. Information shapes the labels..
arxiv-2603-00065: Schnitzer, Hoeving and Zillner study how working practitioners sort AI systems into the four risk tiers of the EU AI Act, which took effect in August 2024. Through a web-based self-service decision tool tested in two phases with 78 practitioners, they find legal definitions and scope hard to interpret. Clear explanations and worked examples markedly improve the sorting process. They offer practical guidance for tool builders and policymakers seeking smoother compliance in practice.
arxiv-2603-00365: Visokay and colleagues present Randomized Recruitment Driven Sampling, a cellphone version of Respondent Driven Sampling adding researcher-controlled randomization to each wave. Standard sampling of this kind needs no frame, but peer invites bias results when similar people cluster. The new method suits low-stigma groups hard to reach for logistical reasons, such as pandemics or conflict. It enforces the random-recruitment rule traditional sampling rarely achieves. Simulation and a test with Bangladeshi garment workers during COVID-19 show less biased estimates and better interval coverage than old sampling.
arxiv-2603-00765: Nascimento and Zhang extend sharp regularity and nondegeneracy results for local minima of elliptic functionals with strong absorption and unbounded sign changing sources. Such problems sit between Bernoulli cavity problems and obstacle free boundary problems. Earlier work assumed bounded positive sources, but the new analysis handles weak source assumptions. The result shows how nonlinearity interacts with weak source rules to preserve both traits.
arxiv-2603-01365: Honari and five colleagues tackle policy lag in async on-policy RL, the gap between the acting policy making data and the learning policy updated. Spread training and frequent updates speed learning but worsen this lag, blocking scaling to larger problems. They name policy lag sources from distributed learning and high update pace, then propose total Variation-based Advantage aligned Constrained policy Optimization, a usable fix for policy lag. Tests show better toughness to policy lag in old RL tasks and a modern RL task for language model math thought.
arxiv-2603-01565:
Yi Gu, Yanqing Liu, Chen Yang, and Sheng Zhao study how to make sounds from text prompts in this 2026 work. Modern audio models still stumble on complex prompts with layered effects, where words and sounds must line up well. Thin or vague captions in training data make that alignment even harder to learn.

The team first uses a large language model to write rich, detailed captions for training sounds. Then they fine-tune a diffusion transformer audio model with a group-based reward method. They test several reward mixes that score text fit, sound quality, and drift from the base model. Careful reward design proves key, and the tuned model gains a lot in fidelity and prompt fit. The result helps map how reward choices steer audio synthesis.
arxiv-2603-01765:
Minseok Seo, Wonjun Lee, Jaehyuk Jang, and Changick Kim fill in missing depth values fast at test time in this 2026 work. Depth completion turns sparse range readings into a full depth map for a scene. Zero-shot versions adapt to new places with no new training data, but past test-time tuning was slow.

The team finds that tuning only the decoder of a depth model suffices for strong adaptation. Depth facts cluster in a low-dimensional subspace inside that decoder, so updates can stay small. Their method tunes just that subspace with sparse depth readings as the guide. Accuracy and speed together set a new best trade-off in their tests. Gains hold across five indoor and outdoor data sets, which makes fast zero-shot depth more practical for robots and cameras.
arxiv-2603-01865:
Ziyi Zhu, Olivier Tieleman, Alexey Bukhtiyarov, and Jinghong Chen remove bias from AI judges that grade open-ended answers. Their 2026 work notes that judge bias can rival the real gaps benchmarks try to measure. More test cases cannot wash out a bias that sits inside the judge itself.

They split benchmark score variance into parts due to scenario, generation, judge, and leftover noise. That split shows exactly how much of a ranking is judge artifact rather than model quality. Their fix, CyclicJudge, rotates judges across scenarios in a round-robin cycle at the same cost as one judge. The rotation cancels bias precisely while each judge is called just once per cycle. Tests on two known benchmarks confirm the predicted gains in both general and domain-specific grading.
arxiv-2603-01965:
Federico Caretti and Guido Sanguinetti build a generative model that keeps the links between data types intact. Their 2026 work revisits multimodal variational autoencoders, which compress mixed data like images plus measurements. Standard fusion in the latent space destroys the joint statistical structure of the data.

That loss harms both generation quality and honest uncertainty estimates downstream. Their model, CoVAE, adds a correlated latent structure that captures how modalities move together. Cross-modal reconstruction then respects those links instead of treating each stream alone. Tests span a number of real and synthetic data sets with varied modality mixes. Results show accurate reconstruction across modalities and effective quantification of the linked uncertainty. The design suits data-rich-in-kind but modest-in-size fields like biomedicine, where each channel counts.
arxiv-2603-02265:
Shibing Mo, Jiarui Zhang, Jiayu Xie, and colleagues predict how well networks resist attack in this 2026 paper. A network is controllable if a few driver nodes can steer the whole system. Robustness checks usually run attack simulations, which are slow and suit only small networks. Past learning methods also miss group links that involve many nodes at once.

Their model reads a network as a hypergraph, where one link can join many nodes. A dual attention design learns plain structure, local group links, and hidden traits at once. It then predicts the full robustness curve under attack. The authors say this is the first study of group knowledge in this task. Tests on fake and real networks beat prior methods at low cost.
arxiv-2603-02465:
Emadeldeen Hamdan, Ahmad Faiz Tharima, Mohd Zahirasri Mohd Tohir, and colleagues adapt wildfire detection to peatland fires in this 2026 paper. Peat fires smolder with low flames, thick smoke, and burning below the surface. Detectors trained on open forest flames miss those signs easily. Labeled peat fire data is scarce, which blocks training from scratch.

Their approach starts from a general wildfire detector's pretrained weights. Fine-tuning on Malaysian peatland images and videos then adapts it to the new domain. Transfer learning beat training from scratch clearly in their experiments. Gains held under low-contrast smoke, partial blocking, and changing light. The method offers a practical path to early peat fire warning. Real-time monitoring for prevention and environmental protection is the target use.
arxiv-2603-02665:
How does a lone long-legged ant actually move when left by itself? This 2026 paper models the paths of isolated A. gracilipes ants tracked closely in the lab. Ant research often stresses signals between ants, but each ant's own motion pattern matters just as much.

The authors test random-motion models against the recorded tracks. A blend of two styles, steady active wandering plus sudden run-and-tumble bursts, matched the real paths well in both shape and numbers. Turn angles, run times, and waiting times followed stable patterns across individual ants. A working model like this helps predict ant movement in new settings. It may also hint at how the ants sense their surroundings.
arxiv-2603-02765:
George Bredis, Nikita Balagansky, Daniil Gavrilov, and Ruslan Rakhimov strengthen world models by predicting embeddings instead of pictures. Their 2026 agent, NE-Dreamer, learns inside a model of the world for reinforcement learning. In partly hidden, high-dimensional settings, guessing the next raw observation wastes effort on detail that does not matter.

A temporal transformer instead predicts the next encoded state from the latent state history, training representations to stay coherent over time. No decoding losses or extra supervision are needed. On the DeepMind Control Suite, the agent matched or beat DreamerV3 and leading decoder-free rivals. On harder memory and spatial tasks from DMLab, it gained by a wide margin. The result favors compact prediction targets for model-based agents.
arxiv-2603-02865:
Haruto Yoshida, Keito Kudo, Yoichi Aoki, and colleagues look inside vision-language models to see when diagram parts become readable. Models do well on diagram tests yet often misread arrows and links between elements. Their 2026 study probes internal signals using synthetic diagrams built from directed graphs.

Node information and overall layout were already readable in single states of the vision encoder, in a simple linear way. Edge information was not: it became linearly clear only later, inside the language model's text tokens. In short, nodes register early and edges register late. That delay may explain why these models stumble on relations such as arrow direction, which demand combined, abstract processing.
arxiv-2603-03265:
Yufu Wang, Evonne Ng, Soyong Shin, and a large team reconstruct human motion in world coordinates from ordinary, messy video. Casual footage brings noise, gaps, and moving cameras, so recovered motion must generalize while staying globally consistent. Their 2026 method, DuoMo, splits the job between two diffusion models.

The first model estimates motion in camera space from the video. The second lifts that estimate into world space and refines it for global coherence. The system outputs mesh vertices directly, skipping parametric body models entirely. On two standard benchmarks, world-space reconstruction error fell by sixteen and thirty percent against prior state of the art, while foot skating stayed low. The factorization also completes motion hidden by occlusion.
arxiv-2603-03365:
Helmut Prodinger shortens a computation in combinatorics, the study of counting patterns and number sequences. His 2026 note concerns the Pell-Padovan tetranacci numbers, a sequence where each term is built from three earlier terms with fixed weights. The task is to find generating functions, compact formulas that encode a whole sequence, for the term-by-term product of this sequence with classical second-order sequences.

An earlier paper handled eight such products one at a time, using symmetric functions case by case. Prodinger gives one quick general method that produces all eight generating functions at once. The trick is to write the partner sequence in a single general form with adjustable constants, so one derivation covers every case. The note is brief and purely computational, aimed at researchers who work with recursive sequences.
arxiv-2603-03565:
Alejandro Breen Herrera and seven colleagues publish a blueprint for improving conversational shopping assistants in production. Grocery shopping is the hard case: requests are vague, tastes are personal, and budgets and stock constrain everything. Their 2026 paper, built around a production-scale grocery assistant, tackles the two problems prototypes dodge: judging multi-turn quality and optimizing many coupled agents at once.

A structured rubric splits shopping quality into dimensions, and a calibrated language-model judge, aligned against human annotations, scores them. Two optimization strategies then compete. One tunes each sub-agent against its local rubric. The other, the novel system-level method, tunes all prompts jointly using multi-turn simulation and whole-trajectory scoring. The authors release rubric templates and evaluation guidance so other builders can copy the recipe.
arxiv-2603-03665:
Binh M Le and Simon S Woo protect faces from recognition systems by changing the expression, not the makeup. Facial recognition now watches everywhere, and older defenses, like transferred makeup styles, fail to transfer in black-box settings and fit some demographics poorly, including men and darker skin tones. Their 2026 method, MAP, edits perceived emotion to disguise the original identity as a chosen target identity.

A score network is fine-tuned on two objectives at once, the target identity and a human expression, with gradient projection steering both toward one shared optimum. Local smoothness regularization and a score matching loss keep the protected images looking natural. Experiments beat noise-based, makeup-based, and freeform attribute baselines on quality and metrics alike. MAP also defeats a live commercial recognition service and adapts to uncommon photographic situations.
arxiv-2603-03765:
Qihao Sun and seven colleagues let a car's lidar teach its cameras depth. Self-driving perception needs metric depth that is accurate, consistent across views and time, and portable to new places. Camera-only stereo struggles on all three counts. Their 2026 framework, DriveMVS, starts from one observation: sparse lidar returns are few but metrically exact, so they can serve as geometric prompts anchoring the whole estimate in absolute scale.

The lidar prompt enters twice, as a hard prior fixing the cost volume's scale and as soft feature guidance fused with image cues by a triple-cue combiner. A spatio-temporal decoder then enforces consistency using neighboring frames. Across several benchmarks DriveMVS leads in metric accuracy and temporal stability. It also transfers zero-shot to new domains, a practical virtue for fleets that cannot retrain everywhere they drive.
arxiv-2603-03865:
Wang Jian and others analyze backdoor attacks in federated learning from a structure-aware angle. Federated learning keeps data private, but it also lets hidden perturbations in model updates persist. Earlier attack studies focused on trigger design or poisoning strategy and assumed identical perturbations behave the same across architectures. The authors argue that model structure matters. They present two metrics, a Structural Responsiveness Score and a Structural Compatibility Coefficient. These capture how sensitive a model is and how well it accepts fractal perturbations.

Tests with their fractal perturbation injection approach show that multi-path feature fusion networks amplify and retain such perturbations even at low poisoning ratios, while low-compatibility models resist them. The compatibility coefficient correlates strongly with attack success, offering a predictor of backdoor survivability and a basis for structural defenses.
arxiv-2603-03965: Mahdi Hejrati and others develop modular shape control for robotic manipulators with uncertain inertial settings, using an adaptive method. The manipulator decomposes into rigid-body and joint modules, with rigid-body motion on the Lie algebra se(3). Local shape control laws are built at module level, linked by power-conjugate twist-wrench pairs. A shape adaptation law on symmetric positive-definite matrices handles inertial uncertainty with proven bounded errors.
arxiv-2603-04065: Ling and colleagues study online order fulfillment with replenishment under demand uncertainty. Firms jointly handle replenishment and real-time fulfillment, and low one-cycle regret need not mean a small profit gap when replenishment repeats, since fulfillment changes inventory. Against a myopic offline benchmark knowing current-cycle demand, the authors give conditions for regret bounds to transfer. For base stock the bound holds with separately optimized targets, while constant orders allow two-sided comparison via a count-loss bound. Cycle-restarted Bayes Selector bounds are constant in horizon.
arxiv-2603-04465: Mandal and colleagues compute quantum scattering for excited HD plus HD collisions. With a good H2-H2 potential, they find near resonant transitions conserving rotational momentum and nearly conserving internal energy. Anisotropic terms and partial waves behind low energy resonant features are found. Results match prior experimental cross sections, including resonances. Low energy cross sections show a strong l equals 3 resonance, and rates peak between 1 K and 10 K near a shape resonance. The match with lab data is thus strong.
arxiv-2603-04565: Xu and Prasanna make histopathology images with Dual-LoRA diffusion. Repair and making share the goal of steady tissue making under missing data. Past methods treat them apart with weak shape guides. Their centroid guided setup unifies Local Structure Completion and Global Structure Synthesis. Multi-class nuclei centroids give light, label light spatial guides when data is partly or fully gone. Two LoRA adapters tune a shared backbone without training twice. Tests beat GAN and rival models on both tasks, with masked LPIPS and global FID much better.
arxiv-2603-04965: Partha Mondal and the rest of the team present a multiband hybrid metasurface with a metal-dielectric-metal stack holding several plasmon modes. The stack pairs a bottom aluminum layer, a silicon dioxide spacer, and a top bar-disc hybrid resonator. Tuned shape yields four distinct peaks across near-infrared and telecommunication bands from gap-surface and local mode mix. How much bounces back shifts with shape and polarization, tests match number guesses, and second-harmonic light strengthens at peak wavelengths through the field being trapped in the cavity.
arxiv-2603-05265: J. Prathap and the rest of the team split radio-source energy budgets between star making and black hole action by unsupervised grouping. Grouping multiwavelength diagnostics from GAMA, EMU, and WISE, grouping recovers most star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei. Their new infrared-radio diagnostic spots radio nuclei among infrared star-forming galaxies and nuclei, matching a KMeans cluster at 90% reliability. A three-dimensional diagnostic from observable settings selects radio sources near 90% reliably and fully. An EMU catalogue with optical-action probabilities favors fractional sorting.
arxiv-2603-05465: Kogilathota and colleagues test whether hallucination risk in vision-language models can be forecast from internal representations before generation begins, using one forward pass. Across eight modern models and varied tasks, they test visual-only features, vision tokens inside the text decoder, and query tokens that fuse visual and textual information. Probes on these representations detect risk without decoding, reaching 0.93 AUROC on three models: Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4-VL, and Molmo 7B, with late query-token states most predictive for most models.
arxiv-2603-05565: Chen and Meng frame a formal paradox. Generative AI narrows within-task skill gaps while shifting value to assets in few hands, so even performance may widen total gap. Their task model yields two regimes, with the line set by tech structure and labor rules. What-if tests matching six real targets pin down sizes, while a response split shows most moments pin inner rates without settling total sign. Occupation-level regressions cannot test task-level forecasts, which need within-job, within-task data not yet on hand at scale.
arxiv-2603-06365: Brito dos Santos Filho presents ESAA-Security, an ESAA version for agent aided security auditing, on AI made or AI changed code. Prompt based security review suffers uneven coverage, weak reruns, and no fixed audit trail. ESAA keeps guesswork agent cognition apart from set state mutation, using append only events and replay based checks. Review runs as a governed four phase pipeline with 26 tasks, 16 domains, and 95 checks, covering reconnaissance, domain audits, risk classification, and reporting. The method produces ordered outputs including vulnerability lists, risk matrices, and fix guidance.
arxiv-2603-06465: Reinhardt and team develop radiomics features mixing classical and functional kinds from liver MRI for cancer finding and risk stratification. Their method uses enhancement pattern mapping images to capture variety through information on perfusion. Mapping data come from T1-weighted MRI scans, and quantiles join ones as inputs under an L1-curbed logistic model. Over time, analysis uses Bayesian tensor response fit for smoothing and shaping of patterns. Rich ones beat rivals on sorting and grade ranks, and harsh lesions show a higher share of pixels with mapping drop.
arxiv-2603-06565: Ye and team propose Hybrid Hierarchical RL, a two-stage plan adding symbolic structure into neural reinforcement learning agents without sacrificing power, drawn from humans. Deep learning agents over-exploit early reward signals and drift. Such designs prove complex to scale and difficult for continuous settings. A logical option-based warm-up strategy steers the policy away from short-term reward loops toward goal-directed ways, with the policy refined via environment interaction. In tests, the approach improves long-horizon decision-making and beats neural and neuro-symbolic baselines.
arxiv-2603-06665: Wu and team report a counter-odd trend in medical visual question answering: chain-of-thought asking often lags direct answering. They blame this on a medical perception bottleneck, where cues blur visual grounding and chain-of-thought may grow sense uncertainty rather than correct it. To test this, they bring two training-free interventions, sight anchoring with region-of-interest cues and description linking via textual guidance. Across benchmarks and model families, they improve accuracy, soften chain-of-thought harm, and in several settings reverse the flip.
arxiv-2603-06865: James gives a guide to picking and reading annotator agreement measures in NLP and nearby fields. Human labels underpin trustworthy NLP data, yet measuring agreement gets hard across sorting, splitting, opinion judgments, and graded ratings. He sorts measures by task type and shows how skewed labels and missing data sway trust estimates. He also urges clear, open reporting, with error bars and studies of where raters disagree, pushing for steadier and more repeatable labeling and testing.
arxiv-2603-06965: Feng and Xu realize the full universal enveloping algebras of Borcherds-Bozec algebras geometrically. Their route uses quivers with loops and the motivic semi-derived Hall algebra. A universal enveloping algebra packages a Lie-type algebra into an associative algebra capturing its representations. A quiver is a directed graph, and loops are arrows starting and ending at the same vertex. The Hall algebra builds algebras by counting extensions between representations, and the motivic semi-derived version refines that counting.
arxiv-2603-07065: Keles offers a shared language for hand-made test mutants used to judge fuzzing and property-based testing tools. He sorts five ways to write mutants, from comments and preprocessor flags to patch files, match-and-replace rules, and in-tree edits, then defines an algebra for picking, tagging, and combining them. A lossless conversion path links the forms through one common middle form. The ideas are built into Marauder, a prototype for injecting, switching, resetting, and mixing mutants.
arxiv-2603-07165: Chen and colleagues improve two-arm robot manipulation with RoTri-Diff, a diffusion model guided by robot-object triadic interaction. Past imitation methods, whether robot-centered or object-centered, miss the changing geometric ties among the two arms and the object. That gap causes collisions, unstable grasps, and weak performance on hard tasks. RoTri encodes the relative 6D poses of both arms and the object as triangular constraints. RoTri-Diff combines those constraints with keyposes and object motion in a layered diffusion process.
arxiv-2603-07365: Alnemari, Qureshi and Begrazadah map scaling laws for tiny vision models, a regime below the sizes prior work covers. Training dozens of small networks at varied widths, they find error still follows a power law, with steeper slopes than those reported for large language models. The law is uneven: local slopes fade with scale, and one architecture saturates near the top of the range. Small models also shift which inputs they miss and concentrate on easy classes, while the tiniest stay best calibrated.
arxiv-2603-07765: Ranaivomanana and colleagues use BlackGEM imaging of hot pre-white dwarf PG 1159-035 to show ground finding of many-period pulsations of a few brightness steps. Ground-based work remains crucial for finding compact pulsator hopefuls. Their aim is testing mode naming for pulsations in hot subdwarfs and white dwarfs via size-ratio analysis. Iterative pre-cleaning reveals l equals 1 and l equals 2 modes matching past work, and size ratios split the two mode types. The study paves the way for star-quake studies of faint compact pulsing stars.
arxiv-2603-07865: Barik and colleagues speed up text-to-audio diffusion, which now needs many model calls and so runs slowly. Rather than start from pure noise, their training-free SoundWeaver builds a prompt-shaped sound prior from bits of cached clips and warms up diffusion partway. A composition graph picks cross-clip joins that fit the prompt and keep sound smooth, while a bandit gate picks how deep to skip for each request. Tests show clear speed gains from a small cache, with sound quality also improved.
arxiv-2603-07965: Jing Jingzhe and colleagues tackle Bayesian optimization under tight constraints in high dimensions. Their Local Constrained Bayesian Optimization method uses the smooth landscape of penalized models, mixing rapid local descent with uncertainty-led search. They prove a convergence rate for the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker residual that grows polynomially with dimension. Tests on benchmarks up to 100D beat state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2603-08065: Huang and colleagues improve structured pruning for large language models, which trims inference cost by removing low-importance parts. Pruning can be seen as learning a gate per component under an l0 sparsity limit, but the discreteness of that limit has pushed prior work toward stochastic hard-concrete relaxations. Those relaxations create a train-test mismatch once sampled masks are discretized for deployment, and keep masks in a bounded, near-binary range. Their Deterministic Differentiable Pruning method optimizes masks alone and drops the stochasticity.
arxiv-2603-08365: Berarducci and colleagues prove, assuming Schanuel's conjecture, that the complete theory of the real exponential field is axiomatized by a set of axioms. Those axioms describe definably complete exponential fields satisfying the differential equation exp prime equals exp. This implies the result of Macintyre and Wilkie that, under the same conjecture, the theory is decidable. The approach rests on the model completeness of a similar set of rules for the function restricted to the interval from minus 1 to 1. The authors prove that part unconditionally.
arxiv-2603-08465: Zhang and colleagues solve incompressible flow in triply periodic minimal surface geometries with MUSA-PINN, a multi-scale weak-form physics-informed network. Physics-informed networks minimize point residuals, but that local focus fails to spread global information through winding channels, causing unstable gradients and broken mass conservation. MUSA-PINN instead writes Navier-Stokes constraints as integral conservation laws over layered spherical volumes. It imposes continuity and momentum through flux-balance residuals at three scales. Tests claim it beats rivals, cutting errors by up to 93% while keeping mass conservation.
arxiv-2603-08665: Víctor Mayoral-Vilches and colleagues show that generative AI has broken consumer robot security open. Tricks once needing deep robot expertise now run through open tools. Three cases show a lawnmower fleet breach, an exoskeleton motor and credential leak, and a window cleaner hit by unauthenticated wireless commands. Across the cases, the tool found dozens of flaws, while defenses still lag behind attacks.
arxiv-2603-08765: Tianyu Sun builds a data assimilation frame for a coupled Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard phase-field model. Coarse space observations feed a nudging system through a general linear observer, recovering full trajectories from rough data. The capped finite-element scheme proves one-step well-posedness with a stepwise prior estimate, and tests show recovery from badly mismatched starts, keyed to observation detail and feedback strength.
arxiv-2603-08965: Edward Izgorodin defines a smooth zoom for knowledge graphs to find level edges. Current tools rely on discrete group finding with hand-tuned settings, giving no smooth zoom and no formal guarantees. His Semantic Level of Detail builds a zoom tool from heat spread, proves hierarchical coherence in the tree limit, and detects scale boundaries from spectral gaps without manual tuning.
arxiv-2603-09065: Chloe Su and colleagues learn adaptive decoding policies for large language models instead of fixed sampling settings. Fixed temperature and top-p ignore how task hardness and doubt shift across prompts and steps. Their lightweight add-ons, trained with reward learning and checked rewards, pick tactics per prompt as a context bandit and per token as a partial-view Markov choice process. Scores rise under fixed budgets.
arxiv-2603-10065: Jah proves that his Epistemic Support-Point Filter is the unique best recursive estimator among evidence only filters. Where Bayesian filters chase an assumed truth and minimise squared error, this filter minimises maximum entropy and shows what has not been ruled out. Its criterion unifies with the Kalman filter on one Holder mean curve, Jah shows. A two day orbital tracking run illustrates how possibilistic stress appears in practice.
arxiv-2603-10265: Shane K Panter and Nasir U Eisty introduce MALTA, a scoring system meant to catch abandoned software that plain version lag misses. Three scores track development activity, maintainer replies, and repository health, tested on a large Debian set linked to upstream repositories. MALTA sorts active from declining upkeep well, and most packages called low risk by version lag alone move to high risk once these signals count. The point is to split lag that can be fixed from lag caused by upstream abandonment.
arxiv-2603-10465: Tianyu Xu and co-authors present MoXaRt, a real-time XR system that lets users pull apart tangled sound sources in a scene. A cascaded design first separates audio coarsely while vision spots sources like faces and instruments. Those visual anchors then guide refinement networks that isolate single sources, even with several voices and instruments at once, at about two seconds of latency. Tests on new recordings and a user study showed much better speech comprehension in hostile sound settings, with far lower cognitive load.
arxiv-2603-10665: Surangana Sengupta and co-authors study optomechanical cooling in the few-photon regime, where needing many photons limits quantum control. They consider a cavity with strong nonlinearity, run as a discrete quantum system. Working in the weak-coupling limit, they link the damping rate to the cavity's dressed-state manifold. The rate is set by population imbalance across those states, and can be tuned with standard circuit QED tools. A Josephson photonics platform trades raw cooling power for full control of the mechanical mode.
arxiv-2603-11265: Luis Mora and coauthors extend irreversible port-Hamiltonian modeling from one dimension to N-dimensional conduction-diffusion systems, keeping the framework thermodynamically sound throughout. Conduction and diffusion fall under a single structure. It preserves global energy balance and gets entropy production right. This lays groundwork for modeling and control in complex work with coupled transport. It points toward structure-preserving schemes that enforce these laws at the discrete level.
arxiv-2603-11365: Rokuto Nagata and coauthors return with a spoofing attack that breaks LiDAR localization even in feature-rich streets and rooms. Conventional injection attacks usually fail there. Dynamic SLAMSpoof injects spurious laser returns. Their spatial shapes and time-varying patterns are designed from scan-matching principles. This lifts success rates in real environments.
