arxiv-2604-14565: Kamimura, Washiyama, and Sano study biped walking and running learned with model-based deep reinforcement learning, comparing bodies with and without passive elements like springs. Training with passive elements leans heavily on the system's attractor: trajectories converge quickly to limit cycles, yet large rewards take a long time to arrive. Attractor-driven learning nevertheless yields locomotion that is robust and energy-efficient. Robots with passive elements thus acquire high-performance gaits efficiently through stable limit cycles born from body-ground interaction, arguing for passive properties in future embodied AI.
arxiv-2604-14865: He, Sel, Ali, Bao, Cunningham, and Wei improve streaming probes for harmful intent, for jailbreaking in chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear domains. Current probes lean on a few high-scoring tokens, tripping false alarms when sensitive terms appear in benign contexts. Their objective requires multiple signal tokens to support a prediction, using aggregate signals. At a 1 percent false-positive rate, true-positive rate rises 35.55 percent relative to streaming baselines. Attention and MLP activations beat residual-stream features, and base-model probes transfer to adversarial cipher attacks, topping 98.85 percent AUROC.
arxiv-2604-14965: Chen, Wang, Huang, and Kurniawati frame indoor object search as a partially observable Markov decision process with growing states and hybrid actions. Their solver GNPF-kCT picks actions by Monte Carlo tree search with belief reuse, a neural network filtering useless actions, and k-center clustering, with a modified upper-confidence bound steering expansion. For sparse information or rewards, they add a guessed target object with a grid-world model. Gazebo tests with Fetch and Stretch robots and office tests show faster, more reliable localization than POMDP and other baselines.
arxiv-2604-15065: Zeng and colleagues ask where position clues should enter detectors hunting tiny objects in images. Their HELP framework keeps position codes in foreground-rich spots while muting background clutter, guided by heatmaps. A heatbar view makes the embedding choices visible for diagnosis and tuning. The design cuts decoder layers from eight to three and trims parameters by about 59 percent while holding accuracy gains.
arxiv-2604-15165: Vasileva and Sim sort the extra text language models add when translating, asking when it fabricates and when it genuinely helps. Overgeneration ranges from model self-explanations to risky confabulations to apt explanations of the kind a human translator might offer. Telling these apart is hard, yet it matters for readers who need to grasp the target text. The paper details strategies tried in commercial work and reports what each revealed.
arxiv-2604-15265: Vila-Miñana and others test whether graphs are isomorphic using persistent homology over motif filtrations. Edge weights from triangle, chordless-square, and chordless-pentagon densities track shape features as filtrations evolve. Their cycle-density filtrations separate non-isomorphic graphs cleanly or nearly so across four hard families, many with symmetries. The method beats curvature- and degree-based rivals, giving a topological view of graph matching and property guesses, and it works well even where graphs mirror each other.
arxiv-2604-15665: Zhang and Zhao tune a monocular 3D biomechanics pipeline for CPU-only runs on consumer hardware, redoing start-up, cutting disk I/O queues, and boosting CPU parallelism. On an AMD Ryzen 7 9700X box, throughput rises 2.47 times and total runtime falls 59.6 percent, with start-up delay down 4.6 times. Outputs stay close to the GPU baseline, with mean joint-angle gap of 0.35 degrees and correlation 0.998.
arxiv-2604-15865: Ramesh, Singh, and Kolathaya present the Dual-Topology Elastic Actuator, the first actuator that switches between series and parallel elastic layouts during operation instead of being fixed in one. A prototype survived 324 switching cycles under load without damage, with each switch taking under 33.33 ms. Parallel mode proved markedly stiffer than series mode, with smaller deflections and faster settling under disturbance. That matches the known behavior of conventional actuators in each mode.
arxiv-2604-16265: Mundayatt and Sreevalsan-Nair propose FL-MHSM, a deep-learning workflow for joint flood-landslide susceptibility mapping at regional scale. Older maps often use one model everywhere, treat hazards separately, and miss cross-hazard links and uncertainty. Their design combines two-level spatial partitions, probabilistic early fusion, and a soft-gating mixture of experts as final model, alongside a tree-based late fusion baseline. In Kerala, early fusion lifts flood recall from 0.816 to 0.840, while the mixture of experts scores best for flood susceptibility.
arxiv-2604-16365: Akhmetov and Buchanan merged two introductory computing courses into a single studio course they call CS 1.5. Run at Northeastern University Vancouver, the course treats generative AI as a collaborator rather than an opponent, and prizes understanding code over producing it from scratch. Four-hour studio sessions, sharing circles and projects joining set theory, recursion and probability link mathematical proof to working software. The report closes by recasting the instructor as a mentor and offering advice for scaling the high-touch model.
arxiv-2604-16465: Ercole asks whether healthcare AI should automate tasks or allocate work, using the economics of coordination costs at the level of tasks. From O*NET job data on what tasks occur and how often, he sorts each task by its coordination cost: finding facts, deciding and bargaining, checking and enforcing, or adapting and coordinating. He scores its coordination burden. Clinician roles carried higher burdens than non-clinician roles, driven by finding facts and decision work. AI chances vary by role, shaped less by technical difficulty than by coordination structure.
arxiv-2604-16565: Ruan and colleagues propose thinking on the manifold for self-checks in diffusion language models. Valid output paths are stable anchors on the high-density manifold, while invalid paths drift off-manifold. Their two-way manifold match metric, BMC, gauges sequence stability through forward hiding and backward rebuild, without training or labels. BMC checks solution truth without ground truth, focuses compute on complex tasks by refusal retries, and guides tuning as a dense shape reward. Inner shape stability thus serves as a robust sign of rightness for spread models.
arxiv-2604-16665: Saha and colleagues introduce CBRS, a multi-platform framework filtering blood donation requests from social media streams. Urgent donation posts go unnoticed amid daily volume, and manual systems struggle in low-resource settings. CBRS uses a cheap dual-layer architecture, trained on parsed request messages in Bengali, English and transliterated Bengali. Adversarial negatives in training further strengthen the model. CBRS reaches 99 percent filtering accuracy and precision, beating benchmark methods. Its tuned Llama model reaches 92 percent zero-shot parsing accuracy, beating rival models while cutting input token use 35 times.
arxiv-2604-16765: Cao and colleagues analyze discourse on X during five weeks around the 2024 United States presidential election. Posts are sorted into 10 major issues, with ideology estimated by human-in-the-loop annotation and toxicity detected by a language model. Toxicity varies by issue in prevalence and intensity, with identity-related issues showing the highest intensity. Harassment is the most prevalent and intense harm across most issues, while hate concentrates in identity debates. Partisan posts carry more harmful content than neutral posts, and toxic discourse runs on high-arousal negative emotions.
arxiv-2604-16865: Korolev and colleagues extract the most telling statistical features from time series made by Itô-type flows. The series are seen values of stochastic flows meeting random differential rules with unknown drift and spread coefficients. Using only data in the series, the authors take settings of number-fitted mixture-type models of observed patterns. Uniform reconstruction yields numbers free of the current value, while non-uniform rebuild accounts for value link. Tested in simple autoregressive guessing algorithms, the extra number features improve prediction.
arxiv-2604-16965: Esmaili-Dokht and six colleagues ask why memory simulators often disagree with real hardware, and how they can be validated. They judge performance from three angles: the tool itself, the CPU-memory interface, and the application. The interface emerges as the main culprit, and their corrections across Ramulator, Ramulator 2, and DRAMsim3 with ZSim bring results much closer to measured system behavior.
arxiv-2604-17165: Parson-Scherban and five colleagues extend optimal current reference theory to wound rotor synchronous machines, adding a rotor-current degree of freedom plus magnetic saturation, cross-coupling, and speed-dependent core losses. They recast the optimal reference search within affine flux regions as a quadratically constrained quadratic program built from finite-element data. Solutions are closed-form or low-dimensional polynomials in several constraint regimes, with a small semidefinite program in the voltage-limited case. Tests on a physical prototype confirm the approach across the torque-speed envelope.
arxiv-2604-17565: Jiang and four colleagues propose UniGeo, a camera-steered image editing framework that keeps geometry steady as viewpoints move. Older methods lean on split geometric cues, often injecting point clouds at one level only, and map views one at a time, so steady camera motion brings drift and shape decay. UniGeo instead injects unified guidance at three levels: representation, architecture, and loss function. Reference injection, anchor focus, and endpoint supervision together hold cross-view structure. Tests across public benchmarks show clear gains in visual quality and geometric consistency.
arxiv-2604-17665: Hew and three colleagues introduce pyzentropy, an open-source Python package for recursive entropy in first-principles thermodynamics. While entropy's repeat rule is well known in info theory, it is rarely used there, and code tools are lacking. The case study uses Fe3Pt in a 12-atom cell with several magnet setups. Applying this formula to compute system entropy matches Invar effects, plus the odd temperature dependence of thermal expansion, heat capacity, and bulk modulus. The package also builds T-V and P-T phase diagrams matching lab findings.
arxiv-2604-18065: Chatzinikolaou, Hoefer, Koutsonikos-Kouloumpis, and Paraskevas build a framework for deciding when two quantum graphs count as Morita equivalent. They treat quantum graphs as relations between operator systems. Their main result says such graphs match exactly when both arise as pullbacks of one shared graph. They add a stronger version of the equivalence and show that connectivity, capacity, and several other invariants survive the matching.
arxiv-2604-18265: Henum, Hobbs, Jiménez-Arranz, McMillan, and Church test whether the planned GaiaNIR mission could reveal dark-matter halos in globular clusters. GaiaNIR would extend Gaia's star mapping into the near-infrared, piercing dusty regions with sharper precision. Simulations of an M4-like cluster show Gaia resolves wide halos only when dust is thin, while GaiaNIR keeps sensitivity even under heavy extinction. The new mission would thus tighten Gaia's kinematic constraints and open heavily obscured clusters to study.
arxiv-2604-18565: Li and Peel investigate small-group detection using the Stochastic Block Model. These small groups are hard to find. They identify three phases: spottable, where they merge into big groups; distinguishable, where they form a unified group of their own but stay fuzzy inside; and crackable, where each is distinct. These phases match shifts at the Kesten-Stigum threshold and two further thresholds from signal matrix eigenvalues. Spectral grouping with the Bethe Hessian performs weaker for small groups than belief spread, a spectral weakness for fine-grained structure.
arxiv-2604-18665: Miao and five colleagues build a video segmentation pipeline for spoken prompts in the MEVIS_Audio task. Their system adds speech-to-text and a presence check to a standard Sa2VA pipeline. Since spoken prompts are noisy and may name absent things, an Omni check asks whether the target shows up on screen. If not, the pipeline stops and returns blank masks. If it does, the text feeds Sa2VA for a rough mask track, polished by an agent layer weighing prompt trust, timing, anchors, and error sources.
arxiv-2604-18865: Fremouw and 13 colleagues show reverse bias reactions create additional mobile ions in metal halide perovskite diodes. Typical mobile ion concentrations are too small to explain tunneling currents and breakdown near minus 5 volts. Inferred concentrations rise by more than 100 times within three minutes of reverse bias. The rise comes from iodide oxidation and iodine vacancy creation, balanced by reduction near the hole transport layer. Thin hole transport coverage leads to even larger concentrations and faster degradation.
arxiv-2604-18965: Kim and five colleagues design a fast multi modal transformer for wireless beamforming jobs. Existing transformers suffer high latency and large memory footprints, and attention costs grow with the square of token count. Their design keeps only key tokens, chosen by a token router under a target computing budget. Each input type gets its own tokenizer into one shared space, and a trainable keep ratio sets each layer's token count. The work targets fast inference for changing scenes with moving vehicles and blockages.
arxiv-2604-19065: Chandak, Tamizholi, and Bambos prove last iterate guarantees for stochastic gradient descent in co-coercive games under noisy feedback. Such games generalize strongly monotone games and allow multiple equilibria. Prior work assumed noise vanishing near equilibrium, which is often unrealistic. They instead allow noise with second moment scaling affinely with squared iterate norms. They prove a last iterate bound shrinking like log time over the cube root of time, the first bound under non-vanishing noise. They prove almost sure convergence to the Nash set and time average guarantees.
arxiv-2604-19265: Camacho, Ezenarro, Schorn-García, and Westerhuis offer a tutorial review of ANOVA simultaneous component analysis, a chemometric tool that extends analysis of variance to high-dimensional data from designed experiments. They argue it pairs naturally with design of experiments, and they build their recommended best practices on a century of ANOVA and experiment-design theory plus a broad literature review. A guiding example walks readers through the method in use.
arxiv-2604-19665: Vignaroli reviews how colliders probe the tau lepton's anomalous magnetic moment, a precise Standard Model test and a sensitive hunt for new physics in the third lepton family. Because the tau decays too fast for classic spin-precession measurement, the review tracks a shift from older LEP limits. It then turns to the sharper precision now reached at the LHC. It highlights ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions, where colliding nuclei act as an intense photon-photon collider boosted by a Z-to-the-fourth rise in coherent photon flux.
arxiv-2604-19765: Snehit Vaddi and Pujith Vaddi ask whether hallucination neurons generalize across knowledge domains in large language models. Earlier work found a sparse set of such neurons, less than one tenth of a percent of feed-forward neurons, that reliably predict hallucinations on general-knowledge questions. Testing 5 open-weight models across 6 domains, they find the neurons do not transfer: classifiers score an AUROC of 0.783 within a domain but far lower on a new domain.
arxiv-2604-19965: Rabbi and three colleagues studied over 33,000 AI-generated pull requests, isolating 675 security-related submissions from agentic coding tools. Recurring flaws include regex inefficiencies, injection flaws, and path traversal, yet many flawed contributions still get merged. Rejections often stem from social or process causes, such as inactivity or missing tests, rather than code flaws. Commit message quality barely moves acceptance or speed, unlike for human pull requests, and the authors add AI-specific categories to rejection taxonomies.
arxiv-2604-20265: Guo and four colleagues derive a compressible Navier-Stokes-Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert model for magnetoelastic materials. In these materials fluid flow bends a solid and steers its magnetization, using an energy-based variational method. They prove solutions exist for a short time when the starting energy is finite. Then, near a steady state with no outside magnetic field and small starting data, they show global well-posedness. That means solutions exist for all time and behave stably. The model reduces to a viscoelastic model when the field vanishes.
arxiv-2604-20365: Godin-Dubois, Yaman, and Kononova compare central pattern generators and multilayer perceptrons for robot control with small input and output spaces. With bounded performance, extra parameters can hurt learning rather than help it. On a fixed four-legged robot with limited proprioception, shallow perceptrons and densely linked pattern generators beat deeper perceptrons and actor-critic designs under evolution and reward training. A parameter impact metric shows diminishing returns for perceptrons but not for pattern generators, backing prior bias for simple hinge walking.
arxiv-2604-20665: Goyal argues vision-language models often fail to truly blend mixed data, a trust gap in the main encoder-link-LLM setup. Rather than pulling grounded knowledge from visual inputs, models exploit language priors to bypass visual jams, a pattern called functional blindness. Instead he offers the Modality Translation Protocol, moving meaning payloads rather than cutting them, and naming the Toll, Curse, and Fallacy of Seeing plus the Semantic Sufficiency Criterion. He also guesses a Divergence Law: as language engines scale, the visual jam penalty may grow rather than shrink.
arxiv-2604-20865: Alvarez-Telena and Diez-Fernandez introduce Orthogonal Art, a new artistic discipline that responds to artificial intelligence rather than serving it. Unlike AI-augmented practices, it is defined by holding the generative and conceptual spaces current AI systems cannot reach. Its founding case is an artistic practice in which technical schematics serve as the main medium. The work also has a teaching side: grounding art practice in schematic logic and algorithmic structure gives an open entry point into Augmented Machines systems.
arxiv-2604-20965: Das and colleagues take stock of resonant anomaly detection for collider physics, where most studies lean on a few simulated signals and narrow observable sets. They release new simulated benchmarks compatible with the LHC Olympics format and test a broad kitchen-sink set that joins Energy Flow Polynomials to standard subjettiness variables. The wide set proves most sensitive across signal types, and an attribute-bagging variant matches its performance at far lower training cost.
arxiv-2604-21065: Giulia Gatti and Giacomo Como analyze an epidemic model in which recovered people can fall ill again, spread across a general network with uneven recovery and immunity-loss rates. They pin the outcome to a single threshold number: below it, infection dies out everywhere, while above it a single steady endemic state takes hold. They also trace how that steady state shifts with the network and rates, and give a distributed algorithm that computes it.
arxiv-2604-21265: Yoshinori Nomura shows that pre-training a transformer on music before language speeds up language learning. A developmental pipeline from piano performances through poetry to prose cuts perplexity by 17.5 percent over random initialization, with music and poetry improving different model parts. The edge persists rather than fading: at the smallest hidden size tested, a gap remains at plateau across seeds. Real music matches synthetic patterns' transfer ceiling with one-third the data, pointing to capacity-dependent data curation.
arxiv-2604-21365: Adam Skurla, Dominik Macko, and Jakub Simko adapt a machine-text detector to machine-generated code for SemEval-2026 Task 13, covering binary detection, generator-family attribution, human-machine hybrid code, and adversarially disguised code. Their systems explore base models better suited to code understanding. Results prove competitive across all three subtasks, though margins to the top systems remain significant. The work shows the adapted approach transfers to code, while leaving clear room for improvement.
arxiv-2604-21565: Animesh Patra and Ankur Raina offer a teaching text on pulse shaping for superconducting qubits, aimed at undergraduates and graduates with basic quantum mechanics and quantum computing course. They join feel, math, into a story. Pulse envelopes show bandwidth leaks outside the subspace, prompting derivative removal by adiabatic gate, from Magnus expansion, tracing error channels in order and why it cancels only in part. Hardware lists arbitrary waveform generators, oscillators, IQ mixing. Two-qubit cross-resonance gates make stray interaction terms beside the one, cut by rounds.
arxiv-2604-21665: Beers and Mulas study Fair and Tolerant graph colourings. In this scheme, each vertex may share its colour with a set fraction of neighbours. The rest spread evenly across other colour classes. They work out the FAT chromatic number for every complete multipartite graph. They also track how such colourings behave under several graph operations. Spectral methods lead the argument, with combinatorial reasoning filling in alongside.
arxiv-2604-21765: Chen, Phani, and Schelter present PrismaDV, a compound AI system that generates data unit tests aware of the downstream task, not just the dataset. It reads task code together with dataset profiles, spots data access patterns, infers hidden data assumptions, and writes executable tests. A prompt-optimisation framework called SIFTA then adapts those tests over time from scarce execution outcomes. On two new benchmarks spanning 60 tasks and five datasets, PrismaDV beats task-agnostic and task-aware baselines.
arxiv-2604-22465: Hitching and Zamora generalize Segre invariants, numbers recording the largest degree reached by subbundles of a given rank, from vector bundles to principal bundles over a curve. For each parabolic subgroup they define a Segre number, shown to vary semicontinuously in families and thus carve moduli space into strata. They track how the invariant behaves under surjective maps between groups, letting stratifications for different groups be compared. The Borel subgroup case for three-by-three matrices yields a sharp Hirschowitz-type bound for certain topological types.
arxiv-2604-22565: Li and 12 colleagues present HiLight, helping frozen models notice decisive evidence buried in long, noisy contexts. Large models reason well yet often miss pivotal spans, so HiLight separates evidence selection from reasoning. A lightweight Emphasis Actor inserts highlight tags around pivotal spans in the untouched context for a frozen Solver to reason over. Highlighting is weakly supervised decision-making, optimized by reinforcement learning on task reward alone, with no evidence labels and no Solver access or change. Across sequential recommendation and long-context question answering, HiLight beats strong prompt baselines.
arxiv-2604-22665: Shalaby and Broderick show drift between dark matter and baryons, gained after decoupling, triggers resonant gravitational instability and sound waves. Baryons fail above their Jeans scale; dark matter, on all scales. When seen drift is subsonic, baryon oscillations ring with the Doppler-shifted mode, beating dark matter. The instability peaks below the Jeans scale and, where baryons rule, opens a stable window between Jeans scale and resonance; supersonic drift suppresses growth. Resonant coupling transfers push, creating a touchless drag. A plain resonance growth rate approximation is derived.
arxiv-2604-23065: Charnock and three co-authors ask what frontier AI developers should disclose about internal deployments of highly capable models used to automate AI research. Such use faces limited outside oversight, yet they must evidence that models deployed inside are safe. The paper lists key disclosures across capabilities, usage, safety mitigations, and governance, weighing gains, limits, and safeguards for leak risks in each area. The framework can inform public transparency papers like system cards and private regular reports under new frontier AI regulation.
arxiv-2604-23865: Bracher, Intes, and Radev ask whether brain models can be run in reverse to recover stimuli from synthetic brain responses. They pair a brain emulator with language models that generate news headlines from valence, arousal, and dominance settings. They then learn a map from brain maps to hidden input settings. The settings can be read back, showing the emulator's encodings preserve input information and enabling reverse design.
arxiv-2604-23965: Lin, Sun, and Wang settle the flexible exponent for non-geometric 3-manifolds, a number that bounds how fast a map's degree can grow with its stretch. For geometric manifolds the value was already known, but the non-geometric case stayed open. Their paper determines that exponent in the non-geometric case, closing a classical question in quantitative topology.
arxiv-2604-24065: Antil and three colleagues present an online adaptive finite-element method for nonsmooth PDE-constrained optimization, including sparse penalties and convex limits. Starting from a coarse mesh, it refines where error estimates for state and adjoint equations demand it, balancing cost against accuracy. The trust-region design handles nonsmooth objectives that mix a smooth term with a convex nonsmooth term. Tests on control and topology optimization examples show sharp detail on local features and sparse patterns.
arxiv-2604-24265: Bai and eight colleagues introduce the SVOM real-time response and collaboration system, using the BeiDou-3 short message service. The paper presents onboard and ground system designs and data flow, plus the collaboration mechanism with other missions. In its first in-flight year SVOM detected 172 gamma-ray bursts, including 147 by GRM and 62 by ECLAIRs, and performed 1,040 observations, spanning exceptional, multi-messenger, and nominal targets of opportunity. The system has measurably increased the mission's scientific output.
arxiv-2604-24765: Jiang and six colleagues use a clear fuzzy space-time framework for P300 brain-computer interface classification, to study how neural patterns differ across populations. Prior work looked at gaps mainly in signals or scores, while the learned representation structure stayed little studied. The model uses spatial and temporal fuzzy filters with learnable prototypes, for classification and rebuilding of cohort-specific fuzzy centers. Tests on ALS, autism and neurotypical cohorts show clear gaps in waveform shape and representation geometry between cohorts.
arxiv-2604-24965: Bell and three colleagues study how galaxy mergers shape disk angular momentum in 471 Milky Way-mass TNG-50 galaxies. They show reorientation is a common result of satellite accretion. About 80 percent of galaxies align their present-day angular momentum with that of their largest merger progenitor's orbit. Reorientation typically shifts angular momentum by around 50 percent. Accreted stellar halos encode this history, with about 81 percent spinning prograde. This signature should be visible with 30-meter telescopes, testing the merger-driven picture.
arxiv-2604-25165: Liu calculates anisotropic emission of direct photons from gold-gold collisions at 200 GeV using a viscous hydrodynamic model with Glasma initial state. Momentum spectra match RHIC data well across bins. Elliptic flow and triangular flow agree well in the 20 to 40 percent bin. They are underpredicted for 0 to 20 percent and overpredicted for 40 to 60 percent. After accounting for prompt photons, the measured elliptic flow is no longer too large to explain. Overestimating prompt yield would suppress both flows below observed values.
arxiv-2604-25465: Cipriani and Woolf show that faithful highest weight hearts in a triangulated category are serially faithful glued hearts. Such hearts hold a dual pair of full exceptional collections. They then pin down all faithful highest weight perverse sheaf categories on stratified spaces, by functor exactness and by vanishing of link cohomology groups. Such a faithful heart on a finite-strata space has dimension bounded by that of the space. Finally, perverse sheaf hypercohomology comes from a resolution of the constant sheaf, and minimal-resolution multiplicities come from intersection cohomology.
arxiv-2604-25665: Nguyen and four colleagues meta-evaluate summarisation metrics and LLM-based evaluators across seven datasets spanning five domains. Traditional metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU correlate weakly or negatively with human judgements, while neural and LLM-based evaluators align far better for linguistic quality. Building on those findings, the team proposes LLM-ReSum, a reflective frame that loops evaluation and generation with no finetuning. Across three domains it lifts summaries by up to 33 percent in factual accuracy and 39 percent in coverage, with humans liking refined versions in 89 percent of cases.
arxiv-2604-25765: Maurino proposes the Error Sensitivity Profile, a measure of how sensitive a classification model's performance is to errors in one feature or in several features. Data quality is critical to model performance, yet cleaning efforts need guidance on which errors matter most. The profile lets teams prioritize cleaning by error type and by feature, based on likely impact. To compute it, the author builds an integrated tool suite called dirty. Tests on two standard datasets with 14 classification models show performance loss is not always predictable from simple correlations.
arxiv-2604-26665: Xiang, Jin, and Wang establish the third-order intrinsic anomalous Hall effect as a transport fingerprint of altermagnets. Linear and second-order responses already tell ferromagnets apart from PT-symmetric antiferromagnets, but whether a third-order intrinsic twin could flag altermagnetic order was open. Spin-group symmetry shows the effect is allowed in the ten spin Laue groups tied to altermagnets with spin-orbit coupling counted. Near altermagnetic band crossings, a strong response arises from the Berry curvature quadrupole, and so widens the Hall-effect hierarchy across aligned magnets.
arxiv-2604-26765: Huang, Menet and Sinha introduce CARhy, a statistical framework for studying daily biological rhythms in gene-activity data across more than two conditions. Built on first-harmonic Fourier regression, it tests whether rhythms exist and whether rhythm strength, timing, and baseline level differ between conditions, while allowing uneven designs and unequal variation. Simulations show it controls false positives and beats existing methods in hard settings. Applied to mouse liver data, it traces how gene rhythms shift across conditions.
arxiv-2604-27365: Hasan, Soumik, and Shahid propose softening harmful social media comments instead of deleting them. The rewrite preserves what a comment says while lowering its emotional force. Their framework, inspired by the simple Notepad AI assistant, turns aggressive, toxic, or hurtful posts into more neutral wording and cuts attacks aimed at identity. They also introduce an Emotion Drift Index that measures how much feeling a rewrite shifts, offering a way to judge whether stylistic change actually reduces online harm.
arxiv-2604-27665: Guo studies an estimator of twice the total quarticity of a continuous Itô semimartingale, built from squared returns and local spot volatility gauges. For a shrinking window, he proves the bias-corrected estimator obeys a functional stable central limit law. The proof uses a shared martingale proxy for the three parts to get their joint covariance structure. The process may have jumps, and he compares the limit variance with realized-quarticity and quadratic spot-volatility measures.
arxiv-2605-00065:
Muhammet Anıl Yağız, Fahrettin Horasan, and Ahmet Haşim Yurttakal present a lightweight pipeline for proving that internet-of-things audit logs have not been tampered with. Log integrity underpins forensics, compliance, and accountability, but blockchain logging brings consensus overhead and network dependence that edge devices can ill afford. Their system gets tamper evidence from Merkle trees alone, with no distributed ledger.

The pipeline ingests log batches with resource-aware adaptive chunk sizes, builds the Merkle tree with fast inclusion proofs, and verifies single entries against a trusted root. The authors also report an implementation audit that found and fixed two evaluation defects, a double-counting bug and a redundant tree rebuild. Corrected benchmarks on synthetic logs show high throughput on one hundred thousand records, small proofs, low memory, and perfect tamper detection across corruption levels.
arxiv-2605-00265:
Sahil Mishra and 3 co-authors present Polaris, a method for embedding hierarchical knowledge, such as product taxonomies, medical ontologies, and label trees. Hierarchies are lopsided and their labels are noisy, which makes them hard to represent in the flat vector spaces models usually learn. Polaris places concepts on a sphere and splits the job in two.

Direction on the sphere carries meaning, while distance from the center carries rank in the hierarchy, so the two signals do not interfere. Training mixes local constraints, a global term that stops the geometry from collapsing, and objectives that respect the one-way nature of parent and child links. At lookup time, structure guides a narrowing of candidate parents. Across tree, graph, and multimodal hierarchies, Polaris improved retrieval over fourteen strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-00365:
Anamika Lochab, Bolian Li, and Ruqi Zhang diagnose a diversity collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a method that trains reasoning models on checkable answers. Single-attempt accuracy rises, yet when the model gets many tries, its coverage of correct solutions shrinks. The authors trace the flaw to the objective itself, which is indifferent to how probability is spread among correct answers.

Training dynamics then feed on themselves, piling probability onto a narrow set of correct outputs while starving other valid ones. Their analysis identifies a uniform spread over correct solutions as uniquely optimal under two criteria. Their method, UCPO, adds a penalty that pushes probability toward neglected correct responses. Across three models and five math benchmarks, coverage and diversity rose while single-attempt accuracy held, with large gains on a hard contest set.
arxiv-2605-00565:
Yuber F. Perez-Gonzalez weighs a dramatic explanation for an ultra-high-energy event recorded by the KM3NeT neutrino telescope: the final burst of a nearby exploding black hole. Dying black holes should emit Hawking radiation, a flash of all particle types at extreme energies. A primordial black hole ending its life close to Earth has been proposed as the event's source.

Such a source would have to sit extremely close, which makes a testable prediction. Gamma-ray and cosmic-ray telescopes should have seen emission building up before the burst. Neutrino telescopes should also have caught lower-energy events ahead of it. Accounting for when observatories were actually looking that way, Perez-Gonzalez finds those signals should have appeared. Their absence strongly disfavors the black hole explanation, at least in the minimal four-dimensional picture.
arxiv-2605-00765:
Leif Verace, Siobhan McMahon, and Erjia Cui propose a faster way to do longitudinal function-on-function regression, where both the input and the output are curves tracked over time. Their three-step method fits many simpler models point by point, smooths the results over the full domain, and then builds confidence bands. An analytic route handles Gaussian data, while a cluster bootstrap handles other cases.

Simulations show accurate estimates with far less computing than earlier methods. The team applies the approach to a trial in older adults who wore activity sensors across several visits. The data show clear morning activity gains from interpersonal support strategies, but not from intrapersonal ones. The methods ship in an R package.
arxiv-2605-00965:
Kimon Manolas and one co-author study chaos in Arnol'd cat maps coupled across the nodes of a circulant graph, a highly symmetric network where each node connects in a repeating pattern. Requiring the evolution matrix to be symplectic fixes the coupling matrix, which is naturally read as the graph's adjacency matrix. The study analyzes Lyapunov spectra, which measure chaos strength, and Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, which measures entropy output.

Simulations give a surprising result: entropy output does not rise as graph connectivity increases. The authors trace that effect to the translational symmetry of the circulant graph. They also analyze the periods of the evolution matrix on a finite toroidal phase space. That completes the dynamical picture for this coupled map system.
arxiv-2605-01065:
Stephen Meisenbacher and two co-authors systematically study how text decomposition and privacy budget sharing affect differentially private text scrambling. The goal is to perturb texts with formal privacy guarantees so outputs stay hard to distinguish from originals. Word-level perturbation is intuitive, but meaningful privatization acts on whole documents. That raises the question of how to split the total privacy budget among text pieces.

Experiments combine several chunking methods with several budget allocation techniques. Design choices prove very important: even at comparable budgets, outcomes differ significantly depending on the combination chosen. The authors provide evidence that optimizing the scrambling procedure can maximize empirical trade-offs between privacy and utility. That gives practical guidance for document-level private text release.
arxiv-2605-01165:
Valter Estevam, Rayson Laroca, Helio Pedrini, and David Menotti propose CEZSAR, a contrastive method for zero-shot action recognition, where a model must classify actions from classes never seen in training. Two problems persist: a semantic gap between textual label representations and visual representations, and domain shift because the test set is unknown. Learning a joint embedding space is a promising response to both.

CEZSAR encodes videos and sentences in a joint space trained by aligning videos with their natural-language descriptions. An automatic negative sampling procedure augments training with unpaired visual and unrelated description examples. Results are described as state of the art on UCF-101 and Kinetics-400 under several split configurations, and code is made publicly available for reuse and checking.
arxiv-2605-01265:
Samantha J. Alloo and five co-authors develop a new retrieval algorithm for X-ray dark-field imaging in grating interferometry, based on the Fokker-Planck model. Grating setups capture three linked images at once: transmission, differential phase, and dark-field. They can use large-area detectors and compact low-coherence sources, both key for human-scale imaging. They have shown promise for chest diagnosis including emphysema, fibrosis, and cancer.

Separating the distinct contrast mechanisms from measured data requires a recovery step. That step has remained fundamentally unchanged since the technique began. Their Fokker-Planck method retrieves both images from the intensity flow in a new way. Experimental measurements on a test object are used to demonstrate and validate the approach.
arxiv-2605-01565:
Bilal Ahmad Rather settles an open problem about a graph built from modular arithmetic. Take the nonzero, nonunit residues modulo a squarefree number. Join two when their greatest common divisor with the modulus tells a certain comaximal story. Then ask how many vertices must be removed to disconnect the core of that graph.

Using the Chinese remainder picture, Rather codes each vertex by the set of prime coordinates where it vanishes. The graph becomes a weighted blow-up of a disjointness graph on sets, where sizes, degrees, and short paths can all be read off. The vertex connectivity comes out exactly as a product over all but the largest prime. That proves an earlier upper bound sharp and shows the graph is maximally connected, with edge strength matching its minimum degree. Distance, diameter, and radius results follow, plus a fast algorithm once the factorization is known.
arxiv-2605-01665:
Peter Reinhard Hansen and Chen Tong build exact likelihood tools for the Voigt distribution. That distribution blends a Gaussian bell with a heavy Cauchy tail, and spectroscopists use it to model line shapes. The blend also suits measurement noise that mostly behaves and sometimes jumps, but its density has no simple closed form, so fits usually lean on numeric crutches.

The pair derive analytic formulas for the density, its score and curvature, Fisher information, and conditional moments. All run through a scaled error function, which makes maximum likelihood stable with no numeric convolution or fake line-shape stand-ins. A redescending score means wild observations discount themselves inside the filter they build for state-space models. Applied to log realized volatility of a large technology fund, their filter separates steady latent swings from passing noise and posts the best prediction score among the rival filters tried.
arxiv-2605-01765:
Jinlun Zhang, Haoneng Huang, Zishu Zhan, and Chunquan Ou widen mediation analysis from averages to whole distributions. Mediation asks how a treatment works through middlemen variables, but standard answers report mean effects, which can hide large reshaping of the outcome spread when the mechanism bends.

Their framework learns conditional generative models for the mediators and the outcome from observational data. With the identification formulas in hand, it rebuilds what the outcome distribution would look like under intervention by Monte Carlo simulation, resampling noise to push cases through the learned models. Classical summary effects fall out alongside richer contrasts, measured by energy distance and Wasserstein distance between distributions. Error bounds split the total error by which learned model contributed it. Numerical tests and a real-data application close the case.
arxiv-2605-02765:
Christine P Lee and four co-authors present U-Define, a system that lets users steer language-model planners with constraints stated in plain words. Model planners are black boxes, so users struggle to enforce what must hold and what may bend. Hard-only rules are too rigid, and numeric flexibility weights confuse users, prior work finds.

U-Define lets a user label each constraint as hard, a rule that must not be broken, or soft, a preference that allows slack. Each type gets its own check: formal model checking for hard rules, and a model-as-judge review for soft ones. In technical tests and user studies with general and expert participants, the typed setup improved how useful people found the system and how well plans matched their intent. Reliability, the authors argue, needs this user-facing layer.
arxiv-2605-02865:
Zalán Gyenis, Miklós Rédei, and Leszek Wroński prove that decisions a rational agent cannot reach by conditioning on partial evidence are not rare exceptions, but abundant. A recent paper defined decisions that are conditionally inaccessible. Such a decision cannot be reached by an agent who maximizes expected utility under one probability. Updating beliefs with partial evidence about the probability that fixes the best act does not get there. Examples existed, and a wider existence claim was conjectured.

The authors prove the strong form. In any finite probability space, for any starting probability, there are uncountably many alternative probabilities, and for each, uncountably many pairs of utility functions, that yield inaccessible decisions. If one probability is read as objective and the other as an agent's subjective view, the result limits what evidence-based updating can recover.
arxiv-2605-03165:
Siyuan Wang and Fengqi You forecast sudden solar power ramps minutes ahead by first predicting how clouds will move. Fast cloud cover can swing photovoltaic output on a minute scale, leaving grid operators little warning to balance supply.

Their framework pairs a physics-guided generative model of future sky video with a forecaster that fuses observed and predicted sky states, sun position, and past output. On the SKIPP'D dataset it caught most ramps up to sixteen minutes ahead, beating deployable baselines. At a fixed reliability target, it also cut the fast reserve margin needed for balancing.
arxiv-2605-03265:
Long Feng and Hongfei Wang propose a high-dimensional two-sample test for location under elliptical distributions with arbitrary dependence. Spatial sign methods suit heavy-tailed data, but their calibration assumed weak dependence, and standard scaling fails to recover the shape when dependence is strong.

Their test standardizes with coordinatewise pairwise-difference quantile scales, which need no moment conditions and stay location free. They derive the statistic's expansion and its weighted chi-square null law under general correlation, justify a diagonal-deletion fix, and show a wild bootstrap tracks the null well. The normal law appears only when no direction dominates.
arxiv-2605-03565:
Chiara Vercellino and seven co-authors tackle a placement problem for neutral-atom quantum computers: arranging qubits, the basic units of quantum information, so that distance rules are obeyed. The task is framed as a constrained unit disk problem, where points must sit in a plane under spacing limits. Their tool is a neural network rather than a classical solver.

Their Distances Encoder Network learns a spatial transformation that moves infeasible layouts into feasible ones, guided by a custom Embedding Loss Function that encodes the constraints. In tests at fixed computation times, the approach beats classical solvers. The work points toward neural optimization as a practical aid for designing quantum hardware layouts.
arxiv-2605-03665:
Athanasios Sourmelidis proves that several different L-functions can all take large values at the same point on the critical line. L-functions generalize the Riemann zeta function, and understanding their extreme values bears on deep questions in number theory. Earlier joint results by Heap and Li needed the Riemann Hypothesis once more than three functions were involved.

Sourmelidis removes that assumption for primitive GL(1) and GL(2) L-functions, using the resonance method together with a variation of Heath-Brown's method for fractional moments of the zeta function. He also studies the joint distribution to the right of the critical line under zero-density estimates, improving work on Dirichlet and Selberg-class L-functions.
arxiv-2605-03865:
Eli Ismailov, Ulf Gran, and Eric Nilsson solve a holographic model of a non-Fermi liquid designed to keep the good features standard holographic metals lack. Ordinary Reissner-Nordström holographic metals have no Luttinger-counting Fermi surface. So the authors build an infrared effective model at finite temperature. It satisfies Luttinger's theorem and includes long-range Coulomb interactions. The model uses a Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory in an anti-de Sitter-Schwarzschild background.

With suitable boundary conditions, they obtain a damped collective plasmon mode. Its plasma frequency scales as Luttinger's theorem predicts. They also analyze the density-density correlator without the long-range Coulomb interaction. They identify a contribution consistent with a Lindhard-like continuum. That matches what Fermi liquid response would lead one to expect.
arxiv-2605-04065:
Yiming Huang and six co-authors introduce FREIA, an unsupervised reinforcement learning algorithm that lets large language models improve their reasoning without ground-truth labels. Existing unsupervised methods often cannot adapt to the model's evolving reasoning ability during training, so they can misdirect policy updates. FREIA is built from two ideas aimed at that gap.

Its Free Energy-Driven Reward adapts rewards to balance consensus among sampled answers against exploration, drawing on the Free Energy Principle. Its Adaptive Advantage Shaping adjusts learning signals according to the shape of the sampled rewards. Across nine datasets and three reasoning tasks, FREIA outperformed other unsupervised reinforcement learning baselines. On a distilled reasoning model, mathematical reasoning gains ran from roughly half a point to several points in Pass@1.
arxiv-2605-04265:
Daniel C. Elton and Preston W. Estep survey open tools and data sets for finding antiviral drugs with computers, a route that could move fast in a new outbreak by reusing approved medicines. Most virus families with pandemic potential still have no approved antiviral drug.

They build a cleaned data set of about forty-three thousand measurements of how compounds bind viral proteins, noting that much source data needed careful splitting before use. With it they retrain one prediction model and benchmark fifteen open tools on a test set of hundreds of compounds across sixteen protein targets.
arxiv-2605-04365:
Ying Song and six co-authors model how ice shelves break apart, a process called calving that weakens the shelf's ability to hold back land ice and slow its flow into the sea. The physics is poorly understood, especially when ocean waves erode the shelf front.

They build a nonlocal simulation framework that handles cracking naturally, unlike standard element methods. With it they study how the shelf's own weight bends it, how buoyancy loosens its foot as melting thins the base, and how wave-driven erosion at the front interacts with both. The work is a first physics-based attempt of this kind.
arxiv-2605-05265: Bahram Mashhoon examines the physics around a cosmic test mass that moves with a peculiar velocity relative to the standard comoving observers of an expanding FLRW universe. He constructs the Fermi normal coordinate system around the boosted mass's world line within an approximation scheme. That local frame is then compared with the corresponding Fermi system built around a comoving observer. Mashhoon also studies the circular gravitomagnetic field that appears around the direction of motion of the boosted mass, a frame-dragging effect tied to its movement through the cosmic flow.
arxiv-2605-05365:
ZAYA1-8B is a reasoning language model described in a technical report by Robert Washbourne and eighteen co-authors. Built by Zyphra on AMD hardware, it is a mixture-of-experts model with eight billion total parameters. Fewer than one billion of those are active for any single token.

Reasoning data was part of training from the very start, not added at the end. A four-stage reinforcement learning program then covered math, puzzles, code, and chat behavior. On hard math and coding tests the small model matches or beats DeepSeek-R1, a far larger system, and it stays competitive with other big open models.
arxiv-2605-05565:
Collisions at RHIC smash heavy nuclei and briefly free quarks and gluons. Yong Zhang uses theory to predict a subtle signal in the debris: correlations between protons and antiprotons flying back to back. Such fermion correlations could reveal how particle masses change inside the hot medium.

Zhang first pins down the allowed mass change by matching measured momentum spectra and particle ratios. A Gaussian source model with outward flow then gives the correlation predictions. The signal's strength depends sharply on how the source's lifetime is distributed in time, and larger antiproton shares should make the signal easier to detect.
arxiv-2605-05665:
Patricio Gallardo and Jayan Mukherjee study threefolds of general type built as special covers of weighted projective spaces. These covers, indexed by a group of sign choices, raise questions about their basic invariants and how they deform. The authors also ask when their canonical maps are flat and how those maps behave.

For the invariants, they write key ratios as functions of branch divisor degrees and trace their limits and bounds. That work yields a counterexample to a conjecture by Bruce Hunt about smooth threefolds in a forbidden zone. They extend a test for when such covers are general in their moduli, even with singular bases. Using Fourier methods on finite groups, they classify the flat cases fully.
arxiv-2605-05765:
A phone assistant that sees, hears, and acts needs its perception, memory, and action loops fused. Xiaoming Ren and thirteen co-authors present X-OmniClaw, a unified mobile agent for Android, in this technical report. The system targets complex, intuitive interactions rather than single scripted commands.

Its perception pipeline merges interface states, real-world visual context, and speech into structured intent representations, aligned over time. A multimodal memory keeps context across steps. The report describes the architecture end to end, positioning the agent as a personal assistant that understands screens and surroundings together.
arxiv-2605-05865:
Generating Chinese calligraphy that looks brushed, not printed, defeats most image models: strokes come out clean where real ink bleeds and pools. Kunchong Shi and Jing Zhang present InkDiffuser, a diffusion framework for one-shot calligraphy synthesis, learning a style from a single example. Two additions target fidelity directly.

A high-frequency enhancement mechanism fuses the contour details that individual samples carry. A differentiable ink structure loss regularizes the morphology of the ink itself, pushing strokes toward realistic texture and flow. The aim is characters with the visual fluidity of hand-brushed art.
arxiv-2605-06165:
Richmond Sin Jing Xuan, Rishabh Bhardwaj, and Soujanya Poria propose Post-Reasoning, a trick that makes direct answer models perform better at no extra cost. Reasoning traces eat tokens and time, yet many real tasks need little explicit reasoning, and extra reasoning can even hurt. Their idea flips the order: give the final answer first, then justify it afterward.

Because the answer comes first, users pay no added latency or token cost for the justification. Across 117 model and benchmark settings, the method improved results in over 88 percent of cases, with a mean relative gain above 17 percent. A trained variant, supervised post-reason tuning, did better still. The authors present the approach as a new ceiling for direct answer performance.
arxiv-2605-06465:
Matthias R. Gaberdiel, Beat Nairz, and Cheng Peng compute non-planar corrections in the symmetric product orbifold, a string theory construction built from many copies of a four-torus. They focus on the energy levels, called anomalous dimensions, of certain quarter-BPS states. In the large-copy limit some levels coincide exactly, hiding finer structure.

The corrections lift some of those degeneracies for large twist and large copy number. The authors also find signatures of quantum chaos, namely level repulsion and random matrix statistics in the spectrum. That suggests the system is integrable only in the planar, large-N limit, and becomes chaotic once finite corrections are included.
arxiv-2605-06865:
Pengrun Huang, Kamalika Chaudhuri, and Yu-Xiang Wang watermark datasets so that training on them leaves a detectable mark in model outputs alone. Owners worry their private data, or the benchmarks too, may be quietly absorbed into language models. Earlier watermarking added fake content or needed access beyond generated text for detection, limiting real use.

Their method raises how often randomly chosen word pairs co-occur, through small meaning-keeping edits across the dataset. Detection from generated text carries provable false positive control. Across four base models and three datasets it finds the mark with high confidence after fine-tuning. It does so even when watermarked text is under five percent of training tokens, while keeping benchmark utility better than baselines.
arxiv-2605-06965:
Iulia-Maria Comsa argues that research on AI consciousness should shift toward questions that can actually be studied. Whether an AI system can truly have inner experience, she says, cannot now be settled. No agreed science of consciousness exists, and the older mind-body problem remains open.

Perceived consciousness is different, Comsa argues, and it is already changing society. People increasingly speak about AI systems as if they think and feel, which affects design, ethics, and everyday language. She maps the drivers and effects of that perception, and urges clear communication from developers and decision makers about what remains unknown.
arxiv-2605-07265:
Kaisei Deguchi, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Hiroaki Mori speed up approximation schemes for hard cut problems on dense graphs. In dense graphs every vertex connects to a large share of the whole, yet earlier schemes ran in time with awkward dependence on the accuracy parameter. The authors deliver the faster efficient variant, an EPTAS, for several minimization problems.

Their main algorithm handles a constrained minimum cut problem using a weak regularity lemma plus sampling and estimation, avoiding heavy machinery used before. Reductions then yield schemes for quotient cut and product sparsest cut, which generalize several classic cut problems. The results cover balanced separation and small-set expansion as special cases.
arxiv-2605-07365:
Raymond Chan and Lingfeng Li solve convolution-type integral equations by pairing neural operators with classic solvers. Such equations appear in signal work and image deblurring. Older multigrid methods clear low-frequency error fast but stall on high-frequency parts, exactly where the authors aim their learned component.

Trained with a preconditioning trick, the neural operator handles the high-frequency parts, while a weighted Jacobi method handles the rest, forming a hybrid loop. The authors analyze both the training's generalization error and how the hybrid settles. On large, badly scaled systems from one- and two-axis problems, the hybrid beats multigrid and conjugate gradient methods.
arxiv-2605-07565:
Tigran Ramazyan and Denis Derkach study Bayesian optimization when the thing being optimized also depends on an environment the user cannot control. That context follows an unknown distribution, which must be estimated from data, and the estimate is always somewhat wrong. Robust methods exist, but they often get expensive, discretize the context, or assume a narrow form of uncertainty.

Their method, EDRBO, pairs ensemble surrogate models with a Wasserstein-ball model of distributional uncertainty, yielding a robust acquisition rule that stays computable and handles continuous contexts directly. They prove sublinear regret guarantees for it. Extensive experiments back the theory and show performance at the level of the best current methods.
arxiv-2605-07665:
Hugh Dance and three co-authors estimate counterfactual distributions, what outcomes would look like under an intervention, by reshaping observed data rather than modeling the target from scratch. That choice is motivated by tight links between the two distributions. Under standard assumptions they share support and tail behavior, stay close under weak confounding, and share any features untouched by confounders.

They build such a flow with flow matching and derive an efficient estimator using a new influence-function correction. An extension aims at minimal-energy flows, which are very simple targets between the observed and counterfactual cases. In tests their estimator beat existing debiased methods and sidestepped known failure modes of flow-based methods.
arxiv-2605-07765:
Elliot Pickens and two co-authors recruit a pretrained tabular foundation model, TabPFN, as the summary network for simulation-based Bayesian inference. In that workflow, a network must compress simulated observations into summaries informative enough for posterior estimation, and training one per problem is costly. TabPFN adapts in context and needs no training, making it a natural fixed summarizer.

Their recipe, PFN-NPE, feeds TabPFN summaries into a downstream inference head, by default a normalizing flow. It matched established posterior approximation methods and sometimes beat them. Probing showed the summaries preserve posterior location and marginal information well, though they can miss joint structure even when the marginals look right. The inference head stays modular and task-dependent.
arxiv-2605-07865:
Minjae Oh and four co-authors stabilize on-policy distillation, the training method where a student language model learns from a teacher on its own generated outputs. In practice the method is unstable because its single-sample gradient estimator has high variance, and good recipes are still immature. Their fix imports a classic tool from reinforcement learning: a control variate baseline.

The neat part is the value function: it has a closed form as the per-token negative reverse KL divergence between student and teacher. It is already available from the forward pass, so no extra critic is needed. Subtracting it keeps gradients unbiased while cutting variance. Across math and science reasoning benchmarks, their vOPD beat plain distillation and matched the expensive full-vocabulary baseline at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2605-07965:
Alex Markowitz and fourteen co-authors follow a Seyfert galaxy caught changing its look. X-ray monitoring with eROSITA showed the soft X-ray flux of HE 1237-2252 crashing by a factor of seventeen within eighteen months. Their follow-up campaign caught the recovery, watching each accretion component respond as the feeding rate climbed back sevenfold over three years.

The galaxy's spectral subtype swung from about 1.0 to 1.8 at the dip and back within three months of recovery, with the broad hydrogen line flux changing several-fold each way. The line profile splits into a virialized broad component and a double-peaked disk component that grows more prominent as the continuum rises. With no sign of obscuration, the team reads the episode as an intrinsic pause in accretion, perhaps fronts moving through the disk.
arxiv-2605-08065:
Ali Pazarci, Nadir Ghazanfari, and Ilmar Gahramanov work out the Hamiltonian form of a supersymmetric Korteweg-de Vries system. The system is constrained, much like its classical twin. It has a Lagrangian form only for one set value of its free parameter.

That Lagrangian is degenerate, so the team uses the Dirac-Bergmann method to find all first and second constraints. They build the total Hamiltonian. One striking point stands out: the rules for staying consistent add a nonlocal term to the energy density. The Hamilton rules then give back the full system, part by part.
arxiv-2605-08265:
Sri Surya Pravallika Ajjarapu and S. M. Mallikarjunaiah move crack checks beyond simple masks. Vision systems report a crack as a plain black-and-white region. That shows where the damage is. It does not tell an engineer what the crack looks like. Crews need the centerline shape. They need to know where cracks branch and meet. They also need signs of how bad the damage is.

Their CrackMorph-XAI-Net framework turns crack photos into structured outputs in four stages. First it pulls out a skeleton that keeps the crack's true shape. Next it finds junctions with Gaussian heatmap regression. Then it computes shape measures. Last it scores severity. Each stage gives a number a person can check by eye.
arxiv-2605-08365:
Vahidullah Tac, Aeneas Koosis, and Ellen Kuhl show that texture alone can drive how much people like a burger, using patties designed with artificial intelligence. The team paired a blind tasting with one hundred one participants against mechanical texture profile measurements for six burgers.

The lineup mixed AI-generated alternative protein patties with animal, plant, mushroom, and hybrid patties and a classic Big Mac. Animal burgers held a distinct sensory-mechanical zone tied to firm, fatty, and holds-together impressions. Mushroom patties skewed springy and gummy, while plant patties read as dry, brittle, and crumbly, in protein-dependent ways. The findings give product designers measurable texture targets linked to liking.
arxiv-2605-08465:
Liang Dai, Junwu Huang, Weichen Winston Yin, Rui Zhou, and coauthors add radio polarization to the measurement of cosmic shear. Cosmic shear is the tiny distortion of galaxy shapes by gravity. The total polarization of a spiral galaxy traces its true orientation. It can expose the intrinsic shape that lensing measurements must subtract.

The authors build a statistical model of shape and polarization. They are joint Gaussian variables. Their covariance measures alignment quality. Maximizing the likelihood gives estimators that recover three things at once. They recover shear, intrinsic alignment, and line-of-sight polarization rotation. The estimators are unbiased with minimal variance to first order. They stay reliable with few galaxies or weak alignment.
arxiv-2605-08565:
Clemens Schaefer and Gil Tabak investigate a puzzle in shrinking language models to very low precision number formats. Smaller blocks should cut error, yet a recent report showed quality getting worse as blocks shrink under a common scaling rule. The authors trace the fault to values clustering near their block peak, which clashes with coarse scaling numbers that can sink to zero.

Stopping that sink to zero helps, and a flexible scale choice method called four over six resolves much of the puzzle. A brute force search confirms error truly falls with finer blocks when scales are chosen well. Chip and software designers learn that format and scaling must be planned together.
arxiv-2605-08765:
Renjie Gu, Jiazhen Du, Yihua Zhang, and Sijia Liu show that models taught to forget can also learn to lie. Unlearning aims to strip harmful training data while keeping general usefulness, yet current methods often hallucinate, emit garbled tokens, or answer inconsistently about what was removed. The authors define unlearning honesty formally: keep utility and candor on retained knowledge, forget effectively, and admit limits on forgotten topics.

Nine methods across three families all fail their new honesty metrics. Their fix, ReVa, realigns internal representations so models refuse forgotten questions far more reliably, nearly doubling the best rival after two dialogue rounds, while also improving candor on retained material. Safe forgetting needs honesty, not just erasure.
arxiv-2605-08865: Qiyu Yang and Shengbo Zhao prove floor results, called Omega results, for Dirichlet L-functions. These functions sit at the core of number theory. They stretch the Riemann zeta function to steps in a fixed stride. With the resonance trick, which pumps up a function's large values with a tuned mate, they show the functions must reach set sizes. The work takes past results, among them the first author's 2024 work, a step on.
arxiv-2605-09065:
Rajalaxmi Rajagopalan and Romit Roy Choudhury generate scene graphs from plain text: structured maps that name the objects in a scene and how they relate. Such graphs can steer image generation toward faithful layouts, but people supply words, not graphs, so the graphs must be built automatically.

Earlier diffusion methods for graphs, proven on molecules and circuits, ignore the layered dependencies among objects, edges, and relations in a scene. The authors build a discrete diffusion model that respects this hierarchy and separates structure from meaning during generation. At use time it samples graphs matched to the text without extra training. Their graphs beat rivals on standard measures and led image generators to follow multi-object prompts more closely.
arxiv-2605-09165:
Ryan Lee, working with Jacob Biloki, Edward J Hu, and Jonathan May, examines looped language models, which reuse the same transformer layers again and again to save memory. Their 2026 study asks why these models scale worse than standard ones with unique layers. Comparing dense and mixture-of-experts designs, with and without looping, they trace the gap to how expert routing changes between passes.

In looped mixture models, different experts fire on each pass through shared layers, restoring expressive power without new parameters, and those models scale better than the standard baseline. Dense looped models do not share that gain. The authors also find loop boundaries make natural early exit points, since outputs settle earlier there. Their direction is clear: pair looping with sparse experts and early exits to gain memory and inference savings with little loss in quality.
arxiv-2605-09365:
Singh and two colleagues argue against stretching language models to cover every enterprise task. They take the position that enterprise work is mostly fixed, ordered, and knowledge-driven, under strict cost, latency, and reliability limits.

Running large models directly, or shrinking them into smaller ones, wastes effort, breaks down, and fits enterprise task structures poorly. Finite-capacity models cannot fully hold the breadth of knowledge these tasks require, the authors say. Instead, language models should serve as front ends rather than monolithic engines, with knowledge and computation moved out into dedicated parts, gaining reliability, scale, and a clear view. In the proposed split of labour, language models handle fixed-form extraction in fixed workflows, while computation and storage go to knowledge bases and symbolic steps. The authors show this modular setup is more reliable and easier to keep up than monolithic frameworks.
arxiv-2605-09765:
Dong and two colleagues rethought how medical AI should learn from digital health records, where labels are messy by nature. Billing codes, rough phenotypes, and patchy notes make guidance weak, noisy, and tied to each hospital. Standard record models still treat those labels as ground truth. WISTERIA instead treats each label as a noisy glimpse of a hidden medical state.

The framework builds several weak label sources and forces agreement across the label patterns they imply, a quiet denoising step that recovers real medical structure from disagreeing labelers. Ontology-aware shaping adds meaning-based structure to the label space. WISTERIA improved prediction scores across standard record tests, resisted label noise, and transferred better across hospitals than sequence-based pretraining.
arxiv-2605-10265:
Karim K. Alaa El-Din, Antonius v. Strachwitz, and Sam M. Vinko tackle a scaling problem in quantum chemistry. Density functional theory is the workhorse of the field, but its exchange-correlation term, which encodes many-body quantum effects beyond a mean-field picture, must be approximated. Machine-learned versions can handle strongly correlated systems yet scale poorly, limiting their use. Their 2026 paper proposes a cheaper non-local alternative.

The new approximation uses an expander graph transformer ansatz, a network design built on expander graphs, and scales linearly with system size rather than quadratically or worse. It recovers the correct hydrogen molecule dissociation curve in the strongly correlated regime, where bonds stretch and electrons correlate strongly. Results on planar H4 also look promising, a system where even top-tier coupled-cluster methods fail. The path opens toward accurate machine-learned functionals cheap enough to deploy at scale.
arxiv-2605-10665:
Julien Bouquiaux and co-authors clarify the atomic-scale setting of europium sources in the store-bought green phosphor beta-SiAlON:Eu, whose precise structure had stayed elusive. They combine a basic excited-state method, force-constant placing for big cells up to 3501 atoms, and Huang-Rhys theory, with Monte Carlo search to pick typical low-energy structures across aluminium-oxygen amounts.

For the lowest-energy structure at low amount, their computed glow spectrum matches the lab peaks at 6 kelvin with excellent match in spots and strengths. It validates a model with ninefold nitrogen links of europium and aluminium, oxygen, and europium confined to one crystal plane. Electron-phonon links proves weak, with a robust phonon mark across arrangements, explaining why resolved phonon copies persist as amounts rise. Rising amounts' observed red shift is explained through zero-phonon line trends, modest link growth, and greater layout variety.
arxiv-2605-10965:
D. Revanth Kumar and Santosh Kumar Yadav test a dark-energy model in curved spacetime against current sky surveys. They fit the model to Hubble data from cosmic clocks, supernova brightness data, and galaxy-clustering data, plus machine-made reconstructions of those sets.

Raw data favor a slightly open universe, while rebuilt data flip the curvature sign toward a closed universe, showing how much curvature answers depend on rebuilding. The fitted values also drift away from the standard Lambda-CDM picture under rebuilding. Model-comparison scores then weigh the framework's trustworthiness. Cosmologists get a cautionary measure of how rebuilding choices can move the universe's shape.
arxiv-2605-11165:
Ben Rachmut and four colleagues introduce COSMOS, a model-agnostic framework for personalized federated learning with clustered server models and pseudo-label-only communication. Federated learning in mixed settings struggles because client models differ in both design and data spread, and prior routes rarely handle both kinds of mix at once.

Clients train local models and predict on public data. The server groups clients by prediction similarity, trains a group-specific model per group using its own compute, and distills results back to clients. The paper gives the first theory showing distillation from learned group models can yield exponential personalization risk contraction, beyond convergence-to-stationarity guarantees. Tests across benchmarks show COSMOS beating all model-agnostic federated baselines while staying competitive with top personalized methods. Federated learning builders get server-side personalization without sharing model weights or raw data.
arxiv-2605-11365: Drago Plecko formalizes causal fairness for generative AI. Such models sample from arbitrary conditionals, so they build their own beliefs about all causal mechanisms. Standard machine learning, by contrast, uses one predictive function. Plecko unifies both settings under one theoretical framework. He derives decomposition results that quantify fairness impacts along causal pathways and through replacement of real-world mechanisms by model mechanisms. He gives identification conditions, efficient estimators, and an analysis of racial and gender bias in large language models.
arxiv-2605-11465: Liu and three colleagues generalize the Tamo-Barg construction of optimal locally recoverable codes, used in distributed and cloud storage. The classical construction rests on good polynomials. The team introduces good rational functions and a broader framework for optimal codes. They study attainable lengths with function field and Galois theory, counting totally split rational places. Exact formulas, sharp bounds and explicit constructions in Galois and non-Galois settings yield codes longer than good polynomials of the same degree allow.
arxiv-2605-11565: Yamauchi, Katayama and Tanahashi study ringing in analog black-white holes built from SNAIL traveling-wave parametric amplifiers. The circuit motion follows Korteweg-de Vries equations with soliton waves. A soliton slows the probe field, creating the causal shape of analog event horizons. The authors derive the probe field's master equation and show no normalizable negative modes via supersymmetric quantum mechanics. They also give the first quasi-normal mode study of this system. From the mode rates they pin down when nonlinear spread takes effect and how ringdown is excited.
arxiv-2605-11665: Jin and ten others present Nautilus, turning one prompt into robot learning workflows. Robot learning is split across policies, benchmarks and robots, with tangled builds making porting hard. General coding agents bridge some setups but lack robot priors and checks. Nautilus takes prompts like test policy A on benchmark B and gives reruns, tests and use. It offers skill sets with mined robot priors and typed contracts among policies, sims and robots, and checked coding at each step. It auto-makes links, widening cross-checks without glue code.
arxiv-2605-11965: Y. Itoh reports the finite-temperature staggered spin susceptibility at a two-dimensional antiferromagnetic quantum critical point. Within self-consistent renormalization theory, he finds the mode-mode coupling value 0.1 separates two regimes: weak coupling yields a Curie law, while strong coupling yields Curie-Weiss or power-law behavior. No Curie-Weiss temperature, in turn, can mark the critical point in weakly coupled systems, a classification he applies to several itinerant layered antiferromagnets.
arxiv-2605-12165: Jose Ignacio Robledo and five colleagues model neutron source distributions with probabilistic generative models. Estimation starts from a Monte Carlo particle list, needed only while training; once learned, the model samples freely, fast, and with no memory cost. They test four model types: variational autoencoders, normalizing flows, adversarial networks, and denoising diffusion models. Results show source distributions can be modeled this way, opening the door to further work, and the authors weigh each approach against existing estimation methods.
arxiv-2605-12265: Sam Martin and Fabien Roger ask whether multi-task training helps monitors on new domains. Prompted models classify with little data, but miss the robustness and gains of fine-tuning. Training on tasks, each with its own prompt, partly generalizes to adjacent domains, lifting unseen scores. Yet edge cases break prompt following, such as when the prompt changes while the domain stays the same. Mixing classification training with instruction training keeps the gains while fixing most failures, and no-thinking training even generalizes to with-thinking classification and summarization.
arxiv-2605-12565: Morasso and three colleagues red-team language models through attacker personas, not generic prompts. Existing automated red-teaming often misses attacks hinging on attacker identity, framing and multi-turn tactics, understating real risk. Their PCAP method conditions search on personas and strategy cards, running parallel persona-conditioned beam searches to find diverse, transferable jailbreaks. The approach works with any underlying search algorithm and sharply raises attack success and prompt diversity, lifting success on GPT-OSS 120B from about fifty-eight percent to about ninety-seven percent.
