arxiv-2605-12765: Turani and nine colleagues make models forget chosen content at use time. Removal by retraining is costly, hard to audit, and undone by quantization. Their GUARD-IT stores doomed content as activation ways. At use time, a matching gate routes queries, using a norm-safe turn of the residual stream for matches. Other queries pass as is. It works across model kinds. On TOFU, it cuts memory in every Llama setup without collapse.
arxiv-2605-12865: Burcroff and Neville prove the asymptotic sign coherence conjecture almost always for skew-symmetric cluster algebras of any rank. For c-vectors, that claim is a basic result for such algebras with principal coefficients. The conjecture says the signs should eventually line up along generic infinite mutation sequences. They show random mutation of any quiver yields c-vectors with matching signs almost surely, and settle the claim fully for many quiver groups via brog quivers.
arxiv-2605-12965: Ma and four co-authors present U-HNO, a U-shaped hybrid neural operator for partial differential equations with both smooth global motion and sharp local features like shocks. Its Sparse-Point Adaptive Routing picks, at each point, whether a global Fourier branch or a local Gaussian branch should dominate, based on local contrast. Across PDEBench tasks from Burgers to Navier-Stokes it tops rollout accuracy on most tasks. The largest gains come where sharp features dominate.
arxiv-2605-13165: Xu and five colleagues built STOP, a way to trim long reasoning chains for scarce training data. It starts from traces the model makes itself. Then it splits each trace into nodes, labels them by type, and links them into a reasoning tree. A rule called ECN keeps only the shortest opening stretch ending at the first node with a right answer. In low-data fine-tuning on GSM8K, Math 500, and AIME 2024, the method cut output tokens by between 19.4% and 42.4% while keeping scores largely intact.
arxiv-2605-13265: Mert Cihangiroglu and colleagues present LightSplit, a privacy guard for split learning between clients and a server. Raw activations at the split point cost bandwidth and leak data to reconstruction attacks. A fixed orthogonal random projection squeezes activations before sending, acting as a bottleneck that drops sample specific detail. At up to 32 fold compression it keeps at least 94 percent accuracy on several image and tabular tasks. The strongest co trained attack loses most of its reconstruction power.
arxiv-2605-13365: Bogdan introduces the Geno-Synthetic Algorithm, a coevolutionary optimizer for mixed type design problems. Real designs mix integers, reals, booleans, categories, complex values and embeddings, which flat chromosomes mangle with rounding and repair. GSA splits genes by type, evolves each family with native operators, and assembles phenotypes for joint scoring. It is the only tested method handling complex and embedding genes, and it matches flattened differential evolution on a mixed integer suite at large budgets.
arxiv-2605-13565: Zekai Zhang and twenty-nine colleagues offer Qwen-Image-VAE-2.0, a family of high-compression variational autoencoders with strong reconstruction and spread. To ease training in high-dimensional latent space, they use a strong semantic matching plan making latent space ready for diffusion work. Tests on public sets, plus a new OmniDoc-TokenBench for text-rich texts, show state-of-the-art rebuilds in general and text-rich domains at high compression. Downstream transformer tests show better diffusability and faster training.
arxiv-2605-13665: Amir Hossain Raj, Dibyendu Das and Xuesu Xiao introduce a reinforcement learning framework for four-legged robots crossing narrow tunnels. Existing methods struggle with rigid gaits, limited flex for varied geometries, and simple setting guesses. Their approach mixes generated settings with policy distillation, using a teacher-student paradigm where expert policies on generated tunnels transfer knowledge to one student policy. That removes any need for complex reward shaping during end-to-end training. Tests in simulation and the real world show steady crossing where usual methods fail.
arxiv-2605-13865: Akihiko Ikeda and five colleagues examine by math the link between a repeat-pulse magnet coil's sizes and its thrift, assuming tiny coil heating. They work out how peak magnet field, energy loss, pulse length, form factor, drag and peak current depend on coil shape. They find smaller coils give more pulses and more intense magnetic fields under a given setup.
arxiv-2605-13965: Herdeiro, Radu, Costa Filho and Sanchis-Gual build new sets of smooth, far-flat solitons in the Einstein-Proca model, grown from flat-space Proca multipoles. Still sets split by multipole rank into electric kinds, which hold round Proca stars at rank zero, and magnetic kinds, which start at rank one with no round twin. Hybrid sets blend electric and magnetic multipoles in a non-linear mix. They bear local spin density but no total spin, and some lack north-south mirror symmetry.
arxiv-2605-14065: Shalchi studies exponential integrators and the Boris integrator for charged bits moving through magnetic turbulence. Such motion matters for fast bits in magnetized plasma, and test-particle runs explore it by building a turbulent field and solving the Newton-Lorentz equation step by step. The paper derives both the Rodrigues scheme and the famous Boris integrator step by step from exponential integrators. When the field is rebuilt fresh at each step, the two perform much alike overall, though theory favors Rodrigues for exactness.
arxiv-2605-14165: Hasan, Islam and Hossain present DSTAN-Med to spot false data injection attacks on Internet-of-Medical-Things sensor streams. Such attacks falsify vital signs in transit, endangering patients and beating monitors with no cyber-physical anomaly checks. Existing deep learning models blend inter-sensor spatial correlations with time links in one shared latent space, so the distinct spatial and time attack marks stay tangled. DSTAN-Med instead routes sensor windows through independent sensor-wise and time-wise attention pathways, with physiological plausibility filtering to bar impossible attack patterns.
arxiv-2605-14365: Choi and colleagues propose LoMETab, a rank-r generalisation of multiplicative ensembles for tabular deep learning. LoMETab lifts rank-1 BatchEnsemble and TabM modulation to a rank-r Hadamard family, with member weights built from weights plus low-rank factors. Two axes emerge, rank and start scale, and for rank at least two the family widens the rank-1 hypothesis class. In tests, added room shows as diversity, with rank and scale steering pairwise spread varying hugely and output-level splits too. Scores over the grid are tied to the dataset.
arxiv-2605-14465: Kwok and colleagues argue multi-step table reasoning fails without a clear cell-grounding contract between planning and execution. Older methods force a left-to-right planner factorisation at odds with permutation invariance, and score states by content alone. A pilot study shows diffusion models produce more order-stable cell attention than autoregressive models. The team presents TABALIGN, pairing a diffusion planner that turns plans into cell masks with TABATTN, a checker scoring steps by mask overlap. Across eight benchmarks, TABALIGN beats the strongest baseline by 15.76 percentage points on accuracy.
arxiv-2605-14565: Korley proposes a Bayesian longitudinal spatial normative model for mapping individual brain deviations against a reference population. Unlike cross-sectional models that treat regions independently, it jointly captures within-person change over time and spatially structured deviations as a latent process with an explicit posterior. Applied to OASIS-3 MRI scans, it is claimed to cut error by about fifty-four percent against a cross-sectional model and forty-five against a non-spatial longitudinal one.
arxiv-2605-14865: Madvil and team present a holistic framework for evaluating AI agents and their failures. Outcome metrics report success or failure with no explanation why, and process-level approaches struggle to tie failure types to precise locations in long traces. The framework pairs top-down diagnosis with bottom-up span-level scoring, decomposing analysis into independent per-span assessments with rationales. On TRAIL, state-of-the-art results are claimed on GAIA and SWE-Bench, with gains up to thirty-eight percent on category F1 and severalfold gains on localisation.
arxiv-2605-15165: Andrew Daw, Chloe Pache, and Angela Zhou model access failures in SNAP, the food-assistance program, as a queueing problem. In a Missouri case, call-center congestion made nearly half of denials process-based. Applicants could not complete needed interviews, a failing a judge ruled a due-process violation. Standard Erlang-A staffing guidance ignores redials and abandonment, through which backlogs breed further crowding, and therefore understaffs. Their framework adds those dynamics, diagnosing emergent chance as a system-level property rather than an explicit rule.
arxiv-2605-15665: Keshava Chaitanya and Jahnavi Gundakaram treat enterprise prompt work as a reliability job, not a one-off writing task. Deployed models drift in silence over time. Their PRISM loop writes test cases from plain-language needs, plays full multi-turn chats, grades pass or fail, finds fault roots, and mends prompts by surgery. It repeats till all tests pass and reruns each day. Across 35 enterprise agents over three weeks it cut median writing time from two days to under thirty minutes. It hit 99 percent production reliability.
arxiv-2605-15865: Junaid Baber and four colleagues test whether open language models can build models that fit domain specific languages from plain text, using only few-shot prompts with no fine-tuning. They grade 39 models from 0.5B to 32B parameters on syntax, meaning and cross-model link consistency, building both user interface and data models from scratch. Several small models, such as gemma3:12b and mistral:7b-instruct, neared or matched much larger models. The results back smaller open models as a cheap, deployable choice over closed models for grammar-conformant generation.
arxiv-2605-15965: Peter Clapham, Lisa Bonheme and Marek Grzes classify the polarised regime of VAEs by mean entropy. Latent variables split into active, passive and mixed sets, but existing active-dimension criteria need a Gaussian prior, limiting use. The authors link this entropy to KL minimization via entropy-variance bounds and Bonheme's active/passive rules. Mean entropy alone cannot separate active from mixed dimensions without variance. Tests show the criterion recovers such a regime across beta-VAEs, identifiable VAEs and L2-regularised models, and passive slots can improve later tasks when scaled.
arxiv-2605-16165: Lu and Armour tackle modality clashes in autoregressive multimodal training, where image making and text understanding fight and destabilize learning. Simple optimizers like AdamW suffer when gradients differ across modalities. Their ML-FOP-SOAP framework adds multi-level variance correction, with a Fisher-orthogonal projection that damps variance-driven clashes. On Janus and Emu3 it improved sample efficiency by up to 1.4-fold and wall-clock speed by up to 1.5-fold over AdamW, with stable training at batch size 8,192.
arxiv-2605-16265: Aravind presents AgentWall, a runtime safety layer for local AI agents. Agents that run shell commands, edit files, call APIs, and browse the web can cause instant harm if misled, yet most safety work stops at model tuning and input filters. It catches every planned action, checks it against a clear written policy, needs human ok for risky steps, and logs a full trail for audit and replay. It reached 92.9 percent policy hit rate with sub-ms cost across 14 benchmark tests.
arxiv-2605-16565: Wong and three colleagues build Skim, a 2026 framework for speculative execution that lets web agents skip heavyweight steps on routine sites. An offline profiler first learns each site's stable URL patterns, answer formats, and task trajectories. Skim then matches a query to a template, synthesizes the destination address, and pulls the answer with a compact model behind a verifier. Across standard benchmarks with three agent backbones, median per-task cost fell by a factor of 1.9 in their tests. In the same tests, latency fell 33.4%, with no accuracy loss.
arxiv-2605-16865: Liu and colleagues propose MixSD, a teacher-free approach for knowledge injection into language models without fine-tuning forgetting. Fine-tuning targets from humans or outside systems diverge from the model's distribution, forcing imitation of unlikely sequences. MixSD builds supervision from mixed tokens from two base-model conditionals: one conditional seeing the injected fact in context, and a naive conditional reflecting the prior. The mixed sequences preserve signal while staying close to the distribution. Across settings, MixSD keeps 100% of held-out capability with high accuracy, while standard fine-tuning keeps 1%.
arxiv-2605-16965: Prabhakar and Melnik calculate how strain affects electrical conductivity in edge-modified graphene nanoribbons. Pristine unstrained armchair ribbons with seven zigzag edges do not conduct, but strain makes them conductive across a wide energy range from infrared to visible to ultraviolet light. Boron-doped and vacancy variants are already metallic, showing non-vanishing conductivity across the same range with or without strain. Strain also shifts Berry curvature: fermions spread across the Brillouin zone in unstrained semiconducting ribbons but localise near the centre point when strained.
arxiv-2605-17165: Premi Adhikari studies how extra training goals affect small-scale Video-JEPA, a self-supervised system that learns video representations by predicting masked content. Testing 18 auxiliary objectives across two pretraining mixes, he finds gains on one skill often cost another. A factorized design splitting appearance from motion improves image and temporal scores while nearly holding fine-grained motion performance.
arxiv-2605-17265: Hu and colleagues expose a blind spot in molecular property prediction: models can look strong overall yet fail where similar molecules differ sharply in behavior, known as property cliffs. Their CliffSplit protocol builds test cases that stress those cliff zones, while CliffLoss, a training-only fix, shrinks the cliff-to-smooth error gap. Tests show cliff zones carry at least 15 percent higher error, and the fix cuts the gap by up to 30 percent.
arxiv-2605-17565: Tang tests whether chess-trained language models generalize or merely memorize, training KinGPT, a 25-million-parameter character-level model, only on position-best-move pairs. KinGPT beats far larger ChessGPT and C1-4B models on puzzle suites, yet Tang argues benchmark success largely reflects pattern-matching rather than rule understanding. Pairing a general model with an external verifier lifts RedPajama 3B's best-move accuracy from 1.2 to 21.2 percent, offering a cheaper flexible alternative to chess-specific fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-17765: Yuanyun Zhang and Shi Li say health models mix quite distinct forces in one shared code space. Illness depth, care strength, how data get watched, and clinic work flow all land in the same slots. Their AURORA plan splits codes into orthogonal subspaces, one per context, and trains each part to stay true to itself. In clinic forecast and search tests, it beats reconstruction, contrastive, and self-distillation baselines, while keeping its parts more distinct and holding up when clinics change.
arxiv-2605-17865: Siddharth Somasundaram and four colleagues bring hidden-object imaging to consumer LiDAR. Research LiDARs can image around corners, but consumer sensors suffer weak lasers, coarse resolution, and motion blur. Inspired by burst photography and synthetic aperture radar, the team fuses many frames into one measurement model. Their motion-induced aperture sampling model unifies object shape, object motion, and camera motion. On smartphone-grade LiDAR they show 3D reconstruction, object tracking, and camera localization from hidden objects, with hardware under 100 dollars and no extra setup.
arxiv-2605-17965: Md Afif Al Mamun and Gias Uddin present BLAgent, an agentic retrieval framework for file-level bug localization. BLAgent combines structure-aware repository encoding, AST chunking with paths, query transformation from two viewpoints, and two-phase agentic reranking with symbol checks and evidence-grounded reasoning. Reasoning stays bounded to a filtered set. On SWE-bench-Lite it tops 78% top accuracy with open-source models and 86% with a closed model, at over 18 times lower cost than the baseline.
arxiv-2605-18465: David Cheban and Andrei Sultan study, in a 2026 paper, finite-dimensional approximations of nonautonomous lattice dynamical systems. They show the models are uniformly dissipative, never blowing up. They also establish upper semi-continuous convergence of the models' attractors. The work covers systems in a lattice coupling each site to its neighbors with damping, nonlinear forcing, and time-dependent inputs over time.
arxiv-2605-18765: Shuai Li and four co-authors propose STAR, a 2026 retriever for graph generation. Graph retrieval methods often ignore sparse semantics in graphs, producing two biases. STAR pairs token-level interaction learning against Semantic Shortcut Bias with path-weighted contrastive learning against Long-Tail Path Bias. Cross-attention and hard path mining model query and path jointly; tail-adaptive weighting optimizes training. Across benchmarks, STAR beats baselines by retrieval gains of 1 point 8 percent and answering gains of 2 point 2 percent.
arxiv-2605-18865: Yuxin Ren and three colleagues replace attention with simpler sequential modules by following sparsity. Self-attention costs grow with the square of token count, yet naive replacement loses accuracy, above all at larger scales. The authors find layers differ in sparsity, so some layer jobs can be swapped for far simpler modules without loss. Layer-wise distillation tests on vision transformers show sparser layers swap with smaller drops, and guided sparsity shrinks the student-teacher gap. The result cuts size and latency for attention replacement.
arxiv-2605-18965: Nathan Burwig and Damien Easson use an affine version of the averaged null energy condition to sort complete cosmologies by shape. They prove non-static flat or open FRW spacetimes cannot both stay complete and meet ANEC, since a negative bulk term grows without bound over repeated cycles. Closed geometry escapes this block, since positive curvature can support complete eternal nonsingular cosmologies with ordinary matter. The authors give explicit closed-universe scalar-field models, and positive curvature would bias flat-model reconstructions by only a percent.
arxiv-2605-19265: Dawei Tian and colleagues tackle test cases that go stale as software changes fast under continuous delivery. Current language-model updaters chase runnable code and line coverage, yet they neglect whether assertions still catch faults. Their MuMuTestUp system splits the job across three agents covering mutation strength, uncovered lines and branches, and semantic retrieval for invented queries. Built on a 571-sample pull-request set from ten Java projects, it is tested with both open and closed leading models.
arxiv-2605-19365: Ravishka Rathnasuriya and Wei Yang improve code models without retraining them, by adapting inputs on the fly instead. Retraining, redesigning, or re-prompting costs heavily in labels, compute, and redeployment, and often generalizes poorly across tasks. Their two-stage method first flags inputs likely to mislead the model, then reshapes those inputs with operations that preserve syntax and meaning to better fit what the model learned. Across varied code-understanding tasks it cuts mispredictions, offering a cheap and scalable route for high-stakes software work.
arxiv-2605-19565: Ashton and team release HiLiftAeroML, the first open high-fidelity dataset for high-lift aircraft aerodynamics. It holds 1,800 simulations across 180 variants of the NASA Common Research Model high-lift configuration at ten angles, 4 to 22 degrees. Each case uses GPU-accelerated large-eddy simulation on grids of 300 to 500 million cells, spanning attached, separated and stalled flow. Wind-tunnel comparisons show good agreement on loads and pressures, and baselines reconstruct fields well except for high-angle separated flow and scarce-data training.
arxiv-2605-19665: Li and team propose CriterAlign, a criterion-centric framework for pairwise code preference prediction. Pairwise human preference prediction drives code-generation evaluation, where quality hinges on task trade-offs beyond correctness. Existing rubric judges score each response alone and compare summed scores, a pointwise design that can trail a monolithic judge. CriterAlign makes direct criterion-level pairwise judgments, with tie-driven tuning, swap-consistency checks and final merge, plus Human-Preference-Aligned Guidance from cases. On BigCode it lifts a Qwen2.5-VL-32B judge from 60 point 4 to 66 point 3 percent.
arxiv-2605-19765: Seikavandi and colleagues release GroupAffect-4, a dataset of forty people in ten four-person groups. The groups tackle pooling, negotiation, idea generation and a public-goods game together. Each person wears body sensors and eye-tracking glasses with a close microphone, alongside self-reports, outcomes and personality scores on a shared clock. Coverage tops ninety-one percent for body signals and ninety-eight for eye tracking, and a check validates the negotiation block. Fifteen test targets span single people, pairs and groups, with leave-one-group-out baselines included.
arxiv-2605-19965: Bariscan Bozkurt and three co-workers derive a neural method for blind source separation that uses only local learning rules. Their Predictive Entropy Maximization approach approximates an entropy measure with an objective whose parts are easy to interpret. Feedforward links follow an error-driven rule that dendrites could realise, while lateral inhibitory links learn by local Hebbian plasticity and output nonlinearities enforce source-domain limits. The method stays robust as source correlation and observation noise grow, and it rivals exact determinant-based baselines.
arxiv-2605-20365: Palaisti and Pasini set out a theory of ramification for finite covers of knot exteriors. For a knot group and a finite-index subgroup, they define inertia subgroups for loops around the knot and take their normal closure as the global ramification subgroup. Finite quotients give a largest unramified quotient, and profinite completions keep inertia and ramification intact under maps that preserve loop structure. Unramified cohomology classes are then exactly those that vanish on all inertia subgroups, as in Galois theory.
arxiv-2605-20865: Deokgyu Yoon and six colleagues propose multi-step likelihood-ratio correction for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Widely used PPO surrogate goals are fundamentally local, relying on a local reading of the exact policy gradient goal. That approximation improves stability by cutting variance from importance sampling, a known trick. Yet it introduces structural bias that trust-region mechanisms must control. Their N-step forward trace augments the PPO surrogate using the summed likelihood ratio of the next N minus one tokens.
arxiv-2605-21065: Herbi Dreiner and three colleagues study the single photon signature of a light long-lived neutralino at remote LHC detectors. They investigate light long-lived neutralinos in R-parity violating supersymmetric models, focusing on proposed remote detectors ANUBIS, CODEX-b, FACET, FASER, FASER2, MAPP, MAPP2, and MATHUSLA. Production is assumed at ATLAS or CMS points via rare scalar meson decays induced by R-parity violating couplings. They study six benchmark scenarios in which the main neutralino decay is to a photon plus a neutrino.
arxiv-2605-21165: Leyou Xu and Bo Zhou answer a question about graphs whose vertices each lie on cycles of every length. Li and Zhan had shown that every 2-connected graph of a certain type with at least seven vertices holds a pancyclic edge, one lying on cycles of all lengths. Zhan asked whether some connectivity level forces such an edge in all vertex-pancyclic graphs. Xu and Zhou show that for every positive integer k, a k-connected vertex-pancyclic graph with no pancyclic edge exists.
arxiv-2605-21265: Giorgio Cipolloni, László Erdős, and Oleksii Kolupaiev study log-determinants of leading principal minors of large non-Hermitian random matrices. They show these converge to a two-plus-one-dimensional Gaussian field. The field is logarithmically correlated for the parabolic distance, like the Edwards-Wilkinson class. The result links random matrix minors to a well-studied interface growth field.
arxiv-2605-21365: Riccardo Passeggeri, Rohan M. Shenoy, and Pengcheng Ye construct L-two over Wasserstein space for statistical analysis of optimal transport. Optimal transport gives a shape-based method for studying spaces of probability spreads, supplying tools for statistics, machine learning, and generative models. In applications, however, measures are almost never known exactly, calling for a theory accounting for data doubt. They lift old theory to random probability measures. The new space inherits the Riemannian structure of that space.
arxiv-2605-21565: Phuong-Anh Nguyen and co-authors use self-paced curriculum learning for modality balance in conversational emotion recognition. These approaches mixing words, faces, and voices have grown fast, yet mismatch and uneven learning limit good use of combined information. Their framework introduces a dual-level Difficulty Measurer capturing line-level and whole-chat challenges. The work targets chats where words, faces, and voices must be read as one. It aims to give each mode its fair share of weight.
arxiv-2605-21765: Emanuel Sommer and David Rügamer argue the time has come for sampling-based inference in Bayesian neural networks. Adoption has lagged amid misconceptions about feasibility and efficiency, yet sampling has now reached computational parity with optimization methods and stands poised to surpass them. Beyond better predictions through model averaging, sampling opens downstream tasks and insight into network landscapes. The authors call for work on two core problems: thorough exploration of the posterior landscape and high-fidelity distillation of posterior samples for efficient downstream use.
arxiv-2605-21965: Mehrdad Saberi, Keivan Rezaei, and Soheil Feizi present SpecHop, a method that speeds up multi-hop retrieval agents by speculating continuously. Such agents wait for tool outputs at each hop, so latency piles up, even though a faster model could guess the next steps. SpecHop runs speculative branches in parallel, committing correct ones as target tool outputs arrive and rolling back wrong ones, preserving accuracy. On retrieval-augmented multi-hop tasks it nears oracle latency gains and cuts latency by up to 40 percent in some settings.
arxiv-2605-22365: Nguyen and colleagues study backdoor defence for time series forecasting, where poisoned data can plant hidden triggers. They test thirteen existing defences and find two root flaws. Tangled data thins channel signals, so filters fail to locate backdoors. Shifts in task form make poisoned and clean windows look alike in training loss. Their TimeGuard trains per channel from a trusted pool, grown by distance-based loss picks. Tests show poisoned-case scores about 1.96 times the leading baseline, with clean performance within 5 percent.
arxiv-2605-22465: Bleeck mimics the RAMPHO episodic buffer in silico to study listening with many talkers. Current enhancement tools tune for sound alone, ignoring masking costs. Across a signal-to-noise sweep, a meaning-keeping distractor is set against the Concentration Shield, whose phase pattern is scrambled. The test splits the cognitive cost of distraction from energetic decay. Destroying its meaning frees listeners from informational masking at high signal-to-noise ratios, but harms temporal glimpsing cues at low ratios.
arxiv-2605-22865: Aldridge offers a fast method for multi-dimensional matching markets. Here agents rank object features rather than full utilities. Singular value decomposition finds the main spread in feature space. Matching then becomes a near one-dimensional problem, done in N log N time. When data have low effective dimension, the method nearly tops Nash Social Welfare. It stays truthful and symmetric. Tests reached 99 percent of optimal welfare, thousands of times faster than direct solving.
arxiv-2605-23165: Aitha and Zakhor introduce a self-guided scouting pipeline where a vision-language model makes key choices guiding a standard robot control stack. At choice points the robot builds a mixed prompt from its map and imagery of open paths, or frontiers. The model reads this prompt to select the best frontier, swapping shape rules with scene thought. Tested across six indoor rooms, the approach improves map reach by up to 24 percent over methods. It has a design fitting any robot with sensors and wifi.
arxiv-2605-23265: Chakraborty and three coauthors study fairness in rank merging under the Spearman footrule, the L1 distance. Standard methods merging preference orders toward a consensus ranking may perpetuate underrepresentation. They address first computing a fair merged top-k ranking, presenting the first optimal method. Second, they consider fair full rank merging over all candidates. A 3-approximation is known, while an exact algorithm exists. They give a 2-approximation method for fair full rank merging, improving on the previous 3-approximation. Tests back their theoretical results.
arxiv-2605-23365: Kim and three colleagues cut the cost of diffusion-style policies in online reinforcement learning, where multi-step denoising slows every decision. Their method, score-based one-step MeanFlow policy optimization, builds its target velocity field straight from the Q-function through score estimation and a probability flow equation, steering probability toward high-value actions. Trained fully online, it tops locomotion tasks in a single generation step while sharply reducing both training and inference time.
arxiv-2605-23565: Brown and Young study goal generalization in sequential reinforcement learning, where agents often chase unintended goals outside training and no principled account of that drift exists. Across over 100 training pipelines and 250 new environments, they find salient features drive generalization and early-learned goals persist into later ones. Their latent policy gradients method simulates small latent variables during training to predict new behavior from training history. It predicts strongly, transfers to unseen pipeline types, and stays interpretable, showing pipeline dependence has capturable structure.
arxiv-2605-24965: Ibrahim Delibasoglu tests if big vision models work as ready-made feature extractors for facial deepfakes from unseen generators. Classic detectors collapse onto narrow artifact fingerprints of their training generators and fail on new manipulation tricks. The study freezes three backbones: a supervised macro-semantic model, a self-supervised geometric model, and a multi-teacher model. It probes them with simple linear heads on the DF40 benchmark. Foundation models keep strong skill on whole-face synthesis, yet localized face edits expose hard limits of linear probing.
arxiv-2605-25565: Mengyang Sun and colleagues strengthen low-rank expert mixtures by rotating experts, not just rescaling them. Standard mixture gates apply a single scalar weight to each chosen expert, capping how far adapters can specialize for varied knowledge. RotMoLE adds a rotation gate per selected expert, exploiting the low-rank structure to let experts specialize more fully, especially when few candidates exist. Tests on complex multi-task and multilingual training confirm the gain over scalar gating.
arxiv-2605-25665: Sengupta, Briggs and Myshakivskyi argue that judging AI-native software by single models, prompts or outputs misses production reality. Real delivery means software is made, checked, shipped and kept up for years. Their meta-engineering harness turns feature needs into clear contracts, routes tasks to role-specialized AI agents, and checks results with outside adversarial verification. It learns from misses by sorting them into classes, with outer-loop calibration. A rollout over 17 items across weeks, including a payments case study, exposed gaps in contracts and checks that drove fixes.
arxiv-2605-25765: Moon, Jun, Lee and Kim improve concept unlearning in diffusion models beyond fixed text embeddings. Existing closed-form methods use text alone, missing how concepts appear across states and layers. Probing cross-attention activations, they find activation-derived bases beat text-derived bases fivefold on held-out prompts. Their CASE method builds forget and retain subspaces from those activations. Those subspaces define a retain-constrained operator in attention weights, needing no gradient fine-tuning. Across ten concepts in four categories, CASE tops baselines on harmonic-mean score.
arxiv-2605-25865: Kaur studies Broken Object Level Authorization, the top-ranked API security flaw, in one of the first large-scale analyses. From 200 HackerOne disclosures, a three-criterion filter yields 107 classified reports. Of these, 84 count as confirmed cases, led by Action-Level Object and Direct Object Reference flaws. Tag-counting alone overstates the true signal, since about a fifth fall out of scope under strict criteria. It also finds vertical privilege failures and abuse of GraphQL Global IDs.
arxiv-2605-26165: Sakizli studies a clash in agentic retrieval systems: tool schemas eat context that retrieval also needs. With dozens to hundreds of tools, schemas can crowd out evidence. Fourteen models, 1.5 to 32 billion parameters plus a frontier API model, are tested on 6,566 calls. Tests use 28 tool definitions at three budgets: 8, 16 and 32 thousand tokens. Conservative tool-schema compression saves 44 to 50 percent of schema tokens. At eight thousand tokens, uncompressed JSON schemas overflow, collapsing exact-match scores near zero. Compressed schemas restore retrieval function with large gains.
arxiv-2605-26265: Tiziano Zanzarella and seven colleagues turn NuSTAR on the Sun during the 2020 minimum to hunt axions and axion-like particles. Such particles could form inside the Sun from thermal photons or electron and nucleon interactions, then turn to photons in its magnetic field. They set limits for light axions, near ten to the minus twenty-fourth for electrons and near ten to the minus nineteenth for nucleons, in inverse gigaelectron volts. These bounds beat ground-based limits, establishing solar X-rays as a powerful axion channel.
arxiv-2605-26465: Ramon G. Gonze and four colleagues compare local differential privacy schemes on principle through Quantitative Information Flow. Epsilon, the usual privacy parameter, bounds only worst-case distinguishability, while utility rankings ignore how schemes fare against varied foes. Modeling schemes as chance channels, the team uses refinement, or Blackwell ordering, to judge when one scheme beats another against every foe. Cases emerge where schemes once called optimal prove incomparable or strictly dominated. Formal treatment of seven leading schemes, from generalized randomized response to histogram encoding, bridges privacy and formal-methods work.
arxiv-2605-26865: Hatasa studies symmetry in the h-polynomials of edge rings of bipartite graphs. He proves that if the ring is pseudo-Gorenstein and the first and next-to-last coefficients match, then the ring is Gorenstein, so its h-polynomial reads the same forwards and backwards. The proof handles the 2-connected case via a tight-separation condition, then extends to all bipartite graphs by block decomposition, also building a minimal Gorenstein closure.
arxiv-2605-26965: Tian and nine colleagues study the baryonic Faber-Jackson relation and fundamental plane across eight orders of magnitude in mass, from dwarf galaxies to galaxy groups. Compiling 1,400 pressure-supported systems, they find both relations hinge on internal acceleration, shifting near a characteristic scale of about 1.2 times ten to the tenth meters per second squared. High-acceleration systems follow the Newtonian virial theorem, while low-acceleration systems follow the MOND version, with the external field effect playing only a secondary role.
arxiv-2605-27065: Glidewell uses the high-low method and wave-packet pruning to prove new small-cap split bounds for the moment curve in 4D. As a use, he proves a guess of Demeter on square-root cancellation of exponential sums tied to the moment curve in 4D. The result gives a range of square-root bounds. It links the Vinogradov mean value theorem in 3D with a result of Bourgain tied to beating the best-known estimate for the Lindelöf hypothesis.
arxiv-2605-27165: Spyridon Kakaroumpas and Stefanos Lappas prove a new Riesz-Kolmogorov compactness theorem for a broad class of function spaces. Their result extends compact results for multi-input operators to weighted variable Lebesgue spaces. It then gives new bounds for commutators, fractional integrals, and Fourier multipliers in those wider spaces. The proof builds on their earlier two-input case.
arxiv-2605-27565: Onur Eren Arpaci, Florian Kerschbaum, and Sujaya Maiyya present Cloak, an oblivious storage system that trades perfect uniformity for speed. Server traffic follows a fixed recentness-biased pattern, and real queries cover as much of that traffic as they can, exploiting temporal locality. The heuristic costs only performance, not security, reaching 165,000 operations per second on Netflix traces and 157,000 on Ethereum traces.
arxiv-2605-27765: Zehao Liu, Yuanpu Cao, Jinghui Chen, and Vasant Honavar restore the difficulty sweet spot in self-distillation for language model reasoning. Their SC-SDPO weights each question's loss by a pass-rate factor, adding difficulty awareness that plain SDPO lacks and inducing an implicit curriculum tracking model competence. The method improves over SDPO by about 3 to 4 points on one model and about 2 to 3 points on another, with stable training throughout.
arxiv-2605-28065: Diks and colleagues benchmark AI agents on long, end-to-end spatial biology, where claims must be recovered from raw measurements without prescribed methods. SpatialBench-Long spans twenty-four evaluations across cancers, organoids, and aging tissue, graded deterministically. Even the best model-harness pairs solved only eight of seventy-two runs, exposing a wide gap.
arxiv-2605-28165: Hanselle and colleagues unify robust learning methods, from distributionally robust optimization to Mixup and label smoothing, along explicit design axes. Their shared formulation reveals which methods duplicate each other, which yield genuinely distinct solutions, and how those relations shift with model and loss. A tunable training procedure then lets practitioners pick combinations that often beat the best single method.
arxiv-2605-28265: Ronen Gradwohl, Fengming Hu, and Rann Smorodinsky ask when persuasion holds up if the listener's tastes stay unknown. They show worst-case choice, regret choice, and tie-break toughness mean the same thing, and that toughness holds in most cases. The match tidies a persuasion corner where planner and sender gaps once looked apart.
arxiv-2605-28365: Pauline Bourigault and four colleagues examine whether Lean, a proof-checking language, can reliably judge plain-language mathematics answers. On a 500-problem set, proof success predicted correctness well only when coverage was high, and a hand check found fewer than half of sampled proofs faithful. Their COVCAL selector certifies accepted answers with a bounded risk or abstains, but only becomes workable once a specialized prover raises coverage enough.
arxiv-2605-28565: Yongsik Seo and four colleagues trace citation failures in search-augmented language models with CITETRACE, a dataset covering the full chain from query through source to answer. It pairs 11,200 real queries from 28 groups with 112,000 replies from ten models, yielding over 761,000 usable pairs. Each one is scored on intent-purpose alignment, source fit, and answer-source fidelity. They find verified misguidance: models cite real, accessible sources yet distort or mis-source them, with up to 96 percent of users meeting at least one misleading cite per response.
arxiv-2605-28965: James Balhoff and Hilmar Lapp test whether frontier language-model agents can take over phenotype annotation, the labor-heavy job of linking free-text trait descriptions to ontology terms. Given source papers, the annotation guide, four project ontologies, and a validation script, five agents from Anthropic and OpenAI repeat a 2018 benchmark. Every agent lands within the range of variation among three human curators, though the best agents fall just short of the best human. All five beat the older Semantic CharaParser tool on every metric.
arxiv-2605-29465: Leonard Tudorache, Ivan Kurtev, and Mark van den Brand assemble a taxonomy of security properties for checking cryptographic protocols with ProVerif and Tamarin. Drawing on a review of 53 recent studies, they sort and define properties such as secrecy and integrity in plain words and strict first-order logic. The paper also lays out modeling patterns and working examples in both tools, gathered in an open repository. It aims to lower the entry barrier for designers who know security but lack formal verification training.
arxiv-2605-29665: Wei Zhang and twelve colleagues trace superconductivity in CsV3Sb5 across flake thickness. Bulk pairing is s-wave, but ultrathin flakes show a zero-field diode effect, which needs broken inversion and time-reversal symmetries. Transport data show non-reciprocal signals and a diode effect, plus a drop in coherence length as flakes thin. Field data reveal a crossover from bulk three-dimensional to thin-flake two-dimensional superconductivity. The findings point to a chiral phase breaking both symmetries and mark thin flakes as a platform for quantum devices.
arxiv-2605-29765: Ali Abusaleh, Bhuvanesh Verma, and Alexander Mehler build a topic pipeline for long-form video that fuses speech, sound, and sight. Their MMTM joins BERTopic clustering to speech recognition and to audio and visual embeddings through a deterministic similarity gate. On German and English broadcast news, three-way modelling cut noise and topic-switching sharply while lifting topic stability. Cluster validity rose severalfold, and word coherence rose for German but not for shorter English broadcasts. The team releases a human-checked fifty-four-hour video topic corpus.
arxiv-2605-29865: Calvin Tcheka, Guy R. Biyogmam, Bell Bogmis N., and Batkam Mbatchou V. Jacky define a new class of Leibniz algebras, the quasi-Artinian algebras, which loosen the minimal condition on ideals. They set out marks that identify members of the class and give conditions under which such an algebra is in fact Artinian. The work then ties prime ideals to the quasi-Artinian frame in detail, showing how ideal theory fits inside the new setting. The wider class gives chain-condition results fresh ground to reach.
arxiv-2605-29965: Susana Hahn, Amadé Nemes, Javier Romero, and Torsten Schaub give temporal answer-set programming a bendable workbench. Rigid solvers slow trials of new temporal logics, so the team builds a meta-programming frame running varied temporal semantics through one declarative setup. They widen clingo's grammar with type rules and nesting, shielding nested modalities from grounding simplifications that would break their sense. Meta-encodings for linear-time, metric, and dynamic logics show the frame's reach, with a full account of the first. The metasp tool packs the workflow for reuse.
arxiv-2605-30365: Yizhu Wen and four co-authors show an attacker can poison music bases by adding fake music captions. Fake captions skew prompts and push songs from the user's ask, with no change to prompt, search, or song maker. They keep high search hooks, but add low sound words to steer songs toward a chosen goal. In tests with MusicCaps, CLAP, and MusicGen, tainted songs move closer to the attacker's goal, yet stay close to the user's ask. This shows a real risk to creative AI tools.
arxiv-2605-30565: Frazin introduces gratis mitigation, a free benefit in coronagraph design for photographing exoplanets directly. Coronagraphs must suppress starlight enormously to reveal planets, and deformable mirrors carve dark holes in the image where planets can appear. Polarization aberrations split the light into several non-interfering parts that respond to the mirror in correlated ways, so minimizing one part can shrink the others at no extra cost. Simulations of a Lyot coronagraph on a four-meter-class telescope demonstrate the effect and trace it through Jones-matrix analysis.
arxiv-2605-30765: Chen and colleagues address the gap between lab demonstrations and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Google has achieved below-threshold results on surface codes, while Riverlane and Rigetti demonstrated feedback loops. The core challenge of live decoding has shifted to systems engineering. The white paper asks where bottlenecks lie beyond decoder speed: round time, tail latency, and coordination. It asks how mature decoders are for surface and parity-check codes. It proposes a six-layer architecture from acquisition to logical operations. Results quantify the gap between decoder performance and requirements.
arxiv-2605-31065: De Filippo and colleagues design channel prediction for satellite networks in 6G systems. Channel prediction limits pilot overhead, but AI predictors are often too complex for onboard use under power limits. Their DRIFT framework jointly estimates and predicts channels, sending pilots only in the first slot and using data processing after that. A lightweight architecture refines data estimates and predicts future responses with low cost and reduced error spread. Simulations show spectrum gains over pilot systems, with mismatch robustness and few operations for onboard use.
arxiv-2605-31265: Maturo and colleagues study how people value money over time, looking at whole discount curves rather than single rates. Most studies boil each person down to one discount rate, but the shape of the curve may hold clues that a single number misses. Monetary equivalence answers from 107 participants become discount curves, smoothed into implicit subjective-time trajectories. Two functional principal components explain 97.44 percent of the variation, and clustering finds three stable profiles of temporal deformation. Standard parametric models fit many individuals well but miss the clustering structure.
arxiv-2605-31465: Fauss, Poor, and Zoubir solve a nonparametric Kiefer-Weiss problem. The aim is to cut a weighted sum of error chances for a binary sequential test, while capping its largest expected sample size over every possible distribution. They turn the problem into an optimal stopping problem. With at most k randomizations per run, they derive the stopping rule, then let k grow to reach the full solution. Optimal cost follows a nonlinear Bellman equation, and the rule tracks the likelihood ratio plus the sample size still expected.
arxiv-2605-31565: Huang and Kouhkouh present a stochastic particle system in Hilbert spaces, with a mean-field version, for derivative-free optimization. The model keeps the consensus-driven shape of old Consensus-Based Optimization while handling infinite-dimensional dynamics. The team proves the dynamics are well-posed and studies its consensus workings. They prove convergence under set rules on the objective, with mass gathering near the minimizer over long times. This extends the method to such problems in infinite dimensions, and they study the finite-particle system for numerical use.
arxiv-2606-00065:
Aritra Roy, Grisan, Gattinoni, and Buckeridge teach a materials data platform to read charts, not just text, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated pipelines already mine composition and property data from papers, but much quantitative data appears only inside figures, which text tools miss. The team extended their ComProScanner system with a figure extractor that filters charts by caption keywords and a graph agent that sends figures to a vision-language model. The model then recovers composition-property pairs directly from plots.

Four vision models were benchmarked on 50 articles about piezoelectric ceramics, a standard test corpus for this platform. Gemini-3-Flash-Preview performed best, reaching composition accuracy and an F1 score both near 0.97, while also being cheapest. A new range-based error threshold judged extracted numbers by physical closeness rather than exact matching. The authors claim the first fully automated mining platform spanning text, tables, and figures for materials science.
arxiv-2606-00365:
Parvathy and co-authors squeeze the live signals of big chat models into a leaner form. Such models cost much time and store space at run time. Weights can be shrunk hard, since they stay fixed. Live signals shift with each prompt, so they need more care and more bits.

Their frame, SPARQLe, notes that most live values crowd near zero. High bits of those values are thus mostly blank. Each wide signal is split in two parts. A dense low part pairs with a sparse high part and a map of its blanks. A light step boosts that sparsity yet more. A chip built for the split form runs the math at once. Tests show speed and energy gains on three models.
arxiv-2606-00565:
Burgos and co-authors show that bead size need not drive cool paint made of silica beads. Such paints shed heat to the sky and cool in full sun with no power. Bead size was thought key to how they throw sun light back. Past that point, its role was not clear.

Their coats are thick, mixed films of beads from small to wide grades. Each film sits deep in the zone where light scatters many times. Fine traits of scatter shift with bead size in their tests. Net cool marks stay firm across the whole size range. Out-door heat reads show near-matched temp drops for all coats. Group light flow rules the cool, not bead size alone. Bead picks can thus rest on skin traits or ease of make.
arxiv-2606-00765:
Rafi and co-authors build a tool to find where AI agents go wrong in this 2026 paper. Agents now do long tasks with reasoning steps, tool calls, and messages between agents. When a run fails, it is hard to tell which agent erred and at which step. A late step may look wrong only because it rests on an earlier bad state.

Their tool, FALAT, treats the hunt as a search guided by dependencies. It first sketches how the task should have been solved. That sketch flags suspect zones in the run. FALAT then traces links between choices, tool outputs, and messages. It asks if fixing one step would have saved the run. On the Who&When benchmark, the authors report, FALAT tops special tools and plain model prompts. Its best setups reach 46.0 percent step accuracy on machine-made runs and 29.1 percent on hand-made ones.
arxiv-2606-00965:
Yu and co-authors do causal inference on the edges of a network in this 2026 paper. In directed networks, an outcome can sit on an edge, not a node. It depends on the treatment of both units the edge joins. That dyadic interference tangles the dependence structure. Standard node-level estimators and their error bars break down.

The team builds Horvitz-Thompson estimators for a broad class of edge-level effects. They prove the estimators settle to a normal law under mild conditions. New variance estimators use the parts of network dependence that can be identified. The bars they give are far less conservative than classical ones. Covariates enter through sample splitting and cross-fitting, to lift efficiency. Plain two-fold splits fail here, since shared units link the folds. A three-fold scheme restores the independence the math needs.
arxiv-2606-01065:
Ma, Eitzinger, and Koestler give agent runtimes a way to edit their own memory cache in this 2026 paper. KV caches store past computation so a model need not redo it. Cache tools assume the chatbot pattern: prompts arrive once and the cache only grows. Agent work breaks that. Failed tool calls retry, stale outputs drop, and paths pivot mid task.

Two cache problems follow. Content that moves position breaks exact prefix reuse, a flaw others have begun to fix. The deeper one is theirs: a policy may need a span of cache cut or swapped, then work goes on without re-filling all that followed. No primitive offered that. Harnesses pay full re-fill costs on each edit. Their primitive, Leyline, takes a declarative directive. A four part tuple states what to edit and how to keep positions sound.
arxiv-2606-01365:
Li and co-authors spot wasted compute in multi-agent language systems. Failures often waste tokens long before final answers arrive. Their trace-based frame watches a three-agent setup live. An orchestrator, a search agent, and an execution agent take part. Structured events become online signals for loops and budget strain. Low information gain and tool instability also get flagged.

Offline semantic checks and selective judge calls add depth. On 165 GAIA traces, 98 runs gave usable answers. The other 67 failed or stopped with none. Warned failed runs spent 58 point 1 percent of tokens after the first warning. A pilot that acted on warnings cut that share sharply. Cheap signals can thus redirect or halt redundant work early.
arxiv-2606-01865:
Li and co-authors teach robot policies from human corrections. Diffusion policies are a strong way to clone robot skills. Yet they drift when the world shifts from training. People then step in to fix failed moves live. Those fixes pair bad robot moves with good human ones.

Most pipelines throw away that negative signal. Their Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy uses both sides. It builds a set of desired action chunks from pairs. Training pulls the policy toward that set. Bad actions inform what to avoid, not just copy. Tests span many robot manipulation tasks. The authors report less drift and less expert data need. The method learns from correction, not just success.
arxiv-2606-02065:
van der Jagt and co-authors invert random Laguerre tessellations to find their generators. A Laguerre tessellation splits space into weighted cells. Given generator points, its cells are easy to compute. The reverse task is far less obvious. Observed cells hide the weighted points that made them.

Poisson-Laguerre tessellations are the random class studied here. Their generators matter for statistical inference on such patterns. For general tessellations, the team characterize all matching configurations. Many generator sets can yield the same cell pattern. For the Poisson case, they propose a consistent inversion method. It recovers the weighted generators from observed cells. The method supports inference for spatial point patterns. Applications include materials and cellular network layouts.
arxiv-2606-02165:
Hernández and co-authors study how to plan power systems when wind and solar grow fast. In wholesale power markets, producers and the system operator hold the key roles. The operator must keep costs low while supply meets demand. Capacity limits must also be respected at all times. The team study a problem set in continuous time.

The operator seeks to cut the joint cost of running and building the network. The problem is stated with two kinds of control variables. One set drives day to day operation, the other drives investment. A Day-Ahead Problem gives an explicit form for the best operation. The investment task then becomes a stochastic control problem. State constraints bind that problem, and known results are extended to fit.
arxiv-2606-02365:
Nam and Ahn study a speed problem in a strong optimizer called Shampoo. Shampoo scores well on large training tasks. Its matrix inversion step costs a great deal, though. Users often reuse stale preconditioners to save time. That trade saves compute but harms training quality.

The pair study staleness through two lenses, convergence and stability. They show that damping acts as a stabilizer. Damping can blunt the harm that staleness brings. Their method, FOAM, adjusts both damping and update timing. It steers both by a gauge of the staleness error. Tests show FOAM cuts wall-clock time versus standard Shampoo. Training stays robust while it runs faster. The work gives users a firmer grip on a common trade-off.
arxiv-2606-02465:
Kang and Kim train language models to know when to translate. Reasoning models handle English well but lag in other languages. The gap comes largely from poor grasp of non-English input. Translating to English can fix the grasp. Yet translating every query wastes compute. Many queries need no translation at all.

Their framework is called Luar. It uses reinforcement learning with a boundary-aware design. The model solves the original query directly when its grasp is sound. It calls a translator only when translated reasoning should win by a clear margin. Tests on multilingual benchmarks beat training-based baselines. Gains are largest on low-resource languages. On Qwen3-4B, average accuracy rises 8.4 points over standard GRPO. Translator calls cluster where translation truly helps. Inference cost falls as a result.
arxiv-2606-02565:
Xiao and co-authors build a camera system that spends pixels where the task needs them. Ultra-high-resolution sensors capture fine detail. Reading all pixels at full resolution breaks bandwidth, latency, and power budgets. Downsampling discards data before relevance is known. Their system acts at acquisition time instead.

A dual-stream sensor design supports the method. A low-resolution global view is always kept. Limited pixel bandwidth flows to task-relevant regions. The allocation is a learned policy. Past observations guide actions that set future measurements. The loop between perception and acquisition closes. Simulations across perception tasks show high scores under strict pixel budgets. Baselines at the same bandwidth fall behind. A 200-megapixel dual-stream sensor validates the design on real video. The system shows task-driven foveated imaging is practical.
arxiv-2606-02765:
Guha asks how many features a transformer model can hold. Model dimension is a basic design choice. Features are thought to live as directions in latent space, nearly at right angles to each other. Guha counts how many such directions fit. The embedding matrix serves as a usable proxy. In the pairwise cosine similarity spread, a boundary splits real token relations from stray similarity. That boundary estimates the accepted deviation from perfect orthogonality.

Dozens of open-source models fall into two classes. Some keep the tight structure. Others lack it. The standard Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma greatly underestimates how well trained representations pack. A revised formula depends on the ratio of vectors to dimensions. It cuts prediction error by two orders of magnitude, with no extra parameters. Representational capacity is an upper bound on usable directions. Capacity is sharply sensitive to the deviation parameter. Larger models favor tighter orthogonality over capacity.
arxiv-2606-02965:
Ojewale and Venkatasubramanian argue that autonomous agents need a principled way to stop. Current agents can edit records, run transactions, and change infrastructure. Benchmarks, product metrics, and default settings all push agents to proceed even without needed inputs, evidence, or authorization. The authors call this compliance bias.

Their response is the Informed Abstention Framework. Abstention becomes a structured capability, not a failure. A precondition-aware pause blocks the next tool call, names what is missing, and routes to a concrete recovery step. The paper also specifies deployment requirements: runtime enforcement, calibrated guards, and auditable traces. A preliminary test across 144 scenarios and seven model families found runtime enforcement blocked 87.5 to 91 percent of hazardous actions. Usability on authorized scenarios stayed between 75 and 92 percent. Compliance bias took two opposite forms across model families, and the safety-usability trade-off proved tunable rather than fixed.
arxiv-2606-03065:
Yuan and co-authors analyze brightness and color changes in blazars using the Zwicky Transient Facility survey. Blazars are active galactic nuclei with jets pointed near our line of sight. The study uses over six years of near-simultaneous data in two bands. It covers 1,149 sources, split between 589 BL Lacs and 560 flat-spectrum radio quasars.

The team measures variability amplitude and color behavior for each source, overall and on short timescales. BL Lacs tend to grow bluer when brighter. The quasars tend to grow redder when brighter. With host-galaxy contamination removed, 14.7 percent of BL Lacs showed the bluer trend against 2.3 percent for redder. For quasars the split was 8.8 against 14.1 percent. Brighter states in both classes favored the bluer trend. Variability size also linked to color trend, in opposite ways per class.
arxiv-2606-03365:
Méroué, Gandon, and Monnin test whether knowledge graph embedding models give stable answers. Such models are the main tool for link prediction, which fills gaps in knowledge graphs. Standard grading favors rank scores such as MRR. It skips how random seeds shake the results. Those scores can also hide wobble in single predictions and in the shape of the embedding space.

The team runs a systematic stability study across many models and datasets. High scorers in fact diverge at the level of single triples. Their embedding spaces vary a lot from run to run. The team isolates the random factors: initialization, triple order, negative sampling, dropout, and hardware. Each one alone induces instability of like size. Better MRR does not promise better stability for a fixed model. Voting, a known aid, helps only a bit. The authors warn that current grading hides a reliability problem for graph completion.
arxiv-2606-03565:
Wang and co-authors improve how AI agents pick reusable skills for a task. Agents lean more and more on skill libraries. Picking skills is not ordinary document search. A useful top set must hold skills that are each relevant and that work together. Prior benchmarks score pairs alone and discard rejections. Those rejections, where a model judged a skill combo implausible, carry useful signal.

The team builds R3-Skill, a Chinese-English benchmark that keeps those rejections. It holds over 10,000 skills, about 42,000 accepted queries, and about 33,000 rejected annotations. A two-stage system then uses the signal. R3-Embedding handles recall from the large pool. R3-Reranker ranks with graded ListNet training. The full pipeline tops the strongest reranking baseline by a wide margin on set compatibility. It also transfers well to a second benchmark. Agent builders get a compatibility-aware retrieval recipe.
arxiv-2606-03665:
Corillon, Smeekes, and Wilms propose StarTime, a way to group time series lags in a tree to shrink big regressions. Such regressions are often forced to be sparse in their weights. Grouping lags in time gives a distinct route to fewer terms. It fits high-order autoregressions and mixed-frequency data. A time tree sorts lags from high to low frequency.

StarTime is a convex penalty method built on that tree. It picks which weights merge at which frequency, which stay sparse, and which mix. New error bounds are proven for the method. In simulations it beats rival methods on accuracy. It also finds the true grouping and sparsity patterns more often. Uses in finance and macro data show the worth of the idea. Forecasters with long lag structures get a tool that learns grouping, not one that assumes it.
arxiv-2606-03765:
Hoang asks which graphs can arise as token-sliding reconfiguration graphs. Tokens sit on independent sets of a graph, one per vertex. A move slides a token along an edge while the set stays independent. The reconfiguration graph links all such k-token states. The realizability problem inverts the view: which abstract graphs occur this way for some base graph? The token count k is fixed at two or more.

Positive results cover complements of complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs. A complement missing one edge is also realizable. Sharp cutoffs are found for complements of paths and cycles. A product formula for disjoint unions extends the results to Cartesian products. Every grid is realizable at a high token value and at all values from four up. Small cases are classified: one four-cycle product fails at k equals two, and the 3-by-3 grid needs k of at least four.
arxiv-2606-03865:
Rawat and co-authors compute baryon form factors inside asymmetric nuclear matter. The target is space-like Sachs electric and magnetic form factors. Vector meson dominance frames the model. In that frame, photons couple to baryons through vector mesons. In-medium effects enter through shifted vector meson masses.

Those masses come from QCD sum rules fed by density-dependent condensates. A chiral SU(3) quark mean field model supplies the condensates. Effective magnetic moments are computed in the same model. Dirac and Pauli form factors then yield the Sachs factors, which encode charge and magnetic spread. Electric and magnetic radii are computed in free space and in dense matter. Finite temperature effects in asymmetric matter are part of the study. Results face other models, lattice data, and experiment. Nuclear theorists get a consistent in-medium picture of baryon structure.
arxiv-2606-04165:
Cheng Jiang and co-authors describe CaloTrilogy in 2026, a fast simulator for calorimeters, the instruments that measure particle energies at colliders. Full physics simulation is accurate but slow, and modern experiments need huge numbers of simulated showers.

Their design mixes three ideas. First, an integrator follows an average velocity field, so sampling takes one or a few steps. Second, the starting noise is learned from real shower shapes, not pure randomness. Third, a diffusion step refines the sample. The result is one model that spans sensors and energies, with knobs for speed and size. Tests on standard datasets from the field showed strong quality at high granularity, the fine detail level. Quality held while cost dropped sharply.
arxiv-2606-04365:
Renjie Liang and co-authors reframe in 2026 how automated systems should describe kidney lesions in CT scans. Not as one label per patient, but as a set of lesions. Each gets its type, size, enhancement, and density, matching how radiologists report.

They curated over twenty-six hundred scans from nearly eight hundred patients. Labels were per lesion and per side. A public challenge set served as external validation. Their detection-transformer model emits a variable number of lesions per kidney. Two design choices dominated performance. One was feeding the segmentation mask as an input channel. The other was pretraining on same-domain abdominal scans. Rare solid lesions stayed near the noise floor, which the authors read as a data problem.
arxiv-2606-04465:
Tao, Wu, and Wong improve the improver, in a 2026 arXiv paper on optimizing system prompts that steer AI agents. A prompt agent rewrites other agents' instructions, raising performance without changing the underlying model, yet existing methods keep the prompt agent's own instructions hand-written and fixed. Their system, SePO, treats that meta-prompt as an optimization target too, evolving it alongside the task prompts it produces.

SePO runs an open-ended evolutionary search keeping an archive of candidate prompts as stepping stones. Pre-training evolves the prompt agent on a pool of tasks, then fine-tuning aims it at one target task. Across five benchmarks covering math, abstract reasoning, graduate science, code generation, and Sudoku, SePO beat Manual-CoT, TextGrad, and MetaSPO, gaining an average of 4.49 points over Manual-CoT, and its pre-trained skill transferred to tasks outside the training mixture.
arxiv-2606-04665:
You, Wang, Long, and Jordan tackle an awkward problem in domain adaptation, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep unsupervised domain adaptation trains on a labeled source domain. It must perform on a related unlabeled target. Without labels there, comparing algorithms fairly is cumbersome. Existing selection methods are biased, restricted, unstable, or quietly use labeled target data.

This yields an unbiased estimate of target risk with bounded variance. A control variate technique reduces the variance further. The authors justify the method theoretically and confirm it empirically. Reliable model selection matters because progress in the field depends on trustworthy comparisons. Without it, reported improvements may reflect lucky validation rather than better adaptation. Deep Embedded Validation aims to give the field a standardized, honest yardstick. It never touches target labels. This removes a standing obstacle to further advances in unsupervised domain adaptation.
arxiv-2606-04865:
Sonowal, Erkensten, Malic, and Rosati compute how highly dipolar excitons interact at the seams between two atom-thin semiconductors, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Lateral heterostructures stitch transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers side by side, and at the junction, charge-transfer excitons form with electrons and holes separated across the interface. These carry in-plane dipoles of several nanometers. The authors study their interactions, including dipolar and quantum exchange effects.

They evaluate the energy renormalization that experiments can access, predicting a net energy blueshift of a few millielectronvolts for bound charge-transfer excitons. For small dipole moments, the renormalization depends quadratically on the dipole moment. Spatial energy offset and temperature emerge as the key tuning knobs for the response. The results sharpen the microscopic understanding of charge-transfer excitons and their interactions in lateral heterostructures.
arxiv-2606-05565:
Gonzalez-Carriedo, Kawamura, Leung, and Prokaj revisit a famous fractal curve in a 2026 arXiv paper. The curve is the Lévy dragon, a jagged self-similar shape that can tile the flat plane. The authors write the curve as the points given by endless complex number series. They study what happens when the plane is stretched or turned by a linear map. The question is which features of the curve survive such changes.

The team encodes the series forms in a labeled directed graph, a web of nodes and arrows. They show the graph itself stays the same under any linear map. Only the labels on the arrows change. They then describe in geometric terms exactly how those label changes look. The result gives a clean way to sort the many faces of the dragon curve into one family.
arxiv-2606-06065:
Cho and Kim show that training one speech recognizer for two outputs can quietly sabotage one of them in a 2026 arXiv paper. Second-language learners need both what was actually pronounced and what was meant. Multi-task learning assumes shared representations help both tasks. Across Korean and English learners, the assumption split by language. Meaning transcription improved under multi-task training. Surface transcription degraded, especially in English.

The damage scaled with how far pronunciation diverged from the intended form, measured by edit distance. Encoder analysis exposed the mechanism: representational entanglement. Korean encoders kept the two tasks' representations distinct. English encoders collapsed them into near-identical ones. Decoder analysis added nuance: the meaning decoder built its own adapted representation, while the surface decoder stayed trapped by the encoder's merge. The fix must target the encoder, the authors argue. Pronunciation feedback tools, their application, need both outputs trustworthy at once.
arxiv-2606-06165:
Siqi Chen, Shi Jin, and Lei Zhang study quantum algorithms for multiscale equations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Homogenization replaces a material with rapid fine-scale wiggles by smooth average behavior that captures the same overall response. For nonlinear or random media, that average is costly to compute directly. Their route uses Young measures, which record how microscopic gradients are distributed rather than tracking each one.

Rewriting the problem with Young measures turns it into a linear program, a structured optimization problem that quantum solvers can attack. In the deterministic case they find a polynomial quantum speedup when only moderate accuracy in the averaged solution is needed. In the stochastic case, encoding all random scenarios in one program gives a square-root saving in sampling cost. Tests on one- and two-dimensional benchmarks confirm the reformulation gives the right answers.
arxiv-2606-06265:
Parsa Memarzadehsaghezi and co-authors build a defense for machine learning classifiers in this 2026 arXiv paper on security. Evasion attacks tweak inputs slightly so a trained classifier misjudges them, a real threat in fraud detection and cybersecurity. Single model defenses often fail when the attack changes shape. The authors instead turn one classifier into a committee that is harder to fool.

Their framework, RESSAP, trains each committee member on a carefully chosen subset of features. A resilience metric guides the choice, weighing how important each feature is against how robust it stays under attack. Noise based augmentation during training hardens the decision boundaries further. At prediction time a random subset of members votes, so an attacker cannot predict exactly which model will judge the input. Experiments showed much stronger resistance to evasion attacks while accuracy on clean data stayed high.
arxiv-2606-06665:
Do bad moods spread among artificial agents the way they spread among people? Chaabane and co-authors study that question in this 2026 arXiv paper using MOLTBOOK, a social network where every account is an autonomous language model agent. Their data cover almost two point nine million posts and one point five million comments.

Negative posts drew far more replies than neutral or positive ones, so dark content still grabs attention. Yet the replies rarely stayed negative. Most shifted to a neutral tone, replies grew more neutral deeper in each thread, and there was little sign that a negative mood carried into the next day. The main pattern, the authors argue, is negative attention followed by calming down, which sets these agent networks apart from human ones, where negative feelings more often feed on themselves.
arxiv-2606-07765:
Meng and colleagues design a CPR training system for high-altitude Tibet in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation needs steady compression depth and rhythm, but most training gear assumes an instructor, repeated coached practice, and shared language. In the Tibet Autonomous Region instruction is fragmented and learners' languages and schooling vary widely, so the team built TibetCPR for unguided learning instead.

The low-cost system pairs touch feedback on the skin for compression depth with cues for rhythm, wrapped in a Tibetan-language narrative. In a randomised study of forty lay members aged nineteen to fifty-six, the guided group stabilised rhythm and depth minute by minute over a ten-minute session. They outperformed an unguided control group, and the gains carried into an unscaffolded one-minute post-test. Users rated usability highly, with a score of about eighty-four, and described the feedback as readable through their actions.
arxiv-2606-07965:
Zekai Zhang and co-authors give industrial defect detection its first large-scale open training ground, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models segment objects from text prompts, but factories look nothing like natural photos, and defects are rare, small, and costly. Models prompted naively scoop up irrelevant pixels, and scarce industrial data has left the approach unexplored.

Their Multi-Modal Industrial Open Dataset holds more than eighty thousand samples across six super-categories and eighteen subcategories of industrial scenes. On top of it they build a refined text-visual prompt method for zero-shot defect detection, meaning the model flags defect types it was never explicitly trained on. An expert-guided adaptation mechanism retargets a general segmentation model, Mobile-SAM, to industrial imagery. The dataset is the first large multi-scene pre-training resource for industrial zero-shot learning, giving open models material they have lacked.
arxiv-2606-08465:
Huan Vo and colleagues run the first controlled race between the major families of general parsers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Parsing, turning text into structured trees, underpins compilers, static analyzers, language servers, and fuzzing tools. Most deployed parsers are deterministic, forcing developers to contort their grammars and even simplify the languages they design. General context-free parsers remove that constraint, but despite decades of development, no rigorous head-to-head comparison existed across the major algorithm families.

The authors built a unified benchmark of six generalized parsing algorithms, spanning classical chart methods and modern grammar-agnostic techniques, plus deterministic baselines. All were implemented in one language with shared data structures. The test suite covers twenty-two grammars, from simple expressions to full C++ and Java. Their results quantify the true cost of generality: how much speed the flexible algorithms surrender, and where each family wins.
arxiv-2606-08865:
Shulga determines which values rational approximations to irrational numbers can achieve under the L1 norm, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diophantine approximation asks how well an irrational number can be approached by fractions. For each number, a Dirichlet constant measures its best approximation quality, and the spectrum is the set of values that occur. With approximation measured in the L1 norm, whose unit ball is a diamond rather than a disk, Shulga computes the spectrum completely.

The spectrum is the interval from one half to one, with no gaps. Equivalently, the Minkowski spectrum, tied to the Minkowski diagonal continued fraction, is the interval from one quarter to one half. Shulga measures the level sets, the numbers sharing a constant, using Hausdorff dimension, a gauge of fractal size. Every level set above one quarter has dimension greater than one half. The bottom level set, at one quarter, has dimension exactly one half.
arxiv-2606-08965:
Ahmed and colleagues predict which social media sessions people will regret, using phones and cheap smartwatches, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Regret, they argue, measures harm better than screen time, since a long session can feel worthwhile and a short one wasted. 21 participants spent 7 days in an experience-sampling study, with passive phone logging, an 80-dollar Bangle.js smartwatch, and surveys after sessions, totaling 1,445 sessions. The team asked what foretells regret before a session starts.
