The gap between intended and actual use predicted regret far more strongly than session length, whose apparent effect collapsed once intention entered the model. Regret also grew when a session displaced something valued, especially at night or after using productivity apps. Context known before the session generalized across participants, while body signals from the watch added person-specific lift. Interviews added themes of scrolling as avoidance and time blindness, pointing beyond simple timers.
arxiv-2606-09065:
Do, Shannon, and Santu compress simulations of a million colliding particles into a handful of learned spatial modes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Lagrangian methods like smoothed particle hydrodynamics track matter as particles and excel at violent events, like debris smashing spacecraft shields. They are also expensive. OnlyDense treats the system state as a function in a Hilbert space, approximated by a linear subspace spanned by neural basis functions, like proper orthogonal decomposition but learned.

Projecting onto the subspace gives latent coefficients, no nonlinear optimization, and the representation ignores how many particles discretize the system. On large-scale hydrodynamics simulations with over 1 million particles, including extreme deformation and breakup, OnlyDense reconstructed states and predicted dynamics with an R-squared score above 0.99 using as few as 32 basis functions. That is a compression of about 5 orders of magnitude. The limitation is reliance on a single reference configuration, flagged for future work.
arxiv-2606-09365:
Haoran Sun and a large Fudan University team present SkeMex, a memory system that lets medical software agents learn from experience without retraining, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clinical agents must handle evolving cases over many steps, yet typical memory stores keep raw interaction traces that are redundant and noisy.

SkeMex distils past interaction trajectories into structured skills, compact records of reusable procedural know-how. The skills sit in a repository with general, task-specific, and action-level branches. Each memory carries a utility score estimated from environment feedback, which guides both retrieval and housekeeping. A repeating read, write, assess, and govern cycle promotes helpful skills and deletes harmful ones. Across diverse clinical tasks, SkeMex beat representative memory-based agents in both offline and online settings. Its skill memory also transferred across different underlying models, suggesting the stored experience is genuinely portable.
arxiv-2606-09665:
Aman Raju and his co-authors build a learning framework to weigh black holes from their flicker in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reverberation mapping times how light echoes across an accretion disk, the gas ring feeding a supermassive black hole. The echo shape encodes the hole's traits. The coming Rubin survey will flood the field with light curves, far too many for slow fits.

Their framework first clusters like-shaped curves with self-organizing maps, one per colour band. An attentive latent neural process then learns each cluster's forms without labels. A mixture density model reads out the echo shapes and hole traits. On fake curves, the rebuild beat rival regressors by sixty to seventy percent. Echo shapes came back about a third better than the training guess. Trained on fake data, the system also ran on real curves from the Zwicky survey, a step toward survey-scale use.
arxiv-2606-09765:
Zhenyu Du and his co-authors find a sharp line between quantum states that can be read and those that stay dark in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reading a quantum state wrecks it: measurement forces it into plain data, and some of its content is lost. The team gauge readout by the share of the state's Fisher information that survives. They gauge cost by circuit depth, how many layers the reading device needs.

Below a key depth, readout fades at an exponential pace as the system grows. The content is, in effect, sealed. That depth scales as a power of log n for grid-like builds. For all-to-all links it is just log log n, a far lower bar. Just past the line, the view clears at once. Random readings then win back a fixed share of the full content, for any state.
arxiv-2606-09865:
Manel Slokom, Malek Slokom, and Thierno Kante ask language models to sniff out fake rows in shared tables in this 2026 arXiv paper. Firms share synthetic data to cut privacy risk. The catch is audit: if a sharp eye can tell fake from real, the shield is thin. The team turn the eye itself into a model, asked to tag each sample real or synthetic.

Two setups were run: the table alone, and the table plus spread facts about its columns. Three generators faked two public sets, the UCI Adult and ACS Census data. A run banked four hundred fifty-one sound trials. On Adult, LLaMA scored zero on the tell-apart scale in the marked cells, while Gemini hit a perfect score on two generators. On Census, LLaMA cried fake at most samples, while Gemini stayed sharp alone but dipped with extra facts.
arxiv-2606-10165:
Garcia and colleagues analyze a stochastic infection-like process on a highly branched network, in a 2026 arXiv paper on probability theory. In the frog model, active particles wander a graph waking dormant particles, called frogs, when they visit their sites. Each active particle performs a random walk biased toward the root and dies after a random geometrically distributed lifetime, while inactive particles wait to be awakened.

The central question is survival: does activity persist forever with positive probability, or die out almost surely? The authors give conditions on the drift strength and the survival parameter separating those regimes. Their proofs compare the process with simpler branching processes, both single-type and multi-type, which are easier to analyze exactly. Such comparison arguments are a standard but powerful route in interacting particle systems. The results clarify how inward drift and mortality compete against the waking mechanism that sustains spread.
arxiv-2606-10265:
O’Keeffe studies a model of particles that both move and synchronize as one, when their couplings are drawn at random, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nonlinear dynamics. Swarmalators combine swarming and oscillation: each unit has a position and a phase, and the two influence each other. In his one-dimensional model, the phase coupling for each particle comes from a uniform distribution spanning positive and negative values.

In that state the group splits across the zero-coupling threshold, positives on one side and negatives on the other, with an order parameter set by the positive-coupling excess. The known unsynced, phase-wave, and synchronized states persist, but each stability boundary is governed by its own feature of the distribution: the mean response, the most negative particle, or the full density. With strongly negative couplings present, order parameters instead oscillate without end, adding to the model's known states.
arxiv-2606-10465:
Deng and colleagues present MASTOR in this 2026 arXiv paper, a multi-agent system that writes semantic test oracles for web services built as RESTful APIs. An oracle is the part of a test that judges whether a response is actually right. MASTOR reads the service's source code, first building context for each endpoint, then generating oracles along two paths, one per operation and one across operation sequences. A challenger agent reviews each draft oracle and pushes for targeted improvements before acceptance.

The evaluation covers thirteen open-source projects with 296 endpoint operations and about a quarter-million lines of code. MASTOR generates 10,022 oracles and reaches an average mutation score of 75.4 percent across the projects, meaning its tests catch most planted faults. On a matched subset it beats direct prompting by 30.1 percentage points, scoring 69.9 percent against 39.8 percent in that comparison. The median cost is modest, at fifty-six cents per API tested.
arxiv-2606-10665:
Moore and Althorpe test a shortcut to quantum equilibrium in this 2026 arXiv paper on chemical physics. An open quantum system, one coupled to a bath, settles into a thermal state entangled with its environment. For continuous-variable systems the state has an exact path-integral form, positions tied to the bath, momenta linked to positions by a phase term. The authors ask whether random classical trajectories in that space can reach it. Their motion follows a recent Matsubara generalised Langevin equation, pushing variables into the complex plane to create the imaginary correlations.

Against intuition, they do equilibrate to the exact quantum state, recovering even the purely imaginary momentum-position correlation. The catch: that motion is numerically unstable, yet clean equilibration is shown for a quartic oscillator in a white-noise bath. Taming the instability would open new simulation methods for such systems, from quantum Brownian motion to surface diffusion.
arxiv-2606-10965:
Kresch and Tschinkel discuss when group actions on varieties can be linearized in this 2026 arXiv paper. In equivariant birational geometry, a finite group's action is linearizable if the variety matches a linear representation up to birational change. Twisting an action by a torsor produces new varieties, and earlier work tied stable linearizability to rationality of all twists.

The note's main theorems say one special twist is enough: properties of every twist, from rational points to stable rationality, follow from the single twist built on a generically free versal action. The same reduction holds for equivariant decomposition of the diagonal. The authors also introduce coarser notions, coarse birationality and coarse linearizability, sitting between the plain and stable versions.
arxiv-2606-11665:
Jan Adler, Florian Gast, Gerhard P Fettweis and Rafael F Schaefer study a practical obstacle for 6G sensing in this 2026 arXiv paper. In monostatic sensing, one device both transmits and receives, acting like radar through its communication antennas. The transmitted signal leaks directly into the receiver and can drown the echoes. Digital precoding, shaping the transmitted beams, should suppress the leak. Real hardware performs far worse than theory.

The authors identify quantization noise, the rounding error when signals are converted between analogue and digital form, as a primary culprit. They derive a closed-form formula predicting how this noise limits any leakage estimation and suppression scheme, using only known system parameters. Numerical analysis and measurements on a real hardware testbed confirm the prediction. The result lets engineers forecast suppression performance before building hardware. Future work will add clock jitter, phase noise and amplifier distortions to the model.
arxiv-2606-11765:
Yang Xu, Hengxu Song and Jianqiao Hu model what happens when rough surfaces touch in this 2026 arXiv paper on mechanics. Real surfaces are rough at many scales, and the resulting stress concentrations can permanently deform the material, a plastic response. Hardness itself changes with scale, complicating predictions of how much true contact area carries a load.

The authors build a stochastic model, treating contact statistics as probability distributions that evolve across magnification scales. Three integral equations track the distributions of elastic contact pressure, plastic contact area and non-contact area. They derive from compounded Chapman-Kolmogorov equations, a tool for layered random processes. The model shows a smooth transition from elastic behaviour through elastic-plastic response to full plasticity as load grows. It also yields a new topographic yield parameter and a diagram for identifying which contact regime a surface pair is in.
arxiv-2606-12165:
Deng and Pantuso price carsharing while admitting that prices themselves shape the demand being priced, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most studies treat demand as random but fixed in character, set by outside forces. Here the demand distribution depends on the firm's own pricing choices, a decision-dependent uncertainty. The team casts joint pricing and relocation as a stochastic program, an optimization under uncertainty, then as a mixed-integer linear program of exponential size.

To solve it exactly, they adapt the L-shaped method with routines built on closed-form subproblem solutions. Added inequalities and cut sharing speed convergence sharply, beating a commercial solver by far. On carsharing data, modeling the price-demand link raises profit by 8.39 percent over an elastic-demand benchmark. The gain over an exogenous-demand benchmark is 8.53 percent. Controlled vehicle allocation also lifts service rates at little profit cost.
arxiv-2606-12565:
Collier and co-authors test whether the shortcut linking galaxies to dark matter halos survives modified gravity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cosmological surveys map galaxies to infer the matter field, relying on the galaxy-halo connection. Assembly bias, the dependence of galaxy content on more than halo mass, corrupts that link. The team built catalogs for DESI and Euclid, from simulations run under f(R) gravity, an alternative to the cosmological constant.

In this gravity, a chameleon mechanism hides the modification in dense regions. Halo and galaxy formation prove enhanced for more massive halos as time passes. The halo occupation model, counting galaxies by halo mass alone, underestimates clustering by ten to twenty percent in standard gravity when assembly bias is ignored. Modified gravity complicates things. Adding environment density as a second occupation variable cuts the bias effect to two or three percent at low redshift, in every gravity model.
arxiv-2606-12765:
Kumaresan reverse-engineers the behaviour of Apple's Metal 4.1 tensor compute path on an M4 Max chip, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Metal 4.1 documents the interface of its matmul2d matrix-multiplication operation but conceals whether low-precision formats are truly accelerated and where the operation executes. Using a checksum-gated microbenchmark harness, the study recovers 11 facts the specification hides or contradicts.

The headline finding is that fp8 matrix multiplication, using the E4M3 8-bit float format, is emulated rather than accelerated: it sustains 0.94 times the throughput of fp16 despite reading half the operand bytes, making it a memory-footprint feature, not a speed feature. Three signals show matmul2d runs on the GPU shader cores, with no dedicated matrix unit and no routing to the Neural Engine. A hand-fused matrix-multiply-plus-bias-plus-activation kernel beats the decomposed path by 6.5 to 12.9 percent in the cache-resident regime.
arxiv-2606-13165:
Panov, Theriault, and Vylegzhanin study the algebraic structure inside a family of topological spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their space, the Davis-Januszkiewicz space, is built from a simplicial complex, a combinatorial object made of vertices and faces. Each vertex inclusion gives a map from the two-sphere into the space. Repeatedly applying the Whitehead product, an operation combining sphere maps, to these maps generates substructures inside the homotopy groups, which classify how spheres can wrap around the space.

The authors describe one such subalgebra, giving its generators and relations in terms of the complex. They prove a sharp criterion for a larger subalgebra: it equals the homotopy group when the complex is a flag complex, meaning its faces are determined by pairwise connections. The results connect combinatorics to homotopy theory. Extensions to more general polyhedral products, a broader construction in topology, are considered.
arxiv-2606-13265:
Ramos, Schmidt, and Zimmer study a chain of quantum spins in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system is a trimerised chain, meaning its magnetic atoms group into repeating units of three, and it is motivated by a copper compound. Frustration, where competing interactions cannot all be satisfied at once, can destabilise the chain's magnetic order. The authors combine a cluster mean-field method with exact diagonalisation, a technique that solves small systems, and apply a magnetic field.

When frustration is weak, the magnetisation settles on a plateau at one third of maximum. That plateau reflects a collective state where each trimer acts like a larger spin. Strengthening one coupling reorganises the spin correlations toward a doublon-like pattern, where excitations pair up. Scaling analysis, which extrapolates from small chains to large ones, supports this. The authors argue the plateau survives because the low-energy behaviour reduces to interacting emergent spins.
arxiv-2606-13665: Appearing on arXiv in 2026, this research paper lays out a new study. The subject on the cover page is One-loop five-point gluing analytically. The paper speaks to science and technology — careful study of how the natural and built world works. The paper's pages hold new research, shared openly with the field.
arxiv-2606-13765:
Mattsson, Wager, and Graham develop an electrostatic model for dual-layer oxide transistors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Thin-film transistors using amorphous oxide semiconductors drive displays, and stacking two semiconductor layers can combine their strengths. Their two-equation model distributes electrostatic charge between the top and bottom layers. It simulates transfer and mobility curves of a dual-layer device pairing two indium-based oxides. The model also yields an expression for how charge confines itself in the bottom layer, as a function of the top layer's thickness and the conduction-band offset.

Balancing charge partition against oxygen vacancy traps, defects that trap charge, the model suggests a top-layer thickness in the 9 to 12 nanometre range. It predicts how the turn-on voltage shifts with band offset and thickness. The model extends to dual-layer transistor systems. Device engineers gain a pocket calculator for design trade-offs.
arxiv-2606-14065:
Maiti's team turns tiny beam deflections into a probe for invisible asymmetries in layered materials. When light reflects at an angle, the beam shifts slightly in its plane, the Goos-Hänchen shift, and across it, the Imbert-Fedorov shift. In a layered medium with broken symmetry, reflection becomes non-reciprocal: lighting from opposite ends gives different shifts. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies these shifts for structured light, with and without orbital angular momentum, boosted by resonance and weak value methods.

For a tiny imbalance, forward and backward shifts can carry opposite signs, making the difference giant. A small index mismatch gave theoretical sensitivities of order ten to the minus ninth index units per nanometer. Focusing effects that distort the beam and spawn a side lobe are analyzed, since they can bias centroid estimates. Projective measurements of the transverse shift showed the amplification working. In-plane sensors beat transverse ones.
arxiv-2606-14265:
Chiusole, Kuehn, and Semenowicz extend a classic tool of dynamics to rough equations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Normal forms simplify a system near an equilibrium point, a resting state, by changing coordinates so the essential behavior stands out. Rough differential equations add irregular driving signals that ordinary calculus cannot handle smoothly.

Assuming enough smoothness and a hyperbolic equilibrium, meaning nearby motion clearly moves toward or away along set directions, the authors prove local formal equivalence between solution flows. One flow comes from the full random nonlinear rough equation, and the other from its linearized version. This match means the complicated system and its simpler linear cousin share the same formal normal form near equilibrium. The result lays the groundwork for a normal form theory covering rough equations.
arxiv-2606-14365:
Pauwels and colleagues give photon-counting detectors an honest report card. The question is not how many outcomes the device prints. It is how many photon numbers it can genuinely tell apart. Such detectors underpin quantum communication, sensing, and computing, yet no practical metric certified their resolution. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines genuine resolution operationally, distinguishing photon numbers in a single shot. It also gives a practical testing protocol using coherent-state probes, laser-like light of controlled intensity.

Applied to a 28-pixel superconducting nanowire detector, the protocol certified genuine four-outcome resolution. The device provably distinguishes zero, one, two, and three-or-more photon events, beyond what any lower-resolution device could fake. Statistical margins were overwhelming in the trusted-source analysis, hundreds of standard deviations for the simplest tests. The work also shows how strongly it depends on detector efficiency, giving makers a concrete target and users a benchmark.
arxiv-2606-14465:
Alaimo and co-authors demonstrate a new jamming attack on 5G networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. User equipment, the phones and devices on a network, can turn adversarial. Their framework STORM-RJ uses a software-defined radio to fire precise noise bursts at the uplink channel, the link carrying data from a device to the tower, exactly when a chosen victim transmits.

The system decodes downlink control information to learn each uplink grant, then synchronizes interference with the exact resource blocks assigned to the target, adjusting bandwidth and center frequency in real time. The authors trace the main delay sources in software and radio hardware. Only low-level radio control reacted fast enough, at microsecond scale, to meet 5G timing demands. They close by discussing defenses, including detection through repeat-request anomalies.
arxiv-2606-14865:
Ye and co-authors change how neural networks are hardened against attacks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Adversarial training teaches a network to resist inputs crafted to fool it. Standard training exposes all parameters from the start. The authors ask whether the order of exposure matters. Their idea borrows from developmental plasticity, where pathways form and stabilize over time.

Their framework, GRAPE, pairs two moves. Stabilization keeps local robust training steady. Progressive hidden expansion releases new trainable dimensions bit by bit. A spectral score sends the new capacity to the modules under most attack pressure. On CIFAR-10 under the standard threat model, robust accuracy rose from about fifty-one point seven percent to about fifty-six point nine percent. That is a relative gain near ten percent. The parameter count also fell by about twenty-one percent at nearly the same compute budget.
arxiv-2606-14965:
Islam and coauthors build a new benchmark for noisy-label learning in a 2026 study. Training labels are often wrong, and errors depend on the item itself, since hard cases get mislabeled more often. Most test sets create such noise with fake raters, which hides where the confusion came from. The team instead generates noise through controlled damage to the inputs.

Their framework, CILN, corrupts images or records in known ways, then has a diverse voter pool label the damaged items. Ninety benchmark settings span CIFAR-10, MNIST, and the Adult data, across corruption types and severity levels. The noise proves genuinely item-dependent, with varied confusion patterns. On CIFAR-10 its label spread sits closer to human doubt than an older synthetic benchmark. It also exposes failure modes in Co-Teaching and DivideMix that rater-based noise never revealed, showing that noise structure matters as much as noise rate.
arxiv-2606-15365:
Ortiz and a large collaboration present the sixth PEARLS survey paper in 2026, fitting the spectral energy distributions of X-ray sources in a field watched by the James Webb Space Telescope. A spectral energy distribution records a galaxy's brightness across wavelengths; fitting one yields star-formation rates and black hole growth rates for the active galactic nucleus. The sample holds 261 X-ray sources out to high redshift.

Most host galaxies form stars below the average rate for their mass, while their black holes feed faster than average. The standout result is a strong correlation: galaxies forming stars above the main trend host the most luminous black holes per unit mass. Low-mass galaxies show black holes in growth spurts, while massive ones tick over in maintenance mode. The pattern supports a shared gas supply fueling both, and it surfaces a population of star-forming cold quasars.
arxiv-2606-15465:
Beyer measures the gap between what blockchain security audits find and what actually steals money, in a 2026 empirical study. The dataset pairs nearly twenty-four thousand public audit findings from twenty-two firms with 218 documented exploit incidents over four years, together worth about seven point eight billion dollars in losses. Audits review code; exploits unfold in the wild, and the paper asks whether the two pictures match.

They largely do not. Audit findings stay remarkably stable year to year, with severe findings holding a steady share. Realized losses, though, concentrate in human vectors: private-key compromise, phishing, and social engineering cause about half of all losses yet barely appear in audit reports. Losses are also extremely concentrated, the eight largest incidents accounting for half the total. The lesson is portfolio thinking: code audits and operational security are complements, and programs built for average outcomes underinsure against the tail.
arxiv-2606-15865:
Ithineni and colleagues probe the magnetism of a platinum and cobalt vanadate interface in 2026, using spin Hall magnetoresistance as an interface-sensitive probe. In the bulk, their films turn ferrimagnetic near 150 kelvin, with out-of-plane anisotropy reorienting in-plane below 90 kelvin. The question is whether the interface, where spin currents cross into the platinum, follows the bulk or keeps its own.

The transport data say it keeps its own. Rotational scans at 20 kelvin show strong hysteresis about one crystal direction and none along the other in-plane axes, revealing biaxial anisotropy at the interface, with easy axes along the 110 directions. It persists up to about 120 kelvin, even where bulk data report the opposite preference, so interface and bulk are magnetically decoupled. The spin mixing conductance comes out in line with other oxide spintronic systems. The result establishes the pair as a platform for engineering anisotropy in oxide spintronics.
arxiv-2606-15965:
Hall and colleagues simulate how fusion-born alpha particles affect core turbulence in the ARC tokamak power plant concept in 2026, using linear and nonlinear gyrokinetic simulations. In a burning plasma, energetic alphas dominate heating, but their effect on ion-scale turbulence was poorly understood. The team compares plasmas with fast alphas against artificially thermalised ones.

Fast alphas significantly reduce turbulent heat and particle fluxes in the inner core, out to half the minor radius. The mechanism is indirect: alpha-driven modes pump zonal flows, whose shearing stabilises the background turbulence, shifting the critical gradient for ion-temperature-gradient modes upward. No unstable fast-ion mode, no stabilisation; direct effects are minor. The suppression strengthens with alpha density and plasma pressure, and extends only as far as the fast particles reach. For power-plant design, burning-plasma turbulence may be kinder than thermalised models assume.
arxiv-2606-16165:
Barrett, Chen, and Lopez-Wild ask in 2026 how to understand a statistical postulate that Bohmian mechanics needs for its predictions. Bohmian mechanics is a deterministic theory of particles guided by a wave. To match quantum statistics, it adds a distribution condition on initial particle positions. Whether that condition is a law or a typicality assumption has stayed unclear.

The authors use algorithmic randomness, the study of sequences passing every effective test for randomness, to restate it. In their algorithmic Bohmian mechanics, it becomes a binding law on allowed states and measurements. The payoff is a guarantee: standard Born-rule statistics hold for standard quantum experiments in the limit, not merely with high probability. This gives a sharp condition rather than a vague appeal to most cases. The account clarifies what quantum chances mean inside such a theory.
arxiv-2606-16465:
Xu and co-authors ask in 2026 when it actually pays to let AI agents act autonomously, and answer with insurance mathematics. Agents now take irreversible actions in operational systems, yet agent-caused losses are rarely assigned, priced, or transferred. The authors argue automation is acceptable when its expected benefit exceeds the insurance premium, the control cost, and the risk that remains. That arithmetic needs agents in defined roles with bounded permissions and comparable execution traces.

Their trace-economic underwriting maps each tool-use trace to customer exposure and claimable loss, using deterministic economic labels rather than a model judge. In their trace-to-loss testbed, this pricing cuts the mean absolute pricing error from about 17.7 thousand to 569, and removes a regressive cross-subsidy. An expert audit of 300 traces accepts 295 labels unchanged. General-purpose agents without a defined role fall outside the regime.
arxiv-2606-16665:
Lee examines a light-matter effect in a 2026 theory paper on the metal-insulator transition. Some materials sit close to a Mott transition, the point where electrons stop flowing and a metal becomes an insulator. Lee asks whether light trapped in a nearby material could push such a system across that line without any applied laser field.

The nearby material is hexagonal boron nitride, which hosts a hyperbolic photon mode where light spreads through a greatly expanded momentum range. Lee computes the photon density of states and the zero-point electric field, the field present even with no light switched on. That field can reach strengths comparable to the largest used in terahertz pump experiments. Placing a near-Mott material on the nitride could shift its transition. The effect fades fast with distance, though, so only a few atomic layers would feel it. Estimates cover several candidate materials.
arxiv-2606-16765:
Schröder, Kavane and Köstler present a validated dataset pipeline in a 2026 workshop paper on turbulent flow simulation. Neural operators promise to replace slow fluid simulations with fast learned surrogates. Judging them fairly needs training data that is physically trustworthy, with real benchmarks attached.

Their pipeline uses a lattice Boltzmann solver, which moves fluid packets on a grid, with cumulant collision rules for stability. Flow runs through three-dimensional channels around generated obstacle shapes, at Reynolds numbers in the turbulent range. The solver is checked against experiments on Strouhal number, drag and fluctuation levels, plus grid convergence studies at very high resolution. On that validated base, the team plans systematic tests of Fourier neural operators and U-Net variants on forecasting, super-resolution and error correction. Physics-based metrics will judge whether surrogates capture the turbulent energy cascade, not just pretty pictures.
arxiv-2606-16865:
Das links the shape of quantum states to how fast information scrambles in a 2026 quantum chaos paper. In a chaotic system most states spread evenly, yet scarred states cling to unstable classical paths and keep a spatial memory. Whether those static patterns also govern dynamics was unclear.

The testbed is a peanut-shaped quantum billiard, a particle bouncing inside a curved boundary. Simple localization numbers can flag states that concentrate oddly, but they discard the state's actual shape. Das instead compares full probability density profiles with a scale-normalized overlap measure. That reveals families of distinct states sharing nearly the same spatial morphology. Comparing their out-of-time-order correlators, which track scrambling, shows weak overlap predicts little. Strongly recurring shapes, though, produce nearly identical scrambling growth and saturation. Scarred structures thus act as spatial templates for operator growth, turning eigenstate shape into a quantitative predictor of dynamics.
arxiv-2606-16965:
Bisicchia and colleagues ask how many times a quantum circuit must be run in a 2026 quantum computing paper. Quantum algorithms are probabilistic, so a circuit is executed repeatedly, in shots, to estimate its output distribution. Extra shots cost money and scarce machine time, yet too few shots ruin accuracy.

Their framework, IncrementalExecution, decides online when to stop, with no assumptions about the circuit's structure or the machine's noise. It watches the empirical output distribution as shots accumulate and stops at the point of diminishing returns, when more shots stop changing the distribution in any statistically meaningful way. Policies for managing shots can be customized to trade cost against fidelity. The evaluation is large: tens of thousands of framework configurations across many circuit and backend combinations, amounting to millions of experiments. Within its static-circuit scope, the answer is positive and immediately usable on today's quantum cloud platforms.
arxiv-2606-17065:
Saqur and colleagues make implied volatility differentiable in a 2026 quantitative finance paper. Option learning lives in two worlds: prices, where markets quote and no-arbitrage rules bite, and implied volatility, where surfaces are smoothed. Converting forward is solved, thanks to Jäckel's rational solver, but gradients could not flow back through its branching code.

PIVOT keeps that solver untouched forward, and supplies the backward pass by implicit differentiation through the pricing map. A gating contract handles the low-vega region, where the inverse map blows up. Invalid rows return NaN, healthy rows get the exact gradient, and low-vega rows are damped rather than silently patched. A fused GPU kernel computes implied volatilities at machine precision and enormous throughput. In volatility-surface fitting, PIVOT objectives beat the baselines, cutting held-out price error substantially. The authors stress the gate is not optional: without it, training collapses.
arxiv-2606-17265:
Hvatov and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on finding stop-bands in periodic structures, the frequency ranges where waves cannot pass through. Such gaps underpin noise insulators, waveguides, and sensors built from phononic and photonic crystals. Computing the full dispersion diagram to locate them is costly, so the authors exploit the mirror symmetries of a symmetric unit cell to shortcut the work.

At the high-symmetry corners of the Brillouin zone, the standing-wave problem splits into four smaller problems on a quarter-cell, each with hard or soft boundary conditions. Sorting and pairing the resulting frequencies along each boundary segment gives an explicit formula for the stop-band intervals. The method matched full calculations to within about one percent for the lowest bands in two test systems. It needs eigenvalue solutions at only three wavevectors.
arxiv-2606-17465:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on generative modelling through the Perron-Frobenius operator, the mathematical object that pushes probability densities forward under random dynamics. Their framework, PFOM, matches density evolution directly through that integral operator, and in doing so it covers flow, diffusion, and jump models in one scheme. The work also ties operator theory, long used for analysing Markov processes, to the practical training losses of modern generative models in a precise way.

Among Bregman divergences, only the Kullback-Leibler choice keeps the density-level goal equal to the sample-based one, yielding a usable loss. That loss turns out to match Koopman path matching, linking the two operator viewpoints neatly. Nesterov-style acceleration is added to both training and sampling to steady the discretisation and speed convergence. Experiments show faster drops in several distance measures and better wall-clock efficiency.
arxiv-2606-17765:
Zumalacárregui and Shan present a 2026 arXiv paper on modelling how fields of stars distort gravitational waves passing through a galaxy or cluster on their way to Earth. The big lens magnifies the wave, but hundreds of stellar-mass microlenses add frequency-dependent wiggles that wave optics cannot ignore. Simulating every stellar field afresh is far too slow for data analysis. Their Reduced-Order Stochastic Diffraction models compress libraries of numerical lensing simulations into a small orthonormal basis plus a probability law for its coefficients, ready to drop into inference pipelines.

A worked example built for current detector sensitivity shows truncation choices and recovery tests on injected signals. The basis can be retuned for other detectors, sources, and microlens populations as needed. With such models, searches can test whether a signal's wiggles match stellar-field lensing. The same machinery could probe unseen compact objects, even dark matter candidates.
arxiv-2606-17865:
Ghosh and colleagues propose a fresh cause for a known effect in twisted molecules, in a 2026 physics paper. When current flows through such a molecule, one electron spin is favored over the other, yet no agreed cause exists. Past ideas leaned on the contacts or on spin-orbit coupling in the molecule. Recent tests point to the molecule itself, so the team starts there, with charge flowing in loops inside it.

That loop flow creates an orbital moment, a small internal magnetism. Its sign is set by the twist of the bonds, so it flips with the handedness of the molecule. Tests on heptahelicene show this moment can yield the seen spin effects and the odd response to magnetic fields, all within the standard rules. The model also predicts extra crossings in the current curves of mirror-image forms, which labs can check.
arxiv-2606-18165:
Hoffman and colleagues dissect a long-lived excited state inside the silicon-32 nucleus, in a 2026 nuclear physics paper. The state is a spin-trap isomer, stuck at spin five with negative parity because its natural decay route is heavily hindered. The team probed its single-neutron makeup at Argonne's ATLAS facility, firing deuterons at silicon-31 and watching the protons that emerge as silicon-32 forms, using the HELIOS spectrometer.

The transfer into the five-minus state is dominated by one orbital, the neutron 0f7/2 level, with a large spectroscopic factor confirming its single-particle character. The nearby three-minus state shows a much weaker share of the same orbital. Comparing with sulfur-34, the authors conclude the hindered decay in silicon-32 is not mainly an overlap problem between the two states. Proton participation, or its absence, is the likelier culprit.
arxiv-2606-18365:
Henze and Jiménez-Gamero study what happens to energy distance statistics, a family of tools for comparing distributions, as their tuning exponent shrinks toward zero, in a 2026 mathematical statistics paper. Their setting is data taking values in a Hilbert space, which covers functional data, not just number vectors.

After proper normalization, the distances converge to a logarithmic energy distance built from the logarithm of the distance between points. The authors show this limit keeps the key property that the distance is zero only when the distributions truly agree, and they connect it to Gaussian kernel discrepancies between distributions. Building on that link, they define a logarithmic Gini covariance for comparing several samples, derive its structure and behavior under both equal and differing distributions, and discuss permutation-based testing. The work opens a boundary case of energy statistics with ties to kernel methods and high-dimensional inference.
arxiv-2606-18865:
Mellinand and the team describe the design and first tests of the motorized mount for the first folding mirror of BlueMUSE, in a 2026 instrumentation paper. BlueMUSE is a blue spectrograph under development for the Very Large Telescope. The mount gives two degrees of freedom, tip and tilt. It exists to correct misalignments caused by environmental variation.

The chosen design converts motor motion into fine angular displacement. It uses a rack-and-pinion drive, an inclined ceramic slope, a ball-bearing contact, and a lever arm. That achieves the large motion reduction the precision budget demands. A stainless-steel prototype was made and measured. With a consistent homing-based operating strategy, repeatability reached about half an arcsecond on one axis, and a quarter arcsecond on the other. Both were inside the requirement. Stability measurements showed sensitivity to thermal effects and limits of the test setup, feeding design iterations.
arxiv-2606-18965:
Russell and colleagues study cooperation in 2026 in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with a restart rule. Partners play a run of games, but the pairing restarts when their moves clash. The population evolves by replicator dynamics, where fitter strategies grow in share. The puzzle is stark. Each agent gains by exploiting the other, yet mutual cooperation pays more for both if it can hold in a well-mixed group over time.

Each agent uses a fixed-length run of planned moves. Longer runs let cooperation emerge and stay stable, the authors show. They give exact guarantees for short lengths and key conditions for the general payoff case. One sharp result stands out. Stable runs must start with defection, a hazing phase, before switching to lasting cooperation. Agents also favor weaker runs with longer hazing, since those runs draw in more starting populations. That pull shapes how cooperation can spread.
arxiv-2606-19365:
Ryoo and colleagues analyze the performance of three-dimensional generative diffusion models across GPU architectures in 2026. Diffusion models are essential for high-fidelity three-dimensional medical image synthesis. Their deployment is constrained by heavy GPU demands. Each sample needs hundreds of network evaluations. The team profiles a state-of-the-art medical diffusion model on three generations of NVIDIA hardware.

Training turns out to be dominated by convolution and implicit matrix-multiply kernels from the cuDNN library. Inefficiencies come from memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core use. Guided by the profiles, the team tests two architecture-aware fixes. Turning on TF32 Tensor Cores and a channels-last layout cuts cycles and dynamic instructions sharply. Tensor Core use rises many-fold, and per-cycle throughput improves. Synthesis quality does not degrade. Profiling first, then tuning layout and precision, pays off.
arxiv-2606-19565:
Navin Ranjan and Andreas Savakis shrink vision-language-action robot models in 2026 without losing their reasons. Such models fuse seeing, language, and control in one policy, but their size blocks small robots. Quantization stores weights in fewer bits, and mixed precision gives sensitive layers more bits than sturdy ones.

Older methods judge layer sensitivity by final action drift alone. A shrunk model can match the motion while scrambling the evidence behind the choice. Mix-QVLA instead checks whether task-relevant evidence survives at key internal boundaries. Gradient-weighted evidence maps compare full-precision and quantized models on strength and spread. A soft-bottleneck score rolls boundary damage into layer sensitivity, tracked across task phases. On LIBERO tests, memory falls from about fifteen gigabytes to about four, while success holds near ninety-six percent. Inference also runs about one and a half times faster.
arxiv-2606-19765:
Davide Poderini and five colleagues chart sparse positive maps on qutrits with exact thresholds in 2026. Qutrits are three-level quantum systems, and positive maps on them detect entanglement. Sparse maps with tractable block structure allow exact analysis where general maps resist it.

Choi matrix blocks reduce positivity to a Hermitian biquadratic form. Exact positivity boundaries follow for three parametric families. The same families yield exact transitions between decomposable and non-decomposable maps. Two classes of positive-partial-transpose states come along with the analysis. One class deforms with the entanglement witnesses from the map study. The other gives clean families whose entangled branch is caught by fixed maps. Exact separability thresholds for bound entanglement drop out. A trace-preserving subclass comparison exposes the full gap between plain and higher-order positivity.
arxiv-2606-19965:
Yihao Wang, Zijian He, Jie Ren, and Keze Wang introduce ROSE in 2026, a benchmark exposing the gap between seeing and acting in multimodal models. The same scene can demand different actions under different instructions, and models often fail to switch. ROSE holds the visual scene fixed while varying region constraints and required symbolic outputs, pairing counting tasks with coordinate-action tasks on identical images.

Across nine recent multimodal models, scores fall by up to forty-five points from counting to region-based action, while humans stay near ninety-nine percent. The gap persists even where the same model counted the same region correctly. Control tests show coordinate grounding explains only part of the loss. A distinct bottleneck in turning shared evidence into context-specific action is isolated for future work.
arxiv-2606-20065:
Brand visibility inside AI search engines is measured at scale in a 2026 study built on Ranqo tracking data. People increasingly ask ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini instead of following blue links, so brands face a new contest called generative engine optimization. The study explains how to measure being represented, cited, and recommended by AI engines, and what those engines appear to value when they cite sources.

Over one hundred thousand prompt responses for more than one hundred brands, tracked from March to May 2026, form a three-tier ladder. Household names appear in about seventy-three percent of relevant first-run answers, mid-market brands in forty-four, and small brands in eleven. Corporate sites take about seventy-eight percent of citations, and ranked best-of listicles are the single most-cited format. The findings give smaller brands a first baseline.
arxiv-2606-20165:
Cloud microphysical process rates, the speeds at which droplets and ice particles form, collide, and melt inside clouds, are recovered here by machine learning after the fact. The 2026 study introduces PRecover, a post-processing tool for the ICON weather model. Simulations rarely store every process rate, because output volume is limited, which blocks deeper analysis of how rain forms and how aerosols affect clouds. PRecover trains random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks to reconstruct the missing rates from standard stored variables.

A two-step method first classifies whether a rate is active, then regresses its size. Some rates, like accretion, can be recomputed directly from stored fields, but others, like autoconversion, cannot. PRecover succeeded for most rates accumulated over ten minutes or less, reaching R-squared values near 0.66 for instantaneous rates. Heterogeneous ice nucleation resisted recovery. Calibrated prediction intervals and transfer tests round out the tool.
arxiv-2606-21165:
Juntong Peng and five colleagues present OmniV2X in 2026, a generative foundation planner for cooperative driving where vehicles share information with each other and infrastructure. Cooperative perception is costly. Data for cooperative scenes are scarce. Many fusion methods ignore standard messaging. Their model reads context sequences from many agents and modes directly.

A supervised pipeline trains with a downstream trajectory loss. A large generative sequence planner learns to use multi-modal inputs through cross-attention. Pretraining on large single-agent planning data comes first. Lightweight, standard-compliant vehicle-to-everything tokens then adapt it to cooperative settings. Results on a standard cooperative dataset beat existing end-to-end baselines. Efficient adaptation matters. Cooperative driving will roll out gradually, and models must join mixed traffic where only some vehicles share data.
arxiv-2606-21365:
Kexin Li, Xiao Hu, Ilya Grishchenko, and David Lie introduce LambdaMark in 2026, an audio watermark built to survive both tampering and reuse in voice cloning. Attackers fine-tune speech models on recordings to imitate a speaker. A useful watermark must therefore stay detectable in the audio, and also after a new model trains on watermarked sound, a property called radioactivity. Earlier marks sit in waveforms or spectrograms and wash out under such reuse.

LambdaMark embeds multi-bit messages into semantic audio representations, the learned features that carry meaning, using a light encoder and a decoder trained with a custom loss. Detection reaches 99.92 percent on LibriSpeech with 97.94 percent of bits recovered, and the mark survives every removal attack tested. It also remains detectable after fine-tuning several speech generators.
arxiv-2606-21565:
Noe Flandre, Alexander Nwala, and Philippe Giabbanelli propose checking agentic AI workflows at design time in 2026, before any agents run. Such systems chain language model agents, tools, and external actions, and today's platforms lean on runtime safeguards while design flaws go unnoticed. Borrowing from modeling and simulation, the authors treat a workflow as a composition of reusable building blocks whose fit can be verified in advance.

Twelve structural rules check whether composed blocks interact coherently. A prototype verifier was tested on forty-eight workflows with known design flaws and 168 logic-preserving structural variants. It reliably flagged violations even when flaws were hidden by splitting tasks across agents, a transformation that fools surface checks. The authors suggest pairing the verifier with community block libraries to assemble safer workflows by construction.
arxiv-2606-21765:
Lassounon, Belmiloudi, and Haddou study chemotherapy planning as a mathematics problem in 2026. Success against a tumour depends on delivering enough drug to kill invasive cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue, a balance that intuition alone handles poorly. The authors frame the dosing schedule as an optimal control problem, where drug concentration is the control that a planner may vary over time.

Tumour growth under treatment follows a nonlinear reaction-diffusion equation, a model of how invasive cells spread and react. The work begins with a careful analysis of that equation, then adds mixed constraints on both the drug levels and the state of the tissue. From there the authors derive first-order necessary conditions that any best schedule must satisfy. Numerical simulations for malignant lung tumours show the strategy can drive invasive cell density down under those constraints, demonstrating the approach on a concrete clinical case.
arxiv-2606-21965:
Aliyev and Aliyeva study, in 2026, a Sturm-Liouville problem, a classic eigenvalue problem for a vibrating-string-type equation, in which the spectral parameter appears linearly inside one boundary condition. Their focus is the root functions of the problem: the eigenfunctions plus the associated functions attached to multiple eigenvalues. Whether such a system is minimal, meaning no function can be dropped without shrinking its span, matters for expanding solutions in series.

Working through the problem's characteristic function, the authors obtain explicit formulas for the biorthogonal system and for several special associated functions. Those formulas let earlier criteria for basis and minimality properties be restated directly in terms of the characteristic function and its derivatives at the eigenvalues. Checking a concrete boundary value problem therefore becomes considerably simpler than before. Several worked examples show the approach in action and confirm it agrees with results already known in the literature.
arxiv-2606-22065:
Miao and colleagues show, in 2026, that boundary conditions can steer how fast an open quantum lattice system relaxes without changing its steady state. In such systems the boundary usually alters both the steady state and the Liouvillian spectrum, the set of decay modes governing relaxation, which makes the two effects hard to separate. Their setting is a disordered dissipative quantum link chain.

The steady state there is fixed by an accumulated field built from the link-by-link disorder, and the authors construct exact steady states from that field. They then design a reciprocal cyclic boundary condition that preserves the matter occupation profile while changing the nonzero Liouvillian spectrum. Open and cyclic chains therefore settle to the same reduced steady state, but the cyclic closure relaxes faster. In the strong-dissipation limit, the difference reduces to comparing exclusion processes with open and cyclic boundaries.
arxiv-2606-22165:
Kawakami and Tian introduce, in 2026, cumulative natural direct and indirect effects for causal mediation analysis with continuous treatments. Mediation analysis splits a treatment's effect on an outcome into a direct part and a part passing through a mediator. The standard natural effects can mislead, because they fail two properties of interpretable effects: skew-symmetry and additivity.

The new measures are built by splitting local causal effects, the average rate of change of the outcome as treatment varies, into local direct and indirect parts. The resulting measures decompose the total effect while preserving both structural properties. The authors extend the framework to ordinal treatments with discrete analogues over ordered levels. They prove identification results under standard causal assumptions. Behaviour is illustrated on canonical linear mediation models with interaction and on a real-world dataset.
arxiv-2606-22565:
Zhuoran Jin and seven colleagues, including Jun Zhao, test whether this reasoning style helps multimodal models in this 2026 paper. Chain-of-thought prompting makes models think step by step, aiding text-only reasoning. Whether the same holds when tasks involve images was unclear.

The team evaluated twelve tasks, split between perception and reasoning, on fourteen ordinary and eight reasoning models. It proved to be no free lunch. For perception tasks it caused side effects, reducing performance in visual grounding and object counting. For reasoning tasks, including mathematics, science, and multi-image problems, it genuinely helped. Open-source multimodal reasoning models gave only marginal gains over their base models, possibly because they overemphasize mathematics. The deepest problem is a pattern the authors call Look Light, Think Heavy: during reasoning, verbal reflection rises and falls, but visual reflection steadily fades. Models cannot yet keep inspecting the image deeply while they think.
arxiv-2606-22765:
Nima Dehghani asks what a reservoir computer should look like when evolution, not habit, picks its wiring, in this 2026 study. A reservoir is a fixed network of loops that turns past inputs into a rich internal state; normally only the readout layer is trained. Dehghani instead evolves the network itself, tuning five design settings to predict spatiotemporal chaos.

His test case is the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a standard chaos model. Evolution cut prediction error across the population and stretched the span over which forecasts stayed accurate. The best designs sat on a size-efficiency frontier with diminishing returns: past a point, bigger networks bought little. Their spectra stayed inside a shared envelope, and their grouping locked into a narrow middle band, with wiring cost falling fast inside it. Top designs combined accuracy and cheap wiring instead of trading one for the other.
arxiv-2606-22965:
Evgueni Doubtsov and Andrei Vasin work on composition operators in a 2026 paper in complex analysis. A composition operator takes a function and runs its output through another function. The paper compares two kinds of function spaces. One is the de Branges-Rovnyak space, built from a given bounded analytic function. The other is the Hardy space on the unit ball, a standard space of well-behaved analytic functions.

Doubtsov and Vasin ask when the operator between these spaces is compact. Compactness roughly means the operator squeezes bounded sets into ones with convergent subsequences, a strong form of good behavior. They connect compactness to limits on Nevanlinna counting functions. Those functions tally how often sliced versions of the inner map hit each value. Natural bounds on the tallies turn out to govern whether compactness holds.
arxiv-2606-23465:
Yuval Filmus gives a self-contained exposition of a theorem on Boolean degree one functions in a 2026 paper. The setting is the Grassmann scheme: all k-dimensional subspaces of a finite vector space. A Boolean function there outputs only zero or one. It has degree one when it is a weighted sum of point indicators, the variables marking which points a subspace contains. The obvious examples are constants and single variables. A subtler one detects subspaces orthogonal to a fixed vector. Ferdinand Ihringer proved that, under mild conditions, these are all of them when the space is large enough. The conditions need both the subspace dimension and its codimension to be at least two.

Filmus presents Ihringer's result with the details filled in, for readers who want the proof in one place. The paper is an exposition, not a new theorem.
arxiv-2606-23965:
Jiang proves a structural theorem about a class of generalized spaces, in a 2026 paper on higher geometry. L-infinity spaces generalize smooth spaces. They allow an L-infinity algebra in place of ordinary coordinates. Such an algebra is a hierarchy of brackets obeying coherence laws. Working over a differential graded manifold, Jiang shows these spaces form a category of fibrant objects. In such a category, abstract homotopy theory works without a full model category.

The proof moves the problem into algebra via the global sections functor. It adapts techniques for L-infinity algebras over a field to filtered settings. A companion paper equates these spaces with transitive L-infinity algebroids. The result therefore implies the algebroids also form a category of fibrant objects.
arxiv-2606-24065:
Shetty and Ghosh survey how to keep electrical substations running through extreme floods. Climate change is intensifying so-called 500-year storms, events with a small yearly chance but devastating impact. A large share of United States transmission assets already sits inside mapped floodplains, and hurricanes Harvey and Ida showed the cost of failure through huge outages and losses. Their 2026 review lays out an engineering framework for a resilient substation design.

Practical measures include raising site elevation, stabilising soil with lime and cement mixes, and armoring slopes with articulating concrete blocks that flex instead of cracking. Green infrastructure, deployable flood barriers, rapid dewatering, microgrids, and computer flood modelling round out the plan, aligned with standards such as ASCE 24 and FEMA guidance. The authors report that treated soils can gain large strength increases, while the combined strategies may cut lifecycle costs substantially while keeping power flowing.
arxiv-2606-24165:
Chen and colleagues judge visual tokens by how they change, not how they look at any single layer. Multimodal language models process hundreds of visual tokens through many transformer layers. Pruning the redundant ones speeds everything up. Existing pruners lean on signals from one layer only, such as attention or similarity. They ignore how a token's representation transforms across depth, and they inherit positional biases in the token sequence.

Cross-Layer Spectral Evolution, the team's training-free criterion, tracks each token in the frequency domain as layers progress. Representations travel from high-frequency structural detail toward low-frequency semantic abstraction. Tokens with stronger spectral redistribution are likelier to be semantically active, and worth keeping. Modelling that dynamic yields a stable importance score that resists positional bias. On image and video benchmarks, the method achieves a better efficiency-accuracy trade-off than single-layer rivals, even under aggressive token reduction.
arxiv-2606-24365:
Pang, Tian, Zhang, and Jiang compute how black holes in higher dimensions deform under fermionic tides. Tidal Love numbers measure how a compact object bulges in an external tidal field. Extending their earlier four-dimensional work, the team solves the massless Dirac equation around charged Reissner-Nordström black holes in D-dimensional spacetime. Ingoing coordinates and regular frames isolate the physical solution branch.

Reading the fermionic Love numbers from the solution's behaviour at infinity reveals a rich dimension-dependent structure. Bosonic Love numbers vanish for certain angular momenta in higher dimensions, a famous quirk. Fermionic ones stay nonzero for every angular momentum and every dimension from four upward. Extremal black holes at the charge limit are the exception. The dependence on angular momentum also weakens as dimension grows. It disappears entirely in the infinite-dimensional limit. Pang's 2026 results sharpen the picture of higher-dimensional black holes under fermionic tides.
arxiv-2606-24465:
Bäumler, Briend, and Jorritsma estimate node ages in a family tree seen only as an unlabelled shape. A uniform random recursive tree grows by attaching each new vertex to a uniformly chosen earlier one. Network archaeology asks the reverse: given the final structure alone, rank vertices by arrival time. Their 2026 study takes a pointwise view, analysing the full distribution of relative estimation error, rather than a single averaged risk.

For rankings induced by Jordan centrality, a classical balance measure, the probability of overestimating an arrival time by a large factor decays slowly, like one over that factor. Underestimation decays exponentially. A refined centrality measure sharpens the overestimation tail dramatically, at the price of a heavier lower tail. A trade off between the two error directions is exposed, one the earlier risk functional rendered invisible. The refined measure nevertheless attains the optimal order of the risk.
arxiv-2606-24565:
Paicu, Popa, and Rus solve an inhomogeneous version of the equation that detects inner products. The Jordan-von Neumann equation, a quadratic functional equation, characterises exactly those norms coming from an inner product. Its changed form replaces the zero right hand side with a given function of two variables. It asks which such functions admit solutions, and what they look like.

A smooth solution exists when the prescribed function is itself twice continuously differentiable, and satisfies a single three variable cocycle identity tying its values at different points. When those hold, the solution is exhibited in closed form: an integral expression built from the second partial derivative of the given function, along the first coordinate axis. The build preserves smoothness across smoothness classes, and across smooth and polynomial classes. Paicu's 2026 result converts an abstract existence question, for a classical functional equation, into one checkable identity plus one integral.
arxiv-2606-24865:
Lipika Kolay, Soumitra Nandi, and Shantanu Sahoo show how angular patterns in B meson decays could reveal invisible fermions. Some B decays end with a charged lepton, a D star meson, and something unseen. The unseen particle is normally a neutrino. It could instead be a heavier invisible fermion, such as a sterile neutrino or a dark sector particle. The authors work inside a general weak effective theory. They ask which measurements would expose the impostor's mass.

A massive invisible fermion leaves distinctive marks on the angular distributions of the decay. Kolay and colleagues identify observables with enhanced sensitivity to that mass. Those observables separate such scenarios clearly from the standard one. Other angular structures distinguish left handed from right handed currents linking leptons to the dark sector. Angular observables, the authors argue, turn a missing energy channel into a diagnostic tool.
arxiv-2606-24965:
Anirban Das, Joanne Boisson, and three colleagues automate the benchmarking of neural models. Reasoning over relational structures is hard for neural models, above all when test problems exceed training difficulty, and nobody knows what makes an instance hard. Their Project Auto-World attacks the evaluation problem itself. A world is parametrised by Datalog rules, and an Edge Transformer serves as the model under test. Two search strategies, LLM driven evolutionary search and autonomous agentic search, hunt for samplers that generate hard instances.

The discovered samplers produce hard problem sets. Training the Edge Transformer on this generated data improves it, and the gain generalises to further data changes. The same machinery runs on worlds proposed by language models. Das and colleagues present this as a step toward self directed research in the field. Benchmarks stop being artefacts written by hand; they become opponents that grow harder as the reasoner improves.
arxiv-2606-25165:
Accuracy loss is the standard way to measure catastrophic forgetting, but it only says whether forgetting happened. Ahmed Anwar and four colleagues argue that it saturates at the extremes and jumps at task boundaries, hiding the shape of what was lost. They propose six metrics derived from the softmax output, covering true label rank, predictive confidence, and distributional divergence, each normalised and needing no change to training.

On CIFAR-100 the metrics speak where accuracy is mute: among classes at zero accuracy, the Confusion Margin still spreads widely across classes that accuracy treats as identical. The signal is also usable. Weighting the loss by per sample metric scores cuts forgetting by 1.3 percentage points over uniform replay. Trend sampling over short windows works far better with the continuous metrics than with accuracy, and on TinyImageNet cuts forgetting by 7.7 points.
arxiv-2606-25265:
Approximating a distribution that cannot be sampled directly can be done by herding a swarm of particles toward high density regions. Vincent Pacelli, Akash Ratheesh, and Evangelos Theodorou introduce entropic transport descent in 2026, where each update solves a small optimal transport problem softened by entropy. The transport plan coordinates the whole swarm at once, steering every particle toward promising proposals while keeping distinct modes populated. Earlier particle methods push particles apart with kernel forces and often collapse in high dimensions.

Each iteration reduces to a standard Sinkhorn computation, and the method can run using only pointwise density values, with no gradient information at all. Across collapse diagnostics, logistic regression, neural networks, and molecular energy distributions, it matched or beat the leading alternatives. Gains were largest exactly where older methods struggle, in high dimensional and multimodal problems.
arxiv-2606-25465:
Restyling a video in a painterly look breaks easily: styles leak into the wrong objects, motion warps, and long clips drift. Huaqiu Li and colleagues present EchoStyle in 2026, a text driven framework that restyles videos of any length. Rather than condition on a reference image, a video to video design fuses the original content with the requested style described in words. The training data problem is attacked backwards, by synthesising stylised pairs automatically.

That reverse pipeline produced a dataset of twenty thousand high quality video pairs for training. For long videos, an opening segment sets the style and later windows follow it under a sliding inference scheme, holding motion steady. Across many artistic styles the system performed on par with leading closed source tools in the authors' comparisons, while keeping time consistency that earlier methods lose.
arxiv-2606-25565:
Black holes made of moving fluid, where flow faster than sound traps sound itself, mimic real gravity closely enough to test with telescopes. G Akhtaryanova, R Karimov, U Khidirov, and R Izmailov compute in 2026 how such acoustic black holes would bend light as microlenses in our galaxy. A passing lens briefly magnifies a background star, and the light curve's shape betrays the lens. One tuning parameter controls how the acoustic version departs from an ordinary Schwarzschild black hole, with three known black hole candidates supplying realistic masses.

Raising that parameter widened the Einstein ring, stretched each event's duration, and lifted peak magnification. Event rates also grew, so acoustic lenses should turn up more often in survey statistics than standard ones of the same mass. The authors present microlensing surveys as a practical channel for constraining analogue gravity models.
arxiv-2606-25665:
A model trained in several hospitals or climates should work in a new one it has never seen, the promise of domain generalisation. The standard trick forces the model's inner representation to look identical across all training domains. Tien-Hung Nguyen, Tien-Dat Tran, M.-Duong Nguyen, and Kok-Seng Wong argue in 2026 that this demand backfires. Each added domain shrinks the space of allowed representations. Useful predictive clues, stable in some domains but not all, get thrown away. Their alternative assumes structure is shared only within subsets of domains.

A mixture of experts implements the idea: each expert aligns just the domains it serves, and a router assembles the subset invariant parts for each prediction. Training goals push for selective alignment, confident balanced routing, and experts that genuinely differ. On DomainBed benchmarks the method generalised better out of domain and held up as the domains grew more varied.
arxiv-2606-25965:
Giulio Turrisi, Ozan Pali, Luca Oneto, and Claudio Semini build robot controllers that keep walking after something breaks. Legged robots sent to remote places, including planetary surfaces, cannot wait for repairs when an actuator fails. A single all-purpose control policy, trained by reinforcement learning, struggles to hold the many different gaits that different failures demand.

Fault information drives their design instead. Diagnosis output switches the controller among specialized expert policies, one per failure mode, in a mixture-of-experts layout. Across failure scenarios, these fault-conditioned modular policies beat single policies of similar size on locomotion performance. They also stay competitive when the network is shrunk substantially, which suits the tight computing budgets of space hardware. Code for the system is released through the team's laboratory repository.
arxiv-2606-26065:
Guangqian Zhao proves an operator estimate for centered Gaussian chaoses of second order. Such chaoses are built from products of Gaussian variables with their mean behaviour removed. The setting is continuous frequency rather than a discrete grid. Two Gaussian frequency legs, an input leg, and an output leg couple through a soft incidence kernel. Non-orthogonal profiles enter through covariance maps between Hilbert spaces.

Four oriented flattenings structure the proof. Rectangular Khintchine inequalities supply the random estimates. Soft-incidence Schatten bounds and dyadic summation over Sobolev-Besov scales finish the argument. A time lift yields operator convergence in the stated norms. A Galerkin assumption gives pathwise convergence by the first Borel-Cantelli lemma. Bounds of this kind keep the wildest terms in a hard equation under firm control. The theorem applies to a named branch of localized paracontrolled resonant products. That branch arises in singular stochastic equations.
arxiv-2606-27165:
Zuo describes a new trigger built for the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during its third run. Triggers are fast filters that decide which collisions are worth recording. Long-lived particles, hypothetical newcomers that travel far before decaying, often leave odd patterns that standard filters miss. When such particles decay inside the muon system, they spray unusually many hits across its cathode strip chambers. In the 2026 report, the High Multiplicity Trigger watches exactly that hit count.

Carefully tuned hit thresholds keep recording rates acceptable even when many collisions overlap. At the same time, efficiency stays high across wide ranges of particle lifetimes and motion patterns. Simulated samples and real proton collision data from the run both test the design. Performance holds steady under harsh high-luminosity running. Sensitivity to displaced muon-system decays grows substantially, giving future searches for physics beyond the Standard Model a flexible new tool.
arxiv-2606-27665:
Vue is a popular framework for building web applications. Testing its interfaces automatically is becoming important as the tools grow. Model-based testing needs a page transition graph to guide exploration. Building that graph for Vue is hard. Transition clues are scattered across router files and single-file components. Tao Li and five colleagues propose LLMVue in 2026 to build the graph with a large language model.

LLMVue infers component hierarchies and route transitions from source code. It merges them into one unified graph across components. Ten open-source Vue projects from GitHub served as the test set. GPT-4o was the language-model backbone. The built graphs showed high precision and recall. Their graph edit distance to reference graphs was low. Guided testing improved coverage and exploration efficiency against random exploration under the same time limits. The authors present the work as the first of its kind for Vue.
arxiv-2606-28065:
Shapley values explain a model's predictions by fairly dividing credit among inputs. Their cost at inference time blocks practical use, though. Joshua Stiller and three colleagues introduce OperatorSHAP in 2026 for neural operators, the models used across physics applications. Existing fast explainers assume uniform inputs. Physical data often live on irregular grids and shapes instead. OperatorSHAP is grid-agnostic. Its training fits FastSHAP-like explainers directly for operators.

A theory grounds them in function space. The method connects to Aumann–Shapley values, the continuous version. They match the best discrete Shapley values across resolutions. They also transfer across grid sizes without retraining. Training can mix datasets with mixed grids. The conclusion suggests swapping in stronger Shapley methods as they appear. Other methods could be lifted the same way. Safety-critical uses, from structural loads to clinical diagnosis, motivate the work.
arxiv-2606-28165:
Hannah Hata Williams, Michael E. Mueller, and Luc Deike revisit a basic tool of ocean science: formulas that describe how ocean wave energy is spread across wave sizes. Many formulas in daily use rest on data gathered more than fifty years ago, before modern instruments could map waves across space.

Williams and colleagues compare common formulas against newer field data from three kinds of sea: waves still growing near their wind source, fully developed seas, and mixed conditions. For fully developed seas, a formula whose tail fades more gently fits better than the classic versions. Feeding different formulas into a large simulation of air flowing over the sea changed the surface roughness as much as a real change in wave conditions would.
arxiv-2606-28365:
Adnan Qidwai, Anand Eswaran, Sonam Mishra, Jaydeep Sen, and Sachindra Joshi manage a costly choice inside search systems. Retrieval pipelines often enrich documents with generated summaries or synthetic questions to match how users ask, and each enrichment view helps retrieval. But testing every combination of view and generator across a whole corpus is prohibitively expensive.

Qidwai's team built CAMI, which treats index building as a budgeted portfolio problem. An agent proposes corpus-specific enrichment templates, small test units measure each view-generator pair cheaply, and promising pairs merge into portfolios under a confidence-aware promotion schedule. The framework repeatedly found high-recall portfolios under strict budgets. It beat content-only baselines on recall by up to about nine percent in hard settings, while spending up to five times less than random search.
arxiv-2606-28565:
Xiteng Yao, Taeho Kim, Hengzhi Pei, and seven colleagues simulate language-model serving down to the individual kernel, the small programs a graphics processor runs. Practitioners must forecast speed and cost across hardware and settings, but real benchmarking is slow, tied to one deployment, and hard to generalize as architectures evolve.

KernelSight-LM breaks every serving step into a roofline kernel model that carries a learned efficiency term, plus communication and host-overhead models. All are composed by a discrete-event scheduler that handles prefix caching and continuous batching. With no measurements from a new chip generation, per-kernel latency error lands near twelve percent. One quick microbenchmark sweep on the target cuts that to under four percent. End-to-end errors stay modest across six model families, and the kernel-level breakdowns guide hardware and software design.
arxiv-2606-28765:
Socci and colleagues map cosmic ray effects inside a dark, cold filament of gas and dust called G035.39-00.33, an infrared dark cloud. Cosmic rays, fast particles from space, drive chemistry in such clouds and link the gas to magnetic fields, but their ionization rate is hard to pin down. The team built a new analytical method that infers the electron share and the ionization rate from three nitrogen and carbon bearing molecules.

New observations from the NOEMA telescope array, at a sharpness matching about nine thousand times the Earth-Sun distance, covered the whole parsec-scale filament. Carbon monoxide was heavily frozen out across the cloud, rising with density. The electron share varied a hundredfold, following density as chemical models predict. Ionization rates in most fields averaged around a stated low value, well below many earlier estimates, hinting at weak cosmic ray penetration deep inside the cloud.
arxiv-2606-29165:
Prakash and Tsiotras present a method for estimating contact forces anywhere along a continuum robot, a flexible robot that bends continuously rather than at joints. Such robots suit unstructured environments, but safe operation requires knowing external forces at unknown points along the body. Several contacts at once make an ill-conditioned problem, where small measurement errors can produce wild force guesses.

Their framework estimates shape and forces together on a factor graph linking measurements and unknowns. A Gaussian mixture form describes the forces compactly, cutting dimensionality and easing the ill-conditioning. A discretised Cosserat rod model supplies the robot's mechanics.
