In test tubes, methylating the promoter stopped two activator proteins from switching the gene on. One temperature-sensitive spot is conserved across species, hinting at a general mechanism.
europmc-pmc3276165:
Bryan Howie, Jonathan Marchini, and Matthew Stephens developed a framework for genotype imputation with thousands of reference genomes, in this 2011 paper in G3. Imputation fills in unmeasured genetic variants in a study by copying from densely typed reference panels, boosting the power of association studies. As projects like 1000 Genomes made panels huge and diverse, choosing which reference haplotypes to use became a bottleneck.

Their approximation sidesteps panel selection: for each study chromosome and each genome region, local sequence similarity picks a custom set of the most useful reference haplotypes on the fly. That keeps computation manageable while using all available references, and it sharpens accuracy at low-frequency variants by catching unexpected sharing between populations. Tests on HapMap data and African malaria-network data showed accurate results across many populations. The method ships in the IMPUTE2 package.
europmc-pmc3279365:
Marta Navarrete and colleagues showed that astrocytes, the brain's support cells, actively help store information, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. Astrocytes were long cast as housekeeping cells for neurons, feeding and cleaning up around them. A newer view, the tripartite synapse, gives them a speaking role in synaptic signaling, and this study tested that role in the living brain.

Combining experiments in living mice with work in tissue preparations, the team examined synapses in the hippocampus, a center for memory. They found that astrocytes mediate a form of synaptic strengthening triggered by cholinergic signaling, the system engaged by attention-related transmitters. Without the astrocytes' participation, that plasticity did not proceed normally. The authors conclude astrocytes do not merely support information storage in the hippocampus; they take part in it directly.
europmc-pmc3292965:
Negrini led an international society of scoliosis specialists in updating treatment guidelines, published in 2012. The society, known as SOSORT, had issued its first guidance in 2005 for curved spines in growing children and teens. Members from many professions, plus a methods expert and a patient representative, reviewed the literature and debated drafts before agreeing on the final text at a 2011 meeting in Barcelona.

The guidelines give sixty five recommendations covering braces, targeted exercises, other non surgical treatments, breathing work, sports, and patient assessment. Braces and assessment draw the most recommendations. The authors are candid that strong research evidence is scarce in this field, with no recommendation backed by the highest grade of evidence, and they invite better studies.
europmc-pmc3302865:
Gallo, Tandon, Alevizos, and Illei tested where tiny regulatory RNAs in blood and saliva actually ride, in a 2012 study. These microRNAs are promising disease markers because they are easy to collect from body fluids, but it was unclear whether they float freely or travel packaged. The team separated tiny membrane parcels called exosomes from human serum and saliva and compared RNA amounts in each fraction.

Most of the measured microRNAs sat inside the exosome fraction rather than the leftover fluid. Some markers appeared only in exosomes and were missed entirely in whole serum. The authors advise future marker studies to start from exosomes, since skipping that step risks missing scarce signals and reporting false negative results.
europmc-pmc3304165:
Tao and co-authors reviewed how small wearable sensors can measure the way people walk, in a 2012 article. Watching gait helps doctors diagnose illness, guide recovery after injury, and judge sports performance, but lab based camera systems are costly and fixed in place. Sensors worn on the body promise the same information anywhere, at low cost.

The review first explains the phases of a step, then surveys the sensors available, including motion sensors and pressure sensors. It sorts analysis methods into those measuring body movement, ground forces, and muscle activity. Applications in clinics, rehabilitation, and sport are summarized separately. The authors expect wearable gait analysis to take a growing role in everyday medical practice as sensors and software improve.
europmc-pmc3318765:
Fleming and Dolan reviewed the brain basis of knowing how well you are performing, in a 2012 article. In any skill, people differ not only in how accurate they are, but also in how well their self judgments track that accuracy. Someone can be good at a task yet poor at sensing their own errors, or the reverse, and this self awareness is called metacognitive ability.

Evidence from memory and decision research shows that self awareness varies widely between people and can separate cleanly from task skill. Brain studies point to the front side areas of the prefrontal cortex, behind the forehead, as key for looking back and judging past performance. Judgments about future performance seem to lean on more central frontal areas instead. The authors sketch how these regions may work with inner body sensing areas to produce accurate self judgments.
europmc-pmc3349865:
Sollid and fellow immunologists proposed a shared naming system for the gluten fragments that drive coeliac disease. Research groups had described T-cell epitopes from wheat, barley, and rye proteins under inconsistent labels, making results hard to compare across laboratories and peptide variants.

Their proposal organises epitopes by the HLA-DQ molecule that presents them and the grain protein they derive from, covering the recognised DQ2- and DQ8-restricted sequences. A systematic nomenclature lets researchers state precisely which peptide a study used, including deamidated forms produced by tissue transglutaminase. The authors intend the scheme to tidy a literature central to understanding coeliac disease.
europmc-pmc3361365:
Perše and Cerar examined the dextran sodium sulphate model of colitis, one of the most popular ways to study inflammatory bowel disease in mice. The model is praised for its simplicity: adding the compound to drinking water produces gut inflammation resembling human disease, which makes it attractive for testing mechanisms and therapies.

The authors warn that the model's simplicity hides traps. Outcomes shift with the dose and molecular weight of the compound, the mouse strain, the gut microbes present, and husbandry conditions. Two laboratories can therefore obtain conflicting results from seemingly identical protocols. Their paper catalogues these variables and offers practical guidance for designing experiments and interpreting results consistently.
europmc-pmc3368265:
Maurer and co-workers asked in 2012 how certain proteins find the growing ends of microtubules, the hollow rails inside cells. End-binding proteins, called EBs, home in on those tips and pull other factors along with them. Nobody knew what feature of the tip they actually recognized.

Using cryo-electron microscopy and glowing-tag imaging, the team built a near-atomic model of the yeast EB protein Mal3 bound to a tip. Its grip bridges the tube's strands and sits beside the spot where the fuel molecule GTP is exchanged. That position lets it sense the tip's chemical state. The same region also caps the tube and guards it from falling apart.
europmc-pmc3409365:
Smink, van Hoeken, and Hoek reviewed in 2012 how often eating disorders occur and how deadly they are. The team searched the major medical databases for studies on incidence, prevalence, and mortality. Eating disorders are uncommon overall, but their patterns differ sharply by type, age, and sex.

Anorexia nervosa occurs fairly often among young women, and new cases in girls aged fifteen to nineteen have risen even as the overall rate held steady. Bulimia nervosa, by contrast, may have declined since the early nineteen nineties. Binge eating disorder is the most common of the group among men and older adults. All these disorders raise the risk of death, anorexia most starkly.
europmc-pmc3424165:
Cornman and co-workers surveyed honey bee colonies across the United States in 2012 to see which germs haunt collapsing colonies. Colony Collapse Disorder empties hives with unusual speed and spread, sometimes without signs of known disease. The team measured the presence and load of known bee pathogens in collapsing, weak, and strong colonies.

Collapsing colonies carried more kinds of pathogens, and in greater amounts, than healthy ones. Pathogen loads rose and fell together in collapsing hives but not in controls, hinting that infections either pile onto weakened bees or amplify each other. Deep RNA sequencing found new strains of Lake Sinai viruses and a shifted gut bacterial mix that may mark the disorder. Germ teamwork, they argue, belongs at the center of the story.

europmc-pmc5424465:
Dumas and co-authors review how to rewrite protein recipes with new chemical building blocks. Their review appeared in Chemical Science. Proteins are built from just twenty natural amino acids. That small set limits their chemistry. Adding unnatural amino acids can change the game. Such blocks can tune enzymes or act as probes. The trick is getting cells to insert them at chosen spots.

Most systems reassign codons, the three-letter words of the genetic code. A matched enzyme and tRNA pair does the insertion. The pair must ignore the cell's own machinery. Stop codons, above all the amber codon, are the usual targets. Quadruplet codons and sense codons offer other routes. The review sorts these designs by their logic. It weighs yields, cross-talk, and use in whole animals. Several unnatural blocks can now enter one protein.
europmc-pmc5482965:
Li and co-authors present a review in the Chinese Journal of Cancer on autophagy and drug resistance in cancer. Autophagy is a cell cleanup system that breaks down worn parts. During chemotherapy, it often switches on in tumor cells. Tumors that resist many drugs pose a major treatment problem. The authors examine how these two topics connect.

Autophagy plays a double role in resistant tumors, they explain. It can shield cancer cells from drugs and aid resistance. Yet it can also kill resistant cells when normal death pathways fail. Drug-driven autophagy may even restart death signals and reverse resistance. The review maps the main mechanisms and open questions. Researchers seek ways to tune this system.
europmc-pmc5529665:
Patel and Witt present a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity on a common membrane fat. Phosphatidylethanolamine, or PE, is the second most plentiful phospholipid in mammalian cells. It fills up to a quarter of cell lipid and crowds mitochondrial walls. Its small head group, ethanolamine, comes only from food. PE helps fold proteins and launch the cleanup process called autophagy.

The review traces PE through several disease settings. Strained cell compartments suffer when PE balance slips. Parkinson's disease and the cell death route ferroptosis both involve it. Cancer drugs also target PE chemistry. One modest lipid touches many systems.
europmc-pmc554765:
Escudier and co-authors present a phase I clinical trial report. Fifteen patients with advanced melanoma took part. Each received a vaccine made from their own dendritic cells. Tiny vesicles from those cells, called exosomes, carried a tumor peptide named MAGE3.

Patients got four vaccinations at one of two dose levels. The team reports no grade II toxicity, and the highest safe dose was not reached. One patient had a partial response by standard criteria. A few others had minor, stable, or mixed responses in skin and lymph nodes. Blood tests found no MAGE3-specific T cell response. Readers get an early safety record for exosome vaccines.
europmc-pmc5572465:
Huo and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications. They built a two-step catalyst that makes a toxic agent inside tumors only. Tumor cells use glucose in a distinct way and sit in a mild acid setting. The design turns those traits against the tumor.

A silica carrier holds a natural enzyme and tiny iron oxide particles. The enzyme drains glucose from tumor cells and makes hydrogen peroxide as it works. The iron particles then turn that peroxide into hydroxyl radicals. Those radicals are highly toxic and trigger tumor cell death. Normal tissue lacks the same conditions, so it should be spared. Readers get a proof of concept for selective catalytic medicine.
europmc-pmc5604965:
Tucker and co-authors pool patient-level data on blood pressure self-monitoring in PLOS Medicine. Many patients with high blood pressure now measure it at home. Whether that alone lowers pressure was unclear. The team gathered raw data from the trials themselves.

Data came from 25 trials, with over 7,000 people in the main analysis. Self-monitoring cut clinic systolic pressure by 3.2 points at 12 months. The catch was the support around it. Monitoring alone showed no clear effect. With intensive help, like guided dose changes or coaching, the drop reached 6.1 points. Gains were largest for people with higher starting pressure. Sex and most other illnesses made no difference. The lesson: pair home checks with active support. Readers get effect sizes by support level.
europmc-pmc5717765:
Larsson and co-authors test which changeable risk factors may help cause Alzheimer's disease. They use Mendelian randomisation, a method that uses genes as stand-ins for each factor. This design cuts the bias that can distort plain health surveys.

The study draws on the International Genomics of Alzheimer's Project. It covers 17,008 cases and 37,154 controls, and checks 24 factors in all. These span schooling, habits, diet, heart and metabolic health, and inflammation. Genetically predicted schooling links clearly to a lower risk of the disease. Signs for intelligence, smoking, vitamin D, and coffee were weaker and less sure. Most heart, metabolic, and blood factors showed no link. The results support more schooling as one route to lower risk.
europmc-pmc5778665:
Gong and co-authors review the rise of PD-1 and PD-L1 blockers as cancer immunotherapy. These drugs free T cells from a brake that tumors exploit. Early trials led to the first approvals in 2014 for two PD-1 drugs. Approvals have since spread across many cancers.

The review details the registration trials behind each approved use. It covers both PD-1 and PD-L1 agents now on the market. Open questions get a full section. They include markers that predict response, resistance, fast progressors, and immune side effects. Trial design and treatment length also need more work, they argue.
europmc-pmc5833365:
Shea and co-authors introduce AMSTAR 2, a checklist for judging systematic reviews of health care. Their paper appeared in The BMJ. Clinicians and policy makers lean on such reviews for decisions. Reviews can mislead when their methods are weak.

The first AMSTAR covered trials with random assignment only. Reviews now often include non-randomised studies too. AMSTAR 2 appraises both kinds with 16 items. It keeps 10 of the original domains and adds a fuller user guide. Seven items count as critical domains. Weakness there sets the overall confidence rating. The tool gives no single score by design.
europmc-pmc5844965:
Wang and co-authors explore pairing radiation with immunotherapy against cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Checkpoint drugs freed the immune system for some patients. Radiation, a local weapon, may widen that reach.

Blasted tumor cells spill antigens the immune system can learn. Radiation also remodels the tumor's surroundings for T cell entry. One pathway, cGAS-STING, sounds the alarm after radiation damage. Pairing the two has shown synergy in animal studies. Dose, timing, and extra side effects still block routine use. The authors sketch trials and tricks that may clear the path.
europmc-pmc5847565:
Mohanraj and co-authors built IMPPAT, a database of Indian medicinal plants and their chemistry. Their report appeared in Scientific Reports. India's healers have used plant remedies for centuries. That knowledge sat scattered in old books, hard to search.

The team curated 1,742 plants and 9,596 plant chemicals by hand. They mapped each plant to its compounds and traditional uses. Each compound also carries computed drug-likeness and safety scores. Their shapes differ from store-bought compound sets, yet match other natural products. Some 960 chemicals look druggable, most unlike any approved drug. It sits open online for drug hunters.
europmc-pmc5882965:
Han and co-authors make ultrathin bismuth sheets that turn carbon dioxide into formate. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. The sheets came from bismuth oxyiodide sheets changed in place. The new sheets are single crystals with large surface area. Bismuth had been little studied for this reaction. Tin rivals often gave poor selectivity.

The sheets reached near total selectivity for formate, they report. High current held across a broad voltage range. The catalyst stayed stable for over ten hours. Theory helped explain why formate was favoured. Paired with an iridium catalyst, the system ran full-cell electrolysis. Two AA batteries could power that cell.
europmc-pmc5952365:
Jacobs and co-authors give recommendations for cone beam computed tomography in implant dentistry. Their guidance paper appeared in BMC Oral Health. Dental CBCT gives three-dimensional images of jaws and teeth. It does so at fairly low radiation dose and cost. More than 85 devices are now on the market. Evidence for one machine may not fit another.

Dose and image quality vary hugely between machines and protocols, they note. Planning data can guide surgery through printing or navigation. But measurement accuracy also swings widely across systems. Patient motion and metal artefacts can spoil images. The authors argue each use needs clear justification. Settings should be optimised before clinical scanning.
europmc-pmc6029765:
Alipanah and co-authors review ways to help patients finish tuberculosis care. Their systematic review appeared in PLoS Medicine. Stopping treatment early risks failure and relapse. It can also breed drug-resistant forms of the disease. Many support methods have been tried worldwide.

The search found 7,729 articles in total. Of these, 129 studies fed the pooled analysis. Seven kinds of support were compared. Directly observed therapy worked better than self-given treatment. Community delivery beat clinic delivery on several outcomes. Education, incentives, reminders, and digital tools also helped. Video observation matched standard observed therapy in the data. Readers get a ranked guide to adherence support. Limits from varied study designs are noted plainly.
europmc-pmc6125665:
Wang and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience on a protein called CREB and schizophrenia. CREB sits inside brain cells and switches genes on. Dopamine, a key brain messenger, acts on it. The dopamine theory holds that dopamine signaling runs too hot in schizophrenia.

The review links CREB to that theory in several ways. CREB controls BDNF, a factor vital for brain growth and learning. Schizophrenia risk genes also feed into CREB. Its levels look abnormal in patient brains. Two gene variants were found only in patients. Animal work ties CREB to drug action as well. The authors propose it as a drug research target.
europmc-pmc6155865:
Federico and co-authors wrote a review in Molecules on silymarin, the extract of milk thistle, and chronic liver disease. Its main active compound is silybin. The extract has been used for liver disorders for many years. It is known for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects.

The review covers use in long-term liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Silymarin can soften the inflammatory cascade that drives virus-related liver damage. Given by vein, it also has a direct antiviral effect in hepatitis C. In alcohol-related disease, it raised cell vitality and cut cell death in studies. The authors sum up a long marriage between a plant extract and liver care.
europmc-pmc6199465:
Li and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Pharmacology on PDE4 inhibitors for inflammatory diseases. PDE4 is an enzyme found mainly in immune, airway, and brain cells. It shapes inflammation and the integrity of epithelial surfaces. Blocking it raises cAMP, a messenger that retunes many genes and proteins.

Three blockers have reached approval so far. Roflumilast treats inflammatory airway disease, apremilast treats psoriatic arthritis, and crisaborole treats atopic dermatitis. Trials in other conditions, including Behçet's syndrome, are also reviewed. Strong effects often come with adverse effects, which limit dosing. The review weighs that trade-off across the drug class and its many candidate compounds.
europmc-pmc6208165:
Tonelli and co-authors review how the protein Nrf2 is itself controlled. Their review appeared in Antioxidants and Redox Signaling. Nrf2 switches on a wide set of protective genes. Those genes build antioxidant systems and break down harmful chemicals. They also help cells recycle worn parts and handle energy use. Because Nrf2 reaches so many systems, its own activity is held under tight control.

Control works at many levels, from gene copying to protein breakdown. Signals from stress, food, and cell growth all feed into the system. The authors stress that Nrf2 sits at the centre of a large control network. Seeing that network whole may explain how it shifts in disease. That fuller view could point to safer ways to adjust Nrf2 in treatment.
europmc-pmc6282265:
Bashiri, Halper, and Orvieto review recurrent implantation failure in fertility treatment. Their review appeared in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology. The label covers women with three failed IVF attempts using good embryos. Causes can sit in the womb, the sperm, or the embryo itself. Age, smoking, weight, and stress all add risk. The IVF protocol in use can also play a part.

Workup should check immune signals and womb infection. Growths, birth defects of the womb, and sperm quality all need review. Treatment must then be tailored to the likely cause. The authors add an unusual suggestion. Planned pleasant activity may ease immune imbalance through brain reward paths. That idea awaits testing. The review joins standard care with that fresh angle. It gives clinics a full checklist for a hard problem.
europmc-pmc6293965:
Humphrey and co-authors report the SHINE trial in rural Zimbabwe. The cluster-randomised trial appeared in The Lancet Global Health. It tested cleaner water, sanitation, and hygiene, called WASH. It also tested better feeding for infants and young children. Pregnant women joined from 211 village clusters. Children were checked at 18 months of age.

The feeding program raised growth scores and blood haemoglobin. It cut stunting and anaemia in the groups that got it. The WASH package had no effect on either main outcome. Neither plan cut diarrhoea at 12 or 18 months. The authors conclude that basic household WASH alone is unlikely to fix stunting. Feeding support did the measurable good here.
europmc-pmc6302465:
Zhao and co-authors report early trial results for a CAR T cell therapy in myeloma. The phase 1 study appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. The therapy is called LCAR-B38M. It targets B cell maturation antigen on cancer cells. All patients had myeloma that had returned or resisted past care.

Fifty-seven patients received the engineered cells. Every patient had some side effect. Low white cell counts were the most common severe problem. Cytokine release syndrome hit 90 percent of patients. Most cases stayed mild or moderate. The overall response rate reached 88 percent. Two thirds of patients saw their cancer fully clear. Median time before disease advanced was 15 months.
europmc-pmc6363665:
Sheu and co-authors update treatment options for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae in Frontiers in Microbiology. Carbapenems are last-resort antibiotics for hard infections. Heavy use has bred gut bacteria that resist them, leaving doctors with very few choices.

Older drugs such as polymyxins and tigecycline remain mainstays, despite weak points. The review covers dose tricks, like long infusions and paired carbapenems, meant to stretch their power. It also surveys new antibiotics made for these resistant germs. Pairing drugs is a common theme across the options. The authors stress that new therapies are urgently needed.
europmc-pmc6383865:
Dekkers and co-authors present guidance in PLoS Medicine, called COSMOS-E. It tells researchers how to plan reviews of observational studies on causes of disease. No such overarching guide existed before, the authors say.

Observational reviews face traps that trial reviews do not. Defining exposures and judging bias need special care. The guide walks through each step, from shaping the question to pooling results. It was written by researchers with deep experience in the field. Clearer reviews should help readers judge which cause claims they can trust. Editors and funders can also use the guide to set reporting standards.
europmc-pmc6399265:
Hong and co-authors report a brain imaging study in Nature Communications on autism. Autism pairs weak social and high-level processing with strong sensory detail. The team asked whether that mix reflects a shift in how brain networks are ordered.

Brain scans at rest came from a large group of autistic and typical people. Steps between sensory areas and higher default mode areas differed in autism. The levels of the brain hierarchy were less sharply split. Follow-up tests linked the pattern to gene activity maps. The work frames autism partly as a disorder of network order.
europmc-pmc6440165:
Nourian Dehkordi and co-authors review stem-cell strategies for healing skin wounds, especially chronic wounds that stall and scar abnormally. Normal closure runs through coordinated phases of inflammation, growth, and remodeling, steered by growth factors and signaling molecules. When the sequence breaks, patients face repeated treatment and high costs.

Embryonic stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and adult stem cells each get a full appraisal of published healing results. Stem cells can speed closure and help regenerate skin structure rather than patch it. Drawbacks remain substantial, from safety and supply questions to the controversy around embryonic sources. The survey maps which cell types sit closest to routine clinical use.
europmc-pmc6449365:
Holmes and co-authors scan living brains for synaptic density in depression and PTSD, the first test of whether synapse loss tracks symptoms in people rather than in post-mortem tissue. PET imaging with the SV2A tracer UCB-J estimated nerve terminal numbers in 26 unmedicated patients with depression, PTSD, or both, plus 21 healthy controls.

Depression severity ran opposite to synaptic density: the most depressed patients showed clearly lower SV2A signal than controls. Density also tracked abnormal functional connectivity measured by MRI, tying structural loss to network disruption. The results give treatment developers a measurable target, since therapies that rebuild synaptic connections should move this marker if they work.
europmc-pmc6458265:
Michel and Brunet walk through the practical steps of EEG source imaging, the pipeline that converts scalp recordings into three-dimensional maps of brain activity. EEG is cheap, portable, and fast, timing neural events in the sub-second range, but its blurry spatial picture long limited it beside other imaging methods. High-density arrays, individual head models, and better algorithms changed that.

Each stage from data cleaning to forward modeling and inverse solutions is explained, with the free Cartool software as the running example. Model choices such as boundary element versus finite element head anatomy are compared, including a validation in 38 epilepsy patients. The guide targets clinicians moving beyond waveform reading.
europmc-pmc6483965:
Cage and Troxell-Whitman survey 262 autistic adults about camouflaging, the masking of autistic traits to pass in social life. Reasons clustered around fitting into a neurotypical world and avoiding retaliation; women more often endorsed conventional motives like getting by at work. Mental health context is stark, with one cited study finding 79 percent of autistic adults had a diagnosable condition.

Both heavy camouflaging everywhere and switching it on and off between contexts tracked poorer mental health. Free-text answers voice exhaustion and compulsion, masking done so long it cannot be turned off, felt as protection yet resented. The findings argue camouflaging belongs in clinical conversations about autistic wellbeing.
europmc-pmc6523365:
Young, Sandman and Craske review emotion regulation in adolescence. Their review appeared in Brain Sciences. Emotion skills grow fast across the teen years. The same years bring high risk for new anxiety and depression. Both disorders tie to poor control of positive and negative feelings.

The authors sort evidence by measure type. Self-report studies show firm links between poor regulation and symptoms. Behavioural and body-signal studies give mixed results. Some point to weak reappraisal skill in anxiety. Brain imaging studies implicate amygdala and prefrontal circuits. Their exact patterns still vary. The authors urge designs that split strategies apart. They also discuss training single strategies in treatment.
europmc-pmc6562165:
Twohig-Bennett and Jones pool the evidence on greenspace and health in a systematic review and meta-analysis for Environmental Research. Claims for parks and greenery stretch back to the 1800s, but no one had quantified them across outcomes at this scale. The pair screened five databases and kept 103 observational and 40 interventional studies covering about 100 health measures.

More greenspace exposure tracked with lower stress hormone levels, slower heart rate and lower blood pressure. Risks of preterm birth, type II diabetes, cardiovascular death and death overall all fell, while self-rated good health rose. Stroke, hypertension, asthma and coronary disease also eased. The authors flag uneven study quality, yet urge planners to protect and extend green space, especially in deprived areas.
europmc-pmc6562565:
Vigano and co-authors review adenosine, a metabolic brake on anti-tumor immunity, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. Stressed, oxygen-starved tumors leak ATP, and enzymes named CD39 and CD73 convert it stepwise into adenosine. In healthy tissue adenosine briefly calms inflammation after injury. In tumors it lingers, and the calm becomes a shield.

Adenosine dulls T cells, natural killer cells and dendritic cells while strengthening regulatory and suppressor cells. The review maps how levels are controlled, how its receptors signal, and what it does to each cell type around a tumor. It closes with the counterattack: drugs blocking CD39, CD73 or adenosine receptors, which in early studies restore T-cell attack, especially alongside checkpoint blockade or cell therapy.
europmc-pmc6570665:
Czepiel and co-authors review Clostridium difficile infection for the European Journal of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases. The spore-forming gut bacillus, since renamed Clostridioides difficile, has grown into one of the most common hospital-acquired infections worldwide. Its spores travel the fecal-oral route and survive for months on surfaces.

Antibiotics are the great enabler, clearing rival gut microbes; old age and hospital or nursing-home stays stack the risk further. Illness ranges from silent carriage through diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. Diagnosis rests on finding toxins in stool, though no single test stands alone. Vancomycin and fidaxomicin now lead treatment, with metronidazole demoted, and the review gives special attention to fecal microbiota transplantation for stubborn, returning cases.
europmc-pmc6598765:
Meers and co-authors present three upgrades to CUT&RUN, a chromatin profiling method. Their methods paper appears in eLife. CUT&RUN maps where proteins sit on DNA. It uses an antibody plus a nuclease fusion protein. The approach needs far less sequencing than ChIP methods. It also works with very small cell numbers. Still, the fusion protein was hard to purify. Digestion timing was touchy as well.

The first upgrade is a hybrid protein A and G construct. It binds more antibody types and purifies with a simple tag. The second tweaks digestion to stop early release of complexes. That change cuts background while raising yield. The third uses stray E. coli DNA as a built-in calibrator. Together they make routine profiling easier to standardise.
europmc-pmc6635665:
Shim and co-authors explain how to run a network meta-analysis in R. Their methods article appears in Epidemiology and Health. A network meta-analysis compares many treatments at once. It blends direct trial results with indirect evidence through shared comparators. That reach exceeds what pairwise pooling can do.

The authors walk through two modeling routes. The Bayesian route uses the gemtc package with rjags for simulation. The frequentist route uses the netmeta package. They report effect sizes, heterogeneity checks, and moderator effects. Publication bias tests are included as well. Worked output shows each step in practice. The guide targets researchers without a statistics major. It favors hands-on method over theory throughout.
europmc-pmc6668865:
Wu and Cederbaum review how alcohol drives oxidative stress and free radical damage. Their article appears in Alcohol Research and Health. Reactive oxygen species arise naturally during metabolism. In excess they damage fats, proteins, and DNA. Alcohol promotes their production in several ways. Its breakdown in the liver spawns radical-forming molecules. It also stimulates cytochrome P450 enzymes. Metal balance shifts add further radical output. At the same time, alcohol drains antioxidant defences.

The resulting oxidative stress injures liver cells centrally. The review explains radical chemistry in plain terms. It then covers the cellular systems producing the species. Protective systems and their failure modes follow. The authors close with alcohol injury mechanisms and research directions.
europmc-pmc6695865:
Duni and co-authors review oxidative stress in chronic kidney disease. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Oxidative stress builds from the earliest disease stages. Kidney pro-oxidant enzymes generate excess reactive species. Oxidation products build up as defences weaken. Podocyte damage and proteinuria follow. Scarring of glomeruli and tubules develops downstream. Vessel oxidative stress impairs kidney self-regulation. Inflammation and oxidation reinforce each other. NF-κB activation in that milieu drives cytokines.

Evidence spans several kidney disease models. Diabetic and IgA nephropathy feature in the set. Polycystic disease and cardiorenal syndrome also appear. The authors treat the topic as a whole. Frameworks for intervention are their closing aim.
europmc-pmc6784865:
Integrative HMP (iHMP) Research Network Consortium describe the second phase of the Human Microbiome Project. The U.S. National Institutes of Health ran the project over ten years. Its goal was to link human-microbe interactions to health. Phase two, the Integrative Human Microbiome Project, followed dynamic changes in microbes and hosts under three conditions.

The conditions were pregnancy and preterm birth, inflammatory bowel diseases, and stressors in people with prediabetes. The studies begin to reveal how host and microbiome talk to each other. In pregnancy, certain vaginal microbes and inflammatory signals tracked with preterm birth risk. All data sit at a public coordination center. The project sets a pattern for future multi-omic microbiome studies.
europmc-pmc6796665:
Olusanya and co-authors argue for revising how hearing loss grades align with the international classification of functioning. Hearing impairment is a major cause of years lived with disability. The World Health Organization counted 466 million people with disabling hearing impairment in 2018. That figure is projected to reach 630 million by 2030 and over 900 million by 2050.

The projections rest on a grading system set in 2008. The authors say it does not fully match the functioning classification's view of impairment. They trace the system's history back to a 1976 assembly decision. One change already made lowered the mild threshold from 25 to 20 decibels. People below 20 decibels rarely use hearing aids, a fact supporting the cutoff.
europmc-pmc6816165:
Alonge and co-authors present a software tool in Genome Biology. Genome assembly often yields many short pieces called contigs. To read a genome well, those pieces must be ordered into full chromosomes. RaGOO does that job by aligning contigs to a finished reference genome. It uses the fast aligner Minimap2.

The authors show RaGOO ordering three draft tomato genomes, including the widely used M82 line, in minutes. After building the chromosome-scale sequences, the tool also flags structural variants, even across gaps. They then applied it to 103 strains of the small plant Arabidopsis. That scan showed that genes for defence were among the most variable in the group.
europmc-pmc6861865:
Hamidian and Nigro review a hospital pathogen's rise, in Microbial Genomics. Acinetobacter baumannii infects vulnerable patients in hospitals worldwide. It has grown resistant to many antibiotics, including carbapenems, a class held in reserve. That resistance now counts as a global threat. The review traces how it emerged and spread.

Most resistance comes from acquired genes for enzymes that destroy carbapenems. One gene, blaOXA-23, dominates in most countries, while others lead in certain regions. Spread rode mainly on two worldwide clones, though new lineages now appear. Analysing all public genomes, the authors find four sequence types accounting for most isolates. They chart where each clone and gene prevails.
europmc-pmc6969065:
Franzmeier and co-authors link the brain's wiring pattern to how fast tau protein builds up in Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Tau tangles track closely with mental decline. Evidence hints tau spreads between connected neurons, helped by their activity.

The team combined resting brain scans with repeated tau imaging in two independent samples. They covered 53 patients and 28 controls in one, and 41 patients and 16 controls in the other. Patients accumulated tau faster than controls. Where two of 400 brain regions were strongly connected, their tau levels rose in step. A model using wiring plus starting tau predicted future spread. The results support spread along connections, and may help forecast each patient's course.
europmc-pmc7005265:
Cruz and co-authors review lipid droplets as active players in cancer. Their review appeared in Cell Death and Disease. Lipid droplets are fat-rich packages inside cells. They handle energy storage, signalling, membrane traffic, and the making of inflammatory compounds. They pile up in many cell types during inflammation and disease.

Cancer cells often carry more of them, though whether that build-up helps cause tumours or follows from them is unsettled. The droplets feed growth, help cells dodge death, and shape talk between tumours and nearby tissue. The review walks the droplet through the classic hallmarks of cancer: inflammation, altered metabolism, fast growth, death resistance, and low oxygen. Open questions close the piece, including whether blocking droplet formation could become a treatment.
europmc-pmc7059165:
Yousefzadeh and co-authors track senescent cells through ageing mouse tissues in Aging Cell. Senescent cells, worn-out cells that stop dividing, build up with age and promote ageing through inflammatory secretions. Mice lacking full levels of the DNA repair enzyme ERCC1-XPF age rapidly under spontaneous genetic stress. The team asked whether those mice also pile up senescent cells faster.

Two marker genes, p16Ink4a and p21Cip1, ran about 15-fold higher in blood lymphocytes of young mutant mice than normal, matching levels in old wild-type mice. The same markers were raised in 10 of 13 tissues in the mutants, and aged normal mice showed increases in the same 10 tissues. Other signs agreed: a senescence enzyme activity rose, and Lamin B1 fell. The pattern is tissue-specific rather than uniform, peaking in organs such as the lung. The study shows where DNA damage drives senescence in the body.
europmc-pmc7069465:
Leng and co-authors report a small cell-therapy trial in Aging and Disease. Severe COVID-19 pneumonia can turn deadly when the immune system erupts in a cytokine storm. Mesenchymal stem cells are known to calm and rebalance immune activity. The team transplanted cells, chosen to lack the ACE2 receptor the virus uses, into 7 patients treated at Beijing YouAn Hospital between 23 January and 16 February 2020.

All seven patients improved without adverse effects, and lung function and symptoms were significantly better within 2 days of the infusion. Two ordinary cases and one severe case recovered and were discharged within 10 days. Blood tests showed lymphocytes rising and C-reactive protein falling. The overactivated immune cells driving the storm vanished within 3 to 6 days, while a regulatory immune cell population sharply increased. The authors present the approach as a way to cure or ease severe disease while larger trials are arranged.
europmc-pmc7077965:
Toepfer and co-authors explain a muscle protein's rest states in Circulation. Heart muscle contraction runs on myosin motors that also need to switch off. Myosin molecules rest in two conformations: a super relaxed state that saves energy, and a disordered relaxed state ready for work. The proportion held in each state tunes heart performance and energy conservation over a lifetime.

Mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy disturb that balance, shifting myosins out of the energy-saving state. Patient-derived heart cells carrying such mutations show abnormal contraction, relaxation, and metabolism, and the imbalance tracks with higher risks of heart failure and atrial fibrillation. A small molecule restored the normal proportions and improved the functional, energetic, and cellular defects. Knowing which amino acids hold the rest-state interactions also helps classify variants of unknown significance. The work reframes a common inherited heart disease as, in part, a failure of motors to rest.
europmc-pmc7136165:
Kline and co-authors present the first international consensus statement on diagnosing and managing Cornelia de Lange syndrome, in Nature Reviews Genetics. The syndrome brings intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, limb differences, and unusual growth. It is caused by variants in any of seven genes, all tied to the cohesin complex.

An international expert group set out shared diagnostic criteria for both classic and non-classic forms of the condition, which affects an estimated 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 30,000 live births. Guidance covers genetic testing routes, long-term management, and care planning. Practice had varied widely between countries, the authors note. A single agreed standard aims to make diagnosis faster and care more even.
europmc-pmc7136965:
Cavaillon, Singer, and Skirecki ask why 30 years of sepsis research produced no drug that clearly improves patient survival, in EMBO Molecular Medicine. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, is a World Health Organization global health priority. Thousands of animal studies looked promising, yet none carried into patients.

The authors blame two recurring errors: enrolling the wrong patients in trials and using animal models that poorly mimic human sepsis. They argue against repeating those mistakes and propose a changed research pattern, with hypotheses tested in relevant long-term models. Long-term damage in survivors gets attention too, along with old and new treatment leads that might still save lives.
europmc-pmc7156565:
Fiorillo and Gorwood assess the mental health effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and what they mean for doctors' practice, in European Psychiatry. Psychiatric services everywhere were reshaping care as the pandemic spread. The authors call the pandemic a new kind of stressor. Unlike an earthquake it has no single place or end. Unlike a war, the threat is invisible and can be carried by anyone nearby.

Four groups face the heaviest burden: people exposed to the virus, people already at risk, health staff, and heavy consumers of pandemic news. More mental illness, disturbed behaviour, and substance use are expected in the months ahead. The piece offers simple protective advice for the public and urges services to plan for the surge.
europmc-pmc7185265:
Harper and co-authors test whether fear of COVID-19 pushes people to follow public health advice. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction. They recruited an international community sample of 324 people. Participants rated their fear of the virus and their sense of personal risk. They also answered questions on morals, politics, and behavior changes.

Fear of the virus stood out as the consistent predictor. People who feared it more reported more protective behavior. Moral views and political leanings explained little on their own. The authors call this fear functional when it leads to safer habits. Their results suggest health messages work partly through emotion. The study adds a psychological angle to pandemic planning. It also cautions that fear must stay tied to useful action.
europmc-pmc7219965:
Datta and co-authors review fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy, a technique that reads the timing of light from glowing molecules. Their article appeared in the Journal of Biomedical Optics. Each fluorescent molecule stays excited for a characteristic time before releasing light. That lifetime reveals its chemical surroundings. Color-based imaging alone cannot show those differences.

The review explains the physics behind the measurement. It surveys the instruments used to capture lifetimes pixel by pixel. Analysis methods turn raw timing data into biological meaning. Applications include tracking disease progression and judging whether a drug works. Images of tumor organoids show metabolism readouts from the method. The authors highlight recent advances that make lifetime imaging faster and more practical for clinics.
europmc-pmc7376165:
Blume and co-authors present a faster way to profile blood proteins in Nature Communications. Plasma holds thousands of proteins, but the most abundant swamp the rest, limiting deep surveys. Their trick uses engineered nanoparticles: proteins coat each particle in a corona pattern that depends on the particle's surface.

From 43 candidate particles they chose a panel of 5 whose combined coronas reveal more than 2,000 proteins. The workflow runs 141 plasma samples in 96-well plates with automation, and signal scaled linearly in spike tests. A pilot study classified lung cancer samples with the profiles. Readers get a platform that trades exotic instruments for clever surfaces, aiming at large, precise protein studies.
europmc-pmc7512065:
Khatana and co-authors explain how oxidized low-density lipoprotein drives atherosclerosis. Faulty blood lipids play a lead role in this artery disease. It underlies most heart attacks and strokes worldwide.

Oxidized LDL gathers in the artery's inner layer and triggers disease onset. Plaques build over time in medium and large arteries. When a plaque ruptures, a clot can block blood flow at once. That block causes heart attack, stroke, and other grave events. The review maps the atherogenic steps driven by oxidized LDL. It then surveys ways to slow the process. Lowering LDL, statin treatment, and wider lipid control lead the options. The authors say the treating tools still lag the clear mechanism picture.
europmc-pmc7515865:
Liu and co-authors review the PI3K/AKT pathway as a key link in multidrug resistance of cancers. Multidrug resistance is the dominant cause of chemotherapy failure. PI3K is a lipid kinase that spreads signals inside cells.

Its partner AKT carries the signal onward in the chain. AKT blocks cell death, drives growth, and reshapes cell metabolism. When this pathway stays overactive, tumors shrug off many drugs at once. The review maps the pathway's main resistance targets. They include drug efflux pumps of the ABC family and death-related proteins. Links with NF-kappaB, mTOR, and sugar burning add more paths. The authors say grasping this hub is key to reversing resistance. Future work must pin down exact control points in each tumor type.
europmc-pmc7542465:
Yang and co-authors review targeted therapy advances for esophageal cancer. Standard care uses surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Results remain poor and side effects can be severe.

Targeted drugs act on growth receptors and blood vessel signals. Cetuximab targets the EGFR pathway in tumors. Bevacizumab targets VEGF and vessel growth. Trastuzumab serves patients with HER-2 positive cancer. Pembrolizumab helps some patients with PD-L1 positive disease. Drugs can be used alone or with other care. Dose, safety and best pairings still need study. The review gives a clinical base for precision care in this cancer.
europmc-pmc7618965:
Datoo and co-authors report a phase 3 trial of the R21/Matrix-M malaria vaccine in African children. An earlier phase 2b trial showed over 75% efficacy with seasonal dosing. The larger trial tested safety and efficacy at scale.

The trial ran at five sites in four African countries. Children aged 5–36 months were enrolled for the study. A total of 5477 children were screened for entry. Of those, 3434 got the malaria vaccine. Another 1705 got a control rabies vaccine. A total of 4878 children received a first dose. Three doses were given 4 weeks apart. A booster followed 12 months after the third dose. The vaccine was well tolerated in the trial population.
europmc-pmc7710765:
Webster and co-authors review inflammation as a cause of muscle loss in cachexia. Cachexia is the involuntary loss of muscle and fat seen in cancer and chronic disease. It raises death rates and blunts treatment. No specific therapy exists for it yet.

Inflammatory signals such as TNF-alpha and IL-6 run high in many patients with this wasting. These signals can act direct on muscle, cutting protein building and raising breakdown. They can also work through the brain, gut, and liver to suppress appetite and shift fuel use. Muscle itself releases signals that feed the loop. The authors call for markers that can catch cachexia early.
europmc-pmc7726165:
Mohanan and co-authors review microbes and enzymes that can break down synthetic plastics. Common plastics such as polyethylene and PET resist natural decay for decades. Some microbes can attack them, at least in lab tests. Their enzymes have in some cases been cloned and read in full.

Breakdown speed depends on the plastic's structure, weight, and crystal share. Enzymes first stick to the surface, then cut the polymer bonds. Sources include microbes from many habitats and the guts of some invertebrates. The authors see a path to recycle plastic into monomers or turn waste into products of higher value.
europmc-pmc7759465:
Walkowiak and co-authors sequence many wheat genomes to expose variation from world breeding. Wheat feeds the globe, but its genome is huge and complex. Past work lacked assemblies for multiple lines. The team built ten full chromosome assemblies and five scaffold assemblies of hexaploid wheat.

Comparison showed wide structural rearrangements between lines. Chunks from wild kin had been bred in for local adaptation. Gene content differed thanks to complex breeding pasts aimed at yield, quality, and stress resistance. The authors map the gene set for disease resistance in detail. They also pin down a gene tied to insect resistance, as proof of the resource's worth.
europmc-pmc7801665:
Christensen and co-authors show that perineuronal nets keep the grid cell network stable. Grid cells help animals navigate and remember space. Their tidy firing patterns appear late in development. Perineuronal nets form around the same time. These matrix webs wrap around inhibitory neurons.

Removing the nets lowered inhibitory cell activity. Grid cells then built weaker maps of a new space. Stored maps of a known space were also corrupted. Relations inside grid cell groups broke down. Downstream hippocampal cells showed distorted spatial signals too. The authors conclude that the nets are a key steadying part of the network.
europmc-pmc7831265:
Marofi and co-authors review CAR T cell therapy for solid tumors, with its blocks and open chances. CAR T cells are immune cells fitted with a built receptor. The receptor has a targeting head taken from an antibody. Inside the cell, it carries activation signals. The therapy has reshaped blood cancer care.

Solid tumors resist this treatment in many ways. The engineered cells struggle to enter dense tumor tissue. The tumor setting shuts down their attack. Safe targets on solid tumors are scarce. The authors sort these hurdles one by one. They also gather the fixes now in testing. Smarter receptors and combo treatments lead the list. The review aims to guide the next design round.
europmc-pmc7862065:
Kantarjian and co-authors report ten years of the ENESTnd trial in chronic myeloid leukemia. The trial set two drugs head to head as first care. One arm took nilotinib, and the other took imatinib. All patients were newly found to have the disease in its chronic phase.

Nilotinib gave deeper responses over the ten years. More patients hit the deep response marks that let some stop care. Disease worsening and deaths from the leukemia were less common on nilotinib. Overall survival at ten years was near nine in ten patients in all arms. Side effects were much alike for the two drugs in most ways. Heart and blood vessel events were more common with nilotinib. The authors back nilotinib as first care for most patients who aim to one day stop treatment.
europmc-pmc7916865:
Sachdev and co-authors present a review of reactive oxygen species in plants under abiotic stress. Plants cannot move away from drought, heat, or salt. Climate change is making those stresses stronger and longer. Plants turn 1–2% of the oxygen they use into reactive oxygen species. These by-products form in chloroplasts, mitochondria, and other cell parts.

At low levels, the species act as signals that help plants adapt. Under stress, their output surges past what plant defences can clear. The burst then damages key molecules and upsets cell balance. The review maps where the species are made and how they signal. It covers the enzyme and non-enzyme systems that keep them in check. New tools such as molecular priming and phenomics close the account.
europmc-pmc7920465:
Sallam presents a systematic review of COVID-19 vaccine acceptance rates worldwide. A vaccine campaign works only if the public accepts the vaccine. Acceptance among health workers matters just as much. The review gathers survey results from the first year of the pandemic to map that acceptance across countries.

The search covered peer-reviewed surveys indexed in PubMed to late December 2020. Results from 31 studies formed the final estimates, drawn from 33 countries. Ecuador led general public acceptance at 97.0%. Kuwait sat lowest at 23.6%. Most country surveys still showed acceptance at or above 70%. Among health workers, rates also varied widely by country. The author warns that low acceptance in some regions could stall control of the pandemic.
europmc-pmc8007165:
Nogal and co-authors examine how short-chain fatty acids link gut microbes, diet, and cardio-metabolic health. Gut bacteria ferment resistant carbohydrates from food into these fatty acids. Fiber-rich and omega-3-rich diets raise their production. The acids help guard the gut barrier and shape glucose and fat metabolism. They also tune the immune system, inflammation, and blood pressure.

The review first ties gut microbe imbalance to diseases such as type-2 diabetes and obesity. It then sets out what acetate, propionate, and butyrate each do. Last, it weighs diets that boost fatty acid output. The aim is care that improves heart and metabolic health through the gut.
europmc-pmc8012365:
Singleton and co-authors recover over a thousand microbial genomes from activated sludge. Microbes do the real work in wastewater treatment, from breaking down waste to recovering resources. Yet their genomes were mostly missing, so community data could not be tied to function. The team sampled 23 Danish full-scale treatment plants. They combined long-read and short-read sequencing.

The authors report 1,083 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes. Among them sit 57 closed circular genomes. The genomes cover roughly 30% of the community by abundance. All meet strict quality standards, with full-length rRNA genes. Paired with over 13 years of marker-gene data, they exposed abundant undescribed lineages. Several belong to groups that matter for plant performance.
europmc-pmc8039965:
Cao and co-authors test stem cell exosomes as a repair treatment for ischemic kidney injury. Exosomes from mesenchymal stem cells promise cell-free therapy for acute kidney injury. Where the vesicles go in the body, and how they heal, stayed unknown. The team used human umbilical cord stem cells as the source. Imaging tracked the vesicles in mice with ischemia-reperfusion injury.

The vesicles homed to the injured kidney and settled in proximal tubules. Surface proteins VLA-4 and LFA-1 guided that targeting. Treatment eased the injury in a dose-dependent way. Tubule cells escaped cell cycle arrest and apoptosis alike. The cargo molecule miR-125b-5p did the work by repressing p53. Blocking that microRNA erased the benefit. The study names both a vehicle and a mechanism.
europmc-pmc8158965:
de Melo and co-authors link COVID-19 loss of smell to lasting virus and inflammation. They studied the olfactory epithelium in people and in hamsters. Smell loss was a hallmark symptom early in the pandemic.

The team found SARS-CoV-2 persisting in the olfactory epithelium for months. Inflammation stayed with it in that tissue. Hamsters also showed infection reaching the brain. The work helps explain why smell loss can linger long after other symptoms fade. It raises care in judging claims about the virus in nerve tissue. Samples came from both human tissue and the hamster model.
europmc-pmc8295265:
Hu and co-authors present flDPnn, a tool that predicts disorder in proteins and its functions. Disordered regions do much work in cells. Computer prediction carries most of the load in finding them.

The tool predicts plain disorder and fully disordered proteins. It also predicts four common disorder functions. Tests in the CAID assessment showed strong accuracy. Other datasets backed the result. Speed counts as a design goal as well. Coupling disorder with function sets the tool apart. Protein researchers gain richer maps from sequence alone. Four disorder functions are covered beside disorder itself.
europmc-pmc8475765:
Barbara and co-authors explain how inflammation and gut microbes govern the intestinal barrier. This barrier is one of the body's largest contact zones with the outside world. It must block harmful antigens and microbes while letting nutrients and water through. That balance is tightly run.

Solutes cross the barrier through cells or between them. Tight junctions, built from many proteins, control the between-cell route. Cytokines, microbes, and food parts all tune these junctions. Microbe products such as short-chain fatty acids help guard the lining. When immune signals damage the junctions, antigens leak in and stir more inflammation. The review maps this control system.
europmc-pmc8613465:
Zhang and Ning review the signal pathways that drive sepsis and the drugs that target them. Sepsis is organ failure caused by a runaway host response to infection. Death rates stay high, and many drug trials have failed. The authors set out the main pathways and the treatments aimed at each one.

The review moves from germ traits to host response as the core problem. It covers how immune cascades switch on and harm organs. Each pathway gets a look at drugs that block or tune it. Some trials show promise, while others fall short. The authors stress that sepsis differs from patient to patient. Care may need to match the pathway at fault in each case.
europmc-pmc8636265:
Lednicky and co-authors identify a pig coronavirus in blood samples from three Haitian children with fever. Human coronavirus infections so far came from two of the four known virus genera. These cases came from a third genus, the deltacoronaviruses. The children had fever with no clear cause.

Genome work showed the cases came from at least two separate jumps from animals. Both viral lines gained the same changes in two genes. One change sits in the spike protein's binding region. It may affect how the spike bends and binds to host cells. The findings warn that animal coronaviruses can adapt to people in new ways.
europmc-pmc8657965:
Zhao and co-authors review cytochrome P450 enzymes and their central role in drug metabolism in humans. These enzymes clear drugs and keep body chemistry in balance. One group of them handles about 80 percent of oxidative drug metabolism. They also clear about half of all common clinical drugs.

The review covers enzyme structures and what they reveal about drug handling. It then looks at why drug response varies by person. Gene variants, gene regulation, and outside factors all play a part. These enzymes can also change drug safety and effect at the site of action. The authors frame them as both workhorses and drug targets.
europmc-pmc8701665:
Jia, Pang, and Liu review how people seek health information online and what shapes that behavior. Online seeking has grown with social media and mobile tools. It can help users make better health choices. Yet no recent review had pulled the newest work together.

The team searched studies from 2016 to 2021. Of 97 papers found, 20 met their rules for inclusion. Age, gender, income, and education all shaped seeking habits. Job status, country, and care roles mattered too. Online groups, privacy, and live chat helped users seek more. The authors offer guidance for governments, health groups, and platforms.
europmc-pmc8882865:
Rudrapal and co-authors review dietary polyphenols as shields against oxidative stress diseases. Polyphenols fill grains, fruits, vegetables, spices, tea, coffee, and wine. Classes include flavonoids, tannins, lignans, and stilbenes. Their antioxidant power draws steady research interest. Long diets rich in them link to lower chronic disease. The review gathers that evidence in one place.

The authors explain how oxidative stress drives disease. They then detail polyphenol chemistry and food sources. Disease sections cover cancer, diabetes, and heart disease. Brain disorders and inflammatory conditions follow. Infections are included as well. For each, the authors set out protective effects and mechanisms. They also note a pro-oxidative side at some doses. Named compounds, such as resveratrol and quercetin, anchor the examples. The piece suits readers weighing diet and prevention.
europmc-pmc8962665:
Yang and co-authors review how the protein SIRT1 is regulated and how it steers inflammation. SIRT1 removes acetyl marks from proteins. It needs the fuel molecule NAD+ to work. Its targets include histones and many signaling proteins. Through them it touches aging, metabolism, and stress defense. Its anti-inflammatory action draws drug interest. Small shifts in its level can sway whole cell responses. The review gathers the control layers one by one.

Gene-level controls come first. Upstream activators and suppressors tune its expression. Post-transcriptional controls follow. Activity controls form a second half. The NAD+ ratio, binding partners, and chemical edits all matter. Sections then trace SIRT1 in inflammation pathways. AP-1 and p38 MAPK routes feature. The authors close with therapeutic prospects. Tuning SIRT1 could treat inflammatory disease, they argue.
europmc-pmc9024665:
Gajic and co-authors review the methods used to test whether microbes resist antimicrobial drugs. Fast, accurate testing guides treatment and stewardship as resistance spreads worldwide. Classic lab methods are reliable but slow and costly, so doctors often prescribe broad drugs on a guess. The review weighs the strengths and limits of each common technique.

Newer systems promise speed and deeper insight into how resistance works. The authors stress that wide checks are still needed before these tools enter routine care. They call for portable, rapid tests that can track resistance across health, farming, and the environment.
europmc-pmc9208265:
Gao and co-authors review four non-apoptotic death paths and their ties to tumor immunotherapy. Many tumors resist apoptosis, the classic form of cell death. Other regulated paths are autophagy, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis. Each can either help or hinder anti-tumor immunity.

Turning immune-cold tumors hot is a key unsolved problem for checkpoint drugs. Death paths that stir immunity may help make that switch. The review maps the two-way links between each path and immune responses. It then covers drugs that trigger or block each path. Combining those drugs with immunotherapy may work even in resistant tumors. Readers get a full survey of a fast-moving treatment idea.
europmc-pmc9259665:
Li and co-authors review trends in insulin resistance, how it works, and how it might be treated. Insulin resistance means tissues respond poorly to the hormone's signal. It sits behind obesity, diabetes, fatty liver disease, and heart disease. A century after insulin's discovery, no drug is approved to treat resistance itself.

Fat tissue sends out signals that promote resistance in the rest of the body. The review sets out how insulin acts and where that action fails. Lifestyle change comes first among the responses, through diet and activity. Drugs that improve sensitivity are then summarized in turn. The authors aim to spotlight new targets for drug design. Treating the root mechanisms, they argue, may help the wider metabolic syndrome as well.
europmc-pmc9404765:
Urban-Chmiel and co-authors review antibiotic resistance in bacteria, a global problem that kills hundreds of thousands of people each year. Bacteria that resist many drugs at once are spreading in humans and animals. Laws have cut farm uses of these drugs, including growth feeds for livestock.

The review sets out how bacteria gain and share resistance. It covers the defense steps strains use against drug attack. It lists gene finds for the main drug groups. Foodborne germs get close attention, among them E. coli, Salmonella, and Campylobacter. Data show how common resistance is by region. The authors add results from their own lab work. They close by urging prevention and new ways to control bacteria.
europmc-pmc9637765:
Wang and co-authors review epigenetic regulation of aging and what it means for interventions. Aging brings a steady fall in body function. Genetic and epigenetic shifts mark that fall in clear ways. These shifts also feed many diseases of old age.

The review covers the main epigenetic change types. DNA methylation and histone marks come first. Chromatin reshaping and non-coding RNA control follow. RNA marks round out the set of mechanisms. Animal work shows that tuning these marks can slow aging. Some tuning even stretched lifespan in model species. Reprogramming plans aim at a form of cell youth reset. Small drug molecules form a second therapy family. Daily habits matter as well in the evidence. Calorie limits, exercise, and steady body clocks all delayed aging signs. Trials in humans are now under way.
europmc-pmc9718665:
Pachitariu and Stringer introduce Cellpose 2.0, a package that lets users train their own cell outline models. Ready-made neural models work well on many image types. They cannot bend to a lab's own outline style, though. New image types far from the training set also trip them up.

The new release ships a zoo of varied ready models. It adds a human-in-the-loop path for fast custom builds. Models tuned on just 500 to 1,000 marked regions did well. They nearly matched models trained on up to 200,000 regions. The loop path cut the needed marks to 100 to 200 regions. Outline quality stayed high at that low mark count. Tools include a marking screen for the user's own images. The authors aim to put custom models within any lab's reach.
europmc-pmc9806465:
Markus and de Leeuw review cerebral small vessel disease, its recent advances, and future directions. The disease causes small deep strokes and brain bleeds. It is the most common base of vascular thinking decline. Its reach extends to gait, balance, mood, and behavior.

Two pathologies drive most cases of the disease. Vessel wall stiffening from aging and blood pressure is one. Amyloid deposits in vessel walls form the second type. Brain scans show its marks in many community adults. New imaging reads tissue damage at finer grain than before. Ultrahigh field scans can now show single tiny arteries. Network analysis links scattered damage to single symptoms. Proven treatments remain few despite the disease's weight. Hard blood pressure control slows white matter damage growth. It also delays the onset of thinking decline. Trials of new vessel targeted drugs are under way.
frus-1861-d165:
Horace Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 June 1861. Perry served the American legation in Madrid. The dispatch is document 165 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Legation staff kept the post running between ministers and during absences. Perry's reports from Madrid gave Washington a steady line on Spain. His June letter shows the second tier of the service at work, far from the famous names. Staff men like Perry rarely signed the great notes, yet the record keeps their names. Names of staff men in the headings honor work that great notes often hide.
frus-1861-d265:
A State Department letter of 2 November 1861 told James Shepherd Pike what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 265 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the autumn of the war's first year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d65:
Writing from London on 2 August 1861, Charles Francis Adams laid the post Bull Run picture before Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 65 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

August brought the full weight of the Bull Run defeat to London opinion. Adams reported how ministers and papers now sized up the Union's strength. His letter helped Seward judge how much firmness the British would bear, and how much they would test. Cotton, credit, and pride all pulled London toward the South in that bleak month. Each of those pulls can be felt in the wary tone of his August pages.
frus-1862-d165:
Two Seward letters to London bear the date 20 October 1862, and this one is Document 165 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, received it at the legation in London.

Splitting one day's business into two letters let clerks file each topic apart and let the envoy answer point by point. It also means no single letter holds the whole picture for that date. Read with its same-day pair and the reports Adams sent back, this dispatch helps rebuild a week of Anglo-American dealings in full. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d265:
Dated 8 April 1862, Document 265 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It appears in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward wrote the day after Shiloh's second day ended in Tennessee, though full news had not yet settled. Battles of that scale moved foreign markets and ministries within days. A dispatch sent in their wake carried Washington's framing of events to Paris before French papers fixed their own version, which was half its purpose. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d365:
On 20 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, in a letter printed as Document 365 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward's May letters to Mercier came in the season when France, checked at Puebla, was deciding how deep its Mexican venture would go. Washington's interest was plain: a France busy in Mexico had less freedom to aid the South. The letter is part of the careful spring exchange in which each side measured the other's intentions. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d465:
George Perkins Marsh in Turin received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862. It is Document 465 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote four days before Antietam, in the same mid-September round of orders that went to Vienna, Madrid, and The Hague. Marsh's Italy had just been shaken by Garibaldi's clash with royal troops at Aspromonte, news that filled his reports that season. The instruction kept the Turin legation aligned with Washington's line as the war reached its autumn crisis. Small posts received the same careful handling as great ones in Seward's system, and this letter is proof of it.
frus-1862-d565:
Henry Shelton Sanford wrote from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 March 1862. His report is Document 565 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

By March 1862 Union victories in the West had improved the American position in Europe, and Sanford's reports tracked the change from his crossroads post. Belgium's industries felt the war through lost American trade, and its court watched France's Mexican venture with concern. Sanford also kept watch on Confederate agents working in Europe, a duty he pursued with zeal. His spring letter is one of the steady reports by which Washington measured opinion in the smaller capitals that autumn's councils would consult.
frus-1862-d65:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 15 May 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 65 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d665:
The President of the United States sent this formal letter to the Tycoon of Japan on 1 August 1861. Tycoon was the name American papers used for the shogun, Japan's military ruler. The letter, signed in President Abraham Lincoln's name, is document 665 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Heads of state wrote such letters on great matters of friendship and form, and envoys bore them by hand. This one kept up the bond that Commodore Perry's visit and Townsend Harris's treaty had made in the 1850s. It stands out in the file: amid piles of desk mail, here is the top of both governments speaking at once.
frus-1863p1-d165:
Late April brought this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams in London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 23 April 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 165 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-April mail from London took stock of a spring that had gone the Union's way on the ships. Adams still watched the yards and the courts, since one held raider did not end the trade. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. It shows the legation's watch kept at full care even as the news grew kind.
frus-1863p1-d265:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 August 1863. It is document 265 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d365:
From the British legation in Washington on 19 January 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 365 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Lyons reported each exchange to Lord John Russell in London. What he wrote to Seward, and what Seward answered, shaped British choices about the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d465:
A 16 April 1863 dispatch from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d565:
Document 565 in the volume is a letter of 16 June 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.
