Resistance depended on which cell type hosted the virus, not on the virus alone. That nuance can mislead drug testing if only one cell line is used. It also matters for dosing, since body tissues differ like lab cells do. Knowing the host effect could rescue therapies judged as failures too early.
plos-pone-0011365:
K Viswanath and colleagues used a national survey in 2010 to test whether screens shape tobacco use in India. India carries a heavy tobacco burden, and films and television there reach huge audiences, often showing smoking as glamorous or normal. The team asked whether people more exposed to such media were more likely to use tobacco themselves.

Drawing on survey data from across the country, they found a clear link between screen exposure and tobacco use. The pattern held as a population-level signal, not just an anecdote about a few viewers. The result gives health officials in India evidence for tighter rules on smoking in films and shows. It also supports media campaigns that counter the image of tobacco that entertainment so often sells.
plos-pone-0011465:
Matthew Peirce and co-authors identified in 2010 a scaffold protein that selectively tunes alarm signaling in macrophages. Macrophages spot germs through Toll-like receptors and answer by releasing cytokine alarms. Many proteins pass that signal along, but scaffold proteins decide its strength and flavor by holding the relay team together. The team characterized one such scaffold, Themis2, also called ICB1.

The scaffold regulated macrophage Toll-like receptor signaling in a selective way, affecting some cytokine outputs more than others. A selective knob is more useful than a master switch, since it might calm harmful inflammation without silencing defense entirely. The finding adds a control point on the immune front line. For diseases of runaway inflammation, selective tuning of this kind is exactly what safer drugs will need.
plos-pone-0011565:
Michael Wilson and co-authors tested in 2010 the paradox of carbon monoxide as a lung treatment. The gas is famous as a silent killer in faulty heaters, yet the body makes tiny amounts of it naturally, and small doses calm inflammation in animal studies. The team gave inhaled carbon monoxide to mice with pulmonary inflammation and measured both benefit and safety in the same experiment.

A therapy that is poison at one dose and medicine at another lives or dies on its margin, so testing efficacy and safety together is the honest design. Their results inform whether the gas can soothe injured lungs without harming the animal that breathes it. Inhaled delivery is attractive because the lung, the target, receives the dose first. The study is a careful step in judging a provocative idea, neither dismissing it for its reputation nor trusting it for its promise.
plos-pone-0011665:
Qiong Xue and co-authors traced how anthrax spores break into lung cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Spreading from the airway surface is a critical early step in inhalational anthrax. Recent evidence showed the Bacillus anthracis germ can pass through the lung lining by entering the epithelial cells directly.

The team found entry depends on actin, the cell's structural protein, and requires two signals, c-Src and PI3K. In effect, the spore tricks the cell into pulling it inside. Mapping each step of that break-in exposes points where a drug might block entry before the germ establishes infection.
plos-pone-0011765:
Kristiina Rajamäki and co-authors linked cholesterol crystals to arterial inflammation, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chronic inflammation of the artery wall is a key element in atherosclerosis, the disease behind most heart attacks. What triggers and sustains that inflammation had remained elusive, though protein complexes called inflammasomes were known to mature inflammatory signals.

The team showed cholesterol crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in human macrophages. Sharp crystals thus act as alarm triggers, not just debris. That crystal-to-alarm link ties cholesterol handling directly to the inflammation driving heart disease and suggests new treatment angles.
plos-pone-0011865:
Richa Tiwary and colleagues investigated in 2010 how a vitamin E relative kills cancer cells. The compound, called alpha-TEA, had already shown anti-cancer effects in lab and animal studies across several tumor types. The team looked at whether stress inside the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's protein-folding workshop, helps drive the killing.

They connect that stress to a death pathway running through TRAIL and its receptor DR5, which pushes cancer cells into apoptosis, an orderly self-destruction. Showing that two stress systems cooperate gives a fuller account of how the compound works. Details like these help judge which tumors might respond and what drug partners could strengthen the effect.
plos-pone-0011965:
Simone Mocellin and colleagues presented in 2010 a database built to match cancer patients to targeted treatments. Standard cancer therapy still fails many patients, and drugs aimed at specific molecular faults were in their infancy. The missing piece was organized knowledge: which molecular profile calls for which targeted drug.

Their Targeted Therapy Database model links a patient's tumor profile to current knowledge of cancer biology and available targeted options. A structured model matters because the knowledge changes monthly and no clinician can hold it all. Resources of this kind are the plumbing of personalized medicine, turning gene reports into treatment shortlists.
plos-pone-0012065:
Luciano Drager and co-workers measured in 2010 how much sleep apnea adds to the problems of people who already have metabolic syndrome. Obstructive sleep apnea, in which the airway repeatedly closes during sleep, is tightly linked to parts of the syndrome. Most earlier evidence studied single components, or patients already sent to sleep clinics for complaints.

Studying consecutive patients with metabolic syndrome, the team gauged apnea's impact on metabolic and inflammatory markers. That design shows the added burden in an unselected group, not just in people who felt sleepy. If apnea measurably worsens the syndrome's markers, screening for it becomes part of metabolic care rather than an optional extra.
plos-pone-0012165:
Wanlong Ma, Hagop Kantarjian, Xi Zhang, and co-authors reported a rare gene change in blood cancer patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. A gene called JAK2 drives several chronic blood diseases, usually through one famous mutation that speeds cell growth. Their lab had tested more than ten thousand samples for that mutation, and a much rarer change, loss of a whole section of the gene, sometimes appears instead.

The authors set out what this rare deletion means for patients who carry it. Rare variants matter because a patient's exact mutation can shape diagnosis, outlook, and drug choice. Cataloguing them keeps genetic testing honest, so an unusual result is read correctly instead of missed or misread.
plos-pone-0012265:
Faten Bougatef, Suzanne Menashi, Farah Khayati, and co-authors studied a surface protein that worsens melanoma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, EMMPRIN, shows up in melanoma tissue where patients fare poorly, but the route from its presence to a worse cancer needed proof. Working with two melanoma cell lines grown from patients' tumors, the team traced what EMMPRIN switches on.

They show it raises a growth-factor receptor on the cancer cells, through a low-oxygen response protein, and that this makes the cells migrate and multiply more. Each named link is a place a drug might cut in. For melanoma, which resists most treatments once spread, a chain of targets beats a single hope.
plos-pone-0012365:
Jayne Sutherland, Bouke de Jong, David Jeffries and colleagues searched blood signals that separate active tuberculosis from silent infection, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of a West African group. TB germs infect about two billion people, and most carry them quietly for life. Doctors need tests that tell who is truly sick now and needs full treatment.

The team measured three signals — TNF alpha, IL-12, and IL-17 — made by blood cells after TB exposure. Together, the pattern of the three split active disease from latent infection well. A blood test built on such signals could speed up diagnosis in clinics that lack advanced labs, helping patients start care sooner.
plos-pone-0012465:
Marcin Piechota, Michal Korostynski and Ryszard Przewlocki built a database of gene switch elements in mammal genomes, described in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes that switch on together often share control elements — short DNA motifs where regulator proteins land. Gene expression datasets let computers hunt those shared motifs across many co-expressed genes at once.

Their database, cREMaG, stores predicted control elements for the mammalian genome in a searchable form. Any researcher can look up a gene set and find its likely switches. Shared public resources of this kind speed up thousands of studies, since each lab need not redo the same genome-wide hunt.
plos-pone-0012565:
Gal Ribak, John Swallow and David Jones filmed diving ducks feeding along the bottom, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Ducks propel themselves underwater with webbed feet, but to stay down and feed they must fight buoyancy the whole time. Earlier views assumed they simply paddled harder; the team measured the actual hydrodynamics and energy cost of holding position.

The ducks use a drag-based hovering method, paddling in a way that resists rising while staying nearly still. The measurements price that hovering in energy, explaining how much food a duck must find to make bottom feeding pay. The work enriches both animal biomechanics and the physics of paddling propulsion.
plos-pone-0012665:
Lin, Liu, Huang and co-authors found dense acid-sensing channels on a little-studied brain cell type. The cells are NG2 glia, a fourth kind of glial cell in the mammal brain that reacts to many kinds of injury. Their 2010 study worked on the rat hippocampus, a region central to memory.

The channels, called ASIC1a, pass calcium and open when tissue turns acidic, as in stroke. Finding so many on NG2 glia gives these quiet cells a possible role in injury response. That role could matter for how the brain heals after damage.
plos-pone-0012765:
Deans, Peterson and Wong described a protein found only in the inner ear's balance and hearing structures. The ear's otoconial membrane holds tiny mineral crystals that sense gravity and motion. Their 2010 paper names the protein otolin, a multi-part glycoprotein specific to the inner ear in mammals.

They show otolin works with two partner proteins in the matrix that holds those crystals. Faults in this system can bring dizziness and balance loss. Naming its parts is a first step toward explaining inherited balance disorders and age-related falls.  The protein builds a mesh that holds crystals in place.
plos-pone-0332565:
Staying active controls blood sugar, yet adults who are blind or have low vision face extra hurdles. Emily J Nicklett and co-authors studied thirty adults in Bexar County, Texas, who live with both type 2 diabetes and serious vision loss, for this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Surveys and long interviews pointed to barriers at every level. People described fear of falling, unsafe sidewalks, few ride options, and programs that never planned for them. Supportive family, guide dogs, and accessible gyms helped others stay moving. The authors argue fixes must reach from personal coaching up to city policy, not stop at advice to exercise more.
plos-pone-0336765:
HIV needs its protease enzyme to mature, and blocking it is a proven drug strategy. Ali Sultan Khazaal Nazal and colleagues went hunting through an approved drug library for a fresh blocker, using the enzyme's shape as the guide, in this 2026 PLOS One computer study.

A shape template from a known enzyme and blocker pair screened the library and surfaced one candidate compound. Docking simulations placed it snugly in the enzyme's grip, slightly better than the reference drug. Longer motion simulations showed a dense web of bonds, though the enzyme wobbled more than usual around it. The candidate is a lead for laboratory testing, not a medicine.
plos-pone-0342165:
Christopher Wang and co-authors propose judging biological sensors by their mistakes rather than by a single information score. Cells and organs sense their surroundings, and the usual yardstick, mutual information, can be computationally brutal and hides detail. Their 2026 work builds maximum-entropy estimators that guess the environment from a sensor's state.

From those guesses they compute bias and variance for graded environments, or confusion matrices for discrete ones. Examples span molecule binding in gene control, nerve signalling, bacterial navigation, and cultured neuron networks. The error-based view proved cheaper to compute and revealed structure that information scores smoothed over. Wang and colleagues offer the toolkit as a companion for sensor analysis across biology.
plos-pone-0342965:
Richard Fleet led a team of eight authors who studied rural emergency care in Quebec, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Small-town emergency rooms often run short of staff, gear, and backup, while their patients have few other options nearby. The team set out to map the blocks to fair care and rank what should be fixed first.

Fleet's group mixed counts with interviews and open-ended input to build a full-circle view of the problem. Their ranked list gives health planners a clear order of needs, from staffing to transfers to distant hospitals. For rural regions far beyond Quebec, the study shows how to ask local staff what would help most before money is spent.
plos-pone-0343565:
Nibas Pal and seven colleagues search gut bacteria for new drug targets against colorectal cancer. Their 2026 study is computational, mining gene data rather than patient tissue. Existing cancer drugs lose power as resistance builds. The team reasoned that the microbes living with the tumour might offer alternative targets. They compared bacterial profiles from twenty-four cancer patients and fifty healthy people. Gut communities differed significantly between the groups.

Forty-two bacterial taxa shifted in abundance. Four were prioritised by effect size and prior evidence, including three Bacteroides species. Key genes from these bacteria became the hunting ground. An antibacterial agent aimed at a microbial gene the tumour depends on is a fresh strategy. It attacks the cancer's ecosystem rather than the cancer cell directly. The work stays at the hypothesis stage, as its authors frame it. Still, it charts a route around the drug resistance that defeats conventional colorectal therapy.
plos-pone-0345165:
Chi Li and colleagues recreated a rain-triggered landslide in the laboratory, building a large physical model of a loess layer resting on mudstone and soaking it with artificial rain. Sensors buried in the slope tracked water and earth pressure, while laser scanning mapped the surface movement hour by hour. Such interface slides are a recurring hazard where soft rock underlies loose soil.

The mudstone drank water and crumbled fast, losing most of its strength within three hours as a slippery water film formed at the interface. Pressure followed a three-stage rise and fall. Laser scans spotted surface warning movements more than two hours before the buried sensors reacted, making a strong case for scanning in early warning systems.
plos-pone-0345965:
Soumaya Ibrahimi and seven colleagues tackle some of industry's dirtiest water in this 2026 study of a working electroplating plant in Tunisia. Wastewater from metal finishing carries nickel, chromium, and salts at wildly variable levels, and the plant's existing treatment swung unpredictably. Over twenty-four weeks the team compared three chemical treatment setups side by side.

A lime-based treatment proved the most dependable, removing nearly all the chromium and nickel while cutting treatment costs sharply. The team then built a statistical model that treats incoming nickel levels as a design input rather than noise, letting operators compute the right chemical dose in real time. Under the model's settings, leftover nickel stayed below legal limits despite big swings in the incoming wastewater, pointing to treatment that adapts instead of failing.
plos-pone-0346065:
Erik Håkansson and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on a rare heart disease. In transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, abnormal protein stiffens the heart. The authors test whether dapagliflozin, a drug first made for diabetes, can reduce symptoms in this condition.

The design is a series of n-of-1 trials run as a pilot study: each patient serves as their own comparison across treatment periods, and results are pooled. That design suits rare diseases where recruiting large trial groups is hard. Cardiologists treating amyloidosis patients are the readers watching whether this drug class earns a place in care.
plos-pone-0346465:
Sara Linde Neven and co-authors tested how reef fish judge attack speed when deciding whether to flee. Prey must escape real strikes without wasting energy on harmless passers-by. Their 2026 study presented controlled looming images at varied speeds to two damselfish species and compared reactions with real predator speeds nearby.

Escape probability rose sharply with stimulus speed, and slow approaches never triggered flight. The speeds that did trigger escape matched genuine predator attack speeds closely. One species ranged farther from shelter and fled more readily; the other hugged shelter and fled less. Group setting made no difference. Neven and colleagues say approach speed is a finely tuned cue in reef prey decisions.
plos-pone-0346965:
J. Daniel Tejero-Díez and co-workers update the checklist of ferns and their kin in Mexico's Sierra Madre Oriental mountain range. These seedless plants thrive in moist mountain forests but records were scattered. Their 2026 study merges regional floras, field trips, and herbarium sheets into one verified list and maps where species richness peaks.

The range holds five hundred sixty-seven species, most of them true ferns. Richness crowns the southern mountains and mid-height slopes, where single grid cells held close to two hundred species. Northern stretches were far poorer. Twenty-two species carry official risk status. A solid checklist gives conservation planners the baseline they need to protect the richest fern forests first.
plos-pone-0347365:
David Pujal, Guillem Ylla, Agustina Pascual, Josep Bau, and Maria-Dolors Piulachs wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on a cockroach, Blattella germanica. It tracks how piRNA expression rises and falls in the ovaries. piRNAs are small RNA molecules that guard the genome, mainly in reproductive tissue.

Expression dynamics means how these molecules rise and fall as eggs develop. In ovaries, piRNAs silence jumping genes that could damage the next generation. Insect biologists use such basic work to understand reproduction in a species that is also a major household pest, and pest control researchers watch for weak points.
plos-pone-0347565:
Emanuela Pasculli and colleagues test whether a microRNA from apples can talk to human genes, in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory paper. MicroRNAs are tiny gene regulators, and evidence suggests plant versions can survive eating and enter other species' cells, a cross-kingdom exchange that remains controversial.

Two apple microRNAs entered cultured human intestinal cells and slowed their growth. One of them was traced to a specific target, the human c-MYB gene, a driver of cell division, using prediction software, expression tests, and a reporter assay that confirmed direct binding. If confirmed in living bodies, food-borne gene regulation of this kind could reshape how nutrition science thinks about fruit.
plos-pone-0347665:
Rana A. Genedy and Jactone A. Ogejo track how temperature varies inside an earthen pit storing dairy manure across seasons. Heat inside the pit drives microbe activity, which in turn drives gas emissions and nutrient loss. Their 2026 study plants sensors at several depths in the pit and matches the readings with weather records and pit management.

Manure stayed warmer at the bottom during cold spells, while surface layers sometimes beat air temperature in warm ones. Layers differed by as much as ten degrees, and the gradient occasionally flipped, mixing heat through the column. Air temperature ruled the pattern, though the amount of manure present softened the swings. Emission models that treat the pit as one uniform mass will miss this layering.
plos-pone-0347765:
Kaleb Amsalu Gobena and colleagues built LiteCrackSeg, a compact artificial intelligence model that outlines cracks in photographs of roads, bridges, and buildings at the level of individual pixels. Cracks are thin, faint, and vastly outnumbered by healthy surface, which defeats many detectors, and inspection devices have little computing power. Their 2026 design blends local pattern detectors with a transformer that sees the whole scene.

A special bottleneck shaped to follow winding crack paths, plus training that punishes missed crack pixels, sharpened results. On three public datasets the model set new accuracy marks while running in real time on modest hardware. The authors target drones and handheld scanners for infrastructure inspection.
plos-pone-0347865:
Reza Taherian, Maryam Karimi Ghahfarokhi, and Farid Zayeri charted life expectancy for one hundred ninety countries from 1960 to 2023 in work published in 2026, then projected trends to 2050. They set the figures against a combined index of schooling, income, and health spending.

World life expectancy rose steadily overall. Poorer regions gained faster in percentage terms but swung more sharply year to year, and wide gaps between regions remain. Expectancy tracked the development index closely. The projections offer governments a sober baseline: progress is real, yet the distance between the longest and shortest lived nations is closing slowly at best.
plos-pone-0348065:
Ruinan Hu and colleagues ask if one protein worsens COVID-19 lung damage. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The protein is called Poldip2. It was known to drive lung inflammation in another acute lung injury. It also makes blood vessels leaky there. The team found it rises in human lung vessel tissue after infection.

Mice bred with less Poldip2 looked just as sick at first. A week on, their lungs told a different story. They carried less virus than normal mice. Fewer invading immune cells had entered. Tissue damage was lighter too. The results mark Poldip2 as a drug target. The work is early and rests on animals.
plos-pone-0348365:
Veronica Milos-Nymberg and colleagues compared two ways of sizing up heart risk in one hundred twenty Swedish primary care patients living with mental illness. This group dies early from cardiovascular disease, often through lifestyle factors. A standard European risk score uses mainly age, blood pressure, cholesterol, and smoking, while Sweden's structured health dialogues probe diet, activity, sleep, alcohol, and body shape as well.

Many patients rated low risk by the score still carried several fixable problems, including inactivity and unhealthy waist size. The dialogues surfaced these hidden risks in both sexes and at every score level. The authors propose pairing the two tools so prevention conversations catch what the calculator misses.
plos-pone-0348565:
Chenxu Sun and colleagues ran a randomized trial on pain relief for hip replacement patients, comparing two strengths of the anesthetic ropivacaine in a nerve block given before spinal anesthesia. Lying on the side for the spinal injection is painful with a broken-down hip, so blocking the hip's nerves first helps. One hundred two patients received either the weaker or the stronger mixture.

The stronger mixture gave lower pain scores during positioning and longer relief after surgery, lasting up to two days, without more side effects. Both strengths beat standard intravenous pain medicine on positioning quality, opioid use, and recovery. The difference between the two was modest, which itself is useful: it tells anesthesiologists how much extra benefit the stronger dose buys.
plos-pone-0348765:
Jinxin Chang, Pengcheng Qu, and Yindong Li test a broken-down form of Tai Chi stepping for stroke survivors whose legs move in stiff, linked patterns. Slow, weight-shifting steps might retrain walking better than standard synergy drills. Their 2026 trial randomly assigns fifty-two patients within six months of stroke. One group adds Tai Chi steps to usual rehabilitation. The other adds standard drills instead. Both sides train five days a week for eight weeks.

Both groups improved, but the Tai Chi group gained far more on leg function scores. Nearly all of them reached walking grades that most of the comparison group missed. Hip, knee, and ankle motion also opened up more widely. Graceful stepping drills could give stroke therapy a low-cost, equipment-free boost.
plos-pone-0349265:
Neck pain is common in desk workers, and the trapezius muscles running from neck to shoulders are often blamed. Markus Koch and colleagues pooled measurements from seven research institutes, recording both sides of this muscle across a full workday, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

About five hundred thirty workers gave same-day data and about two hundred fifty-six were followed over time. Uneven activity between the left and right muscle, at very low effort levels, went with stronger neck pain. Some mid-range effort bands showed links too. The authors suggest lopsided muscle use, even when gentle, may matter more than total load alone.
plos-pone-0349465: Martínez-Rodríguez and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in genetics on how cells copy their DNA. A harmful change in ORC, a protein complex that starts DNA copying, would normally kill the cell. The team found that changes in other parts, some tied to RNA polymerase II, can cancel that harm. Such rescues reveal how the copying and gene-reading systems back each other up.
plos-pone-0349565:
Lili Bai, Ping Li, and Lina Zhao used computer analysis of public gene and drug databases to ask how two common anaesthetics might affect people with type two diabetes. Sevoflurane and propofol are widely used to keep patients asleep in surgery, yet both can disturb blood sugar and heart function. The team hunted for genes that the drugs and the disease share.

Two genes stood out across repeated checks, one that breaks down tissue scaffolding and one that trims sugar chains on cell surfaces. Both connect to cell cleanup pathways and to shifts in immune cells seen in diabetes. Computer docking suggested the drugs can bind these targets. The authors present the pair as leads for safer anaesthesia choices in diabetic patients, still needing lab proof.
plos-pone-0349665:
Abigarl Ndudzo and colleagues developed a fast field test for a virus that curls and damages tomato leaves in Kenya. Standard lab tests need equipment that many low-resource areas lack, so infections can spread before anyone confirms them. Their method pairs a simple DNA extraction from tomato and chili leaves with a loop-based amplification test sharpened by a probe.

The extraction uses an alkaline gel recipe tuned for speed and reliability, and the test targets a gene found in Kenyan strains of the virus. Results can be read by gel, by a real-time signal, or by a simple color change, and the test caught infections in plants without symptoms. Early detection like this lets farmers act before a field is lost.
plos-pone-0349765:
Marius Golubickis and a large team tested a common claim, that societies have grown more self-focused, by listening to fifty years of hit songs. They took the ten most popular songs each year from nineteen seventy to twenty nineteen in the United States, Germany, Japan, and Hong Kong. Counting personal pronouns in lyrics served as their marker of self-focus.

Self-focused language rose over the decades in the United States and Germany, both classed as individualistic societies. No matching rise appeared in Japan or Hong Kong, which lean more collectivistic. The split suggests the trend is cultural rather than universal. Beyond the headline, the study shows how everyday products like pop songs can be mined as records of how whole societies talk about the self.
plos-pone-0349865:
N Thirupathi Rao is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE paper presenting a new computer system for reading mammograms, breast X-ray images. Diagnosis is hard because imaging styles vary, lesions look very different, and past cases are rarely used when judging a new scan.

The system, named ViT-MultiRAGNet, pairs an image model with a memory bank of past cases. For each new scan it fetches the most similar stored cases and blends their evidence into its judgment. Tested on two datasets with repeated cross-checks, it beat single-image and simpler fusion methods on accuracy and related scores. Border alignment of lesion outlines also improved, the authors report.
plos-pone-0350165:
Jittaporn Mongkonkansai and colleagues in Thailand studied how school bags affect young children in 2026. Thirty-two pupils aged seven to twelve walked a short course while carrying a standard bag, a redesigned bag, a bag on one shoulder, or no bag at all.

Heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and head and neck angles were measured during each walk. The standard bag pushed heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure higher than the redesigned one, and carrying style also changed the strain. The results give parents and schools plain evidence that bag design and two-strap carrying can ease the daily load on small bodies.
plos-pone-0351065:
Children with developmental coordination disorder often struggle with sports skills, so Saeed Nazari Kakvandi and colleagues tested kinder ways to teach golf putting. Their 2026 PLOS One study assigned sixty children aged seven to nine into five teaching groups.

Some children heard a simple picture-like cue, swinging like a pendulum. Others focused on the putter's path, on their own hand, on both picture and path, or got no cue at all. After practice sessions, the children faced memory tests days later and a longer putt. The design tests whether guiding attention outward, through images rather than body parts, helps these children learn movement skills that stick.
plos-pone-0351265:
Md Shahriar Hossain Apu and three colleagues read the public mood about human metapneumovirus from social media, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The respiratory virus, usually mild but dangerous for the elderly and the immune compromised, drew anxious attention during its 2024 outbreak in China and beyond. The team applied sentiment analysis to YouTube discussion to map reactions running from fear to trust, arguing health agencies should know which they face before writing guidance.

Their classifier, built on the XLNet language model, sorted posts with accuracy above ninety-three percent. An explainability layer showed which words and phrases pushed each judgment, so the output can be audited rather than merely believed. The authors pitch the approach as an early listening post for outbreak communication: catch rising fear or carelessness early, answer misinformation precisely, and pitch preventive advice at the audience that actually exists.
plos-pone-0351765:
Pei-Chi Wu and colleagues tested a light-based, hormone-free treatment for the vaginal and urinary symptoms that follow menopause, a condition many women cannot or will not treat with estrogen. Twenty-seven women received eight weekly half-hour sessions of gentle red light delivered by a vaginal probe at one medical center, with health scores taken during treatment and three months after.

Vaginal health scores rose significantly at every check, and by the final visit every participant had crossed back above the atrophy threshold. Urinary symptom scores and several quality-of-life areas also improved and held. Sexual function scores improved on average, though few women reached the usual functional cutoff. No side effects appeared. Small and uncontrolled, the study still makes light therapy look worth a proper trial.
plos-pone-0351865:
Stella F Lourenco, Kylee Novick, Ryno Kruger, and Arber Tasimi tested a simple engine of occupational inequality. People prefer jobs where people like them already work. Across four studies with 1,680 participants, published in 2026, they checked two things. Do adults know the gender mix of many occupations? And does that mix steer interest in a job, even against messages about talent?

Participants knew the gender breakdowns well. The mix predicted interest and belonging in advertised jobs in a dose-like way. More women in a field meant more interest from women. The effect held even for fields stereotyped as requiring brilliance. It outweighed ability messaging, especially among women. The authors conclude that changing who is visibly present may beat changing what a field says about genius.
plos-pone-0351965:
Gro Mjeldheim Sandal and Nathan Smith present this 2026 PLOS One study of how astronauts' personal values shift during long missions aboard the International Space Station. Twelve astronauts on stays of four to seven months repeatedly filled in questionnaires about what they valued, how well their values matched their crewmates', and how much tension they felt. The authors wanted to know whether changing priorities affect crew harmony.

Values such as enjoyment and power rose early in missions and eased later, while kindness and security dipped and then recovered near the end. Feeling out of step with crewmates on most values went along with greater tension. The authors suggest training and in-flight support should anticipate these shifts, since they can either strain a crew or be turned into a strength.
plos-pone-0352165:
Gabalape Sejie and seven colleagues model what stops young Batswana from testing for HIV. Their 2026 survey covers students at one private university-level institution in Botswana. Three hundred fifty-three adolescents and young adults answered questionnaires. About sixty-five percent had tested within the previous year. The rest form the study's real subject. Logistic models searched for traits and circumstances predicting non-uptake, so interventions can aim precisely.

Several barriers stood out. Students in casual relationships were likelier to skip testing than single students. Living more than five kilometres from a testing centre also predicted avoidance. Cohabiting arrangements and religious affiliation carried predictive weight, though some estimates were imprecise. The picture is practical. Distance is fixable with mobile or campus testing. Relationship-linked hesitation needs counselling that speaks to partners, not just individuals. Botswana's epidemic makes every untested young adult a missed chance for early treatment.
plos-pone-0352665:
Md Sohel Rana and Amy Faye study temporary migration inside northern Bangladesh in this 2026 paper. Many poor rural workers leave home for short spells of work. Surprisingly, many choose other villages rather than cities, where wages look higher. The authors ask what drives that choice and what each destination does to household income.

Rural destinations did not raise household income more than urban ones. In fact, money sent home from rural work was lower. Yet migrants still preferred villages for good reasons. Costs were lower, so earnings stretched further. Workers could keep up farm tasks at home and spend less time away. The choice looks like risk management under tight household duties, not a failure to chase the best wage.
plos-pone-0352865:
Barrett and colleagues, in a 2026 economic study, ask whether a talking therapy for men with antisocial personality disorder on probation in England and Wales is worth its cost. The therapy teaches mentalisation, the skill of reading one's own and others' minds, and was tested against probation as usual in a randomized trial. Costs were counted broadly, including health care, courts, custody, and the harm of offending.

Two years after assignment, quality of life barely differed between groups, and missing data cloud some service figures. Still, the therapy group cost less, spent less time in custody, and scored lower on aggression. On the aggression measure, each point of improvement came with a saving rather than a bill. On the standard quality-of-life measure, the therapy looked cost-effective at any price a decision maker might reasonably pay. The authors present a rare economic case in forensic mental health.
plos-pone-0353165:
Gennadyy G Boeskorov led a team of five authors reporting an Ice Age fossil find, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The sable, Siberia's prized fur-bearing animal, lives in forests today. The team reported the first boreal sable found in Pleistocene deposits of Arctic Siberia, far north of its modern haunts.

Boeskorov's specimen extends the animal's known Ice Age range into the far north. A single well-placed fossil can rewrite range maps, showing that conditions once suited forest animals much farther north than now. That helps scientists reconstruct Ice Age climates and how species shifted as the world warmed. Museum and survey teams also gain a reason to re-examine Arctic collections for overlooked small mammal remains.
plos-pone-0353265:
Nguyen Viet Anh and six colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study on recycling orthodontic brackets that have come loose. Reusing debonded brackets saves money, but the cleaning method and the primer used when rebonding may change how strongly they hold. The team bonded one hundred brackets to extracted premolars, removed most of them, and reconditioned them by polishing, flaming, or sandblasting before rebonding with different primers or none.

Bond strength depended on the combination chosen, not on either step alone. Sandblasting with one primer gave the strongest bonds, while two other combinations matched new brackets and proved more reliable across repeated tests. Microscope images confirmed sandblasting cleaned the bracket mesh best. Failures mostly occurred where bracket met adhesive, and the authors say careful pairing of method and primer makes rebonding dependable.
plos-pone-0353365:
Chaieb and colleagues searched bean root nodules in dry oasis soils for helpful bacteria in a 2026 study. Poor, worn soils in dry regions need low-cost ways to feed crops. Certain bacteria living with bean roots can boost growth and soil richness without heavy chemical fertilizer.

Sixty bacteria were collected from nodules grown in twelve oasis soils, spanning seven broad bacterial groups. Five stood out for carrying several growth-boosting traits at once, including types already known to partner with beans. Those five are the top candidates for field trials. If they perform outdoors, oasis farmers could gain a living fertilizer drawn from their own soils.
plos-pone-0353465:
Yihan Hu tests in 2026 whether what drives obesity works the same way across England after the pandemic, or shifts from place to place. Data covered more than a hundred and fifty upper tier local areas, with models that account for neighbours influencing each other. Fancier local models were checked against a simpler spatial model using strict diagnostic tests.

Obesity clustered strongly on the map, yet the simpler model won and left no leftover clustering. Drivers such as inactivity held steady across areas, so local coefficients were not needed. Fast food density linked negatively, a known urban puzzle. National structural action on hardship and activity is favoured.
plos-pone-0353565:
Muhammad Minoar Hossain and Mohammad Motiur Rahman design a face recognition system that cannot easily leak the faces it knows, in this 2026 paper. Databases of faces face real threats, from deepfakes to unauthorized access, and most recognition research ignores the privacy side. Their approach deliberately perturbs stored face images using differential privacy techniques, a mathematical way of adding protective noise, and trains a neural network built to learn from the scrambled images.

They tested three perturbation styles across a wide range of privacy strengths on two face datasets, pairing the network with several simple classifiers. A blur-based method with logistic regression gave the best balance, reaching high accuracy on the easier dataset while keeping the stored images obscured. The authors argue recognition and privacy need not be opposites if the network is designed for noisy inputs from the start.
plos-pone-0353665:
Ayse Bilicioglu Gunes and Serife Zeybekoglu Yesil published this 2026 simulation study of fairness in test score matching. Large testing programs must keep scores comparable across sittings, but anchor questions can drift over time and students leave blanks. The authors simulated thousands of examinees across many combinations of drift and missing answers, then tried to repair the gaps with imputation.

Either problem alone could be managed, but together they inflated matching error beyond what imputation fixed. Gunes warns testing programs to watch anchor stability closely, since small errors shift individual decisions.
plos-pone-0353765:
Geethma Ekanayake and four co-authors describe a wound ointment that mixes plant materials with engineered particles, in a 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. The recipe blends zinc oxide nanoparticles with papaya latex powder and aloe vera gel, held in a base of cassava starch and petroleum jelly. Each ingredient was first tested on its own for antioxidant power and effects on blood.

Bench tests showed the ointment base itself clotted blood strongly and attracted red blood cells, while the papaya latex carried an enzyme that breaks down protein. The combined formula is presented as a low-cost, plant-based candidate for dressing wounds, though all testing so far is in the laboratory.
plos-pone-0353865:
Shakira Khatun and seven colleagues translate and validate two questionnaires into Bangla for use with Bangladeshi students, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One scale measures smartphone addiction, the other the feeling of falling behind academically. Seven hundred and twelve adolescents and young adults completed the Bangla versions, along with a measure of mindful attention in the classroom.

Both scales proved highly consistent and kept their intended structure across age, sex, and survey mode. Heavier phone addiction and stronger feelings of underachievement both came with lower grades and wandering attention. In young adults, self-awareness partly linked the two problems. Validated local tools are the first step toward interventions schools can actually evaluate.
plos-pone-0354265:
Birhanu Betela Warssamo, a single author, published this 2026 national study predicting fever in Ethiopian children under five using machine learning. Fever drives much childhood illness and death in low-resource settings. Working from a national health survey of more than eight thousand children, Warssamo trained five algorithms, balanced the data, and mined rules for patterns linked to fever.

A random forest model performed best at prediction and at picking out the important drivers. Warssamo argues such models give health officials a sharper tool for aiming fever prevention where risk clusters.
plos-pone-0354365:
Gnanaolivu and Hart, in a 2026 paper, work on a blind spot in genetic prediction: spelling changes in the floppy, unstructured parts of proteins. These disordered regions lack a fixed shape, yet more than a quarter of known harmful variants fall in them. Standard prediction tools were built for tidy, folded regions and perform worse here.

Their method adds features that describe a disordered region as a whole: its overall shape, its tendency to clump into droplets, and deep language-model readings of the normal and changed protein text. Added to three leading prediction tools, these features lifted accuracy sharply on held-out test data drawn from a clinical variant database. One tool's score rose the most, nearly doubling its margin over chance-level ranking in their measure. The authors argue that judging a variant fairly means judging the region it sits in, not just the single changed letter.
plos-pone-0354465:
William Lima and co-authors revise a firefly family tree in 2026. The group holds giant New World fireflies and their kin. Old group labels rested on a few signalling traits. Those traits change fast and mislead tree building. The team scored fifty species on many adult traits. Two tree building methods were then compared.

Traits from private body parts proved the steadiest. Signalling traits proved far less steady by contrast. One tribe turned out to hold four separate branches. That forced a full reshuffle of the groups. Two new genera and one new tribe are proposed. Several species move to new groups as well. Fresh keys help readers tell the genera apart.
plos-pone-0354665:
Rekha Bhandari led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of a Nepalese fern known locally as Raani Sinkaa. Traditional healers use it for wounds, diarrhea, and stomach trouble. Working step by step from the crude extract, the team separated three compounds and identified them with lab instruments, then tested them in dishes and computer models.

A pair of quercetin compounds showed the strongest antioxidant action and docked neatly onto enzymes that break down starch, hinting at diabetes relevance. Bhandari recommends animal studies and chemistry work before any medicine is claimed.
plos-pone-0354965:
Hoang Tran and three colleagues work on a hardware problem for future wireless networks in this 2026 engineering paper. Millimeter-wave signals carry huge amounts of data but fade quickly and are easily blocked, so networks use steerable antenna arrays plus wall-mounted reflective panels to bounce signals toward users. In cheaper array designs, some users end up with far worse service than others.

The team frames the design problem as maximizing the geometric mean of user data rates, a choice that forces fairness instead of letting strong users dominate. They develop an alternating optimization method that handles the panel's limited settings and the transmitter's power limits together. Simulations show fairer service across users, faster settling than rival methods, and near-top performance even with coarse, low-cost panel settings, which matters for real, affordable deployments.
plos-pone-0355165:
Courtney Goodridge and co-authors tracked drivers' pupils during hands-off assisted driving to test whether pupil size betrays mental load. Pupil diameter mirrors arousal chemistry in the brain, making it a candidate hands-free workload gauge. Their 2026 simulator study placed thirty-eight drivers in Level 2 automation, where the car steers and speeds but the human must stay ready.

The design separated each driver's resting pupil baseline from the pupil's reaction to critical events. Extra non-driving tasks raised cognitive load before takeover moments. The authors asked whether laboratory links between baseline state and reaction size survive in a realistic driving task. Goodridge and colleagues frame pupil dynamics as a possible input for cars that adapt alerts to driver state.
plos-pone-0355465:
Samantha M. Jones, Faith A. Pasternak, and Erin A. Heerey published a 2026 experiment in PLOS ONE on how appearance-focused TikTok videos change mood through self-objectification, seeing oneself as a body to be judged. More than three hundred women and feminine-identifying participants first rated their tendency to self-objectify. They then watched twenty short videos across five categories, three appearance-focused and two neutral. After each, they reported their state of mind.

People prone to self-objectification slipped into that state more strongly after thinspiration and body-positive clips alike; after thinspiration their negative mood rose more. The twist came with body-positive content: feeling self-objectified there was linked to better mood, not worse. A tendency to self-objectify did not move positive mood in the other categories. The same habit, they say, can cut both ways depending on the message, complicating simple warnings about appearance media.
plos-pone-0355965:
Matilda Holmes, David Orton, Helena Hamerow, and Richard Thomas rebuild the farming story of medieval England from animal bones, across a full thousand years. Earlier accounts chopped the period into set eras, which can hide when change really happened. Drawing on a large bone dataset gathered by a major project on feeding early England, the team tracked cattle, sheep, and other stock uses continuously through time.

Some Roman farming habits lingered into the fifth century at certain sites. Wool output rose from the early seventh century, and teams of cattle used purely for pulling plows peaked around the eleventh and twelfth centuries. After that, demand for milk and beef plus wider horse use pushed draft cattle aside. The timeline gives fresh shape to England's farm history.
plos-pone-0356065:
Ammar AbuMostafa and co-authors tested whether ultrasound improves how well root canal fillings seal the inside of a tooth. Their 2026 laboratory study used extracted human premolars and two calcium silicate sealers. After filling the canals, they scanned each tooth with micro-CT, a detailed form of X-ray imaging.

Ultrasound made no clear difference to total porosity for either sealer. Most empty space sat at the gap between filling and canal wall, not inside the filling itself. The top third of each root held the most voids, and the middle third held the least. For dentists, the work shows that where voids form matters more than brief ultrasonic shaking does.
plos-pone-0356265:
Md Salek Miah maps depression and anxiety among married women in Mozambique in this 2026 analysis of a national health survey. More than thirteen thousand ever-married women aged fifteen to forty-nine completed standard screening questionnaires for the two conditions during the 2022-2023 survey. Miah modeled which traits, and which provinces, accompanied symptoms, with an eye to where scarce mental health resources should go.

About one woman in ten screened positive for each condition. Odds peaked in the late thirties and stayed high into the late forties, and beginning sexual life before eighteen raised the odds of both. Women who shared in household decisions, and those with household assets, were protected, while internet use accompanied higher anxiety. Geography mattered strongly: Cabo Delgado, Zambézia, and Nampula carried higher burdens, and Gaza lower, than the capital. The author urges targeted services for midlife women and the high-burden provinces.
plos-pone-0356365:
Andrew H Rogers and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for the first systematic tally of addiction to nicotine, alcohol, or cannabis in adults who live with chronic pain. Research on pain and addiction has fixated on opioids, the authors note. That focus leaves the three commonest substances uncounted as a group in this population. Each can both drive and follow persistent pain.

The planned review will search five databases for studies diagnosing use disorders, not just use, in chronic pain patients. It will pool prevalence with subgroup analyses and bias checks. Problematic use short of disorder is a secondary target. Clinicians and policymakers need the numbers to size treatment services. Today pain clinics and addiction services pass patients between them.
plos-pone-0356465:
Mingyu Jia and colleagues built a classifier meant to tell apart two stages of cervical disease that can look similar under the microscope: advanced precancerous changes and early invasive squamous cancer. Their 2026 study worked from public gene activity datasets, summarizing each sample by the activity of fifty well-known biological pathways instead of thousands of individual genes, which keeps the model's reasoning readable.

A regularized regression model settled on eight pathways, including estrogen response and a pathway tied to tissue invasion. It separated the two stages well in its training data and held up decently on an outside dataset it had never seen. The authors present it as a research tool for understanding how precancer tips into cancer, not as a test ready for patients.
plos-pone-0356765:
Federico G Segala and colleagues shine precisely tuned light into one or both eyes to learn how the pupils' control system merges signals. Pupil size is run by automatic circuits that combine input from both eyes without asking the visual brain, and different light sensors in the eye take turns across time. A custom two-eye light system let the team excite each sensor class separately by a trick of matched spectra.

Some pathways added the two eyes' signals with a boost, one pathway ignored whether one or two eyes were lit, and one pathway actually responded less to two eyes than to one. A second rhythm in the response showed suppression everywhere. Segala and colleagues fit the pattern with a model where each pathway sets its own balance of help and hindrance between the eyes.
plos-pone-0357265:
Manoj Kumar and a large team use computer simulation to ask how missing oxygen atoms change tin oxide, a material used in sensors and clear electronics. Removing a few oxygen atoms is a deliberate tuning trick, but its effects are hard to see directly. The team modeled a sheet of the crystal with none, a few, and more missing atoms, then computed how electrons, light handling, and hydrogen sticking change in each case.

Missing atoms added electron states that raise charge flow and reshaped how the material absorbs and bends light. A middle level of missing atoms gave the best overall optical behavior. On the surface, gaps also made hydrogen cling more strongly. Kumar and colleagues say controlled oxygen loss is a practical dial for better gas sensors and optical coatings.
plos-pone-0357365:
Ou Deng and a team of cancer researchers hunt for a puzzle. Some ovarian tumors respond to a class of drugs that block DNA repair. They respond even when the usual genetic markers say they should not. Tumors lacking two famous repair genes respond well, yet some tumors with working copies respond too. The team compared sensitive and resistant lab-grown tumor cells, mapping which proteins cluster with the drug's target.

Sensitive cells carried more of a mismatch-repair protein in that cluster, and lowering that protein made cells less sensitive to the drug. A partner protein also behaved differently after treatment, and lowering it restored sensitivity. Deng and colleagues propose their protein pair as a clue for widening the group of patients who might benefit.
plos-pone-0357465:
Julia Kopp and colleagues measure real daily movement in adults living with long COVID, using wrist-worn motion trackers worn for over a week. Lingering illness after COVID often cuts activity, but self-reports blur the picture. Data came from the baseline of a treatment trial and covered about one hundred forty adults whose records were complete, analyzed against fatigue, fitness, and health traits.

Movement levels were low overall, with moderate effort measured in tens of minutes a day and vigorous effort nearly absent. Another chronic illness alongside long COVID and some fatigue patterns linked to lower overall movement, while better functional capacity linked to more. Kopp and colleagues suggest therapy should rebuild capacity and manage fatigue together to get patients moving again.
plos-pone-0357565:
Jennifer Andrews and colleagues published a 2026 exploratory study in PLOS ONE on symptom patterns in hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that can affect many body systems at once. Little is known about its cause, so the team looked for symptom groups that travel together, which might point to shared biology. They compared women with the syndrome against matched controls and hypermobile women without chronic pain, scoring pain, energy, mental health, gut, bleeding, and autonomic complaints.

People with the syndrome scored worse in every symptom area. Clustering sorted participants into low, moderate, and high symptom groups. Nearly all controls landed in the low group, while about three in five patients fell in the high group and the rest in the moderate one. Those groupings were reasonably stable under resampling. Such disability patterns, the authors say, can guide future hunts for mechanisms behind the worst-hit symptom clusters.
plos-pone-0357765:
Wael M Alzahrani led a team of seven authors studying recovery after shoulder surgery, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. After rotator cuff repair, attention goes to the repaired tendon, but the shoulder blade's own stamina and movement matter too. The team ran a cross-sectional mediation analysis linking blade endurance and abnormal blade movement, called dyskinesis, to functional outcomes.

Alzahrani's findings tell rehabilitation specialists where to focus: the blade, not only the tendon. Mediation analysis helps show the path by which blade problems drag down overall function. Rehab programs can then add blade training with a clearer rationale. For patients, better-targeted therapy may mean a stronger, less painful shoulder in daily life.
plos-pone-0357965:
Samaneh Dehghan led a team of six authors testing light therapy for myelin repair, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Myelin is the insulation around nerve fibers, and its loss underlies diseases such as multiple sclerosis. The team used a model in which a chemical called LPC strips myelin, then tested flickering visual light at a theta rhythm.

Dehghan's non-invasive entrainment approach aims to nudge the brain toward rebuilding myelin without drugs. The team measured both myelin-related changes and functional outcomes. A drug-free lead that improves outcomes in a model is worth attention, since current options for myelin repair are few. Human use is far off, but the direction is fresh.
plos-pone-0358065:
Neil Vaughan published a 2026 modeling paper in PLOS ONE on the paths traced by artificial worms moving through a three-dimensional grid. Each simulated worm follows simple movement rules set by a genetic code, and its trail can end at the starting point, settle into a repeating loop, or keep wandering. Vaughan wrote custom simulation software with three-dimensional graphics and virtual reality views to explore every possible worm type in this new grid setting.

Out of a few thousand unique worms, more than half ended back at the origin and a large share fell into loops, some repeating only after hundreds of thousands of steps. A handful were still running chaotically after tens of millions of steps, with no known outcome. The study shows how very simple rules can generate surprisingly intricate three-dimensional patterns, and it catalogs the odd cases for other modelers to study.
plos-pone-0358265:
Yifan Zhang led a team of eight authors reviewing dental cases at a peacekeeping hospital, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. China's level-II peacekeeping hospital in the DR Congo treats more than battlefield trauma. The team analyzed trends in the range of oral diseases seen at the hospital.

Zhang's case study shows what peacekeepers and local civilians alike suffer in oral health, from decay to infection. A field hospital must stock and staff for what actually walks in, and dental needs are easy to under-plan. The record helps future missions prepare the right supplies and skills. It also documents health needs in a conflict zone where routine data are scarce, giving planners rare ground truth.
plos-pone-0358465:
Xiaolin Li led a team of six authors modeling sand behavior under structures, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Dense sand has a quirk called dilatancy: sheared under load, it can expand. That quirk changes how foundations grip, settle, and slip where soil meets concrete or steel.

Li's team built a model whose behavior depends on the sand's current state, then tested how its settings change the results. Engineers can use such a model to predict how structures settle over time. Towers, bridges, and offshore platforms all rest on soil-structure contacts like these. A model that captures expansion under shear helps avoid both costly overdesign and dangerous underdesign in sandy ground.
plos-pone-0358565:
Thomas Muehlbauer led a team of six authors comparing balance training for soccer players, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Players favor one leg, and that imbalance raises injury risk. The team compared training on one leg alone against a combined program that added jump-based plyometric work.

Muehlbauer's group measured balance in still and moving tasks to see which program evened out the legs best. Coaches need that answer in practical form, since training time is limited in a season. A program that cuts asymmetry can lower injury rates while also helping performance. The study speaks to academy and pro settings alike, wherever one-sided sports build one-sided bodies.
plos-pone-0358765:
Anna Szpakowicz leads a team of eight in a 2026 PLOS ONE study searching blood proteins for signs of carotid plaque. This fatty buildup in the neck arteries is an early warning of cardiovascular disease and raises stroke risk, yet it often grows silently. The researchers asked whether a panel of proteins, read by machine learning, could flag who carries plaque before symptoms appear.

They drew on a Polish population study of close to seven hundred adults and measured hundreds of protein markers in each person. Forty-two proteins linked significantly to plaque, and a fingerprint of twenty-five separated people with and without plaque reasonably well in middle aged adults. Surprisingly, the strongest markers had murky known ties to artery disease. The authors stress the list is a set of hypotheses needing outside testing.
plos-pone-0358865:
Xuwei Dong and three colleagues build a featherweight vision model for finding cracks in bridges, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cracks threaten a bridge's safety and durability, but sending people to inspect by hand is slow and inconsistent, while heavy software strains the drones that could do the job. Their network aims for precision that still runs lightly enough for aerial inspection gear.

Two new parts do the work: one fuses wide scene meaning with fine detail, and another repairs thin crack features cheaply where image layers join. On a public concrete dataset the model marked crack pixels with accuracy above eighty percent on the strict overlap measure, beating several established networks while staying small. A companion detector handles messy real world backgrounds, moving the system closer to routine drone surveys of aging bridges.
plos-pone-0359065:
Catalina Canizares, Francisco Cardozo, Abiraahmi Shankar, Raymond Balise, and Pamela Morris-Perez wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on adolescent health in the United States. It examines whether how much plain water adolescents drink is linked to suicide attempts. The evidence comes from the Youth Risk Behavior Survey covering 2017 to 2021.

That survey is a national school-based record of teen health behaviors. A link between something as basic as water drinking and suicide attempts would more likely mark wider hardship or health habits than a direct cause. School health researchers read such associations as signals to investigate, and this one joins diet to mental health surveillance.
plos-pone-0359565:
Lulu Li and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a census of the NHX gene family across the genome of Forsythia, the spring-flowering shrub. Within that family, the authors single out two members, FsNHX3 and FsNHX6, as the likeliest candidates for roles in the plant's defenses against drought, salt, and cold.

NHX genes manage sodium and acidity inside plant cells, core jobs during stress. Naming the family members and flagging two candidates gives breeders targets for hardier ornamental plants. Plant molecular biologists working on stress tolerance, in shrubs and crops alike, are the readers for this gene census.
plos-pone-0359865:
Stefania D'Angelo, Georgia Ntani, Ira Madan, and David Coggon wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on older workers in Britain. It studies early long-term economic inactivity, leaving the workforce for good before retirement age. The findings come from a long-running study of health and work after age fifty, called Health and Employment After Fifty.

The authors weigh factors tied to health, to work, and to social position together, asking which mix pushes people out of work early. Losing experienced workers harms both household incomes and the wider economy. Policymakers trying to keep people working into their sixties, and occupational health teams, are the readers for this breakdown of causes.
plos-pone-0360165:
Jin Guo and Langtao Xing published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It deals with IPT systems, short for inductive power transfer, which send electricity without wires or plugs. The authors focus on choosing the best settings, or parameters, for such a system.

Their tool is the genetic algorithm, a search method that breeds and tests many candidate designs and keeps the strongest ones. Applying it to IPT design is meant to raise efficiency without endless manual trial and error. Engineers working on wireless charging for vehicles and devices are the natural audience for this kind of tuning method.
pmc-13196965:
Sitthisak Chaiyasuk and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on audit data and disability-inclusive public services. Audit data governance means the rules for how check and oversight data are kept and used. The team asked how those rules affect fairness for disabled users of public services.

They gathered 125 studies and reports from 2010 to 2025. Three forces shaped results: how services reach disabled people, how audit data are run, and how much a data-driven culture guides choices. Tensions recurred, such as openness versus privacy and standard rules versus personal adjustments. The authors propose a framework that links the three forces, aiming to make audits support learning, not just rule checks.
pmc-13197165:
Alice Gros and colleagues present a 2026 imaging pipeline for organoids, tiny lab-grown tissue models. Whole-mount imaging can show organoid structure in three dimensions, but dense cell packing blocks deep views and cell counts. Their pipeline joins lab imaging with software steps to fix that gap.

The lab part uses two-photon imaging, a deep-penetrating light method, on stained organoids. The software part corrects image flaws, outlines each cell core, and measures gene activity. It ships as a free Python package with viewer plug-ins. Tests on gastruloids, early embryo-like models, showed how local cell shape links to broad tissue order. The tools should transfer to other layered models.
pmc-13197365:
W Andrew Day and colleagues published a 2026 review of shin bone fractures and failed healing of the smaller leg bone. When both leg bones break, the thin fibula may fail to knit, a state called non-union. Its rate was unknown, so the team reviewed trauma center records.

They covered four hundred patients whose shin fractures were fixed with an inner rod. The fibula failed to heal in twenty-one percent of cases. Breaks in the lower third of the fibula failed most often. Fixing the fibula with plates failed more often than fixing with flexible nails or screws. Whether this failure causes pain is not yet known. The authors call for a forward-looking study.
pmc-13202665:
Malaria still infects many young children in Africa, and a 2026 analysis headed by Alemneh Tadesse Kassie identifies which children face the highest risk. The research article pools Malaria Indicator Surveys from 2016 to 2022, covering 51,457 children under five across seventeen sub-Saharan African countries.

More than a third of children were infected in several of the surveyed countries, the authors report. Risk rose for toddlers, poorer households, rural communities, and areas with high illiteracy among adults. Mother's primary education and sleeping under insecticide-treated nets both lowered the odds of infection. The authors recommend expanding net access and targeted health education for the most vulnerable families.
pmc-13211865:
A virtual walk through the operating room might calm patients before wisdom tooth surgery, and a 2026 protocol led by Saptiadi Oktora lays out the trial to test it. The randomized study will enroll thirty-two patients aged seventeen to forty having odontectomy under general anesthesia at a university dental hospital in Indonesia.

Half the patients will preview the operating room in virtual reality, while the others receive standard spoken education before surgery. Anxiety will be tracked with a validated questionnaire, saliva stress markers, and vital signs at three points around the intervention. The trial runs in late 2026, and the authors hope to establish virtual reality as a drug-free premedication option.
pmc-13213565:
Yating Wang and co-authors design in 2026 artificial enzymes by assembling hemin, a blood pigment component, together with amino acids. Natural enzymes are costly and fragile, while many artificial ones lose activity at the neutral acidity of body fluids.

Three versions were made, and the iron-bearing spherical one mimicked two enzymes at once even at neutral acidity. It generated reactive oxygen species in one mode and released oxygen in the other. That self-supplied oxygen fed a glucose-testing reaction, enabling one-step sensing of glucose and hydrogen peroxide at very low levels. Tests on human blood serum gave reliable readings, suggesting practical diagnostic use.
pmc-13215165:

pmc-13216365:

pmc-13216865:

pmc-13217465:

pmc-13217665:

pmc-13217865:

pmc-13218165:

pmc-13218565:

pmc-13221465:

pmc-13221565:

pmc-13222365:

pmc-13225065:

pmc-13226365:

pmc-13227365:

pmc-13233765:

pmc-13234065:

pmc-13234465:

pmc-13237465:

pmc-13238265:

pmc-13239265:

pmc-13239365:

pmc-13243765:

pmc-13246465:

pmc-13247065:

pmc-13249065:

pmc-13249665:
Bondi argues over the hidden philosophy inside network models of the body, in a 2026 Biological Cybernetics review. Diagrams of linked nodes now dominate biology and medicine, yet what those webs claim about living things is rarely examined. The author criticizes views that dissolve organisms into agentless relations or pure information flow, drawing on systems biology and whole-body physiology.

Through ideas like minimal cognition, tinkering, and stigmergy, where traces in an environment guide behavior, the essay defends the person as a relational, self-regulating organism. It closes by urging epistemic humility: network maps are tools for knowing, the author argues, and should not be mistaken for life itself.
pmc-13250165:
Klamm and colleagues present the first detailed structure of a bacterial toxin called staphylococcal enterotoxin L. Their 2026 Scientific Reports paper covers one of the poisons that Staphylococcus bacteria release into food. Many of these toxins also act as superantigens, switching on large numbers of immune cells at once.

The team solved the toxin's crystal structure at high resolution and confirmed its superantigen action with T cell tests. By comparing its protein sequence with its four closest relatives, they mapped surface patches found only on this toxin. Those unique patches could anchor future tests that detect this specific poison in food or patient samples. The work also supports tools for telling similar bacterial toxins apart.
pmc-13250465:
Farzam Kamrani and co-authors link gut-friendly eating to fatty liver in this 2026 study of young people in Iran. Fatty liver tied to body-wide metabolic problems is rising fast among children and teens with excess weight, and gut bacteria seem to play a part.

The study covered 505 youths aged seven to 18 from a national obesity registry. Food questionnaires fed a scoring system that rates diets by how well they support gut bacteria. Higher scores went with clearly lower odds of fatty liver, and the top quarter scored group had less than half the risk of the lowest. Liver enzyme levels explained part of the link.
pmc-13250765:
Dariganga Munkhtulga and a large team describe a new plant species from Mongolia in this 2026 paper. The plant belongs to Oxytropis, a large pea-family genus of northern lands, and was found in Mongolia's Altai Mountains.

Named Oxytropis ikhbogdicus, it was confirmed as new by family-tree analysis of its full chloroplast genome plus careful measurement. It sits close to three relatives in the same section but differs in stem joints, cup size at the flower base, and petal shape and length. Its home range also sets it apart, since the relatives live in China's high plateau or the Tien Shan range. A formal naming paper like this anchors later field guides.
pmc-13250865:
Hantrakun and colleagues chart clotting problems and long-term outcomes in Thai patients with polycythemia vera. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study reviews one hundred thirty-three patients at a major referral center. The disease makes the marrow produce too many red cells, thickening the blood and raising the risk of clots.

Nearly two in five patients suffered at least one clot, and most events struck before or at diagnosis. Arterial clots, such as strokes and heart attacks, dominated the picture. Being sixty or older more than doubled the odds of a clot, and a past clot marked patients more likely to die. Over a median of almost eight years, scarring, leukemia change, and second cancers each appeared in a small share.
pmc-13252065:
Tracy Murphy and co-authors evaluate a Māori data governance checklist in this 2026 New Zealand paper. Health agencies hold powerful data about Māori communities, and a national model sets out how Māori authority over that data should work in practice.

The team applied a planning checklist built from that model to a screening research programme covering artery swelling and irregular heartbeat. They reviewed documents and held group discussions to test existing habits against the checklist. The tool added real value, they report, by filling a practical gap with structured guidance. The paper shows one route to fairer handling of Indigenous health data.
pmc-13252765:
Maka Tsulukidze and colleagues examine informed consent for medication abortion in this 2026 mixed methods study. Consent is meant to protect patient choice, but as pill-based abortion moves online and through telehealth, what women actually learn and miss was little studied.

A national survey followed. Feeling informed hinged most on worries about fetal remains, emotional well-being, and the risk of retained tissue. Stressed women felt less informed, while women who felt happy felt better informed, showing emotion shapes consent itself.
pmc-13253665:
Luigi di Filippo and co-authors published a 2026 study on vitamin D and Covid infection after vaccination. They looked back at 114 adults who had two doses of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine and no prior infection. Seventy patients took vitamin D drops long term, and the team tracked infections for 12 months.

In all, 27 patients (23.7%) got infected after vaccination. Infection was less common in the vitamin D group, at 17% versus 34%. Blood vitamin D level was the only factor that stood alone as a predictor, with lower levels tied to higher risk. The authors suggest keeping vitamin D levels up may aid vaccine protection.
pmc-13254665:
Thanate Sailuenarm and colleagues measure what rotavirus vaccination changed for young children in Thailand in a 2026 national database study. Thailand added the vaccine to its national program in February 2020. The team analyzed surveillance records covering about ninety percent of public facilities, comparing 2014 to 2019 with 2021 to 2024 for children under five.
