Rates of intussusception, a bowel complication historically watched with this vaccine class, stayed stable. The authors read the pattern as strong real-world evidence that the program is working in a middle-income setting.
pmc-13254865:
Yun Huang and colleagues identify a metabolic shield that helps acute myeloid leukemia resist chemotherapy in a 2026 study. Anthracycline drugs kill leukemia cells partly through ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, and resistant cells are exactly those that withstand it. The enzyme ALDH3A2 ran high in patients with poor prognosis and higher still in chemo-resistant disease.

The team found the enzyme degrades 4-hydroxynonenal, a toxic byproduct of the lipid damage ferroptosis depends on, while also reshaping the fatty acid makeup of the cells. Together those actions protected leukemia cells from doxorubicin-triggered ferroptosis. Overproducing the enzyme also stiffened cell membranes in a way that reduced drug uptake, a second line of defense. Its levels are switched on by a histone-modifying enzyme, HDAC2, which binds its promoter. Blocking either the enzyme or its regulator restored chemotherapy's killing power in the team's experiments.
pmc-13254965:
Ismaila Mbodji and co-authors report a 2026 imaging case of advanced urinary schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection common in parts of Africa. Their patient was a middle-aged man with years of painful, frequent urination and blood in his urine. He had repeated freshwater contact since childhood in a region where the parasite is widespread.

A CT scan without contrast showed the bladder wall coated in calcium, a pattern called porcelain bladder. Calcium also lined both ureters, and the right kidney drainage system was swollen, while the kidney tissue itself looked normal. The authors explain that damage climbing upward from the bladder helps separate this infection from urinary tuberculosis, which usually starts in the kidney.
pmc-13256365:
Hatice Terzi and colleagues report a 2026 cell study of apigenin, a plant flavonoid found in foods like parsley and chamomile, against blood cancers. The team treated a chronic myeloid leukemia line and a B-cell lymphoma line, checking survival and signaling, with ordinary mouse fibroblasts as a selectivity comparison.

Apigenin reduced cancer cell survival in proportion to dose and froze cells in the S phase of the cycle. It dampened four growth and survival signals, EGFR, MAPK, PI3K, and NF-κB, while raising two executioner enzymes of cell death. The fibroblasts tolerated the compound better, losing viability only at top doses. The authors argue that hitting two major pathways at once, EGFR/MAPK and PI3K/Akt, makes apigenin interesting, and they recommend animal studies before any clinical talk.
pmc-13256765:
Wilton Amaral dos Santos and co-authors study in 2026 how blending unaged cachaça with spirit aged using jackfruit wood changes the drink's chemistry and taste. Cachaça, Brazil's sugarcane spirit, gains acids and phenolic compounds from wood during aging, and producers want those qualities faster than barrel aging allows.

They mixed white cachaça half and half with spirit stored three ways: in wooden barrels, in steel tanks with wood chips, and in steel tanks with chips plus aeration. Chip-based blends carried more acidity, esters, and phenolics than the barrel blend, and tasters described balanced, mildly woody flavors. Consumers preferred the chip-aged blends, suggesting a faster route that keeps quality.
pmc-13257065:
Zhanna K. Nazarkina and colleagues report a 2026 materials study of drug-carrying fiber mats for heart and vessel devices. Polyurethane is common in medical products, and electrospinning can form it into fine scaffolds. Two drugs were loaded to calm inflammation and limit cell overgrowth.

Blends used a polyurethane called Carbothane with human serum albumin, and mats stayed stable in saline and blood plasma for one hundred twenty days. One sirolimus formula released drug most slowly and scored best overall. Blood contact tests showed good compatibility for most versions. Cell tests with vessel and gum cells varied by formula, while diclofenac lowered an inflammatory signal. Device designers get a ranked candidate plus clear trade-offs to weigh before animal work.
pmc-13257165:
Zuzanna Ratka and co-authors review in 2026 the modest record of immune checkpoint drugs in ovarian cancer. These drugs transformed care for several cancers, yet ovarian tumors usually respond weakly. Trial evidence for single and combined checkpoint blockade is weighed in detail.

Single-drug treatment gave low response rates and little survival gain in unselected patients. Pairing two checkpoint drugs helped more in clear cell tumors but caused more immune side effects. Large first-line and maintenance trials mostly failed in groups chosen without biomarkers. Combinations with vessel-blocking drugs, PARP inhibitors, or chemotherapy helped select subgroups modestly. Early work on TIM-3 targets is noted as preliminary. Gynecologic oncologists get a clear message: progress depends on picking patients by biology, not treating all comers.
pmc-13257265: Frane Bukvić and co-authors publish a 2026 fix to their 2024 study of blood tests in water polo players after hard training. The notice is a correction only. The age range in the methods was wrong. The fixed text states twenty male players from Croatia, aged fifteen to thirty-one, with a median age of twenty-one. The consent note now states that all players and their guardians agreed. The authors state that their findings stand as before, and the first article has been updated.
pmc-13257365:
Yanan Zhang and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that gut microbes belong inside perinatal drug research. Medicines in pregnancy are usually judged as short interventions, yet early life can program later drug response. Maternal gut communities shift across pregnancy and pass signals to the fetus.

Microbial products tune immunity, metabolism, and the enzymes and transporters that handle drugs. Those signals shape maternal drug levels, placental control, and fetal exposure during sensitive windows. After birth, microbes pass to the infant through contact and milk, while newborn drug handling stays immature. The authors propose a mother-placenta-infant framework for drug discovery. Pharmacologists gain a missing dimension that could explain puzzling variation in response and toxicity across the life course.
pmc-13257665:
Hongfei Wang and co-authors simulate gas films that cut flow drag in tiny channels in a 2026 study. Grooves on a water-repelling wall trap bubbles that can merge into a slippery gas layer. Groove count, groove shape, and double-layer layouts were varied in numerical models of microchannel flow.

More grooves made the gas film more continuous and stable. Rectangular grooves spread the film furthest and delivered a slip length well above triangular grooves. Double-layer structures, especially with tight spacing, sped film spreading and thickened the layer, raising slip further. Microfluidic designers gain concrete geometry rules for drag reduction. Stable gas films could lower pumping energy in cooling and lab-on-chip devices. The study is computational, so bench confirmation of long-lived films under real flow remains the follow-on task.
pmc-13257765:
Anna Krawczuk reviews hybrid joints that combine welding with structural adhesive in a 2026 article. Studies from 2000 onward cover four main process families, from resistance spot welding to laser methods. Heat input, adhesive survival, load paths, and failure modes are compared across the fragmented literature.

Low-heat friction processes preserved adhesive better and improved fatigue life in the reviewed work. Resistance spot weld-bonding remains the most established industrial choice despite harsher heating. Epoxy, polyurethane, acrylic, and thermoplastic adhesives differ in heat tolerance, flow during welding, and durability. Hybrid joints usually outlast purely welded ones under static, fatigue, and impact loads. Modeling methods for heat and damage are graded as well. Lightweight vehicle and aircraft builders gain a selection framework, plus research gaps in testing and digital optimization.
pmc-13258065:
Fenglin Shao leads a 2026 scoping review of serious games in nursing education. Serious games are games built for learning rather than entertainment, used here for clinical simulation, skills practice, and feedback. The reviewers searched nine databases up to January 15, 2026 and screened 6,078 records. Studies had to report original research on games in nursing education, and two reviewers checked titles, abstracts, and full texts.

Twenty-four studies were included, mostly from Europe and mostly published from 2021 to 2025. Games were used mainly in basic skills training and adult nursing courses. The most common features were scenario-based decision points and points, badges, or leaderboards, each in eighty-three percent of studies. Outcomes focused on knowledge, skills, and engagement. Follow-up beyond the end of teaching was rare, which the authors flag as a gap.
pmc-13258365:
Hui Ma and colleagues redesign carbon nanotube transistors to slash off-state leakage in a 2026 simulation study. Narrow nanotube channels leak through band-to-band tunneling when switched off, wasting standby power. Pairing small-diameter tubes with an asymmetric gate reshaped the channel's electric landscape in calibrated device models.

The design reached extremely low off current while keeping on current high, setting a record switching ratio for its device class at the larger node. Scaled to a smaller node at lower voltage, the simulated device still held an excellent ratio with strong drive. Both polarities of operation were validated in simulation. pmc-13259065:
Antonios Papadopoulos opens a 2026 special issue on wood and wood polymer composites. These man-made materials blend wood fibers, chips, veneers, or farm scraps with binders and extras. Makers control the recipe closely, unlike timber cut straight from a tree.

That control is the point, the editorial stresses. Solid wood carries knots, defects, and wide swings in strength from board to board. Such blends can instead be made for steady, even results in load-bearing and lighter jobs. Recycled biomass also finds a second life inside them. The papers in this issue survey where this trusty product family is heading.
pmc-13259165:
Lungani Ngcungama and coauthors synthesize seed priming results for common bean and soybean in a 2026 systematic review. Priming soaks seeds before planting to boost early vigor. Thirty one studies were compared on growth chemistry and stress defense traits.

Bean gained more than soybean on most measures, including leaf greenness and photosynthesis. Soybean led only on one defense enzyme, catalase. Climate zone shifted which traits responded most strongly. Soil texture and acidity also patterned the soybean results. Correlations linked specific enzymes to crop type and priming agent choice. Farmers in dry regions gain crop specific priming expectations rather than generic promises.
pmc-13261465:
Mingjie Huang and co-authors built in 2026 magnetic microcapsules that store solar heat and answer to a magnet. The team formed them through an emulsion template followed by shell growth at the droplet surface.

The capsules came out round, even in size, and strongly magnetic. Their dark, conductive shell drank in sunlight across a broad spectrum and turned it to heat with high efficiency. Each gram stored a large amount of heat on melting, and the capsules survived four hundred melt-freeze cycles without faltering. The magnetic response lets outside fields move or gather the capsules on command. The authors target solar heat harvesting and smart temperature control with the design.
pmc-13263365:
Luca Joel De Simone and co-authors present a 2026 case report, written as a letter, about preventing bleeding during pelvic fracture surgery. The danger is the corona mortis, a variant blood vessel linking two artery systems behind the pubic bone. Its Latin name means crown of death, because cutting it can bleed heavily.

A 72-year-old man had multiple right-sided pelvic fractures and a corona mortis about two millimeters wide on scans. Before surgery, doctors threaded a catheter to the vessel and blocked it with glue, a preventive embolization. He also had a nearby artery blocked for safety. Surgery two days later needed no transfusion, and he left hospital in good condition twelve days after.
pmc-13263565:

The sublaminar group improved more from its starting point at most check-ins, notably at two weeks. Yet the absolute scores of the two groups ended statistically indistinguishable. pmc-13263665:
Inika Sharma and Soumyadeep Bhaumik examine who owns, funds, and fronts climate-and-health research in South Asia. Researchers from wealthy countries dominate lead authorship even for studies sited in poorer ones, and local partners are often shut out of key decisions. pmc-13263765:

pmc-13264265:

pmc-13264565:

Faulty genes were found in 16 percent of the vessel group, 10 of 63 people, and 29 percent of the tumor group, 10 of 34. pmc-13264765:

pmc-13264865:

pmc-13265165:
Zehao Huang and colleagues identify a DNA-maintenance gene called SMARCAL1 as a driver in lung adenocarcinoma, in a 2026 study. The authors propose SMARCAL1 as a marker and possible target.
pmc-13265865:

Statistical grouping produced four consumer segments from combined habits, knowledge, and attitudes. The author frames the young, digitally connected respondents as an emerging segment for producers to understand.
pmc-13266365:

pmc-13266765:
Woon Hean Keenan Chong and colleagues compare in 2026 two ways of giving clot-dissolving and DNA-cutting drugs inside the chest for pleural infection. pmc-13266865:

pmc-13267565:

pmc-13269165:

Three or more doses went with milder illness, fewer hospital stays, and faster recovery. Patients with no vaccine and no antiviral drugs died at a higher rate. Adding antiviral drugs to three or more doses shortened recovery further, the team reports.
pmc-13269965:
Pan Zhang, Ling Wu, Yunxi Liao, and Hong Li published a review in 2026 on artificial intelligence in anesthesia care around surgery. Uses include judging risk before surgery, monitoring and automating care during surgery, and predicting complications afterward. The authors argue the future lies not in narrow single-task tools. They favor large general models that can merge many kinds of patient data into one system. Closed-loop control and explainable models are also highlighted. Safe adoption, they say, needs team science and testing in real clinics.
pmc-13270265:
Zimeng He, Yunsheng Xu, and Chunyan Wu search in 2026 public breast cancer data for a marker that predicts who benefits from immune checkpoint therapy. Using gene activity profiles, the team sorted tumor environments into four subtypes with differing survival and treatment response.

One molecule stood out: an enzyme that builds chondroitin chains, called CHPF. Tumors rich in it hosted fewer killer immune cells and more scar-forming and vessel cells, and its activity tracked with pathways tied to immune suppression and matrix disorder. pmc-13271065:
Wu-Jie Guo is lead author of a 2026 chemistry journal article on making simple organic molecules glow for a very long time at room temperature after light is removed. The authors show that small tweaks, easing crowding around electron-giving parts and softening electron-pulling parts, help form a twisted charge-transfer state. That state narrows the energy gap and speeds the jump into triplet states. A stiff hydrogen-bond network in a plastic film then holds those states steady. Tiny structure changes, they report, gave dramatic gains in glow.
pmc-13271765:
Ignasi Fernández-Cabello and colleagues assess in 2026 how much wildcats and domestic cats share space and daily timing in northeastern Spain. Over 300 camera traps watched more than 30 plots across the region. The two cats largely kept to separate areas, which may explain low mixing rates there. Their active hours overlapped more during the mating season, and domestic cats shifted timing where wildcats lived only outside that season. Guarding the separation where mixing persists is the authors' main advice.
pmc-13271965:
Stig Arve Sæther and coauthors survey in 2026 psychological stress among elite young female athletes in Norway and how perfectionism shapes it. Talent pathways carry real mental strain, but stressors in female national team players were little studied. The study covered football, handball, and ice hockey players aged sixteen to nineteen on average.

Among 145 players, a regression model explained one quarter of the differences in felt stress. Worry-focused perfectionism and overload injury each raised stress scores, while striving-type perfectionism did not. Handball players reported lower stress than peers in the other two sports. The findings point to where support staff should watch most closely.
pmc-13272365:
Ling Li and coauthors review in 2026 wound dressings built from chitosan and hyaluronic acid, two natural materials with complementary strengths. The review covers material traits, healing activities, and products already on the market, then turns to weaknesses such as chitosan's poor water solubility and hyaluronic acid's instability. Chemical modifications that fix solubility, and blends of acid chain lengths that balance inflammation and vessel growth, receive detailed attention. Dressing forms surveyed include gels, fibers, films, and sponges.
pmc-13272565:
Xiu-Tong Li and colleagues built a biobank of microbes from acid mine drainage in a 2026 study. Such drainage is highly acidic and rich in metals, and most microbes there have never been grown in a lab. Growing them would open a window on how life adapts to extreme settings.

The set covers most of the core microbes found in these sites worldwide. Many isolates actively processed iron or sulfur, including the first pure cultures of acid tolerant sulfate reducers. Genome comparisons showed that microbes gain survival genes mainly from close relatives. The collection can aid metal recovery and cleanup work.
pmc-13273365:

The team pooled randomised trials from Chinese and English databases up to July 2025.

Fifteen trials with 1,108 patients were included, covering picking, wet cupping, and Zhuang medicine forms of bloodletting. Most trials carried some risk of bias, with only one rated low risk. Comparisons included drugs, rehabilitation, and acupuncture, alone or combined. Results are presented in the full text beyond the summary shown here, so this description stays at the level of the study's scope and methods.
pmc-13273465:
Piotr Soszyński and colleagues ran a twelve month exercise program for at-risk adults in Poland in a 2026 intervention study. Weight fell modestly, belly fat shrank more clearly, and insulin resistance dropped. Blood pressure, triglycerides, and predicted ten year heart risk also improved. Quality of life scores rose enough to equal a meaningful gain in healthy life years, the authors report.
pmc-13273765:

pmc-13273865:

pmc-13273965:

pmc-13274865:

pmc-13274965:

Current treatments for this complication can drag on for years with heavy side effects. pmc-13275765:
Shara Maria Bohne and co-authors wrote a 2026 scoping review on a rare cause of high blood calcium in women with gynecologic cancers. Some tumors release a hormone-like protein, shortened to PTHrP, that pushes calcium up. This problem is well known in other cancers but rarely reported in cancers of the ovaries, womb, and related organs.

After the tumor was removed, both the protein and calcium fell back to normal in most patients.
pmc-13275965:
Yingqian Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on spotting hidden heart valve disease during a common heart test. Coronary angiography uses X-ray video to inspect the heart's arteries. Severe valve problems often occur alongside artery disease but get missed, delaying care.

It also beat two other video models the team compared. The authors say such screening could prompt timely referrals with no extra dye or procedures.
pmc-13276065:

Bone-forming cells in patients show weak energy production in their mitochondria, the cell's power stations. A gene called TRMT10C helps mitochondria work, but its role in bone was unknown.

pmc-13276165:

Labs usually feed cells with fetal bovine serum, taken from calves, which varies between batches and complicates approval for human use. The team tested two human-derived options for eye tissue engineering.

Both human options kept cells active and supported the right marker proteins as well as calf serum did. Cells also behaved in jelly-like three-dimensional gels lit by blue light. pmc-13276765:
Catherine Clelland authored a 2026 commentary piece on how media mood swings steer psychedelic drug research. Psychedelics served healing rituals for centuries, entered psychiatry mid-twentieth century with high hopes, then vanished under sensational coverage and political backlash. Research and attention have now surged again.

Reporting on psychedelic therapy ballooned, and tone peaked positively in 2020. From 2024 sentiment fell sharply. The drop coincided with United States regulators declining to approve MDMA-assisted therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. Lasting progress, the cited authors argue, needs steady reliance on research evidence over headlines.
pmc-13276865:
Idoia Bilbao and colleagues study when infected breast implants can be saved without removal, in a 2026 report. Implant infection is a feared complication, and taking the implant out is the usual answer. Antibiotics alone may work for some patients, sparing them further surgery.

A draining channel through the skin, called a fistula, predicted failure most strongly. High inflammation markers and positive cultures also pointed to poorer outcomes. Staphylococcal species caused most infections, and successful salvage often lasted many years.
pmc-13277065:

When this chain goes wrong, tumors can grow and spread in ways normal tissue controls would stop. pmc-13277365:
Sanam Hosseinpoor-Dashatani and Narges Ebrahimi present a 2026 bibliometric analysis, a study that maps publication patterns, of randomized trials in Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia. The team searched two large databases for human trials from September 2010 to September 2025 and mapped themes, authors, and citations.

They found 4,482 trials grouped into five themes, from drug treatments to lifestyle and prevention. The United States and Europe led joint work, with Asia growing fast. The map can guide where future trial effort should go.
pmc-13278765:
Kazuma Kawahara leads a 2026 case report of flank pain that looked like a trapped nerve but hid appendicitis. A man in his sixties had localized right flank pain, a discrete tender point, and a positive pinch sign. A trigger-point block brought immediate relief, fitting a diagnosis of lateral cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome, where a skin nerve is pinched in the abdominal wall.

His appendicitis score, though, was moderately high, and a CT scan showed a swollen appendix with inflamed fat around it. Emergency keyhole surgery removed the appendix, and he recovered fully with no return of pain. The authors speculate that inflammation and muscle guarding trapped the nerve. Inner inflammation should stay on the checklist for such pain.
pmc-13280165:

Fillers are known to improve hydration and skin quality, but the mechanism was murky. pmc-13280265:

pmc-13280665:

pmc-13281465:

pmc-13281765:

pmc-13281865:

pmc-13282865:

pmc-13283165:

pmc-13283365:

pmc-13283565:

pmc-13283765:

pmc-13284365:

pmc-13284565:

pmc-13284765:

pmc-13284865:

pmc-13284965:

pmc-13286065:

pmc-13286365:

pmc-13286865:

pmc-13287065:

pmc-13287265:

pmc-13287565:

pmc-13288665:

pmc-13288865:

pmc-13289065:
