pmc-13289265:
Vincenzo Quagliariello led a 2026 narrative review on environmental chemicals that disrupt hormones and their place in cardio-oncology. Cardio-oncology deals with heart risk in people with cancer. The authors argue that past work stressed drug harm and usual risk factors, while daily exposures got little attention in this field.

Chemicals that interfere with hormone signals are widespread and can affect metabolism, blood vessels, and inflammation at once. The review pulls together lab, clinical, and population evidence on cancer growth and heart harm from such exposures. Special focus falls on breast cancer, fat tissue problems, and heart injury tied to cancer therapy. The authors urge clinics to count long-term exposure when judging heart risk for survivors.
pmc-13289365:
Shuyin Li and Thomas Gajewski review a 2026 topic on ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of tumor cell death, and its role in cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint blockade helps many patients, but a large share gain nothing. Tumor traits inside the cancer cell itself, not just immune cells, help explain who resists treatment from the start.

Ferroptosis kills cells when fats in their membranes oxidize in the presence of iron, and killer T cells use this path to destroy tumors. Tumors that lose sensitivity to this death route can escape immune control even when T cells arrive. Internal regulators tune how sensitive each tumor is to the process. The authors weigh how boosting this pathway might widen immunotherapy benefit.
pmc-13289465:
Linlin Lai and colleagues study how meaning in life shapes end-of-life care attitudes among cancer nurses in 2026. Oncology nurses in China often work within a culture that avoids talk of death. The study asked whether a sense of life meaning carries part of the link between fear of death and care attitudes. Nurses completed validated scales on dying-care attitudes, death fear, and purpose in life. Data came from surveys run in mid-2024.

All three measures rose together in the results, which surprised the authors. Greater fear of death went with more positive attitudes toward caring for the dying, not worse ones. Meaning in life explained about 63 percent of that link in the model. Fear seemed to push nurses toward meaning, and meaning supported humane care. The authors suggest training should build life meaning alongside clinical skills. That pairing may strengthen palliative care quality.
pmc-13289765:
Anni Song and colleagues wrote a 2026 response letter defending a qualitative study on nursing assistants in integrated medical and elderly care in China. Critics led by Zhao argued that role theory was applied with data from only one side, registered nurses. The authors agree a fuller design would add assistants, patients, and families, and they note that limit was already stated in the original work.

The study was exploratory by design, targeting nurse views since nurses supervise and work daily with assistants in these institutions. The authors do not claim nurse views alone capture the whole role picture. They endorse paired future sampling of both staff groups. Five critique points are answered in turn without changing the original paper.
pmc-13290165:
Banking and payment apps still lock out many blind and low-vision users, a 2026 scoping review by Louise Puli and colleagues finds. With daily money tasks now mostly digital, poor accessibility can block independent financial life for some of the 2.2 billion people worldwide living with vision impairment.

Following scoping review methods, the team searched eight databases and kept 23 studies from 12 countries, with India contributing the most. Designs ranged from small qualitative studies and technical evaluations to one large population survey. Barriers showed up on every platform type, with signing in and proving identity among the persistent trouble spots. Puli and colleagues map the evidence gaps so designers, researchers, and policymakers can target inclusive fixes.
pmc-13290565:
Stimulating the same side of the brain as a tumor, long avoided for safety fears, caused no seizures in a small 2026 safety study by Ahmad Ali and colleagues. Repetitive magnetic stimulation can help motor recovery after tumor surgery, but only the opposite-side, low-frequency kind had been tried in these patients.

Four patients received high-frequency stimulation on the tumor side, chosen because their motor responses survived surgery, and six received the standard opposite-side approach. All improved in muscle strength grades, with functional scores rising in both groups. No seizures or implant heating occurred. Events were minor or unrelated: one wound revision, a brief faint, and a day of tingling in the healthy foot. Ali and colleagues call the approach preliminarily safe and worth proper trials.
pmc-13290665:
Older stroke survivors score worse on language tests, but they recover at the same rate as younger ones, Sophie Roberts and colleagues find in a 2026 study. The team asked which language skills age touches, what makes the gap bigger, and whether age slows recovery from aphasia.

Language was assessed in 749 participants with the Comprehensive Aphasia Test plus self-reports of speaking, understanding, reading, and writing at one week and one year after stroke. Older age at onset meant worse performance across nearly every domain, most sharply for nonword repetition. The penalty grew when lesions were large and early symptoms severe. Yet no subgroup showed age blocking recovery itself. Roberts and colleagues argue that age belongs in how scores are read and prognoses set, not in lowered expectations for gains.
pmc-13290765:
Immune-based drug pairs give advanced liver cancer patients the best survival odds, especially first, Wenbin Zhao and colleagues conclude in a network meta-analysis from 2026. With many checkpoint inhibitor combinations and no head-to-head trials, the team ranked systemic options across treatment lines.

Twelve phase III trials with 8,138 patients entered the network. Immunotherapy plus anti-angiogenic therapy ranked highest for survival, led by sintilimab plus IBI305 and camrelizumab plus rivoceranib against sorafenib. Combinations also beat single drugs on tumor shrinkage and time without progression. The survival edge over sorafenib was clear in first-line treatment but vanished in second-line, a statistically significant split. Single or dual immunotherapy was gentler, while kinase-inhibitor combinations brought more severe side effects. The authors advise sequencing that weighs both power and toxicity.
pmc-13291065:
Two-way talk between gut microbes and the gut’s own nervous system is reviewed in a 2026 article led by Huimin Li. That dialogue helps keep digestion steady, begins shaping the enteric nervous system early in life, and keeps tuning nerve flexibility in adult years, according to the synthesis.

Signals pass through microbe-made chemicals, nerve-active substances, and immune messengers, working on fast, middle, and slow timescales at once. Roles shift by disease: in irritable bowel syndrome the axis distorts signals, in inflammatory bowel disease it amplifies inflammation, and in colorectal cancer it aids the tumor, the authors propose. Treatment ideas range from tailored markers and built microbe groups to postbiotics, all framed as steps toward precise digestive medicine.
pmc-13291165:
Damp wood can draw pests that damage buildings. Abdelkarim S. Elhenawy and colleagues present a 2026 antenna system to spot moisture without cutting into wood. Early warning could stop insect harm before it spreads.

Two small antennas send and receive signals with opposed circular spin. Dry wood keeps the pair well isolated. Wet wood breaks that balance and boosts received power sharply. Tests covered many moisture levels and heat ranges. Three wood types and varied thickness were also tried. Repeated readings stayed close to each other. The cheap, compact build suits low-cost checks in homes and stored timber.
pmc-13291265:
Feeding goats sprouted fenugreek may lift cheese quality. Marwa H El-Gendy leads a 2026 study on soft goat cheese. Fenugreek can change milk fat and yield. A ring compound, beta-cyclodextrin, may strip some cholesterol.

Thirty-nine goats were split into three feed groups. One got no sprouts, others got low or high daily doses. Milk was made into cheese with or without the compound. High dose raised daily milk yield a lot. Protein rose, and bad fats fell sharply in cheese. Taste judges liked the low dose best. High dose cheese scored lower on taste. The low pairing looks like the sweet spot.
pmc-13291365:
Engineered nickel-iron sheets can help or harm grass and soil. Haocheng Xu leads a 2026 study of these nanomaterials in pots. Such layered materials serve industry and cleanup work. Their effects on plant-soil life were barely known.

Ryegrass grew for fifty days in treated soil. Flat sheets boosted grass growth at some doses. A sulfur-bearing, 3D form curbed growth strongly. Both forms shifted soil chemistry in distinct ways. Enzyme activity rose for some types and fell for others. Microbe and fungus mixes changed under both forms. Higher doses made the two forms act more alike. Shape, not just dose, drives the impact here.
pmc-13291865:
Sachin Gupta and co-authors present three adhesive dentistry cases for front tooth repair in a 2026 case series. Modern bonding lets dentists rebuild smiles without grinding teeth down for crowns. The first case used direct composite veneers to correct crooked front teeth that were still alive inside. The second paired office bleaching with veneers for fluorosis staining. The third rebuilt weakened root-treated teeth using a vitamin C rinse, custom fiber posts, and bonded cores.

All three cases reached satisfactory looks and function right after treatment. Follow-up visits showed the restorations holding stable. The authors stress that results hinge on careful case choice and strict bonding steps. Finishing and polishing routines also guard the final shine and fit. They frame adhesive methods as versatile and cost-effective across many front tooth problems. Longer follow-up across more cases would firm up the claims.
pmc-13292065:
Changyul Kim and co-authors test a 2026 idea for beating drug resistance in blood cancers using short peptides cut from autocrine motility factor. They screened seven AMF variants across 14 cancer cell lines, then built four 14-amino-acid peptides from one AMF region. The peptides were tested in HL-60, CCRF-CEM, and IM-9 leukemia and lymphoma lines for growth, uptake, and stress effects.

One peptide, AAP, most reliably slowed growth while still entering cells through the gp78/AMFR route. It raised reactive oxygen species, disturbed mitochondrial voltage, and lifted p53 levels. Paired with doxorubicin, AAP cut the drug's effective dose by 28 to 53 percent of its original value in the tested lines. The boost came from better drug retention, more oxidative stress, and lower resistance pump proteins in some cell types.
pmc-13292465:
Satoru Morimoto, Chris Kato, Shinichi Takahashi, and Hideyuki Okano review a 2026 treatment frontier for ALS built from three merging strategies. Patient stem cells now drive drug discovery, cell transplants aim to calm brain inflammation, and gene therapies silence toxic genes. The review weighs evidence strength and the field's progress through 2026, with attention to Japanese groups' leading roles.

The FDA's accelerated approval of tofersen in April 2023 was the first treatment aimed at a genetic cause of ALS. Stem-cell-derived candidates ropinirole and bosutinib finished early-phase trials. Regulatory T cell therapies remain promising but unproven at scale. RNA interference and AAV microRNA drugs entered first human trials in 2024 and 2025. A newer thread targets STMN2, downstream of TDP-43 failure, which could reach the roughly 90 percent of cases that are sporadic.
pmc-13292565:
Ben Kavanagh and co-authors survey a 2026 campus on public and patient involvement in research at University College Cork, which recently built a dedicated unit to grow that capacity. An eighteen-item survey went to all staff and students, mixing counts with free-text answers about knowledge, motivation, and obstacles. Two hundred eighty-nine people responded, about two-thirds of them staff.

Most respondents, 64.4 percent of those answering, rated their involvement knowledge as reasonable or better and could spot genuine examples. Yet only about half of those familiar with the practice had actually used it. Funding and time led the barriers at roughly 50 and 49 percent, with tokenism worries close behind at 42.6 percent in the tally. Free-text answers demanded recognition, fair pay for contributors, and cultural change, plus training in recruitment, communication, and funding.
pmc-13292665:
Jasen Vladislavić's team runs a 2026 cheek-cell study asking whether fluoride toothpastes leave genetic fingerprints on the mouth's lining. Eighty-eight volunteers were randomized to a fluoride-free paste or one of three fluoride chemistries: sodium fluoride, sodium monofluorophosphate, or amine fluoride. Cheek scrapings at baseline, thirty days, and forty-five days went through the micronucleus cytome assay.

Every fluoride group showed more micronuclei, nuclear buds, and broken-egg cells than controls at both follow-ups. Amine fluoride and monofluorophosphate produced sustained rises across markers, while plain sodium fluoride crept up more slowly. The authors caution that the findings show modulation of cell markers, not proven harm, and the study has limits. They call for work on what repeated low-level fluoride exposure means over years of brushing.
pmc-13292765:
Olga Halle and a large team present a 2026 study of innate lymphoid cells in people with end-stage lung disease. Groups included cystic fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema, and pulmonary fibrosis, compared with healthy lung tissue.

Type 3 cells made up most of these immune cells in sick lungs and nearby lymph nodes, adding to an inflamed setting rich in IL-17A signals. Healthy lungs instead held mostly type 1 cells. In blood from stable cystic fibrosis patients, type 2 cells were more common, and that pattern held for up to 24 months on modulator therapy despite better lung function. Local and blood patterns thus seem hard to reset with treatment.
pmc-13293065:
William Pickett and an international team track adolescent injury trends across thirty-one mostly European countries over twenty years, in work published in 2026. Their data come from six rounds of a school-based health survey covering more than nine hundred fifty thousand young people aged eleven to fifteen. Injuries needing medical care are common in this age group, so the team wanted to know whether rates were rising or falling.

About half of boys and two fifths of girls reported at least one treated injury in recent rounds. Pooled results showed increases for girls of all ages and for multiple injuries in both sexes, with more countries rising than falling. Rising physical activity appeared alongside the injury increases. The authors argue that sport and activity settings deserve first attention in prevention efforts.
pmc-13293365:
Pavan Vemulakonda and colleagues ask, in a 2026 pilot study, whether patients with inflammatory bowel disease who message more through an online portal have more active disease. Steady contact matters in this lifelong gut illness, yet portal habits are little studied.

Health records covered 442 patients at a city academic center, with messages counted over two years from July 2023 to July 2025. Most patients, 347 in all, sent at least one message, averaging about five each. People with active disease messaged more often and were more likely to be heavy users. No links appeared with sex or race. Portals might help flag flares early.
pmc-13293565:
Yuqing Song and colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, Chinese mobile apps for preventing and managing pelvic floor dysfunction. The condition spans bladder and bowel leakage, prolapse, sexual problems, and chronic pelvic pain, and apps could support care at home.

Stores on Apple, Huawei, and VIVO systems were searched, and 46 free Chinese apps met the rules from 3897 screened. All came from companies, and over half had more than 10,000 downloads. Quality scores on a user rating scale ranged widely, from low to high. App store scores of four or more applied to 24 apps. The study maps what users in China can actually find.
pmc-13293765:
Chuan Xu and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a gene score based on palmitoylation, a fat-tagging change to proteins, to forecast esophageal cancer outcomes and drug response. This cancer kills many patients, and stage alone cannot split who will fare poorly.

Single-cell and bulk gene data from public sources fed a model that settled on seven genes. Risk groups split patients with clearly apart survival over one to three years in checks inside and outside the training set. High-risk tumors differed in immune cell mix, mutation load, and drug sensitivity. One gene, PAH, drove tumor growth through a signaling path and needed its fat tag to do so.
pmc-13294565:
Jolie Bruno and co-authors review mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist use in heart failure care in a 2026 article. These drugs form one of four core drug classes recommended for heart failure, yet they remain the least often prescribed. Underuse persists even though benefit has been shown across many forms of the disease.

Evidence and drug action are set out alongside practical advice on who should receive treatment and how to start it. Common obstacles that discourage prescribing are also addressed. By pairing trial findings with workable steps for clinics, the review aims to encourage earlier and wider use and narrow a major gap between guidance and practice.
pmc-13294965:
Qilin Wen and colleagues fix the weak point of biodegradable packaging film, in a 2026 plastics study. Films blown from polylactic acid blended with PBAT, two compostable polyesters, suffer because the pair mix poorly, leaving weak, leaky material. The team added an epoxy chain extender during processing so the polymers stitch together where they meet, and compared extender grades by molecular weight and epoxy content.

One grade, a heavy extender with low epoxy equivalent weight, glued the phases together best and kept the film-blowing process stable. The resulting film stretched far further before breaking and gained roughly thirty percent in strength in one direction, while letting through far less oxygen and water vapor than the plain blend. It also stayed acceptably clear. The authors see a realistic route to compostable films tough enough for shop shelves and food wrapping.
pmc-13295265:
Andreas Glöckner and Marc Jekel ask whether reflective thinkers actually think differently, or just think better, in a 2026 psychology study. Cognitive reflection, measured by a short test of trick questions, predicts wiser choices, but most evidence comes from tasks rigged to mislead intuition. Here 249 people made hundreds of probability judgments and a set of risky choices that carried no such traps, letting the researchers compare the mental machinery behind reflective and impulsive choosers.

Higher reflection scores meant more rational choices in both task families. Yet one model, a parallel constraint satisfaction account where options and evidence settle into coherence, explained everyone's behavior. Reflective participants simply ran that shared process more efficiently and consistently, weighing the same cues with less noise. The result favors theories where intuition and reflection are partners in one system, not rival engines.
pmc-13295665:
Annabella Di Mauro and a large team present a computer pipeline that flags HPV-driven lesions in whole slide images, in a 2026 study. Teaching software on cervical samples is hard, since stains vary, viral marks are sparse, and cytology shades into histology. Their plan trains the model first on a cervical cytology set, then fine-tunes it on tissue slides.

Careful cleaning came first: finding tissue, dropping blurred patches, and leveling stain color. Tested by leaving one patient out at a time across forty-two samples, the domain-trained start beat a generic image-trained start on accuracy and steadiness. A second check covered nineteen patients and more than one hundred thirty thousand patches. The authors offer the route as a way to stretch scarce data in cervical screening.
pmc-13295765:
David Murphy and colleagues set out a review plan on diet plus activity for overweight heart patients in a 2026 protocol. Atrial fibrillation, the commonest lasting rhythm fault, grows from metabolic strain including excess weight. Diet and exercise have each been studied alone, but combined programmes lack a systematic summary.

Four databases will be searched to April 2026 for trials and controlled studies in overweight adults with the rhythm disorder. Symptom burden leads the outcome list, followed by quality of life, body measures, metabolic markers, and rhythm load. Bias checks use standard tools, and results may be pooled where studies allow, without needing ethics approval for the review.
pmc-13295865:
Olivier Salat and colleagues chart severe mastitis in dairy cows and what follows a single shot of a fluoroquinolone drug on farm visits, in a 2026 study. Severe udder infection is a top killer of dairy cows, often through shock, and death claims about a quarter of cases. Eight clinics across France enrolled 323 cows, scored their illness on a shared grid, and tested milk samples for the germs involved.

Each sick cow got one injection of marbofloxacin plus an anti-inflammatory drug, unless one had already been given. Phone checks at five and fifteen days tracked who lived and who recovered. The design let the team weigh which illness signs and germ findings tracked with success. The work speaks to a tense choice, since these drugs are prized for human medicine and their farm use is tightly ruled.
pmc-13296165:
Ting Wu and colleagues study, in 2026, algae communities in the Nanming River basin, an urban river system in China's karst southwest. They map how algal kinds and functional groups shift along the river and test which forces drive the pattern.

Water chemistry showed clear upstream-to-downstream gradients and proved the strongest shaper of algal makeup, ahead of human disturbance and geography. Human activity still mattered by changing nutrient inputs and water conditions. Diatom groups dominated the story of change. The authors advise controlling nutrient loads and watching key diatoms over time to warn of over-enrichment.
pmc-13296865:
Luisa Piccin and a large team review drug treatment after surgery for advanced skin melanoma in a 2026 article. Patients with stage three or four disease face a high risk of relapse once the tumour is removed. Extra systemic therapy aims to cut that risk and improve survival.

Current standards rest on targeted drugs and immunotherapy, chosen partly by whether the tumour carries a BRAF mutation. Open questions persist, including any role for radiation and whether the lowest-risk stage subgroup needs treatment at all. The review limits itself to therapies approved by major regulators or named in leading guidelines. Clinicians get a map of where evidence is settled and where it is not.
pmc-13296965:
Walaa H. El-Maadawy and colleagues test the antibiotic azithromycin against a parasite-linked gut cancer model in mice in a 2026 study. Chronic Cryptosporidium infection in immune-suppressed hosts can end in bowel adenocarcinoma. The only approved drug works poorly, so alternatives are wanted.

Infected mice treated with azithromycin shed far fewer parasite eggs than untreated mice, beating the approved drug's reduction. Gut tissue kept its structure better, and inflammation eased. The drug also quieted survival signalling inside cells and switched cell-death pathways back on. The authors present azithromycin as a dual-purpose candidate that fights the parasite and counters its cancer-promoting effects, at least in this animal model.
pmc-13297165:
Serban Iancu Papacocea and colleagues study, in 2026, what predicts death in hospital after a traumatic blood clot on the brain's surface. Records for 151 patients admitted over five years to a Bucharest emergency hospital were analysed, with attention to clotting tests on arrival.

Over a third of patients died. Coma score on arrival predicted death most strongly, and clot thickness tied to brain shift, surgery and death. A raised clotting ratio above a set threshold independently multiplied death odds about fourfold. The combined model sorted survivors from non-survivors very well.
pmc-13297265:
Ling Li Vivian Ngiam and colleagues pilot, in 2026, an augmented reality trainer that teaches lay mental health helpers through virtual patients. Five trainees or workers wore a headset, practised with the simulation while thinking aloud, then rated the tool and discussed it.

Scores landed above average for usefulness, information and interface quality, and participants received the simulation warmly. Task-sharing, where trained community members deliver care, is held back by costly role-play training, the authors note. Their design lessons aim at scalable, culturally aware practice tools for under-resourced settings and training programmes.
pmc-13299365:
Hungarian patients venting online blame access problems and poor communication, not the medicines themselves, for unsafe medication use, find Barbara Báldy and colleagues in a 2026 qualitative study. They analyzed 5,174 public comments from health forums and social media posted between 2020 and 2023.

Long waits, rushed consultations, and rural service gaps dominated the complaints, alongside missing information about treatment length and side effects and conflicting advice that eroded trust. Notably, community pharmacists barely featured in patients' picture of medication safety, despite being well placed to fill those gaps. The authors recommend interventions that build awareness, access, and trust together rather than information alone.
pmc-13299565:
Growing gene therapy virus inside stable cell lines yields fewer but cleaner particles, report Maria Toth and colleagues in a 2026 production study. They built HEK293 lines carrying the therapeutic gene in their chromosomes, then supplied the remaining packaging genes on plasmids.

Viral genome output fell 4.5-fold compared with the standard three-plasmid method, yet each dose carried four times the potency, and contaminating plasmid backbone DNA inside particles dropped threefold. Measurements by mass photometry and molecular assays largely agreed for the new route. The authors argue that judging production methods on titer alone misleads, and quality measures deserve equal weight.
pmc-13300265:
M Gabarin and colleagues report a 2026 study linking the anatomy of the cavotricuspid isthmus to ablation workload in typical atrial flutter. Ultrasound imaging from inside the heart let operators grade that tissue bridge before burning it. In a retrospective cohort of two hundred consecutive patients treated without fluoroscopy, anatomy received a score from zero to six based on length, pouches, ridges, valve thickness, and shape.

Most patients scored in the mild range, and acute block of the isthmus was achieved in nearly every case. Each extra point on the score added roughly fifty seconds of ablation time and about four more energy applications. The score did not predict acute success, and its link to later flutter recurrence, seen in seven percent overall, was modest. Complications were rare, so the authors propose the score mainly for planning and operator guidance.
pmc-13300465:
Who answers for a medical decision when an algorithm helped make it? Aleksej Omeljančiuk and three colleagues take up that question in a 2026 ethics essay on AI-assisted care. Their normative analysis builds on the internal morality of medicine from Pellegrino and Thomasma, with support from Kant, Levinas, and virtue ethics.

Machines, they argue, cannot carry moral responsibility, because they lack the epistemic, relational, and practical judgment that clinicians bear. Care with AI must therefore run under Meaningful Human Control, not mere oversight of outputs. Five requirements follow: judgment stays primary, forced automation is banned, outputs stay traceable, patients get transparency, and clinicians keep final authority.
pmc-13301765:
B Jacobs and co-authors examine a 2026 real-world cohort fitted with the Micra AV, a tiny leadless pacemaker placed inside the heart. Unlike simpler leadless devices, this model senses the upper chamber's contraction through motion, letting both chambers beat in sequence. The authors searched for patient and heart-scan features that predict strong sensing at implant and good synchrony one year later.

Ninety-four consecutive patients implanted between 2020 and 2023 had detailed ultrasound measures of chamber size, strain, and filling pressures. Among those paced most of the time, median synchrony reached about ninety percent at twelve months. Preserved atrial strain and absence of earlier heart surgery favoured stronger signals, while higher filling pressures pointed the other way. These predictors can help doctors choose which patients suit this device best.
pmc-13302165:
Y Toyama and co-authors test, in a 2026 single-centre analysis, whether pulsed field ablation pulses must be timed to the heartbeat for safety. The PulseSelect catheter can fire with or without synchronising to the ECG's R wave. Pulses landing on the T wave, the heart's recovery phase, might in theory trigger dangerous rhythms.

Thirty-five patients had first-time vein isolation between June and December 2024, receiving nearly six thousand pulse trains in total. About a third of unsynchronised pulses overlapped the T wave, yet no ventricular rhythm problems or circulation trouble followed. Blood markers of heart injury rose no differently between groups, and procedure times gained nothing from skipping synchronisation. The authors still recommend synchronising when possible, but call the unsynchronised mode tolerable.
pmc-13302465:
José González and co-authors study, in a 2026 engineering paper, how 3D printing settings change the real structure of gyroid scaffolds meant for bone repair. These lattice scaffolds promise strong, open networks, yet printed parts often drift from the digital design. The plastic used, polycaprolactone, melts at low temperature and degrades slowly in the body.

A structured experiment varied temperature, speed, and flow for two nozzle sizes, then compression-tested scaffolds at three target porosities. Printed pores and porosity consistently came out below design values. Which setting mattered most depended on the nozzle: temperature for the wider one, speed for the finer one. Stiffness fell as true porosity rose, in a nozzle-dependent pattern the authors say designers should use.
pmc-13303065:
Tissue imaging at a hundred frames per second no longer costs sensitivity, Mark Towers and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 instrumentation study. A Xevo MRT mass spectrometer with a DESI source mapped rat brain while its multi-reflecting analyzer resolved masses up to 100,000 FWHM. Five drug compounds spotted on liver tissue at known dilutions tested the detection floor.

Every compound registered at 25 picograms per square millimeter, and three remained visible at a tenth of that load with clean signal-to-noise. An enhanced duty cycle mode further lifted signals for small metabolites and lipids in both ionization modes. Finer pixels and sharper spectra, the authors argue, sharpen analyte identification.
pmc-13303465:
Eun Kyung Lee and Min Hee Kim present a 2026 case report of unexplained conductive hearing loss treated with acupuncture and bee venom injections. A twenty-two-year-old man had lost hearing in his left ear for over three months, with normal eardrum, scans, and pressure tests. A stiffened tendon on the smallest ear bone was suspected but never proven.

Average hearing thresholds improved from forty to twenty-six decibels after twenty-three days of the combined treatment, the first gain since symptoms began. The authors are careful to say one case cannot prove the treatment worked. They raise the case because surgery is currently the only established route for such middle-ear problems, and gentler options deserve formal study.
pmc-13304065:
Md Abdul Malek and co-authors profile, in a 2026 study, the full fat inventory of forty-eight wine yeast strains. Lipids decide how yeast weathers the alcohol it brews, shaping fermentation success and wine quality. Untargeted chemical profiling hunted every lipid class at once rather than a chosen few.

One hundred thirty-five lipid species across five major families were catalogued. Strains differed sharply: one carried the richest load of two prized unsaturated fatty acids, and unsaturated fat levels varied nearly fivefold between strains. Storage fats called triacylglycerols peaked in three named strains. A previously unreported family of bioactive lipids was tentatively identified and structurally probed. The authors note the data are semi-quantitative, suited to comparing strains rather than absolute dosing.
pmc-13304565:
Natàlia Segura-Alabart and Francesc Serratosa ask which design traits make computer models predict drug-protein binding strength well in a 2026 analysis. Such forecasts filter huge chemical libraries before costly lab testing begins.

Recent learning-based methods trained and tested on two standard databases were sorted by yes-or-no design traits. Statistical tests picked out the winning features. Models scored best when the protein pocket entered as a graph, when drug-protein contact features fed the input, and when atom gaps and bond types were included. Shape-aware inputs, not raw sequences alone, drive accuracy.
pmc-13304865:
Giorgia Gherardini leads a 2026 chemistry study turning carbon dioxide into methanol with two metals working as a pair. Industry wants methanol from captured carbon dioxide, but under basic conditions the chain stalls at a stubborn formate salt.

Past routes needed large loads of acid or alcohol helpers to wake that middle step. Here a nickel complex grabs the formate while a cobalt partner passes it hydrogen from inside the pair, freeing the path onward to methanol. Tests of full cycles and single steps support the handoff picture. Paired metals may unlock gentler carbon recycling routes.
pmc-13305765:
Ioannis Baltas and a large Greek team compare two lab tests for a new drug pair, aztreonam-avibactam, in a 2026 study of drug-proof gut germs. The pair matters because it can still work on Enterobacterales that shrug off carbapenem drugs, even strains making metallo-beta-lactamases. The germs came from sick patients in 17 Greek intensive care units.

Disc diffusion, the simpler test, called far fewer germs susceptible than broth microdilution, the benchmark method. Many fell into a grey zone of technical doubt, yet all of them tested susceptible by the benchmark. Agreement rose sharply when the team applied a smaller disc breakpoint. Their results warn labs that the current disc cut-off can misclassify treatable germs as resistant.
pmc-13306665:
Felix Maximillian Kuon and colleagues test in 2026 a new way to estimate breathing rate from heart signals using three-dimensional heart axis movement. Nineteen healthy adults breathed at paced rates between six and eighteen breaths per minute while wearing a four-electrode EASI device. Three estimation methods were compared against the known pacing schedule.

Tracking heart movement beat both interval-based and amplitude-based estimates on error and signal quality. Its advantage matters because breathing signals shape how heart rate variability is interpreted. A commercial software package proved sharper at faster breathing, while the new method won below ten breaths per minute. That slow range suits relaxation and vagal activation protocols. The authors call for validation against direct breathing measurement during natural, unpaced breathing.
pmc-13306965:
Longjie Zheng trained three drones to hunt a moving ground target among obstacles in a 2026 simulation study. Teams must search, close in, surround and keep tracking while judging only local views and dodging fixed blocks.

A staged curriculum first teaches basic dodging and search against a still target among fixed obstacles, then adds random layouts and motion. The multi-agent learning method builds cooperation step by step, easing slow learning and poor convergence seen in direct training. Reported gains support staged practice for swarm missions in cluttered ground scenes. The staged plan also cuts wasted flight time in the early phase of team training.
pmc-13307065:
Artem Dmitriev and colleagues measure in 2026 how surface roughness changes the work function of gold and silver films, the energy needed to free an electron from a surface. Films sat on stainless steel with roughness from nanometres to micrometres. Measurements stayed inside vacuum so air could not contaminate surfaces.

Two vacuum methods, photoelectron spectroscopy and Kelvin probe microscopy, agreed on samples with different shapes. Work function fell as roughness rose, following logarithmic or linear patterns depending on which roughness measure was used. Air exposure alone dropped the value notably in later checks, underlining why vacuum measurement matters. Charge redistribution at the rougher surface explains the shift, the authors argue. Their relation between slope, height, and work function gives surface engineers a predictive handle.
pmc-13307465:
Koji OHATA and co-authors check in 2026 a movement quality score that works across illness groups inside a standard therapy assessment in Japan. Their group studied 84 hospital patients in rehab for nerve, muscle, or internal conditions, with 68 patients scored twice by two therapists.

Agreement between raters was excellent, with a score value of 0.93 on the scale used for that check. The movement score also lined up very strongly with a broad daily function score, most of all for transfers and walking. Links were weaker for bladder and bowel control, as expected. The score could sit beside daily life measures to give a fuller view of recovery.
pmc-13307865:
Anh Duc Truong and colleagues infect pigs in 2026 with a recombinant African swine fever virus mixing genotypes I and II, first seen in Vietnam and China since 2023. Disease course, blood values, tissue damage, and immune signals were tracked at two doses. Fever and severe bleeding defined the illness.

Signs began within three to five days, and deaths followed between days six and ten. Viral DNA appeared in blood and in mouth and rectal swabs within two to four days, showing early shedding routes. Skin necrosis and swollen joints stood out at examination. A broad wave of inflammatory messengers stayed high while fever persisted. Blood chemistry barely differed between dose groups, although virus distribution did. The authors confirm these recombinant strains as highly virulent and warn that their spread complicates control across the region.
pmc-13308965:
Ettore Caruso and co-authors report in 2026 their run of repeat pressurised aerosol chemotherapy rounds for spread cancer inside the belly, in 10 patients. From December 2024 to December 2025 they did 24 rounds in ovarian and gut cancer cases, all by keyhole surgery with no switch to open work.

Scarred, hostile bellies and wide spread made each re entry a test of craft for the team. Reused entry sites, picked port spots, cold scissor freeing of stuck loops, and tuned spray aim kept each round on track. Stops came from disease growth and frailty, not from failed access. Repeat rounds can thus stay surgical in skilled hands.
pmc-13309465:
Laura Hannig and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study on a cell-surface protein called CEACAM1 in the healthy eye. The protein helps cells stick together and supports blood vessel growth in other organs. Its role in the retina and the choroid layer behind it was largely unknown.

Staining and cell sorting showed the protein on vessel-lining and immune cells in both eye layers. Mice bred without the protein still had normal vessel patterns, normal layer thickness, and normal immune cell counts. Gene activity in the choroid also stayed unchanged. The authors conclude the protein plays only a minor role in the steady adult eye, or that other molecules cover for it.
pmc-13309565:
Jeremias N. Brand and co-authors study a flatworm that can reproduce by splitting its body in a 2026 genome article. Schmidtea mediterranea lives as both sexual and splitting strains, which makes it a rare test case for why sex persists. The team built a full genome for the splitting strain and sampled wild populations.

Large shuffled chromosome blocks covered all chromosomes in the splitting strain, yet they spared the genes for reproduction itself. Those blocks slowly shut down gene shuffling across the genome, easing the shift to splitting. Harmful mutations stayed scarce despite a recent start to splitting, dated within the last half million years. The authors credit the worm body plan with softening the usual costs of giving up sex.
pmc-13309665:
Haixu Xu and colleagues use computer methods to probe how a plant compound may fight cancer in a 2026 study. The compound, luteolin, occurs in many foods and shows anti-cancer effects in lab work, but its routes of action stay unclear. Network methods can map many targets at once across several cancers.

Public databases supplied compound targets, disease genes, and protein links for breast, lung, colorectal, gastric, and liver cancers. One hub gene, AKT1, stood out for its roles in cell death, cell cycle, and tumor control. Docking and motion simulations supported strong binding between luteolin and AKT1. Tumor data banks showed AKT1 levels higher in some cancers and lower in others. The authors name the AKT1 path as a lead for lab testing.
pmc-13309865:
Mahnum Shahzad and colleagues track in 2026 how insurance coverage for weight-loss use shapes GLP-1 drug prescribing across employer plans run by a large American insurer. Claims from about six million people between 2021 and 2024 were classified by diagnosis history to separate weight-loss use from diabetes or heart indications. All plans covered the drugs for diabetes.

Only about fourteen to fifteen percent of plans covered weight-loss use, and that share barely moved across the four years. Member populations looked similar in the two plan types, including obesity prevalence near twenty-three percent. Days supplied of the dedicated weight-loss brands were far higher where coverage existed, as expected. Cost per member was estimated from published review figures rather than claims prices. Employers weighing coverage need exactly this utilisation picture, the authors argue, since clinical benefit is acknowledged while budgets strain.
pmc-13309965:
Amir Khorram-Manesh and co-authors study how security language shapes health fairness in crises in a 2026 article. Wars, sanctions, and rivalry pull clinics, supply chains, and civilian safety into security-run governance. Less studied is how official words make health harm look normal, forced, or someone else problem.

Policy texts from states, world bodies, and aid groups were read beside scholarly work across five crisis settings, from great-power rivalry to wars and sanctions. Three habits recurred: framing issues as security threats, carving out exceptions to normal rules, and shifting blame away from decision makers. The authors argue these habits quietly deepen health inequity and urge writers of policy to name health costs plainly.
pmc-13310065:
Yanran Li and co-authors sort heart failure symptoms into clusters in a 2026 hospital survey. Patients rarely feel one symptom alone; breathlessness, fatigue, swelling, and gut upset arrive in bundles. Finding the lead symptom of each bundle could help nurses act earlier and more precisely.

Surveys from 354 inpatients admitted between November 2024 and January 2025 were read with grouping statistics. Four bundles emerged: night breathing distress, low blood flow, upper airway irritation, and gut symptoms. Three lead symptoms stood out: waking breathless at night, sweating, and cough. The authors propose watching those lead symptoms as early flags for the wider bundles they announce.
pmc-13310365:
Abbas Khan and co-authors report a young man whose rare hormone channel disease struck as a heart emergency in a 2026 case article. Liddle syndrome overactivates kidney sodium channels, driving severe early blood pressure with low potassium. It is inherited and often missed behind ordinary hypertension labels.

The 21-year-old arrived with severe chest pain, blood pressure of 267/170 mmHg, and a heart injury marker far above normal in the reported values. Heart scans showed thickened heart muscle but clean arteries, ruling out a classic heart attack. Kidney vessel scans and hormone ratios were normal, steering the search toward channel disease. The authors use the case to push genetic causes onto the checklist for young hypertensive crises.
pmc-13310465:
Yusuf Abdullahi Hubow and co-authors review primary health care strengthening in Somalia in a 2026 article. Primary care is the base of fair health systems, yet Somalia fragile setting leaves that base weak. High mother and child deaths, preventable infections, and rising chronic disease fall hardest on rural families, displaced people, women, and children.

Peer-reviewed studies, global frameworks, and Somali policy records were read across governance, funding, workforce, service delivery, quality, resilience, and community trust. Fragmented leadership, heavy out-of-pocket costs, and uneven worker spread stood out as brakes on care. Recent reforms offer openings if services reach displaced and rural groups. The authors set priorities for funders and the Somali government.
pmc-13310665:
Koji Onozawa and co-authors follow dialysis patients aged 75 and older over five years in a 2026 study. Japan dialysis population keeps aging, and older patients carry more illness, frailty, and nutrition risk. Real-world outcome data from regional hospitals for this group stayed limited.

All maintenance dialysis patients at a Fukuoka regional hospital on December 1, 2017 were split at age 75 and followed to death or December 2022. Baseline traits, lab values, gut bleeding, and fractures were pulled from records. Five-year death was the main outcome. The authors compare older and younger groups to guide counseling and complication watch in everyday regional practice, where most such patients actually receive care.
pmc-13310865:
Sevval Gunbay and colleagues load the breast cancer drug tamoxifen into tiny fat particles in a 2026 lab study. Tamoxifen helps hormone driven cancers but dissolves poorly and can cause harm, which limits its use. The team asked if fat carriers could make it work against triple negative cancer cells, which lack hormone targets.

Two carrier types were built and checked for size, charge, drug load, and release over seven months of storage. Particles stayed small, held most of the drug, and released it at distinct rates by type. Loaded particles killed triple negative cells in dishes, mainly by triggering cell death. Animal tests are the next step.
pmc-13310965:
Sina Maskoukian and co-authors test a skin applied epilepsy drug for male pattern hair loss in a 2026 trial. Phenytoin spurs skin cell growth and blood vessel growth, and excess hair is a known side effect, which hints at scalp use. Men with androgenetic alopecia applied a 5 percent solution twice daily for 16 weeks.

Hair counts, density, and follicle counts all rose clearly by week 16 on scan measures. Growth phase share rose slightly without clear proof. Patients noted better hair texture and less scalp oil. Side effects stayed mild and brief, with no serious harm. A blinded trial with a control group must confirm gains.
pmc-13311065:
Chen Xu and colleagues describe brain vessel clots during child leukemia care in a 2026 case series. Clots in the brain are rare but grave during acute lymphoblastic leukemia treatment, and a key drug is a known trigger. Timing, lab shifts, and care paths at one center were reviewed.

Among 1,138 treated children from 2018 to 2025, six had scan proven brain clots at a median age of 10 years in the group. Five events clustered within days after the suspect drug dose. All showed high clot breakdown markers and low antithrombin at onset. Blood thinners or clot removal gave good nerve outcomes, with no repeat events.
pmc-13311865:
Laia Gomez-Muñoz and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, a small RNA molecule called miR-30d-5p and its role in type 1 diabetes. After diagnosis, children pass through a partial remission phase of easier blood sugar control and quieter autoimmunity. This molecule rises sharply during that phase. The team tested it in human pancreatic slices, in mice prone to diabetes, and in blood cells from patients, probing effects on insulin release and gene activity.

In pancreatic slices, the molecule supported insulin secretion. Tracing tests were consistent with new insulin-producing cells emerging. Gene sequencing flagged changes in pathways tied to beta cell function and cell development. Treated mice developed diabetes later, hinting at protective and immune-calming effects. In human T cells, the molecule raised inhibitory checkpoint molecules and altered interferon-gamma release. The authors frame it as a candidate target for preserving beta cell function, pending further work.
pmc-13311965:
Denny Choi and co-authors in 2026 give a systematic review of what jobs and exposures raise the risk of salivary gland cancer, a rare tumor whose workplace causes are barely recognized.

The review screened studies published to September 2023 and kept 24 for deep analysis. Misreading of exposure and confounding were common flaws. Industries with the strongest links included food services, cleaning services, rubber and plastics making, material handling, and construction. Exposures with the strongest links included silica dust, cement dust, chlorinated solvents, and formaldehyde. Effect direction plots rank where prevention should aim first. The authors also list the biases that cloud older studies.
pmc-13312165:
Lichuan Liu and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study achieving the first broadly workable asymmetric version of a useful silicon-forming reaction. Attaching silicon to plain aromatic rings by silylating a carbon-hydrogen bond is prized for making organosilicon compounds. Steering the reaction to favor one mirror-image product had failed because silane reactants prefer to react with themselves.

The team's rhodium catalyst uses bulky substituent effects working together to outrun that side reaction. Under mild conditions with readily available starting materials, the method delivered a broad range of silicon-stereogenic monohydrosilanes in good yields and with enantioselectivities reaching 99 percent. The authors present the protocol as a direct, atom-economical route to chiral silicon building blocks for materials and drug research.
pmc-13312365:
Eva Emanuel and colleagues report a 2026 enhanced surveillance study of laboratory-confirmed acute Lyme disease in England. Routine national surveillance rests on lab results alone and says little about patients' stories. The team sent an online questionnaire to all confirmed cases with specimens between April 2023 and March 2024.

Replies covered 511 of 1,086 cases and matched national patterns of age, sex, and region. More than half the respondents, 57.3 percent, never realized a tick had bitten them, and among those who did remember, most bites happened near home, with 28.5 percent possibly occurring in a garden. The rash erythema migrans appeared in 70.5 percent of cases. The authors urge awareness that ticks thrive in urban parks and gardens too, and that wildlife projects should carry tick prevention advice.
pmc-13312565:
Samuel Yao Mayeden and a large team present a 2026 review of how leadership and management shape maternal, newborn, and child health in Sub-Saharan Africa. Preventable deaths persist across the region despite global pledges, and weak leadership inside primary care systems is blamed for waste, unequal access, and patchy quality.

Following PRISMA rules and searching seven databases for studies dated up to July 2025, the team found 13 studies from seven countries plus one multi-country analysis. Helpful methods grouped into leadership training with close supervision, open and answerable governance, and work with communities. Gains included antenatal care use rising by 12 to 48 percent across studies, skilled birth attendance by 10 to 34 percent, and completed vaccines by 8 to 27 percent. Mentors, routine checks, and data-driven choices reinforced the gains.
pmc-13313565:
Cesar Baltodano Dangla and co-authors present a 2026 case report of severe peripartum cardiomyopathy that appeared to heal completely, until deeper imaging said otherwise. Their patient, a 25-year-old woman, developed acute heart failure seven weeks after a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia. Scans showed both ventricles failing badly, with ejection fractions of 14 and 17 percent, clots inside the left ventricle, and a heart stress marker peaking at 12,241 in the reported units.

Treatment combined anticoagulation, early standard heart failure medicines, and a twelve-week course of bromocriptine. Eighteen months later she felt fully well and her main pumping measure had normalized. Advanced imaging, however, found lingering strain abnormalities and a small patch of scar tissue covering 3 percent of heart muscle mass. The authors argue that recovery judged by symptoms and ordinary ultrasound can hide residual injury, and that strain imaging and magnetic resonance scanning should guide long-term risk decisions.
pmc-13314765:
Bersu Nur Hacıfettahoğlu and Saniye Bilici review the next wave of fermented foods in their 2026 paper. Fermented foods have long aided gut health, microbe variety, and nutrient uptake, and new biology is now reshaping how they are made.

Tailored starter cultures and precision fermentation give makers tight control over microbe mixes and tanks, yielding foods that digest easier and carry more micronutrients. Yet the same tools raise safety flags. Bugs reshaped by Cas9 gene editing or by planned metabolic tweaks spark debate on oversight and long-term health effects, as the authors note. The review weighs richer function against fresh biochemical risks and urges rules that keep pace with the craft, so novel ferments reach tables safely.
pmc-13314865:
Laura Kühl leads a large team that wrote a hands-on guide to growing human bronchial organoids, published in 2026. These 3D cell clusters mimic the airway lining in shape, cell mix, and function, making them a prized model for airway disease.

The guide gathers refined protocols for making, keeping, and checking organoids built from adult somatic cells. Starting material can come from surgical lung tissue or from primary bronchial cells of healthy or ill donors, as the authors describe. Step-by-step methods cover growth, upkeep, and the tests that prove the clusters act like real airway lining. Labs can use the guide to study how airway cells grow and fire up, and how diseases of the lower airway unfold, without leaning only on animal work.
pmc-13315565:
Maxwell Ansong Okai and a large team studied in 2026 how feeding embryos inside the egg interacts with incubation heat in broiler breeder eggs. Both warmth and nutrient supply shape embryo growth, yet their combined effects were little known, so 270 fertile eggs were split across a three-by-three design.

Eggs got salt solution, glucose, or vitamin D3 injected on day ten, and were kept at 36.5, 37.0, or 37.5 degrees, with egg and embryo measures taken daily from day fifteen to day twenty. Clear interplay appeared between the feeding type and the heat level for egg traits and embryo development, guiding hatchery tuning.
pmc-13315765:
Morteza Hosseini and Alireza Fattahi designed a possible JAK kinase blocker in 2026 from natural building blocks, joining nucleobase and amino acid parts. One hundred candidate structures were drawn and optimized on computer, then screened with machine learning models trained against five known JAK inhibitors.

One compound, called AMO, came out on top. Docking showed favorable fits in the active site, with the known drug abrocitinib as closest comparator. Motion simulations found stable binding, supported by several structural measures and compact shape analysis. Drug-like behavior and toxicity checks complete the early, fully computational case for lab follow-up.
pmc-13316165:
Stewart James Clark and Michael Graz tested in 2026 whether a carbohydrate-derived fulvic acid can damage genes, a safety question for a material used for immune and antioxidant products. Natural fulvic acids vary a lot and can carry heavy metals, so the test material was made cleanly from sucrose with oxygen and water under good manufacturing practice.

Three standard tests were run. The bacterial Ames test showed no rise in reverse mutations in two bacterial species. Cell and animal micronucleus tests showed no increase in damaged red cell precursors or shifts in their ratios. The clean profile supports product safety work.
pmc-13316365:
Jenny Engelmann and co-authors wrote a 2026 project report on weaving biochemistry through the whole reformed medical degree in Brandenburg, Germany. Instead of teaching the subject once, early and apart, their spiral plan revisits it inside organ and topic modules across all years of study.

An interdisciplinary group built the plan, then checked learning with the Progress Test Medicine and asked students for their views. Test scores matched those at other universities, and students rated the content as relevant and good for deep learning. Biochemistry kept its own identity while giving up most solo control, a high rung on the integration ladder. The report shows peer schools one proven route to link basic science with clinic work.
pmc-13316565:
Nicole Liddy and co-authors describe a 2026 case of thumb replacement by bone-anchored implant after amputation at the knuckle joint, reported as the first such thumb operation in the United States. The implant head came pre-angled, also a world first according to the team, and the work was done in one stage.

Stability testing at ten weeks gave a solid score, and no loosening showed by 13 months. The patient could touch thumb to small finger, daily tasks improved by six months, and a standard arm test score rose by 28 points in the follow-up window. She even felt heat and cold through the implant. The report lays out design, surgery, and rehab steps for other teams.
pmc-13316665:
Yoni Sacknovitz and colleagues report, in 2026, two liver transplant patients who developed itchy skin eruptions linked to human polyomaviruses 6 and 7. Those viruses usually rest quietly in healthy people but can cause disease when immunity is suppressed. Documented skin cases remain very rare.

One man, three months after transplantation in May 2025, developed widespread velvety pink to brown papules and plaques with fever and diarrhoea while taking several immune-suppressing drugs. A skin biopsy showed damaged basal cells, dying keratinocytes and columns of abnormal scale. Genetic testing of lesional skin confirmed virus type 6 and showed active replication. The report pairs his course with a second case involving virus type 7, covering presentation, tissue findings and management.
pmc-13318165:
Mohamed Lemine Sidi Oumar and colleagues report, in 2026, a parasitic cause of fluid around the lung in a 67-year-old farmer. Fluid rich in eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, has many possible causes, from cancer and infection to parasites. Lung involvement by toxocariasis, a roundworm infection caught from dogs, is rare.

The man had worsening breathlessness, right chest pain, fever and general decline, with a loculated fluid collection on imaging. Fluid tests showed marked eosinophilia, while cultures and tuberculosis tests were negative and no cancer cells appeared. Drainage and broad antibiotics brought no lasting improvement. Antibody tests for Toxocara were positive in blood and fluid. Treatment with albendazole was followed by clear clinical and imaging improvement, although one case cannot prove cause.
pmc-13318565:
Lingyun Zhang leads a 2026 meta-analysis asking whether Helicobacter pylori infection is tied to how severe metabolic-associated fatty liver disease becomes. Earlier observational reports pointed in different directions and used mixed methods.

Searches of international and Chinese databases for studies from January 2015 to December 2024 yielded seven studies with 11,168 participants, about half infected with the bacterium. Pooling with random-effects models gave no clear overall link, with wide variation between studies. A modest link appeared only in Chinese populations, while evidence from the two biopsy studies was too imprecise to judge. The authors call for large prospective work with standard measures before any treatment conclusions are drawn.
pmc-13318665:
Zhuhao Yin and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study of brain artery narrowing. They test whether CT-derived flow reserve predicts another ischaemic event within a year. Their patients had symptomatic narrowing of the middle cerebral artery. The flow measure is borrowed from heart artery practice.

The sample held 124 patients with one-sided narrowing who had special CT scans. Computer models of blood flow were built from the scan images. Nineteen patients had a repeat event within the year. Their flow values were lower, at a median of 0.72 against 0.83 in others. A cut-off of 0.80 linked independently to recurrence after adjustment. The flow measure also beat simple narrowing degree at prediction.
pmc-13319365:
Xinyi Zhu and co-authors report a 2026 study of loneliness and long term stress hormone levels in older adults in China. All 126 people in the group were age 60 or older and faced raised heart risk. Past work on loneliness and stress hormones has given mixed results, and a bent rather than straight link was tested here.

Hair samples gave a long term readout of the stress hormone cortisol, while a short scale scored how lonely each person felt. Hormone levels looked higher at low to mid loneliness and lower at high loneliness, forming a curved pattern. The curve held after many other factors were counted, though a few strong cases drove the result.
pmc-13320465:
Mohammed Jaffer Sherif and colleagues run, in 2026, a randomised trial comparing two anaesthetic induction drugs in patients with a narrowed mitral valve who were having valve replacement surgery. Echo measurements used to grade stenosis shift with heart rate and blood pressure, so the induction drug could distort assessment and stress the heart.

Eighty adults received either propofol or sevoflurane. In both groups the pressure gradients across the valve fell after induction. The sevoflurane group showed lower pressure half-time and larger estimated valve area by two calculation methods. Blood pressure dipped in both groups. Heart rate rose with propofol but fell with sevoflurane at both early time points. The authors judge sevoflurane's short-term heart and echo profile more favourable at the moments studied.
pmc-13320665:
Lynne Peeples and Gene Russo reply in a 2026 letter to criticism of their news feature on acupuncture and the placebo effect. Borst and others had questioned the piece, and the authors clarify that it was not written to promote acupuncture as a treatment. It was made with the PNAS Front Matter editors as a news feature.

The feature surveyed lab work on body tissue, including fluid filled spaces called the interstitium, that might explain some effects patients report. It also weighed placebo responses openly and noted that sham needling may itself stir body pathways through skin nerves and tissue. The authors stress the wide public use of acupuncture for pain as a reason to study it closely.
pmc-13323165:
Philip Leissner and co-authors run a randomised trial of online cognitive behavioural therapy after heart events with clear arteries, in a 2026 multicentre study. Patients with MINOCA or Takotsubo syndrome often face poor mental health and quality of life, with no proven treatments on offer.

Eighty-eight patients with raised stress or anxiety scores were split between the internet programme and a waiting list. After 10 to 12 weeks, the treated group showed a higher share reaching normal stress and anxiety levels, though that main gap fell short of statistical firmness. Secondary checks favoured treatment for anxiety relief and symptom scores, with gains of moderate size. Effects looked stronger in Takotsubo patients than in other cases.
pmc-13324165:
Julia Acker and team asked whether the way rotavirus builds its replication organelles is truly conserved across strains. Their 2026 study focused on NSP5, a disordered protein that forms condensates with NSP2 through liquid-liquid phase separation in species A rotaviruses. Because NSP5 sequences vary widely, the team used machine learning to compare variants and built one carrying features of low-split strains.

The built low-split variant could not phase separate on its own unless tagged with phosphate, yet it still supported droplet formation and virus growth inside cells. Low-split variants needed phosphate tags to nucleate droplets, while high-split variants did not, pointing to distinct nucleation mechanisms. Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry revealed a phosphate-driven switch that alters NSP2 binding depending on the variant. The authors conclude that phosphate tagging tunes droplet assembly in a strain-specific way.
pmc-13324665:
Afnan A. Almuhanna and team mapped the gut flora of chronic kidney disease patients in Saudi Arabia, where Arab population data have been thin. Their 2026 study used whole-genome DNA reading of fecal samples from 189 people spanning healthy controls and patients with chronic kidney disease, hemodialysis, and peritoneal dialysis. The aim was to map germ and working differences by disease stage and treatment type.

Germ profiles differed clearly across all patient groups, and risk scores built from taxa that varied in amount distinguished each patient group from controls with areas under the curve above 0.9. Peritoneal gut flora showed reduced diversity, more Proteobacteria and virulence factors, weaker networks, and a proinflammatory profile. Patients on blood filtering, by contrast, showed partial restoration toward a healthier profile, with more short-chain fatty acid production and less lipopolysaccharide synthesis. The authors see modality-specific targets for microbiome-based intervention.
pmc-13326065:
Yihui Zhao and co-authors coat cherry tomatoes with a fully bio-based membrane that guards them after harvest in a 2026 study. Fresh produce spoils fast, and plastic wraps clash with green goals.

Ferulic acid serves as both filler and crosslinker inside a chitosan and caseinate film. The dense coat reached a strength near 55 MPa and leaked its antioxidant filler slowly, about 50 percent over 25 days. On tomatoes stored at 4 °C for 25 days, the coat cut fat damage markers by over 35 percent. Microbe counts fell by more than 2 log units, and firmness plus vitamin C stayed near starting levels.
pmc-13328365:
Jing He, Shouliang Zhao, and Yanqin Ju characterize a sugar-cutting enzyme in an oral bacterium in a 2026 study. Capnocytophaga ochracea settles early in dental plaque and is linked to gum inflammation, but its sialidase had never been studied. The team profiled the enzyme, blocked it, and deleted its gene to watch biofilm behavior.

The enzyme, Co-NanH, worked best at pH 5.5 and cut both main sialic acid link types, matching enzymes from notorious late plaque pathogens. Without the gene, bacteria grew normally in liquid yet built thin, weak biofilms and gripped gum cells poorly. A common blocker, DANA, also cut biofilm growth, marking the enzyme as a drug target for early plaque control.
pmc-13329365:
Pankaj Kumar Tyagi and team mapped research on gender-based career stall, the glass ceiling that holds women from leadership. Their 2026 field-mapping and joined-up review paired a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review with citation mapping, sifting peer-reviewed English Scopus papers from 2015 to 2025 down to 186 records. Link maps built on shared references, co-citations, and shared keywords with VOSviewer picked out the most weighty authors, papers, countries, and journals.

The study found four linked theme areas in today's glass ceiling research, spanning social sciences, business, economics, humanities, and psychology. It traced how the field's brain structure shifted despite decades of policy reforms, diversity drives, and greater gender equality awareness. The team pulls together structural drivers of gendered career blocks across these themes. It puts forward future research paths, aiming to deepen grasp of why women stay markedly absent from leadership roles in most countries.
pmc-13329665:
Roser Navarro-Soler and colleagues compare immune recovery on two-drug versus three-drug HIV therapy in a 2026 study. Both plans use dolutegravir-based integrase drugs, and the two-drug plan pairs it with lamivudine. The team drew on 21,233 adults in the Spanish HIV Research Network and matched patients to balance group traits.

Focus fell on the CD4 to CD8 ratio, a marker of immune health tied to illness and death beyond AIDS itself. At 3 years, no clear gaps in ratio recovery appeared at any cut point between the two plans in the reported results. The authors read this as a sign that long-term immune recovery does not differ by plan size, at least in this matched real-world group.
pmc-13330665:
Miaojuan Qiu and colleagues build a manganese-based nanomedicine for bowel cancer spread in the belly in a 2026 study. Immune therapy helps few bowel cancer patients, since tumours often stay cold to immunity. Manganese can wake innate immunity through the cGAS-STING path, while alendronate shapes T cell action, yet both reach tumours poorly alone.

Joining the two into manganese-alendronate particles aimed to fix delivery. The particles trigger harmful oxygen species inside tumour cells, driving stress and loud cell death that alerts immunity. Alendronate adds T cell support. Together the pair curbed tumour growth and stirred strong anti-tumour responses in the reported models. Both parts are already clinically known materials.
pmc-13331965:
Yukako Otsuka and co-authors recount a 2026 case in which bleeding around the brain first looked exactly like a major heart attack. A 58-year-old man was found in cardiac arrest, his rhythm worsened into ventricular fibrillation during resuscitation, and his heart tracing afterward strongly suggested blocked coronary arteries.

Urgent angiography showed two main coronary arteries closed at once. Yet blood flow returned on its own to full strength before any stent or balloon was used, and ultrasound found no burst plaque or clot. Because the man stayed in a coma, head imaging was done and revealed widespread subarachnoid hemorrhage with fluid build-up. The authors explain the heart picture as spasm of several vessels driven by the brain bleed, a rare mimic that can send teams down the wrong path.
pmc-13332465:
Megumi Nishimura and colleagues map 2026 how a tail segment keeps the channel protein TMEM63B switched off at rest. TMEM63B belongs to a family of force-sensitive channels, and the team recently identified it as a force-sensitive lipid scramblase turned on by changes in membrane properties. The antibody's binding site and its control mechanism had stayed unclear.

Using hybrid constructs, tail truncations, and internal deletions, the team traced the antibody site to the intracellular C-terminal tail, with a three-amino-acid AQV motif as the core contact. That tail region proved essential for holding the protein inactive under resting conditions. Removing a nearby LQD motif or swapping one leucine switched the protein on.
pmc-13332765:
M D Arefin Hossen and co-authors hunted for inflammation-linked genes that drive chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps, in a 2026 study combining public gene data with laboratory checks. The condition returns often after treatment, and its molecular roots remain murky.

Merging gene expression sets with single-cell data and a curated inflammation gene list, the team used network analysis to narrow 96 key genes, which clustered in IL-17 signaling and cytokine interaction pathways. Three genes, FOXP3, C5AR1, and LIF, stood out as effective predictors, and their expression was confirmed experimentally. Immune profiling showed activated memory CD4 T cells and M2 macrophages enriched in polyp tissue, and a drug-matching search nominated bicuculline as a candidate therapy. The authors frame the trio as diagnostic markers tied to immune cell entry into the tissue.
pmc-13333165:

pmc-13333365:

pmc-13333465:

pmc-13333665:

pmc-13334065:

pmc-13335265:

pmc-13336365:

pmc-13336465:
Wen-Teng Yao and co-authors tested wavelength-matched far-infrared therapy for boosting skin blood flow in a 2026 human study. pmc-13336665:

Growing SnS on a first SnS2 layer shielded it and kept the desired form clean. Path control could help build layered devices with exact crystal forms.
pmc-13336865:
Qiang Zhou and co-authors wrap capacitor electrodes in carbon shells using flash heating in a 2026 energy study. Theory ties the gain to stronger ion sticking at the shell.
pmc-13337765:
Wenbo Ma, Xiangdong Ding, and Nan Zhang study a campus sports peer program for migrant children in a 2026 trial. The program pairs children with peers for training and team contests. Goals include better mental adjustment, healthier growth, and stronger belonging in the city.

The peer group scored higher on adjustment, self-esteem, fitness measures, exercise habits, belonging, and peer acceptance in the reported comparisons. Findings support peer sport as a school support tool for newly arrived children.
pmc-13338165:
Adebayo Jonathan Adeyemo and colleagues test biochar plus urea for rice in southern Nigeria in a 2026 field study. Rice husk and sawdust chars are promoted as climate-smart soil aids, but field evidence across soil types was thin. Trials ran on two soils and in upland and lowland settings.

Soil acidity, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and yield parts were measured after harvest. pmc-13339365:
Abigail K. Mayo and colleagues simulate liver injury from obeticholic acid in fatty liver disease in a 2026 computer study. The bile acid drug won approval for a bile duct disease in 2016 but raised liver safety flags in fatty liver trials. Virtual patients replaced human dosing for the test.

Body-based models predicted drug exposure in blood, liver, and gut for healthy and fatty liver groups. Exposure was lifted two, five, and tenfold in virtual fatty liver runs as described. A toxicology model added bile transport blocking and mitochondrion harm. Predicted enzyme rises and injury plots gauge safe dose limits without exposing patients.
pmc-13341465:
Clear cell kidney cancer is surveyed from genes to treatment by Han Yang and colleagues in a 2026 overview. The commonest kidney cancer subtype usually begins with loss of the VHL gene, letting HIF-2α pile up and switch on growth pathways.

The review walks through disease mechanisms and diagnosis, then focuses on belzutifan trial results, aiming to give clinicians a current map of options for this cancer.
pmc-13341665:
Consciousness as an electromagnetic goo rather than a computation is argued by Tam Hunt in a 2026 paper tackling neuroscience's binding and criticality problems. Hunt cites entrainment of spike timing by fields as weak as 0.74 mV/mm, plus field propagation near 50 km/s against spikes' far slower pace, as evidence fields can bind activity across space and time. pmc-13341865:
A diabetes drug transforms metabolism in transplant-related lipodystrophy, in a 2026 case report by Yuri Tanaka and colleagues. The 37-year-old woman had received a stem cell transplant at age 12 for relapsed leukemia, with total body irradiation, and developed diabetes and fatty liver by 17.

pmc-13343165:

pmc-13343465:

pmc-13344065:
Alia H Zawawi and colleagues studied smoking cessation adherence in 2026 at four primary care clinics affiliated with King Abdulaziz Medical City in Saudi Arabia. pmc-13345365:

pmc-13345865:

pmc-13345965:

pmc-13346065:

pmc-13347265:

pmc-13348065:

pmc-13348165:

pmc-13349365:

pmc-13349965:

pmc-13350165:

pmc-13350265:

pmc-13350365:

pmc-13350665:

pmc-13350765:

pmc-13352165:

pmc-13354465:

pmc-13355565:

pmc-13355665:

pmc-13358565:

pmc-13358765:

pmc-13358865:

pmc-13360565:

pmc-13360665:

pmc-13360865:

pmc-13361165:

pmc-13362165:

pmc-13362365:

pmc-13362565:

pmc-13374265:

pmc-13379565:

pmc-13380765:

pmc-13387265:
