Making aromatic amines without touching other fragile groups in the same molecule is a staple problem of fine chemistry, and water's role in it was oddly unexamined.

With water present, selectivity for 3-aminostyrene jumped, passing 98 percent at a best mix of 10 percent water by volume in the results given. Kinetics, in-place infrared watching and theory agree: water splitting at the platinum-oxide boundary blocks the side reactions. A by-product long ignored turns out to steer the reaction.
pmc-13400465:
Ugonna Ihenacho leads a team asking, in 2026, whether neighborhood segregation shapes breast cancer risk in the Multiethnic Cohort. Segregation by race, income and schooling is known to harm health, but local-level links with breast cancer were little studied. Participants lived in California and Hawaii.

The cohort followed more than one hundred thousand women from five ethnic groups, enrolled in their late forties to mid seventies, through 2019. Over 7,300 developed breast cancer. In California, women in the most privileged areas by income and education segregation faced modestly higher risk than those in the least privileged areas. For Latina women, risk rose steadily with neighborhood privilege across several measures.
pmc-13400665:
Lander Heyerick and a large team identify, in 2026, an inflammatory monocyte population driving primary sclerosing cholangitis, a chronic bile duct disease of the liver. Monocytes and macrophages were suspected players, but their exact role was murky. The team also tested whether blocking the related signal could help.

Profiling blood cells from patients, people with ulcerative colitis and healthy controls, they found circulating monocytes loaded with the messenger CXCL8 in the disease group. Blood levels of its protein, IL-8, ran high and marked worse prognosis, with high levels tied to poorer transplant-free survival. Mouse models, including mice carrying a human-like immune system, were used to probe the pathway as a treatment target.
pmc-13401165:
Zhongbo Bian and colleagues report a 2026 trial of noodles fortified with chitooligosaccharides, given to young male seafarers at high risk of central obesity. Life offshore encourages weight gain around the waist, so the team tested a food-based option that could work on board ship.

In a self-controlled trial, 73 men ate placebo noodles for four weeks, then, after a washout break, the fortified noodles every other day for four weeks. Compared with the placebo phase, waist size, visceral fat area, leptin, and LDL cholesterol fell, and a skeletal muscle index rose, while body weight barely changed. Blood metabolite profiling in 38 men helped trace the metabolic shifts behind those changes.
pmc-13401265:
Alejandro Chen Liang and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter to the editor responding to a meta-analysis by Malvi and co-authors. The review covered quinolone antibiotics for preventing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, a serious infection in people with cirrhosis, and its effect on mortality. The letter questions how the review judged the quality of its trials.

Its main point concerns the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Several trials labelled overall low risk had at least one domain rated as some concerns, often for missing data on results. Yet the tool's guidance requires every domain to be low before a study earns an overall low rating. The writers ask the review team to clarify how those overall judgments were reached, and raise further points about the review's handling of its randomized trials.
pmc-13401565: Francesca Palandri and co-authors are named in a 2026 correction notice in Annals of Hematology for their article on modern, multidisciplinary care in polycythemia vera. The notice is a correction only, fixing article metadata rather than any scientific content: the family names of Michelangelo La Placa and Federica Lo Dato were tagged incorrectly. The notice confirms La Placa and Lo Dato as the correct family names. The original article has been updated accordingly, and nothing in its findings, data, or conclusions is changed by the correction.
pmc-13401665:
Suguru Okami and Alexandros Sagkriotis wrote a 2026 careful case analysis of external control arms in Japanese drug approvals. In such cases a treatment is judged against patients outside the trial, because a randomized control arm cannot be run. How well such evidence is written down, and how leftover uncertainty is handled at approval, was unclear.

Screening approvals from 2019 to 2024, the authors found 23 cases using external controls among 674 approvals in scope drawn from 835 found. Each case was scored against twenty attributes covering planning stages through reporting. Post-marketing requirements were studied to see how uncertainty was managed after approval. External controls grouped in rare diseases with small patient groups. Planning and data-source choices were covered fairly well in public records, while later parts were thinner.
pmc-13402265:
Zibo Gao and co-authors counted and mapped two decades of studies on extended reality, the family of virtual, augmented, and mixed reality tools, in bone surgery training. Searching the Web of Science Core Collection for 2000 to 2025, they kept 420 papers under PRISMA 2020 rules. Mapping tools charted who publishes, where, with whom, and which topics surge or fade over time.

Growth fell into three stages, from early trials through steady output to a recent boom driven by better hardware and pandemic-era demand for remote teaching. The United States, the United Kingdom, and China lead output, and McGill University tops the institution list. Artificial intelligence tied to reality tools showed the strongest citation burst from 2020 to 2025. The authors expect deeper blending of smart tutoring with reality training, plus wider cross-border teamwork.
pmc-13402865:
Amy L. Sobbe and co-authors find that mice lacking the Mdr2 transporter, a model of bile-flow liver disease resembling a human cholestatic disorder, hold less iron in their livers than expected. Bile acid build-up in cholestasis lowers hepcidin, the hormone governing iron, which might suggest iron loading. Their 2026 study measures liver iron and iron-related genes in these mice on different diets.

On a normal diet, the model mice had reduced liver iron stores despite lower hepcidin and higher levels of the iron import protein, a combination that should favour loading. Fed a diet with one percent added iron, they resisted liver iron accumulation even though blood iron rose, pointing to impaired iron uptake by liver cells. The authors conclude cholestasis itself disrupts hepatic iron handling, which may explain why cholestatic conditions show relatively little liver iron compared with other liver diseases.
pmc-13403365:
Fredrik Sundbom and colleagues used a Swedish airway register in 2026 to describe people with severe asthma who receive biologic drugs. Their group covered 416 patients signed up between 2016 and 2024. The average age was 54.1 years at entry, and just under half were women.

Most patients used inhaled steroids, and many still had poor control and frequent flare-ups at entry. After an average follow-up near 193 days, control, lung function, and flare rates had improved. The authors note wide gaps in who gets entered by region, and they urge more even recording so the register can track care across Sweden.
pmc-13404365:
Zakir Hussain and co-authors made a paired crystal form of the wakefulness drug modafinil in 2026, joining it with benzoic acid in equal parts. Plain modafinil dissolves poorly, which limits how much the body can take up. Several lab tools confirmed the new crystal, backed by computer modeling of its bonds.

The paired form melted at a lower point than either part alone, a sign of a true new phase. It dissolved far better than raw drug in both stomach-like acid and near-neutral fluid. In two standard mouse mood tests, the paired form also edged out raw drug at the same dose. Strong linking bonds inside the crystal explain its build.
pmc-13404565:
Tao Xie and team probed a odd pattern: higher peer health literacy context tied to lower solo health literacy among Chinese schoolchildren. Their 2026 multilevel work weighs 3,307 participants in Shaanxi Province from 2021, testing whether web health info hunting carries the link and whether teacher support, policy, and money factors shape it. Peer settings shape teen health habits, yet their literacy routes had been little probed.

Peer health literacy context ran against solo literacy, with a clear negative side-route through web health info hunting at group level. Left-behind status, money markers, and policy factors shaped that route. The authors suggest that peer context and online hunting mix in tangled ways, urging schools to teach critical judging of online health info rather than assuming peer exposure alone helps.
pmc-13405065:
Janice Litunya and a large team study HIV testing offered through bars and alcohol venues in rural Kenya and Uganda, reporting in 2026. Such venues carry high transmission risk, and their features may shape who gets tested. The work sits inside a cluster-randomised trial in eight communities.

Researchers mapped 530 venues, and nearly all owners joined the trial. Cards invited adults for free testing with rapid start of prevention or treatment. Of 480 venues that took part in recruitment, 7,744 adults were screened and 21 percent had HIV in the reported figures. Among people who did not know their status, 2.3 percent tested newly positive. Venue traits such as rooms for sex work and condom availability are examined as predictors of yield.
pmc-13405365:
Fuchao Chen, Jingyue Sun and Xiao Wang review gut microbe products as bone protectors in a 2026 survey. Osteoporosis thins bone and raises fracture risk, and research now links it to the gut through chemical messengers. Two families of messengers take centre stage: short-chain fatty acids and polyamines.

Fatty acids from fibre fermentation slow bone-eating cells and help bone-building cells through named receptor and gene pathways. Polyamines such as spermidine likewise favour bone formation and restrain breakdown. Genetic and multi-omics studies add causal hints tying specific gut microbes to bone risk. The review also covers measurement platforms and a translation mechanism, eIF5A hypusination, as fresh angles for therapy.
pmc-13405965:
Thangasrinivasan Samyuktha and co-authors review drugs that block the NLRP3 inflammasome to protect blood vessel linings, in a 2026 article. A damaged vessel lining opens the door to atherosclerosis, diabetes complications and high blood pressure. The NLRP3 complex pours out inflammatory signals and can kill lining cells by a fiery death called pyroptosis.

Blocking the complex lowered inflammation and oxidative stress in the studies gathered, preserving lining function and aiding repair. Both natural and synthetic blockers are covered, and several have reached early human trials with encouraging safety so far. The review weighs where this drug class might fit among vascular treatments, noting most evidence remains early stage.
pmc-13407065:
Eun-Ji Lee and co-authors build a machine-learning model to predict which patients with traumatic cervical spinal cord injury will need a tracheostomy, a breathing tube placed through the neck. Early tracheostomy reduces complications when ventilation will be prolonged. Their 2026 study uses records from one institution covering 2017 to 2024.

Of 267 patients, 49 received a tracheostomy. The team compared several algorithms using demographics, injury level, consciousness and impairment scores, and treatment details, and used SHAP analysis to explain the predictions. A CatBoost model performed best; with age, consciousness score, impairment grade, surgery, and specific neck injury levels as inputs, it reached strong discrimination and 86.5 percent accuracy. The authors suggest the model can support earlier, better-timed decisions about the procedure.
pmc-13407165:
Lukas Mayrhofer and co-authors examine, in 2026, whether radical climate protests change how news coverage treats moderate activists, an idea called the radical flank effect. Their German case pairs Fridays for Future, the moderate school-strike movement, with Last Generation, known for disruptive road protests.

Using language-model annotation checked by validation, the team coded stance and anger in 2,376 news articles and 225,121 reader comments. Short bursts of radical protest coverage coincided with friendlier treatment of the moderate group in articles and in left-leaning comment sections, while right-leaning comments turned cooler. Longer windows showed no such pattern, and anger in protest coverage generally, not radical coverage specifically, shaped later support. The effect looks brief and politically split.
pmc-13407665:
Liina Veskimäe and co-authors survey, in 2026, Estonian teenagers' use and misuse of addictive prescription medicines, from sedatives to sleeping pills. Their data come from a nationally representative 2024 schools survey of 2,019 fifteen- and sixteen-year-olds, who also reported on mental wellbeing and self-harm.

Medical use was reported by 27.8 percent and misuse by 18.3 percent, both higher among girls, with sedatives and sleeping pills the most common in each category. Misused medicines mostly came from home supplies, and self-treatment was the leading motive. Poor mental wellbeing touched 44.4 percent of misusers and self-harm 17.6 percent, the highest rates of any group. Misuse carried nearly triple the adjusted odds of self-harm versus non-use. The authors argue prevention belongs inside wider adolescent mental-health strategy.
pmc-13407865:
Zhijian Li and co-authors solve, in 2026, a manufacturing headache for perovskite solar cells: coating their delicate surface layers in open air. Two functional layers drink moisture from humid air and spoil. One is a molecular carpet, the other a passivation coating. Production usually flees to dry rooms. The team instead mixed alcohol with a low-polarity alkane. The mix dissolves the materials while suppressing moisture uptake during blade coating.

Chemical and electronic checks confirmed the solvent system works generally for both layer types, even in high humidity. Devices whose every layer was blade-coated in air reached a certified efficiency of 26.1 percent, with negligible loss even when made at 80 percent relative humidity. Scalable, factory-floor fabrication of perovskite photovoltaics is the stated prize.
pmc-13408165:
João dos Santos, Juliana de Araújo, and André Sampaio ask in a 2026 review whether sheep skull bones can train ear surgeons. Human bones for practice are scarce, so courses need stand-ins that still teach real anatomy and real technique. The team gathered every study that cut sheep bones or used them in training.

Twenty-six studies qualified. They covered work under both microscopes and endoscopes, plus a wide range of ear surgery, from eardrum repair to cochlear implants. Sheep anatomy matched the human layout closely. Trainees who practised on sheep worked faster, cut more truly, and felt more sure of their hands. The authors flag a few real differences from human bone. For course directors, the review backs sheep bone as a cheap, easy-to-source, and fair practice model.
pmc-13408765:
Seyed Amirhossein Sadeghi and colleagues combine two proteomics routes in 2026 to read the protein coat that nanoparticles pick up in blood with far greater care. That corona decides how a nanomedicine interacts with the body, yet its proteins come in many subtly different forms, called proteoforms, which ordinary methods blur together. The team studied polystyrene particles coated in plasma from breast cancer patients.

Top-down analysis, which reads whole proteins, catalogued more than five thousand proteoforms from four hundred genes, one of the largest such plasma datasets. Adding bottom-up digestion data sharpened the picture for about a third of the forms carrying unexplained mass shifts. The richer catalogue also surfaced candidate breast cancer biomarkers carried in certain proteoforms. Nanomedicine researchers gain both a reference dataset and a method for safer, better-targeted particle design.
pmc-13409965:
Irene Amigo and her team report in 2026 on touch sensors in human skin and the helper cells wrapped around them. They studied Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles, two kinds of end organs that sense light touch and vibration. Helper glial cells there were long seen as mere support, yet they may help sense pressure too.

Using stored skin samples from 64 donors, the team stained for five channel proteins tied to force sensing. Staining showed up in helper cells for some proteins in some corpuscles, with one protein, TRPA1, reported in these cells for the first time. Pacinian bodies were scarce outside hands and feet, so counts there stayed rough. The authors stress that staining alone cannot prove the channels work.
pmc-13410765:
Camilla Pires and co-workers report in 2026 what happens to malaria parasites when a repeat-rich protein called LRR5 is broken. The parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, must time its growth inside red blood cells and decide when to make sexual forms that spread infection. Broken LRR5 was known to raise sensitivity to drugs and heat.

Single-cell gene reading across the growth cycle compared normal parasites with a mutant strain. The mutant turned down genes for protein folding, export, and reshaping the host cell, while stress genes rose in reply. Sexual-stage genes also switched on too early, and overall timing ran fast. LRR5 thus links cell housekeeping to the parasite's sense of timing.
pmc-13411365:
Jun Liu and colleagues made a methane-reforming catalyst in 2026 that shakes off sulfur poisoning, a flaw that blocks biogas upgrading. Their platinum on ceria catalyst uses carbon dioxide to push oxygen from the support onto platinum. That turns deposited sulfur into sulfur dioxide gas that leaves the surface.

After restructuring during reaction, the catalyst kept steady activity for 100 hours even with hydrogen sulfide present, recovering on its own after each poisoning hit. The paper gives engineers a self-cleaning design rule for turning sulfur-laced biogas into useful fuel gas and for cutting downtime in plants that run on dirty feedstocks.
pmc-13411765:
Samantha Smith and colleagues produce in 2026 Ireland's first national estimate of children living with life-limiting conditions. Counting them is the first step toward planning palliative care, yet Ireland lacks a single patient identifier, so one child with many admissions can masquerade as many. Hospital discharge data from 2019 and 2024 were adjusted under three scenarios.

Baseline estimates put prevalence between roughly 35 and 50 per ten thousand children in 2019, easing slightly by 2024. Correcting for undercounting pushed the range higher still. Boys outnumbered girls, and babies under one year carried the highest rates in every scenario. The method itself is a deliverable for countries in the same data bind.
pmc-13414365:
Yves Janssens and co-authors grow a ferroelectric film on silicon in 2026 to coax a high-order acoustic wave mode from a tiny resonator. Surface acoustic wave devices filter radio signals, and the Sezawa mode promises higher frequencies without shrinking the electrode pattern impossibly. Their barium-doped lead zirconate titanate film, laid down by pulsed laser on bulk silicon, couples strongly while the stiff silicon underneath supports the faster wave.

Resonators sang between 275 and 500 megahertz in the reported measurements. Because the film is ferroelectric, boosting its electric polarization sharpened performance: quality factors climbed from 50 to 200, and coupling rose from two to five percent across their devices. The ratio of film thickness to wavelength stayed under the threshold the mode requires. MEMS filters and sensors are the target uses.
pmc-13415265:
Keita Teruya and colleagues studied 8266 Japanese dialysis patients in 2026 to test whether a routine red-cell measure, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, predicts death and heart events. Anemia in kidney failure already raises death risk. Hemoglobin alone may miss part of the picture, so the team grouped patients by this average hemoglobin per red cell.

Over a median near three years, low values tracked with higher death risk, while both low and high values tracked with higher death and heart-event risk in curved analyses. The paper suggests adding this cheap lab value to anemia care, especially for patients whose hemoglobin already sits in the usual target range.
pmc-13415865:
Wei Zhang and colleagues show that brain coupling from adult to infant carries socially marked information into learning, in a 2026 study spanning the United Kingdom and Singapore. Adults taught infants an artificial language, pairing parts with full, partial, or no eye contact. Neural activity was recorded in speaker and listener during teaching.

Coupling ran one way, from adult speaker to infant listener, and strengthened with eye contact. That coupling predicted which language pieces infants later learned selectively. Coupling beat the infant's own brain activity as a predictor of learning. Social valuation, the brain's judgment of what matters, may ride on this directed signal.
pmc-13416665:
Youxue Zhang and co-authors examine vitamin D levels and a urine marker of kidney strain in adults with high blood pressure, in a 2026 analysis. They use United States survey data from NHANES collected between 1999 and 2018. The urine marker is the albumin to creatinine ratio, which can signal heart and kidney risk even at low levels.

The group included 37,554 people, of whom 19,802 had hypertension. Low vitamin D linked more strongly to a higher urine ratio in the hypertension group, with a bend near 60 nmol per litre. Because measures were taken once, the authors note that cause cannot be shown.
pmc-13416765:
Mingxuan Wan and co-authors map how vegetation returned after landslides from the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, in a 2026 study. Slopes stripped by the quake stayed bare for years in many places. Using Landsat images from 2008 to 2023, they trace recovery paths and look for the climate settings that speed or slow regrowth.

Most areas turned from fast to slower recovery within five to seven years. High, rugged ground lagged behind. A warm, moist setting with moderate light favoured fast recovery in their network model. Radiation limited highlands most, while heat and rain mattered more at low sites. Restoration can thus be tailored by place.
pmc-13417865:
Qin-qin Wang and colleagues review inflammation in the brain as a driver of Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases, in a 2026 article. No current therapy targets this brain inflammation directly. Protein clumps central to each disease, amyloid, tau, and alpha synuclein, activate support cells called glia and keep inflammation simmering, which speeds neuron loss.

Outside influences also feed the process, including body wide inflammation, environmental exposures, and gut to brain signals. A neglected actor, the precursor cells that make insulation for nerve fibres, gets special attention. New imaging, single cell, and lab grown tissue tools are sharpening targets, and immune calming trials are reviewed.
pmc-13417965:
Jiazhen Zhao and colleagues model smoke driven lung inflammation in mice and in cultured immune cells, in a 2026 preclinical study at a Shanghai hospital. The work targets chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, where macrophages, the lung's cleaner cells, skew toward an attack mode. Mice breathed cigarette smoke for 15 weeks with two bacterial signal doses, while cells received smoke extract for a day.

Exposed mice showed poorer airflow, higher lung resistance, and damaged air sacs. Attack mode markers and inflammatory signals rose, while a calming signal fell, in both mice and cells. A pathway pairing NF-kB with the NLRP3 inflammasome stayed active, suggesting a target for calming smoke driven inflammation.
pmc-13418765:
Nima Kianfar and colleagues map how well people across Georgia can reach emergency heart care, then test how that reach lines up with heart disease deaths. Heart and vessel disease kills more than 21,000 people in the state each year, making access to fast care a pressing question. Their 2026 study uses a refined catchment method that weighs distance and crowding at each care center.

The model scores each area by the care supply within reach of its people, with nearer centers counting more. The team then linked those scores to local death rates while adjusting for social vulnerability. Gaps in access fell unevenly across the state rather than in a smooth urban-to-rural fade. The linked maps give health planners a sharper view of where new capacity or transport help might save the most lives.
pmc-13418965:
Philipp Braun and colleagues develop an MRI approach that measures body fat while the patient breathes freely, with no breath holds. Water-fat separation scans in the belly usually demand held breath, which many patients cannot manage well. Fat share in the liver and pancreas together gives a fuller picture of metabolic health, so a free-breathing route has real value.

The method pairs a standard grid scan order with spiral ordering of the profile lines and corrects phase errors that spoil fat values. A digital body model helped the team tune the settings before human scans. Motion during breathing is estimated after the fact from the scan data itself, with no extra hardware fitted to the patient. The setup aims at sharp, wide coverage of the belly in a single free-breathing run.
pmc-13419465:
O'Brien surveys zoos about a neglected welfare topic in this 2026 study: animals living with disabilities, defined as losing a critical adaptation that affects stability, mobility, behavior, or perception. Research has leaned on individual case reports and mammals, so the survey went to organizations accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums to map prevalence and practice.

Responses came from 115 people across 45 organizations, roughly 19 percent of accredited members. All but one organization, 98 percent of those surveyed, reported currently caring for at least one disabled animal, and cases spanned every vertebrate group plus spiders, insects, and other invertebrates. Birds, mammals, and reptiles were most likely to receive modified care, and staff judged the welfare of disabled animals similar to that of their able-bodied counterparts. The author offers the dataset as a foundation for systematic disability research.
pmc-13420165:
Mana Mohebbian and colleagues count substance-induced mental disorders across British Columbia in 2022 and 2023, conditions that services often miss. These disorders follow drug or alcohol use directly, bringing psychosis or mood collapse on top of the substance problem itself. A new case-finding method linked substance events in records to later psychiatric diagnoses to catch them.

Cannabis and hallucinogen cases clustered among younger people, while alcohol and tobacco cases dominated in older adults. Stimulant-linked cases carried the highest rates of hospital admission and involuntary treatment in the province. Combined problems worsen recovery and raise service use, so a true count matters for planning. Health authorities get a base map of who is affected and where the load falls.
pmc-13420265:
Menon and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare blood infection in a 74-year-old man in Ohio. The germ, Wohlfahrtiimonas chitiniclastica, is spread by parasitic flies and is linked to maggot-infested wounds. The man arrived with sepsis, meaning a dangerous body-wide infection, and neglected pressure sores containing maggots.

A mass-spectrometry method, MALDI-TOF, finally identified the germ six days after the blood draw. Cultures also grew three other germs, showing how mixed the wound infections were. His course was worsened by metastatic cancer and by tumour lysis syndrome, a burst of waste from dying cancer cells, which eased after a targeted drug. Antibiotics cleared the blood infection, but care shifted to comfort and he died on day thirty. The authors stress expert lab methods for rare germs in neglected wounds.
pmc-13421265:
Aral and colleagues report a 2026 surgery study on repairing one torn shoulder tendon, the subscapularis, with a single anchor holding two suture loads. They reviewed 27 patients, none in heavy physical work, treated between 2014 and 2020. Function, pain, movement, and tendon healing on scans were tracked for at least five years.

By final follow-up, at an average of about 81 months, function scores had nearly doubled from their starting levels. Pain fell to near one on a ten-point scale, and inward rotation improved by several spine levels. Positive results on two squeeze tests for this tendon dropped sharply, from over nine in ten patients to under one in five. For patients without heavy job demands, one anchor gave lasting repair, which keeps surgery simpler and cheaper than multi-anchor fixes.
pmc-13421465:
Mazen Balat, Esraa Mamdouh, Rewaa Awaad, Mohamed Elhoseny and Ahmed M Anter present SignatureGuard in a 2026 paper, a system that checks handwritten signatures while correcting a Latin-script bias in the field. Most verification systems are trained on English signatures, leaving Arabic handwriting nearly absent from benchmarks.

Their framework handles three tasks — forgery detection, writer identification and forgery source identification — and tests six hybrid designs pairing convolutional networks with vision transformers. They also released ASVAR, an Arabic dataset of 3,471 signature images from 70 people. The best hybrids detected forgeries at about 98 percent accuracy on both Arabic and English sets, with consistent rankings across scripts. The authors note their closed-set protocol flatters real-world performance.
pmc-13421565:
Aslı Arslan Kulcan examines, in a 2026 study, whether membrane filtration can split red beetroot juice into a health-rich concentrate and a sugar stream. Beetroot is prized for betalain pigments and phenolic compounds, yet its natural sugars limit some uses, so separating the two fractions has commercial appeal.

Ultrafiltration through two pore sizes came first; the tighter membrane held back more phenolics and betalains. Washing the retained fraction with added water — diafiltration — then flushed out small sugar molecules. At the best wash volume, recoveries reached about sixty-nine percent for phenolics and seventy-three percent for betalains, while under a fifth of the sugar stayed behind. The author presents the combined process as a route to enriched beetroot ingredients.
pmc-13422065:
David Fishwick leads a ten-author team using an online tool, in a 2026 study, to ask European workers whether their jobs are hurting their lungs. Inhaled workplace hazards stay under-recognised by workers, employers and clinicians alike, so the team built industry-specific digital questionnaires linking breathing symptoms to work.

Over twenty-four months, 22,393 people answered, most often in English, Portuguese or French. Nasal symptoms and cough were common, and well over a third reported at least one work-related symptom, while workplace training and guidance were rare. About six percent had changed jobs because work affected their breathing, with bakeries, mines, sports centres and farms standing out. Training, where it existed, cut that risk. The authors promote social media outreach for occupational lung health.
pmc-13422865:
Bhandari and co-authors mine a traditional Nepalese fern in this 2026 study. They isolate compounds from Aleuritopteris bicolor. The fern is known locally as Raani Sinkaa. Folk healers use it for wounds and stomach complaints. Guided by activity testing at each step, the team split the fern's methanol extract into three compounds. Two were quercetin sugar conjugates.

The quercetin pair proved potent antioxidants. They cleared free radicals at a half-maximal concentration of 1.56 micrograms per milliliter. That beat the vitamin C standard's 4.15 in the same assay. The pair also partly curbed Staphylococcus and Klebsiella germs. Against two starch-breaking enzymes tied to diabetes, the mixture scored half-maximal effects at 99.48 and 68.53 micrograms per milliliter. Those figures cover amylase and glucosidase respectively in the reported tests. Docking backed the enzyme binding. The authors urge animal studies toward an antidiabetic phytomedicine.
pmc-13423065:
Sophia Lubna Kara and three co-authors ask health workers in private facilities across Tanzania what they know and do about climate change and health. Their multicentre survey drew 216 completed responses from clinical and non-clinical staff working at several levels of care.

More than 90% of respondents saw climate change as a serious threat to health, and nearly 80% agreed that health facilities themselves harm the environment. The main obstacles to greener practice were low awareness among colleagues, tight budgets, and weak backing from leadership. Staff who did act pointed to careful energy use, waste and water management, and climate teaching. The authors argue facilities could do far more with clearer institutional support.
pmc-13423165:
Jing Zhang and six colleagues pool published findings on stroke risk in people whose high blood pressure has damaged the eye's retina, a sign of wider organ damage. Hypertension is the leading cause of stroke, and the team asked whether this retinal change marks extra risk beyond blood pressure alone.

Searching four databases to December 2025, they combined ten studies with 26,776 participants. Stroke occurred in 20% of people with retinal damage, and their pooled risk ran 1.87 times that of patients without it. Severe retinal damage carried still higher risk, roughly triple the rate seen without damage. Both major stroke types were included in subgroup checks, supporting eye examination as a simple risk signal in hypertension care.
pmc-13423365:
Derek Maas and nine co-authors review whether pairing topical tretinoin with topical minoxidil beats minoxidil alone for pattern hair loss. The condition is common in men and women and weighs on quality of life. Tretinoin is thought to help minoxidil penetrate the scalp and switch on inside the follicle.

Laboratory evidence shows tretinoin cream applied first nearly triples minoxidil absorption into the body. Clinical proof, though, is thin: the single randomised trial found dual therapy no better than minoxidil alone, while smaller reports suggest some non-responders convert when tretinoin is added. Seventy-one social media posts leaned positive but often mentioned irritation. The reviewers place the pairing as an add-on for non-responders, not a first choice.
pmc-13423465:
Kei Miyata and six colleagues describe a stroke caused by a vertebral artery squeezed at the first neck vertebra. An incomplete bony arch, called an arcuate foramen, pressed on the vessel, and a floating clot formed there. Such compression is a rare stroke mechanism, and the case shows how the team untangled two-sided disease.

The older woman arrived with vertigo and unsteady walking, and scans showed fresh infarcts in both lower cerebellar territories. The left artery carried the clot at the squeeze point, while the right artery, on which brain flow depended, was also narrowed lower down. Surgeons stented the right artery first, then closed the left one to remove the clot source, in a single session.
pmc-13424365:
Shaikh Nabi Bukhsh Nazir and Amna Asim run a randomised trial in knee osteoarthritis. They ask whether the joint responds better to training the trunk or training the foot and ankle, two ends of the same loading chain. One hundred patients aged forty or more took part. All had moderate joint damage. Half followed an eight-week core stability programme and half a foot-ankle programme, both layered on standard knee exercises.

Pain at rest was the main measure, joined by knee function scores, walking and standing tests, and structural measures of the Achilles tendon and arch. The core group improved significantly more on every outcome than the foot-ankle group over the eight weeks. The authors argue that proximal control deserves priority in knee rehabilitation.
pmc-13424465:
Businge and colleagues report early safety results in 2026 from a trial in Kampala, Uganda. The trial tested whether the measles-rubella vaccine can be given at six months instead of the standard nine months. Many infants lose their mothers' protective antibodies by six months.

The open-label trial randomly assigned 450 infants to first doses at six or nine months, with boosters at 12 or 18 months depending on the group. Reactions near the injection site and whole-body reactions occurred at nearly the same rates in both age groups. Most local reactions were mild and settled within four days. Five of six hospital stays followed common childhood illnesses, and one death was unrelated to the vaccine. Sixteen confirmed measles or rubella cases appeared before the booster stage.
pmc-13424565:
Mai Haidar and Nabih Raslan ran a 2026 trial in children aged 6 to 12 whose back upper molars were weak from a mineral defect. Each child needed filling work, and each received two numbing shots on separate visits, one a lidocaine mix and one an articaine mix, both with epinephrine.

Pain at injection was rated by the children with a faces scale and by watchers with a behaviour scale covering face, legs, movement, crying, and comfort. Early results showed no clear gap between the two mixes in injection pain on either scale. Dentists get a head-to-head test that keeps the choice grounded in child comfort rather than habit.
pmc-13425465:
Jacqueline L. Chen and coauthors published a 2026 reply concerning evaluation of artificial intelligence answers to medical education questions. They agree that newer models are improving quickly in reasoning and diagnostic performance and that benchmarking must keep pace. Their original study, however, judged the prose explanations behind multiple-choice answers rather than answer accuracy alone.

Even with strong test scores, ChatGPT-4 explanations often contained wrong reasoning, missing clinical details, or advice that could harm patients, according to their analysis. The reply defends explanation quality and safety as the right focus when models may teach or advise clinicians.
pmc-13425965:
Marina A Bustamante-Ordoñez and colleagues report a newborn boy, aged 7 days and small for his gestational age, with a rare and aggressive leukaemia. Neonatal leukaemia accounts for under 1 percent of childhood leukaemias, and the mixed-phenotype form is rarer still.

His white cell count peaked at 615,400 per microlitre, with severe anaemia, low platelets, and purple skin spots of the blueberry muffin type. Clotting trouble and a high risk of tumour breakdown added danger, so staff used manual partial exchange transfusion when machine filtering was unavailable, gaining a brief fall in counts. The case shows how fast teams must act when standard tools are absent.
pmc-13426065:
Shim and co-authors engineered virus-like particles decorated with peptide-MHC complexes. Those complexes are the display molecules that show T cells their targets. The goal was to find and upgrade the rare tumor-specific T cells inside a patient's repertoire. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy is limited by how few of those cells exist, and by how dysfunctional they often are.

The particles selectively prime and expand only the T cells matching the displayed tumor peptide. They ignore bystander cells entirely. They also deliver base editors, precision gene-editing tools. Those editors enhance the killing power of the selected tumor-specific cells. In the reported experiments, the platform armed mixed lymphocyte populations with stronger anti-tumor cytotoxicity. The authors present the system as a way to improve lymphocyte therapy. It avoids the off-target engineering risks of treating all T cells at once.
pmc-13426365:
James Nelson Okema and colleagues report a 2026 case of orbital compression syndrome imitating severe malaria in a refugee settlement in northern Uganda. A 9-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease arrived at a primary facility in Palabek Kal settlement. He had one day of severe frontal headache on both sides radiating to the eyes, high fever, and rapidly swelling eyelids with tearing and light sensitivity. He stayed alert without seizures, vomiting, or breathing distress, and his temperature measured 39.3 degrees.

Blocked blood flow infarcting orbital bone marrow with bleeding under its lining explains this rare, sight-threatening sickle complication. Overlap with orbital cellulitis and malaria makes recognition hard where resources are thin, and the authors stress early suspicion.
pmc-13426465:
Martins and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study on checking mouth sores from a distance. Children on chemotherapy often develop oral mucositis, painful sores inside the mouth. In-person dental checks are not always possible during cancer care. The team tested whether phone photos could stand in for a chair-side exam.

Dentists reviewed 224 photos from 21 young patients through a special app. The remote checks caught every case of mouth sores found in person. The catch was false alarms, which cut the accuracy for ruling sores out. Tongue surfaces gave the clearest photo reads, while lips misled readers most often. The authors see photo checks as a backup tool, not a full replacement. Caregiver-taken photos are the next test the authors want to run.
pmc-13427065:
McDonough and colleagues laid out in 2026 a study to co-design workplace training for pharmacists who now work on-site in Australian aged care homes. Since July 2024 the federal government pays pharmacists to embed in these homes to improve medicine use for frail residents. The role is new worldwide, and its holders work apart from other pharmacists, with few chances to learn from peers.

The project will run focus-group style workshops with pharmacists, other health staff, residents, and families, guided by a consumer advisory group of people with lived experience of aged care. Themes from the workshops will shape a pilot training program, which participants will then test and refine. The authors expect the first co-designed program of its kind, with output data due the following year.
pmc-13427465:
Yuki Saito and colleagues profiled what stem-cell-derived heart muscle cells secrete during manufacturing in a 2026 study. Transplanting human induced pluripotent stem cell cardiomyocytes shows promise for ischemic heart disease, and benefits likely flow from secreted factors, including vesicle-carried signals, rather than cell engraftment alone. How that secretome changes across production time points was poorly understood for clinical-grade cells.

The team combined RNA sequencing, protein analysis, and vesicle microRNA sequencing with functional tests of cell growth, migration, and vessel tube formation. Defining the mode of action and candidate quality attributes should help regulators judge batch consistency for cell therapy products. Cells were drawn at set points in the build, so the team could watch the broth of signs shift as the heart cells grew ripe for use.
pmc-13427565:
Mohamed Hajri and colleagues tell, in a 2026 case report, of a huge cyst on an adrenal gland that caused steady back pain. Their patient was a 54-year-old man whose scan showed a fluid-filled mass about 19 centimeters wide. The mass pushed his kidney and pancreas out of place. Such cysts are rare, and scans alone could not rule out cancer.

Surgeons removed the cyst through an open operation, draining it in a controlled way first to make removal safer. Under the microscope its wall was lined by flat vessel-like cells, confirming a benign endothelial cyst, meaning a cyst lined by blood vessel lining cells. He recovered without problems. The case shows why very large cysts still call for surgery and tissue checks.
pmc-13427865:
M. Sindou and colleagues demonstrate, in a 2026 technique paper, their operation for classic trigeminal neuralgia, the severe one-sided facial pain syndrome. In the classic form, an artery presses on the trigeminal nerve root near the brainstem. Their operation, microvascular decompression, moves the artery away through a small opening behind the ear. Long-term series report lasting pain freedom in roughly 75 to 95 percent of well-chosen patients.

Success rests on freeing the whole nerve root, from the brainstem to where it enters its bony canal. The surgeons prefer shifting the vessel rather than padding it, since padding can create new pressure points. Preoperative MRI must show the conflict clearly before they operate. A linked video shows each step. Surgeons and patients weighing options get the reasoning of a highly experienced team.
pmc-13429265:
Holmgren and colleagues compare what happens after a first heart attack in adults born with heart defects. Their 2026 nationwide Swedish study identified 214 adults with congenital heart disease who had a first acute myocardial infarction between 2000 and 2022. Each was matched with ten controls of similar age, sex, and risk profile drawn from the general population.

The congenital group was younger at their heart attack, averaging 58 years against 70 in unmatched controls. After matching, there was no significant difference in death or repeat heart attack at one year. At ten years, mortality looked higher in the congenital group before adjustment, but the gap disappeared once other clinical factors were included. The authors conclude outcomes are broadly similar and stress lifestyle and risk-factor management for this growing patient group.
pmc-13429565:
Xinyue Huang and colleagues raise dextranase output, an enzyme prized for oral care and industry, by mutating and re-hosting its maker. Wild strains yield too little, so the team combined plasma mutagenesis, mechanism study, and promoter tuning in a new host.

A stable mutant, Chaetomium gracile B12, lifted enzyme activity 30.6-fold to 16.23 units per millilitre over its parent. Sequence study plus AlphaFold2 models and 100-nanosecond simulations suggested the change stiffened the protein and refined its substrate site. Bioprocess teams get a high-yield system plus a testable reason for why the mutant works better.
pmc-13430765:
Ahmed Abdinasir Abdulle and colleagues model the timing of first marriage among women in Somalia, where early marriage is common and timing shapes health, fertility, and economic life. Data came from the 2020 Somali Demographic and Health Survey, covering 16,428 women aged 15 to 49.

Time from birth to first marriage was modelled, and after a standard hazards model failed its proportionality check, parametric models were compared. The Weibull hazards model fit best by an information criterion. Policy readers get a survival-analysis base for finding which social factors pull marriage earlier or later, rather than relying on simple averages.
pmc-13430865:
Pouyan Aminishakib and colleagues present nine cases of cherubism, a rare bone disorder of the jaws passed down in families through SH3BP2 gene faults. The series focuses on treatment choices and outcomes, including denosumab in a stubborn case, plus a proposed diagnostic and treatment algorithm.

Nine Persian patients took part, seven boys and men and two girls and women, with onset from age 2 to 14. They had clinical, scan, and tissue workups, plus genetic tests in some cases, with mutations found in two of three tested. Care ranged from watching and steroid injections to surgery, denosumab, and calcitonin. Denosumab and calcitonin controlled progression after surgical relapse in one case, showing options when surgery fails.
pmc-13432765:
Derkacz and collaborators dissected how Streptomyces, the filamentous soil bacteria behind many antibiotics, build their cell walls at growing branch tips, using a genetic screen in Streptomyces albus. Forcing overproduction of the tip organizer DivIVA killed the cells, so the team hunted for mutations that rescued growth and thereby revealed tip machinery partners.

One rescuer was pknB, a gene for a protein kinase that tags other proteins with phosphate to control their behavior. Deleting it restored growth after DivIVA overproduction, confirming a functional link between the two systems in tip growth. Phosphorylation mapping showed the kinase modifies CslA, the enzyme that weaves cellulose-like beta-glucan into the wall of these bacteria. A CslA version unable to accept the phosphate made less beta-glucan and left cells hypersensitive to lysozyme, an enzyme that chews bacterial walls, identifying this phosphorylation as a central control point.
pmc-13432865:
Lilian Koppensteiner and co-authors showed a hidden effect in 2026. Talks between tumor support cells and T cells in lung cancer switch on a pathway. That pathway drains a cell fuel and brews a calming chemical in its place. That brew helps tumors hide from immune attack. Support cells form the most common stromal crowd in the tumor's rim.

T cells grown with the support cells raised two surface tools that run the drain-and-brew chain, and lab gauges confirmed fresh brew output. Large tumor data banks tied strong brew signals to worse paths in one lung cancer kind. Fine-scale gene maps of early tumor rims showed immune genes turned down in that same kind. The authors cast the two-way talk as a driver worth blocking in future care.
pmc-13432965:
Garcia-Pastor and colleagues present a 2026 case review of two patients with metastatic bowel cancer whose tumors carried extra copies of the HER2 gene.  The team used liquid biopsy, a blood test that reads tumor DNA, to watch HER2 levels over time and time a second round of HER2 drugs.

In one patient, blood tests showed HER2 copies persisted after the first HER2 treatment failed, with no new resistance changes. A fresh HER2 drug pair then held the disease for thirteen months. Later, when HER2 copies vanished, the team switched drugs; when copies returned, another HER2 round steadied the disease again.  Blood-guided timing thus turns a spent drug class back into an option.
pmc-13433265:
Cong Shen and co-authors present MolDr, a deep learning framework that predicts how cancer cells will respond to drugs. It represents molecules as multiscale simplicial complexes, shapes that capture connections among groups of atoms, not just pairs. Pairwise descriptions miss much of a molecule's structure. Their 2026 paper integrates these topological representations with cellular profiles in one model.

Across multiple benchmarks, MolDr matched or beat leading methods at predicting continuous drug responses such as sensitivity scores, and it also generalised to classification tasks that sort responses into categories. Tests removing parts of the model confirmed that using several topological scales at once improved performance. The authors argue that higher-order molecular representations make predictions more accurate and robust across varied drug and cell contexts, and they release the code freely for other researchers.
pmc-13433765:
Huizhong Liu and colleagues propose an automated vision system to replace manual splitter control in spiral concentrators, gravity separators that sort minerals in a flowing film. The devices are cheap, power-free, and widely used for iron, tin, titanium, tantalum-niobium, sulfur, and coal ores.

Today, operators watch mineral bands by eye and shift the splitter by hand to match the concentrate-tailings boundary, a subjective task prone to delays and grade swings. A machine-vision system that tracks the boundary automatically would steady the separation index. Mining plants get a design for steadier grades without constant human watch over each spiral.
pmc-13433865:
Fei Le and co-authors found a crowd of guard cells in 2026 inside thyroid tumors. The crowd mutes killer T cells through a three-step chemical chain. Blocking the chain wakes attack back up. Cell-by-cell reads of patient tumors and mouse models mapped the crowd in fine grain. The crowd bears a named surface mark and runs a fat, calm profile.

Its chain ends in a waste product that dulls killer cells, which lets the tumor slip immune watch. Drugs that block the chain's first or mid step flipped the mute in lab and live tests and shrank tumor loads. The authors pitch the chain as a drug aim to lift immune care for thyroid cancer, above all for hard, spread, or back-again cases.
pmc-13434465:
Andrew Plackett and Marco Catoni ask where seeds came from in 2026, using a fern as a stand in for early land plants. Seeds were a huge step in plant history, yet their first form is still debated. Fern egg chambers grow after mating, much as seed parts grow after pollen lands.

Gene maps of fern sex organs were matched against genes at work in a model plant ovule. Those genes were rich in genes that run the fern egg chamber after mating. The match suggests seed parts arose when that old program switched on in a new place. The model gives fossil debates a gene based test.
pmc-13434565:
Kervin Blanco Untalan, Genessa Jesy Teroy Pagote, and Kyle Renz Gomez Tejero argue in 2026 that refugee food aid must go past handing out information. Leaflets and classes help, yet hunger among refugees tracks pay swings, high prices, and lack of foods that fit home cultures. Transport gaps add to the strain.

Short term gains in diet often fade in the studies cited. Cash aid and food aid show the same uneven pattern over time. Placing the load on workers and families alone misses the wider blocks. The authors call for outcome based plans that fix price, supply, and access together. Measures should track lasting food security, not leaflets delivered.
pmc-13434765:
Wei Luo's team tackled overconfidence in large language models in 2026 with a framework called Predictive Metacognition. Such models often state wrong answers with high confidence and invent facts, which limits their use where stakes are high. The design borrows from brain ideas about prediction and self-checking, training models to answer and judge their own reliability at the same time through error-driven tuning and dual checks.

Fine-tuned on 4,000 crafted cases, two small models cut calibration error against strong rivals while holding task accuracy, and the gains held on new tasks. AI builders get a workable route toward models that know their limits and say so. The paper is a methods advance, so real-world safety gains will depend on tests beyond these benchmarks.
pmc-13435765:
Zoumenou and team audited prescribing registers for 2,200 medical visits across 11 public and private primary care facilities in South Benin. The audit covered 2020. It checked how often the antibiotic metronidazole is used and why. Most consultations in this setting are handled by nurses. Resistance among gut pathogens is a rising concern for the region.

Metronidazole was prescribed in 18 percent of visits. That made it the second most common antibiotic after aminopenicillins at 27 percent across facilities. Antimalarials appeared in 52 percent of visits. Patients had a median age of 19 years, with 57 percent female in the sample. Digestive symptoms raised prescription odds nearly ninefold, with an adjusted odds ratio of 8.86 in the model. Genitourinary symptoms carried an odds ratio of 6.65. Private facilities prescribed it more than public ones, at an odds ratio of 2.31. That prompts calls to study appropriateness.
pmc-13436665:
Arthur H Yancey and coauthors model 911 call data around Super Bowl LIII festivities in 2019 to sharpen outbreak spotting in 2026. Nine days of game events in three host towns supply the test data. Call volumes by hour were set against the same nine days before and after the events.

Tables, bar charts, and heat maps turn raw dispatch logs into pictures staff can read fast. Mass gatherings strain host towns, and faster pattern spotting speeds response. The World Cup in 2026 gives the method a near term stage. Dispatch data arrive faster than hospital reports, which is the core edge. Visual models may join standard syndrome watch toolkits.
pmc-13437365:
Ya Zou and a large team argue the standard two-box view of macrophage behavior hides why these immune cells fail in chronic disease. The old model sorts macrophages into attack mode or repair mode. Their 2026 framework claims the true control lies in cholesterol handling. A cell that cannot ship out excess cholesterol slowly loses its balance, and that failure drives its harmful state rather than merely following it.

Evidence they cite shows that restoring cholesterol outflow can flip an inflamed cell back toward calm. Two cell compartments sit at the heart of the model: mitochondria, which supply energy, and lysosomes, which process waste and fat. Gene switches, small RNA regulators, and chemical marks on DNA then lock the broken state in place, across diseases like clogged arteries and diabetic kidney damage. The authors favor therapies that repair the cell's inner machinery over those that only damp inflammation.
pmc-13437765:
Mohammed Almosfer's team compared metformin, daily-habit change, and both jointly in 2026 for bone renewal in newly found type 2 diabetes in Saudi adults. Early diabetes care shifts weight and metabolism, which may briefly stir bone remodeling, yet bone effects of first-line options were uncertain in this population. One hundred fourteen untreated adults were randomized equally to metformin, daily habits, or paired therapy for six months, with bone-loss and bone-building markers tracked.

Only daily habits cut the bone-loss marker CTX clearly after six months. Bone-building markers and sclerostin did not shift much in any group, and all groups lost weight and lowered blood sugar, most with paired care. Diabetes clinicians get reassurance that short-term metformin does not clearly harm bone turnover, plus a lifestyle bonus. Longer fracture data are still needed.
pmc-13438765:
Paula Abola and colleagues write to add a missing pillar to a published plan for fighting the Parkinson pandemic. The plan they praise sets out a timely vision as cases climb worldwide. Their 2026 letter argues every plank quietly assumes patients can understand their disease, weigh options, and speak as partners in decisions. That capacity, called health literacy, varies widely and is unevenly shared.

Studies show stubborn gaps in what patients know about care, and a mismatch between how involved doctors think patients are and how involved they feel. Voice alone is not enough, the authors note: being heard requires the tools to judge evidence and state an informed preference. Without deliberate teaching and clear materials, even a well-meant plan will widen the gap between confident and confused patients. The letter asks the field to name health literacy as core infrastructure for Parkinson care, not a soft extra.
pmc-13439065:
Romane Cecchi, Sebastian Gluth, and Stefano Palminteri examine how attention shapes the worth people assign to rewards while learning, in work published in 2026. Learners often judge a reward against the range on offer, a habit called normalisation. Choices among three evenly spaced rewards break that pattern, and the authors suspected that looking behaviour explains the break.

Three experiments with 105 people tracked eye gaze while rewards were learned. Tasks steered attention from above and below, and watched options gained in judged worth. A learning model that lets gaze length lift an option's value before range scaling fit choices better than rival models. The results cast attention as an active part of how the brain prices options, not a side effect.
pmc-13439365:
Raza and co-authors built a time-delayed math model of whooping cough transmission. It adds the real-world lags older models ignore. Those lags cover delayed vaccine effects, waning immunity, and slow behavior reactions to outbreaks. Pertussis keeps coming back despite vaccination. The United States saw 5,436 cases in 2023, an 8 percent rise on the prior year.

Their model sorts people into boxes: susceptible, infected, vaccinated, recovered, waned-immunity, and again-susceptible. Delays sit between the moves from box to box. Balance analysis using standard tests showed the basic reproduction number decides the switch. It governs whether the disease dies out or persists. Delays pushed the system toward swinging or damped epidemic waves at certain threshold values in the model runs. Adding delay to vaccination lowered the share infected. Tuned well, it could shift the system toward wiping the disease out. That gives guidance for timing actions.
pmc-13441265:
Guson Kang and colleagues revisit heart failure counting inside a large dialysis trial, asking how much central judging changes the tally, in a 2026 report. The EVOLVE trial randomised 3,883 haemodialysis patients with overactive parathyroid glands to cinacalcet or placebo and tracked cardiovascular events. Site doctors reported suspected heart failure, while a central committee independently defined and judged each event, also hunting for missed ones.

Sites reported 1,366 events, yet the committee confirmed under half as true heart failure endpoints. The committee's own sweep found forty extra candidates and confirmed seventeen. Treatment effects pointed the same way under both counts, with the judged data giving fewer events but a nominally significant benefit for cinacalcet. The authors conclude that heart failure is genuinely hard to identify and classify in dialysis patients, so trial design must budget for expert adjudication.
pmc-13443165:
Xiang Zhang and colleagues build a scan model that grades armpit lymph nodes in breast cancer in a 2026 paper. Node state steers how much surgery a patient needs, yet checks before surgery stay rough. Their deep learning model, BCALN-Net, reads MRI scans to call spread in first nodes, load size, and spread past them.

Training and tests drew on 6,271 patients in all. Scores stayed strong across tumor types, stages, hormone marks, and age bands. A pooled check of 4,081 patients showed the model beats clinic rules at spotting who can skip deep armpit surgery. The authors offer the tool as one scan path for three linked calls. Safer surgery cuts may follow if outside tests back the marks.
pmc-13444265:
Leopoldo Silocchi Pergo and colleagues test a breath score for child asthma attacks in emergency care in a 2026 study. The score, PRAM, grades how hard a child works to breathe. Records ran from August 2023 to March 2025 at a large child emergency unit, with 428 visits from children aged 2 to 17 years.

Scores were logged each hour for five rounds. Ward admission followed 35.0 percent of visits in the set. At triage the score split admissions with an AUC mark of 0.791, which marks fair sorting power. By hour two the mark rose to 0.829, the best read of the series. Long-stay calls stayed weaker. The authors back repeat scoring over one first read for safer sorting.
pmc-13445665:
Manel Ennaceur and coauthors report the first 2026 find of mcr-1, the mobile colistin-resistance gene, in hospital Klebsiella pneumoniae in Tunisia, a worrying sign for last-resort drugs. The team screened 143 carbapenem-resistant samples from a Tunis hospital during 2024, testing drug fight-back by broth dilution and checking genes by PCR and gene reading.

Sixteen samples, 11.2 percent, fought off colistin, all multidrug resistant and rich in carbapenemase and other fight-back genes. One sample carried mcr-1 with moderate drug fight-back plus multiple fight-back genes. Chromosome-based routes still rule locally, but the mobile gene's arrival demands stronger watch and drug care across North Africa.
pmc-13446265:
Cabrera-Cosme and Kent's team used image-enabled cell sorting, which photographs each cell as it is sorted, to split blood-forming stem cells by how their mitochondria look under a green dye. Standard sorting reads only total fluorescence, blind to pattern, yet stem cell subsets differ in staying power and the blood lineages they favor.

Sorting on mitochondrial dye intensity and diffusivity, a measure of how spread out the signal is inside the cell, separated stem cells with different quiescence behavior in single-cell culture assays. The fraction with low total intensity and low diffusivity held the serially reconstituting stem cells, the rare cells able to rebuild the blood system repeatedly in transplant tests. Sister fractions exited quiescence and proliferated on different schedules, revealing functional splits invisible to marker-only sorting in these experiments. The authors present imaging features as a prospective handle for isolating primitive stem cell subsets.
pmc-13446365:
Theophilus Afum and colleagues study what makes tuberculosis hit harder in some patients than others, in a 2026 multi-center cohort from Ghana. Severity swings widely at first sight, and gene tests now count the bacteria quickly, which tempts a simple load story. The team set host traits and bug traits against a standard severity score.

Body mass, a plain mark of nutrition, foretold severity on its own, apart from how many bacteria the gene test found. Self-reported ethnic group also split severity patterns. HIV and diabetes riding with TB bent the picture further. Host and pathogen together, the authors conclude, explain the spread of illness better than bacterial count alone, a point for feeding and comorbidity care.
pmc-13446465:
Olivia Gautier and colleagues trace spinal motor neurons in an ALS mouse model over time and find a distinct sick state that arrives before the cells die, in a 2026 study. ALS wastes the neurons that drive movement, and most patients live only a few years after diagnosis. Single-cell gene and chromatin reads, plus place-based mapping, followed the model built on the SOD1 gene fault.

The most fragile neuron kind shifted by thousands of gene changes into the new state, which the team calls disease-associated motor neurons. Switch networks that govern the shift were mapped, and forcing those switches in human motor neurons copied key traits of the state. Human ALS cord data held the same signature, and its open regions were rich in ALS risk variants.
pmc-13446565:
Megan N. Michalski and colleagues settle a clash over the Frizzled 2 gene in mouse development by building a fresh, fully checked knockout model, in a 2026 study. Frizzled receptors pass Wnt signals that shape the embryo, and Fzd2 was long thought a spare part beside two close kin. One global knockout line died before birth, which hinted at a core role, while an older tissue-specific model turned out not to cut the gene at all.

The team's new model plants two cut markers around the gene and proves the cut makes a true null. Wiping the gene out body-wide did not kill embryos, which clears the earlier clash. Cutting it only in limbs shortened the limbs, which supports a real role for Fzd2 in limb growth.
pmc-13447065:
Pierfrancesco Greco and colleagues ask whether the womb lining works poorly for years after fertility-sparing treatment for womb cancer, in a 2026 case series. Donor eggs give a clean test, since egg quality is held high and only the lining varies. Women aged forty or more who had cleared the cancer and kept their womb took part.

Sixteen patients ran twenty-seven transfer cycles with top-grade embryos and sound lining build in every case. Even so, live birth came in under a fifth of transfers, and under a third of patients overall. Patients whose disease returned fared worse than those who stayed clear. Lining thickness showed no link to success. The authors urge early fertility care once the cancer clears, before the window narrows.
pmc-13447565:
Reiko Masubuchi and co-authors present a pictured 2026 case of a one-sided inflammatory flare after HIV treatment began. A man in his fifties arrived with severe Pneumocystis pneumonia, a lung infection of weakened immunity, alongside newly found advanced HIV. Standard therapy cleared widespread hazy changes on scans, and he went home after three weeks.

Seven days after starting HIV drug therapy, fever, breathlessness and low oxygen returned. Fresh scans showed new net-like, scar-like changes gathered on the left side, a strikingly uneven pattern. Doctors diagnosed a paradoxical immune recovery flare, where reviving immunity attacks residual infection, after ruling out likelier alternatives. The case widens the known scan appearance of this flare, which usually looks diffuse rather than one-sided.
pmc-13447665:
Jinhui Wang and coauthors spot a 2026 study naming SERPING1 as a forecasting marker tied to killer T-cell entry in diffuse large B-cell lymph cancer. Mixing multi-omics, machine learning, single-cell analysis, docking, and gene-luck lottery across public data sets, the team picked four hub genes linked to CD8 T cells.

SERPING1 emerged as central among the four, with immune looks showing CD8 T-cell buildup and pathway links to signal protein and backup signals. The gene carries hope for spotting, outlook, and immune therapy guidance. The joined approach offers a template for marker finding, with medical checks still ahead.
pmc-13448065:
Yinfang Wu and coauthors report a 2026 study showing that SREBP2 drives other guard cell switch-on and allergy airway swelling free of blood fat making. In asthma mouse lungs, M2-tilted in-between guard cells grew with raised SREBP2 pathway action, and IL-4 set off SREBP2 ripening in guard cells.

Blocking SREBP2 ripening curbed IL-4-driven M2 switch-on in cells and animals, while blood fat itself held back ripening and switch-on. Mature SREBP2 tuned IRF4 output and teamed with it to promote switch-on, and myeloid Scap loss cut swelling. The SREBP2-IRF4 axis offers a fresh asthma target beyond blood fat cutting.
pmc-13449365:
Victoria Schouela and colleagues profile in 2026 patients whose upper neck pain may come from the small lateral joint between the first two vertebrae, the C1-C2 joint. This source is usually considered only after tests at the levels below come back negative. Fifty patients with persistent pain after such negative work-ups joined a prospective study at a specialty clinic between 2022 and 2025, receiving a guided injection of anesthetic and steroid into the joint.

At thirty minutes, 22 of 49 patients, 44.9 percent, gained at least half pain relief from the diagnostic block. Facial pain predicted a poorer response, while dominant neck pain or combined neck and head pain predicted a better one. Three months out, a third of patients still met the benefit criteria, and an immediate block response did not predict who they would be. Electric shock-like pain lowered the odds of lasting benefit, while pain on touch raised them.
pmc-13449465:
Zahra Souri and colleagues tested seed priming with zinc oxide and biochar particles to protect wheat from arsenic in 2026. Arsenic in soil harms wheat growth and physiology, and it can accumulate in the plant. The particles were made in one carbonization step from grape leaf waste, then characterized with microscopy and spectroscopy.

Seeds were primed at several particle doses and grown under several arsenic levels. Arsenic alone impaired growth in a dose-dependent way, but primed seeds grew better, carried less arsenic in their shoots, and showed stronger antioxidant enzyme activity. The team links the benefit to reduced oxidative stress. The approach offers a low-cost, waste-based way to shield wheat on contaminated ground.
pmc-13449765:
Alexa E. Richardson and co-authors report the discovery of VU6081679, a molecule that boosts the activity of the brain receptor mGlu8 and eases Parkinson's-like symptoms in rodents. The compound is a positive allosteric modulator, meaning it enhances the receptor's response rather than activating it directly. Their 2026 paper follows the molecule from screening to animal testing.

A high-throughput screen and follow-up chemistry produced a compound potent at rat, mouse, and human versions of the receptor, able to enter the brain and be taken orally. Computer docking placed it in a pocket at the interface between the receptor's two halves, matching a published three-dimensional structure. In rats and mice, it reversed the frozen posture caused by the drug haloperidol, a standard Parkinson's model. Mice lacking the mGlu8 receptor lost the benefit, confirming the effect works through that receptor.
pmc-13449865:

Earlier models matched those feats only with finely tuned allosteric links between parts.

In their model, receptors instead gate far-from-equilibrium enzyme reactions between neighbor kinases. The logic is taken from zero-order ultrasensitivity rather than allostery. Gain can grow as large as you like, simply by splitting reaction speeds. No magic point or fine setting tuning is needed for the gain. The scheme also copies broad lab results that older lattice models struggle to match in the authors' tests. pmc-13450565:

They frame the drug as a hopeful option for people who cannot stay on stronger immune drugs, while noting that proof is still early.
pmc-13451865:

Serious heart events at 90 days were rare across the whole group. The authors question routine reflex testing in this pathway.
pmc-13452165:

Across test datasets, the combined tool matched or beat both earlier methods on prediction accuracy while giving users direct control over result list size and run time. It reports links at the finest level available, down to single sequence variants or species. The authors offer it as a user-friendly way to generate testable biological ideas from large microbiome studies.
pmc-13452365:
Cifuentes-Uribe and colleagues evaluate a blood marker in this 2026 study of acid sphingomyelinase deficiency type B, a rare inherited disorder in which fatty material accumulates in organs and scars the lungs. Larger cohorts are needed to confirm its value.
pmc-13452865:
Marta Martos Rodríguez and others analyzed surgery for bilateral Wilms tumor in 2026, seeking the best strategy to control tumors while preserving kidney function. No standardized surgical strategy existed.

Nephron-sparing surgery preserved kidney tissue in 45.9 percent of kidneys, while total nephrectomy was common for chemotherapy-resistant histologies. Single-stage bilateral surgery trended toward more total removals, tumor rupture, and death, though not significantly. Surgeons gain evidence favoring staged, kidney-sparing approaches where feasible.
pmc-13453565:
Danjie Jiang, Yan Zhang, and Dandan Zhang draw global lessons for China's rollout of HPV vaccine through its national program. China added the vaccine, which guards against cervical cancer, to the program in November 2025. School based delivery by grade reached the highest coverage, passing 90 percent in Rwanda, and mixing school with clinic catch up worked best overall. For China, strengths include home grown vaccine supply and a strong school system. The authors warn of parent hesitancy, regional gaps, and online false claims as the main threats to fair coverage.
pmc-13453665:
Atsushi Ishimura and others set brand and store-brand metronidazole gels side by side in 2026, to see if flow traits change smell control for cancer survivors. Fungating wounds give off strong smells from germs that thrive with no air, which wrecks life quality for patients and carers. Metronidazole gel on skin is first choice for smell, but gels may spread and stick in unlike ways.

Both thinned when stirred, but the brand gel stayed thicker at all stir rates, most of all at slow rates that match wound use. Fillers differed by pack notes. Doctors gain a cause to weigh gel make, not just drug, when picking smell control.
pmc-13454565:
Yves Levy and others tested a CD40-targeted HIV vaccine in 2026, assessing long-term and recall immunity in uninfected volunteers. The ANRS VRI06 trial studied CD40.HIVEnv, an antibody fused with gp140 Env to target dendritic cells. Initial results in seventy-two volunteers showed safety and immunogenicity up to forty-eight weeks.
