pmc-13468065:
Shengjia Huang and co-authors catalog in 2026 the GPAT gene family in olive, the enzymes that take the first committed step in making the triacylglycerol oils the fruit is prized for. Earlier work had flagged one family member, GPAT4, as a key regulator, but the family as a whole was unmapped. The systematic analysis found 12 olive GPAT proteins falling into four subclasses, all carrying the family signature domain.

Seven of the genes, when switched on strongly in test plants, significantly raised total oil content in leaves and seeds. The genes sit scattered across the olive genome with conserved building blocks but varied structures. For an ancient oil crop now bred with modern tools, a complete map of the oil-making gene family points breeders to the exact switches that raise oil yield.
pmc-13468365:
Zykova and co-authors expanded a 2026 vaccine carrier made from virus-like particles of bacteriophage Beihai32, a virus that infects bacteria. Such empty shells display foreign peptides on their surface to train the immune system, and the shell's back end already tolerated long inserts. The team tested whether the front end is equally permissive.

Hybrid shell proteins carrying one to four copies of a flu peptide at the front end were produced in E. coli bacteria. Zykova found the four copy version still self assembled into spherical particles displaying the peptide outside. Mice injected with these particles made high levels of peptide specific antibodies after immunisation. Even a large green fluorescent protein, 238 amino acids long, could be attached and stayed fluorescent on the particle surface.
pmc-13468465:
Jeffrey Justin Margret and Sushil K. Jain review in 2026 a hormone triangle that may connect body fat to Alzheimer disease: adiponectin, vitamin D, and the amino acid L-cysteine. Adiponectin, secreted by fat tissue, calms inflammation, improves insulin response, and in Alzheimer models helps neurons survive, protects synapses, and shields the blood-brain barrier through its two receptors. Human blood studies, though, give inconsistent readings, the so-called adiponectin paradox.

High adiponectin in older or Alzheimer patients may signal frailty, weight loss, or a compensatory response rather than protection, the authors note. Vitamin D raises circulating adiponectin and aids metabolism, while L-cysteine feeds glutathione production and restores redox balance. The review argues the pair may act in synergy on oxidative stress, inflammation, and adiponectin together, sketching a low-cost nutritional strategy that deserves direct testing in Alzheimer prevention.
pmc-13468665:
Zhang and colleagues engineer a better battery anode in this 2026 study, targeting a known weak point of iron oxide. The compound Fe2O3 can store far more lithium than the graphite used in today's batteries, but it conducts electricity poorly and swells badly during charging, which quickly breaks it apart.

Their answer is a three-layer composite grown on nickel foam. Iron oxide nanowires were grown directly on the foam's three-dimensional skeleton using a hot-water chemical method, then sealed under a dense coating of polypyrrole, a conductive polymer. Each layer plays a role: the foam gives strength and conductivity, the polymer buffers swelling and adds nitrogen doping that helps charge move, and the oxide stores the lithium. After prolonged cycling the structure stayed intact, which simpler iron oxide electrodes fail to do, and the authors present the design as a route to higher-energy lithium batteries.
pmc-13469865:
Shaohong Wang, Da Lei, and Qihui Zhen describe in 2026 a ground sensor that reads electric fields in the earth without touching buried electrodes. Such fields guide mineral exploration and warnings for geological hazards, yet contact probes drift, suffer in rough terrain, and pick up interference. Weak natural signals at the microvolt level also defeat many contact free designs, which couple poorly to the ground.

Their sensor stacks three layers. A silver paste plate sits on top, and a ceramic layer with a high dielectric constant sits in the middle. A flexible silicon base hugs small bumps and closes air gaps. Acting like one plate of a capacitor facing the soil, the stack gathers the field signal without burial. The authors report design and performance checks aimed at cleaner low frequency readings for field surveys.
pmc-13470065:
Ji Won Han and colleagues built a machine learning liver safety score in 2026 to predict decompensation during systemic therapy for unresectable liver cancer. Portal hypertension raises bleeding and liver failure risk on therapy, yet treatment choice rarely weighs it formally. A random forest model trained on 1,262 patients and validated on 764 predicted significant portal hypertension and prognosis.

The score reached 0.840 area under the curve, and high-score patients faced decompensation risk 3.25-fold, bleeding risk 4.90-fold, and death risk 2.21-fold higher. Atezolizumab-bevacizumab helped low-score patients but brought bleeding without survival gain in high-score patients. Simulated score-guided choice cut decompensation 24%, bleeding 40%, and mortality 26%, backing personalised regimen selection.
pmc-13470265:
Christopher D Hamad tested weed effects in 2026 on results after lower leg fracture repair, with and without smoke. Weed use is rising fast in the United States, yet surgery-time risks in trauma patients stayed murky. TriNetX records from 2015 to 2023 split adults into weed-only at 2,421, smoke-only at 36,966, joint at 2,338, and non-users.

Weed-only users faced more deep implant sepsis, no-heal or bad-heal, re-do surgery, blood top-up, return trips, anxiety, and low mood than matched non-users. Smoke-only users faced a longer list including wound problems, lung bug, heart attack, and death. Joint users fared worse than weed-only users on wound infection, limb loss, breathing failure, and pain, adding risk for surgeons to flag before repair.
pmc-13470365:
Xin Yang built a clear testing model in 2026 for MP illness in children with acute fever or cough. The germ causes 10% to 40% of in-care childhood pneumonia, yet early spotting is hard. Blood-test-defined cases from two Chinese clinics in 2023 were split 7:3 for training and testing, with 2024 data for later testing.

The best model, using 11 signs, reached area under the curve 0.89 inside and 0.84 on later testing, with TNF-beta and IL-2 as top signs. Age-split models also did well, and doctor trust rose clearly after three months of Streamlit use. PCR testing and cause-based study remain needed before clinic uptake.
pmc-13470565:
Sahid Afrid Mollick leads a seventeen author survey in 2026 of gut microbes in Indigenous tribal communities across India. The study focuses on five especially at risk tribal groups. The groups live along a gradient from older ways of life to more modern ones. A new analysis framework scores how strongly each microbe ties to the wider group, flagging candidate keystone taxa whose presence may hold the whole system together.

The method found 121 candidate keystone microbes, most unique to a single population, with a smaller set repeating across traditional groups. Some keystone candidates linked both to steadier communities and to several disease conditions. Beneath the variation sat a shared core of body chemistry. As communities took up more modern habits, microbe variety fell and disease linked microbes grew more common.
pmc-13470665:
Ya Li and eleven colleagues published this 2026 retrospective cohort study of Shengmai Injection, a traditional Chinese medicine formulation used alongside care in sepsis and septic shock. High-quality evidence for the injection is scarce. At a Guangdong hospital, the team identified what the injection contains by mass spectrometry. They compared outcomes for sepsis patients who did or did not receive it between 2016 and 2024, balancing the groups by propensity matching.

Profiling found 130 components. In the matched comparison, treated patients left intensive care sooner, and spent less time on ventilators and with fever. They also showed lower organ-failure and severity scores plus lower procalcitonin and lactate levels after treatment. The septic shock subgroup showed similar improvements in ventilation time and scores. However, the injection did not reduce 28-day mortality in the cohort. The authors present Shengmai as an adjunct that eases illness, rather than a proven survival treatment.
pmc-13471465:
Jiahe Hu and colleagues report in 2026 a counterintuitive link between cholesterol and scarred tissue inside the heart upper chamber. In persistent atrial fibrillation, low voltage patches mark advanced remodeling and predict relapse after ablation. Their single center study covered 404 patients undergoing a first ablation, and just over half showed such patches on the mapping done during the procedure.

Age, female sex, wave shape, chamber size, and LDL cholesterol all tracked with the patches. Higher LDL cholesterol came with lower odds of low voltage areas, a link partly explained by smaller chamber size in those patients. Split into quarters, the cholesterol groups behaved unevenly for both patches and later relapse, results the authors label descriptive. They present the metabolic angle as understudied rather than settled.
pmc-13471565:
Eskandari and co-authors report a 66-year-old man who developed a spinal bone and disc infection six months after a kidney stone procedure through the urethra. Their 2026 case report traces the infection to E. coli matching the bacteria found, untreated, in his urine before the operation, with no antibiotics given around the procedure.

Imaging and a CT-guided biopsy confirmed infection of the spine's bone and disc, vertebral osteomyelitis with spondylodiscitis, at the T9–T10 level, with a small abscess beside the spine. The isolate resisted ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone but remained susceptible to cefepime, which he received intravenously for six weeks. Within two weeks he had improved substantially, and he ended pain-free with normalized blood markers and clear follow-up imaging, a warning about screening urine before urinary tract procedures.
pmc-13471665:
Han and colleagues built mouse models for the emergent monkeypox Clade Ib, the variant that spread from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2023. They compared it head-to-head with the older Clade IIb. Their 2026 study infected four mouse strains through the nose, including two with crippled interferon defenses, and profiled tissue damage, viral loads, and gene activity.

Susceptible strains lost marked body weight, carried high viral loads, and showed severe tissue lesions, and Clade Ib caused clearly worse disease than IIb under identical conditions. Spleen gene profiles early in infection lit up interferon and inflammatory pathways while adaptive immune genes were switched down. The team also evaluated the antiviral tecovirimat in this system, offering a testbed for countermeasures against the new clade.
pmc-13471965:
Eric A Macklin leads the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial group in 2026 comparing breathing capacity measured at home against the clinic standard in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Breathing strength guides trial eligibility and tracks decline in this fatal motor neuron disease. Home measurements, coached live by video and reviewed centrally, were paired with clinic readings taken within two weeks, across 233 participants followed for a year.

The two settings agreed well, with no systematic bias in either direction. A home reading above the trial threshold predicted a passing clinic reading nine times in ten, though a failing home reading was less decisive. Decline slopes correlated moderately, with home readings falling somewhat faster but varying less between people. Both slopes predicted survival time similarly. The authors back home measurement for future trials.
pmc-13472565:
Yan Xie and six colleagues published this 2026 review on the role of mouth microbes in oral submucous fibrosis. It is a stiffening, precancerous condition of the mouth lining, driven by areca nut chewing. The authors review how chewing reshapes the oral ecosystem. They cover which microbes bloom or vanish, how the shifted mix feeds scarring, and therapies that aim to reset mouth microbes rather than suppress symptoms.

In patients, species such as Fusobacterium nucleatum, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Candida fungi are enriched. Lactobacillus and Streptococcus shrink. The review traces how this imbalance breaches the mucosal barrier and fires inflammatory circuits including the TLR/NF-κB and NLRP3 pathways. It also skews immune cell balance, disturbs tryptophan and short-chain fatty acid metabolism, and adds oxidative stress. Candidate options include probiotics, antimicrobial peptides, light-based therapy, oral microbiota transplantation and diet change. Cause and effect needs multi-omics proof, they caution.
pmc-13473465:
Zihan Li, Tianmin Zhang, and Hongzhen Hu present an upgraded search algorithm in 2026 for hard math problems with many possible answers. The base method mimics school contests, where learners improve through rounds of rivalry. The upgrade adds an early stage that spreads search points wider, plus a late stage that sharpens the best finds. A restart step jolts stuck points back into motion.

Tests ran against six rival methods on standard problem sets with up to one hundred unknowns. The new method ranked first or near first across all sizes tried. Seven real design tasks, from beams to pressure tanks, confirmed the gains hold outside test sets. Engineers gain a steadier tool for tuning complex designs.
pmc-13474665:
Qiu and co-authors gave hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg gas the body makes in traces as a signal. They gave it to diabetic mice whose leg arteries had been tied off to mimic human limb ischemia. Their 2026 study tracked gut microbes by metagenomic sequencing at four time points across diabetes induction, artery surgery, and 21 days of gas-donor treatment.

Treatment improved leg blood flow, restored blood hydrogen sulfide levels that diabetes and ischemia had depleted, and spared the starved calf muscle from structural and functional damage. At the same time the diabetic-ischemic gut community, knocked off balance by the double insult, shifted back toward healthy composition under treatment. The disease burden framing is large: peripheral artery disease affects over 230 million people worldwide, and diabetes plus arterial disease drives more than half of leg amputations in the United States.
pmc-13474865:
Meyer and co-authors interviewed Australian obstetricians in 2026 about what shapes their intent to support normal physiological birth, meaning labor that starts and proceeds on its own without drugs or instruments. Rates of such births have fallen as interventions rise, especially for first-time mothers. The team spoke with eight obstetricians working in varied care models across most Australian states and territories, and sorted the answers into themes.

Two broad themes organized the interviews, each holding three sub-themes about knowledge, beliefs, and outside pressures on the doctors. Knowledge and beliefs covered how doctors define normal birth, how they learned their craft, and how fear of legal claims colors their choices at the bedside. Outside influences included colleagues, hospital policy and resources, and the expectations women and communities bring, leading the authors to recommend stronger teamwork and support for midwives' full scope of practice.
pmc-13476565:
Masiques and colleagues compared pork-based and salmon-based diets in rats in 2026 to see how each shapes fat oxidation during digestion. The diets matched in overall nutrients but differed sharply: pork supplied far more saturated fat and fourteen times more heme iron, while salmon supplied fourteen times more omega-3 fats.

Pork feeding raised several oxidation products in stomach contents. One aldehyde rose seventeen-fold and another rose 27-fold, while an oxidation marker in blood climbed by about 45 percent. Salmon instead raised a local oxidation marker in the upper intestine and a blood inflammation marker by about 30 percent. Gut microbe changes were small, and a gut inflammation marker did not differ between diets.
pmc-13478365:
Taşkin and colleagues compared three laboratory methods for measuring HbA1c in 2026, the blood marker that summarizes average sugar control in diabetes and guides treatment changes. Small reading differences can flip clinical decisions, so agreement between machines matters. Fifty patient blood samples were run on all three systems: a chromatography instrument, a capillary electrophoresis instrument, and a general autoanalyzer using an antibody-based method.

Electrophoresis and chromatography agreed almost perfectly, with a correlation of 0.998 and an average bias of only 0.07 points between them. The autoanalyzer correlated strongly too, at 0.997, but its bias was larger, at 0.52 points against electrophoresis, and the gap widened at higher sugar-control values. The authors warn that autoanalyzer readings near decision thresholds may mislead, while noting the small sample of 50 means the warning needs confirmation in larger work.
pmc-13478465:
Sertaç Oruç and two colleagues improved in 2026 drought forecasts for Norway with hybrid neural models. They used monthly rain records from 1970 to 2025 for Bergen, Kristiansand, Oslo, and Tromsø, scored with a standard 12-month dryness index.

They paired a convolutional neural network with a signal-splitting method called TQWT, plus random forest and tuning methods, and tested four input setups. The CNN-TQWT hybrids beat the other models at all four sites, with the best correlation scores above 0.97 and the best fit scores above 0.91 at every site. The results point to the TQWT split as the key gain, offering planners a steadier base for farm and water plans.
pmc-13479565:
Mohammad Ali Saeedi, Mosayeb Rostamian, and Yadollah Bahrami present a 2026 systematic review of human infections with Edwardsiella tarda, a water-dwelling bacterium that rarely infects people but can kill them. Four databases were searched for reports from January 2000 to October 2025. Fifty-nine unique case reports survived the screening rules.

Cases skewed toward older adults, and Japan contributed the most reports. Many patients had eaten seafood or handled aquatic animals shortly before falling ill. Fever and abdominal pain dominated the presentations, with blood tests typically showing high inflammation markers. Antibiotics used included meropenem, ceftriaxone, ampicillin, metronidazole, and levofloxacin among the most frequent choices. The review gives clinicians a consolidated picture of a pathogen most will meet only through its case literature.
pmc-13479865:
Sintayehu Daba Wami and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a pilot randomized trial of team-based rehabilitation for chronic low back pain in Ethiopia. Back pain is the world's leading cause of years lived with disability, and team rehabilitation works in wealthy countries, yet low-income settings have barely tested it. The pilot will randomize forty patients between the interprofessional program and usual care.

An embedded process evaluation using mixed methods will watch how the program runs in practice. Feasibility questions dominate: recruitment, retention, session attendance, and whether outcome measurement works in this setting. A future full trial depends on these answers. The authors detail the rehabilitation components, the professional mix, and the outcomes a definitive trial would judge.
pmc-13480965:
Marilyn D. Thomas and colleagues present a 2026 study of whether attending a historically Black college relates to later death rates for Black adults in the United States. The team drew on a national cohort recruited in 2003 to 2007 and focused on 1,960 Black graduates who went to high school in a state with such a college. Deaths were tracked from 2012 to 2023, split by the era when each person reached college age.

Overall death rates barely differed between the two college types, with a hazard ratio near one and wide error bounds. Hints flipped by era. Rates ran lower for those of college age in the decade before the Civil Rights Act, and higher for the youngest era, with near-flat results for the oldest. Wide bounds rule out firm claims either way. The authors stress that earlier health gains linked to these colleges showed no clear survival edge here.
pmc-13482565:
Adugna and colleagues build one neural network in 2026 that does two farm jobs at once, naming soybean leaf diseases and detecting pesticide presence from the same images. Splitting the work between two separate models wastes time in the field, so their design shares one feature-reading backbone and branches into task-specific outputs. They tested three backbone designs on a dataset of 429 soybean leaf images prepared with standard augmentation.

All three backbones performed strongly inside the shared framework, with MobileNetV3 reaching 95 percent accuracy, VGG19 reaching 96 percent, and ConvNeXt reaching 97 percent across the joint tasks in the test split. Heat-map explanations showed where each decision looked on the leaf, keeping the system auditable for the agronomists who would act on its calls in practice. The authors pitch the model as a field-ready monitoring tool that flags sick plants and chemical traces together, at phone-friendly computing cost.
pmc-13483865:
D Bhanu Prakash builds a mathematical model of a crop pest and its predator to guide biological control of the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Published in 2026, the system gives the predator extra food beyond the pest and lets predators compete among themselves, with feeding following a type-III response that saturates at high pest density. Field observations of the predator Orius albidipennis eating the whitefly check the feeding assumption.

Analysis shows the model always settles to a single sensible positive solution rather than blowing up or dying out spuriously. Stability checks reveal threshold crossings where control flips, plus ranges where two stable outcomes coexist, which creates hysteresis. Extra food can therefore help or hinder suppression depending on where the system sits. Growers get a warning that more predator support is not automatically better.
pmc-13485865:
Feng Guo, Yi Song, and Guijun Qin review stem cell strategies for diabetes, where replacing or rescuing insulin-making cells remains the central prize. Published in 2026, the survey covers laboratory-grown insulin-producing cells from embryonic and reprogrammed stem cells for insulin-depleted disease. Blood-forming and connective-tissue stem cell transplants receive equal attention for their immune-calming effects.

Beyond replacement, transplanted cells can quiet autoimmunity, coax the pancreas to regrow its own beta cells, and preserve whatever beta cell function remains, jointly improving islet performance and insulin sensitivity. Immune rejection and safety worries still shadow the replacement route, and every approach needs stronger proof of durable benefit. The review weighs promise against those limits and maps the molecular routes each cell type uses.
pmc-13486665:
Okitsu and Sakai challenged a standard idea in learning theory: that the brain runs two separate learning systems, one thoughtful and one habitual, and blends their answers. Their 2026 paper proposes a single reinforcement-learning system that cooperates internally instead of competing, and folds in Pavlovian conditioning, the automatic responses animals learn to signals. Simulations tested whether one system could reproduce three classic animal behaviors at once.

The unified model reproduced habit formation, where behavior becomes automatic with practice, without bolting on a second system. It also captured Pavlovian conditioning and the transfer effect, where a signal for one reward energizes work for another. Earlier hybrid accounts needed separate modules arbitrated by a controller to cover the same ground. Okitsu argues the brain may not need that arbitration machinery, simplifying theories of how animals and perhaps robots should learn.
pmc-13486865:
Volkow and colleagues give the National Institutes of Health perspective in 2026 on ten years of the ABCD Study. The landmark project follows nearly 12,000 United States youth from ages nine or ten through their teens. The study gathers brain scans, thinking tests, genetic samples, and detailed measures of environment, substance use, and mental health.

Its open data model has produced over 1,600 publications by outside researchers. A headline finding is that social and family context predicted early substance use more strongly than brain, thinking, or genetic measures alone. Lifestyle and layered environmental exposures also shaped youth mental health. Economic deprivation affected brain development, but positive supports softened those effects. As the cohort reaches early adulthood, the authors expect sharper answers on addiction and illness trajectories.
pmc-13487965:
Yinpeng Xu and colleagues mine safety report databases for harms linked to givosiran in a 2026 pharmacovigilance study. The RNA-based drug treats acute hepatic porphyria, a rare disorder causing severe attacks and nerve symptoms, by lowering production of a liver enzyme. Reports came chiefly from the United States FAERS system, with checks against the global VigiAccess database, using several statistical signal methods.

More than twelve hundred reports named the drug as the main suspect in each source. Known risks such as raised homocysteine, kidney problems, and pancreas inflammation appeared again. Signals for belly pain, seizure, and mental disorder are not yet on the label and need study. Onset times varied widely, suggesting risk does not fade in a simple pattern.
pmc-13488065:
Yik-Zheng Lim and a large Malaysian team investigate a chikungunya outbreak in Perak state during 2019 and 2020 in a 2026 report. The mosquito-borne virus had been quiet in Malaysia for about a decade before cases surged again. Blood came from seventy-eight people in three hotspot villages, tested for viral RNA and antibodies, and the virus was grown and fully sequenced for family-tree analysis.

Nearly seventy percent of samples tested positive, and a few people carried dengue virus as well. The 2019 virus differed from the strain behind the 2009 Malaysian outbreak and matched recent epidemic strains from Thailand most closely. Several mutations linked with better spread by a common mosquito were present. Import from a neighbor is the likely story, the authors argue.
pmc-13488365:
Sharma, Chen, and Agler studied in 2026 how a leaf rot fungus reshapes germ life around its kills in Arabidopsis thaliana, a small lab plant. The fungus rots leaves across many crops. Such plants store mustard oil type defences that turn toxic when tissue breaks. The fungus breaks those toxins down with an enzyme called SaxA, a step it needs to stay harmful.

Dead patches left by the normal fungus teemed with a wide mix of bacteria. A strain that lacked SaxA caused rot but did not change the local germ mix at all. That split shows the cleanup step, not the rot alone, opens dead tissue to guests. Other defence stores in the plant likely add their own push on which bacteria thrive. Host traits and germ traits thus jointly build the crowd around a lesion.
pmc-13489565:
Desiana Desiana and four colleagues published this 2026 cross-sectional study of inflammation and blood vessel markers in hypertensive patients in Aceh, Indonesia. They measured serum C-reactive protein, an inflammation signal, and nitric oxide, a marker of vessel lining function. Patients numbered 120, from three ethnic groups of the region: the Gayo, Aneuk Jamee and Aceh. They compared levels and correlations between the groups.

C-reactive protein levels did not differ between the three groups. Nitric oxide levels did differ, running highest in Gayo patients at a mean of 51.79 micromoles per litre, then Aneuk Jamee, then Aceh. The two markers correlated strongly, with a coefficient of 0.81 in the Acehnese group. The authors conclude that ethnic background shapes how inflammation and vessel function interlock in hypertension, and that this local detail could inform prevention strategies.
pmc-13491665:
Thach Ngoc Pham and three colleagues present in 2026 the case of a five-year-old Vietnamese boy whose sudden belly pain traced to a rare malformation of lymph vessels inside his small intestine. Such growths usually appear in the head and neck, and bowel involvement is uncommon. His symptoms were one day of pain, vomiting, and fever, with only mild tenderness on examination.

Ultrasound showed a mixed cystic lump, and CT revealed a thickened bowel segment with scattered calcium spots and twisted vessels inside the wall. Surgeons opened the abdomen, found a dark purple, thickened stretch of bowel, removed it, and rejoined the ends. Microscopy confirmed tiny lymph channels threading every layer of the wall. The boy recovered smoothly, and the authors urge doctors to keep this rare cause in mind.
pmc-13491765:
Ying Long and four co-authors use whole-genome data in 2026 to test whether several named pygmy grasshopper species in East Asia are truly separate. The Tetrix japonica complex had been split into multiple species and even two extra genera, mostly on wing shape, a trait that varies within species. Fifty specimens from across the region were resequenced against a chromosome-level reference genome.

More than a million DNA variants painted one unified gene pool with no clusters matching the named species. Genetic differences were tiny and grew simply with geographic distance, and a machine learning classifier could barely tell the supposed species apart. Two named genera nested deep inside the complex beside their geographic neighbors. The authors conclude that taxonomists oversplit one widespread, shape-shifting species.
pmc-13492365:
Paparella and colleagues performed a nickel-catalyzed coupling reaction, joining two carbon fragments into diarylmethanes, in a 2026 study. The reaction ran inside a eutectic solvent made from choline chloride and urea, instead of the amide solvents this work demands. Diarylmethanes, two aromatic rings linked by a carbon, are prized building blocks for medicines and materials. The solvent here is not a backdrop but a participant.

Paparella's reaction ran at fifty degrees in air, finishing within three hours with zinc as the reducing agent and a phosphonium salt as additive. It produced a range of diarylmethanes in yields up to ninety-five percent and scaled to gram quantities. Mechanistic and electrochemical work showed benzyl radicals formed along the way being funneled into cross-coupling rather than wasted on self-pairing. Chloride in the solvent boosted zinc's reducing power, and the additive stabilized the nickel catalyst's states.
pmc-13492765:
Olivia A Smith leads a twenty-two-author team validating in 2026 a bead-based test that sniffs out antibodies against several filoviruses at once, the family that includes Ebola. Such multiplex tools could power outbreak surveillance and vaccine evaluation, but only if results travel reliably between laboratories. The same samples were therefore run in Honolulu and in Kinshasa, in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Forty-six samples from Ebola survivors and close contacts, plus more than nine hundred samples taken around vaccination, anchored the comparison. Variation within and between the laboratories stayed below preset limits for every target, and readings correlated strongly across sites. Antibodies to the vaccine virus jumped after immunization while responses to other filoviruses stayed flat, showing the panel can tell its targets apart. The authors endorse it for comparative serology work.
pmc-13492865:
Bansal and colleagues surveyed patients in 2026 about complaints with blood-drawing services at a large teaching hospital in eastern India. Patient views of phlebotomy, the drawing of blood for tests, reflect both skill and how staff treat people. High-volume public hospitals face long queues, so weak points matter.

One hundred patients answered a 35-item survey in English or Hindi and gave open comments. Nearly all praised hygiene and staff conduct, and most were glad that needed tests were on offer. Complaints centered on long waits, with over a quarter unhappy, and on dirty toilets. Women rated staff behavior and communication higher, while men rated speed and test handling higher. The authors urge fixes to waiting flow, sanitation, and how staff explain each step, with care for the differing views of men and women.
pmc-13493765:
Janell L. M. Smith and others map one branch of the cellular stress response that leads to secretion of GDF15, a signal protein that rises with aging and disease. In 2026, the study uses RNA reading from fiber cells exposed to eleven energy disturbances, including genetic and drug-induced power unit defects. It builds an index for this GDF15 arm of the integrated stress response.

The index checked in tests activating stress kinases, showing rapid changes before GDF15 gene levels itself rose. Applied to forty-four postmortem human tissues, it correlated with age and rose in hearts of people who died suddenly in emergency care. Brain results differed for people who died after long hospital stays. The index gives teams a tissue-specific tool for studying stress switching on.
pmc-13495365:
Liru Liu, Wanfang Li, and Sheng Ye engineer, in a 2026 study, a human enzyme variant that arms a harmless compound against cancer cells. The strategy, called enzyme-prodrug therapy, parks an enzyme at the tumor to switch a mild drug into a killer. The enzyme IDO normally runs a tryptophan pathway tied to immune control, yet it can oxidize indole-3-acetic acid, a plant hormone, into cell-killing products.

The natural enzyme's day job in immune pathways blocks use, so the team cut it down to a variant named IDO268C. The variant kept action on the prodrug while losing the pathway work. In breast and lung cancer cell lines, the pair killed cells strongly, whether the enzyme was made inside the cells or delivered as protein. Being human-derived, the enzyme may dodge immune rejection. The authors present the pair as a candidate for targeted cancer therapy.
pmc-13495465:
Wan Zheng, Hairong Ma, John R Dutcher, and Hongjun Liang present, in a 2026 study, a new class of germ killers built from natural nanoparticles that aims to sidestep drug resistance. Standard antibiotics derail germ machinery, and germs adapt fast. Membrane-active killers punch holes instead, yet older ones also harm human cells because they love fat. The team coated sugar-based particles with water-loving polymer brushes to change that.

The coated particles stayed gentle to body cells yet killed germs by opening pores only in membranes rich in the curved fats germs favor. That mode of attack is harder for germs to out-evolve. After use, common enzymes in nature break the killers down and switch them off, so they do not linger as pollution. The authors frame the work as a template for antibiotics that are potent in the body and harmless once discarded.
pmc-13495865:
Qipeng Wu and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, microneedle patches disguised in macrophage membrane to heal diabetic wounds that stall for months. Such wounds drown in inflammation while new blood vessels fail to grow, so immune cells and vessel lining cells stop coordinating. The patch carries a plant compound inside a metal-organic framework, wrapped in the outer coat of the very immune cells that patrol wounds.

Gene and mechanism studies found the patch switches on a signaling pair, SPP1 from calming immune cells and ApoE on vessel cells, that links inflammation control to vessel growth. The framework's nanozyme action mops up damaging oxygen radicals, freeing the calming cell state. In diabetic mice and mini pigs the patches cooled inflammation, rescued vessel growth, and closed wounds far faster. Restored vessels then fed back to keep immune cells calm.
pmc-13498865:
Pei and colleagues found a three-part gene module that controls tomato resistance to bacterial speck, the leaf disease caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato, in a 2026 plant genetics study. The disease is among the most common and damaging in tomato growing. The team started from a sugar-splitting enzyme gene, SlFBA3, whose activity rises during the resistance response.

Pei showed that raising SlFBA3 levels strengthened resistance while removing it weakened resistance. Its partner protein SlSGR did the opposite, suppressing early immune signaling triggered by molecular patterns from bacteria, and SlFBA3 partly blunted that suppression by binding to it. A third factor, the growth-regulator gene SlARF6A, sits above both, switching SlFBA3 on. Mapping this module, in which one enzyme and its brake are governed by a single upstream activator, gives breeders precise targets for breeding speck-resistant tomatoes without blanket immune changes.
pmc-13499265:
Veitia and Birchler reviewed why gene expression often behaves like a switch rather than a dial, in a 2026 article. They show how that explains the dosage sensitivity of transcription factors. Halving the dose of a gene regulator sometimes causes disease, a phenomenon called haploinsufficiency, though an output drop would seem tolerable. The authors connect that observation to nonlinearity across the steps of making RNA.

Veitia surveys sources of S-shaped responses, including cooperative DNA binding, where one factor eases the next, plus transcriptional synergy between activators. It covers chromatin features, three-dimensional folding, and the condensates that concentrate the transcription machinery. Epigenetic hysteresis, in which a state remembers its past, and network feedback that locks cells into states add thresholds. Because switch-like steps in series can align their transition zones, dosage changes can flip a gene. The authors argue haploinsufficiency emerges from this architecture rather than a mechanism.
pmc-13499865:
Sujaytha Paknikar and Kalpana Muthusamy review in 2026 the medical treatment of severe obesity, defined here as a body mass index at or above fifty, a measure comparing weight with height. This heaviest group is growing fastest worldwide and carries an outsized load of metabolic disease, disability, and health care use. Their clinical features can change both risk and response to therapy, so the review sets out how medicines fit alongside lifestyle change and weight-loss surgery.

Drug trials underrepresent patients at this severity, the authors note, leaving outcome data thin exactly where need is greatest. Medicine alone often falls short, and best care layers lifestyle support, drugs, and surgery, with drugs serving before surgery to reduce risk and after surgery to protect results. Unequal access, high dropout rates, and weaker real-world drug effects temper gains, pointing toward individualised, team-based long-term care.
pmc-13499965:
Rose Barham and colleagues study in 2026 how well combined medicine-pediatrics residency programmes, which train doctors for both adult and child care, integrate into their two host departments. Belonging in both worlds matters for trainee success, yet the drivers of good integration were little known. Building on a national survey, the team ran focus groups with 33 programme leaders at the specialty's national meeting in March 2025 and analysed transcripts for recurring themes.

Every programme taking part rated itself at least somewhat well integrated into its medicine department, and nearly all said the same for pediatrics, with no clear statistical gap between the two. Four factors supported blending in, namely residents joining cross-programme activities, personal relationships across departments, a seat in department business, and a distinct programme identity. The authors offer those levers to leaders building combined training elsewhere.
pmc-13500465:
M Prabhakar and co-authors describe in 2026 a power converter that lifts low direct-current voltage twentyfold for DC microgrids, the local power networks fed by solar panels, wind turbines, and batteries. Such sources deliver low and variable voltage, so boosting it efficiently to a high-voltage bus is essential. Their two-stage design first doubles the gain of a classic boost circuit, then applies an inductor-capacitor gain cell for a squared gain effect, while interleaving keeps input current smooth.

A laboratory prototype converting 20 volts to 400 volts at 200 watts ran at high full-load efficiency in the reported tests. It held its output steady across wide input and load swings with small overshoots. Switch stress stayed at a small fraction of output voltage, easing component demands. Comparisons with rival designs supported the circuit as a fit for microgrid use.
pmc-13500665:
Saori Ishibashi and colleagues examine in 2026 the joint capsule tissue of bunion patients, asking why the sore spot on a hallux valgus foot hurts. Fifty feet from 49 patients having corrective surgery provided medial capsule samples. The tissue was examined under the microscope and stained for a pain-related peptide called CGRP, a tissue-degrading enzyme, and two collagen types. Patients rated their pain and function on a standard foot questionnaire.

Capsule degeneration tracked deformity severity closely in the reported analysis. The pain peptide concentrated around blood vessels and cartilage-like cells regardless of deformity degree, and its level rose alongside the degrading enzyme. Crucially, higher peptide expression matched worse pain scores, and tender bunions showed more of it, even though deformity size itself explained pain poorly. Blocking or calming this peptide pathway becomes a candidate strategy for bunion pain relief.
pmc-13501265:
Dagmar Mudronova and colleagues compare in 2026 how young Atlantic salmon respond to vaccination depending on the water system that raised them. Salmon are vaccinated in freshwater before transfer to the sea, and farms use either flow-through tanks or recirculating systems that reuse water.

Gill samples came from ten fish per system, taken a week before and two weeks after vaccination. Before vaccination, recirculating-system fish already showed higher activity in three defense genes. Afterward, the two groups moved differently: recirculating fish raised a bacteria-fighting gene and lowered a calming one, while flow-through fish raised both attack and calming signals together. The authors conclude that housing water quietly shapes a fish's immune starting point and its vaccine response.
pmc-13501665:
Sanjivani Nikhil Kamble leads a five-author team presenting a 2026 scoping review of core strengthening exercise for primary dysmenorrhea, the severe period pain that occurs without pelvic disease. Core training conditions the deep muscles that stabilize the spine, which may help the body withstand menstrual strain. The team searched five databases for trials and experimental studies in English published between 2019 and 2025. Drug-focused studies and unrelated physiotherapy methods were excluded, leaving trials of core or lumbopelvic stabilization exercise.

Eleven studies qualified, totalling 445 participants. Most reported significant drops in pain intensity after programmes lasting six to twelve weeks, measured on visual analogue or numerical pain scales. Several also found better quality of life, daily function, sleep, and psychological well-being. Head-to-head studies favoured core work over stretching alone, and versions adding pressure biofeedback gave stronger pain relief. The authors map a generally positive but small evidence base.
pmc-13502565:
Tim Köglmeier, Thomas J Tiefel, and Oliver Reiser report a 2026 chemistry route to cyclopropanes, the strained three-membered rings prized in drug molecules, that avoids hazardous diazo reagents entirely. Making these rings is thermodynamically uphill, and classic methods pay for it with explosive precursors or throw away stoichiometric byproducts. The team instead banks light energy first: aldehydes and furan undergo a photochemical [2+2] cycloaddition to form oxetanes, four-membered rings already charged with the needed energy.

A Lewis acid catalyst then triggers an internal rearrangement that contracts each oxetane into a cyclopropane, with ideal atom economy because nothing is added or discarded. The route reaches meso-cyclopropane dicarbaldehydes, versatile building blocks that shorten the path to several difficult bioactive motifs. Because the starting aldehydes and furan are abundant and renewable, and the conditions are mild, the authors present oxetanes as a general gateway to densely functionalized cyclopropanes from simple feedstocks.
pmc-13503665:
Zhenghan Li puts forth a plan joining a long-context language model with multi-sided knowledge graphs for broken archive texts. In 2026, the work targets decayed and half scanned papers whose missing context, broken flow, and unclear items defeat plain pulling. Cross-modal focus and gated merging let neural text codes and set graph knowledge inform each other.

Knowledge filling draws on time, layered, and spatial graph sides to infer missing items, while multi-hop thinking traces hidden links across paper edges. Tests on corpora from three local vaults reached Hits@1 of 0.578, mean return rank 0.648, and link thinking F1 of 0.769, a lot above old marks. Archive keepers gain a route to recover dark data.
pmc-13503765:
Xiaodan Wang, Yuhan Dai, and Keli Mu explore how patients in China view occupational therapy during rehab, in a 2026 interview study. Contentment with care shapes how well rehab works. In China, strong respect for authority may color how patients meet their therapists, yet patient voices are rarely heard.

The team spoke at length with ten patients at one rehab unit and grouped their words into four themes. Most entered therapy by a doctor's order and took a passive role, with tasks that felt dull and not shaped to them. Patients still reported gains in body function and daily life. Warm, clear talk from therapists pleased patients most, while cost weighed heaviest against contentment. The authors call for more shared choice in care.
pmc-13504765:
Dakun Huang, Haixin Li, and Shudong Yang use genetics to test whether sodium passed in urine truly causes kidney stones, in a 2026 study. Salt intake has long tracked with stone risk in diet studies, yet habits like fluid intake can muddy those links. Genetic tools can cut through some of that noise.

The team used gene variants tied to urinary sodium as stand-ins for lifelong sodium output, with data from more than three hundred thousand people. Higher predicted sodium output went with more than double the odds of stones. A second data set gave a like result. Checks found no sign that the variants act through other paths, and results were steady across methods. The findings back salt limits as a stone prevention step.
pmc-13504965:
Meng Zhu leads a team linking sleep habits to fatty liver risk in people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 study. Fatty liver tied to metabolic faults is common in diabetes and can scar the liver over time. Night sleep quality and daytime naps both shape metabolic health.

The cohort held 1,900 patients followed for about three years, with 379 new liver cases found on ultrasound. Poor night sleep alone more than doubled risk against good sleep with short naps. Long naps raised risk even in good night sleepers, and the worst mix, poor nights plus long naps, carried the highest risk. Adding sleep patterns to a standard liver index sharpened its forecasts. The authors suggest sleep review belongs in diabetes liver screening.
pmc-13505065:
Gao, Wang, and Lv ask whether subway networks tilt a city's carbon balance, the ratio between what its land absorbs and what its people emit. Earlier work counted subway emissions or absorption separately and treated lines as simple point-to-point links. Their 2026 study of Chinese counties builds station-level network measures, using social network analysis to capture how accessible the whole web is. It tracks those measures over time against the carbon balance ratio.

Better subway accessibility significantly improved the carbon balance, and the benefit ran strongest in poorer regions, compact urban forms, and areas with low household electricity use in their models. The mechanism unfolds in three phases: tunnelling preserves surface green space during construction, riders shift from cars during operation, and transit-oriented industry change amplifies gains where institutions and technology support it. Road density pointed the other way on green space.
pmc-13507165:
Ming-I Chen, Ying-Lin Hsu, and Yi-Hsin Chen evaluate, in 2026 work, AI help for hospital diagnosis coding with an eye on payment, not just accuracy. Coding errors change what hospitals are paid under group-based payment systems in the United States and Taiwan. The team tested eleven models on intensive care records and built two money-aware scores for coding risk.

A fine-tuned language model led on standard accuracy, while general chat models used cold scored far worse in early tests. Money-aware scores exposed a wide gap between best and worst tuned models that plain metrics missed. Guiding human review by money risk at a fifth of cases captured most of the ideal gain. Live hospital trials are still needed.
pmc-13507265:
Christopher Weekes leads a 2026 team that maps, near single-letter resolution, how the MCM2-7 helicase wakes up and first melts DNA at replication origins. Two inactive helicase rings sit loaded on DNA and must split into active unwinding machines, yet the first melting step was murky. Genome-wide mapping located the earliest strand separation.

Melting begins near the facing surfaces of the two rings, over a conserved sequence pattern rich and poor in A and T bases in alternation. Holding the rings together delayed release of a loading factor, tying mechanics to disassembly. Single strands exit through a dedicated gate between two subunits, needed for activation but not later copying. Origin firing gains a concrete mechanical script.
pmc-13507565:
Sayed and colleagues report a 2026 study of light-activated compounds built to fight cancer and bacteria. Their compounds glow in near-infrared light, clump to boost that glow, and carry a charged part that sticks to membranes. When lit, they release reactive oxygen that damages nearby cells. The team built and compared three versions in cells and bacteria.

The longest version worked best. It clung to membranes, stayed bright, and made reactive oxygen two ways at once. In cancer cells it triggered two forms of cell death, orderly apoptosis and an iron-linked death called ferroptosis, while its glow let the team watch dying cells change shape live. It also killed both major classes of bacteria, and wounds treated with it healed fast. One light-driven compound for tumors and infected wounds could cut the need for separate drugs.
pmc-13508265:
Kjersti Grønning, Liv Eli Lysfjord, and Ann Katrin Hagen Røstad ask people with ME/CFS and their close relatives what support they need, in a 2026 Norwegian study. This illness, marked by deep exhaustion, has few proven treatments, so day-to-day self-management carries much of the load. The team held interviews with 16 people in total, twelve patients and four relatives. Answers were grouped into shared themes about what helps and what gets in the way.

Three needs stood out. Support should be personal and reachable in flexible formats, including digital and mix-and-match modules timed to a person's readiness. Care should be steady over time and should treat patients as credible, countering the stigma described. Peer contact and practical tools, like pacing activity and tracking symptoms, also mattered. Current support often clashed with patients' physical and mental limits and gave mixed advice on activity.
pmc-13508365:
Rui Liu leads a thirteen-author team testing whether activating oxytocin neurons in the brain shields tissue after a stroke, in 2026 mouse work. Oxytocin is a hormone messenger made in a small brain region called the paraventricular nucleus. Inflammation driven by overactive immune cells worsens stroke injury, and oxytocin has calmed inflammation in other settings. The stroke model briefly blocked a brain artery. The team measured oxytocin in several fluids, then used a genetic switch to fire up those neurons in special mice.

Oxytocin levels fell after stroke in brain tissue, blood, and spinal fluid, while its receptor rose near the injury. Switching the neurons on raised oxytocin again, shrank the damaged area, and improved function. Gene reading flagged a calming of an immune draw signal as a key change. The work suggests a built-in brain circuit that can be nudged to limit stroke damage.
pmc-13508465:
Abudounaibi Abudoueryimu leads an eight-author mapping study of research on a CT-based heart flow score used to judge whether narrowed arteries starve heart muscle, in 2026 work. The score, CT-FFR, estimates pressure loss across a narrowing from a standard scan, sparing some patients invasive tests. The team searched a major database for work from 2015 to 2025. Of 730 records found, 582 papers qualified. Mapping software charted output by year, country, institution, journal, and keyword, and flagged sudden bursts of interest in topics.

Output grew steadily at over six percent a year. The United States led in both volume and citations, with China second in volume but lighter in citation impact. The three hub countries for joint work were the United States, China, and Italy, and one imaging journal led the field. Recent bursts point to clinic use, with stable chest pain and diagnosis rising fast.
pmc-13509265:
Shiva Hooshmandi, Nicholas Freestone, and Francesca Arrigoni review how high blood pressure in women is shaped by hormones, vessel aging, and metabolism across life, in 2026 work. Pressure control in women is not static; it shifts with reproductive milestones. Papers that ignored menopause status or reproductive history were set aside or read with care. The synthesis weighed vessel lining function, hormone balance, kidney salt handling, and vessel resistance together.

Menopause, vessel aging, metabolic strain, and the balance of male to female hormones all interact, the review finds. Cell aging and low-grade inflammation add to risk over time. High blood pressure during pregnancy flags women for later heart disease and offers an early chance to act. Newer drug families for diabetes and weight may also help heart risk, though sex-specific prevention proof is still forming. The authors push a life-course frame for judging and treating women's pressure.
pmc-13509665:
Elena-Adelina Toma and eight co-authors survey new options for belly infections that resist standard antibiotics, in a 2026 review. Such infections inside the abdomen grow harder to treat as germs gain resistance, a problem fed by drug use in people, animals, and farming. The review covers new antibiotics in trials alongside less standard approaches that attack germs in other ways.

Candidate options include virus-based germ killers, natural germ-fighting peptides, tiny particles that damage germ walls, gene editing tools aimed at resistance genes, and helpful bacteria that restore gut balance. Each route can bypass known resistance tricks, yet each faces hurdles in delivery, safety, approval rules, and dosing data for belly infections. The authors argue future care will mix several of these tools, guided by fast testing and careful drug stewardship.
pmc-13509865:
Georgii S. Mikhailov and six co-authors test whether natural humic substances can shield an enzyme from damage by therapeutic ultrasound, in 2026 work. The enzyme, alkaline phosphatase, helps build bone mineral and is used in lab assays. The team studied how the enzyme spreads between two liquids that do not mix, how it gathers at their border, and how well it still worked after ultrasound treatment.

Under alkaline conditions, humic substances kept much of the enzyme activity that ultrasound alone would have cost. The sound waves did not change the protein's folded shape, and the activity loss could reverse once treatment stopped. The team proposes that humic pieces bind the enzyme into protective complexes, which break apart under sound and then form again. Treated and untreated samples also made bone mineral at similar rates in a follow-up test.
pmc-13509965:
Chang Wei, Weibin Zhao, and Chengfu Yu study children in China whose parents work away from home, focusing on bullying climate at school and dependence on mobile phones, in 2026 work. Three hundred such children answered surveys twice, six months apart. The team measured school bullying climate, trouble managing emotions, phone dependence, and psychological resilience, a person's capacity to recover from setbacks.

A harsher bullying climate predicted stronger phone dependence six months later. Trouble managing emotions carried part of that link, passing the effect from climate to phone habits. Resilience changed the first step of the chain in an unexpected direction: among highly resilient children the climate-to-emotion link was clear, while among less resilient children it was absent. The authors say protection from resilience may work in narrower ways than often assumed, and they urge care in reading a single survey chain.
pmc-13510165:
Liu and colleagues studied in 2026 how cold and hunger together harm a farmed catfish species during winter, a season when both stresses strike at once. They kept fish for ten days under four setups. The setups paired normal warmth or cold with feeding or no food, and the team then examined livers, gut microbes, and body chemistry.

The combined stress caused the worst liver injury, with cell swelling, cell death, and raised liver enzyme levels. Protective antioxidant defenses fell at the same time. Helpful gut bacteria declined, while likely harmful ones grew, and one genus stood out as the top marker of the combined state. Several cell death pathways switched on only under dual stress. The authors offer these signals as tools to monitor overwintering fish health.
pmc-13515765:
Kawther A Zaher and six colleagues follow one boy's HIV treatment course in a 2026 case report. The child caught HIV-1 subtype C from his mother around birth, and the virus arrived already resistant to key drugs. Gene testing found changes that block protease inhibitors and two backbone drugs, confirmed against a standard resistance database. His starting viral load was high and his immune balance poor.

Early treatment built on a boosted protease inhibitor failed to hold the virus down durably. Care then switched, first to a regimen built on an integrase inhibitor and then to a single-tablet mix of bictegravir with two backbone drugs. From November 2024 the virus stayed undetectable. His CD4 count climbed to healthy levels and the CD4 to CD8 balance normalised. Zaher's team uses the case to argue for resistance testing before a child's first regimen, whenever it is available.
pmc-13516765:
Norman and colleagues set out a 2026 study protocol for screening sleep-disordered breathing in children during dental visits. The condition, which includes obstructive sleep apnea, is underdiagnosed in children despite links to behavior, learning, and heart-metabolic problems, and dentists see children's facial growth over years. The study will enroll sixty children aged eight to thirteen at a university dental clinic.

Norman will classify each child as low or high risk using a validated questionnaire with a preset score threshold. The groups will then be compared on sleep measures from a regulatory-cleared wearable ring monitor worn at home for at least three nights. Measures include apnea event counts and a sleep quality index. Secondary comparisons cover body mass, throat and tonsil grades, anxiety, depression, stress, and sleepiness, with facial X-ray analysis where images already exist. The authors argue dental visits could become an early-warning touchpoint feeding referrals.
pmc-13517465:
Liu and co-authors test whether fermented forage can displace imported feed in pig finishing diets. Their 2026 trial responds to China's heavy reliance on imported soybeans and corn, which leaves swine producers exposed to price swings. The team replaced twenty percent of the base diet with a fermented forage-based mixed feed and fed finishing pigs for 56 days, then measured growth and pork quality.

The substitution caused no harm on either front: growth performance and meat quality matched the standard diet. One measure improved clearly, the antioxidant properties of the pork, which the authors highlight as a quality bonus rather than a trade-off. Because the forage can be grown locally, they present the approach as a practical way to cut dependence on conventional imported ingredients. The paper positions fermentation as the enabling step that makes coarse forage usable for pigs.
pmc-13517665:
Dania M Figueroa Acosta and five colleagues review why HIV's surface protein looks different on free virus than on infected cells in a 2026 article. That protein, Env, is the immune system's main target, and spread from cell to cell resists antibody attack better than free-virus spread. The authors trace the difference to how Env is processed: its cutting step, sugar coats, folding states, and constant recycling through the cell's internal sorting system.

Env's tail, they explain, plugs into that sorting machinery, and new structural models show how the tail's shape steers where Env ends up. Mixed Env populations then present antibodies with moving, mismatched targets. The review closes with countermeasures: antibody cocktails and small molecules that reshape Env to expose it. Figueroa Acosta's team frames trafficking, not just sequence change, as a core immune-escape trick that cure and vaccine design must outwit.
pmc-13517765:
Yuan and colleagues report a 2026 cell study of omega-3 fats and gut cell protection in dogs. Two fats, EPA and DHA, were compared on dog intestinal cells injured with hydrogen peroxide, a standard oxidative stress test. The team measured cell survival, antioxidant enzymes, inflammation signals, aging markers, and the proteins that seal the gut barrier.

Across all tested doses, DHA failed to relieve the injury, while EPA protected the cells clearly. EPA raised antioxidant enzyme activity, calmed inflammatory signaling, and steadied the cell's chromosome-cap structures, slowing stress-driven aging. It also restored tight junction proteins, the seals between gut cells whose loss makes the gut leaky. The split between two similar fats is the surprise: for dog gut health, EPA looks like the active partner, a lead for pet foods aimed at intestinal protection.
pmc-13518665:
Sahrish Nayab and four colleagues examine social and emotional skills among students living at the Child Protection and Welfare Bureau in Gujranwala, Pakistan, in a 2026 study. The bureau shelters children in precarious situations, so skills such as self-control, empathy, and getting along with others shape later learning and well-being.

The team interviewed all 7 teachers and surveyed all 105 students with an adapted skills tool. Children who had stayed six months or longer scored higher than newer arrivals, with gains in sharing, self-expression, and building relationships. Teacher accounts added that personal background affected how each child settled in. Longer supportive stays, the authors conclude, help vulnerable children grow.
pmc-13518865:
Bilal Ahmad Hakim and a large team show in 2026 that losing Nemp1, a protein bracing the inner wall of the cell nucleus, wrecks female meiosis in both flies and mice. Egg cells must pair chromosomes accurately and repair DNA during meiosis, or quality-control checkpoints kill them. NEMP proteins are needed for fertility across many animals, for reasons that stayed murky.

Without Nemp1, meiosis stalled, DNA damage rose at middle stages, and chromosome pairing defects persisted. Damage sensors ATM and CHK2 switched on, driving egg loss, while blocking either sensor rescued the eggs. The findings tie nuclear support to genome protection and help explain the near sterility seen without the protein.
pmc-13519465:
Pazhanivel Kandasamy and colleagues reviewed how mouth lesions can reveal skin and whole-body disease. Published in 2026, the review treats the mouth as a diagnostic window, since its lining shares origins with skin and often shows illness first. Lesions there may precede skin or body-wide signs in conditions from lichen planus and pemphigus to viral infection, connective tissue disease, and immune deficiency.

Mouth conditions reshape how lesions look, since saliva, chewing, microbes, and thin lining turn skin blisters into mouth erosions, ulcers, or red patches. The review walks through infectious, autoimmune, blistering, vessel, genetic, emergency, granulomatous, and histiocytic disorders with mouth signs. The authors urge teamwork among dentists, skin doctors, physicians, and pathologists so early mouth clues trigger full evaluation and referral.
pmc-13519765:
Clara Laffitte Redondo leads a thirteen-author case series in 2026 on liver injury in cystic fibrosis patients taking CFTR modulator drugs. These medicines transformed breathing and quality of life, yet liver damage sometimes forces patients to stop, and the mechanism is unexplained. Six cases of liver toxicity were scored with a standardized causality tool and genotyped for drug-handling genes.

One variant stood out: CYP3A4*22, which slows the CYP3A enzyme, appeared more often than in the general European population, while patients also lacked CYP3A5 expression. Slower clearance could let the drugs linger and stress the liver through oxidative pathways. Other genes governing transport and detoxification may contribute. Larger confirmatory studies are needed, the authors stress.
pmc-13519865:
Meenu Pichholiya and four colleagues compare diabetes drugs head-to-head in 2026 for kidney protection in type 2 diabetes. Diabetic kidney damage is a leading route to kidney failure worldwide, yet no earlier study had directly compared the kidney effects of common antidiabetic therapies. Their prospective study followed 100 patients at a tertiary hospital.

Blood sugar and kidney measures were tracked across follow-up visits. Metformin plus gliptin therapy significantly lowered HbA1c and blood urea. The clearest creatinine improvements appeared with metformin combined with SGLT2 inhibitors or gliptins, while insulin-only patients fared worse. Pichholiya and co-authors conclude oral combinations protect kidneys as well as sugar, while calling for larger, longer studies.
pmc-13520265:
Corné Nel, Jacqueline E Wolvaardt, and Pieter du Toit argue in a 2026 conceptual paper that research ethics in Africa should absorb African value canons alongside the dominant Western frameworks. Helsinki-style ethics rest on individualism, they contend, while African scholarship has long urged communal grounding. A clinical medical practice degree curriculum serves as their worked example of decolonized ethics teaching.

Five canons anchor the proposal, drawn from Swahili and the Ubuntu philosophy of shared humanity: familyhood, calmness, self-giving, fairness, and truthfulness. Centering communal well-being over the lone individual, the authors say, could humanize healthcare as artificial intelligence spreads through it. Inclusive ethics, on this view, protects compassionate care rather than merely policing consent forms.
pmc-13520365:
Rhavenna Thais Alves-Gomes and colleagues map in 2026 repetitive satellite DNA across the genome of the black soldier fly, an insect farmed to turn waste into protein feed. Repeat DNA shapes chromosome centres and ends, yet this species had little chromosome-level repeat data.

Chromosome checks confirmed 14 chromosomes with a sex pair, matching the assembled genome. Eleven satellite families made up roughly 3 to 4 percent of the genome, with varied lengths and base makeup. Some repeats clustered at chromosome ends or centres, suggesting structural roles, while others differed between Brazilian and Spanish stocks. The atlas aids future genome assembly and strain comparison.
pmc-13522765:
Bingfeng Zuo and colleagues combine an exosome vaccine with two drugs against liver cancer in mouse models in a 2026 study. Exosomes are tiny vesicles released by cells; here they came from dendritic cells and were decorated with targeting and immune-recruiting parts. The oral drug lenvatinib releases tumor antigens in place, while the vaccine draws in and activates the immune cells that present those antigens.

The pairing increased tumor-infiltrating killer T cells and suppressed growth in several mouse models, including cancers arising naturally in the liver. Adding a PD-1 blocking antibody eradicated established tumors in the natural model and expanded effector T cells further. The authors describe the strategy as a personalized immune approach that needs no pre-identified antigen and could translate toward clinical use.
pmc-13523265:
Nivetha Uthayasuriyan and co-authors describe a rare brain lymphoma location in a 2026 case report. A fifty-eight-year-old man with a healthy immune system developed worsening headache, vomiting, and cognitive decline. Imaging revealed a well-defined, evenly enhancing mass at a passage between brain fluid spaces and the roof of the third ventricle, blocking fluid flow. Several benign and other tumor types were considered first.

Surgery through a corridor between the hemispheres provided a biopsy specimen. Tissue and marker testing confirmed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the commonest form of primary central nervous system lymphoma. The postoperative course was stormy, with salt imbalance and a lung clot, and the patient died despite intensive support. The authors urge biopsy rather than aggressive removal when lymphoma is suspected, so chemotherapy can start early.
pmc-13523365:
Anthony Wang and colleagues review anesthesia challenges as heart transplantation expands to broader donor and recipient pools in a 2026 article. Donor hearts now come from older and heavier donors, people with heart disease, long-distance retrievals, and donors with infections once considered disqualifying. Preservation devices that keep hearts cold, perfused, or even beating aim to protect these grafts and shorten time without blood flow.

Complications after transplant include widespread vessel relaxation that may resist standard drugs, right heart failure, primary graft dysfunction, bleeding, and clotting problems. Prediction tools for graft dysfunction may allow earlier intervention in high-risk patients. The authors argue that anesthesiologists who anticipate how bleeding, vessel relaxation, and graft problems interact can improve both short and long-term outcomes as the donor pool widens.
pmc-13523465:
Miroslav Stoyanov and colleagues report 2026 laboratory work on drug combinations for cancers carrying extra copies of a section of chromosome 17 known as 17q. PLK4, a protein that controls centriole copying during cell division, is already a drug target in some breast cancers and neuroblastomas with this gain. The team searched for factors that limit how well PLK4 blockade works.

Using cancer genomics portals, the group identified PPM1D, a phosphatase that restrains the tumor suppressor p53, as a key limiter. Blocking PLK4 and PPM1D together switched on p53 target genes and drove cell death in breast cancer cells with 17q gains. Pairing PLK4 blockade with MDM2 blockade had a similar lethal effect, while removing p53 protected cells. Results in two neuroblastoma lines supported the same strategy.
pmc-13524865:
