Kidney disease affects over 850 million people worldwide, with most living in lower-income countries where dialysis access is limited. A 2025 World Health Assembly resolution urged prevention, early detection, and sustainable financing.

Thailand has universal coverage yet one of Southeast Asia's highest kidney failure burdens, above 2,400 cases per million people. A peritoneal dialysis first policy widened access and equity, but the growing dialysis population exposed the limits of a downstream approach. The country now combines community screening, risk stratification, public health measures, disease-modifying drugs, and integrated chronic care, plus nutrition support and conservative care for people nearing kidney failure. The authors present the pivot as a model.
pmc-13525165:
Macrohon and colleagues surveyed pediatric research activity in 2026 across the Zamboanga Peninsula and the provinces of Basilan, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi in the Philippines. They questioned 47 pediatricians and ran group discussions to learn what helps or blocks research after training ends.

Only a small share, under seven percent of respondents, were actively doing research, even though many had done research during training. Peer support, training in methods and statistics, and financial help encouraged research. Weak technical writing skills, scarce funding, and plain disinterest held doctors back, and many saw research as a burden added to clinical work. The authors recommend targeted training and support for the pediatricians who show real interest, rather than pushing everyone equally.
pmc-13525965:
Vicent Llorca-Bofí and colleagues tracked employment among people with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder across Spain from 2018 through 2023. Published in 2026, the register study drew on the Spanish primary care database, covering adults aged twenty to sixty-four with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or other diagnoses. Work is a core marker of recovery in severe mental illness, yet southern European trends were thin.

In 2023, only about one sixth of people with schizophrenia and under two fifths with bipolar disorder held jobs, against nearly two thirds of others. Disability pensions ran far higher in both groups. Employment rose slightly over the period and pensions fell, but a catch-all status category surged sharply. The authors warn that most gains likely reflect administrative shifts rather than true workplace inclusion. Readers get a sober national baseline for reform.
pmc-13528065:
Enes Altın and seven colleagues hunt for tissue markers that warn of return in low-risk bladder cancer in a 2026 study. The cancers had not invaded muscle. Forty patients were drawn from 320 who had tumor removal surgery between 2011 and 2019. Half saw their cancer return and half did not. Stored tissue was stained for seven marker proteins.

Having several tumors predicted return. So did tumor position near the ureter opening. One marker, TSC-1, was strongly tied to recurrence. Patients positive for it had over twenty times the odds in the team's model. Another marker, CD44, pointed the other way, toward lower risk. A third, ELF-3, appeared in every sample and told nothing. The authors suggest staining for TSC-1 and CD44 could sharpen follow-up plans.
pmc-13528165:
Jing Ye and eight colleagues check whether womb lining changes during hormone treatment affect babies from frozen embryo transfer in a 2026 study. The records held 6,331 single babies born after day-three frozen transfers. Ultrasound measured lining thickness before progesterone and on transfer day. Babies were grouped by whether the lining grew, shrank, or stayed flat.

Mean birth weights were nearly identical across the three groups, around 3,350 grams. Low birth weight rates did not rise when the lining shrank. Small-for-dates rates also matched. Adjustment for other factors kept the picture flat. Baby sex and pregnancy length did move birth weight, as expected. The authors conclude lining wiggles after progesterone are not a warning sign. Clinics need not cancel cycles over them, they say.
pmc-13530265:
Keita Fukuyama and co-authors chart cancer care costs across Japan in a 2026 claims study covering 2011 to 2022. National insurance records let the team sort patients by cancer type and track monthly claims and drug use. New targeted and immune drugs have improved outcomes while raising price questions.

Breast cancer was the most common diagnosis, followed by stomach and colon cancers. Lung cancer cost the most overall, while a blood cancer called multiple myeloma cost the most per person each month. Immune checkpoint drug claims climbed fast after those medicines arrived, pushing total cancer spending ahead of economic growth.
pmc-13530765:
Klemt, Sueyoshi, and Chan present in 2026, as conference poster 221, a computer modeling study challenging the ruler surgeons use to judge shoulder instability risk. The glenoid track, the width of socket the ball can traverse safely, is conventionally set at 83 percent of the socket's width from static images.

Building patient-specific finite element models from MRI scans of ten shoulders, the team simulated thirty functional activities under physiological loading. The activities ran from daily tasks to a quarterback's throw and maximum range positions. The track came out significantly narrower under dynamic loading in every single activity than under static assumptions. The narrowest reading, about seventy percent of socket width, occurred in the classic dislocation position. The authors conclude that earlier static work overestimated the safe track, and that the threshold separating stable from risky bone defects may sit lower.
pmc-13531565:
Mannheimer and colleagues analyze a giant primary care cohort in this 2026 New Zealand study of cardiovascular prevention, asking whether having several chronic conditions helps or hinders getting guideline-recommended preventive drugs. The cohort covered 430,286 adults in Auckland's ProCare network without prior cardiovascular disease, stratified by their five-year risk.

At baseline, combined blood-pressure and lipid-lowering therapy reached only 2.5 percent of low-risk, 31 percent of intermediate-risk, and 40 percent of high-risk patients, well short of guideline ambitions for the highest group. Multimorbidity consistently raised the odds of receiving the combination, most strikingly in the low-risk group at a relative risk of 2.90 against patients without multiple conditions, and those patients also maintained therapy slightly better over two years. The authors read the pattern as contact-driven prescribing and flag the persistent under-treatment of high-risk patients as the real gap.
pmc-13531765:
Niloofar Rafati and colleagues survey in 2026 how older hospital patients in Tehran perceive abuse during their stay. Face-to-face interviews covered 422 patients aged 60 and over at university hospitals during 2023 and 2024. A dedicated form scored several forms of poor care, from physical harm to management failures.

Patients rated failures of ward setup and management highest, while direct physical or mental abuse scored lowest. Older age, female sex, living alone, and taking many medicines each raised abuse scores. Together the factors explained about 42 percent of variation. Staff awareness for the most exposed groups is the practical takeaway.
pmc-13534165:
Sertas Erarslan, Turkan P Kilit, and Aycan Acet compare in 2026 two blood sugar markers in people with type 2 diabetes plus excess red blood cells. The usual marker, HbA1c, reflects sugar bound to red cells, so changed cell turnover can distort it. Their study held 62 patients with the blood condition and 40 controls.

Home finger-prick checks showed HbA1c-based estimates ran low by a clear margin in the blood condition group. A fructosamine-based estimate matched home checks much more closely. Six in ten patients would change control category by marker choice, so fructosamine may guide safer care here.
pmc-13534865:
Lathursha Kalaranjan and Eugene Liscio tested whether bloodstain origin analysis works for coughed-out blood patterns. Published in 2026, the forensic study used a mechanical rig to produce expirated patterns at two distances and two angles, plus blind patterns from human volunteers. Expirated patterns form when air pushes blood from a body opening, and origin analysis for them was untested.

Software analysis showed statistically significant errors in origin estimates, largest in distance from the wall, unlike impact patterns where height errors dominate. Fluid type, volume, speed, opening shape, and human factors all limited accuracy. Horizontal and depth estimates still supported two-dimensional origin use for investigations, while vertical errors limited full three-dimensional claims. Readers get a caution for crime-scene reconstruction from cough patterns.
pmc-13536565:
Satoshi Hara and colleagues report in 2026 a male infant with Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum features caused by genome-wide paternal uniparental heterodisomy. In this rare state, chromosome copies come only from the father across the genome, usually with a female chromosome set. Methylation tests showed father-only patterns at many imprinted sites in this boy.

Gene checks found two distinct paternal genomes in blood cells, while other tissues held a normal mixed set, making the child a chimera. Array data confirmed one X and one Y chromosome in each cell type. Careful long-term follow-up is advised for unique signs.
pmc-13536665:
Liping Gong and colleagues surveyed long-term hepatitis C among older antibody-positive patients in Anhui Province, China. Published in 2026, the study took in 4,558 survey forms from patients aged fifty and over found with the marker between 2004 and 2022, with blood testing for viral RNA. Long-term illness was defined by marker signs lasting at least six months.

Knowledge of how to stop and treat hepatitis C stood near one quarter, while over one quarter tested positive for viral RNA and counted as long-term cases. Women, people in the north, and earlier treated patients faced lower odds of long-term illness, while men in the south not treated and with raised liver enzymes faced higher risk. A forecast model using picked factors sorted cases fairly well. The authors call for stronger teaching and screening, most of all for southern men not treated.
pmc-13536765:
Jose Daniel Sanchez Redroban and co-authors compare malaria paths in Ecuador and Venezuela from 2000 to 2023 in a 2026 analysis. Ecuador nearly eliminated malaria while Venezuela saw a historic resurgence. Data on cases, stability, health spending, income, poverty, and oil prices were combined with trend models and a five-part governance review. Trends in other infections in Venezuela were also checked.

Ecuador cut cases by more than 99 percent, with steady declines across three phases. Venezuela cases surged sharply after 2014 alongside an oil price collapse and fiscal squeeze, peaking in 2018. Later declines coincided with weakened tracking and mass migration, suggesting missed cases. Other preventable diseases also resurged. The authors argue that stable governance and protected funding shape whether shocks become outbreaks.
pmc-13537465:
Robert Beaumont Wilson and co-authors review low vitamin C, obesity, and metabolic syndrome in a narrative synthesis. Low vitamin C remains common even where fruit, vegetables, and supplements are widely sold. Highly processed Western diets supply excess energy with few micronutrients, feeding oxidative stress, gut imbalance, and insulin problems. The review weighs possible pathways and asks whether raising vitamin C can help treat weight and metabolic features.

Lab and animal evidence supports vitamin C as both a preventive and a treatment aid. Human trials show smaller gains, covering insulin response, blood fats, inflammation, weight, blood pressure, gut leakiness, and fatty liver. Weak spots include missing starting vitamin C levels in some trials. The authors suggest vitamin C may boost diet and activity programs, while calling for more work on combined treatment.
pmc-13538265:
Zhiya Wu and co-authors build a new outlook index for large B-cell lymphoma treated with standard immune chemotherapy in a 2026 study. Existing indexes sort risk yet miss some poor-outlook patients. Records for 167 newly diagnosed patients treated at a Nanjing cancer hospital between 2016 and 2021 supplied candidate factors. Statistical selection built scoring charts for time without progression and for overall survival, checked by repeated resampling.

Five factors tied to both outcomes, covering age, a blood enzyme level, disease stage, spread beyond lymph nodes, and a helper T cell count. Scoring charts predicted well in internal checks, with strong agreement between predicted and observed results. A simplified index split patients into four risk tiers with clearly separated survival curves. The authors present the index as a practical sorting tool.
pmc-13538365:
Avik Ray and colleagues present a lightweight explainable neural network for spotting crop disease from leaf photos in a 2026 study. Early spotting saves yield and cuts needless spraying, yet expert checks are slow and scarce in rural areas. The design uses efficient layered filters, attention blocks, and skip links to cut computing load, plus heat maps that show which leaf areas drove each call. Testing used a large public leaf collection.

The collection held more than fifty-four thousand images covering thirty-eight diseases across fourteen crops. Test accuracy ran high, with strong balance across disease classes and near-perfect ranking scores. Comparisons showed rival accuracy to heavier models while staying light enough for phones and field devices. The authors offer the tool for real-time farm diagnosis that users can visually verify.
pmc-13539665:
Kiara A Kidman and colleagues simulate how stabilizing small molecules reshape a diabetes-linked protein in a 2026 computational study. The human form of the protein clumps into toxic fibers in type 2 diabetes, while the rat form largely does not. Advanced sampling simulations mapped shape landscapes for both forms across three concentrations of sugar, glycerol, and sorbitol, which are known protein stabilizers.

The additives subtly shifted secondary structure in both proteins. In the human form, spiral shapes grew less likely, especially in the clump-prone core, hinting at lower aggregation drive. Direct bonding between protein and additives stayed scarce, confirming the additives work by avoiding the protein surface rather than gripping it. The authors suggest this exclusion effect could blunt early clumping and cell harm.
pmc-13539965:
Min Zhao leads a 2026 field study in a mature Australian eucalypt woodland asking how adding phosphorus changes the way extra carbon dioxide affects soil breathing. Forests may store less extra carbon when phosphorus runs short, because trees spend more carbon below ground hunting for it.

In the long-running EucFACE experiment, raised carbon dioxide lifted soil respiration regardless of phosphorus supply, and moisture patterns pointed to roots rather than soil decay as the source. Only after phosphorus was added did fine-root growth respond to the extra gas. Within nine months the trees seemed to shift from feeding microbes around roots toward growing roots themselves.
pmc-13540865:
Auany Camila Fantinelli and colleagues use DNA tests in a 2026 study. They named dried sea cucumbers seized at a Brazilian airport. The seizure took place at Guarulhos airport in 2023. Sea cucumbers fetch high prices in Asia. Buyers value them as food and as traditional medicine.

A standard gene marker named eighteen specimens as Holothuria grisea. It named twenty-two more as Isostichopus badionotus. Both species carry a global least-concern label. Unregulated trade could still drain local stocks fast. One species had no reference sequences in public databases. The team had to collect fresh specimens to finish. They argue for fuller open libraries to aid enforcement.
pmc-13542265:
Wei Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 prospective study asking whether a continuous metabolic syndrome score can flag older adults heading toward cardiometabolic multimorbidity. The term covers conditions such as diabetes, heart disease, and stroke occurring together. The score blends waist size, triglycerides, protective cholesterol, blood pressure, and fasting glucose into one number. Cohorts from China, the United States, and the United Kingdom contributed more than 17,000 participants aged 45 and over, all free of multimorbidity at entry.

Across follow-up periods of four to seven years, people in the highest third of the score faced clearly higher risk in every country, most sharply in the Chinese cohort. Pooling the results, each standard-deviation rise in the score lifted risk by about a third. The pattern of risk differed by cohort, rising unevenly in China and steadily elsewhere. The authors propose the score as a practical risk-sorting tool, pending further checks.
pmc-13543565:
Ruixia Liu, Mengmeng Zheng, and Tianrong Pan published a 2026 cross-sectional study asking whether the Fibrosis-4 index, a simple score for liver fibrosis risk, tracks with thyroid nodules in women. The catch is that the score itself contains age, so any link might be an artefact. In 695 women from a health-check cohort at an Anhui hospital, nodules were defined by ultrasound, and models tested the score overall, within two age bands, and with continuous age finely adjusted.

Before the finest age adjustment, the score looked linked to nodules in women under sixty. After adjusting for exact age, the association faded everywhere and lost significance in both age bands, and the age groups did not differ reliably from each other. The authors conclude the apparent liver-thyroid link was mostly age wearing a disguise, a caution for any score that smuggles age into its formula.
pmc-13546165:
Nitika C Panakkal and colleagues mapped low-voltage CT tricks for cutting ray dose in belly-and-pelvis scans. Published in 2026, the scoping review searched five sources for 2000 to 2025 studies of adult contrast-enhanced scans. Belly-pelvis CT drives much of patients' medical radiation, so dose cuts that keep images clear matter.

Thirteen studies with 30 to 907 patients made the cut, using 80 to 120 kV. The 80-kV setting cut dose by 11 to 86 percent, best with hybrid, model-based, or deep-learning rebuilds that tamed noise and held doctor trust. Auto voltage choice and size-tuned plans further tailored dose to patients. Mixed protocols, rebuilds, and dose measures curbed side-by-sides, so the authors urge standard reports and big forward multi-center trials.
pmc-13547365:
Zhulin Wang and Qian Li ran a randomized trial in 2026 of a six-week digital program that teaches new mothers health literacy and self-care after childbirth. Eighty-eight first-time mothers at a Changzhou hospital were assigned within days of delivery to the phone-based program plus standard education or to standard education alone. Eating behavior, activity, and breastfeeding were the main outcomes, with recovery measures alongside.

Eighty-two women finished the study. The program group reported less pain, depression, anxiety, and emotional eating, alongside higher health literacy and more physical activity, and they lost more weight. Bleeding duration ran shorter, some pelvic floor measures looked better, and exclusive or predominant breastfeeding was more common by about twenty-three percentage points. The authors urge caution given the small, single-center design.
pmc-13547565:
Ashraf Al Madhoun and a large team used gene editing in 2026 to split apart the jobs of zebrafish's two glucagon receptors. The question matters for diabetes drugs that target this hormone system. Fish carry two versions where humans carry one. Knocking out each version, and then both, let the team read each receptor's separate contribution through gene activity, feeding challenges, and cell response tests.

The first receptor governed fat and energy metabolism, cholesterol making, and glucose balance, while the second leaned toward fat burning, stress handling, and energy production in cells. Only the second answered to both glucagon and a related gut hormone, a clue to how the pair diverged after an ancient duplication. All knockout fish grew poorly on rich diets.
pmc-13548465:
Tegenu Tento and colleagues modeled in 2026 what lengthens recovery from cholera in a conflict-affected farming and herding region of Ethiopia, where war limits clean water, care, and vaccination. Records from cholera treatment centers were analyzed with survival methods that handle patients recovering at different speeds. How sick patients were, whether they had the vaccine, and exposure history were the candidate factors.

Patients arriving badly dehydrated recovered much more slowly, as did those with a low pulse and those with no vaccine. People who had known contact with a cholera case also improved more slowly, a pattern the authors link to heavier exposure or later arrival for care. Patients with the vaccine and mild cases recovered fastest. The authors push early detection, forceful rehydration, and vaccines aimed at contacts.
pmc-13548565:
Jeongok Park, Youngkyung Kim, and Hyunju Lee explore why hard childhoods still weigh on men's well-being decades later, in a 2026 survey of middle-aged men in South Korea. Midlife brings physical and social change, and symptoms tied to falling testosterone, grouped as andropause, may carry part of the childhood effect forward. The team surveyed 444 community men aged forty to sixty-four online during the summer of 2024.

Men reporting many adverse childhood experiences reported clearly lower well-being than men reporting none. Mediation analysis showed andropause symptoms carried a significant share of that link, connecting early adversity to present-day well-being. Being married, better educated, and better paid each went with higher well-being. The authors recommend community programs that pair trauma-informed counseling with practical management of andropause symptoms for men in midlife.
pmc-13548665:
Xiangqun Ju, Liana Luzzi, and Lisa M. Jamieson chart how mouth problems weigh on Australians' quality of life across fourteen years, in a 2026 population study. Two national surveys, one from 2004 to 2006 and another from 2017 to 2018, asked adults a fourteen-item questionnaire about pain, discomfort, and social difficulty from oral conditions. Thousands answered in each wave, and statistical decomposition asked how much of the change came from the population itself shifting.

Average impact scores fell from seven point three to five point five, meaning daily life was less burdened. Earlier respondents still scored far worse after adjustment. Older age, low income and education, smoking, poor general health, frequent toothache, and visiting the dentist only for problems all marked worse scores. Shifting incomes and visiting habits explained much of the improvement, the authors calculate.
pmc-13551165:
Claudia Grosse, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study of short hormone therapy given before surgery for estrogen receptor positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. Such treatment doubles as a test of hormone sensitivity, with a post-treatment Ki67 growth marker at or below ten percent counting as response. The single-center study compared 180 treated patients, with a median course of 29 days, against 151 patients who went straight to surgery.

Treated tumors showed sharply lower proliferation, and grade fell in over a third of cases, mainly through fewer dividing cells. Progesterone receptor loss and high genomic risk each predicted response independently, while immune cell levels in the tumor surroundings did not. Estrogen receptor levels stayed stable throughout.
pmc-13551265:
Anne Louise de Barros Garioud and four colleagues reported in 2026 on how intravenous melatonin behaves in young children's bodies during surgery. Melatonin may ease anxiety, pain, and delirium around operations, yet dosing data in small children were sparse. Twenty children aged 1 to 6 having elective surgery under general anesthesia received a weight-based dose before surgery ended, with six blood samples each.

Peak blood levels were high and the drug cleared with a half-life near 35 minutes in the reported analysis, values the authors compare with adult data. No emergence delirium occurred, pain scores stayed low, and adverse events matched ordinary postoperative symptoms. The team offers the numbers to guide dose choice in future trials of melatonin for children.
pmc-13551765:
Hengmin Wang, with eleven colleagues, published a 2026 study of a urine test for kidney filter harm in children. Filter cells called podocytes sit at the heart of many kidney diseases in kids. Tests that avoid biopsy are scarce. The team first checked a protein called ANGPTL3 in kidney tissue. They used tissue from 25 sick children and five controls. They then enrolled sick children into test and check sets.

Kidney levels of the protein rose as known harm markers fell. Urine levels, scaled to creatinine, were clearly high in harmed patients. The urine test alone split harmed from unharmed children well in both sets. Adding clinical facts improved it further. The team calls it a strong risk marker that needs no biopsy.
pmc-13551865:
Heon-Young Kim, Jung-Hyun Park, Gwang Hyun Leem, Hyo-Jung Lee, and Jin-Woo Kim published a 2026 nationwide Korean cohort study asking whether acid reflux disease raises the risk of jaw joint disorders. Both conditions are multifactorial, and reflux is increasingly seen as a body-wide disorder. Insurance data covered adults screened in 2010 and 2011, with reflux defined by diagnosis codes plus at least two weeks of acid-suppressing prescriptions, and prior jaw problems excluded.

After matching, 40,755 people with reflux were compared with 115,242 controls. Jaw disorder incidence ran higher in the reflux group, and adjusted modeling gave a modestly raised risk in the reported figures. Survival curves separated significantly as well, so the authors suggest screening reflux patients for jaw symptoms to catch problems early.
pmc-13551965:
Jingru Gao, with six colleagues, published a 2026 study of eating ability and nutrition in very old adults. All participants were aged 75 or above. They filled questionnaires on eating and chewing. Lab tests measured bite force, tongue pressure, and lip seal. Swallowing, taste, and saliva flow were tested too. Nutrition was scored with a short standard form plus body measures.

Factor methods distilled the tests into five abilities. Chewing level and food guiding mattered most for nutrition. Food guiding means moving food around the mouth. Risk fell steeply as these two rose from low levels, then flattened. Blunted taste and weak swallowing also tied to poor nutrition. Chewing mattered most in men, the team notes.
pmc-13554065:
Al Rafy leads a ten-author team building a light vision system that spots sleepy drivers from face photos in a 2026 report. Sleepiness slows reactions and causes many road deaths worldwide. Older systems often fail under new lighting, hide their reasoning, or need too much power. Their model mixes local detail blocks with a token system that reads the whole face, trained on more than 167,000 labelled photos.

Scores topped ninety-nine percent on home data and stayed above ninety-three on new sets. Heat maps show which face regions drove each call, matching signs doctors link to fatigue. Answers came in under a fifth of a second on a small low-power board. A web app gives live warnings with those visual reasons attached.
pmc-13554165:
Tabassum Naz Sindhu leads a five-author team proposing a new one-knob model for count data in a 2026 paper. Counts, such as deaths per day or cell changes per sample, often spread wider than the classic Poisson model allows. Their model blends the Poisson law with a second pattern to gain that extra flex. They work out its averages, spread, and risk curve on paper first.

Computer trials confirmed that their fitting method finds the true knob value well. Two real datasets tested it further: cell damage in rabbit blood cells under a drug, and daily COVID-19 deaths in South Korea. In both, the new model fit better than rival count models. It handled skew, wide spread, and extra zeros at once.
pmc-13554865:
Mohamed Elmorshidy leads a five-author team reporting a twenty-year-old man whose stiff heart sac hid tuberculosis in a 2026 case report. He arrived with worsening heart failure and a heart pumping at a fraction of normal strength. Scans showed a markedly thickened sac around the heart. Standard tests for tuberculosis came back negative, yet doctors treated for it anyway alongside heart failure care.

He kept declining, so surgeons removed the rigid sac in a radical operation. Shock followed, and a heart-lung machine supported him through recovery. Tissue tests at last confirmed tuberculosis in the sac. His heart strength later returned to normal. The authors credit the tight sac, not muscle damage, for the collapse.
pmc-13555865:
Dhiya Mahirah leads a nine-author team tracing three years of care for Singapore children whose body symptoms lack a clear medical cause in a 2026 study. Such symptoms often mirror hidden emotional distress and drive repeat visits. Records covered 4,964 patients aged six to fifteen who visited a children's emergency department in 2018. Use of emergency, inpatient, and specialist care was followed through 2021.

Emergency revisits plunged by year three, and total costs fell by about three quarters. Specialist referrals and hospital admissions stayed substantial in years two and three, though. Younger age, minority ethnicity, and admission at the first visit each raised the odds of repeat emergency use later. The authors see unresolved psychosocial needs behind the lingering care.
pmc-13555965:
Nuttapon Arpornsujaritkun leads a fourteen-author team testing a practice model that grades leaks after trainee surgeons join blood vessels in a 2026 study. Joining vessels is a core surgical skill, yet live practice chances are scarce and risky. Their model adds a pressure-driven leak test giving instant, structured feedback. Thirty-nine surgery residents first stitched without teaching, then watched a standard video, practised with supervision, and repeated the task.

Severe leaks fell from about seven in ten attempts to under three in ten. Average completion time dropped by nearly four minutes. Second- and third-year residents gained the clearest speed improvements. Every trainee rated simulation learning useful, and most felt their hand skills improve. The authors offer the model as a cheap, repeatable training platform.
pmc-13557865:
Jialiang Wen and fourteen colleagues compared in 2026 three operations for central lung tumours in patients who had first received chemotherapy plus immunotherapy. Removing the whole lung was the traditional answer, while sleeve operations cut out the affected lobe and rejoin the airway, sparing healthy tissue. Their review covered 335 patients at Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital who had extended sleeve, simple sleeve, or whole-lung removal after the drug treatment.

Extended sleeve surgery took longer and needed longer drainage than whole-lung removal, yet patients kept better event-free survival. Results split by side: on the right, whole-lung removal carried more complications than either sleeve option, while on the left the three operations looked similar for complications. The authors argue that the extended sleeve deserves a place after modern drug therapy, with the surgical side informing the choice.
pmc-13558365:
Ghada A. Badawi, Rehab M. El-Sayed, and Mohamed N. Fawzy reframed in 2026 multiple sclerosis as a disease of cellular fuel use as much as of misdirected immunity. Modern immune drugs control relapses yet fail to stop slow progression or repair lost myelin. Their review argues that how immune and nerve cells power themselves decides whether they inflame or protect, and that this programming can be adjusted.

Attacking immune cells run on fast sugar burning, guided by growth switches, while calming regulatory cells and myelin repair crews rely on fat burning and efficient respiration. Two established sclerosis drugs turn out to act partly through these fuel pathways, which supports the idea. The authors survey deliberate metabolic strategies, from blocking glutamine use in aggressive cells to metformin-like agents that may aid remyelination, and to supplements that recharge cellular batteries.
pmc-13558565:
Lauren Brakefield-Laird and a large team of colleagues reported in 2026 a drug pairing that exposes a hidden weakness in acute myeloid leukaemia. A survival protein called MCL-1 shields this blood cancer from treatment, yet drugs blocking it alone have disappointed in trials through toxicity and weak responses. Screening for partners, the team found that blocking the first complex of the cell's energy chain makes leukaemia cells depend fatally on MCL-1.

Given together, the two blockers killed leukaemia cell lines and patient-derived tumour grafts far better than either alone, and mice carrying such grafts lived significantly longer. Mechanism work traced the synergy to a cellular stress response switched on when energy production falters, running through a stress messenger protein and a gene switch called ATF4. High-risk forms with rearranged KMT2A genes are a prime target. The authors offer the pairing as a route past single-drug resistance.
pmc-13558765:
Silvia Carboni and five colleagues profiled in 2026 the gut microbes and worm parasites of wild mantled howler monkeys in Costa Rica, while testing how much the method itself bends the answer. Faecal samples from several social groups were stored two ways, in alcohol or flash frozen. They were read with two sequencing strategies, a targeted bacterial gene survey and full shotgun sequencing. Old-fashioned microscopy for worms ran alongside.

Plant-digesting bacteria, archaea, and microbes dominated the gut community, fitting a leaf-eating primate. Alcohol-stored samples looked more diverse than frozen ones, and the targeted survey reported less diversity than shotgun reading, so storage and method each tinted the portrait. Microscopy found worms in about seven of ten monkeys, while gene-based detection proved patchy. The authors give field researchers a clear-eyed account of what each choice buys and what it distorts.
pmc-13559565:
Feng Ding and colleagues built a gene signature meant to forecast survival and treatment response in skin cutaneous melanoma from a measure of how mixed each tumor is inside. Their 2026 study used sequencing data from 472 patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas plus 214 in a second cohort. A heterogeneity score split tumors into high and low groups, and genes differing between them fed a machine learning contest.

Thirty-eight prognostic genes survived screening, and over a hundred algorithm combinations were tried to combine them. The winning model, built with a partial least squares Cox method, separated patients into risk groups with clearly different survival in both cohorts. High-risk tumors carried fewer mutations and showed quieter immune activity, with less immune cell infiltration and lower checkpoint gene expression. The two risk groups also responded differently to classes of targeted drugs. The authors present the signature for risk sorting, pending prospective testing.
pmc-13560565:
Cristina Lagido and colleagues map training resources for open, honest research across Europe under the Horizon Europe project PATTERN. Their 2026 mixed-methods study pulls together desk research, surveys, interviews, and workshops to catalog 571 resources across eight skill areas, from open access and FAIR data to citizen science and research integrity. A subset received formal quality scoring.

The landscape looks fragmented and beginner-heavy. Starter material rules, with thin supply for mid-level and advanced learners, and much content stays generic rather than fitted to local tongues or contexts. Strengths include modular design, open licensing, and active learning formats. Weak points recur around ease of access, unclear reuse paths, and shaky long-term funding. Topic gaps include overlapping bias, policy work, supervision ethics, and native knowledge. The authors call for coordination, deeper advanced training, and weaving the material into school programs.
pmc-13562165:
Jaume Millán i Ichon and colleagues introduce a Trend of Sepsis and Inflammation index that blends brain-wave and heart-rate signals to track inflammatory burden continuously. Their 2026 post-hoc analysis works in two groups: forty-one surgical patients under general anesthesia and twenty-one septic intensive care patients. Heart rate variability alone loses specificity under sedation, so the brain signal compensates.

A neuro-fuzzy system fused variability measures with an EEG-derived brain activity index into one score. Values climbed in clear steps across the three states studied: low at awake baseline, middling after surgery, and high in sepsis. The medians ran roughly two, twenty-five, and sixty-six in the reported results. The index separated the states with strong probability and over ninety percent concordance with expected ranges. The authors propose bedside monitoring use, pending validation against standard biomarkers.
pmc-13562565:
Caiyu Zhang and four colleagues compare blood chemistry in preterm babies who develop a white-matter brain injury and those who do not. The 2026 study drew blood at two weeks of age from 32 affected infants and 68 unaffected ones. A chromatography and mass-spectrometry method measured many small molecules at once, and models hunted for markers that separate the groups.

Most measured compounds differed between groups. Twelve stood out in the ranking model, led by a fatty compound coded C18:2, which also showed the strongest single separation. Higher tyrosine levels pointed away from injury, while higher ornithine and longer intravenous feeding pointed toward it. Breakdown of fatty acids emerged as the likely core pathway. The authors caution that C18:2, promising as it looks, needs more work before it can serve as an early test.
pmc-13563765:
Robert W. Hurley and five colleagues map how researchers measure pain in people with substance use disorders, and find the ruler crude. Pain and addiction feed each other, and sloppy measurement distorts both research and care. Their 2026 review searched five databases for studies from 1990 to 2025 that assessed pain in these populations. Ninety-six studies with 25,872 participants qualified. Each was checked against eight pain domains, from intensity and interference to sleep and treatment satisfaction.

Simple intensity scales ruled: 91 percent of studies used one, yet only 14.6 percent had checked that their tool works in addiction populations. Interference, location, and satisfaction appeared in under sixty percent, and 11.5 percent covered six or more domains. Trials measured more broadly than snapshots, and opioid studies out-measured alcohol or stimulant work. Where links were tested, pain's interference with life tied to substance outcomes more strongly than intensity. The authors propose a minimum measurement set.
pmc-13563865:
T. B. Baum and seven colleagues grow cells from children carrying mutations in DRP1, the protein that snips mitochondria, to watch cortical development go wrong. Children with broken copies of the gene develop the disorder called EMPF1, with delay, optic damage, and epileptic encephalopathy. Which step breaks was unclear. Their 2026 team reprogrammed cells into stem cells, then cortical neurons, with faults in the enzyme's cutting domain or its stalk. Films tracked mitochondria crawling along neurites, and gene profiles followed the cells as they matured.

The mitochondria fused into overlong networks, and their movement faults differed by which domain carried the mutation. Expression shifted in synapse-building and calcium-handling programmes. Recordings across weeks of culture confirmed disturbed calcium signals in the neurons. The authors argue the chain runs from failed fission to stalled transport to miswired synapses, and the domain carrying a child's mutation may shape the disease's course.
pmc-13568165:
Maud De Meyer, Carolina S. Romero, and Marc Van de Velde review, in a 2026 article, fasting before surgery, once ruled by nothing-by-mouth-from-midnight orders meant to stop stomach contents entering the lungs during anesthesia. Evidence now supports shorter fasts, especially for clear liquids, and guidelines worldwide have changed.

Long fasts persist anyway because of old habits, poor communication, scheduling problems, and low priority, harming comfort and body chemistry, with children at special risk. Tools covered include stomach ultrasound, rapid anesthesia techniques, stomach tubes, and the new challenge of diabetes drugs that slow stomach emptying. Clinicians get a practical framework for matching fasting to each patient.
pmc-13571465:
McDonnell and co-authors test a hormonal suspect in this 2026 cohort study of appetite loss in chronic kidney disease, a symptom affecting up to half of patients and tied to worse survival. The suspect is GDF-15, a stress cytokine known to suppress appetite in cancer. The cohort is NURTuRE-CKD, with 2,996 people who have kidney disease but are not yet on dialysis. They were followed for a median of fifty months.

GDF-15 was measured in 2,929 participants, and the 27 percent reporting poor appetite carried clearly higher levels, a median of 2,965 against 2,350 picograms per milliliter in the comparison. Each doubling of the hormone raised the odds of poor appetite by a factor of 1.44 in adjusted analysis, and it also tracked weaker grip strength and lower estimated muscle mass. Doubling predicted disease progression at a hazard ratio of 1.30 and death at 1.72 across follow-up, keeping the cancer appetite-drug analogy alive.
pmc-13572465:
S Murugeswari, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 design for a tiny two-port antenna for 5G phones and wearables. The antenna must work at millimetre waves, where signals carry much data but need careful design at small size. The board is only about twelve millimetres long, among the smallest in its class.

A meandering slot stretches the electrical path without growing the board, and the antenna works in three bands between about 26 and 38 gigahertz. Gain held between 9.3 and 9.7 decibels across those bands. The two ports stayed well apart, with cross-talk at minus 20 decibels and a match score below 0.01. Tests on a layered hand model showed radiation absorbed by tissue stayed within safety limits. Lab measures matched the computer runs closely.
pmc-13572565:
Julia Palma, with 18 colleagues, reports a 2026 regional survey of molecular testing for childhood cancer in Latin America. Gene and molecule tests guide how doctors class a tumour, judge risk, and pick targeted drugs. Access across the region was uneven, above all in public systems, and hard data on the gaps were scarce.

The 2024 survey, run by a regional advisory group with a Latin American paediatric oncology society, asked centres about test availability, access, quality, and barriers. Testing exists in several countries, yet reach stays patchy and inconsistent between places and sectors. Centres flagged cost, capacity, and supply hurdles among the chief barriers. The results give health planners a shared baseline for the region. The authors aim the findings at closing the public-sector gap for children with cancer.
pmc-13573465:
Caifang Qiu and Hui Wang report a 2026 comparison of dancer and non-dancer students on body measures and food attitudes. Dance places strong shape demands on the body, which can shape how young dancers eat and what they know about food. The team asked whether dance students differ from peers on those fronts.

Seventy female undergraduates took part, half dancers and half not, aged 17 to 22. A body analyser measured height, weight, and body mass index for each student. A standard questionnaire, in its Chinese version, gauged food knowledge, and eating attitudes were scored alongside. The head-to-head design isolates what dance training adds beyond student life in general. Results can guide dance schools on food education and early signs of strained eating.
pmc-13574865:
Cesare Mantini, with thirteen colleagues, reports a 2026 MRI study that sorts heart congestion into four stages with scan numbers alone. A backed-up heart raises pressure and floods the lungs, but the usual pressure check needs a catheter. The team built two scan measures, one for filling pressure and one for lung blood volume.

Scans from 262 patients fed the two measures plus tissue maps of heart scarring. Crossing normal or high values on each measure set the four stages. Higher pressure tracked with more lung blood, slower transit, and more scar-like tissue change. Over a median thirty months, twelve percent of patients died of heart causes or landed in hospital for the heart. The worst stage fared poorest, and scar tissue added its own warning. The authors pitch the stages for risk sorting without a catheter.
pmc-13575165:
Poojan D. Shukla and colleagues taped brain signals during real walking and turning in five people with Parkinson's disease, using implants that both record and excite the brain. Turning is a daily yet tricky move that often fails in Parkinson's, causing falls and lost freedom, but its brain basis was unclear. Their 2026 study tracked motor cortex and deep-brain signals turn by turn.

Good turns showed falling beta-band signals and supple cortex-to-pallidum links, while failed turns showed too much beta sync that froze moves. Drugs and deep brain stimulation each helped, but in their own ways: dopamine calmed wayward pallidal beta, while pulses loosened the cortex. The authors point to these circuits as targets for smart pulses aimed at safer turning.
pmc-13576365:
Toni Christoph Berger leads a 2026 study charting, stage by stage, how brain cells change as epilepsy develops in mice. The shift from a healthy brain to one that seizes is called epileptogenesis, and the timing of cell changes was poorly mapped. The team sorted neuron and glia cell nuclei and read their gene activity at one hour, one day, and three months after a seizure trigger.

Most changed genes belonged to a single stage rather than all stages. Early on, both cell types shared a stress and DNA repair programme. At one day, glia swung sharply toward inflammation and regulated cell death routes, while neurons showed immune and plasticity signals. By three months, activity sat mostly in glia, centred on inflammation and vessel growth. The authors mark the early latent window as the best target for preventive treatment.
pmc-13577565:
Jui-Hung Yen leads a 2026 review of fat metabolism as a drug target in acute myeloid leukaemia. This fast-moving blood cancer rewires how it handles fats: leukaemia cells pull in, store, and build more cholesterol and fatty acids to feed growth and survival. Past attempts to starve the cells' energy factories caused broad toxicity, pushing interest toward lipid routes instead.

The review maps the main lipid programmes in these cells, from cholesterol building and fatty acid uptake to fat burning and sphingolipid handling. It explains the control systems that keep those programmes balanced and how their failure feeds cancer growth and drug resistance. Small-molecule blockers for the key enzymes and signals are catalogued with their early results. The authors present lipid targeting as a promising, more selective route that deserves clinical testing.
pmc-13578165:
Po-Yu Chien leads a 2026 study linking smoking, gut microbes, and response to immunotherapy in lung cancer. Smokers often answer checkpoint inhibitor drugs differently from never-smokers, for reasons that were unclear. The team collected stool samples before treatment from 225 patients with non-small cell lung cancer and sequenced the full gene marker of their gut bacteria.

Smokers' gut communities differed in selected species rather than in overall diversity. They carried less Bifidobacterium longum, a species often sold as a probiotic, and more Gram-negative bacteria. Counter to intuition, lower levels of that species tracked with better drug response and longer time without the cancer growing. A bacterial gene tied to coating production also rose with the Gram-negative share and with better responses. The authors read gut makeup as part of the smoking effect on treatment.
pmc-13581465:
Dannewitz and co-authors run a multicentre randomized trial in this 2026 study of a smartphone companion for gum disease care. Nearly two hundred adults with periodontitis at seven German university dental centers received standard periodontal therapy. Some also got the Paro-ComPas app, which supports patients between appointments. Gum bleeding was the main yardstick.

Of 194 randomized participants, 180 entered the analysis and 148 finished. Both groups improved greatly. The adjusted analysis found no significant benefit from the app on the primary bleeding endpoint. The difference was 1.56 percentage points at p equals 0.352 in the model. Nor was there benefit on plaque or probing measures. Delivery of the digital intervention was incomplete, and starting inflammation was low, both limiting sensitivity. One exploratory signal stood out: moderate app users cut plaque significantly more than low users, by 14.95 percentage points, hinting engagement matters more than assignment.
pmc-13585865:
Joumaa Merza and colleagues make a family of pyrrole compounds and test them on nerve cells in this 2026 study. Pyrroles are ring-shaped units found in many natural and lab-made molecules. Starting from one heavily decorated pyrrole, the team reacted it with two partner chemicals to build six new variants, confirming one variant's structure in fine detail with crystal and magnetic readings.

The variants were fed to human nerve-like cells, both healthy and stressed with amyloid beta, the protein clump tied to Alzheimer's disease. Two compounds raised survival in healthy cells, hinting at a protective streak. In stressed cells, though, every compound tested cut survival instead. That split result suggests these molecules interact with amyloid harm in a way that could matter for understanding brain decay, and the authors call for deeper study.
pmc-13589665:
Wenhan Guo and five colleagues ask whether a building's online reputation and its state's staffing rules predict hospice quality inside assisted living. Over two thirds of assisted living residents who die use hospice, and quality there lags other settings. Their 2026 cross-sectional study covered 15,947 assisted living communities, linking their Google Maps star ratings and state rules on care-worker staffing and training to two federal hospice quality scores.

Each extra Google star came with modestly higher odds of being served by a hospice scoring well on the clinical information set, though not on the family survey score. States spelling out staffing rules in more detail had clearly better odds on both scores. Mandating more than twenty-one training hours tracked with better family survey results. The authors see building quality and regulation as quiet partners in end-of-life care.
pmc-13592665:
Ömer Ataç and three colleagues mine fourteen years of posts on X for Turkish talk about Syrian refugee health care. From 4.5 million tweets they pulled 116,172 health related ones. A fine tuned Turkish language model sorted each post by feeling, stance, and topic across five domains, from service provision to medicines. Heat maps and lift scores then linked keywords to public attitudes year by year.

Feeling slid from neutral or warm in 2011 toward open hostility. By 2021 nearly four fifths of posts read negative, and the anti refugee stance peaked the same year. Talk shifted from services toward disease prevention and health staffing. Words like appointment, vaccine, and free clustered with hostile stances. Ataç and the team urge clear, fact based public messaging to counter the drift.
pmc-13595665:
Lina Zhao and co-authors evaluated whether China's county medical community policy, which ties county hospitals and local clinics into one system, made care more efficient in Sanming, Fujian, the model's showcase city. Their 2026 study applied efficiency analysis to ten counties from 2017 to 2022, tracking technical and scale efficiency plus a productivity index.

Average efficiency rose clearly on all three static measures, reflecting better resource use and management. The dynamic index, though, slipped just below the break-even line, hinting that allocation is not yet optimal, a dip the authors partly blame on the pandemic years. Gaps between counties persisted, and front-line primary care institutions trailed the county-level picture. The authors conclude the integrated model improves efficiency overall while leaving primary care strengthening and regional balance as unfinished work.
pmc-13598565:
Sun and colleagues examined in 2026 how patterns of long-term illness relate to depressive symptoms in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. Many older people live with several chronic diseases at once, and depression is common among them. Using a national aging survey from 2020, the team studied 491 people with at least two chronic conditions each.

A grouping method sorted patients into three patterns: a metabolic and heart-vessel group, a digestive and joint group, and a lung disease group. About 37 percent of patients showed depressive symptoms. After accounting for age, sex, and income, the digestive and joint group had notably higher odds of depressive symptoms than the metabolic and heart group. The lung group did not differ clearly. Four or more conditions, or age 70 or over, also raised the odds. The authors say illness pattern, not just illness count, helps flag depression risk.
pmc-13601465:
Rinderknecht and co-authors compared a 2026 mouse study of liver responses after a thigh bone fracture, young animals against aged ones. Fractures trigger immune activity that also reaches distant organs, and older patients suffer more organ damage and deaths. A controlled bone cut with external fixation modelled the fracture reproducibly.

Young mice were seventeen to twenty-six weeks old and aged mice sixty-four to seventy-two weeks at surgery for comparison. Aged sham operated animals already carried higher liver inflammation at baseline, with more neutrophils and inflammatory signals present. Rinderknecht found the bone cut raised liver inflammation in both age groups within twenty-four hours of injury. Aged livers, though, failed to switch on key regulators that coordinate inflammation and repair, including RAGE and sirtuins, which may explain elderly vulnerability.
pmc-13612865:
Heimo Gursch and colleagues describe in 2026 a three-part system for sorting steel scrap by what it actually contains, so steel mills can recycle it into high-grade steel. Scrap is a valuable raw material, since reusing steel saves much energy compared with making it from ore. Stones, plastic, and non-iron metals mixed into scrap can spoil the melt, so mills need to know the mix before they start.

First, a special camera records 437 bands of short-wave infrared light from the scrap. Next, the team tested three kinds of deep learning to name 14 material classes in the images, and a three-dimensional network did best. Last, a math routine picks the scrap blend that best fits the steel grades to be made, turning inspection data into a practical recipe for the furnace.
pmc-13614965:
Lev G. Nemchinov offers a 2026 hypothesis that the genetic code, the universal set of three-letter words that spell out proteins, began with early virus-like particles on the young Earth. Life's code uses four chemical letters read in triplets, yet why each triplet was assigned its amino acid remains unexplained. Before cells existed, selfish RNA strands could copy themselves but were fragile and unprotected.

Nemchinov proposes that these strands wrapped themselves in shells built from amino acids tied to specific RNA letters. A shell would protect the RNA, favouring survival, while the pairing habit hardened into the first code. On this view, the ancestors of viruses were not late parasites but midwives of the code itself. Readers get a bold origin story that links two puzzles: where viruses came from and why the code looks the way it does.
pmc-13615065:
Tee Shao Peng, Nik Adilah Nik Othman, Mohd Normani Zakaria, and Nik Fariza Husna Nik Hassan test two Weber hearing tests in school children. The children have conductive hearing loss, where sound is blocked before it reaches the inner ear. The tests are meant to point to the weaker ear. Both tests place a vibrating sound at the centre of the head; the child says which ear hears it louder. One version uses a tuning fork, the other a clinic audiometer.

Seventy-five children aged seven to twelve took both tests at two pitches each. Accuracy topped 80 percent for every version, and no clear difference appeared between the fork and the machine. Answers also matched what each child's hearing chart predicted. The humble tuning fork, it turns out, holds its own for this job in children.
pmc-13616765:
Dan Guo and colleagues traced how skin nerves pierce deep fascia in early human development. Deep fascia was thought to form after nerves reach under the skin, yet the exact sequence of piercing was untested. Their 2026 study examined tissue sections from 12 early fetuses at 7 to 9 weeks and 10 midterm fetuses at 12 to 18 weeks, covering the neck and front abdominal wall.

Belly-wall nerves reached muscle by week seven while its sheath stayed loose, then a window opened as the sheath firmed, and nerves reached skin by week 12. Neck nerves reached muscle surfaces by week eight, then sprouted twigs through the rising fascia margin. Guo and colleagues conclude fascia and nerve windows develop together, with nerves pausing on the fascia for weeks.
pmc-13618065:
Neeraj Kadian and five colleagues synthesize magnetite nanocrystals doped with gadolinium, a rare-earth element, to see how swapping it in reshapes the crystals's electrical and magnetic behavior. They made the crystals by co-precipitation, a simple mixing method, and checked structure with X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy. Energy storage and electronic devices are the target uses for these spinel ferrite materials.

X-ray tests confirmed a single-phase cubic spinel structure with only minor lattice distortion from the gadolinium. Microscopy showed cluster-like grains. Testing found stronger charge storage at low frequencies, explained by polarization at internal borders, with lower energy loss at high frequencies. Conduction followed a heat-activated hopping pattern, where charges jump between sites over energy barriers. The crystals behaved as soft magnets with low coercivity and moderate saturation, a pairing the authors say suits future energy and electronic uses.
pmc-13618365:
Aiden Ali and four colleagues report an unusual case of hydroxyapatite deposition disease. In this condition, calcium crystals settle in tendons and provoke painful inflammation, usually around the shoulder. Their patient, a forty-two-year-old woman, developed a slowly growing tender lump on the inner side of her forearm that moved when she flexed her wrist. A mass in the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon at that spot is an atypical address for the disease.

X-ray, MRI, and CT imaging characterized the calcific deposit and ruled out the worrying alternatives, since such masses can imitate trauma, infection, or a soft tissue tumor. Treatment avoided open surgery: an ultrasound-guided barbotage procedure, washing the deposit out through a large-bore needle, shrank it and relieved her symptoms. The authors urge clinicians to keep this disease on the list when painful soft tissue masses appear in odd places.
pmc-13618965:
Aniek M. Kolen and twelve colleagues follow eighty-one adults who lost a leg to vascular disease, asking how many are undernourished afterward. Across six hospitals, the team measured food intake by recall and nutritional status with a validated assessment, body mass index, grip strength, and arm measurements within twelve days of amputation. They measured again at five weeks, six months, and nine months, modeling which factors predicted undernutrition.

Eighty-three percent were undernourished in the first days, easing to fifty-six percent at five weeks, twenty-eight at six months, and twenty-four at nine months. Energy and protein intakes rose after discharge, then slid. Living in a care facility multiplied the odds of undernutrition sixfold. Each extra weekly hour of activity trimmed them slightly. All needed nutritional intervention at the first check. Over half still did at nine months, which the authors call an alarming burden.
pmc-13619665:
Alexa Molinari and eleven colleagues compared chemotherapy regimens for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma without a direct head-to-head trial, in a 2026 analysis. They used a matching-adjusted indirect comparison, which reweights patient-level data from one trial so the group resembles published groups from other trials. The newer PET-guided BrECADD regimen faced three older PET-guided options across five earlier studies.

Against the ABVD regimen, BrECADD showed clearly better progression-free and overall survival in both age ranges studied. Against BEACOPP-based treatment the differences shrank to trends favoring BrECADD, with one survival advantage in patients over sixty. Because no shared control arm links the trials, the method rests on careful matching of patient traits. The authors say the results support choosing BrECADD for adults with advanced disease.
pmc-13620165:
Hyomin Park and fifteen colleagues developed a gene therapy aimed at triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form with few targeted options. Their treatment delivers an optimized version of a gene called TIF1-gamma, chosen because it can strike several survival pathways at once. Testing ran from patient tumor tissue kept alive in the lab to mouse models where cancer grows in the breast and spreads.

Treated tissue slowed its shape-shifting growth program, divided less, and died more readily. In mice, tumors grew more slowly and lung spread fell. Lab work showed the gene product tags one growth signal for destruction, blocks a second pathway directly, and cuts a third by destroying its messenger protein. It also lowered two molecules tumors use to hide from immune cells, so scavenger cells ate more cancer. The authors position the single gene as a multitarget strategy against a slippery disease.
pmc-13620265:
Kai Song and thirteen colleagues mapped how gut microbe communities reorganize as colorectal growths develop. Their data came from stool DNA of nearly four thousand screening participants: healthy controls, people with small bowel polyps, people with advanced polyps, and a small group with colorectal cancer. Findings were checked against several independent cohorts.

Two opposing microbe networks emerged. One group of fourteen species, including a Clostridium member, rose together with disease, while thirty-seven other species, including well-known fiber fermenters, formed a health-linked group that excluded the first. The seesaw pattern held steady across outside datasets. A score built from the pattern sorted people by risk, and simple presence-or-absence models using only these species reached moderate accuracy. Chemical outputs of the microbes shifted along with the networks. The authors see stool topology as a possible non-invasive risk tool, pending larger cancer cohorts.
pmc-13621565:
Dima Nasrallah and five colleagues present high blood pressure as a whole-body disorder rather than a plumbing problem in one organ. Primary hypertension drives heart attacks, strokes, and early death worldwide, yet its machinery is only partly mapped. Their review organizes the disease around three engines that feed each other.

The first engine is the hormone system that manages salt and vessel tone, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone network. The second is the central nervous system, whose stress wiring keeps pressure raised. The third is inflammation paired with oxidative stress, which scars vessels and kidneys alike. Around these engines orbit familiar contributors: salty diets, salt-sensitive bodies, disturbed gut microbes, broken sleep-wake rhythms, and insulin resistance. Each acts by pushing the central three. The authors argue that treatments aimed upstream at the drivers should beat chasing single numbers. They frame the model as a guide for prevention research.
pmc-13623365:
Seda Bicici Ulusahin leads a comparison of how shoulders perform and tire in young adults with forward head posture, the habit of holding the head jutting ahead of the neck. Some had scapular dyskinesis, faulty movement of the shoulder blade. The question was whether these posture problems, common in screen-heavy lives, weaken the shoulder at a young age.

Eighty-five adults aged eighteen to twenty-five were split into three groups: posture problems of both kinds, head posture alone, and healthy controls. A timed arm and shoulder test scored how fast and well each person performed set tasks. Both posture groups scored below controls, and the combined-problem group scored lowest on the dominant side. Total and physical fatigue ran higher in both posture groups, while mental fatigue matched across groups. The authors suggest that posture correction and shoulder training may protect young adults before pain sets in.
pmc-13626165:
Zilu Chen and a large team build a two-step nanomedicine that first burns colorectal cancer cells, then sweeps up the survivors it ages. Sound waves switch on their engineered particles, which release reactive oxygen that triggers pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. Some cells dodge death under mild stress and instead turn senescent, and aged cells leak signals that can help tumors return, a known trap of the fiery approach.

The particles' second module, the natural compound piperlongumine, selectively kills those senescent cells. In mouse models under the skin and spread to the liver, the paired treatment shrank tumors by over four-fifths and left very little liver spread. Coupling the two fates in one platform, the authors say, turns a side effect into a scheduled second strike.
pmc-13626865:
Tingting Li and colleagues use a ten-year steppe experiment to test whether living communities truly adapt to global change, rather than merely change. On the Eurasian steppe they dosed plots with nine intensities of extra nitrogen, under fencing or mowing, and tracked how fast plant and soil microbe communities turned over. If turnover signals adaptation, it should rise with pressure, up to the point where pressure overwhelms.

Turnover did exactly that, rising then falling as nitrogen climbed, which marks an adaptive ceiling beyond which communities can no longer keep up. The orderly, soil-driven part of change marched with soil chemistry shifts, while mowing helped plants and fencing helped microbes by damping randomness. Keeping change under the ceiling, and steering the orderly processes, is the management lesson.
pmc-13627165:
Luigi Demarchis leads a large team, publishing in 2026, that reads the protein recipe of bone in acromegaly, a growth hormone excess that quietly weakens skeletons. Why these bones break so easily is not fully explained by hormone levels alone. So the team profiled bone from five patients with the disease and five with non-secreting pituitary tumors. Mass spectrometry did the profiling, on samples taken during surgery. Three hundred twelve proteins were found in each group.

Eighteen proteins differed clearly, six raised and twelve lowered in acromegaly bone. Four of the movers, profilin-1, a periostin form, apolipoprotein E, and caveolin-1, are known bone players, and their levels tracked the patients' growth hormone and IGF-I readings in opposite directions. As a pilot, the study hands the field a shortlist of suspects for skeletal fragility.
pmc-13627665:
Zhimin Li and five colleagues, publishing in 2026, present FairGen, an image-making system designed to keep medical AI honest across demographic groups. Training data for diagnostic models skew heavily toward some populations, and diseases can look different across groups, so rare presentations get missed. FairGen is a diffusion generator steered by physician-aligned preferences, synthesizing balanced image sets that keep the visual marks of disease while widening who is represented.

Across skin images, chest X-rays, and brain MRI benchmarks, fairness gains were large, reaching over ninety percent for skin, while diagnostic accuracy held close to models trained on real clinic data. Independent clinician review and outside cohorts backed the gains. Balanced synthetic data, the authors argue, can patch holes that real-world collection keeps leaving.
pmc-13627865:
Miranda Stavileci, Astrit Kuçi, Agime Dragidella, and Nicola Alberto Valente race four materials at sealing accidental holes in tooth roots. A perforation, a slip of the drill through the root wall, can doom a tooth unless the seal holds against mouth fluids. Fifty extracted human molars were perforated and repaired. The materials were Biodentin, mineral trioxide aggregate, glass ionomer cement, and amalgam. The teeth were then bathed in dye, split, and measured under a stereomicroscope for how far the dye crept.

Biodentin leaked least, with the aggregate a close second and no meaningful gap between them. Amalgam sat in the middle, while glass ionomer leaked most by a clear margin. Under these bench conditions, the authors conclude, the two calcium silicate cements are the surest seals, a practical ranking for a common mishap.
pmc-13629265:
Clare Lewis and two colleagues reviewed international evidence on virtual wards, services that deliver hospital-level care to patients at home through remote monitoring and telemedicine. Their 2026 integrative review compared models in Australia, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, focusing on the part nursing leadership plays.

Across twenty-four sources, senior and advanced-practice nurses sat at the centre of every working model: training staff, writing protocols, running remote assessment, coordinating teams, and managing escalation when patients deteriorated. Medical oversight supplied diagnosis, while nursing leadership supplied the daily operational glue. The authors conclude that empowering nurses to lead virtual ward development is essential if these services are to grow safely beyond pilot scale.
pmc-13629565:
Yanmei Zhu and five colleagues tested whether biochar, charcoal made by heating plant waste without oxygen, can repair soils worn down by continuous cassava cropping. They compared plots with and without a biochar application and sequenced soil microbes to see how the treatment changed soil chemistry and microbial gene activity near roots and in open soil.

Biochar raised soil acidity balance, organic matter, and available nutrients, with the strongest effects in the root zone. Microbial genes for DNA repair and replication grew more abundant there, carbon-cycling genes shifted toward aerobic respiration, and nitrogen-cycling genes moved in several directions at once, including more nitrogen fixation. The authors offer the field results as evidence for biochar in struggling cassava systems.
pmc-13630165:
Emma Hovén and fifteen colleagues present the protocol for UPIC, a nationwide Swedish cohort study of mental health in adolescents and young adults. Rates of anxiety and depression in this age group keep rising, yet the processes driving the trend stay unclear, and most disorders begin in these years.

The study will recruit two thousand people aged fifteen to twenty-nine and follow them for two years under one of three schedules, from yearly check-ins to frequent phone-based momentary assessments. Data will blend app surveys, digital behaviour tests, national registers, smartphone sensor traces of sleep and movement, and home blood samples in a subset. Machine learning will hunt for trajectory patterns, and feasibility measures will judge whether such intensive collection is sustainable.
pmc-13633265:
Hira Mian and nine colleagues published this 2026 analysis of a myeloma drug in frail patients. Multiple myeloma is a blood cancer of older adults, and frailty predicts rougher treatment courses. Data on frail patients receiving newer immune-engaging antibodies are scarce. The drug here, linvoseltamab, links immune T cells to myeloma cells. The team re-examined a trial of one hundred seventeen relapsed or resistant patients, sorting them by three frailty measures.

Frail patients made up roughly a fifth to a quarter of the group, depending on which measure was used. Response rates in frail patients sat close to those in non-frail patients under every measure. Severe side effect rates also matched closely between the groups. The authors read this as a favorable balance of benefit and risk for frail patients. They call for more study of the drug in frail groups, in trials and everyday practice.
pmc-13633765:
Hitomi Shinoda and four colleagues report a rare liver emergency in a twelve-year-old Pembroke Welsh Corgi. The dog collapsed suddenly after months of tiredness and poor appetite. Scans showed a large mass on one liver lobe, with a swirl pattern at its base that signals twisting. A twisted lobe loses its blood flow and can kill if surgery waits. The mass itself proved to be a liver cancer, an unusual partner for this condition.

Surgeons removed the affected lobe without untwisting it first. Tissue study confirmed the cancer with wide dead areas; the cut edge was cancer-free. The dog recovered smoothly, went home on the fourth day, and stayed well a year later. The twist sat at the mass's base, not at the usual pivot point near the liver's center. Seeing that swirl on scans made the diagnosis before surgery possible.
pmc-13635465:
J Odendaal and colleagues ran a large blinded trial of an antibiotic for women with repeated miscarriages and an inflamed womb lining. The inflammation, chronic endometritis, is found by staining a lining sample for the marker CD138. Some guidelines advise treating it, and others do not. More than two thousand women were screened at twenty-seven British clinics, and four hundred thirty-eight with the inflammation entered the trial. Half took doxycycline for two weeks before trying to conceive; half took an identical dummy pill.

Live birth rates came out nearly the same in both groups, at about half. The careful blinded design, covering patients, clinicians, and assessors, makes that null result hard to dismiss. A comparison group without the inflammation did no better, which deepens the puzzle about what the staining marks. The authors conclude the antibiotic, given this way, does not prevent miscarriage in this population.
pmc-13638465:
Diana Montoya-Williams and Scott A. Lorch published this 2026 policy article arguing that paid family leave belongs in the maternal-child health toolkit. Breastfeeding science keeps strengthening: human milk shapes infant immunity and even influences antimicrobial resistance. Yet American families face structural barriers to their breastfeeding goals. The country remains among the few wealthy nations with no federal paid leave program, leaving a patchwork of state schemes.

Leave, where it exists, is strongly tied to starting breastfeeding and keeping it going longer, alongside lower infant mortality and better maternal health. State programs show such leave can run without major labor market disruption, and public support for a national program runs high. The authors reframe leave not as a labor perk but as public health infrastructure. Federal action, they conclude, is the overdue step that would let the science reach population scale.
pmc-13639365:
Theodore Steiner and eight colleagues present a 2026 Canadian subgroup analysis of a fecal microbiota product for preventing repeat Clostridioides difficile infection. The live product, given rectally in a single dose after antibiotics, aims to restore gut microbes in adults whose infections keep returning.

Across five Canadian sites, 117 participants received the treatment. Side effects appeared in about six in ten people and were mostly mild gut complaints. Three quarters had treatment success at eight weeks, and most of those kept their response at six months. Results matched the wider trial, supporting use in Canada.
pmc-13643665:
Marcus Fager Ferrari and four colleagues, with a hemophilia study group, present a 2026 study of what predicts success in immune tolerance work for severe hemophilia A. The therapy aims to erase the antibodies that block clotting factor drugs. Results vary, and the burden is high.

Data covered 237 patients who had lasting antibodies and went through the therapy. Three things meant lower odds of success. One was a large gene deletion. One was a high past peak in antibody level. One was older age when the antibodies first showed. The peak level held most of the power to foretell the result. More gene markers are needed, the authors say.
pmc-13643765:
Anthony Percival-Smith and two colleagues present a 2026 fruit fly study testing whether signaling pathways can substitute for one another during wing growth. A weakened form of the growth signal decapentaplegic leaves wings too small, offering a clean test bed.

The team expressed thirty-five different signaling molecules in the mutant flies and looked for rescue. Three ligands partly restored wing growth: Hedgehog, Semaphorin 1a, and Wnt homolog 2. Two of them did not merely boost the original signal, and one rescue needed its own receptor, suggesting genuine substitution. The authors treat the result as consistent with, though not proof of, shared downstream transcription control.
pmc-13645565:
Kelsie Schiavone and seven colleagues report a mouse study on a protein called UBE2N and its role in helping melanoma tumors grow. The team used mice whose immune cells of the myeloid type could have the Ube2n gene switched off at a chosen time. They then tracked a melanoma line called YUMM1.7. The question was whether removing this protein from those immune cells would slow the tumor.

Switching the gene off did slow tumor growth, and tumors held fewer myeloid cells afterward. Levels of several immune signals in the tumor setting also shifted. In lab-grown immune cells, blocking the protein lowered a signal called SPP1, and fluid from those cells left T cells with fewer exhaustion markers. The results point to myeloid UBE2N as a possible target for future melanoma treatments.
pmc-13645765:
Masato Mitsuhashi and eight colleagues test a blood marker idea for athletes who take repeated head impacts in sport. The team captured tiny particles released by oligodendrocytes, the brain cells that coat nerve fibers, from blood samples. Three surface molecules on those particles were measured, standing for repair, inflammation, and degeneration. Groups included fighters, high school football players, college rugby players, and cross-country runners for comparison.
