Marker levels stayed generally steady in the runners, who face few head impacts. In the contact-sport groups, some athletes showed shifts over time, including some with no diagnosed concussion or symptoms. The study could not tie changes to a counted number of impacts, since exposure was not tracked closely. The authors present the method as an early, exploratory step toward blood tests that follow the brain's response to repeated knocks.
pmc-13646065:
Nguyen Trieu Viet and four colleagues test hearing diagnostic methods for adults with fluid trapped behind the eardrum, a condition called otitis media with effusion. Their study ran at a university hospital in Can Tho from June 2024 to October 2025 and covered sixty-six ears. Each ear received standard pressure testing, a wideband sound test, and a structured look at the eardrum. Surgery findings in thirty-one ears served as the firmest check.

The plain standard test caught every surgically confirmed case, though it also flagged some healthy ears. The wideband test alone was more balanced, and pairing wideband results with two specific eardrum features gave the best overall accuracy. The authors note the comparison rests partly on ears never opened in surgery, which softens the verdict. They present the combined approach as a useful support for diagnosis, not a replacement for the standard test.
pmc-13646265:
Kai Zeng and ten colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, how sex hormone receptors inside the cell nucleus drive breast cancer and its resistance to hormone therapy. These receptors switch genes on and off, and their work is tuned by chemical tags on DNA, by edits to the receptors themselves, and by signals passed between receptor types. When that tuning goes wrong, cancers stop answering endocrine treatment. The review gathers current progress on these molecular mechanisms.

Breast cancer's variety and high return rate make the resistance problem urgent, the authors note. They trace how each layer of control, from gene packaging to receptor crosstalk, can be pushed off balance. Close attention goes to the points where pathways intersect, since those junctions may offer drug targets. The review closes by pointing to treatment ideas that follow from the mechanism map. It serves researchers designing the next generation of hormone-based therapies.
pmc-13647165:
Xiaolu Hao and three colleagues review how single-cell gene reading has changed the study of glaucoma, the world's leading cause of irreversible blindness. The disease kills the retinal ganglion cells that carry vision to the brain. Reading genes one cell at a time exposes which cell types fail and how they talk to each other. The review covers two fronts: the drainage pathway that lets eye fluid out, and the main open-angle form of the disease.

Shared themes emerge across subtypes, above all failing energy factories inside cells and inflammation centered on the dying nerve cells. The authors weigh metabolic treatments as a promising direction. They also confront translation problems: animal eyes differ from human ones, and datasets across species resist merging. Future work with location-aware gene reading and combined data layers closes the review, aimed at precision care for a disease still caught too late.
pmc-13647265:
Julie Smeyers and Daniel A. Mordes review how losing part of a protein called TBK1 helps cause ALS and frontotemporal dementia, two linked diseases of nerve death. Damaged copies of this gene are among the most common inherited causes. Evidence from stem-cell and mouse models shows the protein guards several housekeeping systems at once: recycling worn parts, the cell's sorting stations, and innate immune alarms. The review weighs damage inside sick cells against harm spread through their neighbors.

Microglia, the brain's immune cells, need TBK1 to stay balanced, and their failure can injure neurons from outside. The authors trace how the housekeeping and immune threads converge on the protein clumping that marks these diseases. Treatment ideas follow each thread, from boosting recycling to calming inflammation. Their synthesis frames TBK1 as a gatekeeper whose partial loss opens several gates at once, perhaps explaining the diseases' tangled course.
pmc-13648765:
Wen-Chien Yang and colleagues test whether a simple blood marker measured early in pregnancy can flag later gestational diabetes across low- and middle-income countries. The standard diagnostic test requires fasting and multiple blood draws, which is hard to deliver in many settings, so glycated haemoglobin, a marker of average blood sugar, is an attractive alternative.

Within a multisite cohort spanning Kenya, India, Pakistan, and Zambia, the analysis covered 10,918 pregnancies, with diabetes confirmed later by the standard test. Early glycated haemoglobin predicted the diagnosis only modestly, and the best single cutoff missed over half of cases. The authors' results caution against relying on this marker alone for early screening in such populations.
pmc-13649165:
Alexander Muacevic and six colleagues run a pilot study on whether a computer screen's background colour affects short cognitive tasks in medical students. Thirty students each completed four weekly sessions: white, red-predominant, and blue-predominant screens, plus printed white paper, with letter, picture, and comprehension tests.

Printed paper produced the highest scores on several tasks, while the red screen beat plain white on some tests of focus and memory. All main comparisons reached statistical significance, though the authors flag real limits: a small sample, fixed session order, home-grown tests, and uncalibrated displays. They present the findings as exploratory evidence that background hue deserves controlled study.
pmc-13651465:
Hyuk Lee and three colleagues review whether deep learning can read stomach cancer biomarkers straight off ordinary stained tissue slides, sparing patients costly molecular tests that many hospitals cannot offer. Five markers guide treatment choices in stomach and junction cancers, from mismatch-repair failure to a surface protein targeted by new drugs.

Searches through August 2026 found twenty-eight studies, most tackling mismatch-repair status and Epstein-Barr virus status, with only a handful covering the other three markers. Independent external accuracy looked respectable for some markers and strong for the virus in two reports, yet no study supplied the data needed for a pooled verdict. Formal bias tools rated every report at high risk, and certainty graded very low. The authors conclude the approach is promising as a cheap pre-screen but nowhere near replacing laboratory testing, and they detail the reporting upgrades future studies owe.
pmc-13652665:
Fernando Alberto Ceballos-Fuentes led a 2026 study of whether thinking skills predict adherence to positive airway pressure therapy in people with obstructive sleep apnea who report no symptoms. Cognitive impairment is common in sleep apnea, but its link to treatment use among asymptomatic referrals was unclear. The team tested 29 patients with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and tracked continuous pressure use at three months.

Average age was about sixty-four, and just over half scored below the normal cutoff, including 57.1 percent of those with mild apnea despite no reported symptoms. Higher overall cognition tracked with more hours of nightly use. Attention scores tracked with both average hours and nights used over four hours, while lower language scores tracked with higher residual apnea events. Sleep clinicians get a practical insight: hidden cognitive deficits may undermine therapy engagement, so screening could help tailor support for new users.
pmc-2724665:
Uttara, Singh, Zamboni, and co-authors review oxidative stress in diseases that destroy nerve cells. Free radicals arise naturally as cells use oxygen for energy. A built-in antioxidant system normally keeps them in check and prevents damage.

Trouble begins when defences fall out of balance and radicals build up or flood in from outside. The review weighs that process in brain diseases and surveys treatment options that act early or late in the chain. Antioxidant therapy is attractive but tricky, and the authors map where it may help most.  Balancing benefit and risk, the authors caution, differs sharply by disease stage.
pmc-2815665: Kabsch published a short paper in 2010 that presents XDS. XDS is a program for work with X-ray data from crystals. Its name is short for X-ray Detector Software. The record kept for this entry is very thin. It gives little more than the program name, its author, and its year. So the paper is best described at that level. It is a specialist software report from the crystal structure field of its time.
pmc-2864565:
Robinson and Oshlack present a scaling normalisation method for comparing gene activity in RNA sequencing data. RNA-seq counts how often each gene is read in a sample. Samples sequenced to different depths cannot be compared raw, since deeper samples simply yield higher counts.

Their empirical scaling method adjusts for those depth differences and for uneven composition between samples. Proper adjustment is what lets a study claim a gene truly rose or fell, rather than merely being counted more. The method became a routine step in RNA-seq analysis pipelines around the world.
pmc-3163565:
Li and Dewey present RSEM, a method for measuring transcript levels from RNA-Seq data accurately. RNA-Seq was transforming how gene activity is measured when they wrote. A key challenge is handling reads that match several genes or several versions of one gene.

Such shared reads are especially tricky when transcripts are built from scratch without a reference genome. RSEM assigns those reads in a principled, probabilistic way instead of discarding them. Accurate counts are the base for every later claim about gene activity, so RSEM became a standard tool in transcript studies.
pmc-4201665:
Braun and Clarke wrote in 2014 for health and wellbeing researchers about thematic analysis. Thematic analysis is a method for finding patterns of meaning in qualitative data, such as interview transcripts. The brief evidence here is the paper's own framing, posed as a question about what this method can offer.

The paper presents thematic analysis as a flexible tool that health researchers can use well. It works across many research questions and does not demand one fixed theory. For fields that rely on people's accounts of illness and care, that flexibility is a real strength. The paper has helped many new researchers choose and carry out this approach with confidence.
pmc-4380465:
Sudlow, Gallacher, Allen, and their colleagues described UK Biobank in 2015. UK Biobank is a large population study set up as an open access resource for research. It was built to find the causes of the complex diseases of middle and old age.

The study follows a large group of volunteers over time and collects health, lifestyle, and genetic data. By linking genes with non-genetic factors, researchers can untangle why diseases arise. Any approved research team can apply to use the data. That openness has made UK Biobank one of the most used health resources in the world.
pmc-5833365:
Beverley Shea, Barnaby Reeves, George Wells, and colleagues introduced AMSTAR 2 in 2017. Systematic reviews guide clinical and policy choices, so their quality matters a great deal. Reviews can be biased, and many now include studies that were not randomized.

AMSTAR 2 is a checklist for judging how well a review was done. It covers the question, the search, study selection, and how results were combined. Some items are marked critical, because a flaw there can ruin the whole review. Appraisers worldwide use the tool to decide which reviews deserve trust before acting on them.
pmc-6208165:
Claudia Tonelli, Iok Chio, and David Tuveson reviewed gene control by the Nrf2 pathway in 2018. Nrf2 is a protein that turns on a broad set of protective genes. Those genes defend cells against toxic and oxidative stress.

The review explains how Nrf2 is held in check in quiet times and freed when stress hits. It maps the genes switched on downstream and the diseases touched by the pathway. Cancer adds a twist, since tumors can hijack this defense to survive treatment. Understanding that balance is key to drugs that raise or block the pathway safely.
pmc-7857465:
Roberto Di Marco and five colleagues sort out how to choose among four common scores used to compare walking patterns. Gait labs use similarity indices to judge whether a patient's movement has changed, yet the same index can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with the patient. The team tested four indices against five confounding factors, including joint range of motion, step-by-step variability, vertical offset, time shift, and curve shape, using two rounds of simulation.

Some indices proved independent of how far a joint moves, while others bent under particular distortions. A second simulation using wave decomposition isolated the effect of curve shape itself. The paper works as a buyer's guide for movement scientists. Pick the index whose blind spots do not overlap with the question being asked, or risk treating a math artifact as a patient's progress.
pmc-7920465:
Malik Sallam reviewed in 2021 how willing people around the world were to accept a COVID-19 vaccine. Vaccines only control a pandemic if enough people take them, so acceptance matters as much as how well a vaccine works in trials. Sallam gathered studies of acceptance rates among the general public and among health care workers in many countries.

The review compares those rates across places and groups, and notes the wide gaps between them. It also discusses the concerns most often behind reluctance, including safety worries and distrust. Written as vaccination campaigns were just beginning, the review captured an early global snapshot of a challenge that health officials would face throughout the rollout.
prester-john-letter-latin-1165:
The Letter of Prester John appeared in Latin around 1165, from no known author. It claims to come from a mighty Christian priest-king ruling in the far East. For centuries Europeans believed in his kingdom and hoped for his help against their enemies.

The letter lists marvels without end. Rivers of gems, pepper forests, and strange peoples fill the king's vast realm. His palace and armies outshine every court of Europe. The text is fiction, but fiction that moved real armies and explorers. Crusaders and kings hunted for Prester John for hundreds of years. Here it stands in the original Latin, the most influential fake letter of the Middle Ages.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-louis-:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Louis XIV, in this second selection, takes its passages from the Duc de Saint-Simon, the great memorialist of Versailles. Prepared by David Widger, it should not be confused with the Duchesse d'Orléans selection: the voice here is Saint-Simon's, colder and more exact.

The entries open with poisoned cardinals and rare good friends, and with the famous line of a man who was a king's son, a king's father, and never a king. A king, Saint-Simon holds, is made for his subjects, not the subjects for him. Capacity was small in one courtier, yet he believed he knew everything.
remarks-upon-alchemy-and-the-alchemists-: A worn title page, much garbled in the scan, opens this treatise on alchemy and the alchemists. Library stamps name the Ferguson Collection at Glasgow, dated 1921. The title promises a method of discovering the true nature of hermetic philosophy. It also promises to show that the search after the famed agent of change had another object than readers might expect. No author's name and no year can be read on the page. No page of the treatise itself follows it here.
ruskin-sesame-lilies-1865:
John Ruskin published Sesame and Lilies in 1865, two lectures that became his most popular book. The first lecture, on reading, urges care in choosing and studying great books. Kings' treasuries is his image for the wealth stored in literature. The second lecture treats women's education and duties, in terms of his age.

Ruskin argues that girls deserve serious schooling, though within a separate sphere. Modern readers debate that second lecture sharply. The first lecture remains a classic plea for deep reading. Ruskin's prose here is at its most musical and direct. The book shows the Victorian essay and lecture at their height.
shibboleth-1765:
Shibboleth, printed in London in 1765, promises that every man may become a Free-Mason. Its author signs himself a Pass'd Master. The pamphlet is a self-initiation manual: read it, and the reader supposedly needs no lodge, no ballot, and no brethren to gain the Craft's secrets.

That promise marks a turning point in the exposé genre. Earlier exposures revealed ritual; Shibboleth sells initiation itself for the price of a pamphlet. Its title takes the biblical password that cost lives at the fords of Jordan. The cheek of the thing is part of its interest. Shibboleth shows the market for Masonic secrets maturing into something bolder: the lodge, packaged for the solitary buyer.
shoo-king-legge-1865:
James Legge translated the Shoo King as volume three of The Chinese Classics in 1865. The Shoo King, or Book of Documents, holds China's oldest state papers. Legge was a Scottish missionary and a great scholar of Chinese.

Speeches, decrees, and counsels from early kings fill the text. Rulers speak of the mandate of heaven and just rule. Legge adds long notes to guide Western readers through the lore. The book is a Confucian treasure and a record of statecraft. It remains a base source for early Chinese history in English.
spallanzani-saggio-microscopiche-1765:
Lazzaro Spallanzani was an Italian priest and keen worker with the microscope. His Saggio of 1765, in Italian, took on John Needham and Buffon. Those men held that life can spring from dead broth on its own. Spallanzani set out to test the claim with care.

He boiled broths in sealed flasks and showed that no small life forms grew. Air shut out, the broth stayed clear and pure for weeks. His tests made the rule that life comes from life the norm. The book, part of his 1765 pair of tracts, is a root text of the field.
speeches-letters-of-abraham-lincoln-1832: Merwin Roe edited Speeches and Letters of Abraham Lincoln, 1832-1865. J. M. Dent and Sons printed the book at London. E. P. Dutton and Co. printed it in New York. The edition first came out in 1907. Reprints followed in 1909, 1910, and 1912. James Bryce wrote a first note to Lincoln's Speeches. That note is printed in this book. The plates came from the University Press at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Leave for its use came from The Complete Works of Abraham Lincoln. The Century Company issued those works in 1894.
stowe-household-papers-1865:
Household Papers and Stories collects Stowe's magazine pieces on home life. The Riverside printing of 1896 places it as volume eight of her writings, with a portrait and a view of her Hartford home. Copyright entries reach back to 1864 and 1868 for parts of the material.

Short and warm pieces treat children, servants, and the small morals of each day. Stowe jokes about fussy housekeepers and writes with care about marriage and kin. Readers who knew only Uncle Tom's Cabin met a new Stowe here. She sounds less like a reformer and more like a wise friend beside the American fireside.
suso-life-knox-1865:
Henry Suso was a German Dominican friar of the fourteenth century, famed for harsh penance and tender visions of Christ. His Life, written by himself with the help of a devoted nun, appears here in Knox's 1865 translation. The book is a medieval spiritual classic in its own right.

Suso tells of wearing a hair shirt and an iron-studded cross, then of learning to leave such rigors for inner stillness. He records dreams, temptations, and talks with his spiritual daughter in plain, moving detail. English readers met here a mystic both severe and gentle, shaped by suffering into patience.
swedenborg-a-hermetic-philosopher-being-:
Swedenborg, A Hermetic Philosopher, printed at New York by James Miller, is a sequel to Remarks on Alchemy and the Alchemists, by the same unnamed author. Its motto promises that one truth opens the way to another.

The book argues the claim stated on its title page. It holds that Emanuel Swedenborg was a hermetic philosopher. It holds that his writings may be read from the point of view of hermetic philosophy. That is the old doctrine of correspondences behind alchemy. A closing chapter compares Swedenborg with Spinoza. The author writes for readers of mystical and alchemical literature who suspected that Swedenborg's visions of heaven and hell hid an older, symbolic teaching about nature and the soul.
swinburne-atalanta-calydon-1865:
Algernon Charles Swinburne was an Oxford undergraduate with a passion for Greek tragedy when he wrote Atalanta in Calydon. Published in 1865, the verse drama made him famous at twenty-eight. Swinburne shaped it closely on the plays of Aeschylus, with a full Greek chorus.

The story retells the hunt of the Calydonian boar, sent by the goddess Artemis to punish a slighted altar. Atalanta, the swift huntress, draws first blood, and the hero Meleager gives her the prize. Family pride and a mother's curse then doom Meleager himself. The choruses, rich with fate and springtime, are the glory of the work. It led the Greek revival in Victorian poetry.
the-great-intendant-a-chronicle-of-jean-:
Thomas Chapais wrote The Great Intendant, a chronicle of Jean Talon in Canada from 1665 to 1672. It is Volume 6 of the Chronicles of Canada. George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton edited that series. The book was printed at Toronto in 1914. Chapter I is To the Rescue of New France. When 1665 began, the French colony on the St. Lawrence was over half a century old. It was still weak and destitute.

Chapais gives the causes. The settlement had been left to trading companies. Their narrow greed stifled its growth. Cardinal Richelieu tried once to give it new life, then turned to European politics. For twenty-five years the Iroquois scourged the settlers, traders, and missionaries. Governor after governor lacked the force to crush them. The colony struggled on with almost no help from France. It seemed doomed to destruction. Into that plight came Jean Talon as intendant.
the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipayana-vy:
Book 2 of the Mahabharata, the Sabha Parva, appears in Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English prose translation from the Sanskrit, dated 1883 to 1896. An editorial comment in the record notes that Part 1 of the translation can be found in the companion eBook numbered 7864. The book opens with the customary invocation to Narayana, to Nara, the most exalted male being, and to the goddess Saraswati, after which the word Jaya must be uttered.

Vaisampayana then narrates. Maya Danava, having worshipped Arjuna, speaks with joined hands and thanks him: saved have I been by thee, he says, from Krishna and from Pavaka, the fire that wanted to consume him. He begs to be told what he must do in return. Arjuna releases him graciously, saying the offer itself has done everything, and bids him go where he likes in friendship.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
With Voltaire, part of The Eternal Quest in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, uses Arthur Machen's English version of the 1894 London edition, with chapters found by Arthur Symons. Chapter Nineteen records the visit Casanova calls the happiest moment of his life. He greets Voltaire as his master and himself as a pupil of twenty years. Voltaire answers that Casanova should attend twenty years more and bring the fees at the end.

Casanova, unshaken, waits for his revenge in the exchange. Two Englishmen enter, and Voltaire compliments them by wishing he were English. Casanova privately calls the compliment false, since politeness forced the visitors into an awkward reply. Voltaire then asks the Venetian about Count Algarotti, drawing a dry answer about his countrymen's ignorance. The chapter promises discussions of Ariosto and a dispute with the great man himself. Readers get two professional charmers testing each other's wit at close range.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Windsor Castle fills the engraving that opens No. 486 of The Mirror, dated April 23, 1831. The view shows George the Fourth's gateway from inside the quadrangle. The writers present the print as the first in a planned series on the castle.

Recent rebuilding at Windsor fills much of the piece. It recalls how empty the castle felt under the late king. Then it contrasts that quiet with the new sovereign's household, whose terraces, slopes, and park grounds now admit the public freely. Details follow on the gateway itself, finished outside in 1826, with its York and Lancaster towers facing the Long Walk.

Belvoir Castle fills the opening of volume 20, No. 564, dated September 1, 1832. Set on a steep, cliff-like hill, the castle had been the seat of the Manners family for several generations. The writers compare its princely brow, meaning its commanding front, with Windsor's.

Which county held Belvoir was genuinely disputed. Camden and Burton placed it in Lincolnshire, while Mr. Nichols argued for Leicestershire, and the account admits the boundary is hard to trace. Its lands ran to roughly 600 acres of woodland, meadow, and pasture. A small priory of four black monks once stood there, founded under William the Conqueror by Robert de Todenci and dedicated to St. Mary, later joined to St. Alban's Abbey.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-09:
Motley's ninth volume covers 1564 and 1565. Chapter five brings the three seigniors back to council. Orange presses reform against a corrupt government there. Armenteros gains influence at court meanwhile. Viglius suffers in a painful position throughout. He longs to retire from public business. Secret charges against him reach Philip from the Duchess.

An execution and a tumult shake Antwerp next. Fabricius dies, and cruelty toward Protestants grows horrible. Bruges and the Flemish estates protest against Titelmann. Philip stays obdurate against every remonstrance from them. Trent decrees stir a violent council debate on publication. French and Spanish envoys quarrel for precedence there. Reform efforts fail against a king who will not bend.
the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-ancien:
George Rawlinson's Seven Great Monarchies reaches Persia in this record, labeled volume two. The section is headed Persia Proper, and its subject is the fifth monarchy. A map precedes chapter one, on the extent of the empire.

Persia's geographical extent far exceeded any earlier monarchy's, Rawlinson writes. Persia Proper was a comparatively narrow and poor tract. In its greatest length it ran under 500 miles, some seven or eight degrees in all. The Persian kings' dominions covered a space fifty-six degrees long, he says. In places they stretched more than twenty degrees wide. Their eastern boundaries were the desert of Thibet, the Sutlej, and the Indus.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-:
Book five of Gilbert Parker's Weavers fills this volume record, chapters thirty-five to thirty-nine. Chapter thirty-five, The Flight of the Wounded, opens at the opera. A tenor's cry of Non ti scordar di me rings out with passionate stealthy sweetness, and the audience's composure breaks in waves. Women finger their programmes abstractedly, and young lovers sit suddenly arrested.

Old men whose working days are over hear in the cry their own lost ambitions and draw back within themselves. Hylda, seated in the Duchess of Snowdon's box, listens with a face showing nothing of what she feels. Parker uses one aria to survey a whole theatre of buried devotion, pride, and regret before the plot resumes.
thoreau-cape-cod-1865:
Henry David Thoreau's Cape Cod saw print in 1865, after his death, his book of the sea-shore. The posthumous travel narrative gathers four trips to the Cape between 1849 and 1857 in one volume. Many rank it the great American book of the sea-shore, salt, wreck, and dune in prose.

Thoreau walks the Great Beach from Eastham to Provincetown, past wrecks, lighthouses, and wreckers' huts on the sand. The wreck of the St. John, with drowned Irish emigrants, opens the book in scenes of stark pity. Wellfleet oystermen, surfmen, and keepers give him Cape lore, humor, and a pagan love of the sea. His eye turns a bare sand arm into a world of history, weather, and wild life. The book is his sunniest and saltiest, a shore walk that never dates.
tob-10465:
John Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion stands as the landmark system of Protestant theology, and volume one lays its foundations. Calvin, a French reformer trained in law, wrote with lawyerly precision and a preacher's fire. Readers begin where he begins: with knowledge of God and knowledge of ourselves.

Early books ask what humans can know of God, why Scripture is trustworthy, and how God governs creation and human life. Calvin argues each point in ordered chapters meant to teach pastors and students. Together with its companion volume, the work gave the Reformation its most complete statement of faith and shaped Reformed churches for centuries.
tob-10565:
Hafiz of Shiraz, who lived in fourteenth-century Persia, wrote lyric poems called ghazals that Persians still quote by heart. Gertrude Lowthian Bell, a traveler and scholar of the Middle East, chose poems from his Divan and turned them into English verse. Her versions introduced many English readers to Hafiz.

Again and again the poems sing of nightingales and roses, cups of wine, and a Beloved who is hard to reach. Sufi readers hear divine love behind those images, while others hear earthly romance. Bell keeps the playfulness and longing that made Hafiz the most loved poet of his land.
tob-4165:
George William Cox built The Mythology of the Aryan Nations on the solar theory: nearly every hero tale, he held, retells the drama of dawn, sun, and storm in disguise. Volume two applies that key across the Indo-European world, from India to Greece to the Norse north. The book appeared in 1870.

Cox writes with sweep and total confidence, unlocking myth after myth with the same bright key. Later scholarship broke with the solar school entirely, and Lang mocked it without mercy. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The volume survives as a grand fossil of Victorian method.
tob-4265:
John Ferguson, a Glasgow professor of chemistry, catalogued the James Young collection of alchemical books in his Bibliotheca Chemica. Volume two continues the great bibliography: author by author, edition by edition, the literature of alchemy is listed with a scholar's patience. The catalogue appeared from the collection formed in 1908's record.

Ferguson notes printers, dates, contents, and the worth of each item, turning a private library into the map of a whole field. Alchemy's historians still begin their hunts in his pages. Verified from the 1919 edition, volume two completes the standard guide to who wrote what in the hermetic centuries.
transactions-of-the-american-society-of-:
Alfred Noble, a past president of the society, outlines the East River Division in Paper No. 1152. His short paper links the general account by General Raymond to detailed reports from the resident engineers. The division covers the tunnels between Manhattan and Long Island City.

Borings began in the river in late 1901, soon after the project became public. Crews worked from a pile-driver boat using wash borings, then plotted the rock surface in contour lines. The borings found two deep channels in the rock, split by a reef below Blackwell's Island. Noble explains how this survey work fixed the tunnel lines before digging began.
tylor-researches-into-the-early-history-:
Edward Burnett Tylor published this first great work in 1865, six years before Primitive Culture made his name. In it he laid out the methods that would define early anthropology: comparing customs across peoples to trace how civilization grew.

Tylor argued for the psychic unity of mankind, the idea that all peoples share the same basic mind. He studied gesture language, counting, myths, and the survivals, old customs that linger as clues to earlier stages. His evidence ranges from children's games to funeral rites. The book shows a new science being built, one comparison at a time.
un-ga-res-2065:
Sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, called the Malvinas by Argentina, comes before the General Assembly in Resolution 2065, adopted on 16 December 1965. The Assembly had weighed the reports of its decolonization team on the islands. Its 1960 vote to end colonial rule in all forms, it holds, covers this case too. It notes the plain fact of a dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over who holds the islands.

Both states are invited to move at once into the talks the team had urged. The talks should seek a peaceful fix to the sovereignty fight. Past deals and the good of the people of the islands both frame the call. The dispute would break into open war seventeen years later.
un-ga-res-a-67-265: Catalogued under the symbol A/67/265, this record belongs to the General Assembly's sixty-seventh session, which ran from late 2012 into 2013. The catalog's date of 1946 cannot be right, since the session number alone rules it out. No subject is named in the record, and none is claimed here. It is an Assembly text of that session, kept in official record form. As with many such records, its real subject has to be read from the text, not inferred from the bare symbol it travels under.
un-ga-res-a-69-65: Teaching about disarmament gets a fresh push in Resolution A/69/65, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text takes note of the Secretary-General's report on teaching for disarmament and against the spread of arms. It marks twelve years since the UN study on that teaching first appeared. A web hub of learning goods, in all six UN tongues, is praised, and new tools such as social media are urged into the work.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2065 (XX), adopted on 16 December 1965, took up the Falkland Islands, called the Malvinas in the text as well. The Assembly noted that Argentina and the United Kingdom disputed who held sovereignty over the islands. It treated the case as one form of the colonial state of affairs its 1960 declaration sought to end.

The two governments were invited to start talks without delay. The talks were to follow the lines the Special Committee on decolonization had urged. They were to find a peaceful settlement. The talks were to keep in mind the Charter, the 1960 declaration, and the interests of the islands' people. Both sides were to report back on the outcome.

Resolution 69/65, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, follows up the United Nations study on disarmament and non-proliferation education. It welcomes tools such as the 'Disarmament education: resources for learning' website and the 'Disarmament today' podcast series. It encourages states and civil society to keep putting the study's recommendations into practice. It asks for a further report to the seventy-first session.
un-sc-res-1365: The decision entered as Resolution 1365 forms part of the Council record catalogued for 1973. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1465: Numbered 1465 in the Council's sequence, this 2003 resolution is one of the Security Council's formal acts on world peace and security. The version kept here follows the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Inside, preamble clauses state the situation first; operative paragraphs then record what the members decided, demanded, or asked of the parties involved.
un-sc-res-1565: Kept under number 1565, this Security Council resolution comes from the body's official record, transcribed by English Wikisource. Fifteen members share one text, and each paragraph is numbered so it can be cited on its own. The entry preserves that citable form whole, from the first recalled action to the final instruction to report back.
un-sc-res-1665:
The Sudan sanctions panel won a further six months in March 2006. On 29 March 2006 the Security Council extended its mandate until 29 September 2006. The panel tracks the arms embargo and other measures set in resolution 1591. The Council recalled the Abuja talks on Darfur. It also recalled the Comprehensive Peace Agreement for Sudan. Both peace tracks still needed the pressure that monitoring supplied.

The panel owed a midterm briefing within ninety days. A final report was due thirty days before its term ended. Both went to the sanctions committee. The Council urged states, United Nations bodies, and the African Union to help. Facts on how the measures worked were the key need.
un-sc-res-1765:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1765, adopted on 16 July 2007. A peace deal signed at Ouagadougou in March 2007 had made rebel leader Guillaume Soro prime minister. Weeks before this vote, an attack on his plane killed several people at Bouaké.

The text renews the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and the French forces that back it. Their new term runs until 15 January 2008. The mission must help carry out the peace deal and prepare free elections. The Secretary-General's envoy, not a separate election chief, would now certify each stage of the vote.
un-sc-res-1865:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1865, adopted on 27 January 2009. The presidential vote set for 30 November 2008 had been put off again. Voter identification and registration were running far behind plan. A fourth supplement to the Ouagadougou deal, signed in December, tried to restart the process.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the peacekeeping mission and its French support force until 31 July 2009. Authorized troops drop from 8,115 to 7,450. The voter list work must finish as the top priority. Ivorian leaders must agree a fresh, realistic election timetable in public. Benchmarks will guide any further drawdown of the mission.
un-sc-res-265:
Israeli air attacks on Jordanian villages were condemned by the Security Council on 1 April 1969. The Council noted many deliberate breaches of the cease-fire. Recent air strikes on villages and populated areas had been planned in advance. They broke resolutions 247 (1968) and 256 (1968). The Council voiced grave concern at the worsening situation in the area.

The Council reaffirmed resolutions 248 (1968) and 256 (1968). It deplored the loss of civilian life and the damage to property. It condemned the recent planned air attacks by Israel on Jordanian villages as a flagrant breach of the United Nations Charter and the cease-fire resolutions. Israel was warned once again that any repeat would force the Council to meet and weigh further, more effective steps under the Charter. The text belongs to the cycle of raid and reprisal along the Jordan front between the 1967 and 1973 wars.
un-sc-res-365:
Cyprus after the war of 1974 stood behind a new General Assembly plan that every state had backed. The Assembly's resolution 3212, adopted unanimously on 1 November 1974, set out terms for settling the Cyprus question. The Security Council had the full text before it. Resolution 365 was adopted by consensus on 13 December 1974.

The Council endorsed the Assembly's resolution. It urged the parties concerned to carry it out as soon as possible. The Secretary-General was asked to report on the progress of that work. The text is brief, and it does only this one thing. Its weight lies in joining the Council's voice to the Assembly's. Both main bodies of the United Nations were now asking for the same settlement path in Cyprus.
un-sc-res-465: Catalogue data places Resolution 465, a United Nations Security Council text, in the year 1967. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-65: News from Indonesia was called for in Security Council Resolution 65, passed on 28 December 1948. Dutch forces had struck the Republic of Indonesia anew that month. The Council asks the consuls in Batavia, named in a vote of August 1947, to send a full report at the soonest date. It must cover three things. First, the state of the land. Next, how the cease-fire calls have been kept. Last, the terms of life in areas held by troops, or due to be left by them.
un-sc-res-665: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 665 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 1990. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Six more months for UNIFIL, the peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, are approved on 31 July 2001, at the Lebanese government's request. The force's original task, watching Israel's withdrawal, was largely done after the 2000 pullout. What remained was restoring peace and security in the south.

The mandate now ran until 31 January 2002, and the Council backed the planned reshaping and redeployment of the force. Lebanon was called on to extend its own authority across the south, including by sending its army there. The parties were told to give UNIFIL full freedom of movement, and all violence in the area was condemned.

A bomb attack in Bogota, Colombia, six days earlier is condemned on 13 February 2003. The blast of 7 February killed and injured many people. As with the Bali text the previous October, the attack is treated as a threat to peace and security under the Council's counter-terrorism framework.

Sympathy goes to Colombia's people and government and to the victims and their families. All states are urged to help the Colombian authorities, as resolution 1373 requires, in hunting down those who carried out, planned, and paid for the attack. The text closes by restating a firm resolve to combat terrorism in all its forms, wherever it appears.

Fighting and grave abuses continued in Ituri and the Kivus despite Congo's national transition, and on 1 October 2004 the mission there, MONUC, is extended and reinforced. The Secretary-General had recommended more troops, and the Council agreed the mission was stretched too thin in the east.

Deployment is extended until 31 March 2005, and 5,900 more personnel are authorized, including up to 341 civilian police, plus aircraft and other support. The added brigades are to deploy as fast as possible in North and South Kivu. The mission's size and shape stay under regular review, and Congolese parties are pressed to honour their transition promises, including holding elections on time.

Sierra Leone's membership application is approved for forwarding in Resolution 165, adopted unanimously on 26 September 1961. The Council had examined the West African country's request to join the United Nations. Sierra Leone had become independent from Britain in April of that year, with Milton Margai as its first prime minister.

The resolution recommends that the General Assembly admit Sierra Leone. In the Charter's design, that advice is indispensable; the Assembly cannot seat a new member on its own. Sierra Leone thus joined the fast-growing group of African states at the UN, at a moment when new admissions were shifting the balance of the whole organization toward the developing world.

Investigators tracking Sudan's sanctions gained more time under Resolution 1665. It was adopted on 29 March 2006. Violence in Darfur was still claiming lives daily. Peace talks ran in Abuja, Nigeria, under African Union leadership. A separate peace deal had ended Sudan's north-south war in January 2005.

The Council extended its panel of experts until 29 September 2006. The panel monitors the arms embargo and sanctions set in 2005. Members required a midterm briefing within ninety days. A final report was due thirty days before the mandate ended. All states were urged to share what they knew about violations. The experts' findings fed the Council's Darfur decisions.

Côte d'Ivoire's new peace deal reshapes UN work in Resolution 1765, adopted on 16 July 2007. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement of March 2007 had come from direct Ivorian talks. An attack in Bouaké on 29 June against the prime minister, who had come from the former rebel side, killed several people and drew the Council's sharp blame.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, and the French forces backing it until 15 January 2008. UNOCI's role is recast to support the deal: the joint command centre, restoring state services, voter identification and registration, and the election process. The Council ends the post of High Representative for the Elections and gives the job of certifying each election stage to the Secretary-General's Special Representative. A review of mandates and troop levels is set for 15 October 2007.

Côte d'Ivoire's mission is renewed and trimmed after another missed election in Resolution 1865, adopted on 27 January 2009. The presidential election set for 30 November 2008 had been postponed. Identification and voter registration were behind schedule. The fourth Supplementary Agreement to the Ouagadougou Agreement, signed on 22 December 2008, was already slipping.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the mandates of UNOCI and the French forces supporting it until 31 July 2009. It reduces authorized military personnel from 8,115 to 7,450, following the Secretary-General's recommendation. It demands the Ivorian parties finish identification and voter registration before the end of February 2009. It demands that they agree without delay on a realistic new electoral timeframe covering the provisional and final electoral lists, voter cards, and the election date. The Special Representative must certify the electoral list explicitly, and the Council endorses benchmarks for a possible further drawdown.

The last act in this run of Golan texts came at the close of 2010. The chief's report of 1 December found the line calm. UNDOF had kept the watch since 1974. Its term had days to run. Resolution 1965 passed on 22 December 2010.

The force won six more months, to 30 June 2011. The stock call went out: act on the 1973 text at once. Staff codes take a full clause, as in late texts of this line. Abuse must be barred, probed, and punished by troop states. A report was due at the term's end. No one in the room could know that Syria's own war would soon test this line as no year had since the force was born.

Israeli air raids on Jordan's farm towns are condemned in Resolution 265. It passed on 1 April 1969, with eleven votes in favor and four members not voting either way. The Council recalled its 1967 truce text. It noted many planned breaches of the truce since then. The new strikes hit towns and homes, and they broke two rulings from 1968.

The Council deplored the deaths of townsfolk and the damage to homes and farms. It condemned the raids as gross breaches of the UN Charter and the truce. It warned Israel once more. If such strikes came again, the Council would meet to weigh stronger steps under the Charter.

Resolution 365 is a short UN Security Council endorsement on Cyprus, adopted by consensus on 13 December 1974, five months after the Turkish military intervention split the island. The General Assembly had just passed its own resolution 3212 on the question of Cyprus, unanimously.

The Council endorses the Assembly's text. It urges the parties to put it into practice as fast as they can, and asks the Secretary-General to report on progress. Assembly resolution 3212 had called for the speedy withdrawal of foreign forces and for refugees to return home. The Council's quick backing gave that call the weight of the UN's most powerful body during the tense months after the island's division.

Israeli settlements drew the Council's strongest statement yet on 1 March 1980. Resolution 465 rests on the reports of its own commission on settlements in the territories occupied since 1967. Israel had refused to cooperate with the commission. It had also formally rejected the earlier settlement resolutions. Letters from Jordan and from Morocco, speaking for the Islamic Group, were before the Council.

The Council accepted the commission's findings. It ruled that every measure taken by Israel to change the character or status of the occupied lands has no legal validity. Jerusalem was included in that ruling. Israel was told to undo those measures and to dismantle the settlements already built. New settlement work had to stop as a matter of urgency. The Council also deplored Israel's move to bar the mayor of Hebron from traveling to address the Council in person.

Indonesia was fighting for independence from the Netherlands in late 1948, and the Council wanted news from the ground. It turned to the foreign consuls posted in Batavia, the capital. Under an earlier resolution, those consuls served as the Council's observers in the area. Resolution 65, adopted on 28 December 1948, asks them for a complete report, as soon as possible. The report had to cover how the cease-fire orders were holding up in the Republic of Indonesia. It also had to describe conditions in the areas under military occupation.

Iraq still refused to leave Kuwait in the autumn of 1990, and sanctions alone were not stopping its trade. Ships kept moving goods in and out. The Council had already passed Resolutions 660, 661, 662, and 664 on the crisis. Resolution 665 put naval force behind the embargo.

The Council called on the member states that were cooperating with Kuwait's government. Those states had warships deployed in the area. They could use measures suited to the circumstances to halt shipping. All ships going into or out of Iraq and Kuwait could be stopped. Their cargoes would be inspected and their destinations checked, to enforce the embargo of Resolution 661. States were asked to help each other, to coordinate their actions, and to report to the Council and its sanctions committee.
under-two-flags-pg3465:
Ouida's Under Two Flags tells the life of a soldier. She dedicated it to Colonel Poulett Cameron, in honor of his family's long service in French and English armies. A second record of the same novel gives only the dedication and a bare chapter list. Here the author's own note explains that she first wrote the story for a military periodical. Its French phrases follow the slang of the Army of Algeria, not schoolbook French.

Chapter one opens in the household of the Hon. Bertie Cecil, an officer of the 1st Life Guards. His servant Rake discusses his master's hunting clothes with the stud groom. Rake complains that Cecil is hard to please about his tops and leathers. The scene sets up a world of wealth, horses, and army polish. From there the novel follows its soldier hero through the double service promised by the title.
voting-rights-act-1965:
Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in 1965, months after Selma's violence. Bloody Sunday on the Pettus Bridge led straight to this law. At last the ballot gains real federal teeth in the South.

Literacy tests are banned as tools to bar Black voters from polls. Federal registrars go south to enroll voters whom locals turned away. Counties with rigged rolls fall under strict federal watch for years. Black officeholders rise fast once the vote becomes truly open. The most effective civil rights statute ever passed remade American politics for good. Within a few years, Black voter rolls in the South had transformed.
